Darwinia is a nice little RTS which reminded me a lot of the movie TRON. It is not an overly long game, and you could probably beat it in around 10 hours, less if you try to get through as speedily as possible. The writing is decent. The gameplay is decent. The soundtrack is okay. It should be noted that the game is single-player only, unlike most well-known RTS games.

You can tell that a lot of care went into this game. It runs well, did not have any noticeable bugs, and also includes some nice extras like a map editor. I really appreciated the work that went into the game's startup screens, which are all very nice and fun to watch. Some of them even reveal background information about the game's story. The number of different startup screens really surprised me. I finished the game over many sessions, and I had already finished just over half the game before I saw a startup screen repeated. It is certainly unusual to see so much effort put into something that most people would probably consider an extremely minor part of a game these days.

I have no more to say on the graphics, writing, soundtrack, etc. They are nothing too remarkable, but they are all decent. The gameplay is where my main concern is. Darwinia's gameplay is, honestly, pretty slow-paced. There were a lot of times when I was waiting for my units to get from one place to another. This issue is exacerbated by the fact that this game has the lowest unit cap I have ever seen in an RTS, three units! This is upgradable to five. That's it. Sure, the Darwinians don't count towards that cap, but they are not very useful except for manning fortifications and objectives, which they are required for. The upshot is that building units other than Darwinians is instant and takes no resources, so if you lose a unit you can instantly reconstitute it at the nearest spawn point.

Another complaint I have is that the tutorial does not seem complete. Sure, you get walked through a few things, but some very important basic mechanics are omitted from the tutorial. In particular, the transmission dishes which serve as bridges between parts of levels were not explained to me by the game, and I ended up only finding out about them when they were mentioned by another player. This is a central mechanic that exists on every map and is essential for the later missions! I am not sure why something so critical is not in the tutorial, especially considering that there is such a bridge in the tutorial level, though using it is not required to finish that level or the other early levels. This would not be quite so bad were it not for the fact that this mechanic is non-obvious, as the transmission dishes appear to be part of the level as opposed to something you can control. There are some other, less critical omissions as well, like how to switch a squad's weapons.

The game does have a well-executed Linux port, which I very much appreciate. The game runs natively on Linux, and it runs well. It is refreshing to see a native Linux port which works just fine and has no issues that I noticed.

If you like single-player RTS and computer-themed stuff, this is a good pick.

If Tron and Pac-Man had a baby, it’d be Darwinia.

This game is like falling headfirst into an old-school computer and being handed god-like powers to save a bunch of pixelated stickmen from extinction. It’s weird. It’s charming. It’s gloriously retro.

You don’t command troops – you influence them like some kind of digital dad with a laser pointer. The graphics? Minimalist hacker-vibe meets artsy screensaver. The music? Synthy goodness that’ll make you want to hug a floppy disk.

Gameplay is part strategy, part action, part “wait... what am I doing?” But somehow, it all clicks. Watching your little Darwinian dudes evolve and fight back against viruses is weirdly satisfying.

✅ Unique concept
✅ Retro aesthetic with modern soul
✅ Surprisingly emotional for a game full of green stickmen
❌ No real reason not to try it unless you hate fun

Final verdict: 10/10 would spiritually adopt digital stickmen again.

[h1]Timeless Gem[/h1]
[hr][/hr][i]Game remains an unique gem to this day. There are very few games which tries to portray a feeling of being in a virtual world. It retains an unique aesthetic and feeling. One which was very impressive back then and still holds up to this day. It is a timeless game, but these days and in the future we are cby a mediocre slop.[/i][hr][/hr]
[h1]☠️It should be the sin to be poor☠️[/h1]
I remember seeing this game in a gaming magazine. It struck me as such an unique and good looking game. Back then, games were trying to push 3D graphics into realism, but they were still looking quite unrealistic. Especially real time strategy games. This would put them in an uncanny valley or just make them look bad. Very few games looked graphically great in that period and AAA games were ones pushing the limits. This game stood out, because it was trying to do its own thing. It is an unique, little gem which is still great today. I only regret that I couldn't play it back then when I was a child. It would had blown me away as it would immerse me in a simulated, virtual world. I do regret of not being able to play it back then when games were a lot worse, far fewer and anything remotely good was an instant cult classic. This is one game which plays just as well today as it would had back then and it would had left much greater impression on me in those simpler times. Sadly, affordability was the main issue and childish lack of attention was another reason holding me back.

[h1]💖What makes it special💖[/h1]
Game tries to sell you an idea that you are in virtual world which is alive. Over time, this idea grows on you as game is immersive. It knows what it needs to do in order to try and sell you an idea of a world. It is not trying to be convenient or responsive. It doesn't reduce people in a game into HP and units. This inherent resistance helps you to feel that this is its own world rather than just a level which you have to conquer. Units which you control are explicitly stated to be just programs. They are directly controlled by you and are perfectly obedient. While Darwinians (local sentient inhabitants) on the other hand cannot be directly controlled. This separation goes a long way of making you believe that these two things are different and it helps with immersion. 

Another aspect of an immersion is simulation. World is simulated from Darwinians to terrain or projectiles. Even entire game map tries to portray that it is something in which Darwinians live and work in and everything is connected. Over time, it grows on you through little experiences. It plays badly, but that serves to reinforce that it is not a video game. Simulation also goes a long way. Each particle has to connect with the enemy. Grenades bounce through terrain. You start thinking in terms of line of sight and high ground. You become more engaged with the map terrain and as result, you get emotionally invested with maps themselves. Sound of difficult battle going on in the distance and your Dawrinians lollygagging at the helps to sell you this world. Likewise, you can draft them and send them to die in the war. Seeing them trying to hold on positions which they are slowly losing is a missing ingredient which so many RTS fail to give to you. In those games, map and NPCs feel lifeless where here they have their own charm as they are simulated and reacting to threats which are themselves unscripted. This naturally leads into stories and far more natural situations.

[h1]📋Stories from the front📋[/h1]
I tried to establish Darwinian colony on an island, but couldn't because other 3 colonies would constantly launch raids upon me. I couldn't control my AI units fast enough to respond to two flank assault. Their main strength - perfect obedience was turned into their weakness. So, I started capturing another, starter island so to speak. I managed to establish my colony there. It was far easier cleaning spawn point after spawn point since they were separated by greater distances and were more linear to each other. So, I had time to capture souls and convert it to my population. After conquering, I then could push into that island through transfer point. With ability to rally Darwinians to my side, I managed to make them entrenched on that spawn point. Through greater initial numbers and by carrying turrets to fortify area, I could focus just clearing one spawn point after another. 

Game often turns into a siege warfare where you cannot just use your own directly controlled units. You have to rely on Darwinians who are semi-independent. This is what gives game so much of its charm. It is one thing to see your units fighting, it is another to see local inhabitants trying their best to fight. There was a spider infestation which I couldn't clear myself as they were spawning way too quickly and it would be massive chore to do it solo. So, I had called up Darwinians and established turrets at the entrance. They started to thin the never ending swarm. Each side dragging fallen entities as souls back to the base for revival unto their side. It is trench warfare to the extreme. Then I made several more formations and ordered them to engage spiders from another angle. They went through their mountain chain and occupied at that time, relatively free high ground with my soldiers. My soldiers were shock troops which cleared landing territory and kept enemies at bay until my allies arrived with their transport tanks. They established upon high ground and they started to seriously thin down the enemy horde from two sides. This was the thing which I was looking for since now I could easily use my troops/programs to go in and take their nests out. Once I had broken their numbers, rest was just the cleaning operation.

[h1]🔧Where it falls short🔧[/h1]
This game had a surprisingly long support history. It is clearly loved and is taken proper care of. However, not all is roses and rainbows. I had issues with making Steam screenshots for the game. Steam integration could be better.

More substantial issue is that this game is simply dated. It is a game made in few years by few dudes more or less. Production values as such are low. Its unique artstyle can hide lack of graphical budget to make graphics, maps or music. However, it still has very little content. Enemies are very few and you will see most of them quite soon in the campaign. You have like one troop and one Darwinian troop. Rest are support units or gear. Enemies likewise are just 3 types. Regular lines on a ground, flying worm or a spider. Then there are recoloured Darwinians who are now evil and are fighting you. 

Then you start playing game, it can get tedious very fast. As you don't have unlocks and are not invested into the world, seeing a new map with multiple islands which are teeming with enemies, get old really fast. You need to manually kill each of those enemies and gather their souls for your Darwinias. Gameplay is slow and lacks in any variety. You sure have to get immersed and like what you are playing, otherwise you will be bored to tears.

[h1]An Unique Experiment[/h1]
[hr][/hr][i]I do wish that I could had played this game when I saw it in gaming magazine. Back then it would had struck like a truck. Its aesthetics would offer relief from mud, grey graphics at that time, awkwardly pushing for photo realism. It would be its own indie game when indie games didn't existed. Its mechanics would be seen as cutting edge and lack of content and its tedious nature would had been no obstacles to me. It is one of those rare games which could come at any period in history and still be good or feasible to make. It came out in 2005, but it's one of those rare cases where a brilliant game like this could had came out in 2000 too and be just the same.[/i][hr][/hr]

What invited me to this game in particular was its more cyber fantasy graphics than the oh to typical dystopian or medieval fantasy that's been done to death. And while I've owned it for so many years but played so little of it up to later after the 10000th Anniversary Edition update, it's high time I get to experience it to the end and finally beat it!

Being introduced to a virtual universe created by one man and developed within itself by a species of flat stick-like figures, you jump in unnoticed and are already put to use by borrowing the man's programs to combat a virus and saving his people. Keeping the graphics simple and the game running at a top 60 in a 3D world when playing a real-time strategy is essential, and I like how considerate this game was made to work with that while taking advantage of it with pixelization effects here and there to let you know when a program is about to fall apart. Also, color me impressed as to how the Darwinians were able to project the maker's face in the sky.

The controls are easy to understand well enough once you've pressed 'H' enough times to know how to control each program and get used to the interface. But it was nice and fluid to try the gesture controls for a change, especially if you have a touch-screen. In either case, the learning curve is pretty fair to get you reacting fast enough to know how to push yourself to completing objectives in each of the world's zones.

The difficulty spike can be pretty unpredictable, even with the default setting (1/10). Once you read and predict what your units and enemies are weak against, the way you strategize becomes pretty clear. You will be put under pressure later on in the story as enemies continue to respawn (either from viruses hatching from eggs or the infection that keeps rushing in waves after you). Once you've put enough hours into the game where the creator has done enough research upgrades to give you and your tasks a well-enough advantage, you'll feel like you're making a comeback, and that's very satisfying.

The way that Darwinia was made to be played and explored is a beauty in itself, and I loved how much care the devs put into it to want to keep you coming back for more. Give it a try if you want an interesting new take on a strategy game, or if it's something that'll get you into strategy without the repeat offenders of the past.

Uplink is a pretty realistic hacking sim where the government is 100 km from your house and approaching rapidly. 

Use the inherent weaknesses in IPv4 and telephone systems to make them think your house is elsewhere for long enough that you can destroy the evidence of your crimes. But be warned! Your computer is only as powerful as a potato, you've left logs all over the planet, and if you're still not quite done what you need to, investigators may take MONTHS to hit you with a game over.

In this way, the game has true consequences, akin to an ironman or hardcore mode from today. You can't just start over from an older save, because the feds do not announce their investigation. Sure maybe the last save is OK, or perhaps you were had a few months prior. Maybe you just forgot a single logfile and there's still time, or maybe you were hacking five systems at once in a fugue state and just directly connected to one about a week back.

Uplink, developed and published by Introversion Software, is one of the most distinctive simulation games ever made, offering players an immersive experience in the world of cyber espionage and digital intrusion. Originally released in 2001 and later brought to Steam, it places you in the role of a freelance hacker, an anonymous agent for hire who takes on covert assignments from corporations, governments, and secret organizations. Instead of flashy action or cinematic sequences, the game unfolds entirely through a minimalist computer interface, creating the illusion that you’re operating inside a clandestine digital world. It’s a concept that feels remarkably ahead of its time, blending role-playing elements, economic management, and puzzle-solving into a unique hacking simulator that still resonates with players today.

At the start of the game, you sign a contract with the mysterious Uplink Corporation, which provides you with access to a “gateway” computer. From this base of operations, you begin performing low-level jobs: breaking into public servers, deleting records, and stealing simple files for small amounts of money. Each successful job earns credits that can be spent on upgrading your system—faster processors, better modems, additional memory, or advanced hacking tools. These upgrades are crucial, as each mission increases in difficulty and complexity. Before long, you’ll find yourself infiltrating corporate networks protected by proxy servers, firewalls, and security traces, forcing you to juggle multiple tools while racing against time to avoid detection. The game’s tension lies in that constant countdown: the flashing “Trace In Progress” warning, the slow climb of the trace percentage, and the desperate scramble to cover your digital footprints before you’re caught. Few games have ever captured the thrill of high-stakes hacking as effectively or as convincingly.

Uplink’s minimalist interface is a masterstroke of design. The entire experience takes place through a simulated operating system—a dark blue desktop filled with pop-up windows, status monitors, and email clients. You don’t control a character; instead, you control a system, and it’s the player’s intellect, rather than reflexes, that drives progress. The aesthetic feels simultaneously sterile and atmospheric, with its abstract sound effects, low-key electronic soundtrack, and the steady hum of data streams underscoring every move. The sparse presentation encourages imagination, letting you fill in the blanks of the world beyond the screen. When you see a connection chain trace back through multiple servers or hear the subtle ping of a firewall being bypassed, it feels like you’re part of a larger, shadowy network where every keystroke carries weight. This immersion is something modern games often struggle to achieve even with far more complex visuals, yet Uplink accomplishes it through restraint and suggestion.

What makes Uplink stand out, even decades after its release, is its commitment to player freedom and emergent storytelling. Though there is a central plot involving two rival corporations—Arunmor and ARC—fighting over the fate of the internet via powerful viruses called Faith and Revelation, the game allows players to decide whether to get involved or simply pursue their own career. You can remain a neutral contractor, align with one side, or even double-cross your employers for personal gain. The missions themselves range from simple data thefts to framing innocent users, altering academic records, or stealing classified research. Each task can be approached in different ways depending on your setup, and the game encourages experimentation. There’s no scripted handholding; success comes from learning how each system works and from gradually developing the instincts of a professional hacker. It’s a rare design philosophy that rewards curiosity and persistence rather than spoon-feeding solutions.

The difficulty curve, however, can be steep. New players are likely to fail their first few missions, either by being traced or by forgetting to erase evidence on the servers they infiltrate. The game’s refusal to hold your hand may seem harsh, but it’s also part of what gives it authenticity. Every mistake carries consequences, and the sense of risk makes every victory feel meaningful. The higher-level missions, especially those involving corporate networks and LANs, can feel daunting at first, demanding multitasking and precision timing. Yet this challenge is exactly what keeps Uplink engaging. You’re constantly balancing speed, planning, and resource management, and even after dozens of missions, the thrill of narrowly escaping a trace never loses its intensity.

Beneath its austere interface lies a surprisingly rich simulation of hacker culture. Uplink presents a world where information is currency, corporations are untrustworthy, and morality is flexible. The game doesn’t moralize your choices; it simply lets you act and then face the consequences. This gives it an emergent narrative quality—your story as a hacker is shaped by your actions rather than dictated by cutscenes. You might spend an entire playthrough building a legitimate reputation as a reliable contractor, or you might turn rogue, spreading chaos for your own amusement. Either way, the result feels personal. The slow accumulation of wealth, the satisfaction of upgrading your hardware, and the growing confidence in tackling high-risk jobs all contribute to a strong sense of progression rarely achieved through traditional storytelling.

Uplink’s longevity owes much to its design simplicity and moddable structure. Its interface may look dated by modern standards, but its mechanics remain remarkably intact. Fans have created mods, new skins, and expanded missions that keep the game alive long after its release. Even without modifications, it remains endlessly replayable thanks to procedural generation and open-ended goals. The combination of tension, freedom, and atmosphere ensures that each playthrough feels unique. It’s a game that doesn’t rely on graphics or spectacle but instead on imagination and immersion, allowing players to step into a world of clandestine operations where intellect is your greatest weapon.

Two decades on, Uplink still feels like a blueprint for immersive simulation design. It doesn’t try to simplify or glamorize hacking—it distills it into something abstract yet believable, where strategy and timing matter more than spectacle. Its flaws—repetitive mission types, occasional interface confusion, and a lack of accessibility features—are outweighed by its sense of identity and purpose. There’s a hypnotic rhythm to the gameplay loop: accepting a contract, tracing connections, bypassing systems, cleaning logs, and vanishing without a trace. Each completed mission reinforces that feeling of being part of a secret world, invisible but powerful.

Uplink remains one of the most iconic independent titles of its generation—a cult classic that captures the fantasy of the hacker archetype without resorting to clichés or exaggeration. Its blend of tension, atmosphere, and open-ended design still feels remarkably fresh, proving that immersion doesn’t require realism so much as conviction. It’s a quiet, cerebral experience that rewards patience and cleverness, a game that turns a simple interface into a window into an invisible digital war. For those willing to embrace its minimalist presentation and steep learning curve, Uplink offers one of the most authentic and satisfying cyberpunk experiences ever created—a simulation of solitude, intellect, and danger inside the infinite expanse of the virtual world.

A Timeless Cyberpunk Classic That Still Feels Fresh

Review:
Uplink is a brilliant, immersive experience that stands out as a true pioneer in the hacking simulation genre. Even decades after its initial release, it manages to captivate with its unique blend of strategy, tension, and cyberpunk atmosphere. From the moment you log in as a freelance hacker, the game pulls you into a world of corporate espionage, high-stakes missions, and digital intrigue.

The gameplay strikes a perfect balance between strategy and immersion. Planning your hacks requires careful thought: choosing which systems to infiltrate, managing your software and upgrades, and staying one step ahead of trace programs. Every successful hack feels genuinely rewarding, and the tension as you race against the clock to avoid detection keeps your heart racing.

The aesthetic is minimalist but striking. The interface, with its green-on-black terminal style, perfectly evokes the feel of a 2000s cyberpunk world. Coupled with the moody soundtrack, it creates a persistent sense of suspense that draws you deeper into your clandestine career.

Another standout feature is the freedom the game gives you. You can take on missions from multiple corporations, manipulate markets, steal sensitive data, or even sabotage other hackers. The sandbox nature of Uplink ensures that no two playthroughs are exactly alike.

Even though it’s an older game, Uplink’s design holds up remarkably well. It’s accessible for newcomers to hacking sims, but still offers layers of depth for veterans looking for complex strategies. The sense of accomplishment after a successful high-risk mission is unmatched.

If you’re looking for a game that challenges your mind, rewards careful planning, and immerses you in a retro-futuristic cyberpunk world, Uplink is an essential play. It’s not just a game—it’s a digital playground for anyone who’s ever wanted to live out their inner hacker fantasy.

Pros:
	•	Deep and rewarding hacking mechanics
	•	Engaging cyberpunk atmosphere
	•	High replayability with multiple strategies and approaches
	•	Minimalist interface that enhances immersion
	•	A true classic that still feels relevant

Cons:
	•	Graphics are dated (but perfectly suit the aesthetic)
	•	Some may find the pacing slower compared to modern action games

Verdict:
Uplink is a masterclass in game design. Its tension-filled hacking, strategic depth, and cyberpunk world-building make it a must-play for anyone who enjoys thinking games, retro-futuristic settings, or just the thrill of being a digital ghost in the machine.

Multiwinia, developed and published by Introversion Software, is a fast-paced, minimalist real-time strategy game that reimagines large-scale combat as a vibrant digital playground of chaos and color. Set within the same virtual universe as the studio’s earlier cult hit Darwinia, it trades the introspective tone of its predecessor for a more competitive, arcade-like energy. The premise is simple but effective: the once peaceful digital inhabitants known as Darwinians have splintered into factions, now waging endless wars for dominance across surreal landscapes inside a computer simulation. The game abandons traditional base-building and resource management mechanics, instead focusing entirely on the movement, coordination, and survival of massive pixelated armies. This streamlined approach gives Multiwinia a distinct rhythm that feels both refreshingly immediate and deceptively strategic.

Visually, Multiwinia carries Introversion’s signature aesthetic—abstract, geometric environments and vast swarms of tiny, glowing stick figures moving in synchronized chaos. The landscapes resemble low-poly sculptures painted in bright, otherworldly hues, while explosions, laser fire, and particle effects create a constant sense of kinetic motion. Each battle resembles an abstract painting in motion, and though simple in appearance, the visual design perfectly complements the game’s underlying theme of digital warfare. The interface is clean and minimalistic, allowing players to focus on the ebb and flow of their armies rather than micromanaging menus. This purity of design is one of Multiwinia’s great strengths; it captures the essence of large-scale strategy without clutter or overcomplication, maintaining an aesthetic charm that remains recognizable even years after release.

Gameplay is divided into several distinct modes, each emphasizing different aspects of control and tactical improvisation. These include Domination, King of the Hill, Assault, Rocket Riot, and Capture the Statue, among others. Each mode takes a familiar concept—holding territories, escorting objects, or launching rockets—and reimagines it within Multiwinia’s swarm-based framework. Players command hundreds of tiny units, directing them to capture spawn points, secure objectives, and overwhelm enemy positions. The core appeal lies in managing chaos rather than constructing order; with limited tools, you must adapt on the fly as reinforcements arrive, terrain shifts, and unpredictable power-ups drop across the battlefield. Matches are typically short and intense, lasting around fifteen minutes, which makes the game highly replayable and ideal for quick sessions. Beneath the surface simplicity, there is a surprising amount of tactical nuance in positioning, timing, and reading the flow of battle.

The multiplayer component represents the heart of the experience, offering both online and local play. Matches against human opponents showcase the game’s brilliance—its unpredictable skirmishes, sudden reversals, and emergent moments of humor or desperation. Power-up crates can turn the tide in seconds, introducing temporary advantages like airstrikes, teleportation, or the ability to summon devastating weapons. These elements ensure that no two battles feel alike, yet they also inject an element of randomness that can occasionally frustrate players seeking pure strategy. Still, this unpredictability is part of Multiwinia’s charm. It’s not about perfect control but about thriving in disorder, adapting to shifting conditions, and embracing the absurdity of digital warfare. The artificial intelligence is competent enough to provide a challenge in single-player matches, but the game clearly shines brightest when humans clash over its colorful arenas.

While Multiwinia’s design philosophy emphasizes accessibility and instant action, it also limits the game’s long-term depth. Without a traditional single-player campaign or progression system, the experience can feel transient once the novelty of its modes wears off. Players looking for a narrative-driven strategy game or complex economic systems will find little of that here. The structure is more akin to a competitive playground than a full-fledged grand strategy experience. Yet within this simplicity lies a purity of design that few games achieve—the mechanics are tight, the pacing brisk, and every match tells its own improvised story of triumph and annihilation. The game’s brevity and unpredictability ensure that it never overstays its welcome, but they also mean that Multiwinia functions best as a short-burst experience rather than a long-term obsession.

Technically, the game remains smooth and responsive even during massive battles involving hundreds of units, a testament to Introversion’s careful optimization. The soundtrack enhances the digital atmosphere with electronic rhythms that pulse beneath the chaos, while the minimalist sound effects—crackling lasers, distant explosions, the rhythmic march of pixel soldiers—reinforce the sensation of being inside a simulated world. The presentation is cohesive in every respect, immersing players in a stylized digital war zone that feels both alien and oddly endearing. There is an unmistakable charm in watching countless tiny figures charge heroically into battle, only to dissolve into glowing fragments moments later, as if the game itself is celebrating the beauty of organized disorder.

In the end, Multiwinia stands as an unusual but captivating entry in the real-time strategy genre. It distills the complexity of warfare into a kinetic, visually striking, and immediately playable experience that thrives on spontaneity. While it lacks the narrative and systemic depth of traditional RTS games, its speed, accessibility, and distinctive art direction give it a unique identity that few contemporaries share. For players who appreciate fast, chaotic strategy games that value creativity over control, Multiwinia delivers a satisfying blend of competition and spectacle. It may not satisfy those looking for intricate long-term strategy, but as a snapshot of Introversion Software’s experimental spirit, it remains a memorable and refreshingly original title—one that celebrates both the simplicity of play and the unpredictability of digital life.

I didn't enjoy Darwinia much, so I wasn't expecting to enjoy Multiwinia either, but I figured I might as well check it out since I got both games in a bundle. I was pleasantly surprised to find that some of the things I disliked about Darwinia had been improved, like the painfully slow speed of units and some of the clunkyness around controlling them, and the game feels quite different in general. Unfortunately, despite the six different gamemodes and variety of different maps, it felt like this game got stale extremely quickly, and the gameplay just wasn't complex enough to stay interesting for long.

Regardless of the ultimate objective, most of the gameplay involves selecting groups of units and moving them around the map. You don't really have much control over what they do. If there's something to interact with nearby, they'll probably interact with it. If there's enemies around, they'll probably attack. It's never quite guaranteed though, and sometimes they'll just stand around doing nothing, or wander away. The visual feedback from combat isn't great either, and it's hard to tell exactly why you're winning or losing battles other than the assumption that the winning side had a larger number of units. Crates can be added, which can be collected to provide various items, which make things a bit more interesting. However, where these items spawn is fairly random and feels pretty unfair sometimes, and the power of various items varies wildly, so adding crates does little more than add more luck to the game. You can play this game against friends online or against AI, and playing with friends is definitely more enjoyable, although the gameplay felt about the same in both cases. I don't know if that's because the AI is decent or if it's because this game is so simplistic that it's not hard to design an AI to play it.

The game has the same low poly, simplistic aesthetic as Darwinia, and it looks neat. The game ran well, and I didn't encounter any obvious bugs, other than the same clunky controls when controlling the armor units that Darwinia had.

[b]TL;DR[/b] This is an interesting sequel to Darwinia that shares the same aesthetic and has similar gameplay, although it makes some improvements to the speed of the game and the way units are controlled and used. The gameplay felt pretty simplistic though, with few objectives beyond trying to make sure you have more units than everyone else in every battle, and most additional complexity relies mainly on randomness, which doesn't feel satisfying either. Despite the fairly low price, I still can't recommend this game, as I just don't think there's enough entertaining content here to justify it.

Do you ever have comfort food? Like a good sandwich from a place you've always loved, or a nice book you always re-read every few years. It can take us back to a simpler time, an easier time, when the only thing to worry about is making it to the next bite or the next page. Multiwinia is one of my comfort games. I bought it when originally came out all those years ago and have been playing it every now and then for the past 15 or something years just to get that injection of nostalgia particles into my bloodstream. 

It's not the most perfect game in the world. The graphics are very endearing to me due to my already existing bias, but it admittedly isn't the draw. The pathfinding sometimes has a hard time as well, along with just the AI in general acting like a bunch of weirdos. But there's a core of gold here. If it's your game, you will get it like we all understood Pikmin 1 from only playing real-time-strategy similar to Command and Conquer or Starcraft before. There was even a modding community for this game at some point, with someone working on remaking the map Facing Worlds from Unreal Tournament into this game. 

It's a special game in that it's really not to anyone else. It's a spin off of a bigger, more award winning game. It has never received any sort of HD Update, any new content, and the servers have been dead for longer than some of the people on Steam have been alive. But... It's fun. It's still a fun game. Just send your little green or whatever color team guys to shoot the other guys, have them go get cooler weapons from crates, and just have a good time. 

I'm so happy to see how much Introversion Software has grown since the days of Multiwinia and Darwinia, super proud of you guys. If you guys ever want to remake or remaster Multiwinia, I know one guy that'd be playing it right when it comes out.

Although obviously an older game, it's still the best "modern" subsim there is. Yes, better than [b]Modern Naval Warfare[/b] (2026 early access). If you're looking for an overall modern *strategy* game, [b]Sea Power[/b] is king.

The only problem is that installing (and configuring it to run great) can be a pain, but if you're a "navy nut" like me it's worth doing it. Tip: once you have it running nice, make sure to WinRar your game folder to a backup location for easy quick clean re-install, should you ever need it. You should do this anyway before you begin installing any mods (e.g. Reinforce Alert) so you have a clean "stock" fixed install to go back to.

I have spent thousands of hours playing this. The funny thing is that my Steam playtime only lists a few hours; that's 'cos once you have it installed and configured (and added Reinforce Alert), you don't normally run it though Steam again. For me, I either run the exe directly or through DxWnd.

I'm not going to write a full "for dummies" tutorial how to set it up since that's already been done over and over ad infinitum but let me just say [b]the key[/b] is to simply install the DgVoodoo2 wrapper (all you need are the d3d8.dll and dgVoodooCpl.exe files) and that's it. [b]Don't forget to right-click on the orange DgVoodoo logo in the control panel to enable its extended menu (for the borderless config)[/b].

If you want to run it in a window (in whatever size you like) this can be done properly via DxWnd [b](specifically, version 2.04.36)[/b]. I needed to configure the dgvoodoo wrapper first or DxWnd wouldn't work. I found the "sweet spot" screen size for me is 1680x1050 since then it's not too stretched and squashed. I don't like its supposedly default 4:3 aspect ratio since for whatever reason it looks strangely "squashed" in 4:3. Perhaps (at the time) the devs had intended it to be played on 16:10 ratio monitors, I'm not sure. Whatever, it's all good since 1680x1050 fixes it on a standard 16:9 screen (set 1280x1024 Mode 3 in game options or the font text will be too small and distorted if set higher).

Good hunting and carry on!

Dangerous Waters is a demanding and uncompromising military simulation that remains one of the most detailed portrayals of modern naval combat ever released on PC. Developed by Sonalysts and published by Strategy First, the game was never designed to appeal to a broad audience. Instead, it targets players who crave realism, procedural depth, and a genuine understanding of how modern naval warfare actually functions. From the moment you step into your first mission, it is clear that Dangerous Waters prioritizes authenticity over accessibility, asking players to think like real-world naval officers rather than arcade pilots or action heroes.

The gameplay revolves around commanding a wide range of naval platforms drawn from contemporary military arsenals, including nuclear-powered submarines, diesel-electric submarines, surface combatants, maritime patrol aircraft, and helicopters. Each platform can be controlled at multiple stations, allowing players to jump between sonar, navigation, fire control, radar, and command roles as needed. Rather than simplifying these systems, the game models them with remarkable fidelity, forcing players to interpret sonar contacts, manage sensor noise, plot intercept courses, and carefully plan weapon deployments. Combat is rarely immediate or flashy; instead, it unfolds slowly, often over long stretches of tense silence punctuated by moments of sudden, decisive action.

Submarine warfare is where Dangerous Waters truly distinguishes itself. The game places enormous emphasis on acoustic stealth, positioning, and patience, making undersea combat feel like a high-stakes chess match played in near darkness. Players must constantly balance speed against noise, depth against detection risk, and aggression against survivability. Identifying a contact is rarely straightforward, as sonar returns can be ambiguous or misleading, demanding careful analysis and cross-referencing. This creates a level of psychological tension that few games manage to replicate, where victory often comes from outthinking the enemy rather than overpowering them.

Surface and air warfare add further layers of complexity. Managing a surface ship requires attention to radar coverage, missile defense, and coordination with allied units, while aircraft operations introduce entirely different tactical considerations such as search patterns, fuel management, and sensor range. The game encourages players to think holistically, combining assets rather than relying on a single platform. Success often depends on information superiority — knowing where the enemy is before they know where you are — reinforcing the game’s core theme that modern naval combat is as much about data and detection as it is about firepower.

The structure of Dangerous Waters supports long-term engagement through campaigns, standalone missions, and a powerful mission editor. Campaigns place players within broader geopolitical conflicts, lending narrative context and strategic continuity to individual encounters. The mission editor, meanwhile, has played a major role in the game’s longevity, enabling a dedicated community to create and share custom scenarios that expand the experience far beyond the original content. This community-driven ecosystem has helped keep the game relevant years after its release, especially among hardcore simulation enthusiasts.

Presentation is utilitarian and reflects the game’s age, but it serves its purpose effectively. Visuals focus on clarity rather than spectacle, with much of the action conveyed through tactical displays, sonar waterfalls, and radar screens rather than cinematic views. While the 3D graphics and interface feel dated by modern standards, they remain functional and readable. Sound design plays a critical role, particularly in submarine operations, where subtle audio cues can mean the difference between remaining hidden and being detected. The inclusion of voice command support further reinforces the simulation mindset, allowing players to interact with systems in a way that feels surprisingly immersive.

The most significant barrier to entry is the game’s learning curve. Dangerous Waters demands time, study, and patience, often requiring players to consult manuals or community resources to fully understand its systems. Tutorials are limited, and the game assumes a level of prior knowledge that can be intimidating for newcomers. However, for those willing to invest the effort, this complexity becomes one of its greatest strengths, offering a sense of mastery that few modern games attempt to deliver.

Ultimately, Dangerous Waters stands as a benchmark for realism-driven naval simulations. It is not flashy, forgiving, or easy to approach, but it offers an unparalleled depth of tactical and procedural gameplay that continues to reward serious players. While casual gamers may find it overwhelming or outdated, those with an interest in military simulation, naval strategy, or submarine warfare will discover an experience that remains intellectually engaging and deeply satisfying even years after its original release.

Started out playing Crash Dive on Android. Then Red Storm Rising (venturing into Cold Waters)

And some google search result said DW is the king.

It was all overwhelming at first. So many buttons (like how Highfleet overwhelmed me -- such a great aerial navy sim), so much to read, so much to understand, especially about sonar and TMA.

FPS Chazly really got me into it with his tutorial vids, especially the cumulative series. Worth a watch if you want to really dive deep into DW.

Nothing beats tracking a ghost sonar signal contact, assessing the speed and how near or far it is using the DEMON (brighter intense colors - contact could be nearer, especially at slow speeds), the drawing tools for assessing weapon distance, setting up the activation time and depth ceiling of the torp, and manually flooding, equalizing, and muzzle dooring the torp.


The excitement really begins when the DEMON sonar of the contact goes haywire, passing 5, then 8, then 17 knots, rushing to avoid your torp while you check the narrowband and TMA as to where the hell is your contact going, then adjusting the active torp's bearing.

Then, an explosion. "Loud explosion bearing 105."

A feeling that will never get old, especially when fighting 3 akula improved subs.

非常好的一款游戏，在现代海战游戏中硬核区只有危险水域是唯一真神，冰冷海域只能算是俄罗斯原神高级版。危险水域的突出亮点在于态势感知，那种只能对着仪表盘与电子屏进行水下捉迷藏的沉浸感和在水声学方面的专业程度是其他游戏无法比拟的(举报Sonalysts炸鱼，攀不上美国海军就来碾压游戏公司是吧）什么？现代海战全方面碾压危险水域？但是那游戏都还没出呢！得益于开发商的硬实力，危险水域整体的游戏玩法也是大致还原了现代海战的操作流程，从声呐到火控一应俱全，而且都是相当精细，在这方面也是无人望其项背。
但是油管有个博主说得很好，危险水域最大的缺点不是画面（当你坐在漆黑的声呐显示屏前，无论是蓝光8k超清大屏还是显像管电视机都是平等的），而是愚蠢的AI。这里的AI不会编队航行（除非任务作者强行安排路线，但依然不会分工合作），永远诚信1v1（除非你上了数据链，这也是为啥你的水狗被无畏级揍的时候阿利伯克只是慢悠悠地路过，你得升起天线杆杆告诉阿利伯克它身边顶着AK100的家伙真的不是通美俄军他才愿意开火）甚至驱逐舰在潜艇先发射鱼雷时都无法及时反击。因为这个游戏只是一个零几年的游戏，在这一点上危险水域比冰冷海域差很多，至少冰冷海域的AI懂得编队作战。AI差劲的唯一好处就是，给萌新足够的空间适应游戏操作，不至于游戏还不会玩先被人机一套秒杀。
虽然AI十分差劲，但是危险水域还可以多人联机（虽然人很少，还需要专门的软件）。在多人联机模式中，游戏的难度和复杂程度大大提高，大佬都懂得来骗来偷袭，而萌新基本和我一样TMA都不做就直接发射鱼雷。危险水域还有一个特点，入门门槛极高，没有中文加上极复杂的操作两大劝退幻神几乎来多少玩家就抬走多少玩家，解决办法就是：上网找教程，进群找大佬。B站有翻译的教程，也有大佬亲自操刀教学。
总之，虽然缺点挺明显，危险水域仍然是目前没有替代品的游戏，强烈推荐各位硬核玩家，海军魔怔人，潜艇爱好者游玩。

There’s something deeply absorbing about diving into a turn-based 4X strategy game where the galaxy unfolds not in explosions, but in spreadsheets, diplomacy tables, and tech trees that go on for light-years. Space Empires IV Deluxe is a love letter to an era when complexity wasn’t a bug—it was the feature. It’s not a game for the faint of heart, but for those who enjoy managing empires with the finesse of a galactic accountant and the foresight of an admiral, it offers a unique blend of strategy that’s rarely matched even today.

What It Does Well
The scope is nothing short of staggering. You don’t just pick a race and expand—you design it from the DNA up. Want a species that breathes methane and lives on molten rock? Go for it. You can customize ships down to individual systems, creating fleets that reflect not only strategic choices but personal playstyle. The freedom is intoxicating.

The tech tree is vast—so vast that your first dozen games will feel like tutorials. But once the rhythm kicks in, the discovery becomes part of the satisfaction. Finding obscure techs that shift your strategy or developing doomsday weapons that tip interstellar balance keeps each campaign fresh. Diplomacy, colonization, and warfare are all layered with complexity that rewards long-term planning over impulse decisions.

Multiplayer, while a bit dated in terms of interface, adds a chess-like depth when played against equally obsessive opponents. Battles feel earned, not triggered by luck or rushed aggression. When you win in Space Empires IV Deluxe, it’s because you out-thought the enemy—not just out-gunned them.

Where It Stumbles
Let’s get it out of the way: the interface is brutally outdated. The UI feels like it was lifted from a DOS-era spreadsheet program, and navigating menus is often a lesson in patience. Even with the Deluxe version, which irons out a few bugs and adds quality-of-life tweaks, there’s a persistent clunkiness that no patch has quite polished away.

Graphics are purely functional, bordering on ugly by modern standards. If you need flash and flair to stay engaged, this won’t hold your gaze for long. The tactical battles, while satisfying in theory, play out more like detailed math problems than cinematic spectacles. You have to squint hard to find the drama.

AI, though serviceable, often behaves in ways that break immersion—sending ships into suicide runs or making bizarre trade offers that feel more like random number generation than intelligent negotiation. And while modding can extend the game’s lifespan, setting it up can be an intimidating wall of text and folders.

Verdict
Space Empires IV Deluxe is an acquired taste—but one that can be deeply rewarding for those who enjoy methodical planning over flashy execution. It's not a game that welcomes newcomers with a warm hug; it's more like being dropped into the control room of a star empire with a stack of unread manuals. But for those willing to embrace its depth, the payoff is immense. It's a strategy sandbox that lets you write your own spacefaring saga in excruciating—but satisfying—detail.

Pros:

Immense customization of races and ships

Vast, complex tech tree with meaningful progression

Deep strategic layers across diplomacy, colonization, and warfare

Hugely replayable with different strategies and setups

Satisfying for long-term thinkers and micromanagers

Cons:

Outdated UI and clunky interface

Poor graphics and minimal visual feedback

AI inconsistencies in both combat and diplomacy

Steep learning curve with little in-game guidance

Tactical battles feel dry and overly abstract

Final Score: 7.5 / 10

This is not a polished blockbuster, but a dense and rich strategy gem buried beneath an avalanche of text and data. For the right kind of player, it's a galaxy worth ruling.

Из особенностей стоит отметить:

1. Графика.
Размер игры составляет около 350 мб при огромных внутриигровых возможностях. Соответственно ожидать чего-то завораживающего глаз не стоит. Графика простая до безумия, уровня игр 90-х годов. Но этой простотой она и притягивает.

2. Озвучка.
Фоновая музыка, озвучка элементов интерфейса, звуки боя - все на манер космоса. Не 8 bit музыка, но и не мощные саундтреки современных шутеров.

3. Геймплей.
Интерфейс и управление сначала кажутся сложными. Много не понятных символов, практически ничего не доступно для взаимодействия. Но стоит слегка начать разбираться, как начинаешь втягиваться в игру с головой. Даже банальная колонизация планет поэтапно заставляет задуматься над каждым своим шагом. Тут тебе и исследования технологий для колонизации, и постройка судна, поиск планеты и заселение. Не каждая планета подойдет, и даже если подошла, то нет гарантий что она будет с подходящим климатом и условиями, а не ад. Огромное количество технологий для исследования составных частей кораблей, построек, развития жизни, шпионажа, саботажа, вплоть до манипуляций со звездами и создание своих планет! Плюс к этому добавить черные дыры, космические штормы, руины древних цивилизаций, туманности и прочие космические объекты, которые разнообразят Ваши исследования. И конечно же противники. С реальными игроками будет практически не возможно играть в силу долгих ходов каждого, а боты прекрасно подходят для компаньонов. Они вполне интерактивны, а на высоких уровнях сложностях довольно сильны и могущественны, так что без просчета своих ходов тут не обойтись.

В общем, если есть желание быть в своего рода "песочнице" галактических масштабов, то эта игра идеально подойдет. В ней нет современной ультраграфики, крутой музыки, интригующего сюжета, но тем не менее, она стоит того, что бы в нее играть.

Но главная трагедия этого мира не в этом, а в том, что вы потратите на его спасение (или уничтожение) чуть больше времени, чем планировали. [h2]📜Описание[/h2]
[b]Disciples II: Rise of the Elves[/b] — это третье и, к счастью, последнее дополнение к легендарной пошаговой стратегии Disciples II: Dark Prophecy. В отличие от двух предыдущих аддонов, которые представляли собой скорее платный косметический ремонт, это дополнение наконец-то делает то, чего фанаты ждали годами: добавляет новую играбельную расу — эльфов. И да, они такие же мрачные, циничные и готовые на всё, как и остальные обитатели этого умирающего мира. Вы получаете новую кампанию, 14 карт для сражений и возможность примерить на себя роль либо благородного, либо дикого эльфа. По сути, это та же Disciples II, но теперь с остроухими, и это именно то, чего все и хотели.

[h2]🎨Графика и звук[/h2]
Графика в [b]Disciples II: Rise of the Elves[/b] — это классический пример того, как художественный стиль побеждает технологии. Технически игра, конечно, устарела: 3D-модели юнитов на поле боя выглядят так, словно их вырезали из картона и покрасили гуашью. Но двумерные иллюстрации, портреты персонажей и карты выполнены с такой мрачной, готической эстетикой, что вы будете прощать игре эти угловатости. Это не технологичная, а именно художественная красота. Мир Невендаара умирает, и вы чувствуете это в каждом пикселе. Звуковое сопровождение — это отдельный шедевр. Мрачная, давящая музыка от Филиппа Шаррона идеально дополняет атмосферу безысходности. Вы будете сидеть и планировать захват вражеской столицы, а в наушниках будет играть саундтрек, от которого хочется закутаться в плед и тихо плакать. В хорошем смысле.

[h2]🎮Геймплей[/h2]
Геймплей [b]Rise of the Elves[/b] остаётся верен классической формуле Disciples. Вы управляете героем, нанимаете юнитов, исследуете карту, захватываете ресурсы и, конечно же, сражаетесь. Боевая система проста, как пробка: поле боя разделено на 12 клеток (по 6 с каждой стороны), и каждый юнит выполняет строго определённую роль. Здесь нет места тактическим изыскам вроде перемещения по клеткам. Главное — правильный состав армии и грамотное расположение бойцов. Эльфы привносят в эту формулу свою изюминку: у них есть мощные лучники с несколькими ветками прокачки, крепкие кентавры в роли танков и... ну, маги у них так себе, будем честны. Но это не мешает им быть грозной силой. Игра затягивает своим ритмом: «ещё один ход, ещё одна битва, ещё один уровень». И вот вы уже смотрите на часы, а там 4 утра. И вам на работу через два часа. Но вы всё равно нажимаете «Следующий ход», потому что оторваться невозможно.

[h2]📖Сюжет и атмосфера[/h2]
Сюжет кампании за эльфов продолжает историю этого древнего народа. Бог Галлеан, пробудившись от комы и обнаружив, что его жена стала злобной нежитью, слегка тронулся умом и приказал эльфам идти войной на бывших союзников — Империю. Вам предстоит вернуть былую славу эльфийскому народу, попутно решая, каким путём идти: благородным или диким. Атмосфера в игре — это её главное достоинство. Мир Невендаара пропитан декадансом и упадком. Здесь нет места добру и справедливости. Каждая фракция преследует свои корыстные цели, а нейтральные монстры только и ждут, чтобы сожрать вашего героя. Это мрачное фэнтези, которое не пытается быть милым или героическим. И именно за это его любят.

[h2]✅Плюсы:[/h2]
[list]
[*] ⭐ Новая раса — эльфы. Наконец-то вы можете играть за остроухих, и они действительно ощущаются как полноценная фракция со своими сильными и слабыми сторонами.
[*] ⭐ Неповторимая атмосфера. Мрачная, готическая эстетика и великолепный саундтрек создают уникальное настроение, которое вы не спутаете ни с чем.
[*] ⭐ Уникальная боевая система. Простая, но глубокая. Вам не нужно быть гроссмейстером шахмат, чтобы побеждать, но и бездумно кликать не получится.
[*] ⭐ Высокая реиграбельность. Кампания за эльфов, 14 новых карт, редактор сценариев и, конечно же, возможность играть за другие расы.
[*] ⭐ Огромное количество контента. Более 200 анимированных юнитов, 100 заклинаний, множество предметов и квестов.
[/list]

[h2]❌Минусы:[/h2]
[list]
[*] ⚠️ Устаревшая графика. 3D-модели юнитов выглядят откровенно плохо по современным меркам.
[*] ⚠️ Отсутствие русского языка. В Steam-версии нет официальной локализации, что может стать проблемой для тех, кто не дружит с английским.
[*] ⚠️ Технические проблемы. На современных системах игра может работать с ошибками, и для нормальной работы часто требуется установка фанатского патча (например, Disciples Wrapper).
[*] ⚠️ Дисбаланс. Эльфы, при всех своих плюсах, могут показаться как слишком сильными, так и слишком слабыми в определённых аспектах (особенно это касается магов).
[*] ⚠️Отсутствие системы достижений для истинных коллекционеров прекрасного.
[*] ⚠️Отсутствуют дополнительные материалы в Steam вроде обоев или карточек.
[/list]

[h2]😈Заключение:[/h2]
[b]“Disciples II: Rise of the Elves”[/b] — это классика, которая не стареет, но требует к себе уважения и понимания. Это игра для тех, кто ценит атмосферу, стиль и глубокий геймплей, а не для тех, кто гонится за графикой и спецэффектами. Если вы готовы мириться с некоторыми техническими шероховатостями и отсутствием русского языка, то вас ждёт одно из лучших дополнений к одной из лучших пошаговых стратегий всех времён. Просто помните: когда ваш герой снова погибнет от рук какого-то нейтрального монстра, а вы в ярости захотите удалить игру, сделайте глубокий вдох, загрузите последнее сохранение и попробуйте ещё раз. Потому что Невендаар не прощает ошибок, но он умеет быть благодарным тем, кто не сдаётся.

[h2]💎Итоговая оценка:[/h2]
[h3]Общий балл: 8/10🧝‍♂️[/h3]

There was a time when Disciples II: Rise of the Elves was often compared to Heroes of Might and Magic III. Back then, people argued about which one was better - but today, I don’t really see the need for that comparison. For me, both games are masterpieces that earned their own place in gaming history.

What always pulls me back to Disciples II is its atmosphere. It’s dense, dark, and unapologetically gothic. Every unit portrait feels like a piece of art, and the maps are filled with tiny, handcrafted details that reward slow exploration. The color palette and music tie everything together beautifully, creating a world that feels grim, magical, and alive at the same time.

The factions are another highlight. Humans, Undead, Demons, Dwarves - and, of course, the Elves introduced in Rise of the Elves - each feel truly distinct. They’re not just reskins with minor stat differences; they play differently and force you to adapt. Humans may look weak on paper, but their healers and protective magic make them incredibly resilient. On the other hand, the Undead sacrifice healing and protection for unique abilities like weapon immunity and even draining levels from enemies, reversing their hard-earned transformations.

And those transformations - what a brilliant mechanic. Instead of simply upgrading units, you nurture them. They gain experience, evolve, and take on new forms once certain conditions are met. It’s a system that feels meaningful and personal, making every unit feel like an investment rather than a disposable resource.

The gameplay itself dares to be different. Casting spells on the world map instead of in battle completely changes your strategic approach. Battles rely on fixed formations - front and back rows - with no movement, which at first feels restrictive, but quickly reveals surprising depth. Positioning and army composition become everything, and every decision matters.

There’s also an incredible amount of content. Campaigns (sagas) and standalone scenarios (quests) are rich, varied, and plentiful. And if that’s not enough, custom sagas and quests extend the game’s life even further. It’s the kind of game you can return to again and again without it feeling stale.

Of course, it’s not perfect. Like many games of its era, the hit chance system can feel… unfair. You’ll miss an 80% chance while the AI lands a 60% hit, and it can be frustrating - sometimes enough to tempt you into save scumming. Still, in multiplayer, this unpredictability adds tension and forces a more careful, tactical approach.

Looking back, I know nostalgia plays a role in how much I love this game - but honestly, it doesn’t need it. Disciples II: Rise of the Elves stands strong on its own. It’s one of my favorite turn-based strategy games, and I know I’ll keep coming back to it from time to time, just to lose myself in its dark, beautiful world once again.

Disciples II: Rise of the Elves — это редкий пример дополнения, которое не просто расширяет игру, а усиливает её характер. Атмосфера мрачного фэнтези здесь ощущается в каждом элементе: от музыки и арта до общего настроения мира, который хочется исследовать медленно и вдумчиво.

Эльфийская раса отлично вписалась в баланс и добавила свежие стратегии без потери фирменной сложности серии. Классика, которая до сих пор играется с удовольствием и вызывает чувство ностальгии.

I’ve played a lots of fantasy games over the years, but Disciples II still has a dark fantasy style that I haven’t really encountered anywhere else since the 2000s. There’s something incredibly unique about its art direction, character designs, environments, and overall game design. Everything feels dark, mysterious, and almost haunting, but at the same time beautifully crafted.

The music and audio overall deserves a special mention as well. It doesn’t just sit in the background, it adds so much depth to the atmosphere and perfectly complements the game’s visual style and design. Together, the art, audio, and gameplay create an atmosphere that is difficult to describe but very easy to feel.

And, of course, there’s the nostalgia. Coming back to this game brings back that feeling of playing it years ago, and somehow the atmosphere still holds up.

Unfortunately, the other Disciples games that came after Disciples II never came close to capturing the same combination of art style, atmosphere, music, and game design for me. Disciples II feels like a truly unique piece of dark fantasy gaming that hasn’t really been replicated since.

Still one of my favorites after all these years.

《信徒 II：光明守护者》是一款独立扩展包，让你以帝国或山地氏族的身份潜入《信徒 II》的奇幻世界。

[h1][b]Disciples II: Gallean's Return - Mroczne Hirołsy dla Dorosłych już Dzieci[/b]

[i]Droga Czytelniczko, Drogi Czytelniku.
3 maja - Święto, które jak większość polskich świąt - obchodzimy z mieszaniną dumy i zdezorientowania po majowej rozpuście.
I oto jesteś. Wstajesz rano, jeszcze z dalekim echem wczorajszego BBQ w żołądku i w głowie. Słońce bije przez okno z tą bezczelnością, która należy się tylko majestatowi wiosny. Włączasz PC, bo co innego robić z wolnym dniem, jeśli nie zastanawiać się, dlaczego kraj od ponad dwustu lat próbuje być Europą, a wciąż czuje się jak gorsze dziecko historii.[/i][/h1]

[b]Konstytucja 3 Maja 1791 roku.[/b]
Drugi taki dokument na świecie, pierwszy w Europie. Chwilę potem rozbiory, zdrady, magnaci sprzedający kraj za obce złoto i obietnicę, że ich folwarki przetrwają. Piękna idea, brutalny finał - Targowica, Sierakowscy tego świata kopiący pod własnym stołem, bo tak im wygodniej. I tak sobie przez wieki: wielka idea, małe ludzkie zdrady, sierota-naród taszczący swój patriotyczny, bogo-ojczyźniany krzyż przez kolejne dekady i przemiany.
Brzmi znajomo?

[b]Oczywiście, że brzmi - Nevendaar też tak wygląda.[/b]
Disciples II: Gallean's Return wyszło w 2002 roku - a więc w czasach, kiedy polska klasa średnia dopiero uczyła się, że można mieć więcej niż jeden telewizor, a Internet był dobrem luksusowym. Strategia turowa studia Strategy First, która dotarła do Polski przez CD Projekt - tych samych od Wiedźmina i Cyberpunka - i stała się dla pewnego pokolenia tym, czym Konstytucja Majowa była dla oświeconej, rozwarcholonej szlachty przyzagrodowej: objawieniem, iż coś takiego w ogóle jest możliwe.

[b]Nie jest to gra dla każdego - Nigdy nie była.[/b]
To nie jest Heroes of Might and Magic w baśniowym, przaśnym fantasy, z zamkami jak z obrazka w blasku słońca i blond elfami w białych tunikach tańczącymi po łące. Disciples to przeklęta natura i zimne kamienie, mgła nad martwymi polami i ambient który gra jak Adieu dla świata, który właśnie kończy się za horyzontem.
Nevendaar jest miejscem bez nadziei dla nikogo - Imperium gnije od środka, rozdzierane przez pretendentów do tronu i Inkwizycję siejącą terror. Górskie Klany próbują zebrać szczątki własnej tożsamości po niemal totalnej zagładzie. Legiony Potępionych chcą pochłonąć całe stworzenie w imię upadłego boga. A Nieumarłe Hordy - cóż - mają własną tragedię i ranę której nie da się zasklepić.
Brzmi jak polska scena polityczna, prawda?

[b]Co i z czym.[/b]
Gallean's Return to kompilacja - baza Disciples II: Dark Prophecy plus dwa rozszerzenia: Strażnicy Światła i Słudzy Ciemności. Cztery grywalne rasy, każda z własną kampanią i własnym losem. Cztery perspektywy na ten sam rozpadający się świat. Podobnie jak Konstytucja Majowa, która była próbą pogodzenia czterech sił - szlachty, mieszczaństwa, duchowieństwa i króla. Tamci mieli na to rok. W Nevendaar.
Nikomu nawet nie pozostało tyle czasu.

[b]Technikalia.[/b]
Mechanika jest prosta jak szlachecki honor - złożona jak ichnia moralność.
Poruszasz bohaterem po mapie tura po turze, eksplorując kolejne heksy mgły pozyskujesz złoto, klejnoty ( zasób do rzucania zaklęć ), artefakty i mikstury. Twoje oddziały walczą, giną, ewoluują - i tu jest serce tego tytułu. Bo jednostek nie rekrutuje się bez końca.
Każda urasta - każda ma własną ścieżką rozwoju: zwykły Giermek może z czasem stać się Serafinem lub Inkwizytorem - albo zgnić gdzieś na płowym ugorze, bo źle oceniło się siły oponenta i pchnęło się go pochopnie na starcie.
Tak jak się wysyła niezłomną, lecz nieświadomą młodzież na barykady, bo idea wymaga ofiar, a na decydentach suche buty.
Walka jest turowa, statyczna, pozbawiona fajerwerków i absolutnie wciągająca. Nie ma tu dynamicznej siekany i wysublimowanych animacji. Jest za to ten specyficzny surowy dreszcz, gdy zestawiasz skład drużyny przed starciem, kalkulujesz, czyja inicjatywa jest wyższa, czy Druidka zdąży uzdrowić Wojownika Klanów, zanim Lisz ześle na niego morowe powietrze. To szachy, tyle że z nekromantami i runicznymi olbrzymami.

[b]Antyestetyzm.[/b]
Oprawa z 2002 roku jest tym, czym jest - pikseloza którą przez różowe okulary nostalgii zwiesz klimatyczną. I masz rację !
Bo klimat nie bierze się tu z rozdzielczości. Bierze się z zamysłu - konsekwentnego, ponurego i bezkompromisowego. Disciples II wygląda jak iluminowany rękopis z gotyckiego skryptorium zamoczony w smolistej czerni, zaschniętej posoce, odcieniach ochry i rdzy. Arty jednostek ręcznie malowane, gęste od mroku, pełne tej niepokojąco pięknej brzydoty.
Rycerz Imperium nie lśni jak z bajki - jest cierpiętnikiem, którego zgniata blacha oraz instytucja, która miażdży ludzkie żywoty.
Demoniczna Sukuba nie jest erotyczną fantazją - jest czymś z głębszego i ciemniejszego miejsca w umyśle, jest - limbo rządz.
Nieumarła Zmora - jakby żywcem wypełzła ze szkicu anatomicznego grymuaru, ożywiona wbrew naturze.
A Krasnoludzki Król emanuje srogim majestatem - surowym i dostojnym, jak jego broda i posępne oblicze.
Każda rasa, istota, mówi tu własnym, odpychającym językiem - od Wilka, Chochlika po Wodza zbirów - każde jest w jakim stopniu osobliwe.
To art-direction z prawdziwego zdarzenia. Filozofia wizualna, spójna i mroczna - tonąca w dekadencji - oto jest turpizm wysokiej próby.

[b]Eargasm.[/b]
Udźwiękownie - jak żałobna msza za konającym światem. Każda rasa ma swój motyw, każdy jest odrębnym nastrojem. Imperium brzmi jak chorał za zamkniętymi wrotami katedry. Nieumarłe Hordy - jak pogrzeb, na który nikt nie przybył.
W walce szczęk oręża, chrząkanie jednostek, odgłosy rzucanych zaklęć.
Ale prawdziwa magia dzieje się w warstwie ambientu - każda mapa, ma swój oddech, swój szum wiatru i burzy, swoje odległe echo bitwy. Szepty i zawodzenie pokutników, brzmienie kościelnych organów, ponure bicie dzwonów katedr i nekropolii, gdy w tle słychać brzęczenie trupich owadów, krakanie kruków, wycie wilków - albo ciszę - która jest donioślejsza niż jakikolwiek rumor.

[b]I tu dochodzimy do sedna.[/b]
Disciples II nie jest grą o dobru i złu. Żadne ze stron nie jest tą właściwą - każde ma własny cel, każde nosi na sobie ciężar własnych win i klęsk, każde próbuje przetrwać w świecie wojny - zaszczucia - beznadziei.
*Imperium nie jest wspaniałe, choć jawi się jak gargantuiczny kolos - jest ono skostniałe i pożarte przez uber-brutalny, teokratyczny totalitaryzm, ku fanatycznej wierze we Wszechojca.
*Klany nie są dumnymi wojami krasnoludzkich twierdz pod górą - są, upartymi wyrzutkami, próbującymi odbudować coś z ruin dawnej chwały i potęgi danej przez ich porywczego boga Wotana, który był bardziej niszczycielem niż budowniczym.
*Demony nie są karykaturalnym złem - mają plan, mają zdradzonego boga - upadłego anioła Bethrezena, który stworzył świat a teraz pragnie utopić go we krwi i mają rację przynajmniej co do tego, iż reszta też nie jest bez skazy.
*Nieumarli - Nieumarli są może najbardziej ludzcy ze wszystkich, bo ich wolą nie jest żądza władzy ani fanatyczna wiara, lecz coś bardziej bolesnego: odrzucenie, żal i resentyment skrzepły w wieczną, zimną determinację. Mortis wskrzesiła boga elfów Galleana z miłości - a on ją odrzucił, bo stała się czymś, czego nie mógł już kochać. Istotą bez serca. I to serce, którego nie ma, napędza całą jej armię. To nie jest zło dla zła - to jest ból, który nie może umrzeć, bo już skonał. Memento Mori i Requem w malignie dla i tak wymarłej krainy.

[b]Brzmi to wszystko jak Polska po kolejnych wyborach.[/b]
Cztery strony sporu, każda z własną racją, żadna bez winy, wszyscy w tej samej rozpadającej się matni, z mgłą na horyzoncie i niepewnym jutrem.
Konstytucja Majowa była próbą. Dobrą próbą.
Skończyła się rozbiorami ale sam fakt, że ją napisano, że ktoś miał na tyle odwagi i wizji, żeby spróbować - to zostaje.
Tak jak zostaje Disciples II: turowy, zapomniany, melancholijny klejnot dark fantasy.

review:
Пожилая, но отличная смесь пошаговой стратегии и рпг. Если нет аллергии на древнюю пыль, то крайне рекомендую попробовать, т.к. лучше, имхо, уже не сделают.
От tbs здесь глобальная карта с перемещением героев
От рпг - прокачка всех юнитов (в игре драки максимум 6(8) на 6 в отличие от героев).
Чтобы было понятнее, в менеджменте инвентаря и юнитов, в боевке игра ближе к darkest dungeon, чем к героям, aow и кингс баунти. Кстати, именно поэтому мне третья часть не зашла: в ней юнитам дали возможность ходить по полю сражения, но это вызывало диссонанс, хотя визуально это были те самые диссайплс, в отличие от последующих частей, окончательно повернувших к корейским ммо.
У игры великолепный арт, атмосфера, стиль, цветовая гамма, музыка, звуки. Трек боевки отсылает к первым диссайплам. Эмбиент мрачный и атмосферный. Если арт зацепил, то можете поискать концепт арты Патрика Ламберта, которые офигительные.
Внимание к деталям: на глобальной карте можно залипнуть, глядя на водопадики или рассматривая интерфейс.
Если что, то в редакторе карт можно отдельно рассмотреть все объекты и героев.
Сюжет не откровение, но для игры сойдет. Если пройти кампании в d1, то будет понятнее, что это за Утер из вступительного ролика. Это будет в плюс для атмосферы и погружения. Кстати, на релизе было забавно, когда после wc3 ты получал сюжетно похожую историю. Только Утер был теперь в другой команде) Арка мортис/солониэль и галлеана тоже неплоха.
Почему лучше уже не будет: визуально-атмосферная часть тащит на себе несложный по сути геймплей сюжетных кампаний. И, имхо, даже если сделают ремейк игры или выпустят идейного наследника, полностью повторяющего д2, то получится, как с iratus и darkest dungeon. Первый - копия второго, но выглядит, как очередная мобилка. Я уверен, что повторить d2 и собрать такой же мрачный визуал не удастся.
ЗЫ: если будете играть, то первым делом ткните возле миникарты кнопку включения знамен. Так хотя бы врагов будет видно.

[h2]📜Описание[/h2]
[b]Disciples II: Gallean’s Return[/b] — это сборник, который вобрал в себя всё самое лучшее из легендарной пошаговой стратегии начала нулевых. Внутри вы найдёте базовую игру Disciples II: Dark Prophecy и два самостоятельных дополнения: Guardians of the Light (за Светлые расы — Империю и Горные кланы) и Servants of the Dark (за Тёмные расы — Орду Нежити и Легионы Проклятых). Общий сюжет закручен вокруг возвращения бога Галлеана и того, как его воскрешение (а точнее, месть его жены-нежити Мортис) переворачивает мир Невендара с ног на голову. В игре четыре расы, каждая со своей кампанией, уникальными юнитами и взглядом на то, как правильно насаждать справедливость (или хаос). Русского языка нет, но вам же не нужен перевод, чтобы понять, что инквизиторы — не очень хорошие, а нежить — романтики.

[h2]🎨Графика и звук[/h2]
Визуальный стиль Disciples II — это отдельный вид искусства. 2D-изометрия с ручной отрисовкой, которая до сих пор выглядит шикарно, если вы любите мрачное фэнтези. Арты в готическом стиле: рыцари в ржавых доспехах, гномы с рунами, демоны с явным комплексом неполноценности, и, конечно, нежить — красивая, жуткая и бесконечно печальная. Анимации заклинаний радуют глаз: падающие метеоры, ожившие тени, взрывы тёмной энергии. Звук — это отдельная симфония мрака. Музыка величественная, траурная, иногда тревожная. Звуки боя: лязг, стоны, шепот. А голос рассказчика в кампаниях звучит так, будто он сам уже лет сто как мертв, но продолжает вещать. 

[h2]🎮Геймплей[/h2]
Пошаговая стратегия с глубокими RPG-элементами. Вы ведёте героя по карте, захватываете города, нанимаете войска и выполняете миссии. В отличие от Heroes of Might & Magic, здесь нет строительства замков — вы просто покупаете существ в городах, а вся экономика завязана на рудах и золоте. Главная фишка — ранги юнитов. Ваши солдаты развиваются от новичков до элитных форм (например, солдат → рыцарь → паладин), но для этого нужно выиграть определённое количество боёв. Потеря ветерана — это потеря часов прогресса, так что берегите их, как зеницу ока. Магия мощная и зрелищная, более 100 заклинаний. В сборник добавлен генератор случайных карт, улучшенный ИИ, режим автобоя (для тех, кто не хочет смотреть, как его паладинов рубят вручную) и поддержка больших карт 144x144. Дополнения приносят новые кампании, юнитов, музыку и даже концепт-арты.

[h2]📖Сюжет и атмосфера[/h2]
Сюжет — это тёмное фэнтези с налётом греческой трагедии. Основная драма крутится вокруг Мортис, королевы нежити, и её мужа Галлеана, который был богом, но умер, воскрес и отверг её за то, что она стала бессердечным монстром. И она решает ему отомстить. Жестоко. В дополнении Guardians of the Light вы играете за Империю и гномов: империя раздираема внутренними склоками и инквизицией, которая пытает всех подряд, а гномы восстанавливают свои кланы после почти полного уничтожения. Servants of the Dark даёт возможность поиграть за демонов и нежить: демоны хотят украсть силу возрождающегося эльфийского бога, а нежить — просто преподать урок Галлеану. Атмосфера мрачная, безысходная, но эпичная. Диалоги написаны высоким штилем, с пафосом, который здесь уместен. Чёрный юмор в том, что в мире, где боги воскресают и мстят друг другу, обычные люди (и гномы) просто пытаются выжить. И, как правило, не выживают.

[h2]✅Плюсы:[/h2]
[list]
[*] ⭐ Огромное количество контента — базовая игра + два полноценных дополнения, кампаний на десятки часов.
[*] ⭐ Уникальная мрачная готическая атмосфера, которая не имеет аналогов.
[*] ⭐ Глубокий геймплей с развитием отрядов и героев — каждая потеря болит.
[*] ⭐ Генератор случайных карт, редактор, режим автобоя — реиграбельность зашкаливает.
[/list]

[h2]❌Минусы:[/h2]
[list]
[*] ⚠️ Нет русского языка — придётся учить английский или играть с переводчиком (но интерфейс простой).
[*] ⚠️ Устаревший интерфейс и графика — это ретро, а не минус, но не всем зайдёт.
[*] ⚠️ Высокий порог входа — новичков могут оттолкнуть сложность и отсутствие подсказок.
[*] ⚠️ Баланс хромает — некоторые расы и юниты сильнее других, а заклинания могут решать всё.
[*] ⚠️ Отсутствие системы достижений для истинных коллекционеров прекрасного.
[*] ⚠️ Отсутствуют дополнительные материалы в Steam вроде обоев или карточек.
[/list]

[h2]😈Заключение:[/h2]
[b]«Disciples II: Gallean’s Return»[/b] — это эталон пошаговой стратегии для тех, кто любит мрачное фэнтези, сложные механики и готов прощать игре возраст. Если вы скучаете по временам, когда игры делались с душой, а не по формуле, если вам нравится терять элитных паладинов из-за одной ошибки и переигрывать миссии по десять раз — это ваш идеальный выбор. Если вы ждёте ярких красок, простоты и дружелюбного обучения — лучше пройдите мимо. Но если решитесь, то откроете для себя мир, который не отпускает годами. И помните: Мортис всё равно достанет Галлеана. Даже если для этого придётся воскресить пол-континента.

"Бетрезен умирает" - с этих слов началось мое погружение в безумный, пропитанный ненавистью, кровью и безысходностью мир Невендаара. Борьба богов и их последователей на фоне грядущего разрушения мира, который в конце концов лишь чудом удается спасти (если вы играете за условно "хорошие" расы. ибо в дисциплах по-хорошему и они не святые), становится во главе повествования кампаний всех рас, становясь краеугольным камнем сюжетного нарратива игры. Мрачная красота сеттинга этой стратегии передана на уровне третьего варкрафта, что, на мой взгляд, является редкостью для стратегий. Также не могу не похвалить портреты юнитов и их анимации на тактической карте. Они выполнены ну ооочень круто. 
Однако хорошее повествование служит лишь красивой оберткой, способной создать первоначальный интерес. Дальнейшее погружение происходит благодаря грамотному балансу между рпг-составляющей и стратегическими механиками. 
Начнем с первой категории. В игре (особенно в кампаниях) имеется огромной количество полезных предметов (перманентных и разовых), усиливающие ваших героев и армию. Между ними имеет смысл переключаться, поскольку на вашем пути могут оказаться совершенно разные по силе и способностям отряды врагов. Собственно, здесь все как уже в упоминавшемся 3 варкрафте - менеджмент предметов зачастую может помочь игроку выиграть сражение. 
Что же касается второго аспекта, то он, несмотря на простоту, исполнен не менее прекрасно. Дисциплы - это игра про апгрейды бойцов, а потому вариативность прокачек, предоставленных для каждого типа юнитов, позволяет использовать разные стратегии. Более того, ничего не мешает попробовать собрать армию из однотипных юнитов. Главное, успевать строить здания для их апгрейдов. В общем, простая механика, но зато сколько в ней возможностей для использования различных тактических комбинаций (особенно будет полезно на харде). 
Итог: Дисциплы, несмотря на древность, хорошо состарились. И я искренне не пониманию многих фанатов третьих героев, считающих эту игру "рядовой бирюлькой". Лично для меня Герои, как бы сложны и тактически совершенными они ни были, никогда не заменят сеттинг и красочные (пускай и скоротечные) бои вторых дисциплов.
