This is literally the saddest story in my steam library. This awesome game went from hundreds of people playing it during the open beta - every server full, every new server instantly filling - to dead in months. Why? Price. Hyperbol was $20 for most of its lifespan, and while it's still not technically dead, it's still also not $5 (e: Oh hey, this happened, wonder when). This game would have been a tremendous success had it come out as a F2P game (something Steam didn't support back in 2007) but instead the developers were stubborn and steadfast in killing their own game.

There is literally no reason for this to be more than $5 right now. I say that as someone who waited for the pre-purchase to end in 2007 so that I could pay the full price for the game. It was worth $20 then, but now? Well, there's not a single active game to be found, unless you like playing with half-baked AI. Should this ever go on sale for less than $2, I'm buying it for 20 people on my friends list. Take that as you will.

2022 Update 

I want to be clear that I do not recommend you purchase this game without a plan. There is no way it is an enjoyable experience with no one else playing (it really needs a full game to be fun, and really needed a playerbase large enough to enable skill based match making which is what ultimately killed it) and I do not want you to waste $5 on a game that has been dead for over a decade. I still loved this game, and I think if you could arranged a group to play it somehow it would still be a fantastic experience and there's nothing else out there like it. That's why this review says "Recommended". Do not buy this without a plan or without the understanding that you're essentially buying a relic of the past.

Don't get me wrong, this is a phenomenal game and concept and some of the most fun I've ever had in a PVP-focused game. It was genius. Was. I think it was just before it's time, if it had come out maybe 5 years later it would have been able to thrive with a course adjustment to a F2P model probably. There was, in retrospect, a wealth of opportunity to make the game free and charge for ship customization, it just wasn't a common thing in 2007.

I cannot underscore enough how popular this game was during the free beta and how sharply its population dropped off when the $20 barrier to entry was erected. It was like instantaneous. Makes me sad to this day.

I remember the game being too hard for me back in the day of youth. It's still hard for me now, and there are many frustrating parts, but I simply enjoyed the story and gameplay. X2 is basically T-tension, but with better graphics and the addition of a story. X2 erweitert X: Beyond the Frontier um viele Inhalte, verschlechtert für mich aber gleichzeitig Wirtschaft, Progression und Bedienung.

Das größte Problem ist die fehlende Skalierbarkeit der Verwaltung. In BTF konnten Transporter einer Fabrik einfach in der gewünschten Anzahl zugewiesen werden. In X2 muss praktisch jedes Schiff einzeln gekauft, ausgerüstet, einer Heimatbasis zugewiesen und mit einem Handelsbefehl versehen werden. Bei vielen Fabriken wird dadurch nicht mehr Geld oder Produktionsplanung zum Engpass, sondern die Bedienung der Menüs.

Das Bonus Pack(in der steam version enthalten) löst dieses Problem kaum. Viele Scripts machen einzelne Frachter komplexer, teilweise mit Pilotenrängen und langen Ausbildungszeiten, statt Massenkauf, Massenkonfiguration und einfache Gruppenverwaltung zu verbessern. Grundlegende sinnvolle Handelslogik wird dadurch unnötig hinter zusätzlichem Aufwand versteckt.

Auch die Wirtschaft selbst ist dafür erstaunlich simpel: weitgehend feste Produktions- und Verbrauchsraten, stark standardisierte Fabriken und wenig echte Unterschiede zwischen Produktionsketten. Gleichzeitig sind Fabriken deutlich teurer und amortisieren sich viel langsamer als in BTF. Dadurch entsteht mehr Wartezeit und Verwaltungsaufwand, aber nicht entsprechend mehr wirtschaftliche Tiefe.

Ähnlich bei den Schiffen: Es gibt deutlich mehr Auswahl, aber viel davon ist horizontale Variation mit unterschiedlichen Nachteilen statt klarer vertikaler Progression.

X2 hat weiterhin eine gute Grundidee aus freiem Flug, Handel, Kampf und Fabrikbau. Für mich fügt es aber vor allem Reibung und Mikromanagement hinzu, ohne die zugrunde liegenden Systeme im gleichen Maß zu vertiefen.

[h1][b] Reseña de X2: The Threat[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
X2: The Threat es ese tipo de simulador espacial con alma de hoja de cálculo: te suelta en un universo abierto de ciencia ficción para que hagas lo que quieras… siempre y cuando “lo que quieras” incluya comerciar, explorar, pilotear naves y armar un imperio económico con mentalidad de contador intergaláctico. Sí, hay acción y combate, pero la verdadera guerra aquí es contra tu propia paciencia y tu necesidad de “optimizar rutas”.

Como juego de Estrategia, su encanto está en el sandbox: planificar intercambios, decidir en qué invertir, qué naves operar, cómo expandirte y cuándo dejar de jugar a ser emprendedor espacial para convertirte en el problema armado que todos temen. La primera impresión es clara: esto no te toma de la mano… te empuja por una esclusa y te dice “aprende a respirar”.

Y ojo: es estrictamente un jugador. Si te equivocas, no hay un amigo que te reviva; solo tú, el vacío del espacio y tus decisiones financieras cuestionables.

[h2][b]Mercaderes Estelares vs. Asteroides en el Zapato[/b][/h2]

Lo Bueno:
 Universo abierto tipo sandbox: libertad real para explorar, comerciar y construir tu propia historia   
 Economía y sistema de intercambios con enfoque estratégico: si te gusta planear, aquí hay banquete   
 Mezcla de simulación espacial + acción: puedes pasar de “CEO” a “pirata con licencia” en una tarde   
 Steam Cloud: por fin puedes guardar tu vida de trabajo galáctico sin rezarle a la suerte   
 Subtítulos disponibles: útil cuando el espacio decide hablar en tecnicismos   

Lo No Tan Bueno:
 Sin logros: cero medallitas para tu ego, solo satisfacción existencial (o frustración)   
 Comunidad diminuta (7 jugadores actuales): el universo es enorme, la conversación alrededor no tanto   
 Curva de aprendizaje exigente: si vienes buscando “arcade rápido”, te vas a estrellar con estilo   
 Un jugador: para algunos esto es paz; para otros, soledad espacial premium

[h2]Conclusión (Muy Bueno)[/h2]
X2: The Threat es “muy bueno” en el sentido más peligroso de Steam: no es para todos, pero para quien conecta con su economía, exploración y libertad sandbox, se vuelve una relación tóxica de horas y horas. Vienes por la ciencia ficción, te quedas porque ya invertiste demasiado en tu flota como para abandonar.

La parte controversial: si necesitas validación moderna (logros, guiado constante, ritmo de shooter), este juego te va a parecer un museo interactivo con tareas de oficina. Pero si tu idea de diversión es optimizar rutas, escalar poder y sentir que el universo te pertenece a base de decisiones estratégicas, aquí hay oro espacial.

Con 7 jugadores activos, no esperes una plaza pública enorme; esto es más bien un club de veteranos. Aun así, 428 recomendaciones totales dicen lo obvio: el juego se ganó su lugar, aunque no le interese caerle bien a todo el mundo.

I am playing through all the X-Universe games and finished my playthrough of X2: The Threat. It's a large leap forward from X-Tension. The graphics and overall style feel like a big jump in quality, and the presentation holds up surprisingly well for its age. It also combines a proper storyline with the open-ended sandbox in a way that works naturally.

The story itself is decent, and the cutscenes are neat even if the animations are a bit janky and the dialogue/voice acting leans into early-2000s cringe. What I appreciated most is the pacing. Characters actually tell you to go build up your money and factories between certain missions, so the game encourages you to explore the sandbox instead of rushing the plot.

This is also the first entry with the Artificial Life system and scripting engine, which makes the universe feel more alive and opens the door for modding. Combined with the expanded economy and deeper mechanics, it’s a big step up from the earlier games.

Combat is much improved, especially capital ship battles. Seeing massive turret volleys filling space while fighters weave around them is genuinely cool. The game also introduces proper carriers, and the whole combat experience feels more dynamic and satisfying than anything in BTF or XT.

Automation and empire management are also better here. The property menu has improved filtering, and running a corporate empire feels smoother overall. That said, the universe is more dangerous, and the increased complexity makes the game a little less relaxing than the earlier entries. I played on my Legion Go, and while it worked, I had to set up an extra layer of controls for entering numbers and managing menus. It’s doable, but not as chill as X-Tension on handheld.

Despite that, I really enjoyed X2. It strikes a great balance between story and sandbox, and it’s more stable, more fun, and (in my opinion) has better UI and controls than X3: Reunion which I am now in the middle of playing. I’d recommend X-Tension for players who want a more laid back trading empire experience, but X2 is the one I’d recommend to almost anyone interested in the series.

X2: The Threat, developed and published by Egosoft, represents a significant evolution of the sandbox space simulation formula established in X: Beyond the Frontier. Expanding both the narrative scope and the systemic complexity of its predecessor, X2 invites players into a vast, interconnected universe where trading, combat, exploration, and empire-building coexist within a living economic framework. Rather than presenting a tightly scripted experience, the game embraces player freedom, offering a universe that operates independently of the player’s immediate actions and rewarding long-term planning over short bursts of action.

Set once again in the X-Universe, the story follows Julian Gardna, whose personal journey becomes entangled with the emergence of a mysterious and aggressive alien race known as the Khaak. The narrative provides structure and occasional urgency, especially during key missions that advance the plot. However, like many sandbox simulations, the storyline is optional in spirit if not in design. Players can follow the narrative threads at their own pace or temporarily ignore them in favor of building wealth, exploring uncharted sectors, or assembling fleets. The game’s real strength lies not in its cinematic storytelling but in its capacity to support player-defined goals within a sprawling galactic economy.

The economic system is the beating heart of X2: The Threat. Every station, factory, and ship participates in a dynamic supply-and-demand network. Prices fluctuate based on production levels and consumption rates, creating opportunities for savvy traders to buy low and sell high across dozens of sectors. Early in the game, players often start with modest ships and limited cargo capacity, forcing careful planning of trade routes. As profits accumulate, options expand—larger freighters can be purchased, automated trading ships can be assigned to generate passive income, and eventually entire industrial complexes can be constructed. This gradual progression from small-scale merchant to interstellar magnate is one of the game’s most satisfying arcs.

Combat in X2 adds another layer of depth, though it is rarely the sole focus. The universe contains pirates, hostile factions, and the looming Khaak threat, each capable of disrupting trade routes or attacking vulnerable assets. Players can outfit ships with a variety of weapons, shields, and upgrades, customizing their vessels for defense or offense. While dogfighting can feel less refined than dedicated space combat simulators, strategic fleet management compensates for this. Owning multiple ships and coordinating their deployment across sectors introduces a grander tactical dimension. Large-scale engagements involving capital ships and carriers create moments of spectacle, particularly when defending valuable infrastructure from enemy incursions.

The scale of the universe is impressive, comprising well over a hundred sectors connected by jump gates. Each region has its own economic profile, faction presence, and environmental character. Some sectors teem with trade opportunities, while others are dangerous frontiers patrolled by aggressive forces. Exploration feels purposeful, as uncovering new sectors often reveals lucrative trade possibilities or strategic locations for station construction. The sense of space is reinforced by ambient sound design and the relative isolation of deep-sector travel, contributing to immersion even when gameplay unfolds at a deliberate pace.

Despite its ambition, X2: The Threat demands patience. The interface, while improved over its predecessor, remains dense and occasionally unintuitive. Navigating menus, configuring ships, and managing multiple assets can feel overwhelming for newcomers. The early hours are especially slow, as players work within tight financial constraints and limited ship capabilities. Yet this slow start is intentional, mirroring the climb from obscurity to influence. The game rewards persistence; mastering its systems transforms complexity into empowerment.

Visually, X2 offered notable improvements at the time of release, with enhanced ship models, atmospheric nebulae, and more detailed station designs. While modern standards may reveal the age of its graphics engine, the aesthetic still conveys a sense of scale and cosmic vastness. Ship interiors and menus are functional rather than flashy, reinforcing the simulation-driven focus. The soundtrack and ambient audio contribute to the mood without dominating the experience, allowing players to settle into the rhythms of space commerce and exploration.

Ultimately, X2: The Threat stands as a defining chapter in Egosoft’s space simulation lineage. It successfully broadens the sandbox concept by layering narrative, economic depth, and fleet management into a cohesive universe. It may not offer immediate gratification or streamlined accessibility, but its systemic richness provides enduring appeal. For players who relish autonomy, complex economic systems, and the gradual construction of a personal interstellar empire, X2 delivers a rewarding and expansive journey through the stars.

I bought this game about a decade ago along with the rest of the X games up to X3 Albion Prelude. When i first tried them i found them overwhelming and fairly intimidating. Flash forward to this year, i tried X2 again. As you can tell by the hours i put into it i finally got into it.

to be honest it's not as complicated as i first thought. Even the weird economic management stuff is more or less about finding the right places to build and then setting up a network of ships to handle everything (though i am by no means a master, i've barely scratched the surface). That being said the menu-driven ui does not present everything in a very convenient way. 

Even before you start building factories and sell space weed at competitive prices, there is a real immediacy with how the game plays. after the initial briefing you can go wherever you want and so long as you have some instincts you can mostly figure everything out. Online guides are available if you need them, but observation really helps. And the space battles you get into can be a lot of fun, especially in the big squad battles you can enter through missions. 

That being said, the game shows its age. As of writing this i have yet to play the other X games but it goes without saying that they massively expand everything this game does. I had some problems getting it to run well in the first place (DXVK and SpecialK were required to play the game at a good frame rate for some reason) so you should be prepared. Nonetheless i still feel that it holds its own even if the sequels are more developed experiences. 

Lastly i also want to highlight something that i thought was really cool. Not only do the X games have robust modding support, but the developers actually released a bonus pack filled with user mods that add a lot of essential features like the ability to automatically transfer resources across your stations. I highly recommend reading the readme files for the bonus pack to get the most out of this game.

Присутствует даже какая-никакая драма, чего от экономического космосимулятора вообще не ждешь. Геймплейно - карта большая (настолько большая, что сюжет задействует максимум от неё максимум 10%), кораблей и пушек - много, добавили систему спутников связи, нормальную карту сектора и галактики. Когда понимаешь чем торговать выгоднее всего - процесс значительно ускоряется. Но надо сесть и разобраться... Обучение здесь не просто обязательно - но крайне необходимо, чтобы разобраться что к чему и как этим всем управлять. Но даже оно не гарантирует, что вы не застрянете. Хардкорненько. Новичкам рекомендую исключительно легкий уровень сложности, если вы не хотите перезагружаться и переигрывать одно и то же по 50 раз. Для своего времени игра - офигенная. Кому зайдет - играйте во все части и читайте книги (я это и делаю)

Но совру если не упомяну минусы:

- местами кривой перевод в критически важных местах, где обозначаются названия секторов и станций. (В квесте где написано прилететь на верфь к Сае Хо ЛЕТИТЕ НЕ НА ВЕРФЬ а во второй сектор бОронов на станцию квантовых трубок - ОНА ТАМ.)
- даже с прокачанной на максимум кораблем NOVA - хааки будут очень сложными в сюжетных заданиях, умирать будете только так.

This is the third time I am returning to this game. This is one of those rare games where no one is leading you anywhere. There is a story line, but you can ignore it or return to it at will. You can play without it at all. What to do and how, it all just depends on your desire. If you want to deal only with the economy, the game has calm galaxies where you can build a trading empire and not fight with anyone. If you want wars, you can build a fleet and fly to distant worlds where you will find enemies for every taste. If you want to become a pirate, go ahead.
What I always liked about this game is that when playing it you do not feel like you are being imperceptibly led to some goal, as often happens in other games. And it seems like you are in a free world, but still the developers have created some kind of plan according to which you are led and imperceptibly led to some decision.
Here, you set your own goals in the game and no one knows what will come of it. You get a small ship without control instructions, it is not clear at first how to fly, you even want to quit and not suffer, but if you do not quit on the first day, then you learn more and more and it begins to drag you in. The on-board computer becomes easy to operate, if at first you did not know what to press, then you play it like a piano. You stop paying attention to the graphics of the game, which of course by modern standards seems unsightly, because Napoleonic plans appear, in which the graphics no longer play any role. In general, in my opinion, this is one of those freelance games in which you just live in space and do what you want.

이 시리즈 자체를 모르는 분들을 위해 간단하게 설명하면, (Space Trader(1974)) -> Elite -> Freelancer 계보의 우주 트레이딩 심 게임입니다. 한국 사람들 중 좀 나이 있는 분들 상대로는 대항해시대라고 말하는 게 오히려 이해하기 쉽겠군요. 서양권이면 Sid Merier's Pirates! 로 생각하시면 되겠고.

어쨌든 추천 시점에서 이미 21년 된 물건인데 요즘 하는데 재미있습니다. 세상에.

3는 어떻게 팬 분들이 정성들여 한글화를 했고, 4도 그 한글화 하신 분들 덕에 공식 한글화가 되었지만 2는 한글도 아니니 패스하시는 분들이 많을 겁니다. 저도 추천하긴 하지만 언어 장벽 수준이 적당히 있고(BBS 게시판에 글의 길이가 좀 많이 깁니다. 뭐 대부분은 그냥 반복되는 뉴스 + 반복되는 랜덤 퀘 정도이니 패턴 인식으로 때려 맞출 정도는 되지만) 3 -> Rebirth -> 4로 가면서 다듬어진 UI도 없으니 귀찮은 점도 꽤 있습니다.

그러니 모두를 위한 추천은 아닙니다.

하지만 이 당시 게임에서 이미 배 한척으로 시작 -> 여러 배를 얻기 시작하면서 자기 함대를 만듬 -> 자기 공장을 만들고 나는 손 안대면서 자동화된 수익을 즐김(생각보다 어려움) -> 공장들끼리 연계하면서 완성된 회로 생태계를 만듬(중간 정도 되면 적자가 더 심함. 태양열 발전소만 지으라는 조언이 괜한 게 아니었음) 이 구조가 이미 완성되어 있었습니다.

이걸 하나 하나 이루는 맛은 이미 이때 완성된 것이지요. (사실은 전작 X : Beyond The Frontier 의 스탠드 얼론 확장팩익 X-tension 때부터)

Histoire :
X2: The Threat plonge les joueurs dans un univers de science-fiction ouvert où vous incarnez Julian Gardna, un jeune pilote qui se retrouve rapidement impliqué dans une lutte intergalactique contre la mystérieuse race alien des Kha’ak. L'histoire principale vous guide à travers un scénario intrigant qui implique des trahisons, des batailles spatiales et des alliances fragiles entre factions. Bien que le scénario reste un peu en retrait par rapport à l'exploration libre, il est engageant et aide à immerger le joueur dans un univers vaste et complexe, peuplé de personnages et factions aux motivations variées. L'histoire sert de bon point de départ pour les débutants tout en offrant des intrigues secondaires qui enrichissent l'expérience pour ceux qui veulent s'y plonger.

Gameplay :
Le gameplay de X2: The Threat combine exploration, commerce, et combat spatial dans un monde ouvert, offrant une liberté impressionnante dès le début. Vous pouvez choisir de suivre la campagne ou d’ignorer l’histoire principale pour vous consacrer au commerce, au piratage, à l’établissement de votre propre empire industriel, ou encore à la chasse aux primes. La gestion des ressources et la construction de flottes deviennent progressivement essentielles, car vous pouvez acheter et équiper différents vaisseaux, de petits chasseurs aux gigantesques transporteurs. La complexité du jeu réside dans ses nombreuses options de gestion : acheter, équiper, et personnaliser des vaisseaux, gérer des stations spatiales, établir des routes commerciales automatisées, et même former des escadrons de combat. Le gameplay en monde ouvert peut être intimidant pour les nouveaux joueurs en raison de l'interface et de la courbe d'apprentissage raide, mais il offre une profondeur et une liberté rarement égalées dans les jeux de simulation spatiale.

Graphismes :
Pour un jeu de 2003, X2: The Threat propose des graphismes impressionnants, avec des effets lumineux et des modèles de vaisseaux détaillés. Les environnements spatiaux sont variés et captivants, chaque secteur ayant une atmosphère et des couleurs distinctes qui contribuent à l'immersion. Les vaisseaux, stations et stations spatiales sont bien modélisés, bien que les textures puissent sembler datées par rapport aux standards actuels. Les scènes de batailles spatiales sont souvent spectaculaires, avec des explosions et des effets lumineux immersifs, même si les animations de personnages lors des dialogues sont assez rudimentaires. Visuellement, le jeu réussit encore à capturer l’immensité de l’espace et la beauté des galaxies, même si les joueurs modernes pourraient trouver les graphismes un peu vieillissants.

Difficulté :
X2: The Threat est un jeu exigeant, avec une courbe d'apprentissage raide, surtout pour les nouveaux venus dans les jeux de simulation spatiale. Les mécaniques de commerce, de gestion de flotte, et de combat demandent du temps pour être maîtrisées. L'interface utilisateur, dense et complexe, peut nécessiter un temps d'adaptation, mais ceux qui persévèrent découvrent un système très gratifiant. Le jeu devient particulièrement difficile lorsqu’il s'agit de bâtir son propre empire : équilibrer les ressources, sécuriser les routes commerciales et protéger vos installations demandent une attention constante. Le jeu encourage les joueurs à être stratégiques et à planifier leurs actions à long terme, un aspect qui plaira aux amateurs de simulation et de stratégie.

Durée de vie :
Avec son monde ouvert et ses nombreuses possibilités de gameplay, X2: The Threat offre une durée de vie quasi illimitée. La campagne principale prend environ 30 heures à compléter, mais les joueurs peuvent facilement y passer des centaines d'heures s'ils s'investissent dans le commerce, l'exploration, et la conquête galactique. Les missions secondaires, les interactions avec les différentes factions, et les possibilités de création de stations et de flottes permettent une rejouabilité élevée. Les fans de sandbox et de simulation spatiale auront de quoi s'occuper pendant longtemps, surtout s'ils décident de suivre différentes approches ou de se spécialiser dans un secteur en particulier.

Prix (en solde) :
En solde, X2: The Threat est souvent proposé à moins de 5 euros, ce qui représente un excellent rapport qualité-prix pour la profondeur et la durée de vie offertes par le jeu. Bien que le jeu date un peu, il reste un choix judicieux pour les fans de jeux de simulation spatiale, en particulier ceux qui cherchent une alternative aux jeux plus récents et plus coûteux. À ce prix, le jeu est une affaire pour ceux qui souhaitent plonger dans un univers riche et complexe.

Conclusion :
X2: The Threat est une simulation spatiale immersive, offrant une liberté totale aux joueurs qui souhaitent explorer, commercer, combattre, et même bâtir leur propre empire dans un univers vaste et détaillé. Bien que le jeu exige un certain investissement de temps pour maîtriser ses mécaniques, il est gratifiant pour ceux qui aiment la gestion et la stratégie en monde ouvert. En solde, X2: The Threat est un excellent choix pour les amateurs de science-fiction et de simulation spatiale, malgré des graphismes un peu datés et une interface exigeante.

I bought this god knows how long ago hoping it would be a "cheaper and easier" Elite Dangerous game. Even though I enjoy Elite Dangerous and wanna play it more and do a review for it sometime I just end up rarely playing it so I was hoping something like this could scratch that flying a space ship itch I've been having recently. Smaller download size, easier to run, probably a lot more easier to understand as well... Or so I was hoping. Almost 5 hours and I can tell I'd rather not continue. There is nothing necessarily wrong with the game, its what I expected it to be. Its just that I'm 5 hours in, the very few combat I've seen has been incredibly boring, the trading is fun mainly because I enjoy trading not because the game does it in a fun way, the ships look cool and stuff but its not enough. I can tell that if I really wanted to squeeze fun out of this game I'd have to commit a lot more hours into it and currently I don't really see why I should.

+The menus while very confusing at first can be fun to use once you figure out how they work. That just applies for the controls in general very confusing at first but once you get used to it its not bad at all. A few keys on your keyboard and your mouse is all you need to navigate through the entire game both in space and in the UI.
+Many different ships, they all look nice some even come with turrets. Big stuff, small stuff all the fun things you'd hope to see in space.
+The voice acting can be surprisingly good at times. There were a few lines I really liked. There were times where it was meh as well, some things got annoying too quickly. You do get some dialogue options they're nothing big but they exist.
+The trading in the game is fun but thats mainly because I enjoy trading in games like this, the game doesn't really make it interesting on its own. Yeah prices change for the goods you're trying to sell and each station needs different resources and produces different goods thats all cool but thats what I'd expect in a game like this so I'm not giving it too much praise. Maybe it was super impressive in 2003 but thats the price you pay with older games I guess.

+/- Wtf is a mizura? And all the other weird words they keep using? Mizura, Jizura, This-ura, That-ura. Just say years, hours, minutes. You can get missions from stations they'll just be there for you to look at, read through and accept if you think you can do it and like lets say a mission says "we need 180 of this thing but it has to be delivered to us in 3 mizuras" like sure it sounds different and unique but you're just making my job harder to keep track of time. Maybe its because I didn't play the earlier games but a lot of terminology is just so fucking weird and its never explained to you, just figure it out yourself.

-I usually don't mind older graphics that much and with some games I even find it charming but in here it just looks bad. I like the design of the ships, I don't like their textures.
-The fighting in the game is very very very boring.
-Its an incredibly slow burning game and you can tell early on that you're gonna need to invest a lot of time to get things really rolling or you need to follow a guide to try and min-max everything. I didn't wanna do either.
-Its a space game, it takes place in space. Now thats wonderful, exactly what I wanted. Unfortunately that means things can turn anywhere they want, anytime they want and things turn a lot. What the hell do I mean? Imagine docking into a station and trying to find a parking spot for your ship. There are several in front of you, some occupied and one or two empty spots for you to park into. They're all stationary. But the walls of the station? They're rotating. It fucks with my brain to look at it I've seen similar stuff in other games but they didn't fuck with my brain as much as this game did. I think this is the first space game where my brain got messed up while I was trying to park into a stationary location while all the walls were rotating around me. Oh and another thing about that as far as I know there isn't a "free look" camera mode. Not being able to look left or right inside of your own cockpit makes things hard.

You can do a lot of stuff in game and even though there is a story you don't really have to do the missions and follow it. Its not that its an awful, unplayable game. Its just that it clearly needs a lot of time and effort which I'm not willing to give. I do not want to suffer slowly for god knows how long before things get really off the ground. I came here because its an older game, smaller download size, easier to run on any PC. Had I been using my older, worse computer maybe I would have liked it more but now that I have a stronger PC I don't really have a need, a reason to commit to this game. If you are going to buy a game where you drive space ships and trade and fight... There's better options I believe. If you really want something from the X series go for the latest one, X4, the screenshots look great and its probably improved in a lot of ways too. If you really do want X2 The Threat I assume you have some nostalgia with this game or you were in a situation like me where you didn't have a great PC but you really wanted to play a simulator type of game that took place in space. If you are in those situations, sure. If not then I don't think you should buy this game.

Gott, wenn ich schon die idiotischen Bewertungen von Metacritic sehe, kriege ich das kotzen. Deutsche Spiele werden international einfach mal völlig falsch bewertet, was sich leicht auch durch die meist wesentlich besseren User-Wertungen belegen lässt. 
X2 ist und bleibt eine der besten Weltraumsimulationen aller Zeiten, die mindestens eine 80er Wertung verdient hätte. 

Natürlich ist die Story ohne Belang, die enorm große Spielwelt etwas generisch, aber dafür bekommt man eben auch eine für die damalige Zeit riesige Sandbox. Kein anderes Spiel hat mir jemals eine derartige Auswahl an Schiffen gegeben. Vom Scoutschiff, über den Jäger bis zum Schlachtschiff oder Trägerschiff kann man alles fliegen. Man kann am Ende des Spiels sogar gewaltige Flotten aufstellen, ganze Systeme mit eigenen Stationen und Sektorpatrouillen vollpflastern, so man denn will. 

Die Schiffe unterscheiden sich wohltuend, so dass man motiviert ist, stundenlang Geld zu verdienen, um sich z.B. endlich sein kleines Westentaschenschlachtschiff namens Teladi Adler zu verdienen. 

Atmosphärisch ist das Spiel zu seiner Zeit einfach konkurrenzlos im Genre gewesen. Der Vorteil von X2 ist zudem, dass hier eine gute Mischung besteht, denn das Spiel lässt sich sowohl gut für Leute spielen, die unbedingt hunderte von Stunden in ihre Raumstationen und den Handel investieren wollen, aber genauso gut für Leute, die mehr auf Action setzen. Die können vor allem durch Kaperei und insbesondere Verteidigungsmissionen unglaublich viel Geld generieren und sich somit haufenweise Schiffe und Stationen kaufen, natürlich erst nach harter Arbeit.

X2 ist zudem deutlich besser gelungen als der Nachfolger X3, der zwar sehr hübsch aussah, allerdings derart viele idiotische Fehlentscheidungen beinhaltete, dass das Feeling aus X2 zumindest für mich vollkommen verloren ging, bspw. fehlende Cockpits, fehlerhafte Nebel, grottenschlechte Großkampfschiffe und Verkomplizierung der Kaperei.

X2 ist somit für mich klar der beste Teil der Serie, obwohl X3 so viel Potenzial hatte,

It’s an X game... If you want the definitive sandbox experience of the classic X3 era, Terran Conflict is honestly the better choice. I am moving over to it the second I finish the Bala Gi missions (I just need to buy my TL and the trading station, otherwise I'm completely done).
The only real reason to play Reunion today is if you are deeply interested in the lore and want to see the conclusion of the original Brennan trilogy (X: Beyond the Frontier, X2: The Threat, and this one). Ironically, this campaign feels like the longest but easiest in the trilogy, and unfortunately, the least fun.
Personally, I still prefer X:BtF because it felt tighter, simpler, and more like a true space adventure. X2 didn't quite feel like an Alpha, but it did feel like a Beta. I liked X2's visual style more because it feels less empty, more colorful, and much more lived-in and atmospheric—especially with its cool cockpits. X3 feels a bit dull and colorless by comparison, and it completely lacks cockpits. X3 trades that unique charm for a more 2000s modern, Homeworld-like ship design. There is nothing wrong with that look, but I honestly prefer X2's 90s-style toy spaceships.
It makes me sad that Egosoft never put enough effort into their story campaigns to make them tight and genuinely fun. It always feels like they had a mountain of very cool ideas and features in mind that they simply never implemented. I bet there was originally a much bigger adventure game segment buried in the design—complete with dialogue choices, puzzles, mini-games, more varied missions, and better fleshed-out characters (I very much got that impression from playing X2). I genuinely liked the premise of the Brennan plotline, but it is sadly just a very unpolished, rushed story that was completely abandoned after this game. With that said, I do appreciate the banter between the characters in X3 (even if it's a bit buggy), and it was nice that Egosoft actually gave Julian a voice actor.
In Reunion's main story, you don't actually need to grind or trade much. If you capture or steal an upgraded M3 fighter, you are set, but you could honestly finish the entire narrative in your starting Buster with a bit of luck. The campaign has a very "alpha," unpolished feel and isn't particularly engaging, but at least it's relatively quick and doesn't force a massive grind on you. For both the main plot and Bala Gi, I highly recommend keeping a walkthrough handy. The game can be a bit tricky and buggy at times, and using a guide will definitely save you from some massive headaches.
The Bala Gi endgame missions unlock after you hit 5 million credits and some flight time. They are completely optional and have absolutely no relation to the main plot or lore of the X universe—except maybe for explaining how the M3+ class ships came into being :P There is no real story to it, just a series of semi-hard but short tasks (minus the brutal part where you suddenly need 40 to 60 million credits to buy a TL and a Trading Station to finish it).
Ultimately, unless you are a completionist who wants to experience the full narrative trilogy, feel the retro history of the franchise, and see how the X series evolved into what it is today... you can easily skip Reunion and just jump straight into X4.

[h1][b] Reseña de X3: Reunion[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
X3: Reunion es ese tipo de “Estrategia” que no te toma de la manita: te avienta al vacío del espacio con una calculadora, una nave modesta y la expectativa tóxica de que tú solito armes un imperio. Aquí la estrategia no es mover soldaditos en un mapa: es sobrevivir a base de comercio, rutas, gestión económica, expansión tipo sandbox y decisiones que hacen que tu productividad suba… o que tu flota explote de forma poética.

La primera impresión es clara: esto es un simulador espacial con alma de hoja de Excel, donde el “mundo abierto” significa “felicidades, tienes libertad total para perderte durante horas”. Si vienes buscando acción inmediata, X3 te contesta: “sí, claro, ahorita… cuando termines de entender el ecosistema económico y tus naves de carga no se suiciden”.

Y ojo: es un juego de un jugador, con subtítulos, Steam Cloud y préstamo familiar; o sea, ideal para compartirle tu sufrimiento a un familiar y decirle “mira, es divertido”, mientras él te deja de hablar por una semana.

[h2][b]Bitácora del Capitán: Lo que te hace rico vs. lo que te hace llorar en el hangar[/b][/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Sandbox espacial enorme: explorar, comerciar y expandirte con libertad real.  
  Economía y comercio con sabor a “soy un genio”… hasta que el mercado te humilla.  
  Mezcla sabrosa de simulación de vuelo + estrategia: no solo mandas, también piloteas.  
  Steam Cloud: para guardar tu imperio… y tus malas decisiones interestelares.  
  Préstamo familiar: comparte tu nave… y tu crisis existencial.

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Comunidad muy pequeña (5 jugadores): el espacio está vacío, y no es por inmersión.  
  0 logros: Steam no te aplaude, aunque hayas levantado un imperio desde la nada.  
  Curva de aprendizaje exigente: la “estrategia” se siente como un curso intensivo no solicitado.  
  Si esperabas una experiencia guiada: aquí te sueltan y te dicen “resuélvelo, campeón”.

[h2]Conclusión (Muy Bueno)[/h2]
X3: Reunion es “Muy Bueno” porque hace algo que pocos se atreven: te deja construir tu historia a base de decisiones estratégicas, comercio y exploración en un universo abierto que te puede devorar si llegas con mentalidad de juego rápido. Es un simulador espacial con estrategia de largo aliento, más cercano a administrar un sistema que a “disparar por disparar”.

Ahora, seamos controversiales: si necesitas recompensas constantes, logros, y una comunidad enorme para sentirte acompañado… aquí no hay aplausos, solo vacío interestelar. Con 5 jugadores actuales, esto se siente como un club privado donde todos se conocen por nombre y por trauma.

Aun así, 568 recomendaciones no salen de la nada: es un clásico para quien disfruta la economía, el sandbox y el control de una flota/imperio con paciencia. Si lo tuyo es el “yo aprendo jugando”, este juego te responde: “perfecto, aprende… o perece”.

Si disfrutas juegos de estrategia que te exigen pensar, planear rutas, optimizar recursos y aceptar que el espacio no tiene piedad, X3: Reunion vale la pena. Si buscas algo directo, social o con gratificación inmediata, mejor no te subas a esta nave: aquí el piloto automático es tu orgullo rompiéndose lentamente.

I’m playing through the entire X-Universe series, and X3: Reunion has been the first real stumble. While it looks visually impressive for its time, almost every part of the experience feels like a step backward from X2 in terms of usability, pacing, and overall fun.

The biggest issue is the UI. X2’s interface was nicer, faster, and easier to navigate, while X3’s menus, property management, and ship commands all take noticeably longer to use. On my Legion Go, this was even more frustrating, the extra complexity made my controller setup feel awkward and slowed down basic empire management.

Stability was another major problem. The game crashed often and randomly, so I had to save constantly. Some saves even became corrupted, which meant keeping multiple backups. The in-game save menu is clunky as once you fill all the slots scrolling through them becomes a chore. The Steam version also has cutscene playback issues, and I had to download an older patch from Egosoft just to get them working properly. 

The story is weaker and far less engaging than X2’s. Missions frequently take control away from you, forcing you into specific ships or turret roles and preventing you from interacting with your empire until the mission is finished. This completely breaks the flow between story and sandbox that X2 handled so well. The pacing feels off, and the two halves of the game never really gel.

The economy also feels more grindy, and while automation is slightly improved, the clunky menus cancel out most of the benefit. The universe does feel more alive and dangerous, which is a positive, and combat is a bit better than X2 but not enough to outweigh the other frustrations.

Overall, I enjoyed X2 far more as a complete package. It had better pacing, better story integration, better UI, and was simply more fun to play. X3: Reunion feels like a downgrade in usability and enjoyment, and I wouldn’t recommend it unless you’re playing through the series for completion’s sake. X2 is the better experience, and X3: Terran Conflict is essentially a refined, improved version of Reunion in every way.

X3: Reunion to jeden z tych tytułów, które nie próbują być przystępne. To kosmiczny sandbox w najczystszej formie — ogromny, skomplikowany i absolutnie bezkompromisowy. Jeśli szukasz gry, która od pierwszych minut daje ci spektakularne bitwy i prostą fabułę, to… X3 nie jest dla ciebie. Ale jeśli chcesz prawdziwej symulacji życia w kosmosie, z ekonomią, handlem, walką i budowaniem własnego imperium — to jest gra, która potrafi wciągnąć na setki godzin.

Największą siłą X3: Reunion jest skala.
Galaktyka jest ogromna, pełna sektorów, stacji, frakcji i statków, które żyją własnym życiem. Handel działa naprawdę — ceny zmieniają się w zależności od podaży i popytu, fabryki produkują towary, a ty możesz w to wszystko wejść, manipulować rynkiem albo stworzyć własną sieć przemysłową. To nie jest gra, w której jesteś bohaterem. Tu jesteś jednym z wielu, a twoja pozycja zależy tylko od tego, jak dobrze potrafisz wykorzystać system.

Walka jest wymagająca, ale satysfakcjonująca.
Statki mają masę, bezwładność, różne klasy i role. Nie ma tu arcade’owego latania — każdy manewr ma znaczenie, a starcia potrafią być chaotyczne, intensywne i pełne adrenaliny. Kiedy pierwszy raz zestrzelisz pirata, czujesz dumę. Kiedy pierwszy raz stracisz statek za kilkaset tysięcy kredytów — czujesz ból.

X3: Reunion to także gra o budowaniu.
Możesz tworzyć własne fabryki, łączyć je w kompleksy, zarządzać flotą transportowców, a później nawet dowodzić całą armadą. To powolny proces, ale niezwykle satysfakcjonujący. Każdy kredyt, który zarobisz, ma znaczenie. Każda inwestycja może się zwrócić — albo zbankrutować cię na amen.

Fabuła? Jest, ale nie jest najważniejsza.
To raczej pretekst, żebyś miał cel na początku. Prawdziwa gra zaczyna się wtedy, gdy przestajesz śledzić misje i zaczynasz tworzyć własną historię: jako handlarz, pirat, przemysłowiec, najemnik albo wszystko naraz.

X3: Reunion to tytuł, który nie jest dla każdego.
Jest trudny, powolny, momentami nieprzystępny.
Ale jeśli dasz mu szansę, odpłaci ci się czymś, czego nie daje żadna inna gra:
poczuciem, że naprawdę żyjesz w ogromnym, funkcjonującym kosmosie.

To nie jest gra, którą się przechodzi.
To gra, którą się zamieszkuje.

X3: Reunion from Egosoft is a space simulation that fully commits to the idea of player-driven freedom, offering a universe that feels less like a guided experience and more like an open-ended system waiting to be understood and shaped. Rather than funneling players through tightly scripted missions, it drops them into a sprawling network of sectors connected by jumpgates and lets them decide what kind of life they want to build among the stars. Whether that means becoming a trader, a mercenary, a pirate, or an industrial magnate is entirely up to the player, and that sense of autonomy is the game’s defining strength.

The structure of the game revolves around a living economy that operates independently of the player’s actions. Stations produce goods, resources fluctuate based on supply and demand, and factions interact within a dynamic framework that continues regardless of player involvement. This creates a world that feels active and reactive, where opportunities emerge naturally rather than being handed out through scripted events. Players can start small, hauling goods between stations for profit, and gradually scale up to managing fleets and building entire production networks. Over time, this progression transforms the experience from a simple trading loop into a complex economic simulation, where efficiency, logistics, and planning become just as important as piloting skill.

One of the most compelling aspects of X3: Reunion is how it handles growth. Advancement is not handed out quickly; instead, it is earned through careful decision-making and long-term investment. Acquiring better ships, expanding trade routes, and establishing factories all require time, resources, and patience. This slow progression can feel daunting at first, but it also makes success feel meaningful. Reaching the point where you command multiple ships or oversee automated income streams is deeply satisfying because it reflects a genuine buildup of effort rather than a series of quick rewards.

Exploration also plays a key role in the experience. The universe is vast, with each sector offering its own layout, stations, and potential opportunities. Traveling between these areas reinforces the scale of the game, though it also highlights one of its more divisive qualities: pacing. Movement can be slow, and much of the gameplay involves long stretches of travel or waiting for economic processes to unfold. For some players, this enhances immersion, making the universe feel expansive and real; for others, it can come across as tedious, especially in the absence of faster-paced alternatives early on.

Combat exists as an important but secondary element. Dogfights can be engaging, particularly when piloting more advanced ships equipped with a variety of weapons, and larger engagements add a sense of spectacle as multiple vessels clash in open space. However, the mechanics are not as refined as the game’s economic systems, and encounters can sometimes feel inconsistent. While combat provides excitement and variety, it is clear that the game’s primary focus lies elsewhere, in the broader systems that govern trade, production, and expansion.

The game’s complexity is both its greatest asset and its most significant barrier. X3: Reunion does very little to ease players into its systems, and the interface can feel dense and unintuitive, especially for newcomers. Learning how to navigate menus, manage assets, and optimize trade routes requires a considerable investment of time. There is a steep learning curve that may discourage players who are not prepared to experiment and learn through trial and error. Yet for those who push through this initial hurdle, the depth of the systems becomes a source of lasting engagement.

Visually, the game captures the grandeur of space with detailed ship designs and expansive environments that emphasize scale. Stations and capital ships feel massive, and the lighting and visual effects contribute to a strong sense of atmosphere. While it may not match modern graphical standards, its presentation still succeeds in conveying the vastness and isolation of its setting, reinforcing the immersive quality of the experience.

Despite its ambition, the game is not without flaws. Its pacing can feel uneven, its interface can be cumbersome, and its complexity can be overwhelming. These elements combine to create an experience that demands patience and persistence, and it will not appeal to everyone. However, these same qualities are also what allow it to offer a level of depth and freedom that few games attempt.

In the end, X3: Reunion stands as a deeply immersive and system-driven space simulation that rewards players who are willing to engage with its intricacies. It is not a game of instant gratification, but one of gradual mastery, where the satisfaction comes from building something meaningful within a vast and dynamic universe. For those who appreciate open-ended gameplay and complex economic systems, it remains a standout experience that continues to hold its own despite its age.

This game is beyond awesome. It has the bones to be the best space simulator ever made. 

There are automation elements where you can autopilot your ship to do practically anything you can manually do. You can do the same with ships you own, creating vast fleets of warships that can patrol sectors to eliminate enemies or destroy a specific factions trade routes. You can use the same automation to set up your own trading empire, with factories to produce basic goods like solar energy cells up to extremely elaborate super factories that create highly complex goods like weapons, ships, missiles, shields, and pretty much anything you could imagine. 

The factions are fun and interesting though the dialogue will get repetitive after a few dozen hours. Each faction controls their own territories and in Reunion they tend to go to war with racial enemies which can change the power dynamics in a sector at a moments notice. 

Ship to ship combat is fun up to a point. Flying your own ship is great, nothing is cooler than jumping into a system and chasing down a fat transport and lowering his shields until he ejects. You can either capture his goods, his ship, or the pilot himself. That is until your combat rating gets higher and the fights start getting unfair. You can be the best pilot in the universe in your M3 but when that capital ship or corvette shows up, you are pretty much guaranteed to lose. It will have dozens of support ships that will all simultaneously wreck your face. You can get creative with ship builds and last a good while, but eventually you will require fleets of your own ships to support you and thats where things fall apart.

The NPC AI is fantastic and believable. Your AI, however, is incredibly dumb. Ships in sectors you aren't present in are notorious for mysteriously exploding out of nowhere because they got too close to an enemy faction. Even ships in your own sector can fall prey to stupid decisions like coming through a gate the same time a capital ship is going into it and colliding. Trading ships can be incredibly dumb and will make a bee-line for the first enemy ship in a sector and get wasted. Entire stations can get destroyed because your support fleets break and don't patrol sectors correctly. There are lots of bugs in the AI on the player side. Patches and the like have come out to address some issues but if there is a major weakness in this game, your AI is it.

As for the rest of the game, its and absolute blast. I mostly played as a pirate and had the most fun I have ever had in a video game ambushing ships at gates to add to my collections. I even managed to capture a few capital ships and started my own shipyards up. That was until I invested most of my credits into a behemoth battleship that I couldn't possibly afford to arm. I had the lasers and the shields but it took an army of trading ships just to transport energy cells and missiles back and forth to it and the better equipped enemy AI's ate it for dinner.

Like I said at the beginning, this game has the bones to be the best spaceflight simulator ever made. It has everything. A graphical overhaul and some addressing of the AI would put this game a century ahead of it's time.

Si habéis jugado al X2: La Amenaza, en su modo historia puedes ir progresando poco a poco y avanzado en ella sin problemas. De hecho te proporcionan una nave de transporte de mercancías, lo que ayuda, si sabes que materias comprar y vender, para obtener mejoras y naves.
En este juego, es lo contrario. Joder, estoy en la tercera misión y me machacan nada más aparecer con naves de exploración piratas. ¡Y EN NORMAL!.

Así que:
  Gráficos: 5/5. Siempre me han gustado los simuladores del espacio, manejar naves y negociar en estaciones orbitales. Mejorados de la versión anterior.
  Historia: 1/5. No cambian. Dificil al inicio. (Al menos para un patoso como yo)

  Jugabilidad: 3/5. Algunos cambios, como el desplazamiento de la nave por efecto de la inercia, atraque de la nave, ...

Tudo sobre: X3: Reunion
(Valxb21)

#### 1. **História:**
   - **Enredo:** Em "X3: Reunion", a narrativa te joga em um universo de comércio espacial e combate, onde você deve proteger a galáxia de ameaças alienígenas e desenvolver seu império econômico. O jogo é continuação direta de "X2: The Threat". Você encarna Julian Brennan, que continua a saga de seu pai, envolto em conspirações e lutas contra a raça Xenon.
   - **Positivo:** A profundidade e riqueza da história atraem fãs de ficção científica que buscam mais do que apenas batalhas espaciais. A trama tem uma pegada cinematográfica, com reviravoltas, traições e uma grande expansão do lore do universo X.
   - **Negativo:** A narrativa, embora intrigante, é complexa e pode ser difícil de acompanhar para jogadores novos na série. Ela fica em segundo plano, sendo ofuscada pelo gameplay denso e livre, o que desagrada quem quer um foco maior na história.

#### 2. **Jogabilidade:**
   - **Mecânicas Principais:** O jogo é um simulador espacial de comércio, construção e combate. Você pode construir estações, minerar, negociar mercadorias, e claro, participar de combates intensos. O gerenciamento econômico é uma parte crucial e altamente detalhada.
   - **Positivo:** A liberdade é imensa! Você pode ser um comerciante pacífico ou se tornar um pirata galáctico. O sistema de economia é robusto, permitindo criar impérios ou falir completamente. A variedade de naves e estações para administrar dá um nível de personalização excelente.
   - **Negativo:** A curva de aprendizado é brutal. A interface pode ser um verdadeiro labirinto e algumas mecânicas não são intuitivas, exigindo uma boa dose de paciência. O ritmo lento e a necessidade de microgerenciamento podem ser um grande desmotivador para jogadores casuais.

#### 3. **Conquistas e Desafios:**
   - **Progresso e Metas:** O jogo recompensa aqueles que investem tempo, com conquistas variando desde derrotar inimigos até estabelecer um império econômico próspero. As conquistas são amplamente focadas em progressão econômica e domínio espacial.
   - **Positivo:** As conquistas são uma celebração do esforço do jogador em dominar tanto o combate quanto o comércio. A sensação de "grandeza" quando você finalmente conquista sua primeira frota ou estação é incomparável.
   - **Negativo:** Muitas conquistas são absurdamente demoradas. Se você está procurando um jogo que respeite seu tempo, "X3: Reunion" pode não ser o ideal, já que algumas metas podem levar literalmente dezenas de horas para serem atingidas.

#### 4. **Bugs e Glitches:**
   - **Experiência Geral:** Lançado inicialmente com vários bugs, o jogo enfrentou problemas técnicos, desde falhas gráficas até problemas com a IA.
   - **Positivo:** Muitos bugs foram corrigidos por patches ao longo do tempo e pela própria comunidade modder.
   - **Negativo:** Mesmo assim, alguns problemas persistem, especialmente relacionados à inteligência artificial e à gestão de grandes frotas, com naves que às vezes agem de forma imprevisível. A lentidão e travamentos ocasionais em grandes batalhas também podem frustrar.

#### 5. **Parte Gráfica:**
   - **Visual Geral:** Para a época, "X3: Reunion" impressionou com seus visuais espaciais. O design das naves, planetas e estações espaciais é detalhado e variado, e os efeitos de luzes e sombras nas batalhas espaciais são deslumbrantes.
   - **Positivo:** As naves têm um design variado e as vistas do espaço são verdadeiramente de tirar o fôlego. A sensação de imensidão do espaço é bem capturada, e as explosões são um verdadeiro show.
   - **Negativo:** Embora impressionante para 2005, os gráficos hoje parecem datados. A falta de diversidade nos interiores das estações e a repetitividade de alguns ambientes pode tirar parte do encanto depois de longas horas de jogo.

#### 6. **Trilha Sonora e Efeitos Sonoros:**
   - **Música e Sons:** A trilha sonora de "X3: Reunion" é atmosférica, acompanhando bem a vastidão do espaço e o isolamento que ele proporciona. Os sons de combate e as comunicações entre naves adicionam tensão e emoção.
   - **Positivo:** A música cria a ambientação perfeita, com temas calmos para exploração e faixas mais intensas durante combates. Os efeitos sonoros das batalhas, explosões e comunicações dão uma imersão satisfatória.
   - **Negativo:** A trilha sonora pode se tornar repetitiva depois de longos períodos. Com tanto tempo de gameplay, você provavelmente vai acabar ouvindo as mesmas músicas várias vezes, o que pode diminuir a imersão.

#### 7. **Educação e Complexidade:**
   - **Valor Educacional:** Para quem gosta de economia, estratégia e administração de recursos, o jogo oferece uma verdadeira aula de como gerir complexas cadeias de produção, além de ser um bom exercício de paciência e planejamento estratégico.
   - **Positivo:** "X3: Reunion" pode ensinar muito sobre como funciona uma economia, especialmente a de oferta e demanda. Para fãs de simuladores, é um prato cheio.
   - **Negativo:** O nível de complexidade pode ser um pesadelo para quem não está familiarizado com simuladores desse tipo. A necessidade de aprender tantas mecânicas pode afastar muitos.

#### 8. **Nota Final:**
   - **Nota:** **7.5/10**
   - **Justificativa:** "X3: Reunion" brilha em termos de profundidade e liberdade, especialmente para aqueles que amam simuladores espaciais complexos. Porém, a curva de aprendizado acentuada, a interface complicada e alguns bugs persistentes podem frustrar jogadores que não estejam preparados para investir muito tempo no jogo. É uma experiência densa, mas recompensadora para quem superar seus desafios.

#### 9. **Crítica Geral:**
   - "X3: Reunion" é como aquele professor de física do ensino médio: fascinante, mas pode ser bem complicado e exigente. Ele te joga no fundo do oceano e espera que você aprenda a nadar, o que pode ser encantador ou sufocante, dependendo do seu perfil de jogador. É o tipo de jogo que recompensa planejamento, paciência e estratégia, mas que também pode testar seus limites de tolerância com seus menus complexos e lentidão.

   Se você ama simulação espacial e está disposto a dedicar tempo e esforço para dominar suas complexas mecânicas, vai encontrar um universo cheio de possibilidades e conquistas. Caso contrário, talvez seja melhor procurar por algo mais direto e acessível.

2026年了，还推荐玩x3吗？
我的评价是，是的，但是需要你做到以下几点
1.脾气要好
2.有足够耐心
3.领悟能力很强
好了，如果你满足我说的以上几点，或是在续作x4中建立了造船厂及全产业链，那么我相信你能够品鉴x3的全部内容
第一个问题，重聚，地球人冲突，阿尔比恩序曲，这仨有什么区别?
答：这仨按时间线顺序展开，但是互相独立，其中阿尔比恩序曲是地球人冲突的资料片，类似于红色警戒2与尤里复仇的关系，你建立的存档也是三游戏互不相通，我建议新人直接去玩阿尔比恩序曲，其时间线最靠后，内容最丰富。
第二个问题，为什么我上面需要你做到那三点?
首先从保存说起，保存只能停靠空间站或者购买消耗品救命保险才可以，如果飞了好长时间但是坠机了，那只能重头再来了。
接下来就是碰撞伤害的问题，x3中碰撞伤害极高，如果你不小心与小行星、空间站、更大的船只发生剐蹭，尽管是轻轻贴上去，你的小船会瞬间爆炸，所以不要与任何东西贴贴，在建设空间站是也是如此，一定，不要，穿模，如果你本人不在星区内，这样不会计算碰撞伤害。
再接着是攻略问题，深度时空网站已于2026年初关站，因此x3的大量攻略属于意识状态，仅有贴吧和github上的少量留档（想要的可以dd我），mod或者说脚本也是如此。
然后是游戏几乎为0的新手引导，光是玩家可以选装的软件就有十级种，每种软件功效又只能自行体验，甚至是跨星区贸易、命令飞船靠港等行为都需要特定软件完成，十分复杂，这里我不得不批评ego当年的小巧思，复杂的东西太多，看似硬核实际上十分劝退的机制，甚至地球人冲突的某个任务里还有做数独……
在舰队建设和空间站建设方面，也是无比繁琐，每种武器、每种导弹都需要单独空间站生产，搭起全产业链需要花费你巨量时间，甚至生产一艘战列舰也需要2天10小时，开了十倍加速也需要你挂机四个小时，毫无疑问，这是一个极长线的游戏。
如果你只是想体验，那么去买NPC的武器也可以，但是作为长线游戏，NPC生产武器也是论小时记，无论怎么样，在不开挂不抢船的情况下需要很长时间才能配好一艘m2。

坏的说完了，接下来是x3的优点
首先，比起x4各家孱弱的武器和飞船，x3时代的各国可谓武德充沛，一艘m2身上40多根炮是正常情况，冲入敌阵光翼展开（窝窝屎德战belike），但同样的，你也可能会被对面走过来的导弹鱼雷激光打飞（bushi）
其次，本作各种武器各种导弹丰常丰富，提供了很多的战术选择，舰船类型也十分丰富，从航母m1到驱逐（战列）舰m2，再到护卫（巡洋）舰m7，再到护卫艇（m6），重战机（m3）拦截机（m4）侦察机（m5）轰炸机（m8）。
当你真正入迷，开着小飞机跑商揽任务买到了心仪已久的更强大的座驾，回过头把曾经欺负自己的小飞机踩死的时候，成就感是无与伦比的，这也是太空游戏吸引人的点，都想更高更快更强。
最后是个题外话，本作和浴火银河2的各种内容有很多相似之处，比如等级越高报酬越高的任务，买了武器之后需要在飞船面板安装，跳跃引擎需要充能，可以看出00年代老一辈太空游戏的思路，不过即使x3作为端游的，难度也是太高了，这也是为什么本系列一直不温不火的原因。
作为一个x3x4都有涉猎的玩家，也许我用现在的眼光批判x3过于苛求，但玩了x3我也知道了制作组在x4里做出的让步，武器改为用材料在配装范围内手搓，空间站可以存放大量模块，飞船建造时间的缩短，航母下属丢失可以直接下单建造等等，不过我依然希望未来的x5有着x3般的内容，x4般简化（相对于x3）的游戏流程与等待时间。

Do you like any kind of tutorialization at all in your game? Do you like games that actually give you ways to figure out how get the tools you need to complete the missions it starts throwing at you before penalizing you for failing them? Do you like missions that aren't mathematically impossible to complete, or that actually give you some way of knowing whether or not they're doable before you accept them? Do you like ship retrieval missions where the ship you're retrieving is actually fast enough to be capable of getting where it needs to go before the hour-long timer expires? Do you like assassination missions where it is actually possible to reach your target in the fastest ship you can get before the timer runs down? Or, if the game does throw impossible jobs at you, you like being able to turn down or cancel the mission without penalty once you realize your ship can only cross two sectors in the time you've been given and the target is four sectors away?

Do you like being able to hit the broad side of a barn without finding and buying an upgrade we don't tell you you need and then also don't tell you how to turn on? What about games where you're actually able to have some idea of who's shooting at you and which direction the damage is coming from? And how about games where, if a single missile is instant death even with your ship fully upgraded, we actually give you a way to reliably target the missile and shoot it down instead of having to keep cycling through every enemy ship in the sector before maybe it decides to take pity on you and highlight the incoming doom before you have to reload your prior save yet again?

Do you like games about managing vast remote trading fleets where your giant maxed-out freighters *don't* lose all their shields and die to a handful of light fighters before the "Alert, ship under attack" announcement even finishes playing? How about games about buying and upgrading ships where there are actually guns available to buy, and they're not permanently sold out at every single equipment dock in the galaxy so no matter how hard you look you're stuck with the same two laser cannons that your starting ship comes with forever? Do you like your merchant sims to contain people who will actually *buy* the things you've purchased that are currently taking up freight space as you cross the whole galaxy searching for anyone who will take it off your hands?

Do you like games where the gamepad bindings actually stick, and don't have to be manually rebound every single time you load a save just to be capable of basic menu navigation?

Do you like mandatory progression missions to be completable without needing to use debug tools provided by development as the actual, officially-recommended path through the main questline? If you do have to use the official debug tool, would you like it to *do anything* to fix the blocker that they published it specifically to fix?

Well too bad, we don't do any of that here.

I had been searching for a game in which I could relax and chill out, preferably with my own set of music, and I was fed up with my usual go-to games for this purpose. I needed something else entirely. That was the moment when I remembered I had a game exactly for that. Flying in space. That's the stuff! The X3 game for relaxing purposes? Insane, isn't it? Well, I'm not swayed that easily. Yeah, I was in the past, but not this time.

It was... HELLA GRINDY! Absolutely confusing. I was pushed into infinite-universe dark waters without any understanding of what to do or how to do it. The learning curve is bonkers! Never in my life have I been so lost. Or was I? Yes, I suppose I was lost at the start of my gaming journey, when everything was so fresh and unknown. Just like in this game. Learn how to swim or drown, and failure wasn't an option.

Despite its age and a terrible learning curve that put my many previous games to shame, the game itself was absolutely brilliant! The sandbox aspect is phenomenal. It can blend into whatever game you want: a Space Truck Simulator, a space combat game, an economy simulator, a strategy game, a taxi game, and even an idle game! Basically, whatever space-something you prefer.

The X universe has vast lore! Sadly, the plot is not backing it up and is serviceable at best. Which is a shame. The premise for the first Terran campaign involving political intrigues and rogue artificial intelligence was mildly interesting. It took me 30 hours to finish, and there are at least 5 more? The world IS actually living, and being a part of it is so fun. Something is always happening in the universe!

Starting with one ship and building your own trading empire with a huge trading fleet. Getting ahead of your trading competitors by mere seconds gets your heart pumping so hard. Exploration, and I don't mean in the usual sense. I found out about JumpDrive only after 48 hours. That'll certainly put my competitors to shame! Building your factories and flying on patrol missions with your boys. There's so much more to explore even after 95 hours. It's a great time sink. And you know what? The more you break into the game's complexities, the more addictive it becomes. And it's only the vanilla game! I still haven't tried Albion Prelude, which improves the game drastically. There's a huge modding community! It's scary. I didn't expect it to turn out like this!

After a long reflection, I can finally write a review on this game.
2000 hours on a single player game, how is that possible?

It wasn't until 20 hours into the game that I found the game inside this game, the realization that I can own every ship I see.
There was also a lot of research into the game while I was having lunch at work, first smartphone, browsing the x3tc wiki, while in line at a Chinese takeout (also realizing I will never have to wait again, I will always be able todo something while  in line).

Due to the mod like development, many feature where hidden behind strange menu choices, not obvious to discover. This added a lot of excitement. Any normal developer would have would have highlighted new features, would have shown their work. But that would have spoiled the discovery.

So, I boarded my first Hyperion maybe 200 hours into the game? Again, part of the excitement was the research to figure it out.

Building my first 22 station mega complex... then sitting there and wondering: "How do I turn this thing on?", did not roll over by itself, so awesome.

Someone said this game changes from a first person shooter to a spreadsheet game, they're not wrong. Macroing the traders, in your trade empire, is a whole new game in itself.

Collecting all the ships and.... Hunting for the Aran, I was hallucinating seeing a ship in a sea of asteroids, finally found it. It did not blow up, I was lucky. Later I shot it with a repair laser and had better marines. Even space walked it once from a Hyperion (or was that in X3AP?)

Then the Perma Death plan. Getting a UPC so the PC power would stay up, removed unneeded Windows services that could interrupt the game play, no windows update plz. Played a normal game in parallel with the Perma Death game, so I could practice the next steps, take notes. I do not count attempts that ended in under 24 hours. First run ended after 400 hours, with 6 main missions done, my Boreas appeared inside a Tyr after I went through a gate in Terran space. I took 6 months off. Second try, now with satellites at every gate in Terran space, I managed to grab the achievement.

The final act was reversing the WAD file, pulling all the sector data into a html/js file. I kinda knew I'm done playing, because now I'm peeking behind the curtain. Funny note, some asteroids have duplicates, that explained why I could not tow one of my mines.

I don't think the experience I got from this game could be replicated today. The was a multitude of website that supported this game (at the time, for me): X3TC wiki, x3tc.ru sector map (now .net), Roguey guides, Wolfsburgs complex calculator, Seizewell community and of course the developers boards.

TL;DR a game should hold features back, hide them from the player, allow for surprising discovery. Allow for research outside the game.

[h1][b] Reseña de X3: Terran Conflict[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
X3: Terran Conflict es ese simulador espacial sandbox donde te sueltan en el vacío con una nave, una economía que no te debe nada y la dulce promesa de “haz lo que quieras”… que en realidad significa: “aprende sistemas, administra, comercia, pelea, explora y no llores”. Es Acción, Simulación y Estrategia en un mismo coctel, pero servido en vaso grande y sin instrucciones amables.

La primera impresión es clara: esto no quiere ser tu amigo, quiere ser tu jefe. Puedes pasar de piloto mercenario a magnate corporativo intergaláctico montando rutas de comercio, estaciones y flotas, mientras el universo sigue moviéndose. Es un mundo abierto espacial con mentalidad 4X, donde el capitalismo no es una mecánica… es una religión.

Y sí: es atmosférico, tiene exploración, administración y esa vibra de “si te equivocas, el juego te mira y sigue como si nada”. En resumen: libertad total… con consecuencias totales.

[h2]Lo Bueno y lo No Tan Bueno (Versión: “Imperio Galáctico vs. Manual Inexistente”)[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Sandbox espacial enorme: exploración, comercio y combate con sensación real de “universo vivo”.  
  Economía y comercio con sabor a “MBA en el espacio”: rutas, producción y ganancias que enganchan.  
  Compatibilidad total con mando: sorprendentemente útil para volar y sobrevivir sin contorsionismo.  
  Steam Cloud + Préstamo familiar: tu imperio y tus malas decisiones te siguen a donde vayas.  
  Gran banda sonora y atmósfera: cuando estás perdido, al menos suena épico.

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Curva de aprendizaje: el juego te enseña a base de “descúbrelo o muere”, y ni se inmuta.  
  Estrategia/gestión puede sentirse como trabajo: administrar flotas y estaciones no siempre es “diversión”, a veces es oficina.  
  Voces y narrativa: cumplen, pero no esperes una ópera espacial; a ratos es más “trámite” que drama.  
  Acción con fricción: el combate puede ser satisfactorio, pero no siempre se siente tan fino como uno quisiera.  
  Comunidad activa baja (33 jugadores): hay recomendaciones, sí, pero el bar está casi vacío.

[h2]Conclusión (Excelente)[/h2]
X3: Terran Conflict es el tipo de juego que te da libertad real: puedes ser un piloto de combate, un comerciante obsesivo, un administrador de estaciones o el CEO más despiadado del sector. Y ahí está lo controversial: su “diversión” muchas veces se parece sospechosamente a trabajar… pero con naves y sin recursos humanos.

¿Vale la pena hoy? Con 2061 recomendaciones totales, está claro que hizo escuela y que mucha gente lo considera una joya del sandbox espacial. Pero con 33 jugadores actuales, también se nota que no es precisamente el antro de moda: esto es más un club de veteranos que un fenómeno masivo.

Si te atrae el espacio, la economía, la exploración y la estrategia con mentalidad de imperio, es una experiencia potente. Si necesitas que el juego te lleve de la manita y te premie cada 5 minutos, este universo te va a cobrar peaje.

review:
Egosoft is 12 german dudes in a trenchcoat who love space as a concept first and design games as a distant afterthought. Lots of 'vibes' here. Cool background music and great ship designs to drool over. The actual gameplay is passable at best. 
Like Bethesda games you'll need to install some extra shit to make it playable:
First is the bonus pack. You can find in the DLC section on steam or from the Egosoft website directly.
Then there is the vanilla safe mod list: Egosoft forum topic 278257 
There is a great steam guide for this game all about modding the game without getting the modded tag. To check in game you look at the bottom of your pilot stats for yellow text, if it's not there then you're good.

With that said. I really cannot suggest actually trying to do the plots in this version of the game. They are like pulling teeth. Playing X without the station building script is agony. You get that script with the default bonus pack in the next game, Albion Prelude. That script alone is why I would suggest AP over TC any day. 

So if you're going to play TC, then forget achievements and instal the station builder script.

Immersive sand box-esque space sim, build a galactic merchant fleet or become an ace pilot hunting xenon across the known galaxy. Heavy time sink's assigned to some achievements. Dead is dead requires you to play defensively, as your save is loaded into cloud & is deleted on death. Download the free DLC is a must! 8/10

The absolute gold standard when it comes to autistic sandbox space sims, if that is what you fancy then look no further!

I feel it is on par with the likes of Oxygen not included, Factorio, Kerbal Space Program and the like, even if they are a totally different genres, in a sense that they allow you to do super complex stuff that takes a lot of knowledge about all the various systems these games offer, planning and preparation beforehand, and it is so goddamn rewarding to actually get stuff done lol

I've been playing this game on and off since it came out almost 20 years ago and i can safely say it is one of the most difficult games to fully master, but one that gives a back a LOT when you do.

A true diamond for sure, albeit a rough one.

There are stations that can form whole production complexes, a huuuge galaxy of many sectors that has a whole simulated economy, an ultra complex logistics system that you can set up and let loose, with hundreds of ships that ferry goods all over the place, like mining resources, feeding your factories, hauling stuff to be sold or to be stashed for later, or to be used to make more ships, or weapons to outfit these ships, and so on and so forth.

Also there's like epic space battles and stuff, a handful of different story campaigns, exploration, factions, pirates, you name it X3 got it.

But again, and this is really important - it is very hard to get into.

All in all - i love it, easy 11/10 on my scale, one of the greats, no doubt about it.

Terran Conflict is a game that allows you to enjoy the entirety of what space games have to offer, from the largest scale to the smallest. The learning curve is steep, but the rewards are endless. A real-time economy and combat simulation for *every single entity in the game* goes on while you explore, perform contracts, and purchase more ships and stations. The options are limitless.

In no specific order, you can play this game as if it was:
A pure space combat game, with enough diversity of builds to keep you doing optimizations forever
An exploration game, for the people who just love the gorgeous art direction and aesthetics
A story driven game, with at minimum 5 lore heavy plots and a fascinating setting to dive into
A space trucking simulator, for those who just want to see the money numbers rise
And for those who like it all, a real-time 4X game where you can build your own company, transport network, and command the flagship of an entire fleet performing operations to improve that company

The main attraction to this is that you have *complete authority* on how you want to play this game, what aspects interest you, and the game's systems support every playstyle to a degree that it's hard to get bored if you're pursuing your own desires. All in all, if you like space games of any type, you will be ale to enjoy X3TC as long as you invest the time into learning it's systems.
