The game is good, but it takes up a lot of time. Time, specifically, which is not particularly engaging. A lot of it is gonna be spent flying around in space from one destination to the other, and it's gonna be especially aggravating whilst playing the story, which is going to be mostly nothing but flying to places (with a few interesting events), and will require you to get larger (and therefore slower) ships to progress in a meaningful way. You can start on the story initially, but I would highly suggest exploring the sandbox portion first until you've acquired funds and or better ships, or both, depending on how much of a pirate you arr.

In addition to this, save judiciously. This game has a few bugs, but the ones which are there can be catastrophic, and will cost you hours of flying around in space. Such bugs include but are not limited to: Certain questlines breaking for no reason, one of your ships crashing into you under the follow command, and autopilot deciding that your continued existence is not necessary to reach it's destination. You also cannot save on the fly unless you're in a station or have a stockpile of items called "salvage insurance", which makes it really hard to actually keep up to date saves unless you ping pong across stations.

There's a really large time investment here, unprecedented for a singleplayer game, not all of it is gonna be interactive. In a way, it's a bit like life. When you do get somewhere, it's very gratifying, but there are tons of risks along the way.

X3: Terran Conflict is a sprawling space simulation and trading game that stands out for its ambitious scale and intricate depth, offering a truly immersive experience for fans of open-ended sci-fi sandbox games. Developed by Egosoft, this title is part of the long-running X series, and it refines and expands upon the core mechanics that have defined the franchise for years. Released on Steam, X3: Terran Conflict invites players to lose themselves in a vast universe filled with dynamic economies, complex politics, and massive fleets, blending space combat, trading, and exploration in a way that few games can match.

At its heart, X3: Terran Conflict offers unparalleled freedom. Players begin with a single small ship and a basic understanding of the universe, but from there, the game opens up into a seemingly endless playground of possibilities. Whether you want to become a trader amassing wealth by buying and selling goods across star systems, a feared pirate commanding fleets and raiding convoys, or an empire builder constructing massive stations and managing resources, the game gives you the tools to carve your own path. This freedom is both exhilarating and daunting—the steep learning curve can be a barrier to entry, but the reward for patience is a richly detailed and reactive universe that responds meaningfully to your actions.

One of the standout features of X3: Terran Conflict is its incredibly detailed economic and faction systems. Each star system has its own economy, complete with factories producing goods, trading stations, and fluctuating supply and demand. Players can influence these economies by trading, investing, or even sabotaging competitors, making the universe feel alive and interconnected. Factions have their own agendas and relationships with one another, and your standing with each affects how they treat you. Aligning yourself with one faction can open doors to unique missions and technologies but may also invite hostility from rivals, adding layers of political intrigue to the gameplay.

Combat in X3: Terran Conflict is both tactical and satisfying. Ship-to-ship engagements range from small skirmishes to large-scale fleet battles, requiring players to manage shields, weapons, and positioning carefully. The variety of ship classes—from nimble fighters to massive capital ships—allows for diverse combat strategies, and the game rewards players who take the time to upgrade and customize their vessels. While combat can be challenging, especially against tougher enemies or in hostile territories, it rarely feels unfair. Instead, it encourages players to learn enemy patterns and optimize their loadouts, adding a layer of depth that complements the game’s strategic elements.

Visually, the game’s graphics may feel dated compared to more recent space sims, but the detailed ship models, colorful starfields, and varied station designs still convey a convincing and immersive sci-fi universe. The sound design, including an atmospheric soundtrack and dynamic combat noises, further enhances the experience, immersing players in the vastness of space. While the UI can feel cluttered and overwhelming at first, especially given the game’s complexity, it is functional and improves with familiarity, offering detailed information on everything from ship status to market conditions.

The storyline of X3: Terran Conflict is relatively light compared to the game’s sandbox elements but provides a solid framework that introduces players to the universe and its key factions, especially focusing on the Terran faction, humanity’s role in the galaxy, and their struggle to carve out a place among alien civilizations. The campaign missions are well-crafted and often challenging, serving as a useful guide to the game’s mechanics while also telling an engaging sci-fi tale. However, many players will likely spend most of their time in the open sandbox, creating their own stories and objectives.

One of the biggest challenges of X3: Terran Conflict is its learning curve. Newcomers may find the sheer volume of systems, controls, and economic intricacies intimidating. However, the game’s depth is also its greatest strength; for those willing to invest time, it offers one of the most rewarding and complex space simulations available. The community has also created numerous mods and quality-of-life improvements, which can help smooth the experience and add even more content, further extending the game’s lifespan.

In conclusion, X3: Terran Conflict is a monumental space simulation that delivers a rich, detailed, and expansive universe for players to explore, conquer, and influence. Its blend of trading, combat, and empire management, coupled with a dynamic economic system and faction politics, creates a living galaxy that feels both vast and responsive. While it demands patience and dedication to master, the depth and freedom it offers are unmatched in the genre. For players looking to immerse themselves in a complex, open-ended sci-fi sandbox with endless possibilities, X3: Terran Conflict remains a definitive and enduring choice.

Personally, I played this as a nostalgic time piece from my childhood. I never understood what the game really was as a very young kid. I was like 3 when it released probably 5 or 6 when I first played it. It captivated me and was a favorite for my brother and I growing up. 

That said, I don't think this game is for most people. Some things are very frustrating, like when you shoot your weapons your ship straight up has a seizure. It's so bad that by the end, when you've got good shields installed, it's almost better just to ram your ship into the enemy's ship just to destroy them. Not fun. The sim portion is very easily exploitable and you're basically just waiting for the credit numbers to go up by using SETA (a time warp device) to speed up the process. I had around 5 million credits by the end which is way more than anyone needs in a playthrough. Once you enough money to outfit your ship with the best weapons and shields, all there is left to do is complete the story, which is very short and not very engaging. To top it off, the last stretch of the story has you waiting on a painfully slow ship to return home. Again, you're basically just passing time using SETA until it reaches home.

This pretty much only exists as a piece of nostalgia for those of us who played it back in the day. You're better off watching a Let's Play on YouTube if you're legitimately interested in it for some reason. I love it and I'm glad I finally checked this game off the list of ones I never completed as a kid.

[h1][b] Reseña de X: Beyond the Frontier[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
X: Beyond the Frontier es ese simulador espacial con alma de hoja de cálculo que decidió ponerse una capa de “estrategia” y llamarse aventura. Aquí no vienes a “ganar”: vienes a sobrevivir, comerciar, explorar y aprender a volar mientras el universo te mira con cara de “¿y tú quién te crees?”. Es un sandbox de ciencia ficción donde el progreso se siente más como una inversión a largo plazo que como una misión heroica.

La propuesta es clara: pilotaje, economía, intercambios y expansión en un mundo abierto espacial. La primera impresión es una mezcla de fascinación y sospecha: fascinación por la libertad de exploración, y sospecha porque el juego te suelta con esa energía de “no hay tutorial, hay carácter”.

[h2]Motores al 100%: Lo que despega y lo que se estrella[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
 Libertad tipo sandbox: exploras y te metes en problemas por decisión propia   
 Economía e intercambios con enfoque estratégico: aquí el “grindeo” se disfraza de empresariado espacial   
 Sensación de mundo abierto real: el espacio se siente grande, y tú te sientes pequeño (como debe ser)   
 Ideal para quien disfruta simuladores espaciales: vuelo, gestión y exploración en un mismo paquete   

Lo No Tan Bueno:
 Cero logros: Steam no te aplaude ni cuando respiras, y eso duele más de lo que debería   
 Comunidad muy baja (3 jugadores actuales): si buscas conversación, el vacío del espacio te responde primero   
 Curva de aprendizaje exigente: el juego te entrena a base de golpes, no de cariño   
 Enfoque de “acción” más circunstancial: si vienes por adrenalina constante, te vas a quedar administrando paciencia

[h2]Conclusión ([Muy Bueno])[/h2]
X: Beyond the Frontier es como ese clásico exigente que no te pide permiso para volverte su empleado. Si amas los simuladores y la estrategia económica en el espacio, aquí hay una experiencia con identidad: exploración, vuelo y progresión tipo “hazlo funcionar o muere intentando”. Es entretenido… si tu idea de diversión incluye administrar decisiones y aprender sistemas.

Ahora, la parte controversial: con 3 jugadores actuales, este universo se siente más deshabitado que la vida social de un trader intergaláctico. Aun así, las 278 recomendaciones totales sugieren que el juego se ganó su lugar en el nicho. ¿Vale la pena? Sí, si eres de los que disfrutan el sandbox espacial y no necesitas que Steam te dé una estrellita por cada logro inexistente.

I never thought that I would spend 61 hours playing a game from 1999. It has quite a unique and tedious gameplay (I think the only proper way to play this game is with pen and paper). But that unique gameplay is what makes this game special. This is the definitely among one of the best games I've ever played.

 By the way, if you think this is a game about spaceships and battles then be assured: it is not. Personally I made a mistake thinking this is a game about spaceships and battles, but I don't regret making it.

It is a space docking sim. If you want to drive around a space ship, fight some other space ships while you try and make money in a space station economy, this game is for you. It has lots of "hurry up and wait" in 15-30s chunks but it still got enough fun it to begin with.

Die Urwiege des X-Universums. Dieses Spiel ist wirklich nur was für Core-Fans oder Nostalgiker. Der Spielstart gehört mit Abstand zu den langwierigsten und schwierigsten überhaupt. Wer sich davon aber nicht abschrecken lässt, der lernt ein Stück deutsche Videospielgeschichte kennen. Die Einflüsse ziehen sich durch die ganze Reihe bis hin ins aktuelle Spiel X4 Foundations. In diesem Urspiel kann man leider nur auf das Xperimental Shuttle zurück greifen. Das heißt ihr fliegt hier wirklich das ganze Spiel über in ein und demselben Schiff. Die Weltraumschlachten sind dementsprechend auch eher verhalten und ohne viel Abwechslung. Das ist aber gar nicht weiter schlimm. Die eigentliche Stärke des Spiels liegt in seiner Wirtschaftssimulation. Damit verbringt man auch die Hauptzeit im Spiel. Es werden neue Fabriken gebaut, man muss Nachfrage & Angebot bedienen und langsam aber sicher steigt man zum Herrscher über das ganze Universum auf. Egosoft hat hier etwas erschaffen das bis heute Einzigartig in seiner Form ist. Darum läuft auch das aktuelle Spiel X4 völlig ohne Konkurrenz und wird trotz des inzwischen hohen Alters weiterhin kräftig gespielt!

Recommended for fans of the X-Universe or anyone who enjoys chill trading sims.

X: Beyond the Frontier is definitely showing its age. The graphics are old, the UI is clunky, and you’re stuck with a single ship for the entire game. But once you settle in, it becomes a surprisingly relaxing trading and factory building experience.

You start with basically nothing and slowly trade your way up, upgrading your one ship until it becomes a real powerhouse. The core loop will feel familiar if you’ve played later X games: buying low, selling high, filling economic gaps, and building a few stations. But everything here is much more manual. There’s no galaxy map, no property menu, and very little automation. The economy is simpler, and you'll most likely only ever build a handful of factories. 

One big thing worth mentioning: this game comes from an era when reading the manual and readme was expected. There are controls, mechanics, and bits of guidance documented there that never appear in‑game. Spending a few minutes with those files makes the early hours much smoother.

I played on both my desktop and Legion Go handheld. Cloud saves worked perfectly, and binding keyboard controls to a controller made it easy to play on the couch or in bed.

I mainly played this to see how the series began, and the storyline was worth the trip. Combat is basic and limited, so most of the experience is trading and light factory management, which made it easy to unwind with after a long day.

If you’re a fan of the X-Universe and want to experience the series’ origins or if you enjoy slow, methodical trading games with a bit of factory building than X:BTF is a neat little time capsule that’s still worth playing.

В целом, если не ставить себе целей наиграть 100500 часов и строить какие-то глобальные империи, то всё очень-очень круто. Как раз потихоньку получается наладить торговлю, собрать хороший корабль, закрыть сюжетку, да и, собственно, и всё.

Завязка сюжета восхитительна: минимальное обучение по нажатию на кнопочки управления кораблём и вас телепортирует в неизвестный космос. Там вас встречает станный пришелец на огромном корабле, который радует вас тем, что установил на ваш корабль щит, чтобы вы не погибли. Теперь вы должны ему за это 3500 кредитов(вы вообще не понимаете где вы и что такое "кредиты"). Осчастливив вас долгом, он даёт вам 100 кредитов и отправляет "торговать", чтобы этот долг выплатить. Всё. С этого момента вы сами по себе и должны найти дорогу домой, на Землю.

С управлением нужно немножко освоиться. Навигация по меню и т.д. своеобразна. Количество удобств в игре минимально. Например, нет ни нормального журнала квестов, ни характеристик оружия, ни карты секторов. Я карту честно рисовал себе сам. Всё это ни коим образом не считаю минусами, т.к. это не новодел для жертв тиктока, а настоящая качественная старая игра.

К сожалению, большую часть игры играл на клавиатуре, т.к. старые джойстики за много лет начали плохо себя чувствовать. Наличие хорошего джойстика(не гейпада) добавит удобства игры и погружения.

В целом, от игры нет никаких эмоций, кроме крайне позитивных. Считаю, что тем, кто смог распробовать этот шедевр в начале 2000х, очень и очень повезло. X: Beyond the Frontier, developed and published by Egosoft, marks the beginning of a long-running space simulation series that would go on to define a particular niche of sandbox-driven, economy-focused gameplay. Released at the end of the 1990s, it arrived at a time when space simulators were either heavily combat-oriented or fading in popularity. Instead of following the fast-paced dogfighting model of many contemporaries, X: Beyond the Frontier chose a slower, more methodical path, emphasizing trading, economic systems, and open-ended exploration. The result is a game that feels less like a traditional action title and more like a living simulation of a complex interstellar society.

The narrative premise is straightforward but effective. Players assume the role of Kyle Brennan, a test pilot who becomes stranded in an unfamiliar region of space after an experimental jump drive malfunctions. Cut off from Earth and without immediate means of return, he must survive and adapt within a network of alien-controlled star systems. This setup provides context, but the story never aggressively dictates the pace of play. Instead, it functions as a loose thread woven into a much larger sandbox. The player is free to pursue narrative objectives or ignore them entirely, carving out their own path through commerce, exploration, and gradual expansion.

The true heart of X: Beyond the Frontier lies in its economic model. Each star system contains stations and factories that produce and consume specific resources, creating a dynamic supply-and-demand network. Players can buy goods where they are abundant and cheap, then transport them to sectors where they are scarce and valuable. Over time, profits allow for ship upgrades, better equipment, and eventually the construction of player-owned factories that generate income autonomously. This progression transforms the experience from a lone pilot scraping together credits into a budding industrial magnate influencing entire trade routes. The economic layer is surprisingly deep for its era, demanding attention to market fluctuations and logistical efficiency.

Combat exists but is not the primary focus. Encounters with pirates or hostile factions can occur, and upgrading shields and weapons becomes necessary for survival. However, dogfighting lacks the arcade immediacy found in more action-oriented space games. Battles tend to feel deliberate rather than frantic, reinforcing the broader theme that preparation and investment are more important than reflexes alone. In many cases, avoiding conflict or building enough economic power to outpace threats proves more rewarding than direct confrontation. This design choice underscores the simulation-driven philosophy at the game’s core.

Exploration plays a significant role in shaping the player’s journey. The universe is composed of numerous interconnected sectors linked by jump gates, each with distinct layouts and economic profiles. Discovering new systems often means uncovering fresh trading opportunities or encountering different factions with their own technologies and ships. The scale of the universe fosters a sense of isolation and curiosity, enhanced by ambient sound design and the quiet vastness of space. Unlike tightly scripted games, X: Beyond the Frontier allows long stretches of peaceful travel punctuated by moments of tension, mirroring the rhythms of real commerce and exploration.

Technically and visually, the game reflects its late-1990s origins. Ship models and station designs are simple by modern standards, and the interface can feel clunky to newcomers. Navigating menus, managing cargo, and issuing commands require patience, particularly for players accustomed to streamlined contemporary design. However, beneath the dated presentation lies a robust simulation that rewards dedication. The learning curve is steep, and early hours can feel slow or even confusing. Yet for those willing to invest time, the gradual mastery of systems and accumulation of wealth becomes deeply satisfying.

One of the game’s defining qualities is its emphasis on player autonomy. There are no rigid mission structures forcing progression, no scripted sequences dictating every action. Instead, X: Beyond the Frontier trusts players to set their own goals. Some may focus entirely on trading, others on exploration or incremental military strength. The emergent stories that arise—from narrowly escaping pirate ambushes to watching a newly built factory begin generating profit—often feel more personal and memorable than scripted events.

In retrospect, X: Beyond the Frontier stands as a foundational entry in the space simulation genre. It established the economic and sandbox framework that later entries in the X series would refine and expand upon. While its age is evident in both visuals and interface design, its ambition and systemic depth remain noteworthy. For players who appreciate open-ended progression, complex economic networks, and the quiet satisfaction of building an interstellar enterprise from humble beginnings, it offers a uniquely immersive experience. It is not a game of instant gratification, but rather one of patience, planning, and steady growth in a vast and indifferent universe.

Holds up fairly well despite its age, but I would not recommend it except to fans of Egosoft's X series. Newcomers should probably look at X2 or one of the X3 titles to start with. Those games are of much higher quality, and are a bit less frustratingly cryptic. If you do buy this and get stuck, a walkthrough is included in the game files.

For fans of X though, this game is pretty nice. You get to see how it all started. It has a bit more of an atmosphere than the more recent games (X4, Rebirth). It is also much simpler than later games, which is both a blessing and a curse. Less complexity, but also less to do. You will probably finish the main plot, and then move on to one of the more recent titles.

As for compatibility, despite Egosoft's best efforts this was still made for Windows 9x, and there is only so much they can do. They still patch the game to try and keep it working. But realistically you will need to spend some time debugging in order to get this working on anything newer than Windows 7. Also, you may have issues getting gamepads and joysticks to work. I had no issues with the keyboard or mouse controls.

Ironically, you may actually have an easier time getting this to work on Linux. The game runs out of the box on Proton Experimental as of September 2024, but is prone to crashes, so save often. Also NPC portraits are broken and only display a test pattern. I highly recommend installing GE-Proton. With GE-Proton9-11, the game runs much better and portraits mostly work, although sometimes the wrong portrait will be displayed. Lutris' Wine-GE also works fine and is more stable. Even Lutris' Wine-GE still crashes periodically, so remember to save.

Overall, a very strong showing for a 25 year old game. One of my all-time favorites, even if it is a somewhat niche title.

A fabulous early 3d space trading/economy sim, with some combat elements. The combat is not nuanced, enemy ships will happily fly right into you, and large scale management of your factories is impossible. View it as a prototype or an experiment that was heavily refined in coming years, and you'll respect it more.

Surpassed in most respects by its successors, I recommend playing it through mostly as an exercise in historical appreciation (i.e., you like vintage gaming), or for hardcore X-series fans looking to experience the start of the series themselves. You'll learn the early lore, and playing this game will make it abundantly obvious that X:Rebirth was an attempt to return to the series' origin, however successful or unsuccessful it was.

But right now it is costing me about 1 million credits to upgrade the cargo bay each time.  I would probably need another 20 mil credits to fully upgrade the cargo bay.  I destroyed the Xenon Shipyard in the Unidentified Enemy Sector by hiding inside the open door of the station and getting it down to about 20 percent then nuke time.  I obliterated every single Xenon ship in all the sectors except for of course the ones that spawn in. Ohh... and something interesting after 20 million credits.... you cannot get any more credits... the money just disappears after 20 million.  When you try to transfer more than 20 million to your ship, all the money after 20 million just disappears.   Anyways... here is the most important thing... pressing Shift-J gets you into super S.E.T.A mode.. once you get about 25 engine tunings, your shield doesn't disappear when in super S.E.T.A mode... and once you get to 30 engine tunings, then your shield will recover even in super S.E.T.A mode. In a future where Chat GPT has had enough of everyone's bullsh!t, a lone pilot must trade to save the fate of the universe.

Imagine this:
You're dropped into an alien star system. You don't have anything: no local means of exchange, no technology, no knowledge of even where you are. The only reason you can communicate with aliens at all is because they translated your language out of pure whim. 
You are loaned a pocket change simply because a local fleet commander comes from a species believing in allowing others to take a chance at "profits." 
You have two goals: return the pocket change (at the risk of being disposed of as an unholy contract breaker) and a name of a system "somewhere out there" where "there might be somebody who knows anything about your situation."

That's it. The universe is your oyster. 

Dozens of systems. Dozens of supply chains. Dozens of enemies. 
What you do is up to you. The perfectly polished gameplay is there for you to engage in it. 

When you arrived, dear Brennan, you had nothing, not even shields to protect you from space dust. 
When you finished, oh dear Brennan, you had the world. 
It was not given to you. It was earned by your own tenacity, acumen, flying skills, and patience. 
You weren't born a hero. But you became one.

This game can be broken down into 4 distinct phases:
1. Fish out of water, but Capitalism (Trading Empire Simulator)
2. Docking Computer Any% (Your real-life sanity depends on getting this done)
3. Preparing for Story Missions (You must prepare... with profit)
4. Doing the Story Missions 

As the player, you will spend most of your time in Phase 1 until you are ready to do Phase 3. The bulk of game play is the cargo moving, factory building and supplying, SETA flying trading empire simulator. Even following the guides available, this can get very time consuming. 

This game does have space combat, but it is tuned to be less rewarding than the trading simulator. For its time, the combat is good. Move on to X2 and after for more rewarding space combat scenarios.

That being said, if you want to understand the origins of the X Universe, be the hero, build a scrappy trading empire, or have no problem editing your save to give yourself up to 21 million credits, this game is for you.

Beyond the Frontier offers an interesting first look into the X universe, but is really more a proof of concept than it is an enjoyable experience. While the presentation (for a late '90s game) is rather captivating, the gameplay itself is clunky and underdeveloped. 

Regarding performance. This game will not allow you to play in certain resolutions such as 1440p and has strange UI scaling if you change the resolution beyond the default setting. Performance-wise the game is solid and I managed to keep a stable 120fps throughout my near 50 hours of play, though this would drop to a jarring 30 whenever I had to interact with other characters, something that happens a lot in this game. The audio has some compression though not as bad as some other period games, but mixing issues and cuts occurred infrequently during cutscenes and other bits of dialogue. 

Onto the presentation side of things, the art designs for the ships were mostly distinct and other than in a few cases really sold the scale of the universe being populated by five different alien races. The musical direction here is also pretty good, gives off deep-sea exploration vibes which really start to kick in as you explore neighboring sectors in the first few hours. One more thing to mention is that the CG for the aliens is amazing- there is a grotesqueness to every single creature you meet that makes the effort of exploring the universe all the more rewarding.

I'm not sure I would say Beyond the Frontier is for everyone, though. The first few hours involve tedious grinding for money, sped up by a ship upgrade that effectively lets you speed-hack the game temporarily in exchange for control of your ship. Everything, from travel to trade, and even combat, takes a good amount of time to accomplish. The game records how many hours you would've spent without the time dilation machine, and for me that number was beyond 100. In order to speed these things up you need lots of money, and this is the primary failure of the game's design.

The main way to make money is to build factories that sell goods for you while you fuck around and do better things with your time, not like there's much else to do. The map is ginormous and traveling from one side to another can take up to an hour or more without upgrades. This isn't much of a problem at first since the game is trying to convey a sense of embarking on a great journey, but when it asks you to make the same trek back-to-back so you can talk to a single NPC, it gets old fast. You also can't remotely retrieve money from your factories, you have to fly back to the sector you built them in and land directly on each and every station to collect your cash.

Player convenience, or rather a lack of it, is X: Beyond the Frontier's greatest flaw. It is a chore to play, and this is summed up perfectly by the end section of the very last quest in the game. I won't say what it is, but I will criticize it as an incredibly padded mission for what was clearly supposed to be an exciting conclusion. 

I won't spoil the story but I'll just say that I really just played this game so I'd have some context for the later X games, and I was left very disappointed by what this had to offer. If you're interested in the beginning of the X story line I'd suggest reading the official novel Farnham's Legend instead- it'll save you from a headache and free up time for the hopefully much better X2!

Полноценный ретроспективный обзор на X: Tension помогает понять, почему это дополнение (адд-он) к оригинальной X: Beyond the Frontier 2000 года фанаты жанра считают истинным рождением знаменитой серии космических симуляторов от Egosoft.
В то время как оригинал жестко вел игрока по сюжетной линии и заставлял всю игру летать на одном-единственном корабле, X: Tension полностью перевернула концепцию.
🌌 Игровой процесс и концепция: Абсолютная свобода
Разработчики пошли на смелый шаг: они практически полностью убрали линейный сюжет, оставив игрока наедине с огромной вселенной. Вы снова берете на себя роль пилота Кайла Бреннана, но теперь перед вами — чистокровная «песочница».
Масштабное расширение мира: Количество доступных звездных систем выросло до 90 секторов (было добавлено более 40 новых зон для торговли и войн).
Смена кораблей: Это главное нововведение. Игрок больше не привязан к экспериментальному шатлу. Стало можно покупать, детально настраивать и пилотировать около 40 видов кораблей разных рас — от юрких разведчиков и истребителей до тяжелых грузовых транспортов и огромных кораблей класса TL.
Управление империей и флотом: Появилась развитая система удаленного контроля. Находясь в одном конце галактики, вы можете через карту отдавать приказы своим наемным пилотам, координировать целые торговые флотилии и настраивать работу собственных фабрик.
Абордаж и пиратство: В игру добавили механику катапультирования. Если в бою сильно повредить вражеский или пиратский корабль, испуганный пилот может сдаться и покинуть судно. После этого пустой корабль можно присвоить себе или выгодно продать на верфи.
⚖️ Итог: Кому стоит играть?
X: Tension — это знаковый симулятор, который заложил прочный фундамент для будущих шедевров вроде X3: Reunion и современной X4: Foundations. Игра умудряется сочетать в себе элементы симулятора, экономической стратегии и тактического управления флотом.

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
X: Tension es ese simulador espacial con alma de hoja de cálculo que se disfraza de “estrategia” para que te sientas un almirante… cuando en realidad eres el contador del espacio. Aquí vienes a volar, comerciar, armar tu imperio económico y jugar al sandbox de ciencia ficción donde el universo no te toma de la mano: te empuja por la esclusa de aire y te dice “aprende”.

La primera impresión es clara: mundo abierto, economía, naves y decisiones. Mucha libertad, sí, pero también mucha responsabilidad (y muchas ganas de pausar y preguntarte por qué te metiste en esto). Es un juego para un jugador que premia la paciencia y castiga a los que quieren acción inmediata como si fuera un arcade.

[h2][b]Lo que Te Hace Capitán vs. Lo que Te Hace Renunciar a la Flota[/b][/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Sandbox espacial con libertad real: exploras, vuelas y te armas tu camino sin que el juego te ponga rueditas.  
  Economía y comercio con enfoque serio: si te gusta optimizar rutas y progresión, aquí hay carnita.  
  Ambientación sci‑fi y sensación de “espacio grande”: el mundo abierto se siente amplio y con posibilidades.  
  Steam Cloud: al menos tus decisiones cuestionables se guardan en la nube.  

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Un jugador y punto: si buscabas compañía, te toca hablarle a tu nave (y que te ignore).  
  0 logros: nada como invertir horas para que Steam no te dé ni una palmadita en la espalda.  
  Curva de aprendizaje con vibra de “manual no incluido”: el juego asume que ya naciste sabiendo economía espacial.  
  Acción… pero con prioridades: a veces se siente más “administración con disparos” que acción como tal.

Recommended for fans of the X-Universe or anyone who enjoys open ended trading and empire building.

X-Tension takes the foundation of X: Beyond the Frontier and expands it into a true sandbox. There’s essentially no story here, only random generated missions for trading/combat, and just one actual Story mission that only triggers once you hit a few late game requirements. 

This entry feels much closer to a modern X-Universe game. You get a proper galaxy map, a property menu, the ability to own multiple ships, and almost double the number of sectors compared to X:BTF. It’s a big jump in usability and scale, and I was genuinely impressed by how much they added considering it released only about a year after the first game. The graphics are still old, but noticeably improved.

Everything is more expensive in X-Tension, and factories take longer to become profitable compared to X:BTF. The slower economic ramp actually fits the sandbox, but it’s something to be aware of if you’re coming straight from the first game expecting quick returns. But with SETA time acceleration, I sometimes left the game running while making dinner or running errands and came back a few million credits richer.

Most people recommend skipping straight to X2 for the story, and that was my plan. just a small dip into X-Tension and move on. But I actually got hooked. The gameplay loop is still incredibly addictive, and with fewer mechanics than the newer games, it’s surprisingly relaxing to sit or lie down (I played on my Legion GO a lot, binding the keyboard keys to the controller) and manage your growing trading empire. I started with a handful of remote traders, built out several factory loops, and eventually expanded into a full blown industrial network. I even set myself the personal goal of buying a TL and using it as a makeshift carrier with fighters docked inside.

Combat is still basic, but it’s definitely improved over X:BTF. The overall experience feels smoother, more flexible, and more rewarding as your empire grows.

As with X:BTF, this game comes from an era when reading the manual and readme was expected. There are controls, mechanics, and bits of guidance documented there that never appear in game. Spending a few minutes with those files makes the early hours much smoother.

I did run into issues with Steam Cloud saves switching between my desktop and Legion Go. X-Tension adds five extra save slots, but the Steam Cloud storage limit wasn’t increased to match. Each save is about 10 MB, and the game only has 100 MB of cloud space, so the saves can get out of sync. Keeping your total saves to around nine will probably avoid the problem, also probably won't happen if you only play on one system.

Despite that hiccup, I really enjoyed my time with X-Tension. I ended up completing the late-game story mission that leads into X2 and built a pretty substantial trading empire and combat fleet along the way. If you’re interested in the roots of the X-series sandbox or just want a chill, open ended trading and factory building experience, X-Tension is absolutely worth playing.

X: Tension, developed and published by Egosoft, is a space simulation sandbox that significantly expands upon the framework established in its predecessor, X: Beyond the Frontier. Rather than functioning as a traditional sequel with a tightly scripted campaign, it acts as a large-scale evolution of the original concept, broadening the universe, increasing player freedom, and deepening economic and fleet management systems. The result is a title that prioritizes autonomy and systemic complexity over narrative guidance.

At its core, X: Tension places players in a vast interconnected galaxy composed of dozens of sectors, each governed by dynamic economic rules and populated by diverse factions. Unlike story-driven space games that funnel players toward fixed objectives, this title encourages self-directed progression. You are free to pursue commerce, piracy, bounty hunting, or large-scale economic expansion. The galaxy operates in real time, with goods being produced, transported, and consumed regardless of player involvement. This creates an ecosystem where supply and demand fluctuate organically, rewarding attentive traders who study market trends and identify profitable routes.

One of the most significant improvements over its predecessor is expanded ship accessibility. Players are no longer confined to a single vessel; instead, they can pilot a wide range of ships, from agile fighters to heavy transporters and freighters. Over time, this freedom extends into fleet management and station ownership. Establishing factories and production chains transforms the experience from simple trading into empire building. Constructing and defending your own industrial network adds strategic depth, as economic success must be balanced against threats from hostile factions and pirate activity.

Combat remains an integral but optional component of the experience. Dogfights occur in open 3D space, requiring careful maneuvering and energy management. Hostile factions such as the Xenon present ongoing dangers, particularly in border sectors. However, unlike pure action space shooters, combat here serves as part of a broader sandbox system. You may choose to avoid conflict entirely and focus on commerce, or you may invest heavily in military hardware to dominate contested regions. The game rarely forces a singular approach.

The interface and mechanics reflect the era of its release. Menus are dense and sometimes unintuitive, requiring patience to master. Yet beneath this complexity lies an intricate simulation system that rewards long-term investment. Learning how to manage automated traders, optimize supply chains, and monitor sector maps becomes part of the strategic appeal. The early hours can feel slow and methodical, but as wealth accumulates and fleets expand, the scale of operations grows dramatically.

Visually, X: Tension is unmistakably a product of the early 2000s, with modest ship models and relatively simple environmental textures. However, the sense of scale remains impressive. Vast starfields, distant nebulae, and the quiet hum of space travel create a contemplative atmosphere. Long trade routes and jump gate transitions reinforce the feeling of traversing a living galaxy rather than isolated mission zones. The soundtrack complements this tone with ambient compositions that emphasize exploration and solitude.

Narrative elements are minimal compared to the first game. While there is a loose framework connecting events in the X universe, the emphasis shifts strongly toward sandbox autonomy. Story moments exist primarily to provide context rather than dictate direction. This design philosophy makes the game particularly appealing to players who prefer emergent gameplay over scripted sequences.

Ultimately, X: Tension stands as a foundational entry in the X series that helped define Egosoft’s long-running formula. Its expansive economy, player-driven progression, and open-ended structure laid the groundwork for future installments. Though dated in presentation and occasionally opaque in interface design, it remains a compelling sandbox for players who appreciate deep simulation systems and the freedom to shape their own path through a living galaxy.

Histoire :
X-Tension est une extension de X: Beyond the Frontier, mais elle abandonne en grande partie le fil conducteur scénaristique du jeu de base. Le joueur incarne un pilote, toujours dans l’univers des X, mais cette fois avec une plus grande liberté d’exploration. Il n’y a pas de véritable histoire centrale à suivre, ce qui permet une expérience sandbox pure où vous êtes libre de construire votre empire commercial, devenir un redoutable pirate ou un explorateur. Pour ceux qui apprécient les récits dirigés, l'absence d'une intrigue forte peut être décevante, mais l’aspect immersif de la liberté offerte compense largement.

Gameplay :
Le gameplay de X-Tension repose sur une expérience spatiale ouverte où vous pouvez vous adonner à diverses activités telles que le commerce, le combat, et l'exploration. Vous pouvez désormais piloter plusieurs types de vaisseaux, ce qui offre une grande variété dans l'approche des missions ou des affrontements. Le jeu reprend la mécanique de base de X: Beyond the Frontier avec une amélioration notable des systèmes économiques et des mécaniques de gestion de flotte. L'univers est vaste, avec des dizaines de secteurs à explorer, chacun rempli de stations, de vaisseaux et d’opportunités commerciales. Cependant, la courbe d'apprentissage est assez raide, et les joueurs qui recherchent une prise en main rapide pourraient être découragés par la complexité du système économique et la gestion des vaisseaux. La liberté est énorme, mais le manque de direction peut rendre certaines sessions de jeu un peu vagues ou répétitives.

Graphismes :
Pour un jeu sorti en 2000, les graphismes de X-Tension étaient impressionnants à l’époque, avec des environnements spatiaux vastes et des modèles de vaisseaux détaillés. Toutefois, avec les années, les visuels ont pris un coup de vieux, surtout en comparaison avec les standards actuels. Les stations spatiales, bien que fonctionnelles, sont assez basiques dans leur design, et les arrière-plans stellaires manquent parfois de détails. Cela dit, l'immersion est toujours présente grâce à la diversité des systèmes stellaires et aux effets de lumière qui, bien que datés, parviennent à créer une atmosphère unique. Des mods et des paramètres d'affichage peuvent aider à améliorer l'expérience visuelle, mais il est évident que le jeu montre son âge.

Difficulté :
X-Tension est un jeu difficile à maîtriser, surtout pour les nouveaux venus dans les simulations spatiales. Les commandes sont complexes, la gestion des ressources demande une attention constante, et le jeu ne tient pas la main du joueur. Le côté sandbox ajoute une dimension d'exploration libre, mais cela peut parfois laisser le joueur un peu perdu sans direction claire. Les combats spatiaux nécessitent de bonnes compétences de pilotage et de gestion des systèmes d'armes, et le commerce demande de comprendre les subtilités du marché galactique pour en tirer profit. La courbe d'apprentissage est donc raide, mais pour les amateurs de simulation spatiale hardcore, la satisfaction vient avec le temps et la persévérance.

Durée de vie :
En termes de contenu, X-Tension propose des centaines d’heures de jeu potentiel. C’est un véritable bac à sable où vous pouvez choisir de vous concentrer sur le commerce, la conquête ou simplement l'exploration de l'univers. Il n'y a pas de fin claire, ce qui signifie que vous pouvez passer autant de temps que vous le souhaitez à développer votre flotte ou à découvrir de nouveaux secteurs. Pour les joueurs qui apprécient les expériences ouvertes avec beaucoup de liberté, X-Tension est une mine d’or. Cependant, sans véritable objectif final ou progression narrative, certains joueurs peuvent trouver que la motivation diminue après avoir exploré la plupart des mécaniques du jeu.

Prix (en solde) :
X-Tension est régulièrement proposé à un prix très bas lors des soldes Steam, souvent à moins de 5 euros. À ce prix, c'est un excellent choix pour les amateurs de simulations spatiales ou ceux qui souhaitent découvrir les racines de la série X. Même à plein tarif, le jeu reste abordable et offre un excellent rapport contenu/prix pour sa taille et sa profondeur, surtout si vous appréciez les jeux de gestion et de commerce dans un cadre spatial.

Conclusion :
X-Tension est une extension qui donne aux joueurs une liberté presque totale dans un vaste univers spatial. Bien que l'absence d'une histoire centrale puisse désorienter certains, la profondeur de l'expérience de simulation, le commerce et les combats spatiaux compensent largement. Si vous recherchez une simulation spatiale open world complexe, avec une bonne dose de gestion et d'exploration, ce jeu offre une expérience riche et captivante. C'est une recommandation forte, surtout à prix réduit, pour les fans de jeux de gestion et d’exploration spatiale à la recherche d'une immersion totale dans l'univers des X.

Excellent follow-up to the first game. However, this is more of a game for fans of Egosoft's X-series. For newbies, I recommend looking at X2, or one of the X3 titles. With that being said, this is WAY more accessible than the first game, with an enormous number of useful features being added.

This game is very light on plot, so some players may pass it over if they prefer a more story-driven game. There is exactly one plotline, which is unlocked fairly late (you need good relations with the Paranid) and which is quite difficult, so you will want to take your time and expand your resources before starting it.

There are some annoyances. Viewing sectors that you are not in REQUIRES a navsat in that sector. This also goes for using the jumpdrive and ordering ships. If you are not in the sector and do not have a navsat there, then you CANNOT jump to that sector or give orders to your ships and stations there. People coming from X2 or newer games will probably find this very irritating. There are also some other details, like a lack of sell orders for trade ships, for example. In general, the complexity is higher than the first game but still much lower than X2.

This game is complete enough that you might play for some time after finishing the plot, but due to the aforementioned annoyances and lower quality compared to later games you probably would not make this your mainstay as an X-series fan. The first game in the series to really nail the 'I could just keep playing this for hundreds of hours' feeling is X2: The Threat. In my opinion.

Compatibility-wise it suffers from similar issues to the first game. Compatibility with versions of Windows newer than 7 is flaky at best. Linux users may have an easier time as the game works on Proton Experimental as of September 2024. However, while the game is more stable than the first on Proton, intermittent crashes are still a problem. And NPC portraits are still broken. GE-Proton9-11 made the game more stable and fixed the portrait issues. Lutris' Wine-GE also works and was more stable than GE-Proton in my experience.

[i][b][u]IMPORTANT[/u][/b]: If you end up buying the game, read the manual - as you always should with any game released before 2004. The main guide of X-Tension is actually very well made, at least compared to X:BtF.[/i]

This game is a standalone DLC for X: Beyond the Frontier. I've made a review for it [u][url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/hanapon/recommended/2840/]here[/url][/u]. Keep in mind that many of the things I said in that review still apply to X-Tension, so I'll focus on stuff added compared to X:BtF. This can make the game look better than it actually is, since many of the negatives present in the original were solved. but the main thing that pushes the game score down is still present.

X-Tension made huge improvements compared to the original game. First and foremost, you can drive any ship instead of being locked to a single vessel. This in itself increases massively the amount of stuff you can do in game. You can fly a transporter class ship and make copious amounts of money by trading - but having a bad cruise/rudder control and being vulnerable to pirate ships -, or you can buy and use a small hunter ship, which is fast and has great firepower to face any other ship - but also does have a small cargo space, making trade with it inefficient.

Furthermore, the game improves it's UX/UI. You can manage your factories remotely even if you're in a different sector. You can take a look at everything you've discovered in the galaxy without moving an inch. You now have menus that makes sense and makes your life so, so much more comfortable (in a good way, since the difficulty of the game wasn't a positive of it, but rather a catalyst of boringness). You can finally center your attention on managing your commerce empire, which is the somewhat fun part of the game.

The biggest weakness of the original game, however, is still here. Your early game still comprise or you going from place to place doing basically nothing, and it feels just as boring as the first one, with nothing to do or look at while doing it. At least now you can do this boring work while looking forward to something to experience later in the game. If you like space games, X-Tension is at least worth checking out. There are people who can find pleasure in it's gameplay loop.

Arguably the first proper X game, all staples of the series (the classic games up to X3 and its expansions, anyway) - direct and remote control over your ships and factories, ability to fly any ship (almost any, I guess M1/M2 were cut for time), much improved background simulation, galaxy map, generic missions - were introduced here, and the sequels build upon this framework without altering its core, mostly adding features and polish on top of what this game invented. Which begs the question - is there any point in playing X-Tension over its sequels? Well...

The tagline of the series is "Trade - Fight - Build - Think", and while "Think" is too abstract to describe in gameplay terms, trading, fighting and building are the three primary ways of obtaining riches, which is a reasonable self-appointed goal in place of an absent plot. Yeah, while X-BTF had central plot and an ending, X-Tension ends only when you think you had enough of it. There are a couple mission threads, most notably the Perseus mission, but they only appear under hidden conditions and are more like a side-activity rather than a proper goal.

Trading is interesting for maybe first 20 deals, then the novelty of dynamic pricing wears off and you understand that the economy is a Brownian motion where prices fluctuate like crazy, yet are balanced to keep your earnings on the same level no matter what you're buying and where you're selling, so a long-distance route is as profitsssssable as carrying goods between two stations in the same sector. It is a viable way of obtaining starting capital, but too boring and grindy to bring you to your end goals.

Building your stations is where the economy shows its better sides - you need to be aware of the supply and demand in the region, building supply chains (albeit quite simplified compared to NPC stations), sometimes play around competition. The station prices were completely overhauled compared to X-BTF - in that game, you could blink and discover your station pay off its cost tenfolds, in X-Tension however, the stations are balanced to return its cost in 50 hours on average (which is no less than 5 hours in real life), so you gotta invest early and build often, your empire's profitssss will snowball with time and care. At times it feels like an idle game, which is not necessarily a bad thing. I wish there were more freighter command options and money auto-withdraw, but otherwise it's the best feature in the game.

The combat, on the other hand, is the worst. Every aspect of movement or shooting is critically flawed in one way or another. Turning has heavy inertia so you often overshoot when trying to catch your target in crosshairs, throttle control is twitchy and sensitive so matching your speed with target is plain impossible. All that's combined with outright horrible shooting - your guns don't swivel to help you hit the target even if they are spread far away from the center your ship, your ship shakes violently when you get hit, and just as violently whenever you shoot, your ship gets randomly disoriented like 5 degree with each shot, so you need to be very close to your target to have a chance to land more than the first shot, and explosions after each hit obscure the enemy AND your UI. What's insulting is that NPCs don't have those disadvantages - they turn towards you without any inertia, their guns swivel, and their aim is not affected by anything, and all that is balanced only by their stupidity.
The combat is made worse by Hornet missile, which one-shots any combat ship you're allowed to fly, so whenever an enemy launches a missile, you must cease your attack and either try to shoot it down in panic (with inertial controls and wandering aim, yeah), or abuse strafe-drive physics to run away and wait out until the missile runs out of fuel.
Why would you engage in combat then? When you destroy a pirate ship, you may receive up to 1k credits in bounty and sometimes around 10k in cargo. In comparison, the cheapest TL class ship costs 16mil. So yeah, combat as a way of earning money is useless, though you can engage in it to clear out the pirate and xenon problems for the sake of your industrial empire, which is admittedly a good mix of gameplay systems.
Oh, also this game introduced the ship capture mechanic which remained unchanged throughout the series - you can force the pilot of a non-capital ship to bail out, and then sell his ship for good profitsss (up to 500k depending on the ship class). For that, you need to bring the enemy's shields to a low level and keep shooting at him without destroying the ship. Maybe the pilot will jump out immediately, maybe he will jump out after an hour of sitting on his back and sloowly shooting at him while trying to match your speed to his with the controls as finicky as those. 

Graphically it looks leagues better than X-BTF, with higher-resolution textures and better models. Stations have such a cozy glowiness to them, I wish they retained that even in low LODs, they look too dark from afar. The UI is also glowy and cute, looking like teletext, though while functionally it is much improved over X-BTF, it is not exactly responsive, and its animations block you from doing routine operations in an efficient way, to the point that accidentally pressing "R" during the combat paralyzes your ship control for a few good seconds.

The game is stable and without critical bugs, the only two thinks which bothered me were framerate dropping to single digits whenever you intercom with someone, which can happen during combat, and gates sometimes being immediately destroyed when you enter a sector, permanently cutting off access to regions of space (so save often). A recent patch made the game playable without any hurdles on Win10 (and maybe Win11), though on widescreen resolutions, you'll have top and bottom parts of your screen cut off, and those parts sometimes contain useful information.

So tldr, while this game improves sandbox greatly over X-BTF, the only thing this game has over its sequels is its atmosphere, which is a copy of X-BTF with higher fidelity. X2: The Threat has practically the same economy and includes all mechanics from X-Tension, but with better polish, accessibility and enjoyment.

I'll have to be honest about this. The game itself is fun to play, but Egosoft needs their knuckles rapped for the pathetic story line (if you can even call it that).  One should expect to see continuity between XBTF and X:Tension, but X:tension simply doesn't provide it.  Hey, remember me? I'm  Kyle Brennan, the Hero of Argon and loved by all of the races for my part in the Xenon War. So then why does no one even know me now, plus the Split and Piranad are downright hostile? I was in a sector called Brennan's Triumph, and the Split told me to sod off. What happened to my trading empire and my million plus credits I usually carried with me?  Egosoft no doubt spent quite a bit of money developing that video with the kid telling us about Captain Brennan. Unfortunately, the video does nothing to explain what happened to Brennan's mines and fabs, or why the prices of almost everything have skyrocketed. Would it have been so hard to find a reason?  Of course not. I took a few minutes and came up with this:   After the Xenon's mother ship was destroyed, Ban Danna gave Brennan those fantastic 125mw shields, which he promptly used to wipe out the Xenon ships and bases in all of their sectors. In retaliation, the Xenon staged a major attack that destroyed all of Brennan's possessions and caused prices to skyrocket among all of the races. The Xenon also put a large bounty on Brennan's life, causing Ban Danna to advise him to go incognito for a while. Danna gave him an Argon buster and a few thousand credits to start out on his own. (Brennan couldn't draw on his own account, since that would reveal where he was.)  And then the game could proceed as it does, but at least there would be a reason for Brennan's sudden poverty and unpopularity. Surely their professional writers could have done even better. Having said that, I do like the way the game is put together and recommend it for many hours of fun.  Still, Egosoft really dropped the ball when it came to setting the stage for Brennan's new adventures.

Ok, so I have been playing this game (X-tension) after starting with X: Beyond the Frontier.

The first thing that immediately stands out is that it fixes a lot of the problems with the UI that made the first X game so painful.  This is a much more pleasant experience - far from perfect, but a vast improvement.

It's also a lot less directed.  There is no primary story mission that points you where to go - you stumble on missions as you travel, and initially this was fine, but ultimately this just led to frustration on my part.  While just being let loose on this space to make your own way feels attractive for a while, once I'd set up some factories, made a bit of money, upgraded my ships a bit, I was left with that "why am I playing this?" which never went away.  I didn't get close to 'finishing' the game (whatever 'finishing' might mean) - there was clearly content that I wasn't getting to, but without any direction or clues as to where to go (and worse, when to go) it just became this overwhelming feeling of 'well I might stumble across something if I just wander aimlessly and do mostly the same repetitive stuff for ages, but seriously why would I bother?'.  I could make lots of money and become bestest friends with everyone, but I'm already bored of what it would take to do this and without some indication of why I should be doing it it just bored me to quitting eventually.

Steam shows a lot of hours played here, but a fair few of those were AFK or mostly AFK because the game seems designed to make AFK the most obvious way to achieve things, which is never a good thing in a game.  The tuning of the economy is such that you need a lot of cash and a lot of time to build up anything substantial - orders of magnitude more tedious than the first game, and it just seems to want to push you into getting time to pass in the game so you can get some more cash to get you slightly closer to whatever goals you might have.

Worse your computer has to be pretty much dedicated to this AFK play because the game pauses when you switch out of the game so you can't do anything else while you're waiting for whatever it is of the many things that you have to wait for.

Sure, you can go off and try to stumble across some more of the same missions that you've done a dozen times already (find 50 BoFu, and drop it off here, yay, destroy these Xenon ships which you may or may not get help with in time to save this dumb freighter, escort this ultra slow ship which is more than likely going to be blown up regardless of what you do) while you wait, but really, why?  Serious balance problems all over the place.

The OCD in me kept me wanting to do more for a long time, but in the end the tedium defeated me.

As I said at the start, there are some big improvements in key areas for this game over the first installment, and that gives me hope that some of these bigger plot/story/point issues will be tackled in the subsequent titles, but this one left me deeply frustrated and unsatisfied, and I think a lot of that just comes down to the complete lack of direction.  Just some hints or suggestions about where to go to look for things to follow up on would have done wonders I suspect.  And strangely for this day and age the net is surprisingly sparse in terms of resources or guides for this particular game which means there's not a lot of obvious help if you end up frustrated as I did.

Интерфейс решительным образом развернули лицом к публике и заставили рисовать карту галактики, отмечая уже открытые сектора, а также показывать в деталях каждый регион с указанием названий всех объектов. Теперь, чтобы быстро найти нужную цель, достаточно вызвать карту, ткнуть курсором в нужное имя из списка и выбрать «Select as Target». Удобно — нет слов! Более того, запустив в сектор спутник-шпион, вы сможете оставаться в курсе всех политико-финансовых событий, находясь даже на другом краю вселенной. Помимо этого пилоты-бизнесмены отныне могут при помощи все тех же спутников управлять фабриками на расстоянии («да-да, вот этому клиенту ничего не давайте, пока не заплатит, а аргонцам сделайте скидку!»). По мелочи следует отметить возможность бесплатного savegame’а (долой извращения с покупкой «сохраненок»!), гораздо более удобное меню торговли и наличие встроенного notepad’a для законченных маньяков, что решат вести собственный бортжурнал. Интересно, сколько человек попросили о введении в игру последней «фичи»? Получив кучу зуботычин за попытки ограничить свободу игрока, авторы подумали-подумали, да и выкинули его в утиль. Все, что осталось — длинное, плохо озвученное интро, вкратце излагающее содержание предыдущей серии. Оказывается, герой X-BTF — землянин по фамилии Бреннер, умудрившийся в процессе починки своего звездолета подружить инопланетные расы и вынести нацию роботов-убийц, так и не сумел вернуться домой. Чтобы не умереть со скуки, дожидаясь, пока ученые приладят выскочившие болтики на свои места, он одолжил у приютившего его аргонского правительства кораблик, немного карманной мелочи и улетел восвояси — выполнять квесты и зашибать деньгу. В принципе, с квестами все ясно, как божий день. По достижении хоть какой-нибудь известности к игроку начинают приставать с просьбами все, кому не лень: возьми-отвези, найди-пристрели и подобное в том же духе. Выполнять их вас никто не заставит — дело это сугубо добровольное, однако, если сулят хороший барыш, почему бы не поработать DHL-заменителем? Тем более что авторы уже пообещали выпускать новые миссии вместе с патчами… Вести бизнес в мире X-Tension значительно веселее, чем работать наемником, и, что важно, прибыльнее. Выбираем подходящий регион, покупаем и ставим там фабрику, нанимаем грузовики, истребителей-охранников, швыряем неподалеку спутник и раскрываем карманы пошире. Кстати, командовать подсобным хозяйством до неприличия легко. Изменить цены на фабрике, натравить охранников на пиратствующих гостей или отправить грузовики за покупками можно через систему специальных меню и при наличии верного спутника. Фактически, авторы подарили нам вполне законченный экономический симулятор! Браво. Думаете, это все? Никак нет. Отныне можно покупать корабли, составляя целый парк летательных агрегатов, коих в X-Tension доступно более тридцати (впрочем, знающие люди утверждают, что тут есть и секретные объекты, скажем… НЛО…). У каждого летала свои кокпит, скорость, броня и грузоподъемность, что заставляет быть внимательней при покупке корабля и апгрейдов, хотя тратить свои кровные вовсе необязательно. Не в меру злобные и жадные могут попробовать отбить приглянувшийся кораблик у хозяина, силой принудив его катапультироваться из кабины. После этого остается лишь пристрелить космонавта и, облачившись в скафандр, лететь на абордаж. Между прочим, угон кораблей — тоже бизнес, ибо за это можно получить не только плазмой в лоб от первого же блюстителя закона, но и хорошие мегадоллары на судоверфях. Заметьте, некоторые агрегаты, например, ксенонские, в магазины не завозят… Вот и приходится мародерствовать. Единственной проблемой на пути к нечестному обогащению остается боевая система игры. Любители Tachyon или Starlancer поначалу будут долго отплевываться, пытаясь расправиться даже с самыми дохленькими недругами: здесь так же, как и в X-BTF, побеждает тот, у кого круче пушка и щиты, а кремниевый мозг всем прочим видам атаки по-прежнему предпочитает лобовой таран. Халявщик электронный… Давить. Нет, таранить! Главное, чтобы у вас щитов больше было. Там еще кто-то плачет по «Элите»? Прекратите сию же минуту. Утрите слезы, купите X-Tension и хоть всю оставшуюся жизнь летайте в безумно красивом космосе под бесподобный эмбиент, торгуя, разоряя, убивая и творя добро (ненужное вымарать). Ностальгировать не надо — нам еще нужно заработать 2000 миллионов долларов, скупить все доступные апгрейды, стать мега-магнатом, собрать целый ангар звездолетов и выяснить правду о происхождении таинственных НЛО. За работу, друзья! Жизнь продолжается!

Miután Kyle Brennan egy csúfos hiba miatt belecsöppent galaxisunk egy rég elveszettnek hitt zugába, az ott átélt izgalmak után úgy határoz, ideje hazatérni. Sajnos a technika ördöge még mindig Kyle vállán vakációzik, így a kísérlet kudarcba fullad és hősünk kénytelen megbarátkozni a gondolattal, hogy új hazára lelt. A játék nagyjából itt abba is hagyja a történetmesélést, hiszen olyan, mint fő küldetésszál, nincs. Be kell érnünk azokkal az elvétve felbukkanó rövid kis feladatokkal, amikkel néha megkeresnek minket a helyiek. Az űr a személyes homokozónkká válik, amiben azt csinálunk, amit akarunk - de továbbra is a kereskedelmen van a hangsúly. Szabadságvágyunkat kielégítendő kibővítették a bebarangolható szektorok, a forgatható nyersanyagok és termékek, valamint a meglátogatható és birtokolható gyárak számát. Nem utolsósorban pedig annyi hajónk lehet, amennyit elbír az egyenlegünk és abba ülünk bele, amelyikhez kedvünk van, ami nagy előrelépés az alapjáték egyetlen járművéhez képest. A tulajdonunkban lévő hajókat, gyárakat most már nyomon is követhetjük egy dinamikusan változó menüben, valamint a helyi és világtérképen, aminek hála cégünk sokkal könnyebben átlátható és irányítható. Aki néha ki szeretne szabadulni a kereskedelem határai közül, az belevághat a kalózkodásba, amivel nem csupán rakományuktól foszthatjuk meg a pórul járt hajókat, de gyávább pilóta esetén el is foglalhatjuk azokat. Mértéket természetesen nem árt tartanunk, ha nem szeretnénk magunkra haragítani az adott fajt, aki minden további nélkül ránk uszítja rendfenntartó szerveit, vagy csak egyszerűen nem enged leszállni egyetlen szektorukban sem. Legtöbb problémánk viszont továbbra is a kalózokkal lesz, akik időről-időre megpróbálják rátenni mocskos kis kezüket (mancsukat, csápjukat) nehezen megszerzett értékeinkre.

A játékmenet mellett az űr képi megjelenítése is kisebb fejlődésen esett át, a több űrállomásnak köszönhetően a látványvilág is sokat nyert változatosság terén. A gyárak belseje kisebb-nagyobb ráncfelvarrást kapott, a statikus háttérhez ezúttal több effekt is dukál. Ezek ellenére a grafika mai szemmel nézve elég ósdinak tűnik, bizosan nem szépségével fog minket elcsábítani.

Zenei téren viszont nem sok újdonság ér minket, az alapjáték felhozatala köszön vissza néhány új darab felbukkanásával, továbbá a hangok is köszönik szépen, nem kérnek új köntöst. Amennyiben megfelelt nekünk a nagy előd hangzásvilága - és még nem untunk rá - akkor nem csalódhatunk nagyot.

Az X: Beyond the Frontier önmagában is helyt álló kiegészítője több fronton is hozzátett őse érdemeihez. Szinte minden téren tovább gondolták, így akit nem riaszt el a történet hiánya, az jobban jár jelen kistestvérrel. Ugyan ki ne akarna egy saját kereskedőbirodalmat egy hozzá illő flottával?

Next up, I get into the new "Highway" system. And quickly find out that you can not only hit and run into other ships. But doing so chucks you out of the highway at insane speeds and very far from it. Meaning I now have to fly back to the highway.

[h1]Ну здравствуйте, спустя 12 лет!!![/h1]
[b]X Rebirth[/b] — космический симулятор от немецкой [b]Egosoft[/b], перезапуск знаменитой серии X, с которой я познакомился в 2014м. В интернете пишут, что игра задумывалась как [b]«точка входа»[/b] для новичков: разработчики хотели сделать сложный космос серии проще и ближе к игроку. Мой опыт показал, на старте не сработало, хотя проект стал противоречивый (смешанные отзывы), у фанатов говорят бомбануло, но у него всё равно есть своя аудитория, ну и в целом я дошёл же)

[h3]Сеттинг и сюжет[/h3]
Действие происходит в далёком будущем, где рухнула привычная система межзвёздных врат, а галактическое сообщество переживает кризис. Вы начинаете как пилот в секторе Альбион. После нескольких миссий, связанных с повстанцами [b]Сердце Альбиона[/b], против [b]Плутарх Майнинг Корпорэйшн[/b] узурпировавшей власть в секторе, мы окажемся в [b]Де фризе[/b]. Пройдя цепочку миссий и постройки [u][b]Верфи БЛА[/b][/u]!!!, нас закинет в [b]Омикрон Лиры[/b], ну а далее война с [b]ксенонами[/b] в секторе [b]Мальстрим[/b]. Сюжет не слишком глубокий, но он даёт знакомит со вселенной. Важную роль играет напарница [b]Йиша Тарен[/b] —которая помогает освоиться и даёт подсказки.

[h3]Геймплей [/h3]
Главная идея [b]X Rebirth[/b] — «один корабль вместо флота». В отличие от прошлых частей, где игрок мог командовать десятками судов и строить огромные производственные цепочки, здесь фокус смещён на личный опыт пилота:[list]
[*][b]Управление одним кораблём[/b]. Вы [b]Рен Отани[/b], мелкий предприниматель, который после смерти отца ищет себя и пытается заработать, он лично пилотируете [strike]Гордость Альбиона[/strike] [b]Альбионский Скунс[/b].
[*][b]Вид от первого лица внутри корабля и на станциях[/b]. Можно ходить по отсекам, осматривать оборудование[spoiler](через пару станций поймёте что всё однотипно!)[/spoiler], заходить на станции и взаимодействовать с NPC[spoiler](необходимо и со временем достанет, благо есть удалённая доставка)[/spoiler].
[*][b]Экономика как живая система[/b]. Ресурсы не появляются из воздуха: производство, спрос и логистика зависят от реальных цепочек. Вы можете влиять на рынок, возить дефицитные товары и [u]зарабатывать на разнице цен[/u].
[*][b]Строительство станций[/b]. Доступна механика постройки собственных станций, и весьма сложная, особенно когда тебе нужны термоядерные реакторы что бы строить станцию и продвинуться по сюжету, а изготавливает их ТОЛЬКО Плутарх. Процесс долгий, но даёт долгосрочную экономическую базу (ставьте моды на «auto crew», иначе достанет искать крутых специалистов!
[*][b]Абордажи и десант[/b]. Возможность захватывать корабли, высаживая команду захвата (жаль нет возможности пострелять самому!) Вот что меня зацепило в 2014м году, наверное на меня тогда повлиял [b]Assassin 4 black flag[/b] и я весь 2014й только и захватывал [b]Титуэли[/b], прокачав своих десантников до [u]48 ветеранов и 2 элитных[/u][spoiler](я захватил 65 Марадёров Титуэль)[/spoiler] Успешные операции повышают опыт бойцов: обычные становятся ветеранами, ветераны — элитными. Это не покупка, а прогрессия через действия.[/list]

[h3]Плюсы[/h3][list]
[*][b]Масштабный живой мир[/b]. В секторах постоянно что-то происходит: NPC воюют, летают конвои, меняются цены. Мир ощущается «настоящим», а не декоративным.
[*][b]Глубокая экономика[/b]. Если нравится считать прибыль, оптимизировать маршруты и строить цепочки производства — здесь для этого много пространства.
[*][b]Тактические бои и модульная система повреждений[/b]. Важно не просто стрелять, а целиться в конкретные узлы: прыжковый двигатель!, двигатели, щиты, оружейные системы (в таком порядке!).
[*][b]Атмосфера и звук[/b]. Космические пейзажи, звуки работы оборудования и музыка Алексея Захарова создают узнаваемую «космическую романтику» серии.
В [b]Альбионе[/b] немного гнетуще, но очень спокойно, в [b]Де фризе[/b], станет очень светло), меня достала музыка данного сектора, [b]Омикрон лиры[/b] наслаждайтесь!, [b]Мальстрим[/b] пустой, у [b]Полей возможности гнетущая[/b], а вот после почти 200 часов я кайфанул от музыки в [b]Обители света[/b], она прям реально не бесит а мотивирует!!![/list]

[h3]Минусы и проблемы[/h3][list]
[*][b]Сложный и неудобный интерфейс[/b]. Исправили по сравнению с 2014м, когда приходилось аватару поворачиваться к Йише направо, добавили быстрое меню! Многие функции спрятаны глубоко в меню, логика действий не всегда очевидна. Это сильно мешает освоению?![spoiler] (гугл? + лётная школа!)[/spoiler].
[*][b]Технические проблемы и баги[/b]. На релизе игра была очень сырой: вылеты, зависания, проблемы с сохранениями. Почти всё исправили, но «осадок» остался (сраный контейнер с [b]Камнем созерцания[/b] в [b]Альбионе в Спящем медведе[/b]!).
[*][b]Упрощение ключевых механик[/b]. Отказ от полноценного управления флотом и сильное сокращение стратегических возможностей разочаровали давних фанатов.
[*][b]Неудачные решения в управлении и камере[/b]. Вид из кабины с ограниченным обзором делает бои неудобными: ставишь кабину ястреба и видно почти всё!, а вот с тылами проблемы, не это же симулятор, а вообще есть кнопка F2!
[*][b]Дисбаланс и «узкие места» [/b]. Некоторые механики (например, сюжетный спавн Арауна могут сломаться из-за мода [b]Captain and Defense Officer AI Overhaul (Ignore Jump Fuel[/b]) могут ломаться, и это блокирует важные действия. Ставьте мод на защиту корабля, который берёте на абордаж, командира десанта вы ещё можете найти/прокачать, а вот прокаченных десантников терять очень жалко!
[h3]Хотите пройти сюжет не ставьте этот мод!, если поставили читайте комментарии, [url= https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=248605513] если что решение тут[/url]![/h3][/list]

[h3]Для кого эта игра[/h3][list]
[*][b]Для новичков в серии[/b], которым хочется «космоса без лишней сложности»: один корабль, понятные задачи, прогулки по станциям.
[*][b]Для любителей экономики и логистики[/b], готовых мириться с неудобным интерфейсом ради глубокой симуляции рынка.
[*][b]Для фанатов серии[/b], которые хотят увидеть «перезапуск» и сравнить его с классическими частями. 
Но если вы ищете [b]«классическую» X[/b] с управлением большим флотом, прозрачной экономикой и отточенным UX — лучше обратить внимание на [b]X4: Foundations[/b]: она развивает идеи, не раскрытые в Rebirth.[/list]
[h3]Итог[/h3]
[b]X Rebirth[/b] — это амбициозная, но неровная попытка сделать серию X доступнее. У игры есть масштаб, живая экономика, атмосферность и интересные механики, но они могут быть омрачены тем, что Вам может что-то не понравиться.
