Cossacks: Art of War, developed by GSC Game World and published by GSC World Publishing, builds upon the grand strategic foundations of Cossacks: European Wars and expands them with additional content, refined mechanics, and broader replay potential. Set once again during the volatile conflicts of the 17th and 18th centuries, the game retains its commitment to historical authenticity while amplifying the scale and scope that made its predecessor notable. Rather than reinventing the formula, Art of War deepens it, offering more nations, new campaigns, and expanded tools that strengthen its identity as a large-scale historical real-time strategy experience.

The defining feature of the Cossacks series has always been its massive battles, and Art of War continues that tradition with remarkable ambition. Players can command thousands of units simultaneously, orchestrating sprawling engagements that resemble living, breathing early modern battlefields. Lines of musketeers exchange disciplined volleys, cavalry units attempt flanking maneuvers, and artillery batteries thunder from elevated terrain. The sense of scale is impressive even by modern standards, and it reinforces the importance of formations and positioning. Success in battle depends not only on numerical superiority but also on careful coordination, terrain advantage, and resource sustainability.

Economy management remains deeply intertwined with military success. Players must oversee the collection and distribution of multiple resources, including food, wood, stone, gold, iron, and coal. These resources are not merely abstract currencies; they directly fuel war efforts. Musketeers consume ammunition resources when firing, cannons require ongoing production support, and maintaining large armies places continuous strain on economic infrastructure. This tight connection between logistics and combat introduces meaningful strategic tension. Overextension can quickly lead to economic collapse, forcing players to balance expansion with sustainability.

One of the most notable additions in Art of War is the introduction of new nations, such as Denmark and Bavaria, which expand the roster of playable factions. Each nation carries subtle distinctions in military composition and strategic emphasis, encouraging experimentation across skirmish and campaign modes. While these differences do not radically alter gameplay mechanics, they provide enough variation to enhance replay value and broaden tactical possibilities. Combined with the already extensive selection of factions from European Wars, the overall variety gives players numerous ways to approach each match.

The single-player campaigns offer structured scenarios rooted in historical conflicts involving various European powers. These missions vary in objective design, ranging from defensive holds to offensive expansions and resource-driven survival challenges. The campaigns provide context and direction for players who prefer guided experiences rather than open-ended skirmishes. They also highlight the game’s emphasis on strategic pacing, as each scenario demands careful planning and measured execution rather than reckless aggression.

Another significant enhancement is the inclusion of a robust map editor, which dramatically increases the game’s longevity. Players can create custom battlefields, adjust resource placement, design mission objectives, and tailor scenarios to suit personal preferences. This tool fosters creativity and community engagement, allowing dedicated fans to extend the life of the game far beyond its official campaigns. Custom scenarios often introduce unique challenges and imaginative reinterpretations of historical conflicts, adding depth to an already expansive experience.

Visually, Art of War remains consistent with the sprite-based isometric presentation of its predecessor. While the graphics reflect early 2000s design standards, they effectively communicate the scale and organization of battles. Units are distinct and readable even during dense engagements, and the environments, though not graphically advanced by modern benchmarks, provide sufficient detail to maintain immersion. The sound design complements the visual presentation with musket volleys, cannon blasts, and atmospheric musical tracks that evoke the era’s martial tone.

Despite its strengths, the game inherits some limitations from its engine. Pathfinding can occasionally struggle when managing thousands of units, leading to congestion or awkward movement in tight spaces. The interface, while functional, lacks some of the streamlined quality-of-life features found in contemporary strategy titles. However, these shortcomings are often overshadowed by the depth of its systems and the satisfaction of orchestrating large-scale historical warfare.

Cossacks: Art of War ultimately serves as a meaningful expansion that enriches the core identity of the series. It reinforces the emphasis on economic management, formation-based combat, and massive engagements while offering new content and creative tools that enhance replayability. For players who appreciate historically grounded real-time strategy and enjoy commanding armies at an epic scale, it remains a rewarding and enduring entry in the Cossacks franchise. Though its presentation may feel dated to newcomers, its strategic complexity and ambition continue to stand as a testament to its era’s dedication to depth and scale in RTS design.

After spending countless hours exploring every nook and cranny of Cossacks: Art of War, from its single-player campaigns to its multiplayer skirmishes, I can confidently say that this expansion to the original Cossacks: European Wars is a worthy addition for any strategy enthusiast.

Single-Player Experience
The single-player content in Art of War expands on the original game with new campaigns, scenarios, and challenges. The historical campaigns are engaging and provide a good mix of objectives, from large-scale battles to resource management-heavy missions. The level of detail in the units, buildings, and maps adds a layer of immersion that makes each mission feel unique.

However, the AI can sometimes feel either too predictable or unnaturally aggressive, depending on the difficulty setting. While challenging at times, it doesn't always adapt dynamically, making it possible to exploit certain strategies repeatedly. That said, the depth of gameplay keeps things interesting for those who love micro-managing their resources and armies.

Multiplayer
The multiplayer mode is where Art of War truly shines. It retains the core appeal of real-time strategy battles while introducing new maps and balancing improvements. Whether you're playing with friends or strangers, the competitive nature of the game keeps you on your toes. The addition of new units and nations adds a layer of strategy, allowing for diverse playstyles and tactical approaches.

That said, multiplayer matches can sometimes be lengthy, especially when two skilled players engage in a stalemate. Patience and careful planning are essential, as rushing often leads to disaster.

Improvements Over the Base Game
The expansion introduces several key improvements, including:

New Units & Nations: These add depth and variety to the game.
Map Editor: A fantastic tool for creative players who want to design custom scenarios.
Enhanced Gameplay Mechanics: Subtle changes in unit behavior and balance make the game feel more polished.
Bug Fixes: Many of the bugs and issues from the base game have been addressed.
Graphics & Sound
Although the game is visually dated by today’s standards, it still has a certain charm. The large-scale battles with hundreds of units clashing are a spectacle to behold, even if the animations are a bit stiff. The soundtrack and sound effects are serviceable, though they can become repetitive after long sessions.

Final Thoughts
Cossacks: Art of War is a solid expansion that builds on the strengths of its predecessor. While not without its flaws, its depth, replayability, and improved features make it a must-play for fans of the RTS genre. The game’s steep learning curve and dated visuals may deter newcomers, but for those willing to invest the time, it offers a rich and rewarding experience.

"Cossacks: Art of War" is an ancient game from 2001.  It's a whopping 23 years old at the time of this review.  The game lacks support for any modern gaming display resolutions (or widescreen monitors), hasn't been modernised or updated to run smoothly on modern gaming PCs.  Despite this lack of modernisation, it carries a pretty high price tag for such an ancient game.  This seems to have been put on Steam as a nostalgia gouge, or just a cash grab to try profit from abandonware.

Before we get too deep into this, I have to relate that the game has serious compatbility and stability problems.  For me, the game crashed immediately when I set the resolution to 2160p, and then failed to launch, displaying an error about XGA resolution being unfindable... essentially the game corrupts itself if you try run it on a modern gaming PC.  Because the game is broken and unplayable for me, it may also not work for other gamers.  This is a solid reason to approach this game with some skepticism.

Cossacks was an old RTS game featuring Eastern European nations and troops from the 17th/18th centuries (hence the name, I guess).  There's a lot of scope for such a game but this one is too old and hasn't been properly modernised, and it's not okay for developers to hold their hands out for money for games they haven't tested, patched or otherwise kept up to date.  This would probably be a great buy if it was properly remastered, but this isn't. 

So, should you buy this game?

"Cossacks: Art of War" is relatively expensive for an abandonware nostalgia gouge, at $5 USD, and it's not worth it.  The game is just too old, hasn't been modernised.  And as the old saying goes, you can't go home again.  For comparison, the $5 asking price for this game could get you games like "Payday 2", "Mass Effect 3" or "Mad Max".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.  I also obviously can't recommend people buy games that probably won't even work.  Buyer beware, and all that.

Besonders beeindruckend finde ich, wie viele Einheiten gleichzeitig auf dem Schlachtfeld unterwegs sein können. Es macht Spaß, große Armeen aufzustellen und mit Infanterie, Kavallerie und Artillerie gegen den Gegner vorzugehen. Die verschiedenen Nationen bringen unterschiedliche Einheiten und Möglichkeiten mit, und durch die Formationen bekommt das Ganze auch eine taktische Komponente. Dazu kommen zahlreiche Szenarien und Kampagnen, die für genügend Beschäftigung sorgen. Für ein Spiel aus dieser Zeit ist auch die detaillierte 2D-Grafik noch ziemlich ansprechend.

Natürlich merkt man dem Spiel sein Alter an. Die Bedienung ist nicht immer komfortabel, und bei großen Schlachten kann es schnell unübersichtlich werden. Außerdem ist die Wirtschaft recht anspruchsvoll, weil man mehrere Rohstoffe gleichzeitig verwalten muss. Die Gegner verhalten sich nicht immer besonders clever, und manche Kampagnen können ziemlich schwierig sein. Wer moderne Strategiespiele gewohnt ist, muss sich deshalb erst einmal an die älteren Mechaniken gewöhnen.

Trotzdem macht mir das Spielprinzip auch heute noch Spaß. Der Aufbau der Wirtschaft, die riesigen Armeen und die vielen historischen Einheiten ergeben zusammen ein gelungenes Gesamtpaket. Es ist kein besonders zugängliches Spiel, aber gerade die Komplexität macht für mich einen Teil des Reizes aus. Wer klassische Echtzeitstrategie mag und gerne große Schlachten schlägt, sollte sich das unbedingt ansehen.

Cossacks: European Wars, developed by GSC Game World and published by GSC World Publishing, stands as one of the most ambitious real-time strategy titles of its generation. Set against the turbulent backdrop of 17th and 18th century Europe, the game transports players into an era defined by gunpowder warfare, imperial ambition, and sweeping continental conflicts. Rather than narrowing its focus to a single nation or campaign, it embraces scale in nearly every dimension, offering a wide roster of playable countries, sprawling maps, and the ability to command armies numbering in the thousands. Even decades after its original release, it remains a fascinating example of how grand historical warfare can be translated into intricate strategic systems.

At the heart of Cossacks: European Wars lies a deeply layered economic model. Players must gather and manage multiple resources, including food, wood, stone, gold, iron, and coal, each of which plays a critical role in sustaining both infrastructure and military operations. Unlike many strategy games where ammunition is abstracted, Cossacks integrates resource consumption directly into combat mechanics. Musketeers require iron and coal to fire, cannons drain stockpiles with every shot, and prolonged warfare can cripple an economy if production chains are neglected. This interdependence between battlefield performance and economic health forces players to think beyond immediate tactical gains and consider long-term sustainability. A poorly managed economy can collapse under the strain of maintaining massive armies, creating a delicate balance between expansion, defense, and production.

Combat itself is where the game’s scale becomes most apparent. Few real-time strategy titles of its era allowed players to deploy thousands of individual units simultaneously, forming dense infantry lines, cavalry charges, and artillery batteries that evoke the grandeur of early modern warfare. Infantry can be arranged into formations, officers can improve cohesion and morale, and terrain elevation affects range and effectiveness. The presence of formations encourages strategic positioning rather than chaotic skirmishing, rewarding players who manage their armies with discipline. Watching waves of musketeers exchange volleys while cavalry attempts flanking maneuvers creates a battlefield spectacle that feels both cinematic and mechanically demanding.

The diversity of nations further enriches the experience. Each playable faction comes with distinct architectural styles, unique units, and strategic strengths that subtly influence gameplay. Naval powers excel on water-dominated maps, cavalry-oriented nations can dominate open terrain, and others may boast economic advantages or unique troop types. This variety enhances replayability, as no two factions feel entirely interchangeable. Choosing a nation is not merely cosmetic; it shapes tactical decisions, research priorities, and long-term strategy.

The single-player campaigns draw inspiration from real historical conflicts, weaving structured missions around the broader geopolitical struggles of the era. Objectives vary from defensive sieges to offensive expansions, and the AI can prove formidable, particularly in scenarios that demand multitasking across multiple fronts. Beyond scripted campaigns, the game’s random map generator offers near-endless replay value. Players can customize resource abundance, map size, number of opponents, and victory conditions, crafting experiences that range from brief skirmishes to marathon engagements lasting hours. Multiplayer, whether through local networks or online connectivity, historically extended the game’s lifespan even further by introducing the unpredictability of human opponents.

Visually, Cossacks: European Wars reflects the technical standards of its time, employing detailed 2D sprites and isometric environments that remain surprisingly readable despite the sheer number of units on screen. Battles can appear chaotic, but the clarity of unit design and distinct visual cues help maintain control amid the spectacle. Smoke from cannon fire, marching formations, and animated naval engagements contribute to an immersive atmosphere. While modern players accustomed to high-definition 3D models may find the presentation dated, there is a certain charm and functional elegance in its sprite-based approach. The audio design complements the visual intensity, with musket volleys, cannon blasts, and period-inspired music reinforcing the sense of commanding a grand army.

Of course, the game is not without its limitations. Pathfinding can struggle under the weight of massive armies, occasionally leading to clumsy movement or congestion in tight terrain. Micromanaging thousands of units can become overwhelming, particularly without modern quality-of-life features found in contemporary strategy titles. The interface, though comprehensive, reflects early 2000s design philosophies and may feel cumbersome compared to streamlined modern RTS systems. Nevertheless, these shortcomings are often overshadowed by the game’s ambition and depth.

Ultimately, Cossacks: European Wars distinguishes itself through scale and systemic complexity. It does not merely simulate battles; it simulates the infrastructure required to wage them. The interplay between economy, technology, and massed formations creates a strategic experience that rewards patience, foresight, and calculated aggression. For players who appreciate historically grounded warfare and large-scale real-time strategy, it offers a richly layered experience that still holds relevance. Though time has introduced more refined successors within the genre, Cossacks remains a landmark title—an expansive, demanding, and memorable depiction of early modern European conflict that continues to command respect among strategy enthusiasts.

[h3] [i] How to create a good game? So that it would be interesting not only to spend scarce time with pleasure, but also to get something useful for yourself? This system is used by mass-market educational programs for children from three to seven years old. But what should adults do, tired of the endless fantasy in which the current gaming industry has drowned? There are many options. A completely logical, but elementary example: “Already engage in self-education, really! Raise your cultural level, open a history textbook, buy…” Stop! A textbook? History? This, in general, is not much different from the computer game “Cossacks: European Wars”. [/i] [/h3]
[hr][/hr]
In its image and likeness, "Cossacks" most closely resembles the founder of the genre of all construction strategies "in the Middle Ages", the well-known game Age of Empires. And most of all, it differs from all other RTS. It cannot be classified as "independent" from the conventions of the genre in any case, since the project is commercial from head to toe. Large, cumbersome and labor-intensive. However, GSC Game World knows its worth and, in accordance with its ability to make truly soulful games, presented the gaming community with a bill for three and a half million copies of the game based on historical motives of dusty antiquity.

This work can rightfully be considered a game for gourmets who cannot imagine life without difficulties. Indeed, not everyone will take responsibility for controlling a ramified economic system, commanding thousands of soldiers and peasants, managing a dozen settlements, defending and attacking both on land and at sea.

The peculiarity of "Cossacks" is the most complex character trait of this game. In some places, the player can observe harmony in the economy and in the military arena, and often, having stumbled, has a chance to plunge into the swamp of complete imbalance. It is no longer how the card will fall, but how to correctly take the reins of a riding horse called "primacy". Moreover, this law applies to both network battles between real players and to ordinary tasks from an ordinary, but chicly furnished campaign. If you do not have time to post sentries at the quarries filled with miners in time, you already risk losing them all in a rapid raid of dashing Cossacks waving their sabers at the ready. Peasants are a completely weak-willed people and without the supervision of military forces can easily go to earn extra money in the neighboring field of an unfriendly neighbor. And "capturing" defenseless workers, from a historical point of view, is possible and necessary. The peasant masses flatly refuse to fight with hoes (like in Age of Empires) or whatever comes to hand (Stronghold). For the sovereign's father, there, soldiers from the regular army will lay down their heads, if necessary.

It becomes clear from the very beginning that the player is flatly refused to be shoved into a sandbox. You will have to competently, meter by meter, build your own miniature state according to all the rules of real-time. Over time, resources tend to leak into the bottomless abyss of economic needs: the population destroys food, the gold reserve leaks into the pockets of soldiers and hired thugs, and the regular army spends an incredible amount of coal and iron on military operations. It is not so easy to establish a reliable flow of all these resources. Dozens of workers can work in quarries, but the matter will not be limited to stone supplies alone. At times, the density of deposits on the map can go off the scale below the minimum, but the creators of these conditions are firmly convinced that the player will independently find the ideal way out of the thrown situation, which is successfully masked by the result of the "random" generation of conditions. Developing your empire can be so difficult that the player's soldiers sometimes have to come out with pikes and muskets to defend it from advanced invaders. Against bombards and howitzers.

Sixteen countries are taking part in the battle for total dominance on the world stage, each of which, according to the tradition of the genre, has distinctive features and, oddly enough, a weighty list of shortcomings. Of course, the conscientious work of the artists on the visual component is among the advantages. The settlements of the Swiss colonists, as expected, differ from the British ones as much as the settlements of the French differ from the capital cities of the Russians. Markets, academies and residential buildings with their detailed drawing almost claim to be historically accurate, flaunting a huge number of sprites and a bright color scheme. Inadvertently, the hope arises that the land and sea battles, the work on which must be especially painstaking, should cause at least silent admiration. Therefore, having observed the bustle of dozens of peasants, the majority of whom are engaged in cutting down forests, turning over unliftable blocks of stone or, bent over in three deaths, fiddling around on the sovereign's lands, one can begin to examine the soldiers who have formed one of three possible formations, because contemplating the routine of everyday work becomes boring very quickly.

When it comes to bloody clashes, no viewer sitting on this side of the screen will remain indifferent, although, of course, the duration of battles depends on the number of simultaneously participating combat units, which can be up to eight thousand. Armies on the battlefield are capable of cutting each other up for ten minutes and half an hour - it is simply pleasant to watch, and even more so to control the course of the battle. The conscientiousness with which the developers improved the graphics, reduced the side effects of its shortcomings and brought the advantages to an ephemeral ideal, causes almost affection. A new graphic algorithm was developed, with which the common shortcomings of sprite animation simply disappeared! Many pre-prepared animated movements in sixty-four directions, thanks to which any movement on the screen, be it a marching squad of musketeers, a ship cutting the waves with its bow or eared wheat swaying under the invisible palm of the wind, looks more than believable. But the main reason the visuals are so striking is the amount of detail: the thick white smoke that follows the roar of gunfire; the waves that spread out from the armada of speeding frigates; the flames that devour damaged buildings, the architecture of which is maintained with the same lapidary precision as any other exhibit in this digital military history miniature.

Unlike the titans of the strategy genre Age of Empires or Command & Conquer, where the emphasis in the game is not on the plausibility of the behavior of the surrounding world, but on the scale and diversity of military operations, the game "Cossacks: European Wars" has made a long step forward. Combining incomparable interactivity, its high graphic performance and a deep economic system in an amazingly finely crafted gameplay, this unique offspring of modern alternative gaming culture first strikes you in the heart with something familiar and distant, after which it quickly runs away to the darkest corner, taking with it the most pleasant impressions. Due to the long gradual development, study of technologies and tedious construction of a city that promises to become a giant metropolis of the 16th-18th centuries, the excitement (and often the need) to form a combat-ready army is lost, which, by the way, will also have to be properly maintained. Do not forget that we have pure history before us, in military conflicts of which everyone will have to flounder quite a bit at first. Actual facts and dates are included.

So, what do we have? An aged, but not lost, hit of bygone years. This game of aristocratic elegance deserves to be remembered and loved anew. Even after ten years. Or even more.

Например, режим завоевания Европы /игра на стратегической карте явно задумывались как аналог серии Total War, но вышли очень сырыми и недоделанными. Карта маленькая, провинции огромные, и если на вас одновременно нападают две-три страны, то можно считать себя автоматически проигравшим, поскольку у вас всего одна армия.

[u][b]Кампании[/b][/u]
Много раз я в детстве пробовал их начинать и всегда скипал их чуть быстрее чем сразу. Ну вот не то это было: дома строятся медленно и они огромны, юниты (особенно крестьяне) делаются ещё дольше, ресов мало, войска в полки сводить надо. В итоге ты строишь это всё со скоростью полчаса до первого своего отряда. Приходит противник - залп и твоя армия разбежалась, а ты слит, ибо даже отбиться будет уже нечем.
В стиме я это преодолел. Хотя игра быстрее не стала, это всё такое же унылое медленное построение огромных зданий на очень маленькой территории. Причём зданий бесполезных, ибо на все из них есть ровно одно изучение - открытие гренадёров. Мммммм. По сути, все здания нужны чтобы открыть следующие здания и, в частности, чтобы получить офицеров/кавалерию/пушки. Глупо в общем. Не интересно.
Но на самом деле тут был и подвох определённый скрыт. Ибо как минимум в этом аддоне стабильно такая только первая миссия была (кроме испанцев), все остальные уже сугубо боевые: наступления разные, обороны и т.п. Как по мне, это тоже сомнительно выглядело, но уже пойдёт, я бы даже сказал, что все миссии такими и надо было делать, без строек всяких.

[u][b]Завоевание Европы[/b][/u]
Ох, как же много для меня в этом словосочетании скрыто. Без юмора, но я прошёл это дело за все фракции как на сд-лицухе, так и повторил теперь вновь. В определённый момент запарило конечно, но всё же это и есть сокровище этой игры. Да, оно [i]странное, пыльное, сломанное, но всё равно прекрасное.[/i]

Главная проблема, которую я осознал ещё в детстве, но это настоящий реквием по потерянным возможностям. Этому режиму бы большие масштабы, больше регионов, множество военачальников под управление, больше стран. И вот она - жемчужина геймдева, не иначе. Но нет... Сыграв сейчас, я пришёл снова ровно к этой же мысли. Эта игра могла бы стать тотал варом, о котором я в детстве и не знал, а получилась какая-то "камерная" история.

Отдельно ещё можно поругать поведение нпс в этой "сфере деятельности". Я помнил какие-то проблемы, но теперь увидел их в полной мере. Это буквально какое-то топтание болванчиков на месте, которые почти ничего не делают на карте, от силы нарезая круги друг за другом. На фоне чего уже ты их без зазрения совести  нарезаешь по одному. В бою поведение нпс такое же, кхм, глупое.
Ну и баги. Именно тут все они и были. Причём ровно те же, что и в годы создания этой игры, т.е. патчей от разрабов не было. Типа странного поведение "испанца", который не юзает мушкетёров, из-за чего их приходится длительно искать, а они ещё и убегать начинают, избегая боя.

Но всё же именно этот режим меня и цеплял. Раз за разом я в него приходил, раз за разом покорял карту, чем и был доволен. Именно поэтому я считаю вторую часть (и в частности, этот её аддон) лучшей игрой серии.

Cossacks II: Battle for Europe, developed by GSC Game World and published by GSC World Publishing, expands upon the foundation laid by Cossacks II: Napoleonic Wars and delivers a strategy experience deeply rooted in early 19th-century military conflict. Set during the height of the Napoleonic era, the game shifts focus from broad economic empire-building toward battlefield realism and tactical authenticity. Instead of emphasizing sprawling base construction, it places its weight squarely on commanding disciplined formations, managing morale, and leveraging terrain in massive engagements that mirror the structured warfare of the period. The result is a real-time strategy title that feels more like a historical battlefield simulation than a conventional resource-heavy RTS.

One of the defining characteristics of Battle for Europe is its emphasis on formations and battlefield cohesion. Units are not simply individual soldiers thrown into chaotic combat; they function as organized battalions that rely on leadership and structure to remain effective. Infantry can form disciplined lines or defensive squares, cavalry operate in tight formations to maximize charge impact, and artillery units demand careful placement to avoid exposure while maintaining firing range. Morale plays a critical role, meaning that even numerically superior forces can crumble if flanked or subjected to sustained pressure. Officers and drummers bolster troop effectiveness, reinforcing the idea that leadership and structure are as important as sheer numbers. This system adds a layer of tactical depth that rewards patience and thoughtful positioning over reckless aggression.

The scale of battles remains one of the game’s most impressive aspects. Large armies consisting of thousands of soldiers can clash simultaneously across detailed maps featuring rolling hills, forests, rivers, and urban terrain. Elevation influences range and visibility, wooded areas provide cover but restrict firing lines, and open fields become deadly arenas for cavalry maneuvers. The battlefield feels alive with movement and tension, particularly when two disciplined lines of infantry exchange musket volleys while artillery thunders in the background. The spectacle of these engagements captures the drama of Napoleonic warfare, where timing and coordination determine victory or defeat.

Unlike its predecessor, which focused more narrowly on specific campaigns, Battle for Europe introduces a grand strategic layer that adds significant depth. The titular “Battle for Europe” mode allows players to engage in a turn-based continental campaign where diplomacy, alliances, and territorial expansion shape the broader war effort. Provinces are contested across a map of Europe, and decisions made at the strategic level determine which real-time battles will unfold. This combination of turn-based grand strategy and real-time tactical combat creates a compelling loop. Players must think several steps ahead, balancing military ambition with political calculation. While the strategic layer is not as intricate as dedicated grand strategy titles, it provides meaningful context and continuity between individual battles.

Nation variety enhances replayability. The expansion broadens the roster of playable factions, each with distinct unit compositions and battlefield strengths. Some nations excel in disciplined infantry lines, others field formidable cavalry, and certain factions offer unique unit types that shift tactical priorities. These differences are subtle rather than extreme, but they encourage experimentation and adaptation. Understanding a nation’s strengths and compensating for its weaknesses becomes part of the strategic challenge, especially in multiplayer or higher-difficulty scenarios.

Visually, Cossacks II: Battle for Europe reflects its mid-2000s origins. The isometric perspective and sprite-based units prioritize clarity and scale over graphical spectacle. While the presentation lacks the modern polish of contemporary RTS titles, it effectively communicates battlefield information even during the largest engagements. Units are distinct enough to identify at a glance, and the environmental details, though modest, support immersion. The sound design complements the visuals with musket fire, cannon blasts, and era-appropriate musical themes that underscore the historical atmosphere.

Despite its strengths, the game is not without limitations. The interface can feel dated, particularly for players accustomed to streamlined modern RTS controls. Micromanagement of large formations requires patience, and pathfinding occasionally struggles under the weight of massive armies. Additionally, while the grand strategy layer adds welcome depth, it does not fully match the complexity of specialized strategy franchises. These elements may deter newcomers, but they are often accepted by fans as part of the series’ traditional design philosophy.

Ultimately, Cossacks II: Battle for Europe distinguishes itself through its commitment to historical authenticity and tactical nuance. It is less concerned with flashy innovation and more focused on faithfully representing the structure and discipline of Napoleonic warfare. For players who value formation-based combat, morale systems, and large-scale engagements that demand thoughtful command, the game offers a rich and rewarding experience. Though its presentation reflects its era, its strategic depth and battlefield scale continue to resonate with enthusiasts of historically grounded real-time strategy.

Rating: 8/10

Cossackes II: Battle for Europe ist ein Strategiespiel welches in der Zeit der Napoleonischen Kriege stattfindet.
Es gibt eine Kampagne und die Möglichkeit Gefechte zu spielen. Anders als in vielen anderen Strategiespielen ist möglich echte Schlachten aus der Zeit Napoleons nachzuspielen, so wie Waterloo oder Austerlitz. Geschwindigkeit und Kalkül sind in Verbindung mit der Minikarte Elemente die das Gewinnen erleichtern. Auch Tastaturkürzel können zum verbesserten Spielerlebnis erlernt werden.

In Cossacks II Battle for Europe zählt nicht nur die Waffenstärke sondern auch die Moral und die Ausdauer weswegen es zu spannenden Schiebespielen kommt.

Das Spiel wird geschichtlich interessierten Spielern geraten, da gerade diese an der bunten Uniformenpracht und dem historisch anmutendem Interface Interesse haben könnten.

Die wahre Begeisterung für Cossacks ist durch die schöne Animation der einzelnen Figuren entstanden.
Auch die Ausführung der Befehle läuft nach einem braven und visuell sichtbaren Verhalten der Figuren ab.
Man muss sich nur hineinversetzen in die Zeit um 1800, wo die Menschen halt noch ganz anders gedacht haben.
Heutzutage wo es auch neue und alte Spiele der Reihe gibt, bleibt Cossacks II immer einer meiner Favoriten.
Świetna rozgrywka dla fanów wojen napoleońskich.

I gave Zen of Sudoku a thumbs down, but that does not mean it is a bad game overall.
The game does many things well. 

Pros:
- The difficulty progression is well balanced, offering an enjoyable challenge for both casual and experienced Sudoku players. 
- The graphics are fairly basic, but they suit this type of game well. 
- The soundtrack is also relaxing and helps create a calm atmosphere.

Cons:
However, there are a few issues that significantly impact the experience. 
- The music becomes repetitive during longer play sessions. 
- There is no option to change the screen resolution or UI scaling, which makes the game appear very small when played on a television. 
- In addition, the assistant that highlights cells cannot be disabled, which limits the ability to play the game exactly as I would prefer.

Overall, Zen of Sudoku is a solid Sudoku game with good puzzle design and a relaxing presentation. With a few quality-of-life improvements, especially regarding display options and gameplay customization, it would be much more enjoyable.

Simply Sudoku

Was looking for just a simple sudoku game with no distracting animations or cutesy story or any other distracting add-ons.  I don't want a story path, I just want puzzles!

This is exactly what I was looking for.  The hint button is good, though the explanations for some of the hints didn't make sense until I studied them a few times (finally learned what "x-wing" was).

A pretty basic sudoku game. Each square is divided into 9 pieces that you can left click to assign or right click to mark. You can use the 1-9 numbers on the top of your keyboard to highlight the various numbers for easier viewing. There's several different levels of challenge that feel fine. There aren't any crazy complex solutions, just various levels of basic sudoku. You can get a hint at any time, double click for an explanation of the hint, as well as turn on options like flagging duplicates or incorrect numbers.

The only downside is that it's fairly bare bones in regards to settings. You can't change the font or backgrounds. The rows + columns light up as you hover over the boxes, which is a nice touch, but you can't increase the opacity.

All in all, it's completely fine, especially considering it's free. It'll scratch that sudoku itch you have if you're looking for a quick game to relax with, or give you some easily accessible practice if you're a beginner.

An edit after a few more hours of playing, the game seems to bug out a bit once you start doing master level puzzles. For some reason at this level it starts to see marks that haven't been made. It'll tell you that  a number is locked to a certain row, but that simply isn't true based on your own marks. It seems to only happen at master level though.

Still my favourite Sudokuu game to play, even if it's a struggle to get it to run these days (ironically, it so-far runs no problem on Wine under Linux, but last time I tried, crashed out on Windows..)

Would love to see it updated for higher screen resolutions, but not really that necessary,

О боже, друзья, если вы ещё не играли в Zen of Sudoku, то вы упускаете что-то невероятное! Я скачал эту игру случайно, думая, что это просто очередная головоломка, но теперь она стала моей ежедневной мантрой. Без неё мой день не начинается – это как кофе, но для мозга и души! 

Сначала давайте разберёмся: Zen of Sudoku – это не просто стандартный судоку, где ты заполняешь сетку цифрами. Здесь акцент на релаксе и медитации. Красивые пейзажи, спокойная музыка, подсказки, которые помогают, а не раздражают, и уровни сложности от новичка до мастера. Я начинал с простых пазлов, чтобы успокоить нервы после работы, и вот уже месяц не могу остановиться. Каждый уровень – это маленькая победа, которая даёт такое чувство удовлетворения, будто ты только что спас мир!

Что делает её незаменимой? Во-первых, она тренирует логику и концентрацию, но без стресса. Вместо того чтобы злиться на ошибки, ты расслабляешься и пробуешь снова. Во-вторых, дизайн – огонь! Анимированные переходы, темы вроде леса или океана, которые погружают в зен-мод. Я даже заметил, что после игры лучше сплю и меньше нервничаю. Без Zen of Sudoku моя жизнь была бы хаосом – стресс на работе, пробки, бесконечные задачи. А теперь? Я жду вечера, чтобы сесть с за пк и раствориться в пазлах. Это не игра, это терапия!

Если вы любите головоломки или просто хотите расслабиться, скачайте немедленно. Без неё жить нельзя – поверьте, я проверял!

[h1][b]Zen of Sudoku: A Tranquil Puzzle Experience[/b][/h1]
[hr][/hr]
[h2][b]Gameplay[/b][/h2]
At its core, [i]Zen of Sudoku[/i] is exactly what it sounds like: a digital Sudoku experience with a focus on relaxation and accessibility. For those unfamiliar with Sudoku, it’s a logic-based number puzzle where you fill a 9x9 grid so that every row, column, and 3x3 subgrid contains the numbers 1 through 9 without repetition. The game simplifies the concept, making it approachable for complete beginners like I was before trying it.

The tutorial is a standout feature. It walks you through the basics of Sudoku without ever feeling patronizing. By the time you're done, you'll have the confidence to tackle your first grid. The difficulty levels are highly customizable, ranging from easy puzzles that feel like a gentle warm-up to brain-busting challenges that require serious thought. This flexibility ensures that the game has something for everyone, whether you're a newcomer or a seasoned Sudoku pro.

Controls are intuitive and easy to master, with a clean interface that makes placing numbers or notes simple. There's also an option to highlight conflicts, which is a lifesaver if you're prone to mistakes (like me). The game respects your pace, allowing you to take your time or try speedier solving sessions if you're in the mood for a challenge.
[hr][/hr]
[h2][b]Aesthetics and Atmosphere[/b][/h2]
What makes [i]Zen of Sudoku[/i] stand out from other Sudoku apps is its atmosphere. The visuals are soft and minimalistic, with calming colors and smooth animations that enhance the “zen” experience. It's a game designed to soothe your senses as much as it is to challenge your brain.

The sound design is equally lovely. Gentle, meditative music plays in the background, creating a peaceful environment that’s perfect for unwinding. The sound effects—like the soft click when you place a number—are subtle and satisfying, never intrusive or annoying. It’s clear the developers wanted the entire experience to feel like a meditative exercise, and they nailed it.
[hr][/hr]
[h2][b]History and Context[/b][/h2]
[i]Zen of Sudoku[/i] was developed by the creators of [i]Osmos[/i], another game known for its tranquil, meditative qualities. Released in the mid-2000s, this title aimed to bring the then-popular Sudoku puzzle craze to PC gamers in a way that emphasized relaxation over competition. It was a fresh approach, contrasting with other Sudoku games that often felt sterile or overly utilitarian.

Despite being a relatively niche title, it has aged well, thanks to its timeless gameplay and polished design. It runs flawlessly on modern systems and takes up minimal space, making it an easy addition to your library.
[hr][/hr]
[h2][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/h2]
[i]Zen of Sudoku[/i] is a gem of a game that proves you don’t need flashy graphics or complex mechanics to create something memorable. It’s perfect for beginners who want to learn Sudoku and for veterans who want a relaxing way to enjoy the puzzles they love.

The fact that it’s free only adds to its appeal. With zero risk involved, there’s no reason not to give it a try. If you’re looking for a peaceful, engaging experience that you can return to whenever you need a mental break, [i]Zen of Sudoku[/i] is a fantastic choice.

It may not revolutionize gaming, but it doesn’t need to—it’s content with being exactly what it promises: a calm and enjoyable Sudoku experience that helps you find your inner zen.

I actually bought Zen Of Sudoku (off Steam) back in the day, when they were using it to raise money for, IIRC, Natural Selection II. I randomly stumbled across it, saw it was free now, and decided to dive back in.

This is almost 2 decades old, and, let's be honest; it shows. Chiefly, the low, completely fixed, resolution means that, on my PC, it's far too small to run in a window, but also completely breaks my desktop scaling if I run it in fullscreen... and as someone who loves to have something on my second monitor while playing, that's not great.

But the resolution aside, this is a fine Sudoku game. The tranquil aesthetics are lovely, the screen is very readable, and I still consider the controls for this to be a benchmark for other Sudoku games; none of this zooming over to a number panel to select a digit every time or having one hand permanently on the top row of your keyboard, it's all done by positioning within each cell. Marking is as easy as a left click, pencilling with a right-click, simple. Click a pre-filled number, or hit that number on the keyboard, to highlight every instance of it (marked or pencilled) on the board. Lovely. (Ooh, and: hit Space to auto-generate all pencil markings based on what's already filled. Lovely feature, saves so much time without actually doing anything you wouldn't have already.)

There're also plenty of nice optional features. You can turn off immediate hints for duplicate or incorrect digits, have highlights for redundant pencil markings, that sort of thing. The in-built hint system is nice as well, with one click just highlighting a space worth attention, and a second click explaining not just what you can do in that cell, but how you could have figured it out, completely with relevant highlights.

Put that along with lovely feedback as you fill in the grids, multiple difficulties, and in-game achievements, and this is still a joy to play, my favourite Sudoku game ever. For the real masters out there this may be a bit on the simple side, even on the highest difficulty, but for the rest of us, this is basically as good as it gets. And for free? Get you some.

I was there for NS1 — clans, chaos, and late‑night laughter. NS2 came along, and life pulled us apart. I haven’t touched it in years, but my fondest memory? Being swallowed whole by an Onos, staring into its abyss more times than I care to admit. Some things you never forget.

Recommended for masochists, biologists, and anyone nostalgic for clan warfare… preferably with a strong stomach.

Pros:
+ Fun multiplayer with strong team spirit
+ Unique asymmetrical gameplay (marines vs aliens)
+ Strategy and coordination matter as much as reflexes
+ Nostalgic clan vibes if you’ve got friends to squad up

Cons:
- You do need to actually aim and shoot—no hiding behind strategy alone
- Learning curve can be steep for newcomers
- Player base isn’t as bustling as it once was
- Frequent encounters with the Onos’s digestive tract (immersion, but not the kind you asked for)
- Oh right, and you need to have a stomach for colorful language and a lack of support from people who no longer play games.

I've tried this game a few times, and while it's sometimes fun, the fun doesn't last. It's extremely one-sided with a strong bias towards the aliens. Once they get virtually any of their upper-tier units, the game is already over. If even one player has one, they can run into a group of marines, kill one or two, then run away to recover for a few seconds before repeating. I have never seen the marines successfully defeat one, even in as many as a 4-on-1 encounter, and it gets worse when you remember that any and all of the alien players can become one. Early-game in any match is usually fun, but don't be fooled. Maybe you'd enjoy it as an alien, but it's just not a balanced game.

Natural Selection 2 is the kind of game that makes you question why the industry keeps making the same shooter every year.

One bloke plays Commander, desperately trying to hold the team together like an exhausted manager during a night shift, while everyone else either follows orders or wanders off to become alien food.

It's StarCraft meets Counter-Strike, except everyone is stressed, resources are scarce and a giant alien spider is sprinting towards you at Mach 3.

The atmosphere is incredible, teamwork actually matters and winning feels earned instead of handed out like participation trophies.

Unfortunately, being brilliant and niche is a dangerous combination. Finding populated servers can sometimes feel like searching for Bigfoot.

But when a match clicks? Few multiplayer experiences come close.

Natural Selection 2 didn't deserve to become a hidden gem.

It deserved an entire genre built around it.

El juego de Star Wars mas sobrevalorado de toda la saga, en ningún momento sentís que estas jugando con un escuadrón de élite. Lo único relevante está en la primera hora, después por mas que se intentan crear situaciones nuevas, todo se sigue percibiendo igual. 
La monotonía es el mayor problema del juego, no es el hecho de ir de un punto A hacia uno B, el problema son los enemigos repetidos (en el sentido estético) y reciclados (en el sentido jugable) hasta el hartazgo, tener que hackear 50 mil consolas y vivir en las estaciones de bacta porque son tan élites que no pueden tomar botiquines del suelo.  
¿Terminaste una misión? La república te lo agradece con una foto de la próxima nave donde estarás y un texto de 2 líneas que siempre transmite lo mismo, es decir, muchas ganas de seguir jugando... 
El gunplay es horrible, el rifle automático queda totalmente inútil luego de la primera misión porque en las siguientes todos los enemigos son esponjas de balas que hasta las torretas fijas parecen que tiran piedras del poco daño que hacen. Lo único decente para disparar es el lanzagranadas y la escopeta. lo otro es tosco e incómodo.
Las mecánicas están muy verdes, a veces abrís una puerta sigilosamente y los enemigos están mirando hacia tu dirección, y como de esta forma permanece cerrada, estas obligado a acercarte para que se abra y comerte todos los tiros porque no vas a tener cobertura alguna. Los compañeros se manejan bien en cuanto el juego te lo permite, ponete acá y tira tiros, granadas, curate y nada más, esperaba diseños de niveles con mas coberturas donde, justamente, se cubran y no que estén recorriendo todo el sector o parados frente a una piedra recibiendo todo el daño. 
El año no es excusa y esto no envejeció mal porque los videojuegos no envejecen, siempre fue un fps repetitivo y superficial desde el primer día, por estos años ya estaban los Jedi Knight donde es increíble que tengan un gunplay, diseño de niveles y sentido de progresión muchísimo mejor que esto.

Star Wars: Republic Commando es sin duda uno de los mejores productos concebidos sobre los clones que la saga tiene para ofrecer.

Encarnando a "Boss" desde su nacimiento en Kamino, hasta la famosa batalla de Kashyyk, este juego logra capturar perfectamente lo oscuro y frio de las Guerras Clonicas desde la perspectiva de el Escuadron Delta, que a medida transcurren los eventos de la misma, forman un vinculo de hermandad inseparable.

En términos de gameplay, logra combinar el combate y mecánicas al estilo Halo CE, junto con un toque táctico pudiendo ordenar a cada integrante del escuadrón una serie de acciones para cambiar el rumbo de la pelea.

Si hay algo que debo destacar es lo extenso que se puede volver en ciertas partes, repitiendo en varios niveles el mismo escenario y volviéndolo tedioso o interminable. Y por otra parte, su desenlace brutal, teniendo en cuenta su fecha de salida al dia de hoy todavia no contamos con un final DIGNO para la Delta Squad.

One of if not the best Star wars FPS games. Acomplishes what it sets out to do, giving a gritty atmosphere and regular soldier perspective of the Clone Wars. 

Can get surprisingly difficult and encourages you to use your squad to beat encounters, gunplay is simple but the way you use your squad can turn the tide very easily. The game flips this aspect on its head by having certain levels where you go solo, really highlighting how vulnerable you can be without your team. Enemies can be down right intimidating and melt you in seconds if you don't play smart (Super Battle Droids live up to their name for once).
Fantastic music, you wouldn't be able to tell it came from a Star Wars game, but it does sometimes bring in the classics from the movies. 
For a game as gritty as it is the squadmates have some great chemistry with each other and a lot of humor, bouncing off each other naturally. (Some funny voice lines too if you do something stupid like blowing yourself up). Don't expect a deep story or anything like that, it's a simple adventure of Delta Squad being bad@sses.

Originally played on the Xbox way back, and still lives up to the memories in 2026, absolutely worth the buy, my only complaint is no sequel but knowing Disney these days maybe it's for the better.

Republic Commando is the Clone Clone Wars experience, The Combat is pretty basic and works for the game nothing special or spectacular, The narrative and writing however are absolutely wonderful, They really hit that comradery that's always shown when it comes to the clones, Delta Squad is a delight to hear banter and the writing once again just gives off peak "Clone Wars" (The Show) Vibes (You can actually see Delta Squad in The Clone Wars, Season 3 Episode 14, Which is just stellar).

It is a pretty short game and you can reasonably do pretty much everything in around 10 hours give or take, I'd personally recommend waiting for a sale even though this is a great game, I'd also recommend to check out the various mods after you beat the main game (ModDB is the main hub for this one), There are a ton that add so much to the game and even some that attempt to modernize it, They are a blast and also hit that Clone Wars Vibe so well.

Overall Republic Commando is a wonderful if short game, That anyone who loves Star Wars or the Clones (Who doesn't like the clones?) in general should absolutely play.

Any avid fans of Star Wars should definitely give this game a try. The highlight of this game is definitely the dynamics among Delta Squad. As you go through, you'll get a lot of good banter and comms between the members, of which highlights the tight bonds these troopers have. It really helps that the individual members have their own, unique voice actors.
For more casual fans, I admit that you might find yourself getting a bit sleepy from the gameplay. The shooting can feel a bit clunky, and combat sections can drag for a bit. 
With that being said, I do not think the combat is bad, just a bit tedious. There is an element of strategy involved. As the leader of Delta Squad, you are responsible for leading your brothers into battle, and ensuring that they don't overwhelmed by enemies.
You'll have to consider where your squadmates will be best positioned during a combat encounter. Sometimes you might want them to fall back when the opposition is overwhelming, spread out at different points to cover more area across the arena, or a mix of both where a couple squadmates provide covering fire while you move in.
You also have 5 weapon slots (Pistol, Assault Rifle, Sniper, Grenade Launcher, and an interchangeable special weapon), plus a wide array of grenade options. So, you have many options for approaching combat encounters.

[b]‘Why don’t you ask me something easy, like a nice murder or a boatload of penicillin?’[/b]

[i]Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™[/i] is LucasArts’s twoth [i]Indiana Jones[/i] point-and-click adventure game and is inspired by an actual obsession that certain Fascists had with finding Atlantis. It certainly starts off promising, and for a while I was ready to give it a positive review. However, my experience steadily rolled downhill as I went on and eventually it reached the point where the fun that I had was outweighed by the problems.

The most glaring and persistent worry with this product is something that I like to call ‘adventure game logic’, wherein you can only bypass a game’s obstacles by totally disregarding common sense. A perfect example was the very first time that I got stuck: Indiana can’t get past somebody because he needs to tell him the title of a work. At first you would think that somebody in Azores could help you since he is familiar with said work, but he demands an artefact and the only one that comes to mind is trapped in some ice. Do you learn the title by helping somebody get out the artifact and then giving that to another character? Nope. When I consulted the official hintbook, I found out that after picking a very specific dialogue option with someone, you learn the work’s title from… an animal, and there isn’t even a tip for this built in the game.

Okay, nearly adventure game is bound to have a dud like that, so for a while I brushed it off as an isolated issue. Nonetheless, I noticed more nonsense as I was progressing, like needing to stick gum on one of Indiana’s boots to help him move up somewhere, and discovering a book by destroying something (which somehow leaves the said book undamaged). The latter challenge was so ridiculous that it had me laughing out loud for nearly one minute after I solved it, but believe it or not, for a while I was managing well without reconsulting a guide. I did not even mind the clunky overhead sections in North Africa.

It was when I arrived at the third and final act of the story that my patience was running out and I was forced to repeatedly reconsult a guide. While some of the puzzles in this game remain entertaining, a few of them are obnoxiously frustrating thanks to how poorly written the ‘clues’ are. Not even the official hintbook was helpful when I finally learnt that you have to spin three discs in a very specific direction before you can advance, a direction which contradicts what you would guess from reading the clues.

At one point Indiana arrives at a (mostly boring) labyrinth polluted by a handful of goons. Unfortunately, the janky combat system from [i]Indiana Jones® and the Last Crusade™[/i] is back. The good news is that the combat is less hard to win as well as easier to avoid, with Indiana healing oftener and most of the foes being more willing to take ‘no’ for an answer. That said, the goons in the labyrinth eventually respawn after Indy clobbers ’em and it is boring to repeatedly either fight or evade the goons. Navigating this labyrinth is even more irksome when you realise that you were supposed to reuse an item that you left behind because you naturally thought that you no longer needed it, and there are many items exactly like that. (At least you can’t softlock yourself… as far as I’m aware.) There are more problems that I could name — such as a tediously slow raft and a hideously janky minigame involving a submarine — but I have to keep this review at a manageable length.

I don’t blame others for liking this game: there is no question that it improves over [i]Indiana Jones® and the Last Crusade™[/i] in every single way. It has a gripping setting, there are multiple ways to replay it, some of the puzzles are fine, and for the most part it manages to recreate the tone of the films, albeit with a few pieces of LucasArts’s trademark humour inserted and the action toned down a little. I enjoyed parts of it and it has plenty of good ideas, so it pains me to leave it a negative review, especially being an [i]Indiana Jones[/i] fan, but I have to be honest and say that the fun that I had simply did not make up for the misery that I endured.

The sound is fine. The sound effects feel surprisingly sparser than those in [i]Indiana Jones® and the Last Crusade™[/i], but they are of higher quality and more tolerable. Doug Lee, while not sounding quite like Harrison Ford, did the best that he could and gave a mostly adequate performance. Indy’s sidekick sounds fine, too. The other actors are more amateurish and sound like stereotypical cartoon characters. The music is good: although some of the tracks don’t fit the setting, as they involve ’90s synthesisers, they sound groovy in their own right even if none of them be particularly memorable. Now, here’s the problem: I had trouble getting the music working on the Steam release and had to rely on ScummVM, which I could not get to work with Steam either (which is why it [i]looks[/i] like I hardly played this game). Lastly, the Steam release lacks options for foreign languages, so you’ll have to do some fiddling to make those work.

For an early ’90s title, [i]Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™[/i] looks gorgeous: most of the scenes are beautifully detailed. On the other hand, the character models, while adequate, are less impressive (especially at distances), and nearly all of the animations are jerky, with some being downright crude. The biggest problem with the graphics, though, is that it is not always clear what is relevant or irrelevant to the gameplay, resulting in several pixel hunts.

Ultimately, I can’t recommend [i]Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™[/i] except to diehard fans of the series. You’d be better off watching a longplay or reading the comic book adaptation, but if you must collect it anyway, get it as part of the Indiana Jones Collection when it goes on sale. It certainly has its charm, but the sheer amount of frustrating nonsense makes it harder to enjoy than it needs to be.

[h1]Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis[/h1] (Masterclass point-and-click VGA briliance) https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3794061186&fileuploadsuccess=1 Zde LucasArts definitivně demonstrovali svou nadvládu nad sado-masochistickým designem tehdejší Sierry. Žádné zkoušení všeho na všechno v panice, žádná smrt za každým rohem a žádné otravné bušení příkazů do textového parseru. Jen čistý, geniální point-and-click design. Hal Barwood a Noah Falstein stvořili mistrovské dílo, které svou scenáristickou kvalitou a atmosférou totálně deklasovalo Hollywood a pro milovníky (herní) archeologie zůstává tím pravým vrcholem série. 

Tato plná CD „Talkie“ verze navíc ukazuje absolutní audio-vizuální strop své doby. Zatímco 256barevné VGA rozlišení servíruje nádherné, ručně kreslené lokace od Barnettova muzea až po nacistické ponorky, pod kapotou vrčí zvukový klenot... Atmošku prostě nejvíce tahá a zajišťuje systém iMUSE, kde americký herní skladatel Michael Z. Land (často uváděný jako Michael Land) stvořil prostě klenot. Spolu s ním na soundtracku pracovali Clint Bajakian a Peter McConnell. Hudba totiž dynamicky reaguje na každý váš krok a plynule mění motivy podle nebezpečí na obrazovce, což v kombinaci s kompletním dabingem tvoří naprosto dokonalý interaktivní film. Korunou celého designu je pak volba tří naprosto odlišných herních cest (Wits, Team, Fists) v polovině příběhu, což hře dává nevídanou znovuhratelnost.

GAMEPLAY
Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis is a good point and click game, and a cartoony adventure of Indiana Jones.  Almost all the objects are sitting in plain sight yet you need to discover the creative, non-sensical ways that the game has you combine items with your environment to escape situations.
There are quite a few maze-like sections such as Caves, Lava Doors, Atlantis temples that help if you a draw a map out to remember where to go. There are some movement games such as landing an air balloon, running a camel around, or a car chase, that don't need a lot of gamer skill but are a little quirky to control.
There were probably like 15 or so harder to discover, "ah ha" moments of the game where you feel like you finally see what to do or where to go, rather than just clicking everywhere, and I enjoyed those moments.  A bonus design is that your character cannot fall off ledges as some other point and click adventures sometimes have, and the game respectably gives you a fair warning to get you out of danger.

INDEFINITE
My biggest issue with this game is that it has a few indefinite qualities and randomness that made it feel too loose. After playing the game I am reading that some objects like the Plato book can be in three various places; no wonder the puzzles felt indefinite like I was doing a lot without result.  There are rotating disks puzzles that made me groan every time they occurred, because the supposed "clues" from the book of Plato barely lined up the puzzle, and I would resort to trying every combination. Central to the game are special magic beads that you need to apply to select places, but later you can actually run out of beads if you try them on the wrong places.  Although you can replenish the beads, I don't know why they made this special item CONSUMABLE, and the game does not even tell you how many you have in your "handful of beads".  During the beginning of the game, after you use objects, the game kindly repicks them up for you if you need them again.  Later in the game it stops repicking up items, and you need to backtrack to far away rooms to re-pick up items that you used.

THREE PATHS
The game has three alternate paths (Teams, Fists, and Wits-which I choose) that give the game a variety of methods to pass areas, and each has an alternate area(s) to explore. I thought this variety of paths was confusing as some areas in the game would not yield results.  I spent a lot of time at The Dig Site and confusingly could not find anything to further my adventure, so I do not know if this had to do with various game path logic.  A handful of objects in this game felt under utilized or you wastefully carry them through the rest of the game and continue to try them everywhere to no avail. Perhaps there are more options i missed but it made some parts feel confusing and not definite.

GOOD ENOUGH
I enjoyed this game enough because I was looking for an Indiana Jones story and was willingly to be patient with some of the trial and error style of gameplay.
It ended up to be a decent adventure with enough fair puzzles to rack your brain, and with enough creative solutions to make you excited when your actions finally work to help Indy save the girl and once again beat the Nazis.

[h1][b] Reseña de Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™ es una aventura de apuntar y clic de los años 90 que te suelta en una “película” interactiva donde leer, observar y pensar es el verdadero látigo. Vas de pistas, mapas, diálogos y rompecabezas mientras Indy hace lo que mejor sabe: meterse en problemas arqueológicos que definitivamente NO deberían tocarse.

La propuesta es simple y deliciosa: exploración, conversación, inventario y puzzles con una trama de culto y una vibra retro atmosférica. Primera impresión: esto no te va a “llevar de la mano”; te va a empujar por un acantilado y luego te va a preguntar por qué no volaste. Y sí, es parte del encanto… y del crimen.

[h2]Lo que el Látigo Aplaude y lo que la Atlántida te Cobra[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Rompecabezas clásicos que te hacen sentir inteligente… cuando por fin ceden.  
  Buena trama con energía de aventura pulp noventera: misterio, persecución y “esto es mala idea” constante.  
  Gran banda sonora retro que hace que hasta abrir un cajón se sienta épico.  
  Ambientación atmosférica: pixel-art con personalidad y dirección artística de “clásico de culto”.  
  Steam Cloud y Préstamo familiar: comodidades modernas para un fósil orgulloso.  

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Dificultad con mentalidad de los 90: a veces es “puzzle”, a veces es “adivina lo que pensé”.   
  Interfaz/ritmo de aventura clásica: si vienes de lo moderno, vas a extrañar calidad de vida.   
  Sin logros: cero caramelitos de dopamina para presumir en tu perfil.   
  Comunidad diminuta (12 jugadores): acá no hay “tendencia”, hay arqueología social.

[h2]Conclusión (Muy Bueno)[/h2]
Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™ es de esas aventuras que hoy serían “demasiado lentas” para algunos y “demasiado inteligentes” para otros. Y justo ahí está lo controversial: no está diseñado para complacerte; está diseñado para retarte. Si eso te molesta, perfecto: el juego ganó.

Con apenas 12 jugadores rondando actualmente, esto no es un fenómeno moderno: es un club de arqueólogos tercos. Pero con 1337 recomendaciones totales, queda clarísimo que el culto no es casualidad: hay sustancia, historia y una ambientación que todavía se siente especial.

The Fate of Atlantis isn't just a classic point-and-click; it is arguably the finest Indiana Jones story ever told. It understands the heart of the franchise better than Hollywood itself. Em algum momento da minha vida eu tive acesso a uma demonstração desse jogo, mas eu juro que não recordo quando, da mesma maneira que eu tive contato com a demo do adventure de Ace Ventura. Ele ficou na minha memória como um jogo que eu queria terminar, só não sabia quando. Enfim, o fiz.

Sempre me surpreendo lembrar como o gênero point'n'click já foi grande nos EUA a ponto de atrair franquias renomadas de cinema, motivo pelo qual esses jogos possuem roteiros compatíveis com as obras de origem.

Se Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade é uma excelente adaptação do seu irmão na telonas, Fate of Atlantis estreia um roteiro original, que futuramente também foi adaptado para os quadrinhos e para outro jogo de ação que deus me livre de jogar aquela bomba.

Ele é considerado um dos melhores adventures da história na minha opinião mais pela coerência geral dele e a qualidade típica de Hollywood do que por alguma excelência de game design. Mas isso não tira o mérito de experimentação do jogo com mecânicas diversas interessantes, como controle de veículos, montagem de quebra-cabeças mais "físicos", saindo da interação básica com objetos e pessoas por meios dos tradicionais verbos da linguagem SCUMM.

Mas nem tudo são flores, pois o tenebroso boxe visto em The Last Crusade retorna aqui. O game feel dessa mecânica rivaliza com o combate horrendo de Harvester, outra catástrofe que já tive o desprazer de jogar. É possível jogá-la com o mouse, mas a forma mais eficiente - ou menos torturante - de fazê-lo é usando o teclado numérico...que o meu atual teclado não tem (cry).

Ainda bem que é possível escolher rota onde praticamente não se entra em combate físico, e sempre há uma forma de evitá-los porque...pqp, que gambiarra tenebrosa. Muito feliz que, diferente de seu predecessor, puseram soluções alternativas dos encontros para não precisar recorrer ao mano-a-mano nunca. Sacada de muito bom gosto.

Não tenho particularmente nenhuma crítica ao sistema de IQ Points, mas sinceramente não fede nem cheira, nem agrega e nem estraga. Inofensivo o defende bem.

O nível dos quebra-cabeças é o de sempre da época, né? Não dá pra chamar de particularmente mais difícil que seus contemporâneos, como o caso de Loom, Harvester e Monkey Island 2, que doidera esses jogos, mas também não é particularmente mais fácil que nenhum outro.

Pra todos os efeitos, padece do mesmo mal de ser um jogo curto (até que não tanto, me tomou quase 9h pra terminar) cuja dificuldade de solução de seus quebra-cabeças estende sua duração pra não só criar um atrito característico do gênero, como também incentivar o diálogo com a comunidade online, ou mesmo a compra de guias, na época, claro, já que na atualidade uma olhadinha rápida na Internet resolve qualquer beco sem saída.

A qualidade narrativa não perde para outras mídias baseadas na franquia apesar de, na minha opinião, não ser lá nenhum grande primor de roteiro. É clichê de Hollywood simples, mas um clichê bem redondinho, e isso é capaz de satisfazer qualquer fã do personagem.

Foi muito bom poder fazer esse resgate no tempo de um jogo que por muito tempo ficou na pilha do backlog, e confesso que estou realmente feliz por tê-lo terminado.

Warning: just like the [b]Last Crusade[/b] re-release, press Alt+S to do yourself a favor and remove the horrible smoothing filter.

It would be a disservice to the graphics, which, with reportedly few exceptions, are all pure, amazing pixel art that can still surprise today with its level of detail.
It's far from [b]Fate of Atlantis[/b]' only quality, or even its best: this game is a culmination of everything Lucasfilm/LucasArts did over the previous years. An entirely original Indy story that captures the feeling of his adventures perfectly, bringing the player to a great variety of places throughout the world, with puzzles that can get challenging but rarely suffer from the "moon logic" that plagues other productions.
It's quite long, and that without counting how at least half of it is within one of the three paths, which feature very different approaches to situations; you have a lot of adventuring to do before seeing all it has to offer.
Just like in [b]Last Crusade[/b], the fistfights are the weakest part, but you at least get some alternate solutions to dispatch the tougher Nazis, and they even gave the ability to press the [i]INS[/i] key to just be done with it at the cost of not getting points.

Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™

 Its a classic point-and-click adventure game from LucasArts that transports fans of the legendary Indiana Jones series to the world of the 1930s. With a captivating story, challenging puzzles, and an atmosphere that perfectly captures the spirit of the films, this game is considered one of the best adventure games of its time. It offers a new, standalone story that is nevertheless deeply rooted in the familiar Indiana Jones themes.

Story and Setting:

The game's plot revolves around the mysterious "Atlantis" legend, which Indiana Jones and his companion, Sophia Hapgood, investigate. After the Nazis learn of the existence of the fabled Atlantis, it's up to Indy to unravel the mystery before the ancient powers fall into the wrong hands. The game offers an exciting mix of archaeology, mythology and action-packed chases – all in a beautifully designed, tropical setting.

The story is divided into four major chapters that take Indy and Sophia through various countries and perilous adventures – from Iceland to the desert and the depths of the ocean. The character development, especially the burgeoning relationship between Indy and Sophia, is also a highlight.

Gameplay:

"Fate of Atlantis" utilizes the classic point-and-click mechanic typical of many LucasArts adventures of this era. Players must interact with the environment, gather clues, solve puzzles, and combine items to progress. The game's appeal lies in the variety of solutions. There are three distinct paths that change depending on the player character and decisions made throughout the game:

The Thinker – Here, puzzles are solved through pure reasoning and combining items.

The Doer – This path focuses on more action-packed scenes and physical interaction with the environment.

The Persuader – This variant emphasizes Indy and Sophia's communication and diplomacy to resolve conflicts.

The different paths not only offer increased replayability, but also interesting variations in the plot development.

Puzzles and Challenge:

The puzzles in "Fate of Atlantis" are a true highlight of the game. They are clever and challenging without being overly frustrating. They require a good understanding of the game world and a willingness to experiment. The "Thinker" path, in particular, can offer some real brain teasers, while the "Doer" path focuses more on quick thinking and action elements. The difficulty is very well balanced, ensuring that both adventure game novices and experienced players will find something to enjoy.

Graphics and Sound:
While the graphics were certainly modern in 1992, they now appear rather nostalgic. The characters and backgrounds are rendered in the typical LucasArts style, with hand-drawn animations and detailed environments. The cities and landscapes are particularly impressive, conveying an authentic impression of the various locations Indy visits on his journey.

The soundtrack, composed under the direction of Michael Land, is also a great feature of the game. The music perfectly complements the game's atmosphere and is reminiscent of John Williams' famous film scores. The voice acting is also excellent, bringing the characters to life and further enriching the story.

Conclusion:

"Indiana Jones® and the Fate of Atlantis™" is a true masterpiece of the adventure genre, perfectly capturing the charm and excitement of the Indiana Jones films. With a gripping story, diverse gameplay options, and well-designed puzzles, it offers an exceptional gaming experience that has lost none of its appeal years after its release. It's a game that will not only delight fans of the Indiana Jones films but also adventure game enthusiasts looking for a deep and rewarding experience.

Un vieux jeu qui a pris un coup de vieux visuel, mais qui possède encore le meilleur système de combat au sabre laser.

Il faut être honnête : si vous sortez de Jedi: Fallen Order ou Survivor, le choc visuel est rude. Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy accuse clairement son âge avec des graphismes datés et un level design souvent labyrinthique où l'on tourne en rond à chercher l'interrupteur pour ouvrir la porte suivante. Quant à l'histoire, elle sert surtout de prétexte pour enchaîner les missions aux quatre coins de la galaxie.

Pourtant, une fois qu'on passe outre ces défauts, le jeu a un charme fou :

Le fantasme Jedi ultime : C'est l'un des rares jeux où l'on crée vraiment son propre Padawan de A à Z. Choisir sa race (jouer un Kel Dor comme Plo Koon, un Rodien ou un Twi'lek), personnaliser sa tenue et surtout forger son propre sabre (simple, double lame ou deux sabres) procure un plaisir immédiat.

Un gameplay au sabre avant-gardiste : Pour un jeu de 2003, la physique et la chorégraphie des duels sont incroyables. Les styles de combat (rapide, moyen, lourd), les acrobaties sur les murs et la liberté d'utiliser la Force rendent chaque affrontement nerveux, technique et ultra-jouissif. On n'a jamais vraiment fait mieux en termes de sensations pures.

En bref : Un excellent petit jeu culte à faire absolument si vous êtes fan de Star Wars. Il faut accepter son côté rétro et parfois confus, mais la liberté de création et la nervosité des combats au sabre valent largement le détour.
