[h1][b] Reseña de Runaway, A Road Adventure[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Runaway, A Road Adventure es una aventura clásica de apuntar y clic en 2D con vibra retro y humor caricaturesco: eres Brian, un tipo promedio que termina metido en un caos de misterio, persecuciones y rompecabezas como si su vida fuera un episodio largo de “¿por qué a mí?”. La propuesta es la de siempre… pero bien ejecutada: explorar escenarios, combinar objetos, hablar con personajes raritos y avanzar una trama con “buena historia” (cuando el género se acuerda de que la historia importa).

La primera impresión: esto huele a clásico de PC con banda sonora “gran” y una narrativa que quiere ser comedia, thriller y road trip al mismo tiempo. Y en buena parte lo logra. Eso sí: también trae ese encanto vintage donde el juego a veces te mira y te dice “sí, era 2001, ¿y qué?”, especialmente cuando los rompecabezas se ponen creativos… o “creativos” en el sentido de “adivina lo que pensé”.

Si vienes buscando una experiencia de un solo jugador con misterio, humor y rompecabezas tipo habitación de escape, aquí hay material. Si vienes buscando calidad de vida moderna… bueno, el juego viene de una época donde la calidad de vida era sobrevivir al dial-up.

[h2]Lo Aventura y lo “Aventura porque adivinas”[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Rompecabezas y situaciones estilo escape room que te hacen sentir listo… hasta que no  
  Buena trama con misterio y ritmo de road trip que engancha más de lo que debería  
  Gran banda sonora: acompaña y levanta escenas como si tuviera salario propio  
  Tono de comedia y estilo caricaturesco que le da personalidad retro de la buena  
  Aventura clásica de apuntar y clic: puro “old school” para fans del género

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Algunos rompecabezas se sienten “lógicos” solo si compartes cerebro con el diseñador   
  Envejeció con orgullo: lo retro encanta, pero también puede sentirse tosco hoy   
  Comunidad actual mínima (3 jugadores): si buscas conversación viva… habla con los NPC  
  Sin logros: Steam se queda sin su dosis de dopamina por numeritos   
  Contenido sexual: más “eh…” que “wow”; puede incomodar o parecer innecesario

[h2]Conclusión (Muy Bueno)[/h2]
Runaway, A Road Adventure es de esos clásicos que todavía se defienden por lo que importa en una aventura: historia con misterio, humor funcional y rompecabezas que te mantienen avanzando… aunque a veces sea avanzando a base de “ok, juego, ya entendí, tú ganas”. Su estilo 2D retro y tono caricaturesco son parte del encanto, pero también el recordatorio constante de que esto no fue diseñado con las comodidades modernas en mente.

Con 644 recomendaciones totales, está claro que el juego dejó huella y tiene una reputación ganada. Pero con 3 jugadores actuales, la realidad es que hoy es más una cápsula del tiempo: lo juegas por cultura, por gusto al género y por ver por qué tantos lo recuerdan, no por subirse a la ola de moda.

Si eres fan del apuntar y clic, del misterio y de las aventuras clásicas con banda sonora fuerte, vale la pena. Si tu paciencia con puzzles “a interpretación del autor” es baja, ve con la mentalidad correcta: aquí el verdadero rompecabezas es aceptar que el juego a veces no te debe explicaciones.

Si te laten las aventuras con buena trama, humor y ese sabor retro de “antes todo era más difícil porque sí”, Runaway cumple y entretiene. Solo no esperes que Steam te premie con logros ni que la comunidad esté haciendo fiesta: esta es una cita a solas con un clásico… y con tu paciencia.

I'm really torn if I should recommend that.
It isn't bad per se, but if I ask myself "If someone asked me for a good P'n'C game, would I recommend this one", the answer is no.

It is a nice adventure all in all, but it has many downsides. 
Starts right at the, well, start. The game only runs in exclusive fullscreen on a tiny resolution. Now it is 23 years old, so that's not too much you can blame it for, but even back then at least changing resolutions or running in a window would have been normal. Older games allowed it.
The first one that will hit you ingame is that it has a tendency to tell, not show. The game starts with a guy sitting in a chair just talking about the backstory - instead of showing it. Not only is that quite boring, it also drags on. Many of those sequences show quite little and drag on longer than you'd like, infodumping things you could also have learned by gameplay.
Then the game is very pixelhunty. There's no key to highlight interactables and moving the mouse too fast will "skip over" interactable items, and often they are very tiny. So half the time you're stuck you simply didn't see something you could pick up.
Another issue is the game being not flexible enough. Even if you know or at least guess at the solution, sometimes you can't implement it because you go at it in slightly different ways than the game intended. One time for example you find a new location and at that location is a thing with a phone number. So you go to the person with communication devices, speak with them, have a topic about the new location and... nothing. So you look elsewhere. Turns out, that person was correct but you have to use the item with them, not talk to them.
In a similar vein, something stuck to me where I guessed at the correct solution but the game went out of it's way to dissuade me. It was about filling a huge tank with water. The vessel with which I transported water across 4 screens was very small so the game said "there's a litte water in the tank" after it, no visual difference. Thought I'd try it again, no change in results. Ok rule of three, again. Again no change, same text, same visuals. So I went to search for a bigger transportation method. Turns out I did it exactly right, but it needed 4 repetitions.
The game also likes to give you plenty of red herrings. Half the things in your inventory you either don't need, or need exactly once and never again, yet they stay in your inventory until the end of the chapter. Maybe I'm just too used to other adventures but items that outlived their usefulness should be "used up". Some do, far from all. Also some stuff can be interacted with earlier but don't give you anything - until you did something else. Suddenly the desk that didn't contain anything useful contains something useful. A reverse red herring so to speak. This makes some real life sense, you didn't know you needed that item before, but for a puzzle game it's awful.
Of course, there's the occasional moon logic and character inconsistencies (not touching that skeleton, eww. That other skeleton tho..) but that's kinda normal for P'n'C adventures, can't fault it too much for that.

So.. yeah, all in all not a bad adventure but as you can tell I had my issues with it.

Решил подсесть на иглу ностальгии — и вначале всё действительно сработало. Та самая рисованная графика, музыка, лёгкая авантюрная атмосфера двухтысячных. Первые главы проходятся бодро: диалоги местами наивные, но с шармом, персонажи карикатурные, сюжет абсурдный, но в духе старых квестов.

А потом наступает четвёртая глава — и начинается чистый пиксель-хантинг. Найди крошечную щётку, которая спрятана за дверью так, что её почти не видно. Камера статичная, подсветки активных зон нет, и ты просто методично водишь мышкой по экрану в надежде, что курсор где-то изменится. В какой-то момент это перестаёт быть «разгадкой загадки» и превращается в борьбу с интерфейсом.

Логика задач. Главный герой, например, не хочет копаться в грязи. Нужно выйти на террасу и сбросить цветочный горшок вниз, чтобы… изменить ситуацию. В такие моменты понимаешь, что логика тут работает по принципу «потому что так задумано», а не «потому что это естественно».

Заскриптованность тоже даёт о себе знать. Одни предметы герой подбирает с формулировкой «авось пригодится», другие — только после определённого диалога или скрипта. Листья табака в кладовке — даже не подумает взять. Фонендоскоп из чемоданчика — та же история.

В итоге пришлось открыть прохождение. И вот тут случился флэшбек: в пятой главе я вдруг вспомнил, что в детстве забросил игру именно на четвёртой. Тогда не было ни гайдов, ни подсказок под рукой. Просто упёрся — и всё. Память хитрая штука: мозг оставил приятные ощущения от начала, но заботливо стёр раздражение от середины.

И ещё один момент, который сейчас бросается в глаза сильнее, чем раньше — главный герой. Он оказался довольно неприятным типом. Поджёг больницу, испортил древний артефакт Майя, напоил реставраторшу каким-то сомнительным «кофе», по его вине гибнут люди (уборщик, друг с музея) — и всё это подаётся как весёлое приключение. Такое себе приключение Шурика.

В итоге Runaway работает как капсула времени. Атмосфера и стиль до сих пор цепляют, но механики и логика загадок местами безжалостно устарели. Ностальгия есть — но теперь она с привкусом осознания, что в детстве терпения было больше, а требований к дизайну — меньше.

[h1][i]“As I walk along, I wonder
What went wrong with our love~ 🎶”[/i]
~Del Shannon, Runaway[/h1]

If I ever have to pick one single genre as my favorite, it'll be point-and-click adventures. There's nothing more cozy in the world than sitting in a dark room with some ice cream and coffee, trying to figure out what to do next in order to progress. Unfortunately, there was also a major problem with the genre. I know, I know; you've heard this story, like, a million times before. Bear with me, as it's really important to mention. I'll try to keep it short. Yes, it was the Internet.

While back in the 80s it was quite easy to pull an all-nighter in order to finally learn what happened next to our man Roger Wilco, once the Internet started to be affordable and at least one kid in class had access to all the walkthroughs out there, it was an obvious fun killer. Which was rather sad, since it was also the time when the genre peaked with games like Monkey Island 2, Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis, Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers, Broken Sword, and others. Still, despite those games being absolutely fantastic, investing in such projects started to be a pretty bad idea. I mean, come on. What's the purpose of an AAA project that can be solved in only a few hours? Doug TenNapel's The Neverhood was a nice example of that. It was a brilliant game that involved claymation, a unique setting, and a one-of-a-kind soundtrack by Terry Scott Taylor. The game was a bloody art. Guess what happened with it? You guessed it! It flopped. It's not like we stopped getting major games at that point; The Longest Journey, for example, did pretty well. It sold 200,000+ copies in about three years (which was quite good for a point-and-click title). How many copies did, say, The Sims sell, though? Almost four million. In just a year. Like I said, the point-and-click genre was in agony. It was pretty obvious that point-and-click games wouldn't last long. Publishers felt that way, the press felt that way, the audience felt that way... Guess who didn't? Some devoted devs. And that, my friends, is finally the time for us to start talking about our game of the day—Runaway: A Road Adventure.

Runaway was released in 2001. And as long as we don't count Humongous Entertainment, who were still doing their kid-oriented thing, the genre was considered dead and only small European (also, post-soviet) companies were still making such games. Which were ugly, clunky, and unpleasant about 90% of the time. And technically? Runaway was one of such games too. Technically. See, while being developed by the Spanish company Pendulo Studios (“pendulo” means “pendulum”), it didn't feel cheap. I mean, come on. Thanks to how point-and-click games don't require complicated gameplay mechanics, balancing, or other things, those are pretty easy to make. Because of that, it was often like, “Don't know what to make? Make a point-and-click adventure!” Runaway wasn't like that. If anything, it was exactly the opposite of that.

Pendulo cared. Like, for real. The guys loved the genre and wanted to make something real. And naturally, lots of people who were tired of all those clunky games like The Mystery of the Druids and Zero Critical were ready to welcome it. Did Runaway disappoint? Not at all! Heavily inspired by all sorts of movies (from Tarantino's Pulp Fiction to Stephan Elliott's The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert), it was... quite a trip, really. It had 3 CDs of content (yes, those nasty things were still a thing); there were lots of solid (not perfect, but high quality) animations, an exclusive song (performed by Spanish band Liquor), six story chapters, etc. The storytelling was also unorthodox for this kind of entertainment (one of the many problems with the genre was that devs didn't even try thinking outside the box)... It was a thing. Runaway sold well (somewhere on The Longest Journey level) and together with April Ryan's game and Benoît Sokal's Syberia, it's considered one of the games that helped to halt the genre's decline. Was it perfect, though? Well... about that.

To be completely honest with you, I kind of regretted revisiting this game many years later. See, Runaway was one of those things that shined in the moment but somehow didn't age that well. Back in the day? Seeing a certain amount of quality was more than enough. And it's still there. The game does have that certain aftertaste we all want from such stuff. You can feel Broken Sword, you can feel LucasArts... But at the same time... let's just say a certain amount of clunkiness is still there too.

Take the puzzles, for example. Sometimes, those are OK—quite intuitive, etc. But sometimes? Sometimes it's, “[i]How in the name of rotten Cthulhu's butt was I supposed to guess THAT?![/i]” Items that do nothing and some crazy pixel hunting are included. Don't get me wrong, though; I'm one of those boomers who feel heavily against so-called “hotspot highlighting.” That certain thing where you press a button and instantly see all the active elements on screen. You know, the one that's included in, like, every single point-and-click adventure nowadays (I believe it was Simon the Sorcerer II: The Lion, the Wizard and the Wardrobe that was introduced said feature to us in 1995). Personally? Not a fan. I do believe that a certain amount of pixel hunting is important in order for the player to get dopamine. Without it, the game starts to feel more like a chore. Runaway, on the other hand? Even if you feel like me, it [i]will[/i] make you want that “press Tab to win” thingy. The game also makes certain objects reusable, with absolutely no hints or indications about where exactly it wants you to check a certain container again. Our character (Brian Basco, who totally isn't “We've got George Stobbart at home,” lol) says, “there's nothing else interesting in there,” and then boom! There's suddenly a new item in there. Ridiculous.

Talking about the characters, by the way: I can't say those are terrible (I've seen much, [i]much[/i] worse in the genre), but at the same time, they are anything but iconic. The whole thing screams Broken Sword, except our lady here is a cringey damsel in distress who does nothing but be “sexy” and ask for help. [i]Eugh[/i]. Broken Sword's Nicole was a [i]person[/i]. Gina Timmins? She's nobody. Again, Runaway did fine and it's [i]that[/i] kind of a story; just... make sure not to expect too much.

And that's exactly the problem, I think. When you look back at Runaway from years later (I'm writing this a whopping 25 years since the initial release, and my monitor doesn't even support its default resolution, so I needed to use dgVoodoo 2), it feels like nothing special. Somewhat poor, even (especially since it still has some bugs and, in my case, for example, the game skipped a pretty big portion of puzzles just because I tried to leave the area). Lots of puzzles are questionable, some of the pixel hunting is ridiculous... I already mentioned all that. In other words, while looking at everything good that Steam has to offer, I'm... not even sure I can recommend it. Not in a “[i]Dude! Forget about everything else and go play this one![/i]” way, at least.

Still, it's very important for us to remember that Runaway was one of those games that helped to save the genre back in the early 2000s. And it deserves lots of respect for that. And even with all that aside? It's still quite solid. A bit too old-school for a modern audience (again, some crazy pixel hunting), a bit too clunky, and it doesn't look nearly as good as it did in its moment; but still, it's totally playable. Since point-and-click games are anything but long (you can beat Runaway in about four hours if you use a walkthrough or ask generative AI for help), there's always a demand for new ones, so... yeah. Runaway is worth playing. It totally is. Just make sure not to expect too much. It wasn't nearly as good as some of us probably remember.

I mostly enjoyed the puzzles but Runaway suffers a bit in the latter half from some reeeeaally convoluted and unexpected solutions that I absolutely needed a guide for. For example. A wrench you need falls into a muddy horse trough from a second story balcony. Your character refuses to stick his hand into it to get the wrench so what do you need to do? Obviously not kick the trough over, or find gloves, or tongs. What you have to do is find a flowerpot, and then drop that from the balcony also so it lands in the trough and splashes the wrench out of it. Obvious, huh? Well naturally your character can pick it up now, even though it's still covered in mud.

The convoluted puzzles though I could live with I think because there's not -that- many of them per chapter, but the real problem then is that the game also makes it really hard to find objects you need. You don't have modern adventure game conveniences like hotspots to highlight interactives so you have to scour scenes by eye, but objects blend REALLY well into the background and are often indistinguishable from non interactives. Some of them are also tiny, and their hitboxes seemingly smaller. I had to keep a guide handy to point me at selectable objects that I had no idea were there because their hitbox barely registered under my cursor.

I feel like Runaway is really deserving of a soft remaster and it wouldn't take much to make it solid. Just fix the resolution and graphics issues for modern platforms, make saving the game less clunky, and add a hotspot button. That's really all it needs.

Runaway: A Road Adventure is a lively, stylish point-and-click adventure that embodies the spirit of classic puzzle-driven storytelling while introducing a modern, colorful flair. Developed by Pendulo Studios and published by Focus Entertainment, the game begins with a seemingly ordinary moment in the life of Brian Basco, an introverted physics student preparing to leave New York for graduate school. Everything changes the instant he nearly hits Gina Timmins with his car, drawing him into a tangled conspiracy involving the mafia, a mysterious artifact, and a chase that sprawls across deserts, small towns, and unusual American backroads. This abrupt shift from academic life to high-stakes danger gives the adventure a brisk narrative momentum, plunging players into a story that mixes comedy, danger, and melodrama in equal measure.

The pacing and structure of the adventure reflect the point-and-click classics that inspired it. Exploration is broken into distinct chapters, each set in a beautifully illustrated environment rich with detail. Backgrounds are hand-drawn and vibrant, creating a world that feels both animated and immersive, while the characters — rendered in cel-shaded 3D — stand out against the scenery in a way that emphasizes their personalities and expressions. This stylistic blend gives the game a unique visual identity. It feels like a comic book brought to life, complete with exaggerated reactions, expressive gestures, and cinematic storytelling. The cutscenes, in particular, showcase Pendulo’s ambition to create a narrative experience that feels more like an animated film than a traditional adventure.

Puzzle-solving forms the backbone of the experience, and Runaway embraces the conventions of the genre with enthusiasm. Much of the challenge lies in deciphering how items fit together or how environmental clues interact to unlock new pathways. While many puzzles are logical and satisfying, others veer into the obscure, pushing players into elaborate item hunts or forcing them to notice very small environmental details. This adherence to old-school convention can be nostalgic for some, yet frustrating for others who prefer more streamlined modern design. Nevertheless, the puzzles are integrated well into the story progression, ensuring that every solved interaction feels like another step deeper into Brian and Gina’s twisting mystery.

The game’s humor and writing do much of the narrative heavy lifting. Brian is a somewhat awkward but earnest protagonist whose sudden entanglement with Gina forces him into situations far beyond his comfort zone. Gina herself contributes emotional depth and intrigue, serving as both a motivation and a narrative anchor. Their journey introduces a wide range of eccentric supporting characters, each adding flair to the adventure. The dialogue can be playful, dramatic, or tongue-in-cheek, often switching tones in a way that gives the journey its charm. Even when the plot leans into pulp-thriller territory, the game never loses its sense of fun, and the characters’ reactions keep the tone lively and engaging.

Where the game stumbles is in pacing and clarity. Some sections move briskly, delivering new environments and plot twists with energy, while others bog down in prolonged dialogue sequences or extended pixel hunts that slow the momentum. The linear structure leaves no room for alternate solutions, meaning players are sometimes left wandering until they discover the one very specific interaction needed to continue. These pacing bumps are understandable given the era and genre, but they may test the patience of players unfamiliar with older adventure design philosophies.

Despite these limitations, Runaway: A Road Adventure endures as a beloved entry in the modern revival of point-and-click games. Its polished presentation, charismatic cast, vibrant visuals, and dramatic sense of adventure helped reestablish Pendulo Studios as a major voice in narrative game development. It inspired sequels, cultivated a strong fanbase, and demonstrated that adventure games could still captivate audiences in the early 2000s and beyond. Even today, it remains an enjoyable blend of classic mechanics and modern style, offering a road trip filled with puzzles, personality, and colorful storytelling.

For anyone who appreciates narrative-driven games, charming art direction, and the nostalgic challenges of traditional point-and-click adventures, Runaway remains a memorable and rewarding journey worth experiencing.

[b]Runaway: A Road Adventure[/b] es una aventura gráfica en 2D de [i]point & click[/i]. Interesante y visualmente espectacular aventura de factura española. Algunas decisiones a la hora de progresar o por la resolución de algún puzle pueden resultar poco intuitivas, pero por lo general es muy satisfactorio y avanza a buen ritmo. Una buena aventura que merece tener un hueco entre los clásicos del género.

[h1]Un encuentro fortuito[/h1]
Brian Basco es un joven neoyorquino de veintitrés años que acaba de terminar la carrera de Física y al que le ofrecen la oportunidad de realizar un doctorado en la universidad de Berkeley. Pero en camino a California se topa accidentalmente con Gina quien parece huir de alguien. Querer ayudar a la pobre chica cambiará su vida para siempre.

Algunas de las situaciones son un poco inverosímiles y la transición de una a otra no siempre resulta natural, pero es entretenido y los diálogos están bien escritos. Algo que resulta curioso a la par que un tanto escandaloso es que un juego de factura española no venga en español debido a un tema de licencias, sólo viene en inglés y francés. Por suerte en la [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2859508183]sección de guías[/url] podremos encontrar las voces y textos en español.

Lo cierto es que ha aguantado el paso del tiempo de manera sobresaliente. Pese al formato 4:3, los fondos 2D están dibujados a mano y cuentan con montones de detalles y una buena resolución. Y los personajes, en 3D, están renderizados mediante [i]cel-shading[/i] lo que hace que se fusionen perfectamente con los fondos y apenas acucien el paso del tiempo. Si no fuera por algunas simples animaciones faciales al ver a los personajes de cerca, nadie diría que el título tiene más de dos décadas.

Pese a la falta de algún tipo de tutorial, el control es simple e intuitivo. Con el puntero del ratón observaremos el entorno e indicaremos dónde queremos mover al protagonista o con qué queremos interactuar mediante el botón izquierdo. El botón derecho alterna entre observar un elemento o personaje e interactuar con él, ya sea hablar, recoger, utilizar, etcétera. En la parte superior de la pantalla tendremos acceso al inventario y las opciones, pero también podremos acceder mediante el teclado con Tab y Esc respectivamente.

En cuanto a los puzles, le veo sus más y sus menos. No sería hasta más adelante que algunos de estos juegos incluyeran la opción de pulsar una tecla para ver con qué podemos interactuar o algún tipo de ayuda o pistas. Por ello, tiene algunas zonas en las que habremos de mover el puntero del ratón pixel por pixel para estar seguros de que no nos dejamos nada. Peor es algunos puzles poco coherentes, por suerte no muchos, o cuando está claro qué hemos de hacer pero el juego no nos deja porque hay que hablar con alguien u observar algo antes de poder hacerlo. Esas restricciones lineales pueden resultar un tanto frustrantes (el cuarto capítulo es un tanto nefario en ese sentido).

En cuanto al estado técnico. Lo cierto es que me ha sorprendido que, teniendo el tiempo que tiene, no haya sido necesario dar ningún rodeo o trastear con ninguna configuración para que funcione correctamente. Instalar y jugar.

La historia debería durar unas 8-10 horas. Como ocurre en este tipo de juegos, el tiempo variará un poco dependiendo de si nos atascamos más o menos y nuestra paciencia.

Runaway: A Road Adventure – Recensione

Runaway è un’avventura grafica che sa di anni 2000, di quando le storie si prendevano il loro tempo e le icone point-and-click erano piccole opere d’arte. È un viaggio on the road pieno di colori, personaggi strambi e situazioni assurde, con quel tocco da film d’avventura che oggi non si vede quasi più.

La scrittura è leggera, ironica, a volte sopra le righe. Brian e Gina funzionano: lui è il classico “tipo qualunque” catapultato nel casino, lei è il mistero che mette in moto tutto.
Gli enigmi? Vecchia scuola: logici, ma spesso bastardi il giusto. Qualche volta strappi i capelli, ma fa parte del DNA delle avventure.

Pro:

Storia divertente, con atmosfera da film anni ’90.

Personaggi memorabili e dialoghi ben scritti.

Stile grafico cartoon piacevole ancora oggi.

Belle musiche che ti riportano indietro nel tempo.

Contro:

Alcuni enigmi sono un po’ troppo macchinosi.

Ritmo altalenante in certi capitoli.

Interfaccia datata, ma ci sta: è parte del pacchetto nostalgia.

Verdetto:
Runaway è una cartolina vintage dal mondo delle avventure grafiche. Se ami il genere, se ti mancano quelle vibrazioni alla Broken Sword, o se vuoi una storia scanzonata da goderti con calma, qui trovi una piccola gemma che ancora regge botta.

Voto personale: 8/10 – Una road-trip avventurosa che profuma di altri tempi.

[h1]Uma aventura que mais parece um filme da Sessão da Tarde[/h1]

Runaway: A Road Adventure é um point and click que exige do jogador uma predisposição específica: encarar a experiência como se estivesse assistindo a um daqueles filmes leves e absurdos da "Sessão da Tarde". Se você não entrar nesse espírito, há grandes chances de se frustrar.

[b]Enredo: do nonsense ao bizarro[/b]

A história é uma mistura caótica de elementos: máfia, misticismo, ocultismo, povos indígenas e até alienígenas. Tudo isso tratado com uma leveza quase cômica, como se nada tivesse real importância. O enredo não é envolvente nem surpreendente e nem tenta ser. Ainda assim, de forma quase inexplicável, você se vê envolvido, ajudando personagens por puro acaso. Os protagonistas são meros instrumentos do roteiro, sem profundidade ou carisma. Você não se importa com ninguém, apenas segue adiante, curioso para ver qual será a próxima maluquice.

[b]Visual: bonito, mas problemático[/b]

Graficamente, o jogo impressiona, mesmo hoje. Os cenários são bem desenhados, com um estilo artístico caricato que funciona bem dentro da proposta. Os personagens têm proporções estranhas e rostos esquisitos, mas isso parece intencional, parte do charme visual. O problema é que a direção de arte e o design dos puzzles parecem não ter conversado. O jogo abusa do famigerado "pixel hunting": objetos essenciais ficam escondidos em áreas escuras ou mal sinalizadas. Um exemplo frustrante ocorre logo no início, quando você precisa encontrar uma seringa que simplesmente não está visível só ao passar o cursor por um canto escuro da estante é que o nome do item aparece. Isso quebra a imersão e dá a sensação de que os quebra-cabeças foram pensados depois dos cenários, e não o contrário.

[b]Jogabilidade: simples, mas inconsistente[/b]

A mecânica segue o padrão do gênero: clique para andar, interaja com objetos, use ou examine itens. Porém, a execução é inconsistente. Um exemplo claro é a bolsa da personagem Gina: ao clicar em "olhar", o protagonista apenas comenta sobre ela; ao clicar em "usar", ela vai para o inventário. Mas para encontrar os itens dentro da bolsa, você precisa abrir o inventário e usar a opção "olhar" novamente e às vezes, repetir esse processo mais de uma vez para encontrar tudo. Em outros momentos, o jogo ignora essa lógica e adiciona os itens automaticamente. Essa falta de padrão confunde e atrapalha a fluidez da experiência.
Outro ponto negativo é a mecânica de espera: em certas situações, você precisa aguardar que um personagem conclua uma tarefa para prosseguir. Mas essa espera se resume a sair da área e voltar, o que se torna um vai-e-volta desnecessário. Uma solução mais criativa, como inserir um puzzle nesse intervalo, teria sido muito mais interessante.

Runaway: A Road Adventure é um jogo que pode agradar quem busca uma experiência leve, descompromissada e recheada de situações absurdas. É como assistir a um filme bizarro de domingo à tarde: você sabe que não vai mudar sua vida, mas pode render boas risadas e momentos curiosos. Apesar de seus problemas de design e narrativa rasa, há valor na proposta especialmente se você estiver no clima certo para embarcar nessa viagem nonsense.

The game looks great and starts promising, but soon the fun is spoiled.

- There is a lot of pixel hunting. Sometimes you have to find an object that's only a few pixels wide, or an object that blends in with a much bigger object. Without hotspots these really suck, and the most likely reason you get stuck is because you've missed a small but important item.
- One of my biggest no-go's when it comes to adventure games are objects that either become interesting for the character when it wasn't before ("oh suddenly I need this bucket, while 5 minutes ago I said I didn't need such a rusty thing") or -and this is even worse- items that suddenly hold more items than they previously did. For example, there's a closet in the game that'll give you an item. If you come back at a later time, after having talked to someone, it suddenly contains another item that you need. You might think this is so the player won't get overwhelmed with items, but this game throws so much stuff at you that I don't believe that. It's just padding, and I hate that in adventure games. There's nothing that hints you that there is a new item there.
- The main character is the biggest wuss ever. He literally doesn't want to get his hands dirty. When an object lands in the mud, he refuses to pick it up.
- Straight from the start you get some items in your inventory you're never going to use. Not one, but three of them. Why?
- At some point there's senseless padding in the form of waiting. “I'll do it soon”. You then have to go to the map screen, and come straight back. It's so pointless.

Because of these issues I can't give it a high score. I probably won't be picking up the second game in a hurry, but I hope it'll be a better experience if I do.

🛣️ Runaway: A Road Adventure 

Runaway: A Road Adventure is a classic point-and-click journey that still surprises, even decades later. For a game released in 2003, it’s impressively charming — with a stylish presentation, lively characters, and a great soundtrack. The story may seem a bit cliché at first, but it’s told with flair and that early-2000s movie feel. The protagonist narrates his adventure like in an old road film, which adds personality.

The gameplay is typical for the genre — lots of exploration, dialogue, and item puzzles. However, some puzzles are quite unintuitive: you understand what needs to be done, but not how. Without a guide, it’s easy to get stuck since the game gives no clear hints.

Visually, the blend of 2D characters and 3D backgrounds still works beautifully. The art style feels warm and cinematic. Characters are expressive — the hero is naive yet likable, the heroine is charming, and the side characters are colorful and memorable. It feels like playing through a hand-drawn movie.

✅ Pros:
✔ Atmospheric, movie-like adventure story.
✔ Charming blend of 2D and 3D visuals.
✔ Distinctive, expressive characters and good voice acting.
✔ Excellent soundtrack and ambient music.
✔ Mature tone — crime, deception, romance, and danger.

❌ Cons:
➖ Some puzzles are illogical or too cryptic without hints.
➖ Occasional crashes on modern systems (especially in Chapter 4).
➖ Certain actions only trigger from very specific positions.
➖ Story is engaging but not deeply layered — more like a light adventure film.

📝 Conclusion
Runaway: A Road Adventure is a solid and heartfelt classic of the genre. It’s stylish, fun, and nostalgic — a game that feels like an early-2000s movie brought to life. It’s not perfect, but it has charm, humor, and genuine spirit.

Rating: 7.5/10. A warm, atmospheric adventure with soul — perfect for fans of old-school point-and-click storytelling.

🎮 Fun Facts:
• Developed by Pendulo Studios, a Spanish team that later created Runaway 2, Runaway 3, and Yesterday Origins.
• One of the first adventure games to combine 2D animation with 3D backgrounds.
• Features over 100 animated scenes and 30 minutes of cutscenes.
• The soundtrack, including songs by Lighthouse Family, became a fan favorite.
• The game’s success made Pendulo Studios known as “the Spanish answer to LucasArts.”

Owszem, nie jest to ta sama liga co Broken Sword czy Gabriel Knight czy gry LucasArts, ale jest naprawdę dobrze.

Największym plusem tej produkcji jest jej oprawa graficzna. Wszystkie tła są ręcznie rysowane i są przepiękne oraz bogate w detale. To się nigdy nie zestarzeje, co najwyżej rozdzielczość może być zbyt mała. Mimo że postaci są renderowane w 3D, to zastosowany na nich cel-shading i filtry sprawiają, że zdają się one również być narysowane. Inne gry z tamtych czasów, w których użyto trójwymiarowych modeli wyglądają dziś brzydko i topornie, a Runaway nadal wygląda dobrze. Podobało mi się również to, że wszystkie czynności podejmowane przez głównego bohatera są animowane, co nie jest standardem w przygodówkach, nawet tych współczesnych.

Zagadki są logiczne, raczej wszystkie mają sens, a ich rozwiązanie sprawiało mi przyjemność. W grze brak jest łamigłówek, wszystkie zagadki opierają się na interakcji między przedmiotami i otoczeniem, czyli taki przygodówkowy standard. Trudnością jest to, że gra nie posiada systemu hotspotów, interaktywnych przedmiotów jest masa i w żaden sposób nie wyróżniają się one z tła, więc powodzenia np w zauważeniu jednego gwoździa w jakiejś desce, która znajduje się gdzieś z boku ekranu. Dodatkowo bywa i tak, ze Brian, czyli główny bohater, nie może zebrać danego przedmiotu czy wejść z nim w interakcję dopóki przedmiot ten nie jest mu potrzebny. W efekcie trzeba obserwować otoczenie i zapamiętywać gdzie się widziało coś potencjalnie przydatnego, bo może będzie do tego miejsca trzeba wrócić później. Czasem bohater komentuje dany przedmiot dając znać, że może mu się przydać, ale jeszcze nie teraz, a czasem tego nie robi... Nie zacinałem się w tej grze na zagadkach, tylko właśnie w takich momentach gdy czegoś nie zauważyłem, bądź nie wiedziałem nawet, że czegoś szukam. Polecam stronę Universal Hint System, która nie daje gotowych rozwiązań (chociaż daje, jak ktoś chce), tylko delikatnie i stopniowo nakierowuje nas we właściwym kierunku. Mi kilka razy pomogła.

Fabularnie jest ok, myślę, że mogłoby być lepiej.

Segunda entrega de la trilogía que, aunque creo que mejora a la primera, sigue siendo un juego bastante pasable. Lo primero, es una pena que, por tema de licencias, un juego que es español, aquí esté en inglés y tengas que acudir a soluciones de la comunidad para jugarlo traducido. Menos mal que, como siempre, la comunidad provee a las mil maravillas. Igual que con el bug del capítulo 4, donde los copos de nieve ralentizarán tu juego hasta hacerlo injugable o, por lo que he leído, puede haber otros bugs.

Respecto al juego...es que es muy tedioso, y tiene unos personajes de lo más anodino, bastante planos y poco interesantes. Y lo peor es que el primer con el que ocurre esto es con el protagonista, que en la primera entrega era un nerd convertido en un Indiana Jones, pero que aquí, de repente, se ha convertido en un chulo mazado que se lleva a todas las chicas de calle. ¿A cuento de qué viene esa transformación? Porque tampoco lo hace más carismático.

Luego está la decisión de desaprovechar a Gina. No es que fuera un gran personaje, pero de repente se queda totalmente fuera y pasas a eliminar la dinámica de poder usar a dos personajes. Pero no te preocupes, que meten a otra tía buena para que tengas tu ración de superficialidad.

El guion es muy atropellado e inconexo, desarrollando algunos temas en exceso y, en cambio, otros, pasando muy deprisa por encima, lo que hace que haya cosas, como lo de los extraterrestres, que además de forzadísimas, apenas se entiendan a cuento de que vienen. Tampoco ayuda el hecho de haber forzado la tercera entrega, simplemente partiendo la segunda y dejando un continuará con todo abierto e inconcluso.

En cuanto al tema de puzzles, hay muchos que no tienen sentido y te harán atascarte, pero no porque no sepas qué tienes que hacer, si no porque, por ejemplo, tienes que usar un objeto con otro, pero si haces otro con uno, no vale. O tener que hablar en diferentes momentos con un personaje, repitiendo una conversación que ya has tenido, pero porque desbloquea algo a lo que antes no reaccionaba. Y como encima en las conversaciones, no se eliminan las cosas que ya has preguntado, esto hace que sea complicado de descubrir. Vamos, que quieras o no, más de una vez tendrás que acudir al sistema de pistas casi "obligado".

Por último, en algunos momentos se abusa mucho de las animaciones y vídeos y cosas que podrían haber sido parte del juego para hacer e interactuar, haciendo que estuviera más integrado, las convierten en animación y te pasas más de 5 minutos simplemente viendo una escena, lo cual te saca totalmente del juego.

Casi lo mejor es el apartado gráfico del juego, con esos fondos dibujados tan chulos que le aportan su propio carácter al juego, y haciendo que los personajes 3D queden muy bien integrados (aunque una pena de personajes 3D, que aún sabiendo que están hechos a postas los diseños - espero - da mucha grima verlos a casi todos, con esos rasgos tan desmesuradamente exagerados). Y una pena que hayan quitado la banda sonora del primero, que también era parte de su idiosincrasia.

En definitiva, juego que me ha gustado más que la primera entrega como aventura en sí, pero que sigue adoleciendo de fallos que, para mí, lo hacen ser un "quiero y no puedo" y realmente no te deja con ganas de una 3ª entrega, habiendo otras opciones mucho mejores. No te deja huella y, aunque va en la línea de las aventuras de Péndulo de la época, no acaba de ser todo lo que podría haber sido.

[h1][b] Reseña de Runaway, The Dream of The Turtle[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Runaway, The Dream of The Turtle es una aventura clásica de [b]apuntar y clic[/b] en 2D que te lanza a una historia con aire retro, humor y rompecabezas, como esos tiempos en los que los juegos no te agarraban de la manita… te agarraban del cuello y te decían: “piensa, campeón”. Aquí vienes por la trama y la comedia, y te quedas porque quieres demostrarle al juego (y a tu ego) que no necesitas un minimapa con GPS emocional.

La primera impresión es clara: es un título con [b]buena narrativa[/b] y vibra de “clásico”, de esos que se sienten hechos para gente que disfruta leer diálogos, observar escenarios y combinar objetos como si fuera alquimia doméstica. Si buscas acción, este juego te ofrece lo más cercano: [i]clic… clic… clic…[/i] y una leve crisis existencial cuando el puzzle te mira feo.

[h2]Lo Bueno y Lo “¿En serio era así antes?”[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Rompecabezas que te hacen usar la cabeza (y a veces insultar al monitor)  
  Buena trama con tono de comedia: más historia, menos “ve a matar 30 ratas”  
  Gran banda sonora: el tipo de música que te acompaña mientras fallas con dignidad  
  Sensación retro y de clásico bien marcada, ideal para fans del point & click  
  Momentos divertidos que le dan personalidad y evitan el drama eterno

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  0 logros: Steam te mira y dice “¿y tu dopamina de checklist, papá?”  
  Un jugador y ya: si querías culpar a alguien de tus decisiones, mala suerte  
  Diseño “a la antigua”: encantador… hasta que recuerdas que la paciencia no escala con la edad  
  Puede sentirse “casual” en ritmo: mucha charla, mucha observación, poca adrenalina  
  Rejugabilidad limitada: una vez sabes los puzzles, el misterio se va de vacaciones

[h2]Conclusión (Muy Bueno)[/h2]
Runaway, The Dream of The Turtle es el tipo de aventura que te recuerda por qué el point & click fue religión: [b]historia, humor, rompecabezas[/b] y una presentación retro que no pide permiso para existir. Es entretenido, tiene buena música y sabe sostenerse con narrativa, no con fuegos artificiales.

Ahora, seamos controversiales: si tu tolerancia a “probar combinaciones” es baja o vienes entrenado por juegos que te ponen una flecha gigante diciendo “AQUÍ”, esto te puede parecer lento, anticuado o directamente una conspiración contra tu tiempo libre. Y con 0 logros, Steam tampoco te aplaude… te deja en silencio, como si no hubieras hecho nada con tu vida.

Con [b]1 jugador actual[/b] y [b]317 recomendaciones[/b], queda claro que es un juego de nicho: no está de moda, pero sí tiene gente que lo banca. Si te gustan las aventuras clásicas, vale la pena. Si no, vas a preguntar “¿y cuándo empieza el juego?” mientras el juego te responde “ya empezó, genio”.

[h3]Recomendación de Compra (Recomendado si te gustan las aventuras clásicas)[/h3]

Puntuación Total: 6.8/10

Veredicto: [i]Cómpralo si eres fan del point & click y vienes por historia y puzzles; evítalo si necesitas acción, logros y gratificación instantánea.[/i]

Si te late la aventura narrativa retro con comedia y rompecabezas, Runaway cumple y entretiene con personalidad. Si tu paciencia dura menos que un tutorial, mejor no te auto-sabotees: este juego no corre… [b]te hace pensar[/b].

I think Road Adventure was quite ok adventure titles. This sequel though isn't. It manages to take all the bad aspects from original, moon logic, prolonged inconsistent plot and ungodly amount of back tracking.

Seriously this game is absolutely filled with things like you see item, it might be mentioned, but protagonist won't take it. But you speak to like person next screen and go back and all of the sudden "This item X might be very useful to me". You have to constantly and I do mean CONSTANTLY go back and forth to items and dialogue possibilities and rigorously go through them on-and-on-and-on to progress. Then there's the moonlogic in this game. It's way worse than original. I'll just blatantly throw one scene as it makes 0, absolutely zero sense. You will have to remove spark plug from chainsaw to use it in car, all is ok, makes somewhat sense, but guess what tool you need to remove spark plug? No, not a ratched, not pliers, not a wrench. Noo something like that would make somewhat sense, yes. NO you use friggin' KNIFE to remove SPARK PLUG from engine. Like who the F made some of these puzzles? Good luck getting through this one without walkthrough.

Bad design is really shame as game starts really strong and I really, really liked it from the start. In start there was fairly logical puzzles, fun plot and characters. But everything and I do mean everything falls apart around midway. One of the main character Joshua is just simply badly written character that is supposed to be funny, when it really isn't. Then the dialogue takes weird turn and everything feels like it's dragging along. There were few parts where I was simply annoyed and keep pressing mousebutton to skip dialogue as fast as possible. But wait, it gets even worse. Later on the game it somehow manages to add screens where you likely are trying to go back to speak to character, but you literally have to wait same two character talking sequence over and over again. It doesn't change, but I was grabbing to my phone in the end waiting for scene to end and to try to invoke dialogue to see if something had changed.

Then the very ending chapter. I've never ever seen such inconsistent and weird ending that's wait.... Of course it's cliffhanger that just pretty much states that we'll continue in part 3. Plus the last chapter. It's downright blatant copy of Monkey Island. Yes the game throws you into piratey scene for very lame reason and horribly tries to copy various Monkey Island things, failing in the worst possible way. Seriously at this point I didn't even smile once to stuff it tried to threw at me. It's like game somehow acknowledges it's really bad and tries to distract that it's better "loaning" from MI. Real wtf moments there.

But I'm not sure. I've read that it's supposed to be much better than this, but after completing these two titles, I seriously need a short break.

So shame as at best dialogue IS funny, characters can be interesting, art style is mostly really nice, even some voice overs are really good, though some like Joshua annoying as hell. But anyway game really shines in some parts, but then all of the sudden it falls flat on its face, like everyone making this game just would've gave up and said screw this and let's just throw some filling everywhere.

Score: 6,5 of 10 and it comes from effort it puts in at best. If you get it, get it from the deepest sales possible and download walkthrough before even starting the game

[h1][i]“It was said that you would destroy the Sith, not join them!”[/i]
~Obi-Wan Kenobi[/h1]

Runaway: A Road Adventure was anything but perfect. It was cringey at times, it suffered from some terrible pixel hunting, etc. Yet, it was the right game at the right time. Together with some others (like Benoît Sokal's Syberia, for example), it was one of those games that gave the point-and-click genre support in a time of decline. It was nothing like what Nintendo did after the infamous video game crash of 1983, of course, but still, it was one of those games that helped the genre survive. It was pretty stylish, it had an interesting narrative (for a European point-and-click adventure, that is), it looked good, and it had exclusive songs with vocals (a rare thing to see back in the day). Like I said, it was a thing. And when there's a thing? A sequel is inevitable. So, ladies, gentlemen, and all the others, please welcome Runaway 2. I mean, Runaway: The Dream of the Turtle.

And you know what? The intro looks promising. It's stylish, it comes with a new song (no famous singers, though; I wasn't even able to find out who Ryk-C is), and it feels exactly like what we all expected from a Runaway sequel. I mean, come on. The original Runaway, despite all of its flaws, was very movie-like. Heck, it was actually inspired by certain names. It was, like, the game's most powerful trait. Together with a certain amount of quality, it was something that put the original Runaway above the other European adventures that mostly aimed for quick money and didn't care about such stuff. That's what we all wanted from Runaway 2. Guess what it did? It joined “The Dark Side of the Force.”

I mean, that's it. Runaway 2 is one of those European adventures that some of us fans call “the genre rot.” You know, when the genre's in such a bad shape that no major companies really care to produce quality stuff and only small ones produce games for a quick money grab. What about indies, you may ask? Well, that's another problem. It was still the early 2000s, and the indie scene wasn't nearly as strong as it is today. With no easily accessible engines that were really worth working with (like Unity, for example) and no real demand or support, it was only starting to take form. Dave Gilbert, for example, had just dropped the very first game (as long as we don't count Bestowers of Eternity) in his Blackwell series. So, with nothing else on the market, the old fans had no other choice but to play second-grade stuff like Journey to the Center of the Earth and Agatha Christie: And Then There Were None. But OK, I keep calling those games bad, but what was wrong with them exactly? Well, Runaway 2 is a nice example of that.

What's funny is that lots of the crimes it committed were already present in the first game. All Pendulo really needed to do was learn from their previous mistakes. They didn't. Instead, they made new ones. Let's start with the dialogues. Let's just admit it: everybody hates those in these kinds of games (even when there are famous actors like  Duke Nukem himself, Jon St. John here). The point-and-click genre is built around exactly that—pointing and clicking. And the dopamine comes at the moment when you pick up the right item and put it on the right spot. Combining items included. Dialogues? Those kinda make everything vague for no real reason, aside from adding unfair difficulty. Which was kind of a thing in the pre-Internet time, when people wasted days and weeks trying to figure things out in order to brag to their friends, but quickly became a buzzkill when walkthroughs became easily accessible (wasting days on painfully confusing things was no fun anymore because there were no real-life rewards for it). And Runaway 2? It's, like, dialogue hell. You'll need dialogues to progress (there's even a part where you'll walk from one NPC to another multiple times); very often, our dude Brian will need to [i]know[/i] what to do before such options become available... That's right: the infamous “you can't use this on that because your character doesn't know that such stuff is possible or needed.” And there are, like, [i]tons[/i] of dialogues. And all of them are stupid. Screw that.

Talking about stupid stuff—that's another problem with European (post-soviet too) adventures from that period. The thing is, such games rarely (if ever) took themselves seriously. That's why the first Runaway stood out. It’s not like it wasn't cheesy at times, and yes, it was heavily comedic, but it did take itself seriously, if that makes sense to you. Runaway 2? It's just a bunch of “LOL, we don't care!” stuff tossed together. And it's so-o-o cliché! It's the same exact European thing copy-pasted from, like, every second adventure out there. Witch doctors, stoners, aliens, racist jokes... Eugh. Which is rather sad, since the main concept (and yes, there [i]is[/i] a concept here) suggests a certain amount of depth. You know how in, say, the Vaishnava tradition, the entire universe is seen as a "dream" manifested by Lord Vishnu during his cosmic slumber? The writer of Runaway 2 tried to play with the idea. Unfortunately... OK, you ever had a stoner friend? The one who, after a couple of YouTube videos, started to explain the universe to you? And you're like, “Dude, stop smoking so much!” I'm not trying to say anything about Josué Monchan (the lead writer), but that's how his work feels. And yes, this game has a different writer (the first Runaway had not one, but three: Ramón Hernáez, Rafael Latiegui Antón, and Felipe Gómez Pinilla).

Also, yes: pixel hunting is a b*tch. It was also a problem with the first game, but here it's even worse. Thanks to how dialogues and other factors keep inventing the rules on the fly without letting you know, it feels especially bad. Again, a healthy amount of pixel hunting is good for your dopamine (in my opinion at least), but honestly, this here is a nice example of how sometimes hotspot highlighting can be a good thing. And there's no excuse for not having it here. I mean, Simon the Sorcerer II happened more than ten years before Runaway 2. And the first Runaway clearly showed that pixel hunting there is a problem. Every single review complained about it. But no, Runaway 2 didn't care. At least in both of its major forms: the PC version and the Wii port (which added some sort of a hint system, in which a Jar Jar-like character named Joshua will tell you things like “cards usually belong in slots”). Cyanide (yes, [i]that[/i] Cyanide who made Styx and Call of Cthulhu) did add hotspot highlighting in their port for the Nintendo DS, but mostly because they didn't have a choice—the game is completely unplayable on the DS without it (and even with it, it's not really a nice experience thanks to how hard it is to see a thing).

[i]Anyway[/i], the tragedy of Runaway 2 is that it pretty much destroyed everything that used to make the first one good and became “yet another one of those.” Take any European (or post-soviet) adventure from that time period and that'll be it. Heck, if anything, some of those actually did better. So Blonde, for example, while having a similar approach, felt much smoother and even threw in extra content (mini-games) in the Wii and DS ports (something that Runaway 2 didn't).

So, what's the verdict? Is it worth getting back to this game nowadays? My answer is no. Not a single reason. The genre's doing great with indies today, with most of such games being heavily conceptual. Low budget? Sure. But still heavily conceptual. And it's not like there's a lack of those. You want a good game? Aim for those. As for Runaway 2? Well, it's playable (may require dgVoodoo2 on modern systems, though), but like I said, it's “one of those.” And when it's about “those,” it doesn't really matter which game you pick up—Runaway 2 or, say, Mozart: The Conspirators of Prague. It was said that Runaway 2 would destroy crappy European adventures. Instead, it joined them.

[b]Runaway: the Dream of the Turtle[/b] es una aventura gráfica de [i]point&click[/i] en 2D para un jugador. La primera entrega tenía sus problemas pero en general resultó ser un buen título. En esta ocasión se repiten algunos de los errores del primero junto con algunos nuevos, como un ritmo más lento, una dirección argumental cuestionable que además se queda a medias y personajes poco interesantes. Pese a tener algunos momentos y puzles decentes, no me ha parecido una buena continuación o un buen título en general.

[h1]El sueño de la tortuga[/h1]
Brian y Gina disfrutan de su retiro paradisiaco tras los eventos de la primera parte. Un accidentado viaje en avión los dejará aislados en una isla que no está tan desierta como decían.

Al igual que con el anterior, por el tema de licencias, el juego viene con voces y textos en inglés. Debemos pasarnos por la [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2859559364]sección de guías[/url] si queremos descargar las voces y textos en español originales.

Inicialmente Runaway iba a ser un único juego, pero debido al éxito de la primera parte se convirtió en una trilogía, y eso se nota. Un ritmo más lento y una trama que se apoya más en referencias al cine y la televisión de los 90 hacen que esté bastante por debajo de su antecesor. Al menos esta falta de enfoque le permite mostrar más variedad  de localizaciones pero no me gusta el camino seguido. Tampoco me han gustado los personajes en esta entrega, tanto los que repiten como la mayoría de los nuevos son bastante irritantes, incluso el propio protagonista, quien fuese un buen tipo en el primero que quería hacer lo correcto, ha pasado a ser un tanto caricaturesco.

Mecánicamente no cambia mucho. Seguimos contando con excelentes fondos en 2D dibujados a mano en formato 4:3 (cuadrado) con personajes en 3D, pero bastante mejor detallados y animados que en el anterior. Con el botón derecho alternamos entre observar e interactuar con el escenario mientras pasamos el puntero del ratón por cada píxel para ir recogiendo todo aquello que no esté clavado o le parezca interesante al protagonista y dialogar con un buen nutrido número de personajes variopintos mientras resolvemos puzles… algunos mejores que otros.

Ya en la primera parte había algunos puzles cuya lógica resultaba un poco cuestionable, aquí vuelven junto con objetos de un único uso que debemos recoger más de una vez o esperar varios segundos hasta que termine una animación para que la acción se complete. El ritmo general es más lento. Tampoco ayuda el tema de las conversaciones, donde los temas tratados no desaparecen. En más de una ocasión nos veremos repitiendo diálogos para ver si ofrecen alguna nueva opción, cosa que no suele pasar. Al menos en esta ocasión se añade un sistema de ayuda cuyas indicaciones podrían haber estado un poco mejor trabajadas.

Lo cierto es que ha habido un momento en el que dejé el juego de lado durante varias semanas antes de animarme a completarlo, y sólo porque me gusta terminar los juegos que empiezo. Pese a que tiene sus momentos interesantes aquí y allí, en términos generales no lo he disfrutado y el hecho de que la trama se quede a medias con la tercera entrega en mente y los mencionados personajes irritantes, no ayuda.

En cuanto al estado técnico. Funciona sin más, instalar y jugar, pero por alguna razón, en cada escena donde hay copos de nieve el juego se ralentiza una barbaridad. La única solución que he encontrado es usar algún programa de terceros como [i]dgvoodoo2[/i] o [i]DxWnd[/i] para forzarlo en modo ventana.

La aventura tiene una duración de unas 10-12 horas. Como todos los juegos de este tipo, el tiempo varía en función de cuánto nos atasquemos y nuestra perseverancia antes de consultar una guía o ayuda.

[H1][b]ANÁLISIS DE [i]RUNAWAY 2: EL SUEÑO DE LA TORTUGA[/i][/b][/H1]

Tras el gran éxito de Runaway: A Road to Adventure (lanzado en el 2001), Pendulo Studios demostró en 2006 con esta esperada secuela, que las aventuras gráficas clásicas point & click seguían muy vivas, convirtiéndose por méritos propios en todo un referente del género.

[H1]Argumento:[/H1]

Si en el primer juego acompañamos a un tímido Brian Basco que terminaba envuelto en una persecución con la mafia y el ejército junto a Gina, en esta segunda parte nos encontramos con una historia aún más alocada, donde unas pacíficas vacaciones en Hawái terminan en un accidente de avión en una isla repleta de militares, extraterrestres, piratas y templos olvidados.

El guion está plagado de humor, ingeniosos diálogos y la presencia de personajes secundarios de lo más extravagantes y memorables, al igual que ya sucedía en la primera entrega. Sin embargo, también generó una gran división en la opinión de los usuarios y la crítica especializada. Mientras que a muchos les encantó ese giro hacia una comedia de aventuras gamberra, surrealista y de tipo serie B, otros criticaron duramente que perdía la identidad y parte de la coherencia de la primera entrega, que apostaba por un tono de película de criminales y de misterio mucho más serio y mejor hilado (aunque también guardaba su parte de locura).

Gina pasa prácticamente desapercibida durante todo el juego, relegada a un segundo plano y perdiéndose por completo esa química tan especial que había entre el protagonista y ella en el primer título. Por si fuera poco, el juego termina de forma muy brusca con un "Continuará..." que te obliga sí o sí a jugar la tercera entrega, dejando toda la trama principal por resolver, algo que tampoco me ha gustado nada.

[H1]Jugabilidad:[/H1]

En cuanto al apartado jugable, se mantiene intacta la base del point & click tradicional, pero introduce cambios que mejoran considerablemente la experiencia respecto al primero. Una de las mejoras más destacables es la limpieza de inventario por capítulos, ya que al cambio de episodio Brian descarta los objetos inservibles, solucionando la acumulación molesta del primer juego. Por otra parte, la lógica de interacción se ha suavizado un poco para evitar que Brian se niegue tajantemente a coger cosas sin motivo (como por ejemplo cuando queremos coger algo que nos va a hacer falta, pero que todavía no podemos coger por no ser el momento adecuado), reduciendo la rigidez del original (aunque sigue pasando, pero menos que antes). Además, se añade mucho humor en el que Brian rompe la cuarta pared constantemente para dar pequeñas pistas o comentar de forma cómica cómo guarda los objetos.

En cuanto a la dificultad, se ha disparado de forma notable. Los puzles son en ocasiones excesivamente rebuscados, lo que hace que sea muy habitual quedarse atascado sin saber por dónde tirar. Afortunadamente, se ha incluido un sistema de pistas que me ha parecido una verdadera maravilla: integrado de forma orgánica en la propia aventura, plagado de humor y de una utilidad sobresaliente. Está tan bien implementado que te ayuda a avanzar (casi siempre, aunque hay ocasiones que ni con esas lo verás claro) sin destrozarte la experiencia ni darte la respuesta mascada de golpe, algo totalmente de agradecer. Aun así, prepárate para tener que recurrir a guías externas en más de una ocasión.

[H1]Gráficos:[/H1]

Si el primer juego ya era una maravilla visual con su estilo Cel-Shading tipo dibujo animado para los modelados y sus escenarios pintados a mano, Runaway 2 dio un salto técnico notorio. Pendulo Studios combinó esos fondos 2D con un nivel de detalle sobresaliente y elementos 3D perfectamente integrados. Es en las escenas prerrenderizadas de las cinemáticas donde realmente se notaba la gran mejoría, con una iluminación mucho más trabajada (como en las escenas submarinas), unos efectos meteorológicos más realistas (como la nieve en Alaska con pisadas que se borran progresivamente) y unas animaciones de los personajes que estaban muy por encima de lo visto en 2001, destacando además por la gran variedad de entornos (playas tropicales, selvas, montañas nevadas...). Eso sí, el juego hoy día da muchísimos problemas, por lo que se hace OBLIGATORIO el uso de dgVoodoo2 para que funcione correctamente. Aún así, el juego es muy inestable, he sufrido innumerables salidas al escritorio, por lo que recomiendo que guardéis la partida muy a menudo. 

[H1]Sonido:[/H1]

A nivel sonoro, el juego cuenta con una banda sonora excelente que mantiene la esencia pop/rock de la saga y unos diálogos cargados de carisma. Sin embargo, tal y como sorprendentemente sucedía en la primera entrega, la versión Steam no viene traducida ni doblada al español a pesar de tratarse de un juego desarrollado en España, por lo que es totalmente obligatorio hacer uso de la guía que os facilito arriba para disfrutar de su sublime doblaje profesional en nuestro idioma, en el que encontraremos voces tan míticas como las de Eduardo del Hoyo (Rick Grimes en The Walking Dead, que encarna al protagonista Brian Basco), Nuria Mediavilla (la voz en español de actrices de la talla de Nicole Kidman, Angelina Jolie o Uma Thurman, doblando a Gina) o Iván Muelas (la voz habitual de actores como Will Smith) entre muchos otros.

[H1][b]PROS:[/b][/H1]

✅ Apartado gráfico de gran belleza

✅ Los diálogos

✅ El humor constante

✅ Personajes secundarios memorables

✅ Gran variedad de escenarios

✅ Duración más que notable

✅ Gran salto técnico y de producción con respecto a la primera entrega

✅ Se puede conseguir a muy buen precio de oferta en Steam

[H1][b]CONTRAS:[/b][/H1]

❌ Muy inestable en equipos actuales: se sale al escritorio con mucha frecuencia (¡guarda a menudo!)

❌ Requiere obligatoriamente recurrir a soluciones como dgVoodoo2 para que funcione bien hoy en día (ver la guía de arriba)

❌ Al igual que la primera entrega, sorprendentemente la versión de Steam viene en inglés (usa la guía de arriba si quieres textos y voces en español)

❌ Algunos puzles son excesivamente rebuscados. La dificultad se ha elevado considerablemente

❌ La historia roza a veces el absurdo extremo, perdiendo algo la esencia del primer juego

❌ Gina queda relegada a un segundo plano durante toda la aventura

❌ El brusco final, que te deja con muchas incógnitas sin resolver

❌ No tiene logros, cromos ni artículos de la tienda de puntos de Steam

❌ No tiene sistema de guardado de la partida en la nube Steam Cloud

[H1]Conclusión:[/H1] 

Runaway 2: El Sueño de la Tortuga es una secuela más que decente; es más grande, variada y técnicamente superior a la primera entrega, pero pierde algo de frescura y coherencia narrativa al decantarse por una trama muy disparatada. Sufre de una preocupante inestabilidad en sistemas modernos que exige el uso de guías para solucionarlo, mucha paciencia por las constantes salidas al escritorio y guardar muy a menudo. No obstante, compensa estos problemas con un arte excelente, unos diálogos de lo más ingeniosos y personajes llenos de carisma. Además, una vez tienes el doblaje al español instalado, puedes disfrutar de algunas de las mejores interpretaciones que se recuerden en un juego español. Si disfrutaste del primer viaje de Brian, esta secuela es una parada obligatoria, especialmente si lo encuentras de oferta y siempre siendo consciente de todos los problemas que tiene.

Si mi análisis te ha gustado o te ha servido de ayuda, agradecería que dejaras un voto positivo para que pueda llegar a más gente. Se agradecen también los premios de puntos de Steam. ¡Gracias por leerme! No dudéis en dejar vuestros comentarios o dudas, responderé lo antes posible.

Runaway: The Dream of the Turtle continues the globe-trotting misadventures of Brian Basco and Gina Timmins with a sequel that doubles down on spectacle, absurdity, and cartoonish flair. Developed by Pendulo Studios and published by Focus Entertainment, the game opens with Brian and Gina enjoying what should have been a carefree Hawaiian escape—until a sightseeing plane flight goes disastrously wrong. The crash leaves Gina missing and Brian stranded in an unfamiliar jungle, setting off a chain of events that spirals into a bizarre odyssey filled with eccentric characters, conspiracies, and environments that grow stranger and more elaborate as the story continues. Where the first Runaway blended mystery with light humor, The Dream of the Turtle embraces a far more chaotic, comedic energy, treating the adventure almost like a colorful animated series brought to life.

Visually, the game remains one of the series’ strongest assets. Pendulo Studios maintains its signature hand-painted aesthetic, blending richly detailed backgrounds with stylized, expressive character art. Every location feels distinct—from tropical islands to military bases, frozen arctic outposts, underwater vessels, and more. These diverse settings don’t just add visual variety; they amplify the sense of a journey that expands in scope with every chapter. The animated cutscenes, though limited by the technology of their time, carry an energetic tone that reflects the game’s exaggerated personality. Even when the narrative veers into implausible territory, the visual presentation helps keep the experience grounded in a vibrant, lively world.

Gameplay adheres closely to the traditions of classic point-and-click adventures. Players explore scenes, collect objects, interrogate quirky characters, and piece together puzzle solutions using a mix of observation, experimentation, and sometimes wild leaps of logic. This design will feel familiar to fans of older adventure games: part of the charm comes from solving puzzles through creative item combinations, but it also brings with it the genre’s pitfalls. Some puzzles are clever and intuitive, while others rely heavily on noticing tiny interactable elements or interpreting logic that feels more whimsical than sensible. These fluctuations in design quality can lead to moments of satisfaction followed by stretches of frustration, particularly when progress hinges on discovering one small environmental detail or combining items in ways that aren’t clearly motivated.

The writing and tone of The Dream of the Turtle mark a noticeable departure from the more grounded humor of the original game. Here, Pendulo embraces a heightened level of absurdity, weaving in elements of military intrigue, alien conspiracies, pirates, and pulpy sci-fi tropes—often without worrying too much about coherence. Characters are painted in broad strokes, leaning into comedic exaggeration and cultural stereotypes that may come across as dated or heavy-handed by modern standards. For some players, this over-the-top style is part of the game’s charm, giving it the carefree, chaotic feel of a Saturday-morning cartoon. For others, the humor and narrative whiplash may dampen emotional investment or make the story feel unsteady and unfocused.

Reception to Runaway: The Dream of the Turtle has long been divided for these reasons. Many players admire the artistic presentation, globe-spanning environments, polished character animations, and the overall ambition to create a cinematic adventure. Fans of point-and-click games often appreciate the sheer number of puzzles and environments to explore. However, criticisms frequently target the pacing, the uneven quality of the writing, the reliance on obtuse puzzle logic, and the narrative’s tendency to wander without delivering substantial payoff. The tonal shifts—from light comedy to melodrama to outlandish sci-fi—can make the plot feel stitched together rather than organically unfolding, especially when combined with cliffhanger moments that set up the next installment without offering full closure.

Despite its inconsistencies, The Dream of the Turtle remains a memorable entry in the Runaway series. It is unabashedly colorful, enthusiastic in its eccentricity, and unafraid to swing for the fences with its narrative twists and visual spectacle. Players who approach it with a taste for classic adventure puzzles, an appreciation for bold, exaggerated humor, and patience for unconventional storytelling will find an enjoyable and sometimes surprising journey. Those looking for cohesive writing, grounded characters, or puzzle design that avoids guesswork may find it less appealing. Ultimately, the game serves as a lively continuation of Brian and Gina’s saga—one that celebrates the joy of adventure even as it stumbles over its own ambition.

Huh... where do I even start? Well, obviously, I've seen those negative reviews. But you never know, right? Maybe it's another hidden gem, overlooked and misunderstood by a crowd? So I dived in and... At least initially everything seemed more or less alright. Not without issues, but the first 3 chapters were ok. But the 4th chapter is [b] that [/b] point, where everything goes south. Not only previous issues hit critical mass, but new, even bigger issues appear.

First, the gameplay. I don't mind if protagonist can't perform certain action, until he gets so called 'aha!' moment in a story, as long as it seems reasonable. What I'n not ok with - when the game sets certain rules and then breaks it. For example, in the 4th chapter, our charming snaggle-toothed companion forgets important piece of info. Why? - sudden amnesia. We try to exhaust all dialog options with him, but no matter what we ask - Brian says that it's useless and he needs to find another solution. [b]OK[/b]

I keep playing, speak with the local, learn about solution... but then I hit the wall. After a #$% of wasted time and trials and errors, I finally learn that this solution is not enough. It must be 'slightly' improved. How do you discover this? You need to go back to the dude with [u][i][b]amnesia[/b][/i][/u] and ask him about his distant past. Excuse me? EXCUSE ME?!!

Another example. Same 4th chapter. You need to obtain X item. And you can only get it with another Y item. Tha's the [b]only[/b] possible way. We spend roughly 2/3 of the chapter to get Y in order to obtain X. But when we finallt get Y - Brian just refuses to use it. Then I absolutely accidentally dicovered, that at first, you have to make an obviously failed attempt and try to get X without Y. Like why? This option was never brought to the table. It's totally senseless. There were no any dialogs that it is possible to get X without Y. It was obviously impossible. What the...

Gameplay won't become better later on, but enough about it. Let's talk about the story. The true 'meat' is here. And again, the first 3 chapters storywise were more or less acceptable as well. But then, at the end of the 4th chapter it breaks the dumb meter. Suddenly we encounter comical aliens, like in "Destroy all humans". Then we are teleported to the other end of the world with amnesia (how refreshing). How the game explains this mess? Either with flashbacks, or just by saying "don't worry about it anymore" (literally words from the dialog).

And it won't become any better later either. It looks like the devs had no idea how to continue this mess and eventually we get a vinaigrette of unifinished plots, ideas, settings, etc. Ah yeah, we also get a lot of long and boring dialogs with tons of useless and absolutely not fun information. At certain point the story just ends on a cliffhanger. But honestly, if the story is a mess like this - you are just glad that it has finally ended. Anyhow. 

Even most characters are rather unpleasant here. Losers, dumbs, cuckold, freak, hateful hermit, unsociable brat, mary-sue... Brian also turnt into not that pleasant dude. In the 4th chapter we have to orchestrate a rather nasty trap for an absolutely harmless man, who helped us a lot and even invited to his house. As a result of this trap, the dude will be maimed, r##ed and potentially killed. And Brian also regrets that he missed an opportunity to film this and post on the Internet. Hilarious, right? Tags [Funny] and [Comedy] fit just well. And then we, as a sign of gratitude, will steal his belongings.

What can I say in the end? I assume it is too late to dissuade you to buy it, because most likely you've already got full Pendulo pack at good price. Thus, at least make sure that you will play it with a guide at your hand. Those reviewers who finished this game with a guide, actually made a very smart choice. Coz I finished it without guides and all I got is frustration and regrets about wasted time. And just in case - you can safely play the 3rd game right after the 1st one. Nothing of value will be lost.
