"Telltale's Texas Hold'Em" is a fun poker card game with interactive comedy cutscenes. I just won the whole tournament, and after all that, I can say that this game is good for some quick, fun sessions, assuming you have great time-management skills in real life. Can't believe that this was the very first game created by the legendary Telltale Games!

One huge downside is the lack of modern hardware optimization! The game fails to load in fullscreen and can even crash during the boot-up screen on Windows. To run the game, just delete the "prefs.prop" file from the game's installation folder, then use 'Lossless Scaling's Integer Scaling' to scale it back up to fullscreen from 640p perhaps to your native display resolution. However, it runs fine out of the box on most modern Linux distros. Telltale should really remaster this game at this point, along with a sequel.

Go for it. You will have a great time with it. And if you want to learn about the card game, I would suggest playing 'Balatro' first to get familiar with the poker hand system, or just check it online, your choice. :)

Telltale Texas Hold ’Em is a game that demonstrates how much personality can elevate a simple concept. Developed and published by Telltale Games, this poker title takes the familiar rules of Texas Hold ’Em and surrounds them with a cast of eccentric characters whose conversations, rivalries, and comedic exchanges become just as important as the cards on the table. Rather than presenting poker as a serious simulation focused exclusively on strategy and competition, the game embraces humor and character-driven entertainment, creating an experience that remains surprisingly enjoyable years after its original release.

At its foundation, the game is a straightforward poker tournament. Players sit at a table with four computer-controlled opponents and compete to accumulate chips through a series of hands. The mechanics follow the standard rules of Texas Hold ’Em, making the game accessible to poker enthusiasts while also providing enough guidance for newcomers. The learning curve is gentle, allowing inexperienced players to understand the fundamentals without feeling intimidated. This accessibility is one of the game's strongest qualities, as it opens the door for a much wider audience than traditional poker simulations often attract.

What truly separates Telltale Texas Hold ’Em from countless other card games is its cast of opponents. Each character possesses a distinct personality that influences every conversation and reaction at the table. Harry Weinhead approaches the game with confidence and calculated ambition, while Boris Krinkle attempts to intimidate everyone around him through sheer force of personality. Theodore Dudebrough contributes a carefree and relaxed attitude that frequently results in amusing exchanges, and Grandma Shaky constantly steals the spotlight with unpredictable remarks and bizarre observations. Together, these characters transform an ordinary card game into an ongoing comedy performance.

The interactions between these opponents provide much of the game's entertainment value. Every hand becomes an opportunity for witty dialogue, playful insults, exaggerated boasts, and unexpected reactions. Even when the cards are not particularly exciting, the conversations help maintain player interest. The humor rarely feels forced because it emerges naturally from the personalities around the table. As a result, the game succeeds in creating a social atmosphere that resembles an entertaining gathering of eccentric individuals rather than a sterile poker simulation.

The writing deserves considerable praise because it showcases the strengths that would later become synonymous with Telltale Games. Long before the studio became famous for narrative adventures, it already demonstrated a talent for crafting memorable dialogue and distinctive characters. Each participant feels recognizable and consistent, which helps establish a sense of familiarity over time. Players are not merely competing against artificial intelligence; they are competing against characters whose personalities become increasingly memorable with every session.

From a gameplay perspective, the poker mechanics strike an effective balance between accessibility and strategy. Winning still requires understanding probability, reading betting patterns, and making intelligent decisions. The game does not simply hand victories to players. Success comes from applying real poker knowledge while adapting to the tendencies of individual opponents. Experienced poker players will appreciate that the core mechanics remain faithful to the game itself, while newcomers can gradually improve their skills through practice and observation.

The presentation reflects the era in which the game was released. Character models and environments are relatively simple compared to modern standards, and the visuals occasionally reveal their age. However, the art direction succeeds in emphasizing personality over realism. Expressive animations and exaggerated character designs help communicate emotions clearly, ensuring that the humor remains effective. The visual style may not impress technically, but it supports the game's comedic tone remarkably well.

Voice acting contributes significantly to the overall experience. The performances bring each character to life, adding energy and charm to every interaction. Hearing opponents react to victories, losses, bluffs, and unexpected outcomes creates a level of engagement that text alone could never achieve. The voice work helps establish a lively atmosphere and reinforces the game's identity as a comedy-focused poker experience.

The game's limited scope may disappoint players searching for extensive customization options or large-scale tournament structures. There is no elaborate career mode or endless progression system. Instead, the focus remains on a single poker table and the colorful personalities gathered around it. While this simplicity restricts the amount of content available, it also allows the game to concentrate entirely on what it does best: delivering entertaining poker matches filled with humor and memorable character interactions.

Looking back, Telltale Texas Hold ’Em feels like an early preview of the creative direction that would eventually define the studio. The emphasis on dialogue, character relationships, and personality-driven entertainment is already evident throughout the experience. Even though poker serves as the central mechanic, the real attraction is spending time with the game's cast and enjoying their reactions to the unpredictable nature of every hand.

Ultimately, Telltale Texas Hold ’Em succeeds because it understands that games can be entertaining even when their mechanics are simple. By combining solid poker gameplay with a cast of unforgettable characters and consistently amusing writing, it creates an experience that remains charming long after the novelty of its premise wears off. It may not be the deepest poker simulator available, but it stands as one of the most distinctive and entertaining interpretations of the game. For players who appreciate humor, memorable characters, and accessible card gameplay, it remains a surprisingly enjoyable classic from Telltale's early years.

It's fun for a round or two, but after that, you'll never touch it again. Unless you really have a thing for Janky Old PC Games, definitely skip this.

Also, important note: if you want to play the game, you gotta go into the files and delete the file named "port". Do not enable full-screen either.

Honestly, this is still a solid Poker simulator while also being an interesting history piece regarding TellTales early years and as the predecessor to the Poker Night at the Inventory series. Which is a little funny as of the three Telltale Poker sim games, this is the only one they still hold the rights to as the other two are buried under licencing agreements. 

Gameplay and Mehanics: 
If you know how to play Poker, this won't be a hard game to jump into. If you don't, the game does have tutrials, and the I.A id VERY forgiving so this isn't a bad place to learn the game. Speaking of the I.A, the characters around the table seem to have their own playstyle and tells. The Grandma will seemingly only bet high if she has something to play while Boris will go on in seemingly at random and will often be the first to bust out. Theodore seems to be the best player of the group and will fold often, while Harry seems to be the most balanced in terms of his patterns. That being said all the players will at times bet high despite not seeing the flop. I busted out two players just by matching their all in bets before the flop and just winning due to luck? I also never lost with more than a three of a kind and during my first playthrough the A.I players seem to only get more than a pair twice on the reveal. I watched gameplay from Youtube creators and this seems to be consistent. This was meant as a tech demo afterall so it wouldn't make sense for the game to be too hard. As it stands, it's an easy poker game to kill forty-sixty minutes playing. 

Characters and setting. 
The game is set in what could be called a generic broadcasted Poker setting. The announcer is also kind of plain but fits the setting. The other four characters playing against "The Player: are mainly one note archetypes, but that doesn't make them not entertaining. Grandma is the sweet old lady that hits on being a little crazy... Like when she talks to her chips and states that she needs to "sharpen her knifes" after busting out. Theo is a dude bro that makes movie references and who is the most annoying at the table yet usually LAST TO THE END! Boris is a shady bald guy who hints that he got the money for the tournament from, shady sources. Harry is a Poker Vet? an old man who is easily set off? he's the hardest to read which makes sense as his "I'm better than you" personality fits well at a Poker table without the need to flush him out more. 

Conclusion:
The game is old but isn't as jank as some of the other reviews seem to note. the game is less than two bucks and only took me forty minutes to get through. I'd say it's worth playing through once as if you're like me and have never played the Poker Night at the Inventory series, the first PNI game was just re added to steam. So right now seems like the best time to play Telltale Texas Hold 'Em before jumping into the first Poker night game.

It's a bit dated, sure, but it is also a bit of a classic. The banter is pretty fun, and even if you lose you can still watch the rest of the tournament and root for your favorite players. Given how cheap this game is even before discount, I'd say it is well worth a purchase. So, take my advice, and just go all in!

La premisa es simple, hay 5 jugadores en un torneo de póker que consta de vos y 4 rivales, cada uno con su personalidad, forma de jugar y comentarios divertidos para cada mano.

Cada participante empieza con un pozo de dinero, y al terminarse los fondos, este queda eliminado de la partida.

Son torneos relativamente cortos, en menos de 20 minutos pude ganar, pero todo depende de tu habilidad de mentir o de jugar al póker.

Si bien es más un título experimental, hoy en día es un juego de culto y los primeros pasos de una compañía que sacaría excelentes títulos narrativos.

I'm no expert in twin stick shooters, but I love the visuals of this series. I tend to regard them as like the video game equivalent of a fireworks show. I put more playtime into the original XBLA version of this game at a friend's house like almost 20 years ago, but this is exactly that.

Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved is a remarkable demonstration of how a simple arcade concept can deliver an addictive and challenging experience without relying on complicated mechanics or elaborate storytelling. Developed by Bizarre Creations and published by Activision, this twin-stick shooter focuses on fast reactions, precise movement, and the pursuit of increasingly impressive high scores. Its straightforward design captures the excitement of traditional arcade gaming while introducing an impressive visual identity that remains appealing years after its original release. Although the game offers relatively little content beyond its central survival challenge, the quality of its mechanics makes every attempt feel worthwhile.

The gameplay places players in control of a small spacecraft trapped inside a rectangular arena populated by hostile geometric shapes. Movement and shooting operate independently, allowing players to dodge incoming threats while firing in virtually any direction. The objective is simple: survive as long as possible while destroying enemies and accumulating points. However, the challenge escalates rapidly as additional enemies enter the arena, creating increasingly dangerous situations. Successful players must constantly evaluate their surroundings, identify safe movement paths, and avoid becoming trapped. The responsive controls make this demanding gameplay feel satisfying, ensuring that survival depends primarily on individual skill rather than complicated systems.

Enemy variety contributes significantly to the experience. Different geometric opponents possess distinct movement patterns, ranging from direct pursuit to unpredictable wandering and more unusual defensive behaviors. These differences create encounters that require constant adaptation rather than mindless shooting. As the arena becomes crowded, players must prioritize dangerous targets while maintaining enough space to maneuver. The escalating enemy density produces a thrilling sense of urgency, transforming an initially manageable challenge into an intense test of concentration and reflexes. Even without traditional levels or boss encounters, the changing combinations of enemies provide enough unpredictability to make repeated attempts entertaining.

The scoring mechanics are particularly effective at encouraging improvement. Destroying enemies builds a score multiplier, rewarding players who remain alive and maintain consistent performance. Losing a life resets the multiplier, making mistakes especially costly during successful runs. This system creates an engaging balance between aggressive play and careful survival. Players who eliminate enemies efficiently can achieve impressive scores, but excessive confidence often results in disastrous collisions. Limited smart bombs provide an emergency escape mechanism by clearing threats from the arena, although deciding when to use them requires careful judgment. Together, these mechanics create an excellent foundation for competitive score chasing.

The visual presentation remains one of the game's most memorable characteristics. Bright neon shapes move across a dark arena, accompanied by colorful explosions, glowing projectiles, and dynamic grid effects. The abstract art direction gives the action a distinctive personality without requiring detailed environments or elaborate character models. Every successful elimination produces satisfying visual feedback, reinforcing the excitement of combat. However, the abundance of particles and moving objects can occasionally overwhelm the screen, making certain threats difficult to identify. This visual intensity contributes to the game's energetic atmosphere but can also become frustrating during particularly demanding moments.

Sound design strengthens the overall presentation through electronic music and sharp arcade effects that complement the constant action. Explosions, weapon fire, and enemy destruction produce immediate auditory feedback, helping establish a satisfying rhythm during extended survival attempts. The soundtrack supports the futuristic atmosphere without distracting from gameplay. While the audio selection is not especially extensive, it accomplishes its purpose effectively by reinforcing the speed and intensity of each encounter.

Accessibility is another important advantage. The basic controls are easy to understand, and players can begin enjoying the experience almost immediately. However, mastering the game requires patience, practice, and considerable awareness of enemy behavior. Its difficulty increases naturally as encounters become more crowded, encouraging players to develop better positioning and movement strategies. This makes it especially rewarding for arcade enthusiasts who appreciate improvement through repetition. Short sessions also make it convenient for players who want immediate entertainment without investing hours into complicated progression systems.

The PC version faithfully recreates the original Xbox Live Arcade experience while supporting keyboard, mouse, and dual-stick gamepad controls. Steam Deck compatibility is officially Verified, with functional default controls, readable interface text, and satisfactory performance under the recommended settings. This makes the game an excellent choice for handheld gaming, particularly because its short sessions fit naturally into portable play.

Its greatest weakness is the limited variety of activities available. There is no substantial campaign, character progression, or collection of alternative gameplay modes to maintain interest beyond high-score competition. Repeated attempts may eventually feel monotonous, particularly for players who prefer narrative objectives or unlockable content. Nevertheless, the focused design is also its greatest strength, providing a polished arcade experience without unnecessary distractions.

Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved remains an outstanding example of timeless arcade design. Its precise controls, satisfying scoring mechanics, distinctive visuals, and demanding survival gameplay create an experience that continues to reward dedication. Although its restricted scope may disappoint players seeking extensive content, those who enjoy skill-based challenges will discover a remarkably entertaining shooter that encourages repeated attempts and continuous improvement. Its ability to transform a handful of simple mechanics into such an exciting experience makes it a worthwhile addition to any arcade enthusiast's collection.

A wonderfully addictive and visually spectacular arcade shooter that combines accessible controls with demanding gameplay, delivering an enduring test of reflexes, precision, and determination.

Do you ever have a job that you just f%ing hate? And yet you work there because it's adjacent to a dream — something else you’d rather be doing. So you suffer through the shitty job because it gives you a tiny thread of something that's more awesome.

In 2005, that was me.

I worked for Xbox customer service. Specifically, I was the guy you’d call if your Xbox was broken or you couldn't connect to the Live service — and believe you me, in 2005, there were a *lot* of broken Xboxes.

Oh goddamn, was it awful.

The Three Rings of Death. If you were around in the 2000s and bought yourself a new Xbox 360, you know full well what I’m talking about. That shit was rough. Telling someone who just spent hundreds of dollars on an Xbox 360 that they couldn’t get it repaired because it was out of warranty just completely sucked.

And I need to tell you—at first, the warranty for Xbox 360s was *90 days*. Ninety. Days. Later on, they extended it to a year, because goddamn those Xbox 360s broke down like crazy. And eventually, Microsoft did the right thing and said, hey, if your Xbox had the Three Rings of Death, we’ll repair it or get you a new one.

But that was much later.

Working on the Xbox 360 right after lunch? It was hell. Dealing with those repairs was hell. And I specifically remember Christmas of that year—how many people I had to hear say their Christmas was wrecked because of that issue.

Now—there was *one* good thing about that job. Something that kept me there way longer than I should’ve stayed. And in hindsight, it is just so goddamn stupid that I stayed because of this.

But—before the day started, during breaks, and after work, I got to play video games.

Basically, I got to play Xbox’s greatest hits. Goddamn there were a lot of them. And as much as I hated dealing with customer service and the broken hearts that came with it, oh my God—Microsoft had some *killer* games.

I’m not gonna go on and on about them, but there was *one* game in particular that I completely loved. My heart belonged to it.

*Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved.*

This game was something special.

Let me tell you what actually made it special to *me*.

You see, in the 2000s, we were still kind of in that era where everything had to be 3D. And if it wasn’t 3D, and it was 2D, it had to be an evolution of the whole 16-bit thing.

*Geometry Wars* came along during a time when most gamers had forgotten about '80s arcade games. Early-‘80s stuff — arcade games that came out between like 1975 to 1985. In hindsight, that was the golden age. And arcade games from that era? Massively different from what came after.

Back then, a lot of games were space-themed. Single screen. Cheap thrills. The kind of thing where you’d put in a quarter and *boom*, instant action. No tutorials. No long-winded cutscenes. No crazy overarching story that took hundreds of hours. Just *go*. It was balls-to-the-wall madness.

And like I said, in the 2000s you were either playing wild 3D games—you know, *Metal Gear Solid*, *Ratchet & Clank*, *Halo*—or you were playing what I call “fancy 2D games.” Like *Castlevania: Symphony of the Night*. Maybe, if you were a PC gamer, you’d play isometric stuff like *Diablo* or *Warcraft*.

And I’m not ragging on those games. I *love* those games.

But nothing scratched that old arcade itch.

And I’m not the kind of person who thinks that just because something is old, it’s not enjoyable. Goddamn—if that were true, then everything would just be a time-based novelty. All about some urge to stay “with it.”

*Geometry Wars* came out during that time. But what really set it apart?

It made the most of the Xbox 360’s dual analog controls. And it felt *amazing*. You moved with the left stick. You shot with the right. It felt intuitive. Fresh. That 360-degree movement—it felt like piloting a spaceship. My thumbs just *got it*. It felt natural.

But what really impressed me were the graphics.

The geometry in *Geometry Wars*? Yeah, it was real. This game looked like it was made on graph paper. Everything sat on a grid. Simple shapes — but with lighting effects that *shimmered*. That shimmer made it stand out.

You gotta understand, flat panel TVs were just starting to appear. So on an LCD? This looked like *magic*. The light bloomed. I think that’s where the term bloom effect comes from—how it *blooms*.

And the wobble—when your ship would move and there’d be explosions, or those little black holes—the whole grid would start to warp. It felt like you were about to cross into another dimension. But you never did. It was just a *threat*.

That’s something I always loved about *Geometry Wars*.

It wasn’t a triple-A game. Kinda indie. But not really.

It was developed by Bizarre Creations—the same people who made *Project Gotham Racing*, which was an Xbox 360 classic.

*Geometry Wars* started as a side project. Just a little arcade minigame you could play inside the *Project Gotham* garage. And that little minigame got so popular, it spun off into *Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved*.

But here’s the part that makes me feel dumb.

This wasn’t a massive game. It was ten bucks. You could get it on Xbox Live Arcade.

And yet... I stuck with that shitty minimum wage job—where there was no career advancement, no future—for *two years*. Maybe more.

Just to keep playing *Geometry Wars* at work.

And it wasn’t just about the game. I could’ve bought an Xbox 360. I could’ve played at home.

But there was something about going to work, seeing my coworkers. We’d have this stressful, horrible job that none of us liked—and in between, we’d compete. Try to beat each other’s high scores.

And in some ways, I miss that.

I miss that moment. Because guess what?

Now I own thousands of games. But I don’t have coworkers. I don’t have anyone I see every day. And I’m definitely not playing video games with friends.

Do people my age—I’m in my 40s now—do we even *play* video games anymore?

What do we even *do*?

I don’t know. I’m so disconnected from having a social life. I wish people my age still made friends. I wish there was a place where you could bullshit for a couple hours a day, have a good time, knock out a few challenges. Get that little hit of arcade glory.

But nobody does that.

Everyone’s so serious about their goddamn mortgages.

20 years ago, I had a shitty job. But I also had *people*—people who gave me a few rounds of *Geometry Wars*. And that was enough to keep me there. At least for a while.

I’m gonna be real here: sometimes I wish I could have that *Geometry Wars* moment again—without the soul-destroying minimum wage job attached.

But I’ll tell you something.

I still play *Geometry Wars*. Occasionally.

And yeah, the memory’s bittersweet.

But it’s sweet enough that I keep playing it.

Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved – Hra, která dokázala, že méně je někdy více

V dnešní době, kdy se herní průmysk přehání v ultrarealistické grafice, komplexních příbězích a nekonečných otevřených světech, je snadné zapomenout na to, že podstata hraní může být naprosto jednoduchá a přesto neuvěřitelně návyková. Přesně tohle nám připomíná Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved, hra, která svého času vyšla jako nenápadná součást Project Gotham Racing 2 a následně se probojovala na Xbox Live Arcade, kde definovala éru digitální distribuce.

Od prvního spuštění je jasné, že tady se hraje na jinou notu. Žádné dlouhé tutoriály, žádné složité menu. Jen vy, vaše loď, a nekonečné vlny geometrických nepřátel na ploše, která připomíná staré vektorové hry z arkádových automatů. Hra je brilantní ve své jednoduchosti. Cílem je přežít co nejdéle, ničit vše, co se hýbe, a nahánět vysoké skóre.

Hypnotická akce a vizuální symfonie

Co dělá Geometry Wars tak speciálním, je jeho hluboká hratelnost ukrytá pod povrchem. Zatímco pravá analogová páčka ovládá pohyb lodi, levá míří vaše zbraně. Tento systém je tak intuitivní, že ho zvládnete za pár sekund, ale mastering ho trvá celé hodiny. Brzy se z bezhlavého střílení stane taneční balet mezi explodujícími nepřáteli, uhýbáním laserům a sbíráním bodových diamantů.

Vizuální stránka je kapitola sama o sobě. Retro styl je doveden k dokonalosti, a i když je grafika primitivní, je naprosto hypnotická. Neonové linky, explozivní částicové efekty a dynamicky se měnící pozadí vytváří vizuální symfonii, která vás vtáhne do děje. Vše se navíc odehrává v plynulých 60 snímcích za sekundu, což je pro hru takovéto povahy naprosto klíčové.

Nekonečné skóre a znovuhratelnost

Tato hra nemá konec, a to je její největší síla. Cílem není dohrát příběh, ale překonat sám sebe a své kamarády. Žebříčky jsou naprosto zásadní součástí zážitku a motivují k tomu, abyste hru spouštěli znovu a znovu, jen abyste překonali svůj osobní rekord nebo viděli, zda se vám podaří předstihnout někoho z přátel.

Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved je hrou, která stála u zrodu moderní indie scény a ukázala, že hry nemusí být megalomanské, aby byly geniální. Je to dokonalý příklad toho, jak správně namíchaná akce, design a nostalgie mohou vytvořit nezapomenutelný zážitek, který ani po letech neztrácí nic ze své síly.

Pokud hledáte hru, která vás na hodiny pohltí a vrátí vás k čisté radosti z hraní, nemusíte hledat dál. Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved je nadčasový skvost, který by měl mít ve své knihovně každý fanoušek arkádových her.

I honestly didn't expect to get this invested in EVE Online. I downloaded it out of curiosity, thinking it would be another space MMO where you pick a ship, complete some missions, fight enemies and slowly upgrade your equipment. Well, I couldn't have been more wrong.

The first thing that stands out is just how much freedom this game gives you. There isn't really one correct way to play. You can become a miner, explorer, trader, industrialist, pirate or focus entirely on combat. You can spend hours building your economy, transporting goods between systems, searching for hidden locations or joining other players in large-scale fleet operations. And somehow, all these activities are connected to each other.

The player-driven economy is probably one of my favourite aspects. Almost everything has a purpose, and the market feels like an actual ecosystem rather than a shop with items randomly generated by developers. Players produce ships, gather resources, manufacture equipment and transport goods across the galaxy. Even something as simple as buying a new ship can involve a surprisingly complicated chain of player activities behind the scenes.

I also really like the atmosphere. Flying through different star systems, looking at distant planets, stations and massive ships gives you a strange feeling of being part of something much bigger than your own character. Sometimes I just find myself travelling somewhere with music playing in the background, checking the map and planning my next destination. It sounds boring on paper, but there is something relaxing about it.

Of course, EVE isn't perfect. The learning curve is absolutely brutal for newcomers. There are so many menus, statistics, mechanics and things to understand that it can feel like starting a new job rather than playing a game. The tutorials help, but they only introduce a fraction of what is actually available. You will probably spend quite a bit of time looking things up, watching guides and asking more experienced players for advice.

Another thing worth mentioning is that the game doesn't always respect your expectations. You can spend hours collecting resources or preparing for an expedition and lose everything because of one bad decision or an encounter with another player. Ships are not simply temporary equipment that magically returns after destruction. Losing something expensive genuinely hurts, especially when you know how much time it took to afford it. But strangely enough, that's also what makes the victories feel meaningful.

The community is another interesting part of the experience. You can meet incredibly helpful people willing to explain complicated mechanics, share knowledge and even help you get started. At the same time, there are plenty of players who will happily take advantage of your lack of experience. Trusting the wrong person can become an expensive lesson. I guess that's part of the charm of a universe where other players are not just background characters.

I wouldn't recommend rushing through everything or trying to understand the entire game immediately. There is simply too much content, and constantly comparing your progress to experienced players is probably the fastest way to burn yourself out. Find an activity you enjoy, learn it properly and expand from there. Joining a decent corporation can also completely change your experience.

Despite its age, EVE Online still offers something that is surprisingly difficult to find in modern MMOs: a world where players create their own stories and where decisions can have consequences beyond a simple quest reward.

It's complicated, sometimes frustrating, occasionally incredibly slow, and definitely not for everyone. But if you enjoy space exploration, strategy, economics, social interaction and the freedom to create your own goals, there is a good chance you'll find something special here.

I still have a ridiculous amount of things to learn and explore, and that's probably the best reason to keep playing.

developer_response:
Hey there coolcreeper155,

For what it's worth, nobody needs a background in aerospace engineering to fly a spaceship in New Eden, and finding the first couple of hours confusing doesn't make anyone stupid. EVE throws a lot of new ideas at you at once, and plenty of today's veteran pilots remember feeling exactly as lost as you describe.

The tutorial is only the first step. After it, the Career Program agents walk you through activities like combat, exploration and industry one at a time, so you can learn at your own pace rather than all at once. Joining a corporation also helps a lot: many filter as New Pilot Friendly or New Pilot Focused in the in-game corp finder, and their members are usually happy to answer the 'what does this button do' questions. The in-game help channels and the many beginner guides on YouTube are good options too.

If you ever feel like giving it another go, there's no rush, and Alpha accounts can keep playing without paying anything.

Thank you for trying out and reviewing EVE Online.
-The EVE Online Dev Team

developer_response:
Hey there DapperWolf,

Twenty years of coming back says a lot about the pull New Eden has, even when the individual pieces don't land. It sounds like the part that clicked every time was the corp and the people around you, and that matches what we hear from many pilots: missions, mining and the rest tend to feel like a treadmill when done on their own, and much more meaningful when they feed into something a group is building, defending or fighting over.

If the routine is what wears thin, most activities have riskier, faster-paced variants, such as mining or gas harvesting in wormholes or hostile space, or moving from missions into exploration or Faction Warfare. On losses, part of EVE's design is that everything can be destroyed, but spreading assets around, insuring ships and not flying more than you can afford to replace can keep a single bad day from undoing months of work.

If you do find yourself undocking again in a few years, the door is open, and we hope that time the view from the top is worth the climb.

Thank you for trying out and reviewing EVE Online.
-The EVE Online Dev Team

review:
EVE Online is one of the few games where the players genuinely make the experience, for better or worse.

I've spent countless hours involved in faction warfare, commanding fleets, organising doctrines, sorting logistics, managing corporation activities and dealing with the inevitable chaos that comes with getting a group of people to do something together.

At its best, EVE is exceptional. You can spend days preparing for an operation, only for everything to change in seconds because someone made a decision you didn't anticipate. A well-executed fleet, a close escape, an expensive kill or a completely unexpected engagement can make all that preparation worthwhile.

The politics are just as important as the fighting. Corporations, alliances, rivalries, grudges and friendships create stories that simply wouldn't exist in most other games. Players build entire communities around what happens in New Eden, including their own propaganda, humour and internal drama.

However, EVE has some serious frustrations.

The amount of administration involved can be ridiculous. Skill requirements, fitting ships, moving assets, maintaining doctrines, managing ISK and organising people can turn what should be an evening of entertainment into unpaid management.

Multiboxing is another issue. While there's a distinction between manually operating multiple accounts and input broadcasting, I don't think fleets dominated by excessive multiboxing are particularly healthy for the game. Numbers and account ownership shouldn't overshadow actual player participation.

Then there are the egos. Some people treat corporation positions and Discord permissions like genuine positions of authority. You can have 90 people on a roster and still struggle to find 20 who reliably turn up. The game rewards organisation, but that doesn't mean everyone involved is particularly good at it.

And yet, I keep playing.

Not because every fight is brilliant or every operation goes to plan. Quite the opposite. Sometimes you lose ships, waste an evening, achieve absolutely nothing and spend half the time wondering why you bothered.

But when you've got a good group of people, a capable fleet and something worth fighting over, EVE delivers experiences that very few games can reproduce.

EVE isn't necessarily a good use of your time. But it can be a very good time.

And that's probably the most accurate recommendation I can give it.

[h1]Race07[/h1]

Release: 2007
Entwickler: SimBin
Preis: 7.99€ / Sale: 2.99€ (2024 zuletzt)
Achievements/Collectibles: nein/nein

Ich hab gerade mal ein paar alte Racing Games durchgeschaut, die bei mir auf Steam noch rumflattern und hatte viel nostalgische Gefühle für Race07 übrig, also hab ichs mal angeworfen, den Controller zurecht gemacht und getestet. Und ich muss sagen, Race07 ist noch richtig gut spielbar. Vieles kam mir direkt bekannt vor, war es doch eines der ersten Racinggames, welches ich aktiv und viel gespielt hab. Damals noch mit nem roten Sidewinder FF von Microsoft (und später dann einem Formula Force EX und Race On).
Aber SimBin war damals auch, was Kunos jetzt ist, absolute Simulationsexperten.
Grafisch ist es natürlich sehr angestaubt aber noch passabel. Die Fahrzeugsounds sind aber spitze, kaum Unterschiede zu neuen Releases.

Die Strecken- und Fahrzeugauswahl begrenzt sich auf die WTCC Saison 2006/2007, fügt aber noch ein paar kleinere open-wheel Klassen und andere Touringwagen hinzu, ganz cool, weil es diese Fahrzeuge in kaum anderen Games gibt (mir fällt spontan nur Racedriver Grid ein). Gerade Strecken wie der technische Stadtkurs in Macau oder die beiden schnellen schwedischen Strecken, findet man aber wirklich in keinem anderen Spiel (ohne Mods), was sie zu richtigen Unicorns macht. Allein dafür hat es sich gelohnt, mal wieder reinzuschauen.

Sonst enthält Race07 alles, was man bei einem Rennspiel braucht. Karrieremodus, Zeitfahren, schnelles Rennen und sogar eine, über P2P laufende, Onlineanbindung für Onlinerennen. 
Die Fahrphysik ist okay, mit einem Controller fühlt es sich sehr schwammig an. Ich erinnere mich aber leicht, dass dies damals schon ein Kritikpunkt war (s/o Heiko Klinge). Die Autos liegen nicht wirklich auf der Strecke sondern schweben eher darüber. Dennoch ist Race07 absolut easy fahrbar und erkannte sogar meinen Xbox Series X Controller, mit wenigen kleinen Settings, die geändert werden mussten.

Keine Ahnung, warum ich das Verlangen hatte diese Review zu schreiben aber das Spiel hat die 3/4h gebockt lol

Why am I playing (and recommending) this game in 2026? Through a cruel twist of fate, my gaming laptop is bricked, and now I'm on a decade old Linux notebook. My use case might be niche, but it's not unique. Lotta people out there trying to game on a potato!

Are you looking for a realistic racing sim that runs great on older tech? RACE 07 is worth your time! As others have said, this is a great (and inexpensive) option for people who can't run current- or last-gen titles. Also worth pointing out that this one's acutally still available to buy, which is sadly a rare thing - I miss you, TDU2!

The standard game comes with a great selection of tracks and some interesting vehicle categories. While touring cars are the main focus, you also get open wheel racing with F3000, Formula BMW, and Formula RaceRoom's pseudo F1 cars.

Sure, the graphics are basic by today's standards, and the UI is dated, but the driving is challenging and intense, and the vehicle setup options are many. It's definitely on the serious simulation side of the scale, though one of the DLCs brings in an arcade mode that's not actually all that arcade-y.

Now, quirks: 

First, on my rig it took a few tries to get a gamepad set up. Might be a Proton issue, I don't know. Anyway, I definitely recommend using a gamepad or wheel, as the handling can be very touchy.

Second, the DLCs are sold as separate 'games', which is fine, it just clutters up your library. Great use of the 'Hide Game' option. Any Steam veterans from the mid-to-late '00s will know the drill. The options can be a bit confusing, so look closely before purchasing (Race Injection is a good start).

I haven't tried online play. Maybe someday. I imagine there are people out there who've been playing this since the day it came out, and I can't be bothered to 'git gud' enough to keep up with them. Happy to be a casual on this one.

RACE 07 это капсула времени сохранившая дух гоночного симулятора середины 2000 х в его наиболее отточенной и харизматичной форме. Она не стремится к холодной математической точности симуляции ради симуляции её цель передать драйв напряжение и тактическую глубину реального гоночного турнира и с этой задачей она справляется блестяще даже сегодня. Её физика может показаться устаревшей для привыкших к современным моделям но её внутренняя согласованность и ясная обратная связь делают процесс обучения и совершенствования невероятно удовлетворяющим. Звук и общая атмосфера остаются конкурентными преимуществами.

Лично я считаю RACE 07 не просто устаревшей игрой которую стоит изучить из исторического интереса а по прежнему действующим и чрезвычайно увлекательным симулятором для тех кто ценит ясный честный вызов и неподдельное ощущение участия в гонке. Она предлагает опыт сконцентрированный на сути соревновательного вождения без излишних осложнений или отвлечений. Это не самая продвинутая или самая красивая игра в библиотеке но она одна из тех что понимают самую суть удовольствия от виртуальных гонок и доставляет его с завидной постоянностью. Моё впечатление от неё стойко положительное как от надежного и атмосферного инструмента для определённого типа гоночного настроения.

if you dont care about graphics, this is a great game. tragically, it takes a great deal of effort to get working properly.

I. since this game released on steam after the porsche and ferrari licenses expired, you'll have to manually change the hexadecimal values in the game executable file to get that content back. i'm not going to leave the exact instructions here, but there are many tutorials online and on steam that show you what to do. i heavily recommend reading this --> https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1989373160 guide by GUGA510 for instructions on a bunch of stuff, including how to recover the porsche and ferrari content. this obviously isn't required, but it does bring back a few cool pieces of content.

II. something that IS required is running the game, config, and sudo executables as administrator, while also running the game through compatibility mode with windows xp sp3. if you do not run the game as admin, you won't have access to the driving school within the game. you'll also need to do is put the following string in the launch properties of the game. this allows it to keep track of your playtime properly: (backslashes do not show in steam reviews, replace slashes with backslashes)

"C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/GTR 2 - FIA GT Racing Game/GTR2.exe" %command%

III. the audio while driving will be ATROCIOUS and the game will run poorly if you do not set the cpu affinity yourself. to do this, you can open task manager (after starting the game), go to details tab, right click on game and set the affinity to cpus 0 and 1. this setting doesn't save, so you will have to do this every time the game starts. if you dont want to do that, you can download the free version of Process Lasso and set it to always do that. you could probably set the cpu affinity to all threads, but just using 2 seems to work fine for me.

you have to get your hands quite dirty to make this game fully work, but i'd say that it's worth it.

GTR 2 - FIA GT Racing Game stands as one of the most respected and enduring PC racing simulators ever released, representing the peak of SimBin Studios AB’s philosophy of uncompromising realism and motorsport authenticity. Designed as a direct evolution of the original GTR, this sequel expands every aspect of the experience, capturing the intensity, strategy, and discipline of professional GT racing with a level of depth that still commands admiration years later. Rather than chasing cinematic spectacle or arcade accessibility, GTR 2 dedicates itself to replicating what it actually feels like to compete in FIA GT racing, making it a title that rewards patience, precision, and genuine racing skill.

At the core of GTR 2 is its commitment to realistic driving physics. Cars behave as heavy, mechanical machines governed by grip limits, aerodynamics, tire temperature, and suspension geometry rather than scripted handling tricks. Every input matters: braking too late overheats tires, aggressive throttle application can destabilize the rear, and poor corner exits compound over the length of a lap. The physics model encourages smooth, deliberate driving and punishes sloppy technique, making clean laps deeply satisfying. This approach shines brightest when played with a racing wheel and pedals, but even with a gamepad, the simulation communicates a tangible sense of vehicle mass and traction that defines its identity.

The car roster is extensive and meticulously curated, covering the FIA GT and NGT classes from the early-2000s championships. Iconic manufacturers such as Ferrari, Porsche, BMW, Lamborghini, Maserati, and Saleen are represented with multiple entries, each behaving distinctly on track. These differences are not cosmetic; switching cars often requires rethinking braking points, racing lines, and setup philosophy entirely. Learning a new car feels like learning a new discipline, reinforcing the idea that mastery comes from adaptation rather than memorization.

Track selection and environmental simulation elevate the racing experience further. GTR 2 includes a wide range of circuits faithfully recreated from real-world venues, and many feature multiple layouts to reflect different race configurations. Dynamic weather and time progression add strategic complexity, particularly in endurance events where daylight fades into night and conditions evolve gradually rather than abruptly. Racing through dusk into darkness, managing headlights, tire wear, and pit strategy, creates a sense of immersion that few racing games of its era could match.

Game modes are built to support both accessibility and long-term mastery. Single races and quick championships allow players to jump in, while full championship seasons and endurance events offer marathon experiences that test consistency and focus. The driving school deserves special mention, as it provides structured lessons that teach racing fundamentals such as braking technique, cornering balance, and throttle control. This educational component helps bridge the gap between casual racing fans and full simulation enthusiasts, encouraging skill development rather than simple progression.

Artificial intelligence in GTR 2 is competitive and largely believable, capable of applying pressure, defending positions, and capitalizing on player mistakes. Races feel dynamic rather than scripted, with AI drivers responding to on-track situations in ways that demand respect and awareness. While not flawless, the AI contributes significantly to the sense of realism and challenge, especially in longer races where consistency and racecraft matter more than outright pace.

Visually, GTR 2 reflects its mid-2000s origins, but its clarity and functional design still serve the simulation well. Car models and track geometry prioritize accurate proportions and readability over visual excess, making it easier to judge speed, braking distances, and apexes. Lighting and weather effects, particularly during night racing, still convey atmosphere effectively, even if textures and interface elements feel dated by modern standards. Sound design complements the visuals with engine notes that communicate RPM and load clearly, reinforcing immersion through audio feedback.

One of GTR 2’s greatest strengths lies in its longevity, driven largely by its passionate modding community. Over the years, players have expanded the game far beyond its original scope, adding new cars, historical seasons, modern GT content, and additional tracks. These community efforts have kept the simulator relevant and fresh, allowing it to coexist alongside much newer racing titles rather than being replaced by them.

GTR 2 does demand commitment. Its learning curve is steep, and success comes through practice, setup experimentation, and disciplined driving rather than instant gratification. Multiplayer, while still possible through communities and leagues, is no longer plug-and-play, requiring coordination and dedication. These factors make the game less approachable for casual players, but they also define its lasting appeal among simulation purists.

Ultimately, GTR 2 – FIA GT Racing Game remains a benchmark for serious sim racing. It embodies a design philosophy centered on authenticity, challenge, and respect for motorsport, delivering an experience that values skill over spectacle. While its age is evident in presentation and convenience, the heart of the simulation remains powerful and deeply rewarding. For players seeking a pure, demanding, and historically grounded GT racing experience, GTR 2 continues to stand as a classic that fully earns its reputation within the sim racing community.

Guten Tag meine Lieben,

GTR 2 hat für mich einen ganz besonderen Platz in meinem Herzen. Viele vielen Jahre hat mich GTR 2 als Simracer begleitet. Dadurch, dass GTR 2 sehr modfreundlich ist, war das damals in unseren Ligen natürlich komplett durchgemoddet und nach all den Jahren wird es mir jetzt vermutlich recht schwer fallen mich daran zu erinnern, was im Grundspiel drin war und was durch Mods kam, aber ich geb mein Bestes.

Aber erstmal zu den Fakten. GTR 2 ist eine Rennsimulation von SimBin Studios und seinerzeit ein absoluter Meilenstein. Egal ob es die extrem realistische Fahrphysik anbelangt, von der sich selbst heute noch ein Iracing oder ein ACC eine dicke Scheibe von abschneiden können, ob es das Schadensmodell war, wo auch mal Frontsplitter, Stoßstange, Motorhaube, Heckflügel oder Reifen abflogen, wo Kratzer und Beulen bis hin zu kompletten Deformierungen an der Tagesordnung waren, wo deine Bremsen versagen, dein Getriebe oder der Motor platzen konnte und was generell einfach deutlich fortschrittlicher war als die heutigen Spiele. Auch damals hab es schon einen realistischen Tag und Nachtwechsel, eine super Regendarstellung, die Möglichkeit 24h Rennen zu fahren in Echtzeit und es auch damals kein Problem war mit über 50 Fahrzeugen gleichzeitig Multiclass-Rennen zu fahren. Alles Dinge, auf die man heute bei den meisten Simulationen verzichten muss.

Natürlich gab es dann mittels Mods noch die Möglichkeit realistisch sich veränderndes Wetter einzubauen, was im Grundspiel nicht ging, da war es dann entweder trocken oder nass, aber alleine die auf- und unter gehende Sonne, die dann im Cockpit blendete, war klasse.

Was das Setup anbelangt, so konnte man damals bereits alles einstellen, was man in der Realität auch einstellen konnte, detailreicher ging da einfasch nicht.

Und jetzt kommt's! Das Game hatte eine Ingameschnittstelle zu MoTec. MoTec ist ein Datenanalyseprogramm, welches aus dem echten Motorsport kommt, was man an das Fahrzeug anschließen kann und was alle Daten ausliest. Heißt du lässt dir alles anzeigen, z.B. wo du wieviel Prozent Gas gegeben hast, wo du gebremst hast obwohl es unnötig war, wie deine Temperaturen waren und noch vieles, vieles mehr.

Und das war in dem Game auch möglich. Wenn du MoTec besessen hast, konntest du jede gefahrene Runde auf jedem Fahrzeug damit auswerten um deine Fahrweise und auch das Setup zu verbessern und anzupassen.

Zu meinen Hochzeiten hatte ich über 400 verschiedene Strecken im Sortiment und weit über 1.000 Fahrzeuge. Mit über 80 Fahrzeugen auf der Nordschleife unterwegs zu sein war schon etwas ganz besonderes.

Das Game hat mich über Jahre geprägt, ich meine über 7.000h kommen nicht von ungefähr.

Die ganze Simracing-Community hat Ewigkeiten auf GTR 3 gewartet, aber bis heute sind wir nicht belohnt worden.

Ich kann nur sagen, dass es ein absoluter Meilenstein in der Simracing-Historie ist und dass ich keine einzige Sekunde bereue.

Müsst ihr wissen!

[i]Sid Meier's Civilization[/i] is without doubt a great series. It balanced historical breadth with a deep root in history and culture, and gamified often-ridiculed elements for the fun factor.

A lot of people must had learned a thing or two about history from playing Civilization; my father introduced me to [i]Civilization II[/i] when I was very young. While I was not good at playing it, browse around the game, like simply watching the introduction clips to world wonders, felt touching and moving. That was the weight of history and it was everywhere in the game, including in many of the materials in its visual presentation. The game had a great impact on me.

Sure, the series is not education software; it never meant to be. After all video game needs to be entertaining. While important, the more recent entries seem to treat themselves too seriously as games, especially as board games, where rules and balance need to be rigid. The visuals also turned vivid and cartoony. The later entries feel a lot like physical board game adaptations, but there was never one in the first place. They also felt a lot more "native" as games for entertainment, stripped of historical or cultural reference and importance.

While the design direction for the series shifted towards a more pragmatic and rigid direction, more in line with institutionalized strategy game design, the fourth entry in the series is the very peak, because it still somewhat stayed true to and actively embraced the duality embedded in the identity of the series. In this sense, perhaps it is not too ridiculous to call it the "last good Civilization." – if that sounds overrated, "last good square Civilization." – you can’t argue with this.

Resenha: BioShock 2, um retorno que merecia mais calma

Terminei BioShock 2 em cerca de 17 horas. Foi rápido demais para um jogo tão rico, e fica a sensação de que eu deveria ter jogado com mais calma, saboreando cada canto de Rapture como quem aprecia um prato bem temperado.

 Uma narrativa que amadurece

A história foi expandida de forma notável. Os personagens estão mais ambíguos e complexos, e já não há uma divisão simples entre bem e mal. Também descobrimos muito mais sobre o passado de Rapture, o que enriquece o universo e dá novas camadas a lugares que achávamos conhecer.

Escolhas que pesam

Além do dilema das Little Sisters, que já era marcante, agora também decidimos se poupamos ou não pelo menos dois personagens importantes da trama. O mais interessante é que ambos têm narrativas muito bem construídas, o que torna a decisão realmente difícil. Não existe resposta óbvia, e é isso que faz a escolha ter peso.

 Dois ideais em choque

O primeiro jogo girava em torno da visão de mundo de Andrew Ryan, o individualismo extremo. Aqui, o contraponto é o coletivismo de Sofia Lamb. Ver as duas ideologias frente a frente, e as consequências de ambas para a cidade, dá profundidade filosófica à história.

Ser um Big Daddy

Controlar um Big Daddy muda a experiência. Pela primeira vez podemos sair da cidade e caminhar pelo fundo do oceano, um respiro visual que também reforça o isolamento de Rapture. O jogo também é mais generoso com dinheiro e recursos: dificilmente você fica sem munição, o que deixa o combate mais fluido e menos frustrante.

A coleta de ADAM e a tensão

Coletar ADAM deixou de ser apenas pegar a garotinha e seguir adiante. Agora é preciso defendê-la dos Splicers e, mais tarde, enfrentar as Big Sisters. Isso transforma cada área em um território perigoso e mantém a tensão sempre alta.

 Terror e atmosfera

Há trechos em que somos jogados na escuridão absoluta, enfrentando inimigos que surgem das sombras. A trilha sonora contribui muito para esse clima, e a variedade maior de inimigos evita que o combate fique repetitivo.

 Uma observação pessoal

Na minha experiência, para aproveitar o jogo ao máximo é praticamente necessário entender inglês. Os Splicers falam o tempo inteiro, se lamentam e conversam entre si, e boa parte da ambientação vem dessas falas. Um mod de legendas ajuda, mas só em parte. Também considero imprescindível ouvir todos os áudios possíveis. Cada gravação revela uma nova faceta dessa história tão rica.

Veredito

BioShock 2 expande o que o original construiu com mais ambiguidade, mais escolhas e mais tensão. É um jogo que pede para ser degustado, não devorado. Se eu pudesse voltar no tempo, jogaria mais devagar.

Seguindo a lógica após o primeiro jogo, BioShock 2 é outro jogo excelente. De modo geral, a qualidade do jogo foi mantida em todos os aspectos, seja gameplay, ambientação, músicas. A gameplay, embora em seu núcleo seja a mesma, ganha em dinamicidade cedo, justamente pelo fato de controlarmos um Big Daddy, com o único detalhe de que eu tive a impressão de que desde cedo você parece muito forte (o que faz sentido para o universo do jogo, e para mim não chega a ser um incômodo). 

A história, embora não tenha a mesma magia de BioShock 1, justamente por já conhecermos Rapture (que com certeza é o ponto principal dos dois primeiros jogos em termo de narrativa), é muito boa. A antagonista Lamb também faz um ótimo papel, assim como Andrew Ryan fez, especialmente se você prestar atenção nos diários de áudio. Acho importante falar ainda do quão boa é a DLC, que, mesmo sendo curta, tem uma história sensacional.

De modo geral, acho que uma boa forma de resumir BioShock 2 é fazendo uma comparação com Majora's Mask, que, mesmo sendo um jogo incrível, fica um pouco na sombra do primeiro jogo, Ocarina of Time, da mesma forma que BioShock 2, outra obra-prima acaba sendo posto para escanteio pelo fato de que BioShock 1 é um dos melhores jogos de todos os tempos.

BioShock 2 — шутер от первого лица с элементами RPG и immersive‑sim, продолжение культовой игры 2007 года. Разработкой занималась студия 2K Marin (при поддержке Irrational Games), а действие происходит в «Восторге» спустя восемь лет после событий оригинала. Здесь ты играешь не за обычного человека, а за Большого Папочку — Субъект Дельта, и это полностью меняет ощущение силы и уязвимости в мире игры.

Сюжет и философия
События разворачиваются в 1968 году. Главный герой — Субъект Дельта, один из первых прототипов Больших Папочек, связанный особой связью с Элеонорой Лэмб, «маленькой сестричкой». Он пробуждается, чтобы спасти её от матери — Софии Лэмб. София противопоставлена Эндрю Райану: если Райан верил в абсолютную свободу и индивидуализм, то Лэмб проповедует коллективизм и «благо большинства», доводя его до тоталитаризма.

Моральная дилемма остаётся, но подаётся иначе: теперь ты не просто решаешь, спасать или эксплуатировать сестричек — ты буквально их защитник, и сам геймплей строится вокруг этой роли. Концовка зависит от того, как ты поступаешь с другими сестричками и в финале с Элеонорой: можно действовать эгоистично, можно — ради «блага города», а можно попытаться спасти всех.

Геймплей: сила Большого Папочки и новые тактики
BioShock 2 делает упор на более агрессивный, «тяжёлый» стиль игры:

Двуручное управление. Главное нововведение: можно одновременно стрелять из оружия правой рукой и использовать плазмиды левой. Это убирает паузы на переключение и делает бои динамичнее.
Бур как основное оружие. У Дельты есть фирменный бур — мощное оружие ближнего боя, которое ещё и даёт постоянный урон и контроль над противником.
Защита сестричек. Механика эскорта стала центральной: ты сопровождаешь «маленькую сестричку», отбиваясь от волн сплайсеров. Это мини‑арены, где нужно грамотно расставлять ловушки, взламывать турели и использовать окружение.
Новые гаджеты и инструменты. Появились заклёпочные мины, гарпуны, хакерские дротики (ими можно взламывать системы на расстоянии). Сама мини‑игра взлома изменилась: вместо «трубопровода» — ритм‑механика, которая быстрее, но требует точности.
Экономика и прокачка. «Адам» по‑прежнему нужен для плазмидов и тоников, деньги — на патроны и расходники. Ресурсы всё так же ограничены, поэтому приходится выбирать, что улучшать.
Большая Сестра. Это новый тип врага — бывшая «маленькая сестричка», которая научилась использовать плазмиды. Она быстрая, агрессивная и служит «наказанием» за попытки насильственно забрать АДАМ. Сражения с ней — одни из самых напряжённых в игре.
Мир и атмосфера «Восторга»
«Восторг» стал ещё более запущенным и «живым» в смысле активности: здесь больше сплайсеров, больше следов борьбы, а некоторые районы ощущаются как настоящие зоны боевых действий. При этом арт‑деко и подводная эстетика никуда не делись: роскошные залы, витражи, мерцающие лампы и вода повсюду создают тот самый узнаваемый стиль.

Локации стали просторнее и лучше приспособлены для боёв: есть места для расстановки ловушек, удобные точки для взлома турелей и укрытия, чтобы перегруппироваться во время защиты сестрички.

Мультиплеер (уникальная фишка BioShock 2)
В отличие от первой части, здесь есть полноценный сетевой режим. Игроки берут роли сплайсеров с разными способностями и сражаются за АДАМ, прокачивая своего персонажа. Это не обязательная часть, но для серии она стала необычным экспериментом и добавила игре реиграбельности.

Визуал и звук
Графика — эволюция оригинала: те же арт‑деко интерьеры, но с улучшенной детализацией, более чёткими текстурами и эффектами воды. Анимации лиц и движения сплайсеров стали выразительнее, а костюмы и окружение подчёркивают упадок города.

Саундтрек сохраняет дух первой части: джаз, биг‑бэнд, эмбиент и винтажные песни. Звуковой дизайн усиливает ощущение подводного мира: гул воды, лязг металла, шипение пара и голоса персонажей создают нужную атмосферу. Локализация — русский интерфейс и субтитры, озвучка — английская.

В состав переизданий часто входит DLC Minerva’s Den — отдельная сюжетная история про сотрудника «Восторга», которая многими считается лучшей частью BioShock 2: там меньше «обязательных» защит сестричек, а больше исследования и головоломок.

Плюсы
Более динамичные бои. Двуручное управление и бур делают сражения быстрее и тактичнее.
Центральная роль защиты сестричек. Эта механика задаёт ритм и смысл многим уровням, а также подчёркивает моральные выборы.
Улучшенные инструменты взлома. Дротики и ритм‑мини‑игра делают взлом удобнее и быстрее.
Мультиплеер. Редкий для серии элемент, который даёт дополнительный опыт.
Minerva’s Den. Отличный дополнительный контент, который многие ценят даже выше основной кампании.
Атмосфера «Восторга». Город по‑прежнему завораживает дизайном и ощущением упадка.
Минусы
Сюжет слабее оригинала. История Софии Лэмб и её философии воспринимается как менее цельная, чем конфликт Райана и Атласа.
Повторяемость механик защиты. Многократные эскорты сестричек местами превращаются в рутину.
Баланс против Большой Сестры. Она может ощущаться слишком агрессивной и «несправедливой» на высоких сложностях.
Меньше философской новизны. Вторая часть развивает идеи оригинала, но не даёт такого же сильного культурного удара.
Кому подойдёт: фанатам BioShock, которые хотят снова побывать в «Восторге» и попробовать более агрессивный геймплей; тем, кто ценит тактические перестрелки и моральные дилеммы; игрокам, которым нравится идея «быть защитником» и выстраивать оборону на ходу. Если хочется именно сюжетного откровения уровня первой части — лучше начать с неё, а BioShock 2 воспринимать как более «боевой» сиквел.

I haven't played the Bioshock games in well over a decade, and since I just ran through the Crysis trilogy again, I decided Bioshock was next on my list. I devoured Bioshock 1, demolished Bioshock 2 after that, and finally came time to play the most "modern" installation of the trilogy: Bioshock Infinite.

To preface, this game is, to me, is just not a Bioshock game, at least in the same vein as Bioshock 1 and 2, and System Shock before that. (*Note, I've only ever played the System Shock Remake, but the inspiration and the fact that the Bioshock series is confirmed to be a spiritual successor allows me to say this.)

Overall, I have probably a net negative opinion of this game compared to the previous two, and I'll elaborate on the specifics of why this game fails where the first two succeeded, for there are myriad reasons as to why this is, in no particular order they will be given, except perhaps the amount of sheer anger I feel at what this game provided to its players.

Here's my breakdown of the positives and negatives:

The Positives:

Bioshock Infinite as a game has held up remarkably well in certain aspects, as its forebears did, most notably including graphics and art direction. It is definitely a more cartoonish take on the art style than 1 and 2, allowing the more aged character models and textures of Bioshock 1 and 2 to seem more "in-universe", as it were, instead of going for supreme realism like some other games of the era. The setting of Columbia speaks for itself as soon as the player sets foot there, and it creates one hell of a whiplash when compared to the setting of the first two games:

Where Rapture was underwater, Columbia is in the clouds. Plasmids/ADAM and EVE has become Vigors and Salts, a subtle nuance that the more anti-religion Rapture has named its most prized resourced after Biblical characters whereas Columbia chose otherwise. When the former trades art deco and mid-century style to create a utopia, the latter favors classical, early 1900's Americana for its own brand of nostalgia. While Rapture and Andrew Ryan embody Randian Objectivism, freedom from all government, law, and religion, judging no one by their sex or color, Columbia and the Prophet Zachary Comstock embody hardcore fundamentalist Christianity, a fanatical cult dedicated to the Prophet and his visions, and the early 20th Century hyper-racist, sexist, classist, and anti-worker environment that the America we read about in history books is infamous for. It is meant to be the polar opposite of the first game, while retaining the same core issue: that one man's Utopia is another man's Dystopia, and this game hit a lot closer to home for a lot of us back in 2013.

There are many moments in this game that are spectacular, but most of them are found in the first 35% of the game I would say. The highlights of the game of course are the two main characters: Booker DeWitt, private detective and ex-Pinkerton agent, war hero of Wounded Knee and the Boxer Rebellion, and Elizabeth Comstock, the Lamb of the Prophet, daughter of Father Comstock and Lady Comstock, who has the miraculous ability to manipulate Tears in the fabric of reality. These two characters are the crux of the game, and the dynamic they have is essential to literally everything in the game.

As far as mechanics go, the game is a lot snappier than the first two games. Gunfights are more exciting, more visual flair and blood, more gore, and interesting enemy types are available to fight. Elizabeth is the constant companion in-game, and instead of many games where you have to defend a useless and weak side-character from dying, Elizabeth actively throws you equipment during gunfights to give you an edge, and Elizabeth can never die or force you to restart from a checkpoint because you failed to protect her, a far cry from the Little Sister harvesting missions of the second game. The game has a decent variety of weapons to choose from, although you will be swapping out guns very frequently, creating a fast-paced and chaotic situation in every fight. Elizabeth can also summon through her Tears battlefield augmentations, adding friendly NPC's to deal and soak up damage, decoys to draw enemy fire, add vertical mobility options, and provide extra equipment and weapon containers.

The game is fun to play, skyhook combat adds a vertical option to firefights, and the equipment system is essential for playing on higher difficulties. The Vigor options are tailored more to Columbia's airborne nature, with such abilities like Bucking Bronco and Undertow allowing you to pick up and throw people off into the clouds below, while many others are essentially copies of Bioshock 1 and 2's Plasmids.

The Negatives:

The UI is kind of atrocious, especially the menu to swap equipment and look at Voxophones. You won't be going into the menu screens as much as Bioshock 1 or 2, because there is no map, but it's still irritating to have to go through the clunky faux-1900's themed scrollbars to change your shirt or hat abilities. You can only equip 2 weapons at a time now in Bioshock Infinite, except for the Burial at Sea DLC's where you get a hidden weapon wheel that I was unaware of until I nearly finished Episode 1. Irritatingly there are also Vox Populi versions for many of the weapons that also have their own upgrades, so my recommendation is to just buy the upgrades for the basic Columbia versions of the weapons.

My main and most prominent issues are with the story, as there are two massive, glaring issues that I simply cannot go without explaining:

A. The Vox Populi subplot - In the game you meet the Frank Fontaine equivalent character in Columbia, one Daisy Fitzroy, a black freedom fighter who was falsely accused of murdering Lady Comstock and is leading a nascent rebellion against the Prophet. The beginning of the game sets the player up with a moral choice to either stone a mixed-race couple captured by the Columbia authorities or to throw it at the racist announcer. The game is shouting at you the entire time that Columbia is an awful place to live if you are not a White person by the strictly defined early-1900's definition of White, so no Italians, Jews, or Irish. These people you see in the game are basically enslaved, it's a slave rebellion. The issue is that once you are halfway through the game, Bioshock Infinite literally decides to, "...but both sides are bad actually...", and then the Vox Populi turn into a rabid gang of murderous and implied rapists, and Daisy Fitzroy literally shoots a man in front of his son, wipes his blood on his face, and then says that to stop the cycle of oppression, "you got to pull it up from the root." They literally made a both-sides argument in a conflict between slaves and their oppressors, and to make that work they turned the character of Daisy Fitzroy into a rabid lunatic who would murder a child in cold blood for literally no reason. There is another addition to this that I will tack onto this horrifically written part of the game in the next segment, speaking of:

B. The Multiverse and Time Travel - This game commits the cardinal sin of being a story about the Multiverse and Time Travel, without adhering to common sense rules about both of those concepts, or the actual scientific concept of the Many-Worlds Interpretation, while still expecting the player to care about the plot. As I mentioned before, the first 35% of the game is stellar, until you reach a point where you are forced to hop into an alternate universe where a character who was dead in the "prime" Bioshock Infinite universe is still alive. You then hop universes a number of times as the story progresses, creating lingering and unanswered questions about what universe you are actually in, the ultimate question being, "WHY SHOULD I CARE ANYMORE?".

I just finished BioShock Infinite, and honestly, this was one of those games that was really easy to sit down and knock out over a weekend. It's the kind of game where you can turn your brain off, enjoy the ride, and still stay invested in what's going on without needing a notebook open on your second monitor.

The first thing that stood out to me was the world itself. Even though the graphics don't really hold up to modern AAA standards anymore, the art style, colors, and overall atmosphere still look great. I played on max settings, and while it won't compete with today's visual powerhouses, Columbia is still a fascinating place to explore. The game has a unique identity that helps it age much better than some other titles from the same era.

One thing that took me a bit to get used to was navigation. There's no traditional map that you can open and use to figure out where you're supposed to go. Instead, the game points you in the right direction with visual indicators and arrows. It works, but there were definitely moments where I found myself wandering around wondering if I missed something obvious.

As for the story, this is where BioShock Infinite really earns its reputation. The gameplay is good, the visuals are good, but the story is what carries the entire experience. It's creative, unique, and unlike anything I've personally played before. Even when I wasn't completely sure where the narrative was heading, I stayed invested because I wanted to see how everything unfolded. I played entirely on a controller and had zero issues with the controls. The game felt smooth from start to finish, and outside of a small visual glitch, I didn't encounter any major bugs.

Overall, I'm giving BioShock Infinite a 6/10.

Now, before that score scares anyone away, it's important to understand why. I'll admit I'm probably a little spoiled by modern games. When you've spent years playing newer releases, it becomes difficult not to compare older games to today's standards. But despite its age, BioShock Infinite still manages to hold its own because of its creativity, world-building, and storytelling. Where the graphics may fall behind, the imagination behind the game absolutely does not.

Will this game make me rush out and play the older BioShock games sitting in my library? Honestly, probably not. But am I glad I finally experienced Infinite for myself? Absolutely.

If you're looking for something different, have a free weekend, and want to experience a game that's truly in a world of its own, BioShock Infinite is still worth checking out over a decade later. It won't blow away modern blockbusters visually, but its story and creativity put up a much better fight than I expected.

"The only me is me. Are you sure the only you is you?"

Existe algum pecado grande o suficiente para não poder ser redimido? Todos somos os vilões na história de alguém, e o que fazemos com esse fardo é sempre uma escolha individual. Acho que esse é o tema de BioShock Infinite que mais ressoa comigo. A culpa é um sentimento poderoso, mas talvez o perdão seja ainda mais.

Você joga com um protagonista falho em todos os sentidos da palavra. Um homem com um passado terrível, que aceita sequestrar uma garota para tentar consertar os próprios erros. E, durante toda essa jornada, fica evidente que o certo e o errado se cruzam muito mais do que gostaríamos. Religião, ciência, política, racismo e ganância são temas que permeiam toda a narrativa de forma essencial.

Columbia é uma cidade aparentemente perfeita, quase angelical em sua aparência e em seus ideais, mas que sustenta toda essa beleza sobre aqueles que são explorados, esquecidos e oprimidos. No fim das contas, Columbia talvez seja o maior retrato que a franquia já fez de alguns dos aspectos mais cruéis da natureza humana.

Booker é um personagem extremamente complexo. Desde os primeiros minutos do jogo, Troy Baker entrega, na minha opinião, uma das melhores interpretações de toda a sua carreira. Booker é um homem que não acredita que todos os seus erros possam simplesmente desaparecer por causa de um batismo. É alguém que prefere observar uma injustiça de longe porque, afinal, não foi contratado para interferir nela.

Isso muda quando ele conhece Elizabeth.

Elizabeth tem um sonho aparentemente simples: liberdade. Liberdade para dançar, cantar, conhecer o mundo e descobrir tudo o que ele pode oferecer. Mas, conforme a história avança, ela percebe que nenhuma alma permanece completamente boa para sempre. Ao mesmo tempo em que Elizabeth desperta a esperança e a bondade que Booker havia enterrado, Booker também alimenta nela sentimentos de vingança, desespero e raiva. É justamente essa troca constante entre os dois que faz com que a relação deles seja uma das melhores que já vi nos videogames.

BioShock sempre foi uma franquia extremamente focada em narrativa, mas, de alguma forma, Infinite consegue superar até mesmo o primeiro jogo nesse aspecto. Tudo isso vem acompanhado por uma direção de arte que compete de igual para igual com Rapture, uma trilha sonora emocionante e uma jogabilidade muito mais moderna e dinâmica do que a de seus antecessores.

O resultado é uma obra que, em alguns momentos, chega a ser difícil de descrever. Cada cenário parece uma pintura. Cada linha de diálogo soa como um trecho de uma grande obra literária. Cada música parece ter saído diretamente de uma orquestra. Sim, algumas mecânicas denunciam a idade do jogo — afinal, já se passaram treze anos desde o seu lançamento —, mas é impressionante como praticamente todos os aspectos técnicos continuam funcionando tão bem até hoje.

A DLC Burial at Sea, que considero obrigatória para qualquer pessoa que terminar Infinite, é a cereja do bolo. Além de proporcionar uma revisita emocionante a Rapture em seu auge, ela consegue contar uma história que, de alguma forma, rivaliza com a campanha principal em emoção, relevância e coerência. Mais do que um epílogo, ela funciona como o elo que une toda a trilogia de uma maneira extremamente satisfatória.

Nunca vai existir nada como BioShock. Agora, com a trilogia finalmente concluída, tenho ainda mais certeza disso. É uma daquelas obras que, assim como Skyrim e Red Dead Redemption, parecem simplesmente intocáveis. E Infinite talvez seja o maior exemplo disso: um jogo sobre culpa, perdão, escolhas e consequências que consegue unir filosofia, crítica social e entretenimento de uma forma que pouquíssimas obras já conseguiram. É uma experiência para a qual eu nunca vou conseguir fazer justiça apenas com palavras, e uma recomendação que faço sem a menor hesitação.

"But if grace is within the grasp of one such as you, how can anyone else not see it in themselves?"

BioShock Infinite fue de esos juegos que me dejaron pensando incluso después de terminarlo. Columbia es una ciudad hermosa a primera vista, flotando entre nubes y llena de colores, pero detrás de esa apariencia hay fanatismo, racismo y una sensación constante de que algo está muy mal. Booker DeWitt y Elizabeth hacen que la historia funcione muchísimo: él es un protagonista roto y ella pasa de ser alguien encerrada y curiosa a entender el peso enorme de sus poderes.

La historia de los universos paralelos puede volverse un poco loca, pero justamente eso es parte de lo increíble. El final cambia completamente la forma de ver todo lo anterior y hace que uno quiera volver a jugarlo para encontrar detalles.

El DLC *Clash in the Clouds* no aporta demasiado a la historia, pero sirve para disfrutar el combate y probar todas las combinaciones de vigores y armas. En cambio, *Burial at Sea* es una locura: volver a Rapture antes de su caída, con esa ambientación oscura y elegante, fue como regresar a un lugar conocido pero todavía más inquietante. Además, ver a Elizabeth en ese contexto y cómo conecta Infinite con el primer BioShock hace que todo cierre de una forma bastante impactante.

Para mí, BioShock Infinite no es solo un shooter: es una historia rara, ambiciosa y llena de momentos que te dejan con la boca abierta.
