[h1]电子游戏里的最佳伴侣[/h1]
生化奇兵无限对一直陪伴玩家的游戏伴侣的塑造令人印象深刻，游戏里的伊丽莎白有很强烈的个人性格，不仅体现在剧情演出当中，更在战斗和搜索物资的过程中大放光彩。“[b]战斗时你无需保护伊丽莎白，她可以保护好自己[/b]”制作组在伊丽莎白的ai上花了很大精力，在战斗中，她会递给玩家欠缺的弹药或是血瓶；在添图时，她会为玩家找寻散落在地的钱，或是提醒玩家遗漏的撬门锁。但制作组似乎为了展现这一点而破坏了正常的游戏体验，比如，游戏里枪的备弹太少，通常会出现弹药不足的情况；又比如，游戏里除了药瓶，其他能捡的物品都不太明显。还有多多少少的毛病，使得游戏的gameplay相当一般。
但是话又说回来，一款2013年的线性剧情向游戏，我并不期望它的gameplay能有多好。这游戏最吸引人的，也不是什么动作射击，而是与伴侣的互动。初识时伊丽莎白对男主还有所戒备，直到在旅途中一起经历困难，才逐渐相信了男主。[spoiler]虽然知道真相之后又崩塌了[/spoiler]在旅途过程中，如何能让玩家像男主一样产生对伊丽莎白的情感——互动。在战斗中，伊丽莎白会帮助玩家，但不是像别的游戏一样打打枪杀敌，而是在战场上搜寻玩家需要的物资，然后传给我们。伊丽莎白很弱小，却不需要玩家在战斗中去保护她，她也不会在战斗中直接“隐身”。制作组用这个非常巧妙的设计，既体现了伊丽莎白的个人魅力，又增强了玩家的情感代入。在旅途中，两人互相安慰，男主弹起吉他，伊丽莎白也会伴着奏唱起歌。这个在游戏里出现了不到一分钟的场景，却给人留下很深的印象，很好的增进了二人的情感。
除了令人难忘的角色塑造，游戏的美术和剧情也很值得说道。蒸汽朋克的背景，飘在云上的国度和反乌托邦的故事。游戏别样的美术风格在开场便给玩家留下了极强，甚至是全游戏最强的视觉冲击。剧情上的反转叫人惊讶，而因为前期埋下的伏笔，也不会让人觉得意外。

Я взагалі не фанат BioShock і досі щиро не збагну, звідки навколо цієї серії стільки галасу та захвату. Вперше я пройшов ці ігри ще давним-давно просто тому, що мій друг задовбав мене своїми розповідями. Нещодавно я вирішив дати всій франшизі ще один шанс, перепройшов усе від початку до кінця, сподіваючись, що, може, тоді я чогось просто не зрозумів. Але ні — моє ставлення анітрохи не змінилося. Це все ще абсолютно не моє, геймплейно не зайшло, а перший BioShock за цей час узагалі дико застарів і виглядає дуже архаїчно.

Якщо ж говорити конкретно про Infinite і вибирати найкращу частину серед усього цього, то це, звісно, вона. Хоча б тому, що повітряна Колумбія виглядає незрівнянно приємніше й цікавіше за той похмурий, давлячий Рапчер. Окремий жирний плюс для мене — відмова від цього дурнуватого арсеналу з десятьма тисячами непотрібних стволів. Без цього нагромадження грати стало банально простіше й комфортніше. З тоніками розробники теж вгамувалися: вони винесені на праву кнопку миші, і при цьому на екрані не стирчить постійно рука, як це дратувало в другій частині. Ну а Елізабет як напарниця — це просто чудове рішення, з нею в дорозі справді приємно перебувати. І головний герой нарешті розмовляє, що теж додає грі очок.

Проте під час проходження дуже чітко відчувається, який творчий хаос панував усередині студії і як жорстко Кена Левіна заганяли в рамки дедлайнів. У грі просто гора вирізаного контенту, через що в деяких місцях шви шиті білими нитками, а всередині відчувається деяка недороблена розірваність. Тим не менш, сюжетно все тримається докупи цілком нормально, а фінал видається справді сильним і гарним.

Окремою темою йдуть доповнення, які залишили дуже двоякі враження. Геймплейно Burial at Sea — це суцільний крінж із якимось натужним недостелсом, де ти падаєш від трьох випадкових куль. Навіщо було робити такий хардкорний і незручний темп — загадка. Але от із сюжетного боку друга частина доповнення зайшла мені чи не найбільше з усього досвіду в Infinite. Елізабет там розкрита круто, а сама кінцівка історії закольцьовує всі події неймовірно красиво й елегантно.

Коротше кажучи, бігати в це часом було навіть приємно, але геймплейно серія мене як не чіпляла колись, так і не чіпляє тепер. BioShock Infinite я б оцінив десь на 7 з 10: пройти її для загального розвитку чи заради ностальгії ще можна, але падати в обморок від захвату й молитися на неї я точно не збираюся.


P.S. У цій частині субтитри нарешті з нормальним темпом зроблені, але вони маленькі й їх чомусь зовсім немає для голософонів.

Bioshock Infinite is... a game. From Bioshock it takes only the name and some gameplay aspects, as both the world and the story are totally different from the other two games (in tone, design, etc). There isn't even any direct connection to the other games until the Burial at Sea DLCs, which take you back to Rapture (where they try to reconcile the story of the previous games with this one).

If you take it as an alternative story, then it starts really weak but evolves into a mindf*ck after around 50% of the game. It is a much more modern spin on both the graphics and the gameplay elements, but it's still a product of its time: bloom to 500% and stupid movement/ani-lock controls. It's still a good game regardless.

The artistic beauty of the game shows in several places, from character and world design to animations (of Elizabeth mostly). Speaking of, Elizabeth is a proper companion NPC: it points out relevant information about your surrondings (pick ups, specific enemy types or where they're coming from, etc) and also helps by giving you salts ("mana"), healthpacks, ammo or even money. She can't be hurt so at worst she's a NPC that regularly helps you with whatever you need in that moment.

I'd recommend buying the Bioshock: The Collection version during a sale, as it comes with the previous games and all relevants DLCs. Great to kill a couple dozen hours, even more if you like to complete all the achievements.

BE WARNED! One of the DLCs ("Clash in the Clouds") provides zero additional story, it's just an arcade gamemode where you clear different waves of enemies in different maps. The Blue Ribbon challenges are a grindfest, and these are required for 100%. And some of them are actual torture, not fun at all. 
This DLC does unlock some behind the scenes content (tho it still requires you to grind the gamemode)

Чем ярче горишь, тем быстрее сгораешь - именно так можно описать всю серию BioShock, где вся трилогия вышла за всего какие то 6 лет (с 2007 по 2013), при этом получила восторженные отзывы что со стороны критиков, что со стороны простых игроков, но вот уже 13 лет прошло с момента выхода BioShock Infinite и о продолжении практически ничего не слышно, правда на то есть причины, но об этом в конце моего отзыва.
Первый BioShock многие причисляют к жанру иммерсив-сим, но как по мне иммерсивные элементы в нем сделаны достаточно слабо, скорее это просто шутер от первого лица с небольшими вкраплениями иммерсив-сима. BioShock Infinite же сделал еще больший шаг в сторону от данного жанра и теперь перед нами просто шутер от первого лица с легкой прокачкой. И хоть я обожаю сам жанр иммерсив-симов, но как по мне вышесказанное BioShock Infinite крайне к лицу - игра стала намного динамичнее, подача сюжета стала разнообразнее, а постановка просто улетела в космос. Шутерная составляющая изменилась не сильно, из минусов хочу отметить что главный герой может носить с собой только два экземпляра огнестрельного оружия (в предыдущих играх можно носить с собой полный арсенал), но сами пушки ощущаются тут намного приятнее, а в совокупности с тем, что патронов периодически не хватает мне приходилось сбрасывать свое оружие и подбирать у поверженных противников и хочу отметить что данное действие нисколько меня не раздражало, хотя обычно я не люблю подобные механики. Плазмиды, вернее в данной игре они называются энергетиками попадаются как уже знакомые, так и абсолютно новые, и лично мне показалось что тут они получились более мощными, по крайней мере пользовался я ими постоянно, в отличии от предыдущих игр. Левл дизайн с одной стороны сильно упростился, игра стала максимально линейной, больше никаких запутанных локаций-лабиринтов и скрытых комнат (хотя вру, раз пять за игру скрытые комнаты попадаются, они даже отмечены как дополнительные задания), зато в игре появились аэротрассы - подобие канатной дороги, по который резво можно перемещаться с помощью специального крюка, что добавляет динамики и вертикального геймплея.
Пройдя первый Bioshock я все не понимал почему Кена Левина считают гениальным сценаристом, конечно сюжет там был весьма неплох, но как по мне на гениальность не тянул. И вот пройдя BioShock Infinite я могу сказать - теперь я понял. Это просто натурально взрыв мозга, так переплести между собой научную фантастику, параллельные миры, стимпанк, религию, расовую дискриминацию, реальную историю и культуру США и завернуть все это в драму - на это способен только гений. Сюжет начинается достаточно просто - главный герой Букер ДеВитт (бывший военный, а ныне частный детектив) ради списания карточного долга получает задание в ходе которого проникает в парящий в облаках город "Колумбия" в поисках девушки Элизабет. Постепенно нить сюжета все более и более запутывается, а финальный твист как по мне один из лучших в истории видеоигр. Из персонажей конечно же запоминается Букер ДеВитт, классический нуарный антигерой, за душой которого немало грехов, его образ и характер очень сильно контрастируют с солнечной и на первый взгляд безмятежной атмосферой в "Колумбии". Ну и конечно же Элизабет - это настоящая жемчужина игры, пожалуй это самый лучший и запоминающийся напарник в истории видеоигр, в ходе сражений она не мешается под ногами, может открывать порталы между мирами для помощи главному герою и подкидывать ему аптечки или снаряжение, во время же мирного исследования локация она ведет себя максимально живо, сама подходит и изучает окружение, ненавязчиво указывает игроку на пропущенные предметы, а если герой не спешит покидать локацию то может просто отойти в сторону посидеть на лавочке. Визуально и характером она полная противоположность Букеру - юная миловидная девушка с чистой душой, еще не познавшая грязь и жестокость пусть и красивого окружающего ее мира.
По оптимизации и багам у игры каких либо проблем нет, лично я не встретил ни одной ошибки на протяжении игры. Хоть я и не люблю мультяшную стилизацию графики, но признаю что во первых игры с подобным стилем достаточно хорошо состариваются, а во вторых данный стиль очень идет BioShock Infinite, конечно же не отметить работу художников я просто не могу - как по мне "Колумбия" получилась просто фантастической, и если тот же "Восторг" из первых частей под конец игры начинал немного утомлять своими мрачными коридорами, то тут такой проблемы небыло. Музыка как и в предыдущих частях подобранная великолепно, отдельно хочу отметить интересную задумку с использованием произведений не соответствующих своему времени (действия игры происходят в 1912 а музыку можно услышать даже из 1980-ых), что объясняется тем, что местный композитор через пространственные разрывы подслушивал и переделывал на свой лад музыку из других эпох.
К сожалению после выхода BioShock Infinite глава студии разработчиков и по совместительству главный идейный вдохновитель Кен Левин признал что выгорел и не хочет превращать BioShock в конвейер, после чего покинул студию, а та через непродолжительное время была закрыта. Права же на серию вроде как остались у издателя 2K Games, и вроде там даже ведется какая то работа по продолжению серии, но не думаю что без Кена стоит ждать многого. Сам же Кен Левин работает над долгостроем Judas, и вот эта игра может стать продолжением идей BioShock. Ну а BioShock Infinite это самый настоящий бриллиант видеоигровой индустрии и я настоятельно рекомендую ее к прохождению всем любителям видеоигр.

Freedom Force, developed by Irrational Games and published by 2K, is a superhero-themed tactical RPG that captures the campy charm and moral optimism of classic comic books while delivering a surprisingly deep strategic experience. Released in 2002, it remains one of the most distinctive interpretations of the superhero genre in gaming, mixing lighthearted storytelling with thoughtful design. From the opening sequence, the game establishes its playful tone with bold narration, comic-book panels, and exaggerated dialogue straight out of the Silver Age. It’s a love letter to the era when heroes shouted their attacks, villains monologued endlessly, and good always triumphed over evil through sheer willpower and righteousness. The entire presentation—from art direction to character design—celebrates the colorful, larger-than-life style of old pulp comics, making it a game that feels both nostalgic and timeless.

The premise is wonderfully simple but executed with creative flair. The story begins when a strange alien substance known as Energy X crashes onto Earth, granting superhuman powers to ordinary citizens—both noble and corrupt. Out of this cosmic accident rises a diverse cast of heroes and villains who battle for control of Patriot City and, eventually, the world. As the player, you take command of the newly formed Freedom Force, a team of superheroes dedicated to defending humanity from these new threats. Each mission plays out like an issue of a comic series, complete with over-the-top narration, humorous cutscenes, and cliffhanger endings that keep the story light and engaging. It’s a tone that never takes itself too seriously, yet it’s delivered with such confidence and affection for its source material that it feels genuinely authentic rather than parody.

Gameplay in Freedom Force is a hybrid of real-time tactics and role-playing systems. You control a squad of up to four heroes at once, each with unique powers, attributes, and special abilities that can be combined creatively in battle. Combat unfolds in real time but can be paused at any moment, allowing you to issue precise orders and coordinate attacks. This pause-and-play mechanic is central to the game’s tactical depth, encouraging players to consider positioning, timing, and environmental interaction. Almost everything in the environment can be used strategically—cars, lampposts, and even park benches can be thrown as makeshift weapons, while explosive barrels and destructible cover add layers of improvisation. The balance between chaos and control gives each encounter a cinematic energy. You can charge headlong into battle like a reckless superhero or take a more methodical approach, setting up ambushes and exploiting enemy weaknesses. Both styles work, and the freedom to improvise makes every mission feel dynamic and rewarding.

As the campaign progresses, you recruit more heroes to your roster, each with a distinct personality and playstyle. Some are archetypal powerhouses like Minute Man, who embodies patriotic idealism and brute strength, while others wield stranger powers, such as manipulating time, energy, or even gravity. The variety of characters keeps the gameplay fresh and encourages experimentation, especially as you can customize stats and unlock new abilities through experience points earned in combat. These upgrades give a satisfying sense of progression without bogging the game down in micromanagement. Freedom Force’s design philosophy strikes a balance between accessibility and depth: simple enough for newcomers to enjoy, yet complex enough for strategy enthusiasts to appreciate. Every battle feels like a puzzle with multiple solutions, driven by creativity and the interaction of powers rather than rigid mechanics.

Visually, the game embraces its comic-book roots with enthusiasm. The environments are vibrant and destructible, the animations exaggerated, and the use of bold outlines and onomatopoeic effects—like “BAM!” and “KRAK!”—make every fight feel like a living panel from a vintage comic. The voice acting, though intentionally campy, fits perfectly with the game’s tone, adding humor and personality to even the simplest dialogue. Combined with the rousing orchestral score, the presentation manages to balance parody and sincerity. Freedom Force isn’t mocking its inspirations—it’s celebrating them. Few games have ever captured the spirit of classic comics this authentically, from the melodramatic villains with absurd schemes to the heroes’ noble speeches about justice and teamwork.

Despite its many strengths, the game is not without flaws. The camera and pathfinding can occasionally make managing multiple heroes cumbersome, especially during hectic fights in tight spaces. Some missions feel repetitive after extended play, and the AI can behave erratically at times. Additionally, while the upgrade system is enjoyable, the tactical challenge plateaus in the later stages once players have optimized their team compositions. Still, these are minor blemishes on an otherwise impressive design. The pacing of missions, the variety of objectives, and the interplay between characters and environments ensure that the experience rarely grows dull. What the game may lack in modern polish, it compensates for with personality, creativity, and sheer heart.

Ultimately, Freedom Force succeeds because it understands what makes the superhero fantasy so compelling. It’s not just about power—it’s about camaraderie, idealism, and style. Every mission feels like an adventure, every victory a triumph of spirit as much as strength. Irrational Games managed to combine strategic gameplay with narrative flair in a way that few titles have since replicated. Even decades after its release, the game stands as a cult classic, remembered fondly for its charm, humor, and faithfulness to comic-book storytelling. Freedom Force remains one of the purest expressions of the superhero genre in gaming—a work of love that captures both the innocence and the excitement of a bygone era, where heroes were larger than life, and saving the world was always just another day on the job.

My memory of this game, of playing it off a CD, is that you could read an entire comic book waiting for a new level to load. Unfortunately that's the part of the game that has been preserved here. Bugs galore, including having actions edge off screen and characters 'dropping' through buildings making them unmovable or un-engagable. What was fun about this game originally was the campy concept and bright colors. It doesn't look right now. The bright colors and comic book dashes and dots with this early animation style doesn't scream page-turning immersive world. It's like a cheap, superficial game you'd get on a cellphone. 

The missions can be painfully simplistic and there isn't a sense of team building or world building. Your reward is largely your own imagination as you earn enough to unlock 'sets' of abilities or skills. If you're someone who wants the nostalgia either from the original release or from the really, really old comics, this might scratch the itch. If you have even slightly high standards informed by modern games, you'll be disappointed. 

The idea that something this simplistic came out in the same era as the Halo games or even the early Civilization games is a little shocking to contemplate. The people who designed it loved Patriot City and some of the 1980's kind of super villain tropes. They had fun with this, clearly, I just don't think it aged well and given the depth of both missions and conceptual design of other early 2000's games I remain shocked it was ever reviewed and ranked so highly. 

I guess get it if it's on sale or you're really, really curious about what people did when they weren't playing Quake back in the day.

I read a glowing review 9/10 on Gamespot for Freedom Force in 2002, (just checked, it's still up), and it's been on my "will play at some point" list for 20 years. It was not worth the wait. Re-reading that review by Ron Dulin now, he compares the game to Grim Fandango and Interstate '76. I never got around to Interstate '76, but comparing this to Grim Fandango must be a joke. Ron's review doesn't seem to be parody, but I can only imagine he was playing a prank on us 20 years ago.

The game is a "not good" superhero / superteam game, with a real time and pause battle system. The game starts you with one initial hero - Minuteman, and you can quickly expand the roster to many more, although only 4 can go on a mission. The main appeal, (I didn't care enough to bother), seems to be that people enjoy creating custom superheroes with game breaking superpowers, (the game lets you add these to your roster), but the game isn't really difficult enough to need this, and any custom character has no voice acting, so adding them cuts down on the whacky voice acting, which is a parody of '50s comics, and probably the only good part of the game. 

So, in conclusion, Ron Dulin pranked me twenty years ago, and then I wasted 29 hours on this game in 2022.
On the upside the campaign was fairly short, which was the only reason I decided to suffer through it.

Freedom Force vs. the 3rd Reich, developed by Irrational Games and published by 2K, is a spirited and unapologetically campy tactical role-playing game that celebrates the golden age of comic books with charm, humor, and creativity. Released in 2005 as the sequel to the original Freedom Force, the game once again throws players into a colorful universe of superheroes and supervillains, but this time with a twist of pulp-style time travel. The plot sees the Freedom Force hurled back to World War II after a meddling villain tampers with history, forcing them to join the Allied resistance against an Axis power bolstered by superpowered Nazi forces. The premise is gloriously absurd, and that’s exactly what makes it work—the game embraces its comic book inspirations wholeheartedly, creating a self-aware homage that never takes itself too seriously.

The story unfolds through comic-panel-style cutscenes, filled with over-the-top narration and dramatic one-liners that perfectly mimic the tone of mid-century superhero adventures. Heroes deliver monologues about justice and honor, villains cackle with theatrical menace, and every chapter feels like an issue ripped straight from the pages of a vintage comic. This commitment to presentation gives the game an unmistakable identity. The art direction leans into bright colors, bold outlines, and dynamic poses that capture the energy of the genre. Each mission is introduced as a new comic “issue,” complete with splash pages and captions, and the voice acting—equal parts earnest and exaggerated—cements the feeling that you’re stepping into an animated comic universe. It’s this stylistic dedication that keeps the game from ever feeling dated; while its graphics show their age, the style remains timeless.

Gameplay blends real-time tactics with light RPG elements. You command a small team of superheroes, each with distinct powers, attributes, and energy meters that govern their abilities. Battles unfold in semi-open environments that can be freely rotated and zoomed, with combat emphasizing positioning, timing, and creative use of the environment. Buildings, cars, and streetlamps can all be picked up and hurled, allowing players to improvise attacks that feel true to the chaotic, destructive flair of comic book battles. The variety of powers is impressive—some heroes use brute strength to smash through walls, while others rely on flight, energy blasts, or mind control. The tactical depth lies in managing each hero’s stamina and coordinating their abilities for maximum efficiency, as careless use of powers can leave your squad exhausted and vulnerable. It’s a satisfying system that rewards planning but still leaves room for spontaneous, cinematic mayhem.

As with its predecessor, the game allows for extensive customization. Players can create their own superheroes from scratch, selecting powers, costumes, and origin stories to build the ultimate comic creation. This feature remains one of the most endearing parts of Freedom Force, as it invites players to experiment with bizarre and imaginative builds that feel right at home in its world. The progression system encourages replayability, as heroes gain experience, unlock new powers, and become more formidable as the story unfolds. The sequel streamlines some of the first game’s mechanics while introducing new characters and a more cohesive campaign, though it doesn’t drastically alter the formula. This familiarity works in its favor for returning players, but newcomers may find the interface somewhat dated compared to more modern tactical RPGs.

The campaign structure offers a mix of mission types—defending key points, escorting civilians, stopping enemy waves, or defeating boss villains. While the objectives occasionally repeat, the diversity of environments and enemy types helps maintain momentum. The inclusion of superpowered Nazis and the time-travel narrative gives the game license to explore wild set pieces, from wartime Europe to alternate timelines filled with fantastical twists. Each encounter feels like an episode in a serialized adventure, tied together by the heroes’ charismatic banter and the game’s satirical tone. It’s not a complex narrative by any means, but it succeeds because it knows exactly what it wants to be: a playful, pulpy romp through comic book history.

On the technical side, Freedom Force vs. the 3rd Reich runs smoothly even on modern systems, though its visuals are clearly products of the early 2000s. The cel-shaded art direction ages gracefully, and the exaggerated animations suit the tone perfectly. The camera and controls, while occasionally clunky, remain serviceable once mastered. The soundtrack, filled with heroic brass and adventurous orchestral cues, underscores the tone beautifully—it’s the kind of score that makes even small victories feel triumphant. The destructible environments also add to the immersion, giving combat a physicality that few games of its era managed to achieve. Watching cars explode or walls crumble under superhuman strength never loses its charm.

Where the game falters is mostly in its ambition relative to its scope. The core mechanics, while fun, don’t evolve much over the campaign, and some missions rely on repetition rather than new ideas. The AI can occasionally behave erratically, with teammates or enemies getting stuck or misusing abilities. Yet these shortcomings are minor compared to the game’s strengths. The sheer enthusiasm behind its design—its writing, art, and gameplay—overshadows its technical blemishes. Even two decades after release, it stands as one of the few games that truly captures the feel of commanding a team of comic book heroes in the heat of battle.

Freedom Force vs. the 3rd Reich succeeds not just as a sequel but as a love letter to superhero storytelling. It’s a game filled with heart, humor, and the kind of creativity that modern titles often overlook in favor of polish and realism. Its blend of strategic depth and comic book flair creates a rare experience that is as entertaining to watch as it is to play. Whether you’re flinging cars at Nazi robots, charging into battle with a team of brightly clad heroes, or simply reveling in its retro sense of wonder, it’s impossible not to be swept up in its infectious enthusiasm. This is your classic videogame with heroes, sometimes even superheroes from across the entire world!

Although the graphics are just as simple as the game is old, it's still hanging very well even in comparison to the nowadays' competition with the videogames of similar or the same concept genres.
Not only this game can boast itself by its low price tag (especially during discounts that are fairly frequent), but the hardware requirements are.. Literally none. It'd be more of a trouble to run it due to the optimization for newer hardware, but those cases should be very rare and one in-between, nothing of the ordinary.

Unfortunately, I must also mention that I didn't like the length of the story.
By about three hours, I was already in and more or less finished, things being a lot more simple than I recall from those fifteen years ago when I first stumbled upon this.. Masterpiece of its age.
It's short, does pose a challenge or two and requires some thought for building up your heroes (which ones to call for that mission if they're available, how to play around it the environment and enemies, and so on..).

Huge applause for actually having a built-in offline mode against AI where the player can choose whichever heroes they want, edit their statistics according to their likings, and even their appearances from within what the game offers, and that applies even towards certain game modes where you choose which characters AI gets to control.
Now that I'm at it - The controls are simple, too simple even, so it's back to the old school troublesome navigation that requires constant attention as if the characters lacked common sense on how to.. Say, run around the corner; Nope, you will have to move their path in a zig-zag way to ensure they don't get stuck over the wall. Heh, funny, but also mighta be annoying to some.
Jumping back, this can be repeated as many times as the player decides to, offering a huge variety of possible fights, making it very suitable towards .. Everyone.

The voice acting of each hero is very well done, nowadays appears to me to be more comical rather than serious, giving this game some new appeal.
That said, there were some moments in the story that, when taken seriously, have moved my heart. That was unexpected, but they are there.. Rarely, but they're there and that's what's important to me.


I'd definitely recommend this oldie masterpiece towards the audience that's into heroes and wants to get some feel of what kinds of games have used to come out during those, nowadays referred to as ancient times.

Everybody wants to be a hero .. Right?
Be it towards somebody, towards themselves included..-

The steam version requires a patch to play on modern PCs, but this game works out the box, which is the reason why this game has better reviews.

As a sequel made with the same engine it was clearly made faster than the original with small improvements, with means that in some ways it's "progressed" but in other way it seems cheap and slap-dash. For example, there is no shine on Bullet's armour in his character portrait. It's such an obvious and easy to fix omission that indicates that the game was made quickly and without much attention to detail.

I use the word "progression" because the alterations are either good or bad depending on your outlook. For example, friendly fire has been nurfed. Whenever you use a ranged attack your character will run away from the target to make space, whereas in the original game they would fire from any distance. powers now use energy "bars" instead of just numbers, and they have simplified the intensity system so that you can only increase your attack by one bar, and you can no longer choose to do a less powerful attack. In the old game you could do low intensity attacks to save energy.

These changed are mostly there to simplify gameplay but they make the gameplay significantly less dynamic. This is a trend that ultimately destroyed mainstream gaming.

[h1]Sid Meier's Civilization V – 8/10. One More Turn, One More Empire.[/h1]
[h2]Introduction – Building History, One Turn at a Time[/h2]
I've always loved historical strategy games, especially those that allow me to develop nations, manage economies, negotiate with other powers, and occasionally rewrite history.

Civilization V delivers plenty of that.

There's something incredibly satisfying about starting with a small settlement and gradually transforming it into a powerful civilization spanning entire continents.

However, while I genuinely enjoy Civilization V, it has never quite reached the same level of personal attachment I have to games like Victoria II, Hearts of Iron III, or Total War.
The vanilla experience sometimes felt a little dry to me.
Fortunately, the Steam Workshop changed everything.

[h2]Gameplay – The More Cities, the Better[/h2]
My preferred playstyle was always economic development and diplomacy.
I enjoyed establishing cities, developing infrastructure, researching technologies, managing resources, and maintaining relationships with other civilizations.

But there was one thing I particularly loved: expansion.
The more cities I founded, the more satisfying the experience became.

I wasn't interested in limiting myself to a handful of perfectly optimized settlements. I wanted to build a proper empire, with cities stretching across the map and an economy capable of supporting them.

Watching a small civilization gradually become a prosperous global power was genuinely rewarding.
And although I preferred diplomacy over unnecessary wars, I always made sure my military was capable of defending everything I had built.

Peace is wonderful. Being completely unprepared for war isn't.

[h2]Diplomacy, AI & Gandhi's Questionable Pacifism[/h2]
I spent most of my time playing against AI opponents, enjoying the freedom to develop my civilization at my own pace.
Diplomacy was one of my favourite aspects of the game. Trade agreements, alliances, city-states, and international politics made the world feel more interesting.

Of course, the AI could also be frustrating.
Some leaders behaved unpredictably, relationships could deteriorate for questionable reasons, and diplomacy wasn't always as sophisticated as I would have liked.

And then there was Gandhi.
That supposedly peaceful bastard could be one of the most aggressive neighbours imaginable.

Nothing quite captures the Civilization experience like trying to maintain peaceful relations with someone who apparently considers your existence a diplomatic inconvenience.

[h2]Steam Workshop – Where the Real Fun Began[/h2]
For me, the Steam Workshop was one of Civilization V's greatest strengths.
I experimented with all kinds of modifications, from additional civilizations and historical leaders to changes that expanded the overall experience.

Alternative history was particularly entertaining.
I enjoyed playing as Jefferson Davis and taking the Confederate States into the modern era, imagining how such a country might develop across generations.

Another favourite was Mussolini's Italy, where I could pursue my own imperial ambitions and build a Mediterranean empire.
These scenarios weren't about endorsing historical regimes. They were about exploring fictional outcomes and creating completely different timelines.

And that was exactly what made them interesting.
The Workshop offered so much variety that returning to the original game without modifications sometimes felt rather limiting.

[h2]Presentation & Civilization VI[/h2]
Visually, I still prefer Civilization V's more grounded artistic direction.
The world map, cities, military units, and overall presentation have a style that suits my taste in historical strategy games.

Civilization VI went in a much more colourful, cartoonish direction, which never appealed to me as much.
I also found Civilization V's overall experience more enjoyable and straightforward, even though its successor introduced additional mechanics and systems.

Sometimes more features don't necessarily mean a game will suit your personal preferences better.

The fifth instalment simply feels more like the Civilization I want to play.

[h2]Final Verdict – 8/10[/h2]
Civilization V is an excellent turn-based strategy game with satisfying empire-building, enjoyable diplomacy, and plenty of opportunities to create your own historical adventures.

Its greatest strengths are its accessibility, gradual progression, economic development, and outstanding modding community.

However, the base game could feel repetitive or somewhat dry, the AI wasn't always convincing, and other historical strategy games offered the depth and atmosphere I personally preferred.

I don't return to Civilization V particularly often anymore, but I still appreciate the countless possibilities it gave me.

[b]Rating: 8/10 – A great strategy game made even better by its incredible Workshop community.[/b]
For me, the real pleasure was never simply winning.
It was watching my cities grow, my economy flourish, and my civilization develop into something I could genuinely be proud of.
And if I could rewrite a few centuries of history along the way, even better.

[b]One more turn? Sure. But first, I need to found another city.[/b]

Axel & Pixel is an unusual point-and-click adventure that relies less on elaborate storytelling and difficult puzzles than on the experience of traveling through an imaginative dreamscape. Developed by Silver Wish Games and published by 2K, it follows Axel, a painter who becomes trapped inside a surreal dream alongside his faithful dog, Pixel. Their journey carries them through an assortment of strange locations as Axel attempts to escape while pursuing an artistic goal involving the four seasons. The premise is deliberately whimsical, allowing the game to prioritize visual creativity and environmental storytelling over lengthy conversations or complicated exposition.

Its strongest feature is the distinctive artistic presentation. The environments look like surreal paintings assembled from hand-crafted illustrations, photographic imagery, animation, and unusual visual effects. This combination produces scenery that feels deliberately artificial in the best possible way, reinforcing the impression that Axel is traveling through a world created by an unpredictable imagination. Locations can shift between peaceful, humorous, mysterious, and mildly unsettling without losing their coherent storybook identity.

The adventure contains 24 chapters divided across spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Using the seasons as major stages gives the journey a satisfying visual progression, with each section introducing changes in scenery and atmosphere. Instead of remaining in environments with a single artistic theme, the player regularly encounters new landscapes and situations. This seasonal structure is particularly effective because Axel is an artist, making the changing scenery feel connected to his character rather than merely functioning as a convenient method of adding environmental variety.

Most gameplay follows traditional point-and-click principles. Players inspect scenes, locate interactive objects, determine how different environmental elements work together, and perform actions in an appropriate order. Pixel occasionally contributes to solving situations as well, making the dog feel like an actual participant rather than simply a companion following the protagonist. The interface is straightforward enough that newcomers to adventure games should have little trouble understanding the fundamental mechanics.

Puzzle difficulty generally remains approachable. Many challenges emphasize careful observation rather than complex logical deductions, and this creates a relaxed rhythm that complements the dreamlike atmosphere. However, players accustomed to demanding classic adventure games may consider the puzzles too easy. Some situations involve identifying interactive hotspots or experimenting with obvious environmental objects rather than constructing elaborate solutions. As a result, the game is better suited to players interested in exploration and atmosphere than those primarily searching for difficult brainteasers.

The experience occasionally moves beyond conventional point-and-click interactions. Three vehicle minigames introduce more immediate action, while certain sequences use timed interactions to create urgency. These portions are relatively simple and never become the game's central focus, but they prevent the adventure from settling into an entirely predictable routine. The transition between environmental puzzles and more active sequences gives the campaign additional variety without fundamentally changing its accessible nature.

Axel and Pixel themselves contribute substantially to the game's personality. Their relationship gives the journey warmth despite the relatively restrained narrative presentation. Instead of depending heavily on dialogue, much of the characterization comes from animation, behavior, visual reactions, and the circumstances encountered throughout the dream. Pixel is particularly effective at adding charm to scenes that might otherwise feel lonely, while Axel's identity as a painter provides a thematic explanation for the unusual artistic environments surrounding them.

There are also optional elements and Steam achievements that provide additional objectives for players who enjoy searching scenes thoroughly. The environments reward observation because small details can contribute both to progression and completion goals. Nevertheless, replayability is limited by the fundamentally linear nature of the adventure. Once puzzle solutions and interactive sequences are known, subsequent playthroughs lose much of their mystery. The attraction of returning therefore depends largely on appreciation for the artwork and atmosphere rather than discovering substantially different outcomes.

Steam Deck compatibility requires an important qualification. The game does not have an official Valve Steam Deck compatibility rating, so it should be considered unverified rather than officially Playable or Verified. Because this is an older PC release, players intending to use a Steam Deck should expect that Proton compatibility, controls, display behavior, or other technical adjustments may require experimentation. It should therefore not be purchased specifically for handheld play under the assumption of guaranteed trouble-free Steam Deck support.

The game's age is most apparent in its relatively basic mechanics and presentation technology, but its artistic direction has aged more gracefully. A realistic visual style from the same period could have become significantly dated, whereas the intentionally surreal construction of these environments still gives them character. The tradeoff is that players looking for modern convenience features, sophisticated controls, deep puzzle systems, or extensive narrative branching will not find them here.

Ultimately, Axel & Pixel is most successful as an interactive artistic journey rather than a mechanically ambitious adventure. Its 24-chapter progression, changing seasons, environmental puzzles, unusual dream imagery, vehicle sequences, and charming partnership between a painter and his dog create an experience with a recognizable identity. The puzzles could have offered greater depth, and the linear structure limits replay value, but the unusual visual direction gives the adventure qualities that distinguish it from more conventional point-and-click games.

The imaginative artwork, pleasant atmosphere, seasonal progression, and accessible puzzles make it worthwhile for players who appreciate visually distinctive adventures. Its simplicity and uncertain Steam Deck experience prevent a stronger recommendation, but its creative dream world remains the primary reason to experience it.

As far as these point-and-click adventure games go, Axel & Pixel doesn't do a whole lot to stand out from the pack. In fact, between its level-based structure, surreal visual style, and lack of dialogue, it practically reeks of Samorost. That's not necessarily a bad thing, because the visual style is still beautiful, and I'd say the game's biggest strength is its gorgeous and creative world design. There's lots of clever solutions to puzzles baked into the environment, and the way the two protagonists interact with them is always fun to see. However, that style does make it hard to distinguish objects from the environment, and this happens way too often. It also tries to mix its gameplay up on occasion, and while that leads to cool moments like connecting pipes, it hits a low with three tedious and frustrating vehicle levels (which become more bearable if you set your refresh rate to 60 Hz). Speaking of tedious, the animations can also last way too long for how often you'll probably be repeating them. With that being said, the core gameplay is still fun, the atmospheric music is pretty great, and the minigames make some of the vehicles a lot more enjoyable.

This game may not be polished in all the right places, but it is still charming as heck, and that's all I can really ask for from this genre.

I'm going to keep this brief. Axel & Pixel changed my life.

Firstly, the game is an absolute pleasure to look at. The contrast between the lovingly handcrafted backdrops and the minimalist aesthetic of our two heroes will keep your eyes glued to the screen for hours on end. And once the game has seduced you with the sheer majesty of its design, there is still so much more to love about Axel & Pixel. 

This narratively driven wonder compels the player to progress through its thrilling action, shocking twists, and heartwarming man on dog bonding. For example, who could forget the pickle that Pixel found himself in when Axel was frozen inside of an ice cube? Or the thrill of chasing Evil Rat through a cave in a hot air balloon? These moments, along with countless others, are examples of the tremendous care that surely was taken in crafting this game's exciting, vibrant plot.

In addition to the beauty of Axel & Pixel's majesty and the depth of its story, the game is simply unmatched as a pure video gaming experience. Not only are you in for thought provoking puzzles and high octane point-and-click action, the game also takes risks by introducing side scrolling chase sequences and quick-time button prompts (a la Uncharted) to keep you on your toes.

The only minor gripe I had with Axel & Pixel is the difficulty. The game allots you 3 hints in each level, which is simply far too few. I think infinity hints would be more appropriate.

To recapitulate, Axel & Pixel is truly a marvel. The game surpassed all of my expectations regarding its design, story, and gameplay. I can't wait for the DLC.

I know this may be extremely unfair to say, but the feeling I get from this game is that it tries to pull of that unique, weird and whacky yet awesome art style and atmosphere that Amanita Design (Samorost2, Machinarium, Botanicula) pull off so well. 
Now, I don’t know who came first, I’m not saying this is a copy and I’m not saying Amanita Design is better, I just don't think this game pulls off the style to well. It has very detailed and strange scenes to it, almost a “chopped up photos” kind of look to it, then cartoons and things CGed on top. I really doubt I’m explaining this very well but it just doesn’t seem to look right to me. Maybe you are reading this, and kind of understand what I mean?

Anyways, I have always thought that “gibberish” voices in games for characters communicating are annoying, and this game doesn’t help that at all. In certain games like Sims, it’s pretty bearable. But I found that this bugged me a bit. To kids and such it may be pretty cute or funny, and in fairness I think this would make a great kids game, but for teens/adults looking for a decent point and click game, this is not one I would recommend. 

I don’t mean to be a complete moan about the game, I’m sure not everyone felt the same as me.
it’s an “alright” game, it’s got little mini games and puzzles and little bits of humour in it that again I think would make this an enjoyable game for kids, but I found it a little “meh”. I played through it until the end, so it isn’t like it was so painfully unbearable that I couldn’t even finish it. But now that I am done with it, I don’t ever see myself coming back and playing this game for the fun of it. If I were to come back to it at all, it would be to get all the achievements. If like me, you’re in that point and click adventure game mood and you're looking for one to play, I’d suggest you look elsewhere.

But, if you're any good at the Trials games and enjoyed Botanicula you can blindly buy this one I guess. I might give it another try someday.

Return to Castle Wolfensteil gilt für viele als eins der besten, wenn nicht sogar der beste Teil der Reihe. Ich persönlich bin da jetzt nicht ganz so überzeugt von.

Als Agent William „B.J.“ Blazkowicz kämpft man sich durch feindliche Einrichtungen, mittelalterliche Burgen, geheime Forschungslabore und übernatürliche Schauplätze, um die finsteren Pläne der Nazis zu vereiteln. Die Handlung ist jetzt nicht gerade eine erzählerische Meisterleistung, bietet aber eine unterhaltsame Mischung aus Spionage, Action und düsterem Mystery-Horror.

Das Spiel verbindet klassische Feuergefechte mit Schleicheinlagen und abwechslungsreichen Missionen. Das Waffenarsenal bietet genügend Abwechslung, während die Gegner deutlich Gegenwehr leisten. Die Gefechte fühlen sich wuchtig an und verlangen auf höheren Schwierigkeitsgraden durchaus taktisches Vorgehen und besonders Geschick, da einige Gegner sehr schnell sind, viel einstecken und vor allem viel austeilen können.

Besonders gelungen ist die Atmosphäre. Anfangs erinnert das Spiel an einen klassischen Zweiter-Weltkrieg-Shooter wie Call of Duty, doch mit zunehmender Spielzeit werden die übernatürlichen Elemente immer präsenter. Untote, bizarre Experimente und okkulte Rituale sorgen für einen interessanten Genre-Mix. Gerade die Abschnitte rund um Castle Wolfenstein und die paranormalen Bedrohungen gehören zu den Highlights.

Aber nicht jede Mission ist gleich spannend. Einige Abschnitte ziehen sich unnötig in die Länge und manche Gefechte wirken durch nachspawnende oder ungünstig platzierte Gegner unnötig nervig. Besonders die Schleichpassagen können frustrieren wenn man ständig entdeckt wird, die ganze Anlage Alarm schlägt und man die Mission wiederholen muss. Dazu kommen noch gelegentliche Schwankungen im Schwierigkeitsgrad, einige nicht ganz zuverlässige Waffen und eine Handlung, die ihre interessanten Ideen nicht immer vollständig ausschöpft.

Technisch ist das Spiel natürlich schon in die Jahre gekommen. Das Spiel nutzt die selbe Engine wie Quake III, Grafik und Animationen wirken daher sehr altmodisch, doch das gehört einfach zur Präsentation dazu.
Return to Castle Wolfenstein ist ein unterhaltsamer Genre-Mix aus klassischem Ego-Shooter, Weltkriegs-Action und übernatürlichem Horror. Die abwechslungsreichen Schauplätze und die herrlich absurden Nazi-Experimente machen die Kampagne auch heute noch unvergesslich. 

Kleinere Schwächen beim Missionsdesign, bei der Schleichmechanik und beim Schwierigkeitsgrad könnten das Erlebnis für den einen oder anderen vielleicht versauen. Aber wenn man sich davon nicht unterkriegen lässt, ist das Spiel eigentlich recht solide. 
Daher kann ich das Spiel durchaus jedem Klassikerliebhaber empfehlen, auch wenn ich persönlich das Spiel etwas überbewertet finde. Es ist zwar gut, aber nicht mein Favorit.
Zudem würde ich es sowieso empfehlen die Real RTCW Mod zu nutzen, welche das Spiel nochmal grafisch aufpoliert und etwas modernisiert.

FPS Ultime

Return to Castle Wolfenstein, c'est un de ces FPS qui représente parfaitement le début des années 2000. Une époque où les jeux n'avaient pas besoin de monde ouvert ou de systèmes compliqués pour être mémorables. Il fallait une bonne ambiance, des armes, des ennemis et surtout des niveaux qui donnent envie d'avancer.

Et Wolfenstein avait déjà tout ça.

Développé par Gray Matter et publié par Activision en 2001, Return to Castle Wolfenstein remet au goût du jour une licence qui avait marqué l'histoire du FPS. On retrouve B.J. Blazkowicz, prisonnier des nazis avant de réussir à s'échapper et de repartir en mission derrière les lignes ennemies.

Et dès les premières minutes, le ton est donné.

Château médiéval, soldats allemands, laboratoires secrets, armes expérimentales et évidemment une bonne dose d'occultisme.

Parce que Return to Castle Wolfenstein ne veut pas simplement nous faire combattre des nazis.

Il veut aussi nous faire combattre des zombies.

Et des créatures.

Et des expériences complètement folles.

C'est probablement ce mélange qui donne au jeu son identité.

On commence avec une ambiance presque réaliste, avec de l'infiltration et des missions derrière les lignes ennemies, puis le jeu devient progressivement beaucoup plus étrange. Les laboratoires secrets et les expériences de la SS laissent place à quelque chose de beaucoup plus fantastique.

Et franchement, ça fonctionne.

Le gameplay reste celui d'un FPS très classique de son époque. On avance, on récupère des armes, on tire et on progresse dans des niveaux assez linéaires. Mais les armes ont du répondant, les ennemis sont agressifs et les affrontements restent particulièrement efficaces.

Et surtout, le jeu sait varier les plaisirs.

Infiltration, fusillades, missions nocturnes, véhicules, espionnage et moments beaucoup plus bourrins. Le rythme change régulièrement et évite au jeu de devenir une simple succession de couloirs.

Mais ce que je retiens surtout, c'est son ambiance.

Les châteaux allemands, les bases militaires, les villages, les laboratoires et les ruines donnent au jeu une vraie identité. La bande-son accompagne parfaitement cette atmosphère et certaines zones restent encore aujourd'hui très mémorables.

Et puis il y a les fameux niveaux occultes.

Là, le jeu abandonne complètement le réalisme pour nous emmener vers quelque chose qui ressemble davantage à de l'horreur fantastique.

C'est là que Return to Castle Wolfenstein devient vraiment Wolfenstein.

Un mélange improbable entre film de guerre, aventure pulp et horreur.

Le jeu a évidemment vieilli. Les graphismes, les animations et certains comportements ennemis accusent leur âge. Le level design est parfois très linéaire et quelques passages peuvent sembler datés.

Mais justement...

Il faut le remettre dans son époque.

En 2001, Return to Castle Wolfenstein était une vraie démonstration de ce que pouvait faire un FPS solo. Il avait une campagne variée, une ambiance forte et surtout cette capacité à nous faire passer d'une opération militaire à un cauchemar surnaturel sans jamais complètement perdre son identité.

Et puis il y a B.J. Blazkowicz.

Un héros simple, efficace et parfaitement adapté à ce genre d'aventure.

Pas besoin de longs discours.

Un pistolet.

Une mitraillette.

Et quelques centaines de nazis sur le chemin.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein reste donc un excellent représentant du FPS old school.

Un jeu qui a forcément pris quelques rides, mais qui possède encore ce charme des productions du début des années 2000.

Un château.

Des nazis.

Des expériences secrètes.

Des zombies.

Des armes expérimentales.

Et un B.J. Blazkowicz qui n'est clairement pas venu faire du tourisme.

Une vieille recette,
Mais une recette qui fonctionne toujours.

Score: 9.5/10

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is an outstanding WWII action FPS that combines intense gunfights, atmospheric environments, supernatural elements, and a memorable single-player campaign. It has a great sense of progression as B.J. Blazkowicz moves from military operations into increasingly bizarre Nazi experiments and occult mysteries.

What it does well
🔫 Excellent gunplay — Weapons feel powerful and satisfying, with a good variety of firearms and explosives.
🏰 Fantastic atmosphere — Castles, crypts, laboratories, villages, and military installations create a constantly changing setting.
🧪 Great campaign variety — The game moves between stealth, exploration, firefights, scripted sequences, and supernatural encounters.
👻 Supernatural elements — Ancient rituals, undead enemies, and occult experiments add a memorable twist to the WWII setting.
🪖 Enemy variety — Soldiers, officers, elite troops, scientists, and supernatural enemies require different approaches.
🎵 Sound design — Weapon sounds, enemy voices, environmental effects, and music contribute heavily to the atmosphere.
🎯 Strong level design — Levels contain secrets, alternate routes, hidden areas, and plenty of environmental detail.
Weaknesses
👴 Shows its age — Some mechanics and visuals are clearly from the early 2000s.
🤖 Occasional enemy AI issues — Enemies can sometimes behave strangely or get stuck.
🧩 A few uneven sections — Certain missions are less exciting than the strongest parts of the campaign.
Who will enjoy it?

Players who enjoy WWII shooters, atmospheric campaigns, exploration, supernatural horror, secret areas, and fast-paced FPS combat will find a lot to enjoy.

Standout Features

⭐ B.J. Blazkowicz
⭐ Castle and military environments
⭐ Occult and supernatural storyline
⭐ Excellent weapon selection
⭐ Atmospheric campaign
⭐ Strong enemy variety
⭐ Secrets and hidden areas
⭐ Memorable boss encounters

Verdict

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is an excellent single-player FPS with a fantastic mixture of military action and supernatural adventure. Its atmosphere, level design, weapons, and campaign variety still make it a highly enjoyable experience decades later.

9.5/10 — A fantastic WWII FPS with an unforgettable supernatural twist. 🏰🔫👻

review:
Schlecht gealtertes Spiel. 
Hakenkreuze, Bilder vom Addi und absolut verwirrende Levelführung.

[h1]Return to Castle Wolfenstein[/h1]

kam schon 2001 für den PC raus. In Deutschland war es wegen den NS Symbolen verboten gewesen. Im März 2026 wurde das Game vorzeitig von der Index-Liste gestrichen und ist nun ungeschnitten im deutschen Steam Store erhältlich.

Ich hab das Spiel auf meinem Windows 11 PC angezockt oder besser gesagt es versucht. Ich konnte das Spiel starten, habe im Hauptmenü die Auflösung geändert und bekam eine Fehlermeldung (GLW_StartOpenGL() - could not load OpenGL subsystem). Das Game ist abgestürzt. Ab diesem Zeitpunkt bekam ich die Fehlermeldung immer wenn ich das Spiel gestartet habe. Ich habe das Spiel gelöscht und neu installiert, die Fehlermeldung kam aber trotzdem.

Dann habe ich RTCW auf meinem alten Retro PC mit Windows 10 installiert. Ich konnte dort die Auflösung ändern und das Spiel ganz normal zocken. Ich wollts eigentlich nur kurz anspielen, habs aber dann doch ganz durchgezockt. Auf dem Win10 PC ist das Spiel nicht einmal abgestürzt.

Wer noch einen Win10 PC hat, wird wohl keine Probleme beim Zocken haben. Wer nur noch Win11 hat, müsste sich ggf. nach Lösungen umschauen.

Erwähnenswert ist noch, dass es 3 Schwierigkeitssufen gibt, wobei das Game auch auf der leichtesten schwer ist. Ich selber bin unzählige male gestorben. Um Frust zu vermeiden, sollte man regelmäßig manuell speichern. Ansonsten müsste man jedes mal das Kapitel neu starten.

Das Spiel an sich ist ganz ok. Grafik und Soundeffekte sind ziemlich betagt. Der Soundtrack und die Steuerung sind aber immer noch gut und passend. Das Game ist komplett auf Englisch, es gibt nicht mal deutsche Untertitel. Das war aber zur damaligen Zeit öfters so.

Wäre schön, wenn es hier Errungenschaften gäbe. Gibt es aber leider momentan nicht. Und leider funktioniert der Multiplayer nicht. Da müsste noch nachgebessert werden.

Die Spielzeit betrug bei mir ca. 11 Stunden. Für den Vollpreis von momentanen 5 Euro ist das vollkommen ok.

[h3]Return to Castle Wolfenstein macht immer noch Spaß und hat ne akzeptable Preis-Leistung. Daher empfehle ich das Game weiter.[/h3]

review:
Played through the entire first segment and then realised I wasn't really hooked. The exploration feels a lot less satisfying overall, the weapons don't pack a significant punch and the enemies don't really react to being hit. I was also really curious to see how they integrated the rpg mechanics, but they seem to be more for flair than anything.

I might give it another shot one day to see if it clicks, but my first impression was sour. A real shame, the visuals looked really nice and I loved the first one.

Damals hatte ich bereits Quake 1 und 2, Doom 1 und 2 sowie Duke Nukem usw komplett durchgespielt und war immer auf der Suche nach dem nächsten guten Shooter. Eines Tages entdeckte ich in meinem Spieleladen des Vertrauens im CD SOUND in Passau eine Spielehülle mit einer Grafik die mich stark an Quake  erinnerte. Der Titel Hexen 2.

Ohne vorher jemals etwas von dem Spiel gehört oder gelesen zu haben, kaufte ich es einfach auf gut Glück. Und was soll ich sagen? Es war verdammt gut! Die düstere Atmosphäre, das einzigartige Setting und das Spielgefühl haben mich sofort gepackt. Für mich war Hexen 2 ein echter Geheimtipp, auch wenn es damals gefühlt nur wenige gespielt haben.

Heute, im Zeitalter des Internets, wird gefühlt jedes Spiel schon vor der Veröffentlichung bis ins kleinste Detail analysiert, zerlegt und bewertet. Im schlimmsten Fall wird es sogar schon lange vor dem offiziellen 1.0 Release auf Steam gespielt und komplett auseinander genommen. Überraschungen sind dadurch die Ausnahme geworden. Dieses Gefühl, zufällig auf ein Spiel zu stoßen, absolut nichts darüber zu wissen und dann völlig begeistert davon zu sein gibt es einfach heutzutage nicht mehr.

Hexen II war für mich genau so ein Überraschungshit. Keine Reviews, keine YouTube-Videos, keine endlosen Diskussionen in Foren. Einfach die Hülle gesehen, gekauft und in ein verdammt gutes Spiel erhalten.

Das waren noch Zeiten! Die gute alte Zeit, in der man Spiele noch wirklich entdecken konnte und es steht immer noch im Regal und mittlerweile auch in der Steam Biblio.

Hexen II looks incredible. The art direction, texture work, mapping, enemies, everything looks cool and sounds great in this game. If you are interested in Quake 1 graphics then you will really enjoy this aspect. There is a lot of variety in locations, too - over the course of the game there are four different settings you explore: Medieval Europe, Mesoamerica, Ancient Egypt and Ancient Greece.

I liked the game until I reached Egypt. It filtered me. I don't like hand-holdy games, but Hexen II takes the fucking cake. The game does not have a map and it has point-and-click progression logic. You have to find items, bring them to other maps to transform them, then bring them to another map to unlock doors. This is decipherable and even fun in the first two chapters of the game, but the Egypt chapter was way too obtuse for me to finish without the assistance of a guide. It doesn't help that it also has a floor puzzle from Hell which I am convinced is bugged. I quicksaved and attempted to solve it for 20 minutes to no avail. The guides were confused on how to complete it and YouTube wasn't helpful. Just ridiculous.

I would recommend playing through the first two chapters but I would not recommend playing past that without the use of a guide. I really hope this gets a NightDive remaster with some alterations because Hexen II is a great game buried under some serious bullshit.

I haven't actually beaten Heretic OR the original HeXen.
That being said, from what little I've played of HeXen 1, HeXen II is MILES better! The levels and progression from area to area can be a bit obtuse, but it beats the Hell out of needing to find a dozen switches just to open a door. And I would argue that unique items relating to each unique area being the driving force of unlocking secrets to get to the next stage is far more interesting anyway.

The combat takes some getting used to with certain weapons and/or characters, ESPESCIALLY if you insist on playing without a crosshair (which I do 🙃), but just choose a difficulty that feels fair in order to get used to the combat. And then once you're ready, move up a difficulty level on your next playthrough!

It still has some jank, you'll need some community patches and a source port to get the best experience, and there WILL BE parts that make you go "What the HELL am I supposed to do?!" but honestly, it's par for the course when it comes to these early action adventure games.

It's not DOOM, it's not Heretic 2, and it's not Unreal, but it's a Raven game, and that's enough for me. 👌

Два змеиных всадника пали, но дело их живёт, ибо третий и по совместительству самый могущественный из них, Эйдолон, продолжает своё странствие. Компанию ему, помимо россыпи монструозных сущностей в диапазоне от пауков, скорпионов, рогатых лучников и бараноподобных магов до големов и импов, составляют четыре всадника рангом пониже — Голод, Смерть, Чума и Война. Одному из четырёх героев — паладину, крестоносцу, некроманту или убийце — предстоит собраться с силами и бросить ему вызов. Основные концептуальные принципы сохранились со времён оригинального Hexen: Beyond Heretic (1995), но в геймплейном контексте отныне это скорее не шутер, а экшен с примесью приключения.

Арсенал. Как и ранее, каждый класс имеет свою специфику. Доступных каждому орудий по-прежнему четыре — с той разницей, что последнее отныне собирается не из трёх, а из двух частей. Возьмём для примера убийцу — единственную женщину в отряде. Начинает своё странствие она с довольно слабым клинком, чуть позже обзаводится дальнобойным арбалетом, потребляющим синюю ману. В доступном ростере она, возможно, может показаться наиболее сомнительным выбором, но, как в своё время было с магом, первое впечатление обманчиво — третьим доступным ей орудием, требующим зелёную ману, становятся достаточно мощные бомбы, а четвёртым, как, впрочем, и у остальных персонажей, является посох, снаряды которого сами наводятся на противников. Помимо этого, если ей удаётся подобраться к недоброжелателю со спины, то есть возможность нанести критический урон.

Инвентарь. Знакомые предметы вроде синих склянок, употребляемых для пополнения здоровья сразу, и фиолетовых, которые можно унести с собой, а также томов силы дополнились новыми разновидностями. Так, отдельно среди них можно выделить возможность призывать на помощь дружественных летающих импов, куб, который бьёт супостатов подобием электрического разряда, кольца, моментально применяемые при подборе и дающие разные бонусы — вроде возможности дольше плавать под водой. Импы и кубы вполне эффективны против наиболее опасных разновидностей монстров — в частности, ангелов смерти, блокирующих большинство атак, и упомянутых магов, которые любят телепортироваться. Они также могут временно отвлечь на себя боссов. Осталась на месте и возможность превращения монстров в домашний скот, в Hexen II представленный овцами.

Базовые RPG-элементы. По мере продвижения выбранный герой увеличивает свой уровень, что, с одной стороны, даёт прирост к базовым характеристикам, а с другой — открывает пассивные способности числом две штуки. У убийцы, помимо упомянутого выше критического удара, есть возможность замереть на месте и потенциально стать невидимой для противников, а некромант получает способность похищать здоровье у окрестной живности и таким образом восполнять своё собственное.

Антураж. В основе игры лежит ядро Quake (1996), что, в свою очередь, сказалось на стилистике и местной атмосфере. Локации довольно угловатые, в эстетике брутализма, с не очень существенной детализацией. Повествование разбито на четыре тематические зоны, охватывающие вымышленные континенты. Blackmarsh — Средневековье, Mazaera — Мезоамерика, представляющая собой некую помесь ацтеков и майя, Thysis — Древний Египет, Septimus — Античность. По мере продвижения обнаруживаются новые виды противников, уникальные для конкретной местности. Люди-ягуары, люди с головами шакалов (отсылка к богу смерти Анубису), каракатицы и медузы-горгоны, которые могут попытаться превратить героя (или героиню) в камень. Новые технические возможности позволили добавить чуть больше точечных элементов разрушаемости.

Сюжетный аспект. Лаконичен, ограничен интро и текстами, разбросанными по локациям.

Туда-обратно. Оригинальный Hexen славился своими запутанными головоломками и хитро запрятанными переключателями. Здесь же эта составляющая вышла на новый, иной уровень. На этот раз дело не ограничивается только бегом, прыжками, поиском ключей и многочисленных квестовых предметов. Так, в Древнем Египте — наиболее красочном, но наименее линейном и наиболее сложном в прохождении сегменте — потребуется расшифровывать загадки, построенные вокруг времени и мифологии, разобраться в которых без сопроводительного руководства будет непросто.

Оценивать получившийся результат можно по-разному. Экшена здесь хватает, но рассматривать данный проект по привычным стандартам шутеров нет смысла. Повествованию не стали уделять больше внимания, и это разочаровывает. Есть визуально примечательные сегменты, но общая атмосфера довольно блёклая. Звуковое сопровождение есть, но ничем не запоминается. Усложнённые загадки потенциально способны отбить желание к прохождению. В то же время, если рассматривать тот же список в плоскости приключенческого проекта, то фактически оценка может оказаться на несколько баллов выше.

* Хронометраж ~ 9,5 часов, сложность "Cutthroat" (2 / 4), класс - убийца (assassin).

* Source-port - FTEQW.

-----

Portal of Praevus (1998).

Действие дополнения разворачивается сразу после гибели последнего змеиного всадника, Эйдолона. Основным антагонистом отныне является четырёхрукий маг — Прайвус. С одной стороны, он жаждет по своему усмотрению воспользоваться останками падших всадников, а с другой — подчинить местный мир своей власти. Принципиальных концептуальных изменений по сравнению с оригинальной игрой не так много, но в целом их достаточно.

Новая героиня. К ростеру из четырёх знакомых персонажей примкнула демонесса, согласно заложенной концепции являющаяся плодом нечестивых экспериментов Эйдолона, который хотел вывести собственную демоническую армию. Если же погрузиться в мифологический контекст чуть больше, то можно выдвинуть предположение, что она является отсылкой к мифам Тибета, в одной из версий которых представляется кем-то вроде местной богини из периода, предшествующего приходу буддизма. Новая особа полагается исключительно на дальнобойные атаки. Может кидаться кислотой и призывать столбы огня, а при сборе двух фрагментов четвёртого орудия — оперировать мечом, который разбрасывает по земле что-то вроде шаровых молний. Сочетание последнего с томом силы позволяет бить противников направленным электрическим зарядом. Помимо этого, она передвигается несколько быстрее других героев и легче преодолевает сегменты, где требуются прыжки, так как может ненадолго замирать в воздухе.

Локации. Доступны два хаба. Первый — перекочевавший из предшественника Blackmarsh в антураже Средневековья, с поправкой на то, что теперь исследуем (помимо "штаб-квартиры" ранее павшего злодея) деревню, крепость, катакомбы и чертоги мёртвых. Второй — Tulku, отдельный континент, стилизованный под крайне редко встречающийся в играх стиль — заснеженный Тибет, состоящий из десяти сегментов. Среди них окрестности храмового комплекса, ледяные пещеры и сами храмы, представляющие собой гремучую смесь из отсылок к шаманизму, индуизму и буддизму. Из чего-то похожего по контексту в памяти всплывает только Skyblazer (1994), некогда выходивший на Super Nintendo.

Монстры. Пять новых разновидностей. Пентаклы — прыгающие, стреляющие издалека и в довесок взрывающиеся существа, представляющие собой некое подобие комбинации слизней и пиявок. Люди-яки (два вида) — могут пытаться атаковать с разбега, швыряются льдом. Чем-то напоминают ослабленных малотавров из Heretic (1994). Людей-ягуаров больше нет, зато есть схожая вариация на тему снежных барсов и встречающихся ближе к эпилогу тигров. И те и другие могут осуществлять атаку в прыжке.

Предметы. Новых расходников не замечено, но ввиду наличия нового класса изменилось возможное свойство бомб — отныне они могут распылять ядовитый газ.

Новое музыкальное сопровождение. Субъективно — более интересное.

Графическая составляющая осталась на уровне. Красоты Тибета вполне сопоставимы по уровню с представленным ранее Древним Египтом. Имеется поддержка рендера Glide со своей спецификой вроде несколько иначе выглядящих спрайтов оружия.

This is probably the game I would use as a prime example of bad level design. This is one of those "where the actual fuck do I go?" or "play with an open guide" kind of game, but in the worst was possible. The objectives are unclear, the puzzles are too cryptic and the level design is confusing as hell, probably even more so than Hexen 1. The combat (using the Paladin class) is kinda weird and janky in the way that damage might feel random at times and the enemies have poorly telegraphed moves like dodging, deflecting or just regular attacks; even if it's subpar it's not even close to being the worst part of the game, the level design and progression take that spot. There are also soft RPG mechanics tacked on, like gaining experience and leveling up from killing enemies, they just translate to higher stats (such as max health) and passive skills that may not be that good or are just underwhelming: the Paladin has a skill to move faster underwater and not drowning; and a skill that has 20% chance (at max level) to revive him when dying. I just hope if or when Microsoft/Nightdive/ID/MachineGames makes a remaster that they address these issues because otherwise I don't think I would come back to it, I'd also change my review if they "fix" it enough to be at least decent.

[h1][b] Reseña de HeXen II[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
HeXen II es ese shooter en primera persona noventero que se levanta de su tumba gótica para recordarte una verdad incómoda: antes los juegos no te daban la mano… te la arrancaban y luego te pedían que resolvieras un rompecabezas con el muñón. Acción rápida, fantasía oscura y un ritmo de “avanza, dispara, explora, te pierdes, vuelves a disparar”.

La propuesta es simple y deliciosa: boomer shooter con sabor a mazmorra, con ambientación atmosférica y un toque de rol (más por feeling y progresión que por sistemas modernos). Entras por la puerta buscando adrenalina y sales con PTSD de pasillos idénticos y enemigos que te castigan por existir. Primera impresión: envejeció con dignidad… pero no con paciencia para tu agenda.

[h2]Hechizos Prohibidos y Maldiciones del Reino[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
 Acción FPS retro con personalidad: rápido, directo y sin cinemáticas eternas   
 Ambientación gótica/fantasía oscura muy marcada, de esas que te “ensucian” la pantalla mental   
 Tiene multijugador y cooperativo (incluye LAN), ideal para sufrir acompañado   
 Steam Cloud y Préstamo familiar: al menos tus partidas (y tu trauma) viajan contigo   
 Sensación “clásico de ayer”: para quienes extrañan cuando los juegos eran menos terapia y más castigo   

Lo No Tan Bueno:
 0 logros: Steam no te va a validar nada, aunque hayas sobrevivido como campeón   
 Comunidad actual: 1 jugador. Sí, UNO. El multijugador existe, como los unicornios: en teoría   
 Dificultad vieja escuela: a ratos es reto justo, a ratos es “te moriste porque sí”   
 Elementos de rompecabezas/exploración pueden sentirse crípticos si vienes con cerebro moderno   
 Presentación retro: si esperas glamour visual actual, este juego te mira y se ríe en 320x200

[h2]Conclusión (Bueno)[/h2]
HeXen II es “Bueno” en el sentido más honesto: un clásico de acción en primera persona con identidad, oscurito, atmosférico y con ese ritmo de boomer shooter que te obliga a jugar despierto. No intenta seducirte: te reta, te empuja al barro y te dice “a ver si muy gamer”.

Lo controversial: su multijugador y cooperativo son una carta de presentación simpática… pero con 1 jugador activo, hoy se siente más como un museo interactivo que como una plaza pública. Aun así, con 547 recomendaciones totales, queda claro que tiene su culto: gente que aprecia el diseño de otra época, con sus virtudes y sus pecados.

[h1] HeXen II [/h1]

[h3] Positives: [/h3]
+ Retro and nostalgia feel
+ Good graphics (for its time)
+ Ok sounds and atmospheric dark music (if you bother to fix the missing soundtrack)
+ A lot of abilities and items to use
+ 4 different classes to choose from
+ Some cool weapons
+ A lot of nicely detailed environments
+ Some parts are actually quite enjoyable
+ There are walkthroughs available online (thank God!)

[h3] Negatives: [/h3]
- The most complex, confusing and labyrinthy level-design I have ever encountered from the 90s
- Some way too hidden items, confusing puzzles and crazy things you must do to progress
- You'll most likely get stuck many times during your playthrough
- Almost no hints on where to go or what to do next to progress
- No objective tab or in-game map
- You have to do everything in exact order (which you have to guess yourself)
- A lot of back and forth
- You can go to multiple levels making it even harder to know what to do next
- A lot of wandering around frustrated without knowing what small thing you have overlooked
- A lot of bugs and glitches
- The game is unstable (even with the Hammer of Thyrion Source port)
- Gets grindy and repetitive
- Hard difficulty in general (with difficulty spikes)
- Not enough ammo or health potions
- The fun of playing disappears way too fast
- Almost unplayable out of the box without fixes
- The Mission Pack Portal Of Praevus is not included

[h3] Conclusion: [/h3]
[b] Hexen 2: [/b]
I played this game as a little kid when it was released in the 90s, but didnt get past the first level.
Thought it would be better now that Im older, but man I understand why I struggled so much with this game.
Luckily there are walkthroughs online, or else I would have given up on the game for the second time in my life.
Why isnt there an objective tab or in-game map? With such confusing labyrinthy level design it should have been included.
And the puzzles and things you must do to progress sometimes makes little to no sense.
So would I play this game ever again? Thats a no.
Are there people who would like this game even with all its problems? Sure.
If any of the above dosent scare you away, just go ahead.

[b] Mission Pack Portal of Praevus: [/b]
After playing the original, I also played the not included Mission Pack to see if it was any different.
And man am I glad I did, its so much better than the original game.
First and foremost the confusing labyrinthy levels of the original is toned down to a more simplified and understandable design.
The game is more linear and straight forward, making progress way more joyful and entertaining.
And also there is an objectives tab this time around (finally!).
The graphics feel crisper and better, the level themes and textures are better, so the overall feel is better.
Its also less dark and more mysterious. And in my opinion, thats a nice way to go.
The new class Demoness has a ranged starting weapon with infinite ammo, a major upgrade from the original melee weapons.
So yeah, do yourself a favor and play the Mission Pack as well.

5. Set options for mouse/mouse look to "on", and adjust the graphics to you liking under OpenGL Features and Video Modes (It can make the game look quite amazing for a 90s game)

7. To fix the field of view open the console command with "|" (the key next to "1") and type FOV 120 (or values to your liking from 60-170)
Remember to do this every time you start the game (or the FOV will be at the standard 80)
8. If the game suddenly hangs or gets major framedrops, either force close the game and restart, or tab in and out of the game
(Its also more stable if you play it in window mode rather than in fullscreen)
9. If you get stuck for a longer period of time (trust me, you most likely will!) be kind to yourself and use online walkthroughs
