[h1] Está olhando em um DLC de um dos maiores jogos de RTS do mundo. [/h1]

[u] Você sabe o que é Company of Heroes? Não? Deixe eu te explicar! [/u]

Company of Heroes é um jogo de estratégia em tempo real sobre a Segunda Guerra Mundial. Neste DLC, ele adiciona mais campanhas de um jogador e, junto com isso, adiciona duas novas facções: os Britânicos e a Panzer Elite alemã. Estes dois servem como suporte no jogo, e eu vou falar sobre estas coisas nessa análise.

[h1] Panzer Elite Alemã [/h1]

A Panzer Elite é uma nova facção do lado do Eixo, e é focada puramente em rapidez e guerra mecanizada.  Do mesmo jeito aos Britânicos, eles precisam de um veículo mecanizado para controlar pontos estratégicos. O que são pontos estratégicos? Bem, pontos estratégicos são basicamente a sua fonte de recursos. Existem três tipos de pontos estratégicos: Ponto estratégico, combustível, e munição. Cada um deles dá mão de obra, que você precisa para colocar unidades na fronteira.

[h1] Britânicos [/h1]

Os britânicos são outra nova facção adicionada por este DLC, focada puramente em infantaria e artilharia. Ela é boa para jogar se você quer focar em defender ruas que ajudarão na campanha. Eles precisam da sua unidade mecanizada de HQ para controlar pontos capturados mais eficientemente, mas é melhor não fazer isso enquanto a área está em combate. 

Em conclusão, eu completamente recomendo que você use Opposing Fronts no jogo de Company of Heroes, se quiser mais unidades de suporte. Como os britânicos, eu gosto de capturar a maioria das ruas e fortificá-las, enquanto como os Panzer Elite eu geralmente ataco os inimigos para meus aliados ajudarem e capturarem pontos.

[i]«Командовать англичанами — это искусство превращения чаепития в кровавую баню под аккомпанемент 'Бог хранит короля', играющего на заедающей патефонной игле.»[/i]

[quote][i]Всем привет. Автор не несет ответственности за причиненный вред своими обзорами. Любое сходство с другими обзорами случайно. Данный обзор является лишь мнением автора и вы можете всегда оставаться при своем мнении! Спасибо за понимание и приятной игры![/i][/quote]

[h2]Описание[/h2]
[b]Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts[/b] — это это дополнение к Company of Heroes, где вас ждут две новые фракции: британцы с их чопорной обороной и немецкая танковая элита, для которой «блицкриг» — не тактика, а стиль жизни. Здесь вы освободите французский Кан (или героически провалите операцию «Маркет Гарден»), а заодно узнаете, что война — это как чаепитие у королевы: либо вы пьёте чай, либо чай пьёт вас.

[h2]Графика и звук[/h2]
Визуал — как дорогой коньяк: с годами только лучше. Разрушаемость осталась на высоте: дома крошатся под танками, а трупы летят так грациозно, будто участвуют в балете. Дождь и грозы — теперь немцы горят под аккомпанемент молний, как в голливудском блокбастере.

Лязг гусениц «Тигров», вопли «томми» под пулемётами MG-42 и бравурные речи офицеров — идеальный фон для медитации. Особый шик: звук британской гаубицы, от которого у соседей сыплется штукатурка.

Минус: На некоторых ПК игра тормозит, словно пьяный фельдфебель в грязи Нормандии. Зато графика напоминает тушёнку — съедобно, но без изысков.

[h2]Геймплей[/h2]
Две новые фракции — два способа терять солдат с изяществом:
[list]
[*] Британцы: Их тактика — «окопались и ждём». Мобильные штабы на колёсах (чтобы быстрее сбежать?), траншеи для чаепитий под огнём и офицеры, чьи речи поднимают боевой дух... пока снаряд не снесёт им голову. Плюс: артиллерия бьёт так далеко, что можно устроить вечерний чай прямо в штабе врага.

[*] Немецкая танковая элита: Тут вам не пехота — тут «панцер-балет». Лёгкие танки-разведчики, «Королевские тигры» (дорогие, как яхты олигарха) и десантники, телепортирующиеся в здания (видимо, через портал в Берлин). Минус: если техника горит — это катастрофа. Если не горит — вы что-то делаете не так.

[/list]

Фишка дополнения: Система ветеранов. Пехота, выжившая после атаки на танк, получает бонусы: от «крепких нервов» до умения прятаться в кустах с гранатой.

[h2]Сюжет и атмосфера[/h2]
[b]Кампания за британцев[/b]
Освобождение Кана — это 10 миссий обороны. Сидишь в окопе, пьёшь воображаемый чай, отражаешь атаки немцев. Сюжет? «За королеву!» — большего не надо. Историческая достоверность на уровне: коммандос в планерах выглядят круто, даже если приземляются прямо на мины.

[b]Кампания за немцев[/b]
Операция «Маркет Гарден» — редкий шанс поиграть за «плохих парней». Два брата-офицера, философствующие о войне между взрывами. Атмосфера: грязь, кровь и ирония. Когда ваш «Тигр» давит союзников, игра шепчет: «Это не военные преступления, это тактика».

Важно: Ролики сняты так эпично, что даже смерть рядового Джонсона выглядит как сцена из «Спасти рядового Райана»

[h2]Плюсы:[/h2]
[list]
[*] Уникальные фракции: от чаепитий до танковых оргий 
[*] Разрушаемость всего, включая мораль
[*] Мобильные штабы — гениально для побегов
[*] Окопы! Наконец-то можно рыть могилы заранее
[/list]

[h2]Минусы:[/h2]
[list]
[*] Баланс? Нет, не слышали: «Королевский тигр» против пехоты — это цирк
[*] Британская кампания: оборона, оборона и ещё раз оборона
[*] Локализация: немцы кричат «сэр!» вместо «Achtung!»
[*] AI союзников умнее сапога, но тупее лопаты
[/list]

[h2]Заключение:[/h2]
[b]“Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts”[/b] — это как второй кусок торта после пира победы: такой же сладкий, но может стоить вам печени. Хотите артиллерийской дуэли под дождём? Пожалуйста! Мечтали давить союзников «Тигром»? Вот ваш билет в рай для циников. Главное — не задумываться, почему немецкие десантники телепортируются в дома.

[h2]Итоговая оценка:[/h2]
[h3]8/10[/h3]

Если вы всегда мечтали почувствовать себя великим полководцем, но в реальной жизни теряетесь даже в бою с микроволновкой, то Opposing Fronts — идеальная игра для вас!

Что меня впечатлило:

Немецкие тигры – такие же непробиваемые, как моя уверенность, что "ещё одна партия – и спать".

Британские укрепления – наконец-то можно почувствовать себя черепахой в броне, только вместо панциря у тебя мешки с песком и надежда.

ИИ противника – иногда кажется, что он читает мои мысли. Особенно когда я думаю: "А не сдать ли мне эту точку?" – и тут же получаю шквал артиллерии в ответ.

Что заставило меня рыдать в подушку:

Мины. Их так много, что можно подумать, будто немцы закопали здесь не смертоносные ловушки, а свои нереализованные мечты.

Артиллерия. Если в детстве вас пугали словами "придёт бабайка и заберёт", то здесь бабайка – это 88-мм пушка, и она уже пришла.

Спам юнитов. Иногда кажется, что враг играет не по правилам, а на чистом адреналине и злости.

Вывод: Opposing Fronts – это как экстремальный спорт, только без риска сломать шею. Зато можно сломать клавиатуру, когда твой последний "Шерман" взлетает на воздух от фаустпатрона, который выпустил какой-то спрятавшийся за кустом фольксштурмовец. 10/10, будете ненавидеть и перезагружать сейвы!**

P.S. Особая благодарность разработчикам за то, что напомнили: война – это не только про стратегию, но и про жестокие, беспощадные уроки смирения.

I just want to briefly say, for those who experience audio bugs (audio not playing at all). This game was not intended for the hardware we have today. 
So here are a few simple steps that should fix this:
1. Set your audio device (example- Headphones, earbuds, or speakers) as [b]default[/b] audio device in settings.
2. Click on your audio device [b]properties[/b] and change audio to Stereo (16 bit, 48000 Hz). 
3. When the game is running, go into task manager and right click on the (supremecommander.exe). Under [b]properties[/b] make sure that the game is being run in Windows 7 compatibility mode. 

You should be all set. [b]Disclaimer[/b], I only have played this on Windows, so this fix is for Windows system. I'm not a computer guys, just stating a fix for a common/ frustrating audio bug since this is now an old game. Try it out. Definitely recommend the whole series.

Hay juegos de estrategia en tiempo real… y luego está Supreme Commander. Un título que no intenta darte la ilusión de una guerra a gran escala: directamente te lanza dentro de una. Aquí no controlas un pequeño destacamento ni haces microgestión de cuatro tanques. Aquí diriges ejércitos enteros, fábricas interminables, líneas de producción colosales y frentes de batalla que pueden extenderse por mapas gigantescos durante horas… o incluso días.

Lo primero que sorprende es la escala. En la mayoría de RTS tradicionales, manejar veinte o treinta unidades ya se considera una fuerza importante. En Supreme Commander, eso apenas es el comienzo. Conforme avanza la partida, el campo de batalla se llena de cientos de unidades terrestres, aéreas y navales combatiendo simultáneamente mientras enormes robots experimentales arrasan bases enteras. Y aun así, el juego consigue que todo tenga sentido gracias a una interfaz brillante y a su famoso sistema de zoom estratégico, que te permite pasar de ver un tanque individual a contemplar continentes completos en segundos.

Pero lo que realmente convierte a Supreme Commander en algo especial es el ritmo de sus partidas. Este no es un RTS pensado para encuentros rápidos de quince minutos. Una escaramuza grande puede convertirse en una auténtica campaña militar donde las líneas del frente cambian constantemente, las economías colapsan y resurgen, y cada decisión estratégica tiene consecuencias enormes. Hay partidas que empiezan como una simple expansión territorial y terminan, muchas horas después, con armas nucleares cruzando el mapa y ejércitos infinitos chocando en una guerra de desgaste brutal.

Esa sensación de “guerra total” es difícil de encontrar incluso hoy. Mientras otros juegos de estrategia premian la velocidad de clics y la microgestión extrema, Supreme Commander se centra en la macroestrategia: producción, logística, control del mapa y planificación a largo plazo. Te hace sentir más como un comandante real coordinando una maquinaria bélica gigantesca que como un jugador moviendo unidades una a una.

Visualmente quizá haya envejecido, pero su ambición sigue impresionando. Pocos RTS han logrado transmitir tan bien la idea de conflicto masivo. Ver cientos de unidades avanzando al mismo tiempo, apoyar ofensivas desde varios frentes y mantener una economía capaz de alimentar semejante monstruo bélico sigue siendo increíblemente satisfactorio.

Supreme Commander no es un RTS para partidas rápidas ni para jugadores impacientes. Es un juego para quienes disfrutan perdiéndose en guerras gigantescas, optimizando producción durante horas y viendo cómo una pequeña base inicial termina convertida en una potencia militar imposible. De esos juegos que empiezas “para una escaramuza rápida” y cuando miras el reloj han pasado seis horas… y la guerra todavía no ha terminado.

There are many RTS games that focus on fast matches and constant micromanagement, but this game feels different even today. The scale of the battles is still impressive, and very few strategy games manage to create the same feeling of commanding a real futuristic war.

What makes the game special is its enormous maps and the number of units you can control at the same time. Instead of managing a small army, you are building entire production lines, expanding across huge battlefields, and fighting on land, sea, and air simultaneously. At its best, the game feels less like a traditional RTS and more like directing a full military campaign.

The economic system is also one of the strongest parts of the game. Rather than collecting resources in small bursts, the game uses a constant income and spending system. This makes expansion and long-term planning much more important than simple reaction speed. Once you understand how the economy works, the gameplay becomes extremely satisfying.

Visually, it has aged reasonably well. The graphics are clearly from another era, but the art direction and massive battles still look great, especially when dozens of experimental units and explosions fill the screen. The strategic zoom feature remains one of the best mechanics ever introduced in the RTS genre, allowing the player to smoothly switch between detailed control and a complete overview of the battlefield.

However, the game is not perfect. The interface can feel overwhelming at first, and new players may struggle with the complexity. Matches are often very long, and the game demands patience and attention. Performance can also become an issue in large battles, especially on older hardware.

Even with those problems, this game remains one of the most ambitious real-time strategy games ever made. It may not be as accessible as modern RTS titles, but the scale, depth, and atmosphere make it unforgettable for players who enjoy large-scale strategy games.

I just want to briefly say, for those who experience audio bugs (audio not playing at all). This game was not intended for the hardware we have today.
So here are a few simple steps that should fix this:
1. Set your audio device (example- Headphones, earbuds, or speakers) as default audio device in settings.
2. Click on your audio device [b]properties[/b] and change audio to Stereo (16 bit, 48000 Hz).
3. When the game is running, go into task manager and right click on the (supremecommander.exe). Under [b]properties[/b] make sure that the game is being run in Windows 7 compatibility mode.

You should be all set. [b]Disclaimer[/b], I only have played this on Windows, so this fix is for Windows system. I'm not a computer guys, just stating a fix for a common/ frustrating audio bug since this is now an old game. Try it out. Definitely recommend the whole series.

I have spent more than 1,500 hours playing Supreme Commander and have reached a rating of approximately 1900. Even after so much time, the game has never become repetitive for me; on the contrary, I continue to discover new ways to enjoy it.

Most of my playtime is through FAF (Forged Alliance Forever), which has effectively given Supreme Commander a second life. FAF offers an active community, ranked matches, team games, a large selection of maps, modifications, and custom game modes. I particularly enjoy playing Seton's Clutch, Dual Gap, and maps created with the map generator.

The variety of custom game modes also deserves special mention. There is an excellent Roguelike mode, several survival modes, and many other community-created modifications. Because of this, Supreme Commander feels like much more than a single RTS title; it has developed into a broader platform with a great deal of strategic variety.

Even standard matches offer an impressive amount of depth. Players can build large bases, fight on land, at sea, and in the air, deploy experimental units, launch nuclear weapons, and engage in large-scale artillery battles. Team coordination is also very well supported, as players can draw directly on the map and place markers to communicate plans and objectives.

I also appreciate the campaign and its storyline. Even after many years, the single-player experience remains enjoyable, and the scale of the battles continues to be impressive.

I would also like to thank the developers and everyone involved in the FAF project. Their continued work on balance, new features, maps, game modes, and general improvements has helped keep the game interesting and enjoyable. The community itself is equally important, as Supreme Commander is at its best when played with other people.

I have also spent a significant amount of time with other RTS games. For example, I have around 1,000 hours in Company of Heroes, in addition to many other strategy titles. However, if I had to choose the RTS that I continue to return to most often, it would be Supreme Commander.

After more than 1,500 hours, I can still confidently recommend it.

La tercera guerra mundial es la visión apocalíptica que nos ofrece el juego, con un planteamiento sobre la escasez de recursos naturales y la crisis económica en el mundo, controlaremos al ejército de los estados unidos que quiere tomar el último yacimiento petrolífero que queda en la tierra, este se une a la unión europea creando así la coalición occidental. Rusia no quiere quedar atrás y forma junto a china y otras naciones la "Alianza de la estrella roja" y declara la guerra total a Occidente.

Controlaremos a un pelotón llamado los perros callejeros que deberán abrir paso hasta llegar a Moscú para finalizar la guerra, el juego es un shooter muy parecido a otras franquicias más populares, con la diferencia que en esta guerra moderna podremos controlas drones, pequeños vehículos no tripulados para enviar al frente de batalla y crear el caos, también podremos controlar en algunas misiones tanques y helicópteros entre otros arsenales militares.
Solo jugué el modo campaña, cumple la función de divertir y la historia si engancha, pero advertí que siempre comparte el mismo objetivo en todas las misiones, hacerse con determinados puntos de control para seguir avanzando, pero en vez de ser lineal, tú puedes elegir el camino a través del mapa.
Gráficamente es bueno, escenarios detallados y nítidos, pero estoy hablando de un juego del 2008, ya un título viejo, pero se juega de forma fluida y se ve bien. En sonido el fuego de armas es el más potente de todos y la música acompaña los momentos de acción, lo juegue traducido al español y digamos que está bien, los gritos y órdenes de soldados ayudan a recrear el caos que se está jugando manteniendo un nivel de sonido agradable.

En fin, es un buen juego, si te gusta el género de shooter militares no te va a defraudar y lo que lo hace realmente entretenido es poder manejar esos drones para enviarlos a un pelotón de enemigos atrincherados para sacarlos a los tiros de ahí. El juego en Steam presenta algunos errores de compatibilidad, tuve que recurrir a soluciones externas para poder ejecutarlo en la plataforma, además de otro problema que no guarda las partidas, lo tuve que jugar una tarde noche de corrido. El multijugador nunca lo jugué porque no encontré partidas activas, el juego viene con voces en español y lamentablemente no tiene logros, ni cromos en Steam.

I mean for intents and purposes this is just Battlefield Bad Company from Temu and Drones, but personally as the gameplay goes it does it fairly well.

It has destructible environments as a key element and a overall control scheme that works fairly well.

However at the current price of $20 it is a hard pass as the Campaign lasts only about 4 hours in total and the multiplayer scene is basically dead, so I really can't recommend it in it's current state.

But if you were to get it of a larger bundle or a key for $5 or less, it is a pretty fun joy ride of the time it gives, even if it is not perfect.

I actually think with some design adjustments to the core game, this could have really been a decent Battlefield competitor.

However given the time of it's release, and how BF2 released in 05, this is more or less a down grade in every way save the drone gameplay, which is fun while it lasts.

The AI is also surprisingly decent, however it has some noticeable hiccups and by 2008 standards is not that great.

Overall I would give this a 6/10 and while I think if I had some slightly better direction and campaign I would rate it closer to an 8.

However as it is, it wont be higher than a 6 and it really comes down to it's current state of things.

Realistically for most players it is probably closer to a 4 out of 10.

However I am usually a bit forgiving when it comes to games with age so as it is, it is not that bad.

Just too short for the asking price, and BF2 doing most of what it sets out to do better.

The writing is also pretty bad, however some of the VA work is actually decent given what they had to work with.

It attempts to push a serious story with some comedic undertones, but most if not all do not really land, so most if not all the writing is kind of cringe.

For most people I would give a pass on this game and just play BF2, but if you enjoy BF2's general gameplay style and just want to explore other peoples take on it, this is probably one of the better ones on offer despite it's flawed nature.

Pretty okay game at most. The sound design is its absolute biggest strength, and if you just watch a video, you will understand. Sadly, it does not come close to the action of competing FPS games at the time of release (CoD4, WaW, Bad Company 1, Crysis, Far Cry 2) in either campaign or its somewhat dull campaign. Despite some decent visuals for 2008 as well, it lacks in detail and any real style with pretty much a basic Tom Clancy-esque "modern futureism" we'd see in games like Ghost Recon 2, Advanced Warfighter and later Black Ops 2. There is also no interesting or engaging story to be told or found whatsoever. If you think you might enjoy a big shoot fest of a 4 hour long campaign, this might be for you. Maybe you can find whoever is still playing this game (I haven't).

On the topic of the campaign though, "non-linear levels" sound cool until you actually play them, and there isn't much freedom outside of what order you actually do the objectives in. The objectives also repetitively range from "Destroy this" or "Capture this"... or maybe even "Capture this but hold E". Not much variety, and it's very noticeable for the 4 hour campaign. It also does not help you MUST destroy the SAMs with C4 and nothing else (Because anything else does absolutely nothing). Why pretend there is choice when there is no choice? Why make it a selling point how open the game is when it's no more open than an average level in an older CoD title? I don't see the point at all. You can also choose your loadouts in levels... after you die. Oh, and once a "sequence" of a level ends, you are reset to the starting gear on the level, so crappy SMG here we go over and over, every level start. 

As a Steam Deck (Or "on the go game"), it doesn't fair much differently, sadly. The first problem is just getting the goddamn game to work properly, which you need to use SPECIFICALLY Proton 5.13-6. Anything older or newer DOES NOT WORK. Then, you need to disable Steam Input through Controller in Properties (Which you never need to do... EVER with any games). Afterward, the game takes approx. 1-3 minutes just to setup whatever redists (every single time), and then launches. The game's performance is also quite bad, with lots of and quite unexplainable dips I wouldn't even see in other UE3 games (BIA Hell's Highway, MoH Airborne, Wolverine, etc.). To top all of that off, there is no form of aim assist or bullet magnetism, making aiming the incredibly inaccurate weaponry way worse than it really should be. This extends to more than the automatic weapons, but also the pistol (which is pin-point accurate), the sniper, and the suppressed SMG. If there is a work around for this, that'd be okay... but then there is the crashing. The game crashes constantly on Steam Deck for no apparent reason after maybe 10-20 minutes of gameplay, and always at the most inexplicable moments. I still have no idea what makes the crashes, but they exist and are the number reason to not bother playing this on the Deck (Or any other linux handheld or any other linux system for that matter).

Once again, if you can somehow find whoever is playing the MP of this game, it can probably be a fun time, but a shooter is only as fun as its guns, and there are very few and they range from either being incredibly inaccurate but very strong or vise versa. There also some hurdles you need to jump through to even get the game working, like installing PhysX drivers, fixing the horrid FOV, disabling mouse acceleration and finding a way to get the shadows to stop becoming these horrifying square anomalies when you get too far. It does not help that the game's default price on Steam is 20 dollars. 20 dollars for a game where the fundimental element (The multiplayer) does not work, and HAS not worked FOR 15 YEARS. THE GAME'S MULTIPLAYER HAS BEEN LONGER THAN IT LIVED AND IT IS STILL 20 DOLLARS. WHAT THE FUCK. If you find it on sale... maybe give it a try, but not anything more than 5 or 10 bones. Battlefield 2 still gets plenty of folks, so just do that instead (It's free now anyways).

I knew that KAOS made Homefront 2011, but what I didn't know was that they made something else before it, and I found out that Frontlines Fuel of War is that game. I decided to give it a shot and was honestly pretty surprised by what a studio other than DICE and EA could deliver back when this game came out.

Yeah, this game takes huge inspiration from Battlefield and it even had its own Multiplayer, but that died along with the studio. So now you can only play it over LAN or if it's even possible, maybe on some dedicated server somewhere on the internet, though that's just me speculating.

Even after all these years, the game looks great with that classic 2000s "piss filter," which gives me a heavy dose of nostalgia from back when the world still looked normal, unlike today.

The gameplay is on the more repetitive side, the campaign just consists of missions where you have to destroy, capture, or defend something, and it goes like that from start to finish. But the gunplay is great, even if a bit clunky.

The ARC3 is inaccurate most of the time, but it deals a ton of damage when you switch it to grenade launcher mode. The MAG021 and M1000 MIK are awesome sniper rifles that are always a treat to use, especially when you blow off someone's head or even their legs and they fly like 18 meters into the air. The Guardian Rocket Launcher isn't anything special; it has its uses against tanks or helicopters, which are honestly a pain to control (even Battlefield has better chopper controls). The MP15S is the most accurate submachine gun, and whenever I held it, it felt like spreading butter on bread - super smooth. The Shockentry 100 is probably the strongest weapon in the game alongside the snipers, and it's even good at midrange. The M12 Alamo is a pretty fast and powerful pistol; a few shots into the Red Star Alliance troops and they hit the dirt immediately, and it's not even automatic.

Besides the gunplay, you've got vehicles, tanks, and those poorly controlled helicopters I mentioned, but on the flip side, the drones are actually pretty cool. You get a chopper drone that rains down rockets from above, a minigun drone that drives around mowing down enemies, and an explosive drone designed to drive under tanks and blow them up.

The campaign has a story, but it definitely has its flaws. None of the characters are particularly interesting, except for a journalist named Wayne Andrews, who we follow alongside the Western Coalition all the way to Moscow to get to the oil the Red Star Alliance is hoarding.

All in all, I have to say I really enjoyed the game, and if I could, I'd play it again. If you want something similar to Call of Duty or even the Battlefield campaigns, this is a solid choice.

Frontlines: Fuel of War is a large-scale military first-person shooter developed by Kaos Studios and published by THQ. Released during a period crowded with modern warfare shooters, the game sought to separate itself from competitors through its ambitious depiction of a near-future global conflict driven by dwindling energy resources. Rather than focusing solely on traditional military rivalries, the game imagines a world where oil shortages, economic instability, and environmental decline have pushed nations into a desperate struggle for survival. This premise provides a compelling backdrop that still feels relevant years after its release and gives the campaign a stronger sense of purpose than many shooters of its era.

The story places players in the ranks of the Western Coalition as they battle the Red Star Alliance across a variety of war-torn locations. While the narrative itself is not particularly focused on character development, it succeeds in presenting a believable geopolitical conflict where access to resources becomes the primary motivation for war. The campaign unfolds through a series of military operations that showcase the scale of the conflict, giving players the impression that they are participating in a much larger global struggle rather than isolated missions.

One of the game's most notable features is its Frontline Combat System, which changes the way battles progress. Instead of relying on a simple sequence of disconnected objectives, the battlefield evolves as players capture strategic positions. Successfully completing objectives pushes the frontline forward, opening new areas and creating fresh goals. This mechanic helps maintain momentum throughout missions and provides a greater sense of participation in an active war. The system also reduces the feeling of linearity that often affects military shooters, making battles feel more dynamic and unpredictable.

Combat is varied and engaging thanks to the large selection of weapons, vehicles, and support equipment. Players have access to futuristic military technology that remains believable within the game's setting. The drone system is particularly impressive, allowing players to deploy reconnaissance units, remote-controlled explosives, attack drones, and mortar-support platforms. These tools add tactical depth to encounters and encourage experimentation beyond traditional gunplay. Whether scouting enemy positions or launching remote assaults, drones contribute significantly to the game's unique identity.

Vehicle gameplay is another major highlight. Tanks, helicopters, armored transports, and other combat machines play an important role on the battlefield. The maps are designed to accommodate both infantry and vehicle warfare, allowing seamless transitions between different styles of combat. Large-scale engagements often involve multiple layers of action occurring simultaneously, creating memorable moments that capture the chaos and excitement of modern warfare. This combination of infantry combat and mechanized warfare gives the game a sense of scale that remains impressive.

Visually, Frontlines: Fuel of War delivered strong presentation for its time. Built using Unreal Engine 3 technology, the game featured detailed environments, convincing explosions, and expansive battlefields. Although modern shooters have surpassed it technically, the art direction still effectively conveys a world damaged by conflict and resource scarcity. Destroyed cities, industrial complexes, and military installations all contribute to the atmosphere of a planet pushed to the brink. The sound design further strengthens immersion with powerful weapon effects, battlefield communications, and explosive audio that helps sell the intensity of combat.

The multiplayer component was originally one of the game's biggest attractions. Large player counts and objective-based warfare created exciting battles where teamwork and strategic positioning mattered. The game's class-based systems, vehicles, and evolving frontlines offered an experience that blended elements of traditional shooters with larger battlefield simulations. While the online community is far smaller today, the multiplayer design remains an important part of the game's legacy and demonstrates the ambition behind the project.

Despite its strengths, the game does have limitations. Enemy artificial intelligence can occasionally behave inconsistently, reducing the challenge during certain encounters. Some objectives become repetitive over the course of the campaign, and the story never fully explores the potential of its intriguing setting. Players accustomed to modern shooter mechanics may also notice dated elements in movement, gun handling, and overall presentation. These issues prevent the game from reaching the highest tier of military shooters, but they do not overshadow its many accomplishments.

Frontlines: Fuel of War remains an ambitious and enjoyable shooter that successfully combines large-scale warfare, strategic gadgets, and a believable near-future setting. Its innovative frontline progression system, extensive vehicle combat, and emphasis on tactical flexibility help it stand apart from many of its contemporaries. Although some aspects have aged and the multiplayer scene is no longer as active as it once was, the game still offers a rewarding experience for fans of military action games who appreciate scale, experimentation, and battlefield immersion.

Rating: 7/10

Frontlines: Fuel of War is a large-scale warfare FPS much like Battlefield’s multiplayer but in a singeplayer setting. The short campaign revolves around the 125th Strike Division nicknamed "The Stray Dogs" fighting against the evil Red Star offensive in the Oil Wars.

The gameplay is straightforward: Shoot the bad guys, capture and destroy objectives. It trades the lone-hero narrative for an interesting feature: When you die, you simply redeploy as another soldier, keeping the momentum of the battle moving. On the normal difficulty, enemies are too bullet-spongy for my taste, but changing to the easy difficulty solves that problem.

There's environmental destruction as well, although it isn't quite as wild as Battlefield, you can still blast away enemy cover and sentries. You also get to pilot tanks freely in and out of battle, which is basic but remains very fun.

The AI is surprisingly smart for both allies and enemies, contributing heavily to the immersion. You cannot give direct orders to your teammates, but they already follow your lead, automatically seek cover when under fire, and provide useful call-outs. They’ll let you know when an area is clear or pinpoint where an enemy is hiding. Enemies are smart enough to retreat when you capture an objective or advance too aggressively. They make excellent use of buildings and cover, making every firefight feel like a genuine struggle for the frontline.

The game offers a nice arsenal and your soldier can carry a lot of equipment. Most notably, the RC toys with guns which makes you wish they were in more games. The sound design is also pretty good. The gunshots are aggressive and the cinematic score fits to the intensity of each mission.

The main issue with this game is that it’s difficult to run on modern hardware, and its poor performance drains all your computer’s power. So before purchasing it, make sure you’re ready for troubleshooting!

If you enjoy continuous gunfire, soldiers shouting and rockets flying at you, give this game a try.

TLDR: Either my tech was too much for this old beast, or it was always a mess to get going. If it’s almost free or in a bundle it’s good fun for ~4-5 hours, but I can’t recommend based on the technical difficulties.

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

Frontlines: fuel of war (FL) is an old FPS set in the impending resources wars of the early 21st century. We are the Stray Dogs, a border patrol force become strike team on the front line of the erupting conflict for oil between the west and a China/Russia alliance. Our job? Kill the commies, push the frontline, win the war. 

Man. Resources wars pitting what is rapidly becoming historical foes against one another in the midst of global economic depression over raising energy costs on the back of a virus which broke systems… I don’t know if I can say this aged well… I can say that last year was clearly busy, what with world war 3 seemingly breaking out and being fought.

I only played single player, the multiplayer experience is long dead, So let’s see how it stands up today.

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] I was surprised not just by the variety of weapons and vehicles, but how each tool felt different and almost all of them were fun to play with. 
[*] Limited respawns in the campaign gave it an old school feeling. I don’t know what would have happened if I’d lost all my lives… Maybe you have to begin the campaign from scratch, I don’t know, but it sure stressed me out when I got low on lives once or twice.
[*] Decent sized maps with multiple paths and a small degree of autonomy in objective completion make this game feel better than significantly more recent FPS titles. These maps aren’t ground-breaking, or amazing, but the simple factor of letting us pick a path and attack it in a way we want makes it feel [i]nice.[/i] 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] I’d call what I had “Issues running the game.” But it really understates how much work it took to get this game going. Given I completed the whole thing in 4 hours, I’d say it took almost a full third of the time again just to get it working… And it wasn’t a single problem I couldn’t solve, which in many ways was [i]significantly[/i] more frustrating. Because I’d whack a problem, only to have a new and exciting one rock up. All of which were solved in a few minutes, but added up. From drivers, to inputs, to sounds, to resolution, to menus… I don’t think any part of this game worked first time.
[*] Bugs, bugs everywhere. Good lord. The experience of playing this game can be terrible. My list of bugs includes but is not limited to; Guns not firing, or not dealing damage, enemies spawning endlessly on the spawn point after a point has been captured, vehicles falling through the world, not being drivable, crashing the game to desktop when entered, spawning on top of me, cutscenes crashing the game, cutscenes not playing, the game saying its loading in, but just sitting as in-game while not loading, and allies and enemies alike getting stuck inside terrain. 
[*] Weapon aiming is just… bad. Most of the weapons couldn’t hit the side of a barn, at point blank. Except the sniper rifle, which will kill you before the enemy even renders. I don’t mind weapons not landing exactly where I aim, that’s the point of having a spread mechanic. I do mind them being so wildly inaccurate I could rename them ‘blunderbuss’ and still be disappointed with the accuracy. 
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Fix the bugs.
[*] If someone out there still loves this, then building some kind of fan patch to make it playable from a single file would be amazing. 
[*] Honestly, I’d like to see more… a shame the devs are long gone. 
[/list]


[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]
Overall if you happen to see this in a bundle then it adds value for a few hours of knocking about… But I don’t think it’s really worth the time to get it working. It sure as hell isn’t worth picking up for itself alone. 

This game is for folks who are after a bit of 2000’s shooter, chest high walls not included. Though you WILL need to take cover to avoid getting splatted. It’s for folks who aren’t too fussed about the story and the writing. 

This game is not for people who have existential dread. It isn’t for folks who want a prediction a little too close to home, and it isn’t for children.

All in all, I’d say this was probably great back in its time. It’s a piece of archaeology that if you happen to come across, I think it’s worth the evening or two.

I remember having the chance to try it out in 2008 through a PC Gamer magazine disk which had a demo that included the whole multiplayer mode. It took a while for my 12 year old self to get used to the massive recoil of the guns but eventually I had a lot of fun. Unfortunately the game servers are shut down and the campaign doesn't offer enough to be the sole reason for owning this game. If I remember correctly, the story ends with an implication that there will be a sequel but that never happened. All in all, at its current state, I don't think the game is worth the money or time anymore. Looking back, it's a shame Frontlines: Fuel of War never became more popular and that many people never had a chance to experience it at its peak.
I usually don't remember quotes from cinematics but I remember the guy in this game discussing alternative fuel sources and saying "That shit didn't pan out."

Першою Saints Row, про яку я дізнався, була Saints Row the Third зі своїм шаленим стилем та гумором. Другою грою в цій серії, про яку я дізнався (і також яку я вперше зіграв, бо забрав безкоштовно кілька років тому в EGS), була четверта частина, яка взаглі відійшла від гангстерської тематики і натомість зосередилася на Sci-Fi із суперздімностями (останнє було прямо дуже прикольне). Однак вони все ж більше спиралися на ґеймплей, натомість сюжет був радше слабшою частиною.

Однак зі Saints Row 2 інакше. На відміну від наступних частин (не знаю як там з ребутом, бо не грав і, судячи з відгуків, не буду грати) Saints Row 2 має набагато серйозніший сюжет, де присутньо трохи гумору, а все божевілля знаходиться в побічних завданнях, а не вплетено в основну лінію як у наступних частин. Головний герой також більш глибоко розкритий як психопат, який готовий піти на все (навіть втративши деяких побратимів) аби помститися. З ґеймплейної частини мені дуже сподобалася кастомізація практично всього (вигляд, автомобілі, мувсет, характер, лігва, стиль банди і їхній автопарк), зброя, яка в більшості досить приземлена до реальності. Та й загалом ця частина, в хорошому сенсі, більш наближена до ігор серії GTA і, можливо, в дечому перевершує деякі з тогочасних її частин.

Saints Row 2 is what happens when GTA takes a hit of crack and decides to become a legend.

This game is absolute chaos in the best possible way. The story is surprisingly dark, the characters are unforgettable, and the amount of ridiculous shit you can get up to is genuinely unmatched. One minute you're taking over the city, the next you're launching yourself through a windshield, wearing the dumbest outfit imaginable, and causing millions in property damage.

Steelport? Nah. Stilwater is HOME.

The customization, the soundtrack, the missions, the humor, the pure unfiltered insanity... this game has more personality than most AAA games released today.

Sure, it's old. Sure, it's janky. Sure, it might occasionally fight for its life trying to run properly on modern hardware.

But I'd rather play this masterpiece 100 times than another soulless open-world game with a map full of icons and nothing interesting to do.

Saints Row 2 isn't just a game. It's a lifestyle.

Gish is a wonderfully strange example of how a platformer can build its entire identity around a single unconventional mechanic. Developed by Cryptic Sea and Edmund McMillen and published by Chronic Logic, it casts the player as a twelve-pound ball of tar rather than the usual athletic hero. That choice affects nearly every aspect of the experience. Instead of simply running, jumping, and attacking through carefully arranged stages, the player must understand how a soft, sticky, heavy body interacts with terrain, enemies, objects, and momentum. Even after many years, this concept gives the game a personality that remains surprisingly distinctive.

The adventure begins when Gish is spending time with his girlfriend, Brea, only for a mysterious figure to emerge from a manhole and drag her underground. Gish follows her into Dross, a forgotten subterranean city filled with twisting passages, traps, hostile creatures, and increasingly bizarre dangers. The rescue plot is straightforward, but it works because the underground setting becomes progressively stranger as the journey continues. There is an appealing mixture of dark humor, grotesque imagery, and slightly unsettling atmosphere that complements a protagonist who is literally a living lump of tar.

What makes the gameplay special is the way Gish can manipulate his physical properties. His gelatinous body can squeeze through narrow spaces, cling to surfaces, become heavier, bounce, and use momentum to overcome obstacles. Environmental interaction therefore feels less scripted than in a conventional platformer. A simple obstacle may require the player to move an object, build momentum, alter Gish's physical behavior, or exploit the surrounding geometry. Dynamic physics and destructible environments reinforce the feeling that levels are spaces to manipulate rather than static obstacle courses.

This unusual movement system comes with a significant learning curve. Gish deliberately lacks the instantaneous precision associated with many traditional platform heroes. His weight, elasticity, and momentum can make seemingly simple actions unpredictable until the player understands the physics. This produces satisfying moments when an improvised solution succeeds, but it can also result in frustration when a jump or maneuver behaves differently than expected. Players who demand extremely precise platforming may find the controls awkward, while those who enjoy experimentation are more likely to appreciate the underlying design.

The amount of content is another strength. The game offers more than 34 story levels, over 20 collection stages, five hidden levels, unlockable modes, and a level editor. More than 15 types of animated enemies and six bosses add variety to the campaign. There are also six versus modes alongside shared and split-screen cooperative and competitive play. Remote Play Together makes the local multiplayer component more convenient for players who want to experience those modes without everyone physically sharing the same computer.

Its anniversary improvements also help an old game remain reasonably approachable. The package received additional Lost Levels, an updated physics engine, revised levels and menus, and widescreen support. These enhancements do not disguise the game's age completely, but attempting to modernize it too aggressively would arguably damage some of its charm. The visual design remains deliberately grimy and peculiar, while dynamic lighting gives the underground environments additional atmosphere. The simple 2D presentation also makes the physics-driven action reasonably easy to follow despite the frequent environmental chaos.

Combat is closely connected to the same physical systems used for exploration. Gish is not built around conventional weapons, so defeating enemies frequently means using his mass, movement, or surroundings effectively. This helps maintain consistency between platforming, puzzle solving, and combat. Rather than feeling like several unrelated gameplay systems stitched together, much of the adventure revolves around learning additional applications for the protagonist's unusual body.

There are nevertheless elements that show their age. Some interactions can feel cumbersome, the physics occasionally produce awkward results, and partial controller support is less convenient than the comprehensive gamepad implementation expected from modern platformers. The presentation is functional rather than lavish, and players accustomed to contemporary quality-of-life features may need time to adjust. These shortcomings are noticeable, but the core mechanics are unusual enough that the experience rarely feels generic.

Steam Deck users should be especially cautious. The current official Steam Deck compatibility status is Unsupported. Valve's compatibility information indicates that support is still being worked on, so this should not be treated as a Deck-ready title. Individual players may potentially experiment with Proton, alternative configurations, or customized controls, but anyone purchasing specifically for handheld play should understand that there is no official Verified or Playable designation.

Ultimately, Gish succeeds because it commits completely to its eccentric central idea. The protagonist's sticky, deformable body is not simply a visual gimmick but the foundation for movement, puzzles, combat, exploration, and environmental interaction. The physics can occasionally become frustrating, and the game's age is impossible to ignore, yet those imperfections are balanced by creativity and a genuine willingness to experiment. With a substantial campaign, secret content, multiplayer options, a level editor, additional anniversary content, and a memorable underground atmosphere, it remains an intriguing piece of independent game design for players willing to embrace its unconventional controls.

Une bonne idée, mais un gameplay trop frustrant... 😕🪨

Gish part d’un concept original et audacieux : incarner une boule de goudron vivante avec des capacités physiques uniques pour explorer des niveaux remplis de pièges et d’ennemis. Malheureusement, si l’idée est rafraîchissante sur le papier, sa réalisation laisse à désirer. 😬

Le plus gros problème vient du gameplay, qui repose entièrement sur la physique... mais de manière trop imprévisible. Contrôler Gish est souvent un combat en soi : les déplacements sont lourds, les sauts imprécis, et les interactions avec l’environnement manquent de cohérence. On passe plus de temps à lutter contre le personnage qu’à résoudre les véritables défis des niveaux. 🤯🕹️

La courbe de difficulté est mal équilibrée : certains niveaux sont frustrants non pas parce qu’ils sont exigeants, mais parce qu’ils sont injustes. Le level design est parfois trop rigide, ce qui rend l’expérience plus pénible qu'amusante, surtout quand il faut recommencer plusieurs fois à cause d’un saut raté ou d’une collision bizarre. 🚫

Graphiquement, le jeu a un certain charme rétro, mais il a mal vieilli. L’ambiance visuelle et sonore est assez répétitive et manque de variété pour vraiment marquer les esprits. 🎨🔁

En résumé, Gish avait un vrai potentiel en tant que jeu de plateforme basé sur la physique, mais son gameplay peu intuitif et sa difficulté frustrante viennent gâcher l'expérience. C’est une curiosité intéressante pour les plus patients... mais pas forcément un plaisir à jouer. 👎

1. Не липкий.
Ты можешь как прилипать к стенам, так и нет. Предметы то прилипают, то нет. Зато враги всегда липнут.

Данная механика рассчитана на разрушение и убийство врагов, а так же в некоторых местах для головоломок. Но блоки вас раздавят. А врагам часто пофиг. Особенно нравится их бесконечная анимация атаки, пока ты их давишь или пытаешься перелезть. 

4*. Не веселый.
Уровни задизайнены ужасно. Местами можно намертво застрять, местами умереть от лифта или блока для кнопки, который пытаешься дотащить. После долгих секций просто тупо кидают с потолка моба, чтоб он тебя сбил или укусил. Большие мобы в узких коридорах - вообще сказка, особенно в 5-4. Многие уровни собирают в себе нудные перетаскивания блоков на кнопки в начале и разбитый мост над лавой под конец.
Секреты сначала искать интересно, но потом становится настолько плевать, что хочется просто пройти уже уровень.
Музыка однотипна и при рестарте уровня начинает бесить.

Итог.
Брал по скидке ради ностальгии. Ностальгию получил. А еще пару rage quit'ов. По итогу прошел, но даже никакую ачивку не дали, потому что они сломаны (как и вся игра).

[h1] ВСТУПЛЕНИЕ [/h1]
Gish – первая большая игра Эдмунда МакМиллена и его первый успех. Несмотря на то, что я испытываю к ней тёплые чувства, мне было сложно написать на неё хоть какой-то обзор. Я долго метался между двумя оценками стима, не зная какую дать игре. С одной стороны игра хорошая, но с другой… Думаю, что для полной картины и большего контекста мне нужно обозначить одну важную вещь перед тем, как переходить к стандартным пунктам моих стимовских пописулек, а именно ремастер игры.

[h1] РЕМАСТЕР 2020 [/h1]
В 2020-ом году для игры было выпущено обновление-ремастер, которое заметно её перелопатило. Графен стал почётче, физику подредактировали, общее качество убили, игру ушарахали… М-дем… :/
В этом обзоре сравнение ремастера с оригинальной игрой будет примерно везде, поэтому данный раздел пробежим совсем кратко. Однако, забегая вперёд, если таки купите игру, откатывайтесь до старых версий сразу же. Теперь по порядку об остальном.

[h1] СЮЖЕТ [/h1]
Gish – игра времён раннего МакМиллена, тогда он ещё активно развивал свою вселенную, именуемую Бэдлендс. Это значит, что о смысловой нагрузке сюжета (да и про сам сюжет, процентов на 90 всего прохождения) можете смело забыть. Существует история тут только для того, чтобы оправдать геймплей, да и то не всегда.

Порой создаётся странное ощущение, что порядок локаций в игре под конец становится абсолютно рандомным. Если поначалу маршрут Гиша (заглавного, собственно, героя) +/- читаем, то позже вам предстоит из самой преисподней попасть в… египетский храм? По сути-то, даже такое можно вполне себе использовать, но игре жесть как не хватает контекста. В Super Meat Boy, которого Эду ещё только предстояло на тот момент сделать, настолько же, по ощущениям, рандомный разброс локаций +/- склеивался небольшими кат-сценами, в Gish же кат-сцены только две (интро и концовка), да и то они текстовые.

[h1] ГЕЙМПЛЕЙ [/h1]
Геймплейно Gish, как и многие старые игры МакМиллена, экспериментален. Это платформер, построенный на физике гг, который является здесь смоляным шариком, имеющим три состояния (жидкое, липкое и тяжёлое), между которыми вам нужно будет переключаться, чтобы успешно завершить уровень. Так же Гиш умеет прыгать и пружинить в прыжке, набирая высоту с каждым следующим, что можно использовать для того, чтобы попасть в труднодоступные зоны игры.

Вот тут вот начинаются сильные различия старой версии и ремастера. Основные состояния персонажа остались те же, а вот механика прыжка претерпела изменения. Если в старых версиях в прыжках чувствовался вес Гиша, а пружиня он не мог набирать высоту бесконечно, то в актуальной версии, не будь в каждой главе потолков, игрок мог бы хоть в стратосферу улететь. Из-за этого отдельные моменты игры можно просто пролететь, хотя они, вроде рассчитывались как испытание. Играя в оригинальную версию прям сильно ощущаешь, что челлендж, который Эдмунд выстраивал, в ремастере пошёл по пизде.

Однако ремастер кое-что исправил-таки в физике игры, буду честен. Раньше Гиша, при недостаточно аккуратной игре, могло тупо вдавить самого в себя, из-за чего он начинал бесконтрольно получать урон и погибал. Происходило это не так часто, но было весьма неприятным косяком со стороны разрабов, в новой же версии такого не наблюдается.

Хорошо, теперь переходим к тому, как бороться с местной вражиной. А вот здесь уже реальный цирк начинается, дамы и господа, добро пожаловать, так сказать! В старых версиях всё было просто и понятно: давишь мелочь, отрываешь головы здоровякам, элементарно же… только вот актуальная ремастурнатая версия опять насрала! С обновлённой физикой шеи второго типа врагов стали состоять из чистого майнкрафтового обсидиана, из-за чего сорвать головы с их плеч практически нереально. 

На уровне 5-5 это ведёт чуть ли не к софтлоку из-за противника, расположенного в узком коридоре. Это самый конец уровня и если раньше убить его не составляло труда, то теперь либо вы что-то придумываете с ним, либо он забивает вас насмерть. Неплохо обновили игру, господа, на весь просранный геймдизайн обновили.

А теперь вишенка на этот торт, феерия просто – финальный босс. Раньше этот босс вёл себя в соответствии со старой физикой игры, был медленнее и двигался тяжелее. Теперь этот босс ТАКОЙ ЖЕ манёвренный, как и вы (в ремастере), а это значит, что теперь он просто летает по арене и становится почти непроходимым. Эдмунд, вопрос будет нескромный отнюдь, но вы это говно тестировали вообще?

Gish is not just a piece of tar, as its creators claim. It is more like a bouncy ball that has unexpectedly gained softness, a mouth, and a pair of yellow eyes. Gish travels through dungeons, defeats monsters, and solves puzzles to save his beloved. Outside of his adventures, he resembles an illustration from a physics textbook due to his realistic model of object interaction. Newton's laws are embodied in every detail here: from swinging platforms to crossing water obstacles. Even jumps require considering Gish's shape and the surface beneath him, turning each action into an engaging experiment.

Gish stands out because physics is not just a gimmick here, but the core of the gameplay. Every action is tied to the laws of physics. Traps on levels are like small kinematic experiments, and fighting enemies requires using physics to succeed. Jumps, acceleration, and changing mass all require careful attention and calculations.

The game amazes with a variety of obstacles and tasks throughout. Gish gives players the freedom to choose how to solve problems, making the gameplay unique for everyone. This is the embodiment of the "emergent gameplay" idea, where the player creates their own experience and finds unique ways to overcome challenges.

The only drawback of the game is the music. Despite its high quality, the repetition of the same track for extended periods can become tiresome.

The graphics in Gish, although three-dimensional, are displayed in a flat format, creating a clear picture with dynamic lighting and shadows. The game lacks trendy shader effects, but that doesn't prevent it from being engaging. Multiplayer adds even more fun, offering modes like Drag Race and Sumo, which will make you laugh and compete with friends.

Gish is filled with humor and parodies that add charm to the game. The developers at Chronic Logic deserve praise for creating such an original and entertaining game in a short time, demonstrating that they approach their work as art, not just production.

Tarball with the Devil is a studio album by Les Goopool and the Holy Oil Barrel, released in 1996. "Les Goopool and the Holy Oil Barrel" is Goopool's first solo effort. In addition to his usual bass guitar and vocals, he also plays most of the drums and some guitar, and plays with tar. He also self produced and engineered the album at his own studio, "Dross". Credited musicians include Charlie Hunter on guitar for "Me and Gish;" Marc "Mirv" Haggard on guitar on songs such as "El Sobrante Gish LAN Party" and "Sewershot," as well as on the saw for "Cohibas Esplenditos"; Adam "Tar Cock" Gates on vocal; Jay Lane on drums; and Henry Rollins narrating "Delicate Tarball."
The touring band for the album were Goopool, Marc "Mirv" Haggard, Adam Gates, and Bryan "Brain" Mantia. "Brain" Mantia was then a new member of Primus.

[/list]

Sorry guys, but I couldn't stand this game. I'd say the highlight here is Gish himself, who has a surprising amount of depth to his wonky movement and abilities that makes moving around feel weirdly rewarding and satisfying. The mechanics are cool, but the levels built around them are a big mixed bag, often ranging from kind of boring to suddenly unforgiving. It feels like every level after a while is just filled with spots that really bring out the janky physics and can kill you instantly (especially with the buggy squish physics), be it a lava pit you didn't see coming, a hearty dose of enemy spam (and combat is already clunky by itself), or just an incredibly tedious environmental puzzle. Even the presentation is pretty meh; Gish is animated really well but the rest of the visuals are fairly dull and repetitive, and frankly so is the music. There are at least some really cool moments but they're just not worth slogging through the main game for, so I guess the decent side modes are a saving grace in that regard.

I can respect Gish for its incredible legacy, being the game to launch McMillen's career and all, but it really didn't age well and is easily one of his weakest works. And that's all without even mentioning the 15th anniversary update that somehow made it even worse.

Although I REALLY disliked Desperados 1 and thought it could be better, Desperados 2 does the exact thing people always want sequels to be: A literally different genre.

I mean, yeah, you COULD play the game from the top down, but it's way more fun and easier to just go into third person and blast your way through. Because this is what this game truly is, a third person shooter.

Stealth doesn't always work, if I thought the stealth in the first game was wonky in this game it's broken. Everytime you kill an enemy you get such a massive amount of ammo that you can pretty much blast your way through the game with a single character without much problem. Which I think was intended, considering how many levels have forced encounters

The AI is incredibly buggy and unlike the first game it gets stuck on level geometry a lot, note that this doesn't stop it from 1-shot-killing you the nanosecond they see you and turn to face you.

I've heard that the game runs bad on AMD hardware, and on mine the performance drops when going to third person mode are awful, even with the game all on minimum. Keep in mind I'm on an RX570. Not exactly a modern contender for high tier, but it should be easily 2x overkill for a low budget game from 2006.

The story makes absolutely no sense. You get suddenly dropped into the intro cutscene of Cooper's brother that was never mentioned before, him getting tortured and killed, and your path to revenge against a criminal that was never mentioned before. There's absolutely no tie in with the previous game. Adding to that, none of the voice actors of the first game return, which while I am not attached to, still think it's a damn shame, since they did a superb job before.

The game is only 6 missions long, somehow. There's "changes" in the middle of the missions that give you new objectives and refill the screen with enemies but there's still only 6 missions.

Desperados 2: Cooper’s Revenge, developed by Spellbound Entertainment and published by THQ Nordic, is a real-time tactical strategy game that immerses players in the rugged and lawless world of the American Wild West. Released in 2006 as the sequel to Desperados: Wanted Dead or Alive, the game builds upon its predecessor by introducing fully 3D environments while retaining the core tactical gameplay that emphasizes planning, stealth, and precision. Players once again step into the boots of John Cooper, navigating a perilous journey of revenge and justice in a setting that combines open deserts, frontier towns, and dangerous wilderness.

The story picks up with John Cooper seeking to avenge the death of his brother, Marshal Ross Cooper, at the hands of a mysterious criminal known only as “Angel Face.” To accomplish this, Cooper reunites his team of specialists: Kate, the agile and quick-witted sharpshooter; Doc, the veteran with medical and explosive expertise; Sam, the resourceful tracker; Sanchez, the loyal brawler; and the new addition, Hawkeye, a skilled Native American warrior. Each character brings unique skills to the table, and the game’s missions are designed to encourage players to leverage these abilities in combination, whether setting ambushes, sneaking past enemies, or coordinating complex tactical maneuvers.

Gameplay in Desperados 2 emphasizes careful observation, strategic foresight, and stealth over brute force. Players must plan their movements meticulously, using cover, distractions, and environmental interactions to eliminate threats without triggering alarms. The dual perspective system—allowing players to switch between isometric and third-person views—adds flexibility, enabling different approaches to the same challenge. This mechanic enhances tactical decision-making, giving players a clearer view of enemy patrols and the surrounding terrain, and allowing for precise timing when executing coordinated actions across the team.

The game’s visual design captures the gritty atmosphere of the Wild West, with detailed 3D environments that range from dusty canyons and deserted towns to bustling villages and dense forests. Character models are expressive and animations are fluid, adding a layer of realism to interactions and combat. The soundtrack, infused with classic Western motifs, complements the visual presentation, providing tension during stealth sequences and drama during key story moments. Together, the audio-visual elements create a convincing and immersive frontier experience.

While Desperados 2 excels in strategy and narrative, it does come with notable challenges. The game is renowned for its difficulty, with missions that often demand perfect timing and precise execution. Some players have reported frustration with the AI’s unpredictability, as enemies can behave inconsistently, and certain objectives require repeated attempts to master. Additionally, controls can feel awkward at times, especially during complex maneuvers or when coordinating multiple characters simultaneously. Voice acting, while serviceable, occasionally lacks the polish to fully convey the intensity of the narrative.

Despite these drawbacks, Desperados 2: Cooper’s Revenge remains a rewarding experience for players who enjoy tactical depth and strategic problem-solving. Its combination of stealth, planning, and character synergy challenges players to think critically and adapt to evolving situations. The game’s narrative of vengeance and loyalty, paired with its immersive Western setting, offers a compelling backdrop for tense, thoughtful gameplay. For fans of tactical strategy and Western-themed adventures, Desperados 2 delivers a challenging and memorable journey that rewards patience, creativity, and careful execution.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
I used to love the game as a child, but I've clearly forgotten how masochistic you have to be to enjoy the infuriatingly slow and wonky animations and zergling swarms of aimbot enemies. Can't really recommend the game even to those whole liked the first game, and certainly not to people who started with the latest third game that has far more polished gameplay.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The brother of the main character from the first game gets murdered, so the main character sets out on a quest to stop a railroad company from killing random civilians with [spoiler]fake Native American attacks[/spoiler] on the trail for some reason. Where does the revenge play in? Oh, the guy killing people also killed the MC's brother, of course! If that sounds confusing, it's because the game doesn't really elaborate the position you find yourself in half the time, and the brother's death gets mostly forgotten by the plot.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Desperados II is an isometric real-time tactical game with an added third-person view option, allow you to control characters directly. You control a team of six characters, each with unique abilities or gear, in addition to their ranged weapon of choice. The game tries to blend shootout action segments with stealth-focused segments, but leaves a lot to be desired in both departments.

On the action front, the game changed how aiming and weapon ammos works. Instead of guns being infinitely reloadable but overheating with use, you instead have to pick up ammo from dead enemies... which is only relevant at the very beginning of each level when your ammo supplies are reset, but becomes utterly meaningless after a few kills (excluding Hawkeye, since he can't get more arrows from enemies). Enemy AI seems to only have two modes: braindead zombies that literally limp around the map and run straight into your shotgun, or aim bots that one-shot you through walls and obstacles from a longer distance than you can even attempt to shoot them at. Also, characters can't take out their weapons and move at the same time in tactical mode and tend to get themselves killed before they finally comply with your command to stow away their weapons to beat a retreat. And don't get me started on the aiming and reload system... you need to focus your cursor steadily onto an enemy to shoot them (the farther away they are, the more time you need to focus before shooting), but the characters will randomly start reloading and throw off your aim at the worst timing imaginable. Other times, you'll be firing blanks, because the characters can't get it through their thick skulls to reload already. In short, be prepared for a lot of game reloading.

On the stealth front... it sucks. Since practically none of the characters have any decent lures or distractions, it just boils down to using Kate's seduction to lure people out of sight to knock them down. Technically, some characters have other ways to distract/lure people, but they're very cumbersome, and the knockdown animation is so slow (and characters need to get into a standing position before they carry out ANY action) that you have to mad-dash at a seduced enemy to have any chance of K.O.ing them before they shoot you. And there are a WHOLE lot of enemies on the map, so the stealth approach will get VERY tedious. Especially on the FOUR no-kill-no-alarm levels.

While each character has four different actions available, you'll soon realise that most of them don't have any practical use. Either because you need to get too close to an enemy - that can do 180 turns instantaneously - to use them, or because they're too cumbersome to use without decent lures and it's much easier to just take out your gun and be done with it. There's too many enemies around to use your gear anyway.

[h1]Level Design[/h1]
There are 6 missions in the game, each divided into 2-4 sub-missions, usually reusing the same map (or part of it) as the previous one. Excluding the recycled locations, there are 7 unique maps in the game. In the early game, the recycling of the maps doesn't feel TOO obnoxious, since you're either using different parts of the map, or have story reasons to replay the same area, but in the later part of the game, it turns into horribly blatant padding. Instead of going from your starting point A to your end goal B, you go from point A to get reinforcements at point C, then the enemies respawn and the reinforcements decide to wait behind as you go all the way back down from point C, but now stop by point D, after which enemies will respawn again, and only now can you go to point B. What's the point of reinforcements if I have to kill off the entire map twice, only for them to die off easily in the end anyway?

[h1]Overview[/h1]
The Good
+Quick Action feature lets you chain multiple actions, instead of just one like in the other Desperados games
+Map rotation
+Third person mode lets you get around some bugs or poor visibility
+The game tried to innovate

Fazit:
Desperados 2: Coopers Revenge ist der Nachfolger von Desperados - Wanted Dead or Alive. Den ersten Teil fand ich gut, wurde aber von diesem Teil enttäuscht.
Storymäßig war einiges ziemlich verwirrend und nicht ganz klar, worauf man hinaus möchte.
Wieder spielen wir eine Gruppe von bis zu 6 Charakteren, welche alle unterschiedliche Fähigkeiten besitzen. Diese müssen wir nutzen, um in den Missionen voranzukommen.
Die Grafik ist um einiges Besser als im ersten Teil und auch der Wechsel in die 3D-Ansicht ist eine super Idee. Das Konzept passte also, aber leider ist die Umsetzung nicht gelungen. Bei der Steuerung fängt es schon an. Diese ist sehr ungenau und führt zu Frust. Die gegnerische KI ist sogar noch schlechter, als im Vorgänger. Ein Beispiel: Wenn ich einem Feind in den Rücken schieße und aufgrund der schlechten Steuerung nicht treffe, gehe ich davon aus, das dieser sich umdreht und mir ans Leder möchte. Tatsächlich drehte der Feind sich auch um, sah mich an, wie ich auf ihn erneut zielte und ging seiner Tätigkeit (Gebäude runterschauen) weiter nach. Easy-Game für mich, aber bestimmt nicht so angedacht.
Was mir am ersten Teil so gut gefallen hat, waren die abwechslungsreichen Maps. Hier wiederholten die sich sehr oft.
So gut der erste Teil war, so sehr enttäuschte leider der zweite Teil. Den dritten Teil werde ich mir aber definitiv noch anschauen. Von diesem sollte man die Finger lassen. Nicht Empfehlenswert!!!!

Not an amazing game, but a fun western overall with quite a few things to appreciate.

Even thought the game doesn't reach it's potential, it feels like a game with quite a lot of ambition behind it.
While the original was much closer to Commandos, this feels much more like it's own thing without abandoning it's source of inspiration. 

A lot of effort was put in the level design, animations and general presentation of the game. 
The two view modes feel nice to use most of the time, with one providing a more tactical perspective and the other feeling more close and personal (macro/micro). Most issues are related to the core gameplay, which at first glance seems as it should, but often gets tedious especially in stealth segments.

Naja, die Grafik ist im Vergleich zum Vorgänger etwas "moderner" aber alles andere war beim 5 Jahre älteren Vorgänger irgendwie besser.

- keine Videos mehr als Eröffnung, nur noch Bilder mit Ton
- die Figuren bewegen sich "hakelig" und selbst wenn ich einen Gauner von hinten KO schlagen will, erschießt er mich seelenruhig 3 Sek lang, in denen ich dann untätig darauf warte.

- die meiste Zeit kann man frei rumballern (je nach Missionsziel). Fast alle Gegner lassen Munition fallen und die "Aufgeschreckten" laufen ziellos herum und werden einfach umgeschossen. 

Ich werde es ohne Freude durchspielen und hoffe, dass Teil 3 besser ist!

There was a time, in the mid-2000s, when the video game industry was literally obsessed with the term “Tycoon.” You could manage zoos, roller coasters, shopping malls, and even prisons. But in 2006, someone decided to hand us the keys to the world’s most iconic city. Replaying and reviewing *Tycoon City: New York* today isn’t just a trip down memory lane; it’s rediscovering a style of management game that no longer exists: brazen, visually mesmerizing, and scandalously focused on getting passersby to spend money. While classic titles like SimCity punished you if you forgot to connect a water pipe or a power line, Tycoon City couldn’t care less about the bureaucratic red tape. The game dropped you into Manhattan with a single, brutal goal: to conquer the island one neighborhood at a time by turning New Yorkers’ dreams into cold, hard cash. From Greenwich Village to Times Square, the gameplay wasn’t based on urban planning, but on “window-shopping fetishism”.

The game’s most ingenious feature was its micro-customization system. Simply setting up a souvenir shop or a café wasn’t enough. To maximize profits, you had to physically place furnishings outside your establishment: benches, planters, giant neon signs, and even quirky mascots dancing on the sidewalk. It was a sort of *The Sims* on a metropolitan scale, where every single addition expanded the business’s sphere of influence, attracting the attention of thousands of virtual citizens walking down the street. 

Note: The following information is provided for general reference only and should not be interpreted as medical advice; for any specific needs, we recommend consulting a professional.

From a technical and visual standpoint, the graphics engine was, for its time, something of a marvel in terms of atmospheric optimization. The day-night cycle offered incredible views: watching office lights come on at sunset, car headlights reflecting off puddles, and Broadway signs illuminating the sidewalk had a mesmerizing effect. You could zoom in from the sky to within a centimeter of a passerby’s face to read their thoughts and fulfill their capitalist desires (like: “I want a hot dog” or “This nightclub lacks class”), all accompanied by a jazz and lounge soundtrack that imprinted the frenetic rhythm of the Big Apple on your mind. Of course, if we analyze it with the critical eye of today’s reviewer, Tycoon City suffered from a certain lack of real challenge over the long term: once you figured out how to chain together activities and unlocked major landmarks like the Empire State Building, money flowed into the stock market almost automatically, turning the simulation into a gigantic, relaxing urban diorama. But the honesty and charm of this game lay precisely in its lack of pretension: it didn’t want to make you grapple with the economic crisis or crime; it just wanted to make you feel like the kings of New York.

Tycoon City: New York remains a timeless classic for fans of business simulation games. It’s a game that prioritized style and atmosphere over the mathematical complexity of spreadsheets, offering us an idealized, vibrant Manhattan that’s incredibly fun to develop with donut shops and avant-garde theaters.

Small WIn11 guide to get it running half decent for at least 2h without crashing:
- Delete the Folders ANIMS, DRIDS and MODELS in the \Steam\steamapps\common\Tycoon City New York\data\ART folder
- Download the latest d3d9.dll file from GitHub user doitsujin in the dxvk package and extract it to the \Steam\steamapps\common\Tycoon City New York folder
- start a new game

This is a relaxing, fun game with 2 big caveats. The first is the most important: IT WILL CRASH ON YOU! So save often, like every 10 minutes or so (it's a good practice anyway). It's probably also a good idea to fork off multiple save files over time, since I saw one person said that they got into a situation where the game crashed every time right when they start. I haven't had that at all, it just randomly crashes every one in a while. So each time a new district opens up I will save that as a snapshot point.

The other caveat is that you can't expect this game to be very realistic or complete, and just have to take it for the silly shout out to NYC that it is. There is impressive breadth to it but certain aspects are pretty shallow. For example, if you use your upgrade points only on potted conifers then you'll pretty much always have highly rated businesses. Furthermore, you really don't have any liabilities and will just continue to gain money and credits over time. I read that there are cheat codes but you don't really need them, it's a Tycoon game that is built for your success. It can also become somewhat repetitive at points, but as long as you focus on the opportunities and just building out each district more than 50-60% then it keeps moving along.

Despite the abundance of problems and shortcomings with this game, it deserves an endearingly positive rating for 3 reasons. One is that it is soothing to build up your meaningless and impractical business empire with ease and watch it climb the rankings. Reminds me how pointless such a pursuit can be in real life! Another reason is the cultural experience to get a sense for Manhattan, at least in the mid-2000s. And lastly, it's the same reason you might watch an outdated or poorly done movie to be entertained at how dissonant some parts are. There are little nuggets that charm for various reasons. From tired cliches and stereotypes to bizarre technical glitches, even its limitations are adorable!
