What can I say? It's a shame I only recently discovered it, a great game from Cryptic, the creators of Neverwinter and Star Trek Online.

Below is a list of the game's aspects:

- Technically, it's a dated game, and it shows, but in my opinion, it's well-crafted and functional, with decent animations and well-executed Marvel comic-style graphics.

- Character creation is absolutely HUGE; I don't think even current MMOs come close to the depth of this customization. Furthermore, each class isn't really that rigid; you can mix and match many skills and orient your character in multiple directions.

- Excellent combat; it's a well-designed action/tab targeting system; you'll have to parry, charge up attacks, and be careful about energy consumption when using skills.

- The population isn't very high, but it's present. There are still enough players to allow for queues, dungeons, and events at the same time. Also, there is a discord channel still very active

The main hub, Millennium City, is very large and has many quests and frequent updates, a common feature in Cryptic games (see Neverwinter).

In conclusion, it's not a dead game; in fact, it's still quite popular, especially among veteran players. I don't think there are many new players. I see some low-level ones around, but I think they're older players starting new characters, but it's the same thing.
Regardless, don't care about the graphics or the fact that it's not very popular; it's a game that offers a lot of content and variety.

[h1]Champions Online: The Potential MMO[/h1]

For the several years of playing this, I will have to say that the game has a really solid amount of features that can definitely be attractive to newcomers looking for a superhero fix or similar, however with the recent state of events, [b]I'd advise to steer away from playing Champions Online[/b]. This is 100% due to the negative treatment towards the investment players have made across years of playing this game. Spending money on this game as well as time can end up with experiences ruined due to content changes that basically kill playstyles for existing players or content that ends up being forgotten or removed due development changes that the players did not want. The game itself is an acquired taste to an extent, however, if you do manage get to the level cap in this game, your options for content diminish drastically and that is assuming you make it to level 40.

In terms of gameplay, it's just an ordinary tab-target MMO with pretty simple mechanics all things considered. You can definitely play this game casually, especially considering the general difficulty across the game isn't too high itself. The game has a tutorial giving instructions and guides you through basic movements, however past that tutorial, you're not given knowledge on core mechanics that will allow you to excel later into the game. Additionally, leveling ends up being choices between running Grab Alerts (EXP queuing content) or running open world missions, with open world missions being mainly solo as the game doesn't really do a good job at enticing players to do these missions together. These are the primary options for leveling and there are other options to level in this game, however, [b]they are absolutely gimped in comparison[/b]. The development team for this game had lowered EXP rates for open missions which made most OMs less enticing to run for the sake of leveling. This results in a monotonous grind to level 40.

If you've made it past level 40, [b]you're basically already at endgame[/b], the primary content loop are open world raids called "Cosmics". ten man content known as "Rampages" and Lairs if you're looking to gear up. That's it. You have events every now and they can give you some rewards as well. Problem is that there are powerful build defining items that can be locked behind events; this reads similar to Gacha games for those who are familiar. For some of these items, there is no other way to obtain these unless someone else sells them on the Auction House (very likely for an insane price). Once you get everything you need for content, you're at the mercy of the next upcoming patch as you don't whether or not the character you're made to this point will get gutted into obscurity. That's right, if a power choice or style of play is getting nerfed, it's basically being killed off with little to no way to recover. This is due to the nature of the game for the most part being in maintenance mode and since we can't reasonably expect content to scale up, we would have to, of course, scale down our players.

Community-wise, most of your communication will be through the official Discord as the forums for this game have been retired recently. For any support requests, it ends up being a back and forth between requesting assistance via ARC or within the Discord itself for any in-game related issues. In addition to support, the discord houses sections for suggestions and feedback that sparingly are looked into. The biggest and most glaring issue with this is that getting banned within the Discord means that there isn't really too many ways to express your opinion on changes or get support. With recent events, a lot of vocal members have been removed for airing out their opinions regarding the state of the game and the Discord, general mismanagement from Development too.

If there's one saving grace for this, is that at least it has costumes. The customization for this game is still amazing 15+ years later and it continues to do so here in this department. A lot of players that stick around with Champions Online tend to be really attached to their characters and the customization for this game definitely justifies that.

If you're looking to try out this game, it has amazing customization and can be treated as side-game as post-endgame, you'll be waiting a lot for the content you'd want to run and likely AFK in the main hub. I, however, cannot recommend this game until the game's general direction has improved going forward. As it stands right now, Champions sadly does not empower its heroes.

The community can be great, despite the toxic few that still exist, but it's shrinking because of bad decisions, bad nerfs, bad changes, and disregarding criticisms as, again, "toxic" or "Harassment".

So how do we fix this?

1) Start paying more attention to player criticism. I'm not saying drop everything and listen to everything the players say, I'm saying pay attention to veteran players as they've been playing the game for long enough that they have enough knowledge about the game itself. They know what they're talking about usually and they should be listened to, not just Ravenforce, but DJRatchet, Wind, and others.

It's such a shame. Probably one of the most mishandled MMOs of all time. Awful management...utterly tone deaf development team and a support team that's been here over a decade now that take ages to respond to dire situations. That is, if they ever decide not to gloss over your issue entirely.

Yet...while I love this game and the community itself...the head developer doesn't seem to care at all what the community wants. The changes we want are not even massive or requiring some system overall. They are entirely too focused upon balance...and yet, they do not know anything of the gameplay despite having been a player themselves prior to getting the job.

It's clear that they enjoy the suffering of others, it's literally within their title that they have in-game. We were free for a year and picked up briefly by a company called DECA. And, this is just a conspiracy theory...but I feel as though they were set up to fail by the current head dev. It wasn't a great idea to put in the person getting let go do the job of training the soon-to-be new devs taking that job. Utter conflict of interest.

And yet, DECA had done a fantastic job. They listened to the community, which is paramount in such a small MMO. Every now and then, something would break, sure. But it was never something game breaking, it wasn't like things became unplayable. A few costumes have minor rigging issues. Annoying, but not the end of the world. Really fun gadgets, streams, devs who PLAYED THE GAME.

However, that company was gone almost a year in, unfortunately. Picked back up by Jack Emmert's Cryptic Studios...who made the tone deaf decision to bring back that horrid developer (who was in control of Champions for ten years prior by the by). No one in the community was happy about this other than the few friends that she has since she's known since she was a player in the game City of Heroes. Unrelated to a point, but she made one of those friends a moderator in the Champions official Discord...and it was later revealed that friend was a pedophiliac. Who is still not banned from the game despite overwhelming evidence in-game of such deplorable behavior.

The only way this MMO could possibly improve at this point, is to be ripped from the grasp of any sort of company only seeking to make a quick buck off of games. Being placed in the hands of the IP loving community itself would be golden via a private server. To have people who wish to play Champions Online and not just try and make it into some sort of City of Heroes clone.

Otherwise...Champions Online has a great community, albeit shrinking rapidly. The costuming is fantastic and varied to a ridiculous degree. The combat does take some getting used to, as one has to remember this is quite an old MMO, so it lacks the formulaic mechanics of other MMOs...your rotation does not play itself and it will not be ideal to simply tune out on autopilot. In the late game, mobility is important, every role has its use. Creating a Freeform build is difficult as there are so many options available to a new player...but there are some build savvy folks still left in the community.

An amazing concept that has survived to this day for very good reason in an age where MMOs are a dying breed...even when there were no updates for quite a long time at one point, fans still enjoyed the game for what it was. It's a pity that the current development team seems to wish to tear it all down. And Cryptic Studios refuses to see the value in a superhero MMO such as this where the market is wide open. Maybe one day it'll be freed with the release of the codes so its fans may finally have the game they were hoping for.

Edit: And now things are becoming worse...a large number of players are getting banned from the official Discord who haven't even done anything to deserve it. One who was banned hadn't even said anything for over a week. I'd suggest avoiding Champions Online until this dictator-like behavior is settled. This is not okay and not the proper way to moderate.

Star Trek Online has plenty going for it. The storylines, extensive selection of starships, customisation options and space combat make it an enjoyable experience, particularly for Star Trek fans. The developers deserve credit for keeping the game alive for over 16 years.

Unfortunately, much of that enjoyment is undermined by its ridiculously inflated player-driven Exchange.

The Exchange allows players to buy and sell equipment using Energy Credits. However, it is possible to encounter listings demanding over 1 billion credits for individual items, including equipment whose practical usefulness appears difficult to reconcile with the asking price.

It's a problem familiar to players of many online multiplayer games: speculative pricing and excessive mark-ups can make an otherwise useful marketplace frustrating and inaccessible.

Not everyone has hundreds of millions of credits available or wants to spend countless hours grinding simply to upgrade their ship. An in-game economy should enhance the experience, not become an obstacle to enjoying it.

The relationship between the Exchange and the game's monetisation system also deserves scrutiny.

Players can purchase Zen with real money, obtain tradable items such as Master Keys and sell them for Energy Credits. This creates a route through which real-world spending can help players afford expensive Exchange items.

While there is no evidence presented here that the developers deliberately encourage inflated prices, I believe this economic design raises legitimate questions about whether sufficient safeguards exist to protect ordinary players.

Cryptic Studios, the developer behind Star Trek Online, also developed Neverwinter and Champions Online, both of which feature player trading and premium monetisation. Neverwinter players have similarly raised concerns about expensive Auction House listings and the cost of equipment progression.

This is therefore not an unfamiliar challenge for a developer with extensive experience operating online games and their economies.

Other developers have introduced measures to address marketplace problems. EVE Online's developer, CCP Games, acknowledged concerns about speculation and artificial scarcity within its PLEX market in 2025, while RuneScape has implemented transaction taxes and other economic safeguards.

If other developers can take steps to improve their player-driven economies, surely it is reasonable to expect Cryptic Studios to examine whether similar improvements would benefit Star Trek Online.

There is also considerable irony in a Star Trek game, based on a future where humanity has supposedly moved beyond greed and the relentless pursuit of wealth, featuring a marketplace where some asking prices seem completely disconnected from the needs of ordinary players.

It feels less like Starfleet and more like the Ferengi Alliance!

Ultimately, Star Trek Online remains a good game with enjoyable combat, excellent ship variety and plenty of content. However, the Exchange's excessive asking prices and the difficulties casual players can face when trying to improve their equipment seriously detract from the experience.

I believe the developers should take greater responsibility for ensuring that the marketplace remains accessible and balanced, with better pricing transparency, sensible economic safeguards and more opportunities to obtain competitive equipment through normal gameplay.

Star Trek Online should be about exploration, adventure and commanding starships, not struggling to navigate a marketplace where desirable equipment can carry astronomical price tags.

Final Verdict: 3/5 Stars

A great Star Trek experience spoiled by an excessively expensive player marketplace and legitimate concerns about how its economy interacts with real-money monetisation. The game deserves better, and so do its players.

I know I said that I'd recommend the game, but look...

The only reason to play this game is because you're that into the Star Trek universe. As an extension of that universe that you get to interact in, this game's a blast, but as an MMO, it's probably one of the less laudable F2P MMOs out there. The biggest detractor for me is how buggy the UI is, has been, and will likely always be. It's $300 for a lifetime subscription (worth it for a die-hard fan when it's on sale for $200 or less), and with the prices on the Zen shop, they must be making money. In spite of that, they can't afford to troubleshoot and resolve glaring UI glitches. Missions where you have to play as another character or in another ship are infuriating due to those UI issues because they mess up your keybindings and character traits, and you start dying in combat because you don't know you need to go turn all your traits back on or remap your keybindings. The popsicle sticks and Elmer's glue holding this game together are showing really badly, and it desperately needs a coding update that addresses the obscene bugs. Also, Steam users can't file tickets through the in-game system and have to manually dig up a customer service email address that Arc doesn't make easy to find so you can start the process that way. It takes longer, and it feels like Arc doesn't like their Steam users.

Blade Kitten is a rather light platformed with relatively cute graphics and expanded world, that could be checked via comics that are kinda hard to get, at least when i tried to find them.

So audio reflects general direction by being very relaxed and kid friendly, you could put game ost on during some birthday party for kindergartners as well as play it as pop music at disco like 20 years ago. Sounds and voice acting are about same, sometimes cuteish and generally upholding bright impression.

Looks as mentioned are geared towards being lovely, bubbly and in theme of early 2000s platformers, even in few somewhat dark moments, it does not feel scary or oppressive because of art design. Considering how it aimed at comics to 3d, graphics should survive test of time for a while due to stylisation. 

While gameplay has some somewhat intense moments, most of the time it give a lot of breathing room and having flying sword makes it feel easier, at least for me. Besides actual platforming there is lots of fighting, so presence of system that allows upgrading your combat power is a welcome sight, even if it’s very simple. There is a number of cosmetics skins to unlock and stuff to gather, like in all representatives of the genre, but there isn’t overwhelming number of those. Good chunk of stuff would be unlocked by simply playing game, which is not that long either, so there is only a bit of grind, except for I think one of achievements.

Plot feels like it was taken from the middle of general adventuring story - there were events before game started and after it ends, which is confirmed in part by Blade Kitten comics. In general you start game, get in tight situation and spend rest of the game getting out of it. Ofc on the way plot thickens, additional details come into light and so on, but in total it’s very simple. There would be dark forces, femme fatale some conspiracies, what lacks in my opinion are actual reliable allies, but guess there are no such things in life of grizzled bounty hunter, which you play as. Forget Mandalorian with his Baby Yoda Grogu, you have Blade Kitten with Skiffy, they are totally same.

Es un juego sencillo muy de su época (o eso creo).

No le pidas muchos detalles a su historia porque tiene varios momentos en los que se notan demasiado las elipsis. Y otros en los que se podría haber desarrollado un poco más para hacerlo más ameno. Pero, conociendo el contexto de donde viene, creo que está "bien". No es genial, no es perfecto ni tampoco es muy bueno pero aún así, todo siempre se entiende, e incluso hay algún que otro momento gracioso muy ingenioso.

No le pidas un combate muy profundo porque es más como un machaca botones, de esos que no tienen mucha variedad de combate pero, al menos no te cansan el dedo. Golpe básico hacia delante o atrás, golpe a distancia media, golpe en barrida, golpe en caída, golpe corriendo, golpe cayendo sobre los enemigos para después revolearlos y poco más. Hay juegos muy famosos que empezaron sagas super largas con mucho menos, pero las comparaciones son odiosas y no vienen al caso.

No le pidas mucha complejidad a los mapas, no son rectos, pero tampoco son demasiado enredados. Algún que otro puzle para abrir alguna puerta y poco más. Si queres simplemente terminar el juego, rara vez se pone complicado para encontrar el camino. Solo los capítulos de Fortaleza Oculta, Revelaciones y tal vez Oscuridarque pueden llegar a ser tediosos. Pero si queres encontrarlo todo y sos de los que no usan guías, hay algunas cosas que están escondidas de maneras demasiado rebuscadas.

El plataformeo está bastante bien, aunque un poco bugueado. Si te acercas a una pared podes empezar a treparla e incluso podes seguir colgado por el techo. Podes clavar tu espada en la pared para usarla como apoyo para hacer un salto hacia lo alto (siempre que tengas resistencia/aguante) o incluso podes clavarla en casi todos los materiales (después de un salto) para poder explorar los lugares más escondidos del mapa. Esta es la mecánica que más disfrute del juego y me encantaría encontrarla más seguido. Pero, las cosas como son, si solo te limitas a terminar el juego sin buscar nada, posiblemente no llegues a usarla.

En resumen, el juego está bien si no queres complejidad. Leí comentarios de que no se podía terminar porque X puerta en X nivel no se abría y tengo que decir que no tuve este problema ni ningún otro bug que me impidiera avanzar hasta terminarlo. Al fin me saqué las ganas de jugarlo y quedé bastante satisfecho.

Blade Kitten, developed and published by Krome Studios, is an action-adventure platformer that brings a distinct anime-inspired flair to the genre. Centered around Kit Ballard, a feisty cat-like bounty hunter with a whip-like tail, the game invites players into the richly crafted world of Hollow Wish, where exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving are interwoven into a vibrant, cel-shaded landscape. With its colorful visuals and fast-paced gameplay, Blade Kitten aims to capture the spirit of classic platformers while adding its own unique narrative and stylistic twists.

The story follows Kit as she pursues a dangerous fugitive on Hollow Wish, only to uncover a deeper conspiracy threatening the planet’s future. While the narrative injects humor and character-driven moments, it can feel somewhat shallow and predictable, leaning heavily on internet slang and casual banter that may not resonate with all players. Despite this, the character of Kit Ballard stands out as a memorable and charismatic protagonist, with her attitude and personality carrying much of the game’s charm. The plot serves primarily as a backdrop for the gameplay, which is where the game truly shines.

Gameplay in Blade Kitten blends traditional platforming elements with combat mechanics centered on Kit’s whip tail, which players use both for traversal—swinging across gaps or climbing—and for engaging enemies. The combat system is approachable and emphasizes chaining attacks and using special moves, though some players might find it repetitive over time. Exploration is encouraged through level design that includes hidden areas, collectibles, and environmental puzzles, although certain sections lean towards linearity, which can limit the sense of discovery. The pacing balances action and platforming well, making for an experience that’s accessible to newcomers but still offers moments of challenge.

Visually, the game stands out thanks to its cel-shaded graphics that evoke anime and comic book aesthetics. The world of Hollow Wish is detailed and diverse, featuring lush jungles, futuristic industrial zones, and other varied environments that feel distinct and immersive. Kit’s character model is colorful and expressive, and her animations are smooth, enhancing the fluidity of movement and combat sequences. This artistic approach helps Blade Kitten maintain a lighthearted and vibrant tone, which complements its playful narrative style.

The audio design supports the overall atmosphere with an energetic soundtrack that fits the game’s upbeat pace. Voice acting is present throughout the story, adding personality to the characters, though it varies in quality and sometimes lacks polish. Sound effects for combat and environmental interactions are effective and contribute to the tactile feel of gameplay, even if they don’t push any boundaries.

From a technical standpoint, Blade Kitten performs well across various systems, delivering consistent frame rates and responsive controls. The interface is straightforward, allowing players to focus on exploration and combat without confusion. While the game may not offer deep customization or complex mechanics, it remains user-friendly and inviting.

Overall, Blade Kitten offers a fun and visually appealing platforming adventure with a quirky protagonist and a whimsical world. It may not revolutionize the genre or provide a deeply immersive narrative experience, but its charm lies in its style and the straightforward enjoyment of its gameplay. Fans of anime-inspired games and classic action-platformers looking for a lighthearted journey will likely appreciate what Blade Kitten brings to the table, even if it falls short of becoming a must-play classic.

The last third of this game is paid DLC due to the extended development time.  The team dropped the price of the base game, so they’re offering better value, but it’s also meant to lure in unsuspecting buyers, which is kind of sneaky, so I guess it’s a wash.  Just know that the full game is worth $7-8 at full price, not $3.  Is the base game worth buying?  I mean, against the multitude of options in this store and others, all of the possible discounts, not really, but as a bargain bin hack-and-slash platformer with a bunch of collectibles, it’s decent value.

The story is paper thin.  You’ve got your typical Sci-Fi setting with aliens, bounty hunters, and space marines.  Kit, our protagonist, does some jobbing before we’re suddenly confronted with a planetary threat and Kit being a survivor of a genocide, which hits with all the impact of an empty plastic bag.  Any potential for engaging writing is crowded out of the plot by Kit’s banter.  Her delivery isn’t annoying, but her shtick is repetitive, and it makes scenes that should have different tones just melt together.  It’s not like the game is trying to have a deep or exciting plot, but that doesn’t stop it from reeking of genericness.

The presentation is a bit better.  They haven’t aged all that well, but the designs and animations are fine for the year this came out.  Skiffy is cute.  The proprietor with the racist Asian accent isn’t.  The other designs are just kind of… well… generic.  The environments are fine, but they lack personality: the bazaar, the tenements, the fortress, the temple, the factory… I’ve seen it all before.  Maybe I’d get more out of them if the world were more fleshed out, but as they are, they’re long and visually repetitive.

That brings me to the gameplay.  It’s functional, but it’s very uneven.  Searching for hidden collectibles is pretty fun, but the sparse use of direction indicators makes it hard in some levels to tell the main path from side paths.  Since I prefer to search for collectibles before taking the main path, this meant I had to feel things out by the use of checkpoints, which was annoying and time-consuming.  The combat and platforming are pretty easy, but they don’t feel fluid.  There’s a tiny delay between attacks and jumps that might not seem like much, but it slow things down quite a bit cumulatively.  There are also a few glitches: I got stuck in a few places that made the character model blink and twitch, and the screen turned completely white in one small section of one level.  Nothing broke the game for me, but be wary.

I can’t say I really like this game, but with twelve substantial levels, collectibles and time trackers, I think it’s just worth it to grab on sale.  However, I would not buy the DLC unless you came off the base game truly hungry for more.

Ein schönes vergleichsweise kurzes Spiel mit vielen Ecken zum Erkunden und einer einfach gestrickten Story, wo halt eines zum anderen führt. (soll aber kein Kritikpunkt sein, ich fand sie durchaus in Ordnung). Vllt schonmal als kurzes Fazit: An sich hatte ich es als spaßiges, buntes Jump 'n Run mit Gemetzel ohne großes Nachdenken oder sich-Sorgen-machen empfunden und es hat mir Spaß gemacht von vorn bis hinten. 

Was mich ein bissle gestört hat, war, dass es nur recht wenige Gegnermodelle gibt und von den Gegnern, die so in den Leveln herumlaufen, kam es nicht selten vor, dass ich von den Angriffen ge-stunlocked wurde. Aber: Die Lebensenergie erholt sich eh von selbst nach einigen Sekunden, wenn man nicht im Kampf ist. Von daher denke ich, kann man da ruhig drüber hinwegsehen. 
Auch ein kleines bisschen nervig war das Reittier. Absteigen ging nicht immer sofort, vermutlich, weil es von der Höhe her zu eng war. Aber wenn ich absteigen konnte und rüber hopsen wollt, um Gegner zu bekämpfen oder weiterzulaufen, kam es  vor, dass sie sich stattdessen wieder auf das Tier setzt. 
Von der Motion Sickness, wie andere sie beschreiben, war ich jetzt 0 betroffen, von daher kann ich das nicht bewerten.

Die Musik war teils atmosphärisch, manchmal dudelt sie vor sich herum, aber als nervig hab ich sie nicht empfunden. Aber beid er engl. Synchro kann man nichts gegen sagen, das klang super. Hmm.. Was noch? Kostüme gibt es ohne Ende genauso wie reichlich Collectibles. Was mir aber da besonders gefallen hat, war natürlich der/die/das kleine Skiff. Irgendwie ist dieses "Ungeziefer" wie es von einigen Charakteren im Spiel betitelt wird, doch recht putzig. 

Es ist natürlich schade, dass es bei dem Basisspiel und der DLC-Episode bleibt, aber für das, was es ist, habe ich dieses Spiel vom Krome Studios genossen. Trotzdem wurde ich gern mehr über die Hintergründe der Charaktere erfahren, um sie noch besser verstehen zu können. ;)

[b]Personal Comment[/b] Blade Kitten is a charming and fun platformer that really shines with its unique art style and charismatic protagonist. Kit Ballard’s adventures are a joy to play through, and the engaging combat and catchy soundtrack add to the overall appeal.

However, the game has its limitations. The linear levels and simple story might not offer much depth, and occasional bugs can be a bit annoying. The lack of customization options and short playtime are also worth noting.

Despite these issues, Blade Kitten is an enjoyable game that’s definitely worth checking out if you’re looking for a light-hearted, action-packed adventure with a lot of personality.

For most of the game, I would have rated it as neutral to slightly positive. The story is forgettable, but I have no problem with that for the type of game it is. The issue was control of the character which often led to fighting the controls themselves rather than overcoming the environment. The character would sometimes be overly sticky to surfaces while other times not stick when she should have. Combat isn't particularly engaging, and that caused some irritation when trying to find secret areas while dealing with respawning enemies. Extended stun-locks were also an irritating design choice.

The control issues weren't enough to make my review negative until the final boss. The encounter design coupled with the control issues pushed my review to neutral to slightly negative. For me, it went from a passable game to one I just wanted to be over with.

I played on a steam deck, and aside from one crash to the home screen I didn't notice any compatibility issues.
Blade Kitten is a hidden gem, well worth giving a chance.

Pour commencer, j'ai jouer au jeu car le personnage qu'on incarne est une sorte de femme féline qui me faisait penser à ma propre protagoniste qui possède aussi des attributs félins et surtout est doté de la même couleur de cheveux XD. Mais au-delà de ça, j'ai bien apprécier le jeu. Mais je me dois quand même de critiquer certain points qui rendrai le jeu plus "agréable": 
1) Le choix de la barre de vie qui se régénère était sympa mais c'était impossible de voir combien on subissait à certain moment tellement il y avait d'ennemis. 

2) Le fait que les armes n'apporte rien de très particulier et que au final on choisis celle qui nous convient le mieux et on spam la touche d'attaque. Et que la manip spécial pour faire une "technique spé" lorsque l'ennemie est de face et à une lueur bleu à la main...bordel c'est presque invisible si on remarque pas qu'on peu le faire ! résultat j'ai découvert ça au boss de fin ou elle est obligatoire...ce qui m'aurait bien amusée de pouvoir le faire avant. 

3) Le système d'amélioration de santé, on achète des items dans le shop mais il est impossible de réellement constaté l'augmentation des PV ou de l'Endurance. Ce qui nous fait echo à mon 1er point. 

4) Les ennemis, ne pas voir leur PV ok c'est pas un problème, mais on nous balance des nouveaux ennemis sans vraiment ajouter de la "difficulté" mais on est juste surpris qu'il se défendent résultat on spam la touche sans vraiment savoir ce qu'on fait jusqu'à saisir le patern.  Et les niveaux des draques ou il y en a 10 à la sec qui vous harcèlent c'était tellement énérvant que j'ai rapidement speedrun les niveaux démotivé de me faire harceler pendant que je fouillais les recoins. 

5) Dernier point, hors quelque bugs sur l'avant dernier niveaux ou le perso censé aider ne réagit pas nous obligeant à relancer le jeu jusqu'à ce que ça fonctionne, je trouve que du début à la fin les cinématiques sont trop "rapide" et surtout qu'on nous présente très vite pleins de "races" existante. Ainsi pour ce qui ne connaissait pas le Webtoon j'était rapidement perdu avec un goût de "j'aime bien mais je comprend pas vraiment tout ce qui ce passe". 

ps : J'ai acheté le DLC comics, mais l'univers est si vaste que ça demande un effort de savoir par quel PDF commencer. Toutefois les dessins et artwork son splendide très beau travail <3

Conclusion : Le jeu est une très belle oeuvre, la musique marque l'esprit, les designs sont soignée et on ressent la passion et le vaste univers qui pourrait clairement exploiter d'autre aventure je pense. Donc si vous aimez les jeux de plateformes et les univers SF-Galactique et le concept de chasseur de primes ce jeu est fait pour vous <3 ! Et rendez-vous sur WEBTOON anglais si vous souhaitez lire les 12 chapitres de "Dirty Angels Blade Kitten" !

Haunted House rend hommage au classique d'origine, paru sur l'Atari 2600 en 1981. Cette nouvelle édition du tout premier jeu de survie et d'horreur s'adresse toutefois à un public plus familial.

Dans ce jeu, les joueurs devront tenter résoudre les mystères qui hantent le manoir de Graves en incarnant les petits-enfants de Samuel Silverspring, celui-là même qui est disparu sans laisser de traces dans cette maléfique demeure, il y a 30 ans. Pourchassés par des rats voraces, des chauves-souris, d'effroyables squelettes et des fantômes, les joueurs devront explorer une vingtaine de niveaux seuls ou en duo, afin de mettre la main sur les quatre fragments perdus d'une urne magique. Dans les premiers niveaux, les joueurs ne pourront livrer bataille aux créatures maléfiques, ils n'auront d'autre choix que de fuir. Alors qu'ils exploreront cette vaste demeure, les joueurs devront s'éclairer à l'aide diverses sources lumineuses afin de retrouver des ouvrages mystiques et des artéfacts mystérieux. Chaque source (allumettes, cellulaires, bougies, etc.) pouvant être utilisée pour une période limitée, une gestion de l'inventaire, réduit à deux items seulement, sera nécessaire. Certains items pourront révéler des chemins secrets (lanterne) ou blesser des ennemis (torche). En plus de devoir fouiller les lieux pour trouver des clés, les joueurs devront aussi actionner des leviers dissimulés, afin d'ouvrir des portes. Le jeu intéressera sans doute les plus jeunes, qui pourront jouer avec un parent.

Points Positifs:

+ Fidèle au concept d'origine
+ Adapté pour plus les plus jeunes (non-violent)
+ Inclus un mode coopératif à deux joueurs

Points Négatifs:

- Plutôt cher, 19,99$ sur Steam
- Contrôles mal adaptés sur PC
- Trophées à récupérer sans intérêt

A really terrible game that doesn't even come close to capturing the feel of the original. I won't bother you detailing what the game is like. There are plenty of reviews out there. I will get down to the nitty-gritty.

Is it fun?

No. The enemy has no real intelligence. Just fire your weapon and eventually you'll hit something. Capital ships are insanely easy. Strafe and shoot. The most laughable capital ship is supposed to be the hardest: The Zylon Basestar. You remember that annoying glowing basestar from the original? Shielded so you had to hit him just right. In this version, you just fly inside it and sit there, completely protected from attack, while you line up your shots.

It's kind of cute how they use the original symbols on the galactic map. And the space backdrop is nice to look at.

But the over-the-shoulder look you get of your ship should immediately tell you: This is not Star Raiders.

Gone is the (limited, but good for its time) strategy of defending your starbases. But even 1979 gameplay is superior to this where there is no strategy at all. Heck, even Star Raiders II had better gameplay than this travesty.

If you're looking for a recapture of Star Raiders on a modern system, you're looking in the wrong place. And the pitiful thing is: it can be done! Archon, Missile Command, and Centiped were all updated very well while capturing the heart and soul of the orignals.

This Star Raiders is a soulless creature unworthy of the name.

I love how different this is from the original Star Raiders, while still retaining key aspects of the original gameplay. I enjoyed learning all the cool things you can do with your ship, and comparing what you can do now with what you could do in the original. I love all the new abilities and weapons and such! I don't mind that it's mission-based because all the missions are at different locations with different scenery, terrain, and things you have to get done. It adds some nice variety! I like that the cutscenes add a bit of depth to the story, and explain what's happening and why, and how it's connected to the original. I love that Solaris is included here too! 
Not only is the gameplay good, but the graphics aren't bad either! The controls are pretty complicated if you don't have a controller, it definitely just takes time to get used to.

Star Raiders seem to be an interesting reimagining of an old classic, but ended up with horrible controls that makes the game virtually unplayable, wasting a decent engine and a good license. 

(For the record, I am one of those PC kids who NEVER played the original, okay?) 

The intro is quite lame, it's just some static comic-book type panels about how the cabal of friends, including Ruiz, that's you, the geek, joined Atar Academy in order to work your way into the Star Raiders squadron on the Solaris carrier in the war against the Zylons. 

Your ship has three modes: turret (heavy shields and weapons, don't move much), as well as assault and attack (I still can't figure out which mode is better for what, and there's no manual).  In the intro/tutorial you can only use a single mode and it's only later you get to choose the modes. (Why does this reminds me so much of Robotech, i.e. fighter, guardian, and robot modes?) Somehow you have to upgrade the weapons individually in each mode too.  

The graphics are a bit sparse but workable, and it's compatible with modern high-res screens (no problem setting it to 1680x1050). It's annoying though to get prompted with legend of onscreen HUD every time one starts the mission.

I managed to complete the tutorial missions by spamming the sky with missiles and I seriously doubt I could drive the fighter with any precision in an actual dogfight, when I have no problem playing games that require such precisions, but then those work with gamepad. This one doesn't. 

All in all, don't bother buying this, unless you want to spend a while figuring out how to get your gamepad to work, and maybe you still won't enjoy it.

Star Raiders was one of my favorite games on the old Atari 8-bit systems. Packed into a measly 8K of ROM was a surprisingly detailed and complex space dogfighting game. When I saw that Atari was releasing an updated version for the PC, I was both excited and wary. All too often companies dig up a popular title from their vaults and try to squeeze more money out of it (anyone remember Knight Rider 2000?)

Alas, that's exactly what Atari has done with Star Raiders. This version of the game is about as unlike the original as you could possibly get while still flying a space fighter. Now it has a story, it's mission-based, the fighter can transform into different modes and there are cutscenes. There are also a number of new types of enemies to fight, including capital ships. I never got to a point where I could go into hyperspace or use the Galactic Chart or Long Range Scanner, if those things even exist in the game. While the original Star Raiders managed to squeeze the entire game into a mere 8,192 BYTES, this new version weighs in at nearly a full gigabyte.

Graphics are OK, if rather uninspired. It seemed a bit hard to figure out what I was looking at sometimes, with dark ships against the dark background of space, but fortunately enemies have boxes around them so you can always figure out where you need to shoot. The game really looks like a direct port from the X-Box.

The biggest flaw with Star Raiders is the horrendous controls. I could not get the game to recognize the rudder, throttle or hat controls on my Microsoft Sidewinder Precision Pro joystick. It also wouldn't recognize the additional buttons on my Logitech G700 gaming mouse or my Logitech Dual Action gamepad. Without the rudder or throttle, attempting to fly with the joystick is impossible, while trying to fly with the mouse felt like I was piloting a Mack truck through molasses. Keyboard? Don't make me laugh.

As far as gameplay, I really wouldn't know. I couldn't make it past the third tutorial because the controls were so utterly abysmal I couldn't track the enemy fighters to shoot them down. It might have been an interesting game if the controls actually worked.

This game has been out for two years and the publisher has never released an update.  Don't waste your money on it.

Il gioco è costituito da 16 livelli, disposti su due zone. 10 nella prima e 6 nella seconda.

Non esiste storia, non esiste epilogo (tranne una animazione finale, ma giusto per).

E' come se fosse solo una raccolta di livelli.

In ogni livello in pratica lo scopo è giungere alla fine, e fare un punteggio migliore. Quest'ultimo si persegue in vari modi:

-si deve attivare la flora locale. Per fare questo vanno raccolte delle spore da delle piante che le riproducono in continuazione, e spargerle per punti particolari del fondale (lo spargimento è automatico, basta passarci sopra). In pratica si passa sui fondali e per magia crescono piante e alghe che illuminano anche lo scenario e fanno luce. 
-si devono raccogliere degli oggetti (ad esempio dei cristalli) nascosti per i livelli.

ogni livello è diviso in due parti. Si inizia in un punto, si arriva alla fine della prima parte dove si trova una specie di teletrasporto, che riporta alla seconda parte del livello. Si può anche viaggiare a ritroso usando lo stesso teletrasporto nella seconda zona del livello. 

Per potere raggiungere la fine dei livelli bisogna superare dei puzzle che a volte sono anche carini, anche se sempre molto facili. Questi puzzle, ad esempio, richiedono di mettere in modo meccanismi che aprono porte o la distruzione di alcuni oggetti del fondale. Per fare questo a volte servono oggetti particolari (come le bombe o le lampade che permettono di addentrarsi in zone riempite da una nebbia oscura), che sono rilasciati da alcune piante, che bisogna fare crescere con le spore di cui sopra.

Non si muore mai, anche se ci stanno alcuni nemici che impediscono di raggiungere alcune zone. Ma anche questo fa parte dei puzzle: bisogna solo capire che per arrivare in quelle zone non serve fare lo slalom tra i nemici, ma evidentemente c'è un enigma che permette di risolvere la situazione in un dato modo (ad esempio, usufruire di un cannone che faccia cadere l'oggetto verso la mia direzione dalla zona stazionata dal mostro, senza quindi provarci fisicamente).

Tutto qui, si inizia dal primo livello e si arriva alla fine. Al termine di ogni livello viene dato un punteggio e bon.

Il gioco è tecnicamente molto ben fatto con zoom continui e colori cangianti e pulsanti. I diversi livelli non si distinguono tantissimo tra di loro esteticamente, anche se in ognuno si introduce un diverso stile/enigma (ad esempio, nel livello delle batterie gli enigmi sono a base della corrente elettrica, ma non ho capito come sia possibile che nessuno rimanga fulminato in acqua).

Dopo ogni livello inoltre si sbloccano dei "vestiti", ovvero è possibile impersonare un teletubbie diverso (rosa, blu, pallinato, tigrato ecc...) o mettergli un diverso cappellino (vuoi l'elmetto con le corna gialle? Accomodati). Ma è solo questione estetica.

Lo consiglio? Per rilassarsi sì, è carino, ma prendetelo in sconto. Ci ho messo, in tutto, meno di 7 ore (in realtà l'ho ripreso, ne avevo già altre 2 circa in precedenza) e per quello che mi ha dato, imho, il prezzo da non superare non sarebbe di oltre 5 euro.

The UnderGarden is a decent casual game, with cute colorful visuals, nice music, and uncomplicated gameplay. You'll flit about serene mazelike caverns, making plants grow and solving a few simple physics-based puzzles. It's all quite peaceful and relaxing. 

And with the game's deadliest threat being bubbles that knock your character back a few feet, The UnderGarden is about as stress-free as games get.

The UnderGarden isn't for hardcore gamers, but casual gamers and kids will probably enjoy it.

The UnderGarden is a slow casual experience with beautiful visuals and relaxing music. Good for that slow lazy evening yet offers a bit of a challenge if going for gold.

Think Creavures, Aquaria, even Sparkle 2 Evo - a slower-paced adventure with a heavy focus on mesmerising visuals and a soothing soundtrack. The aim of the game is to pollenize the underwater flora and explore the levels for secrets. There's no need to rush so it's perfectly fine to just relax and take time solving the odd puzzle. For those more interested in score it's certainly possible to go for speed as each level is scored and time is recorded. Something to appeal to both casual and core gamers.

The puzzle design is not ground-breaking but does what it has to do without compromising the relaxing nature of the game too much. There are lever puzzles, push-buttons that have to be held down (or up!) by special seeds, and some other physics-based puzzles. Some puzzles have alternative, less obvious solutions that lead to secrets and bonus collectibles so it's certainly worth the while to experiment a little and try to explore every nook and cranny.

I suppose I would recommend the game to anyone looking for a decent time without the fast pace of more modern games. It's not often that I play casual games like this, but the visuals and an overall calm atmosphere are hard to pass up.

The UnderGarden est un jeu relaxant qui vous propose d'explorer de vastes cavernes souterraines, où différentes formes de vie colorées s'animeront suite à votre passage.

Le jeu repose sur des mécaniques de jeu très accessibles. Vous y incarner un petit jardinier, capable de récupérer du pollen et le redistribuer à son passage, permettant ainsi à une variété de plantes de fleurir. Il en résulte une floraison à grande échelle de toute beauté. Bien qu'il ne soit pas nécessaire de polliniser toutes les plantes, les adeptes du jeu s'efforceront d'atteindre l'objectif de 100%. Certaines plantes produiront des fruits, qui pourront être utilisés dans la résolution d'énigmes. Il pourra ainsi déposer des fruits lourds sur une plateforme pour abaisser celle-ci, ou encore relâcher des fruits légers pour les voir s'envoler et déplacer vers le haut une plateforme. Des fruits explosifs pourront également être utilisés pour détruire des obstacles. Des musiciens, jouant d'instruments différents, pourront aussi être déplacés pour influencer la flore locale, uniquement par plaisir.

Votre avatar pouvant flotter, vous pourrez le déplacer lentement en pointant une direction précise, ou rapidement en effectuant une charge. Certains puzzles nécessiteront un peu de précision, notamment ceux où il faut éviter des obstacles pouvant causer la détonation des fruits explosifs, ou encore ceux où il faut emprunter des courants d'air. Dans chacun des quinze niveaux, des fleurs spéciales sont également cachées. Bien que le jeu ne soit pas difficile, certains casse-tête environnementaux vous échapperont à votre premier passage et il ne vous sera pas possible de réessayer de les résoudre sur le champ, vous devrez revisiter le niveau une seconde fois, ce qui pourrait occasionner un peu de frustration. Sinon, avec sa trame musicale paisible, The UnderGarden reste un jeu très zen.

“Vendetta” is the mission that sticks with me. It opens with you lying among bodies in Stalingrad, waiting for a German patrol to pass. Then Reznov appears and talks you through lining up a shot as the sound of bombers passing overhead covers your rifle fire. The mission takes its time, which makes the scramble through a burning building later on feel even more desperate.

The campaign alternates between the Soviet advance on Berlin and the U.S. Marines fighting across the Pacific. The two fronts feel distinct. In the Pacific, tall grass and concealed bunkers make every advance feel exposed. In Berlin, the fighting closes in around ruined buildings and streets. The oppressive sound design ties it all together. The game can push that intensity too far on Veteran, where the sheer number of grenades landing at your feet makes some checkpoints feel more like a test of patience.

Multiplayer has its own highlights. Castle’s courtyards and upper floors make for good back-and-forth fights, and hearing the attack dogs arrive can send a whole team scrambling. The biggest surprise is Nazi Zombies. Nacht der Untoten is just a handful of rooms, some boarded windows, and a Mystery Box, yet it can turn a quiet round into a panic the moment someone calls out that they’re out of ammo.

**9/10.** World at War is worth revisiting for its grim campaign and the simplicity of its original Zombies map. There’s still something satisfying about holding that little bunker for one more round with a friend, right up until you both realize you’ve been watching the same window.

In terms of WW2 shooters, this is one of the most brutal, akin to Brothers in Arms HH. The music and scoring is also top notch. The gameplay is simple, but serves its role in making you feel like one of the grunts on the frontlines. 

Unfortunately, multiplayer is dead, and playing the campaign coop requires utilizing an albeit, easy to install mod, but comes with some bugs and annoyances in the playthrough. Zombies still gets lots of support and is fun for those that like that style of game, though there's probably more complete zombie packages elsewhere which include the WaW maps. 

For a game that rarely goes on sale, I think $20 is still worth it for a great campaign and zombies, just please do your research if looking to play them online.

**Call of Duty: World at War — One of the Greatest World War II Shooters Ever Made**

**Rating: 10/10 — A Must-Play Classic**

Call of Duty: World at War is one of the most memorable entries in the Call of Duty franchise. Developed by Treyarch, this 2008 first-person shooter delivers a brutal portrayal of World War II, combining intense combat, a dark atmosphere, an excellent soundtrack, and one of the most iconic bonus modes in gaming history: Nazi Zombies.

Even years after its release, World at War remains an outstanding example of how to create a memorable military shooter.

**Story and Campaign:**

One of the game's greatest strengths is its two-part campaign, which follows American Marines fighting against Imperial Japanese forces in the Pacific and Soviet soldiers battling Nazi Germany on the Eastern Front.

The American campaign emphasizes the brutality of jungle warfare, with ambushes, fortified positions, and relentless enemy resistance. The Soviet campaign takes a darker approach, following the Red Army's advance toward Berlin through some of the war's most devastating battles.

The characters, particularly Dimitri Petrenko and Viktor Reznov, help make the Soviet storyline especially memorable. The relationship between these characters adds emotional weight to the campaign, while the struggle to survive gives the battles a sense of desperation.

World at War does not attempt to present war as glamorous. Its disturbing imagery, violent encounters, and desperate situations emphasize the terrible human cost of the conflict.

**Gameplay and Combat:**

The gameplay follows the traditional Call of Duty formula, featuring linear missions, intense firefights, weapon variety, and explosive set pieces. The combat feels satisfying, and the different environments provide some welcome variation.

The Pacific missions introduce Japanese tactics such as ambushes and Banzai charges, while the Eastern Front features large-scale infantry battles and the destruction of German defensive positions.

The arsenal includes period-inspired weapons such as the M1 Garand, Thompson, PPSh-41, Mosin-Nagant, and MP40. Flamethrowers and other specialized weapons also add variety to certain encounters.

However, the grenade spam on higher difficulties can become extremely frustrating. Enemy AI can sometimes feel unfair, and friendly soldiers are not always as helpful as they should be. Despite these problems, the core shooting mechanics remain enjoyable.

**Historical Setting and Atmosphere:**

World at War excels at creating an intense World War II atmosphere. The battlefields, ruined buildings, jungle environments, military equipment, and sound design contribute to a convincing sense of chaos.

The game also gives attention to the Pacific theater, which was less frequently explored in mainstream military shooters than the European theater. Its portrayal of the fighting against Imperial Japanese forces gives the campaign a different character from games focused exclusively on the Western Front.

Although it takes creative liberties for dramatic purposes, the game successfully communicates the violence, exhaustion, and desperation associated with the conflict.

**Graphics and Visual Presentation:**

For a game released in 2008, World at War has impressive visual presentation. The environments are detailed enough to establish a strong sense of place, while the lighting, explosions, smoke, and destruction help create intense battle scenes.

The graphics are understandably dated today, but the art direction and cinematic presentation remain effective. The game still manages to deliver memorable moments without relying on modern graphical technology.

**Soundtrack and Sound Design:**

The audio is one of the game's strongest features. Weapon sounds, explosions, battlefield shouting, and environmental effects help make the combat feel chaotic and dangerous.

The soundtrack also deserves recognition for reinforcing the intensity of the campaign. Its music fits the game's darker tone, particularly during the Soviet missions, where the atmosphere becomes increasingly desperate.

Voice acting is another highlight, especially in the Soviet campaign. The dialogue between Reznov and Petrenko helps establish the emotional core of the story.

**Nazi Zombies — An Iconic Game Mode:**

Nazi Zombies is arguably one of World at War's greatest contributions to gaming. Originally unlocked after completing the campaign, this survival mode places players in increasingly difficult rounds of undead enemies.

Players must collect points, purchase weapons, repair barricades, unlock areas, and work together to survive for as long as possible. Every round becomes more dangerous, creating a satisfying mixture of tension, strategy, and cooperation.

The original Nacht der Untoten map is simple but incredibly effective, while later maps such as Verrückt, Shi No Numa, and Der Riese expand the experience with new mechanics, locations, and secrets.

Nazi Zombies helped establish a formula that would become a major part of the Call of Duty franchise. Its replayability, cooperative gameplay, and memorable atmosphere make it one of the game's most important features.

**Multiplayer and Cooperative Gameplay:**

The original multiplayer offers class-based combat, customizable loadouts, weapon progression, perks, and maps inspired by the game's World War II setting. Tank combat also adds an unusual element compared with many other entries in the series.

The cooperative campaign is another welcome feature, allowing friends to experience the story together rather than limiting cooperation to separate multiplayer modes.

However, the online experience deserves a qualification in a modern review. Because the game is nearly two decades old, its original multiplayer ecosystem is less convenient than that of newer titles. Players may encounter compatibility problems, limited populated lobbies, or other technical complications depending on how they access the game.

**Difficulty and Replayability:**

World at War can be brutally difficult, particularly on Veteran difficulty. Enemies are aggressive, grenades can become overwhelming, and surviving certain encounters requires patience and careful positioning.

Although this difficulty can sometimes feel unfair, it gives the campaign a memorable level of intensity. Completing difficult missions provides a genuine sense of accomplishment.

Nazi Zombies adds substantial replayability, while cooperative play, higher difficulty settings, and multiplayer provide additional reasons to return.

**Technical Performance and Weaknesses:**

Despite its strengths, World at War is not perfect. Its grenade-heavy encounters, occasionally unreliable friendly AI, dated animations, and repetitive firefights can become frustrating.

Modern PC players may also encounter legacy compatibility or online connectivity issues. The game was designed for much older systems, and some of its original online features are not as straightforward to use today.

These shortcomings are worth acknowledging, but they do little to diminish the quality of the campaign and Zombies mode.

**Final Verdict:**

Call of Duty: World at War remains an exceptional World War II shooter. Its two campaigns offer memorable combat and a darker atmosphere than many contemporary military games, while its soundtrack, characters, and level design help it stand out among other entries in the franchise.

Nazi Zombies alone gives the game considerable replay value, and its influence on later Call of Duty titles is difficult to overlook.

Although its difficulty balance, technical limitations, and aging multiplayer experience prevent it from being flawless, its strongest features have stood the test of time.

If you enjoy World War II history, military shooters, cooperative campaigns, and classic round-based survival games, Call of Duty: World at War is absolutely worth playing.

I highly recommend getting this collection while it is still available on STEAM. While it is designed to work up to Windows 8, I really have no problems running most of them on Windows 10 or 11, due to the fact that they are running through an emulator which is pretty boiler plate in terms of it being able to play on almost anything.

As for the collection; it has literally everything. Even the enhanced SCI version of King's Quest 1 that is hard to find. These games come from an era where you were designed to sit comfortable, drink your coffee, eat your bagel/pastry, and think about the puzzles you were confronted with. 

You will encounter deaths. You will encounter puzzles that stump you. You will encounter intentional softlocks, that you have absolutely no idea are softlocks and will induce rage or self-pitying laughter as you come to realize it. These were not considered "bad design" back then, because patience was a virtue, and word of mouth helped build mystery around the game.

Conversely, in spite of those things, you will also encounter genuinely funny jokes, whimsical adventure, surprising moments of "combat", alternative ways to solve puzzles or even to advance through the story, memorable locations and characters, and a design ethos and personality to these games that are wholly unlike that of LucasArts. Where LucasArts was safe and coddling, at times feeling a little mischievous, King's Quest is the older brother of LucasArts games, both figuratively and literally. It is not afraid to kill you in comedic or even brutal methods, abruptly and without pause. It is not afraid test your patience with absurdity, or even taunt or tantalize you into making mistakes. This is a series of games where you can defeat a yeti by throwing a pie in its face, while also getting ambushed by a dwarf who stole an item you didn't realize you needed an hour and a half later, unable to continue.

And it's hard not to love it for all its warts and all. It's like an insanely hot woman who is your life's dream to meet, finding out she's interested in you, but then realizing she farts in bed, and they smell like rancid cabbage, but you find out you don't really mind, and in fact after a while, you come to get used to it, even miss it when you're not with her.

If you do not want to stress with worrying about the potential softlocks, there are wikis dedicated to listing all of them outright so you can deftly avoid them and go unimpeded. They are more common in some titles than others, while in King's Quest 7, the whole game is fairly streamlined with no deaths OR dead ends. This series is more than just fun though; they are historical. Mystery House was the first graphical adventure game, but King's Quest 1 is the one that solidified the concept of what they were. This is the series where Monkey Island started...It's where Snatcher started...Hell, it's where Phoenix Wright started. Even if you don't like the gameplay, it should be interesting to anyone who considers themselves a gamer, or interested in gaming as a whole, to check out purely from a curiosity perspective. The historical significance of these games is huge, and while one could argue against not overlooking the faults of their gameplay, they cannot overlook the impact of their influence.
Brings back great childhood memories; I truly wish they would remake them all again but this is still awesome.

I loved this game soooo much when I was a kid, and when I found it for under $10, I was thrilled. Hopefully I will still have some fun with it, but it's clear from my first few hours trying that this was a cheap attempt by the company to squeeze more dollars out of an old product, without doing absolutely anything to prep it for a modern audience.

HUGE example #1. When you attempt to play KQ4, it makes you do a security check by writing a certain word from the KQ4 manual. Which you presumably haven't had in 35 years, if ever...you just bought it on Steam. Did they even LOOK at their product before they put it out there?!? Unreal that something that gaping slipped through. You literally can't play one of the worlds in the package deal. 

Example #2. I played for a while, and went to save the game. It wants me to identify a folder on my computer to save it to. Um....

There are some very basic things they could have done to update the game so that it's playable on a modern computer. I don't care about the graphics, it's an old game. But it has to be playable. I will try it a little bit more, but may just ask for a refund. Only try this if you are a super diehard fan and willing to put up with a lot of hassles to play your old favorite.

Pros:
-Great Puzzles
-Great Retro Art
-Music and Aesthetic still intact

But that's the thing, the only pros to these games are because the original games were so solid, there's been very little effort to make them accessible on modern systems, or to add anything to improve the QoL for new players, or old players on newer hardware.

Cons:
-No proper UI or modern launcher
-Uses a very old DOSBox build
-Poor default display scaling and blurry visuals

-Minimal Windows 10/11 support
-Feels unpolished and outdated for a paid collection

[h3][b]King’s Quest Collection Review: A Nostalgic Journey Through Sierra’s Madness[/b][/h3]
The [i]King’s Quest Collection[/i] on Steam is both a blessing and a curse for fans of classic adventure games. It compiles the legendary series created by Roberta Williams, which laid the groundwork for graphical adventure gaming as we know it. But if you’ve played these games, you already know: Sierra does [i]not[/i] love you. These games were designed to frustrate, enchant, and maybe even break you.

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]What’s Included[/b][/h3]
This collection brings together all seven of the original [i]King’s Quest[/i] games (I-VII) without [i]King’s Quest: Mask of Eternity[/i], which shifted into an action-adventure direction. It includes two collections in one package: [b]King's Quest Collection[/b] and [b]King's Quest Collection Legacy[/b]. You choose edition at launch.  
[olist]
[*]King's Quest Collection is just an updated King's Quest Collection from 2006 that has been optimized to support additional Operating Systems. 
[*]King's Quest Collection Legacy is just unchanged King's Quest Collection from 2006.
[/olist]
The King's Quest Collection changes include adding KQ1 AGI and KQ7 2.0 DOS (replacing KQ1 SCI remake and KQ7 1.5 from the previous 2006 collection). The King's Quest Collection Legacy is the same as the 2006 version with KQ1SCI, and King's Quest 7 Windows 95 1.5 version (16-bit windows only, but can be manually set up to run in ScummVM). 

Here’s the breakdown:
[olist]
	[*][b]King’s Quest I: Quest for the Crown[/b] – Where it all began. Help Sir Graham become king by solving puzzles that range from clever to infuriating.
	[*][b]King’s Quest II: Romancing the Throne[/b] – A slightly more ambitious sequel with a romantic quest at its heart.
	[*][b]King’s Quest III: To Heir Is Human[/b] – Now you’re Gwydion, a young slave trying to escape his evil wizard captor. Arguably one of the series’ most innovative stories.
	[*][b]King’s Quest IV: The Perils of Rosella[/b] – One of the first games with a female protagonist, and the day/night mechanic was groundbreaking at the time.
	[*][b]King’s Quest V: Absence Makes the Heart Go Yonder![/b] – Known for its gorgeous VGA graphics and that owl Cedric. We’ll get to him.
	[*][b]King’s Quest VI: Heir Today, Gone Tomorrow[/b] – Widely considered the best in the series. A great mix of story, puzzles, and memorable characters.
	[*][b]King’s Quest VII: The Princeless Bride[/b] – A more cartoon-like entry that leaned into the whimsical side of fairy tales.
[/olist]

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]Copyright Protection Nonsense[/b][/h3]
Let’s talk about one of the most baffling and infuriating aspects of this Steam release: the publisher left the original [i]copyright protection[/i] in place. Yes, you read that right. To play these games, you’re still required to look up specific information from the game manuals—like it’s the 1980s and you’re rifling through dog-eared papers to find the right spell or coordinates. The kicker? While the manuals are included as PDFs, the sheer laziness of not even attempting to modernize this process is astonishing.

This isn’t a charming quirk; it’s pure garbage. It’s one thing to preserve the gameplay, but to subject players to antiquated DRM is absurd. We’re decades past floppy disks and code wheels, yet here we are, held hostage by a system that should’ve been retired with shoulder pads and mullets. This decision reeks of apathy, showing just how little care went into adapting these classics for a modern audience.

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]Gameplay[/b][/h3]
At its core, [i]King’s Quest[/i] is about exploring whimsical fairy-tale landscapes, solving puzzles, and not dying… repeatedly. Every game in the series has a way of punishing you mercilessly for being curious or, heaven forbid, unprepared. Didn't pick up that one pixelated feather? Start over. Stepped too close to a staircase? Hope you saved recently.

The series evolved from the early text-parser interface (type commands like “TAKE SWORD”) to a point-and-click system in the later entries. The shift was welcome, but the games never lost their knack for frustrating players with obscure logic and random deaths.

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]The Sierra Approach to Love: Brutal Tough Love[/b][/h3]
Sierra Online, led by Roberta and Ken Williams, made games for a very specific type of gamer. If LucasArts gave us forgiving puzzles and funny death screens, Sierra went the opposite way:
[list]
	[*][i]“Oh, you didn’t save before you climbed those stairs? Too bad.”[/i]
	[*][i]“Didn’t notice that small pixel on the ground? You’re doomed.”[/i]
[/list]
But the cruelty often feels intentional, part of the series’ quirky charm. The eagle feather in [i]King’s Quest III[/i] or the labyrinthine catacombs in [i]King’s Quest V[/i] are badges of honor for those who conquer them.

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]Characters and Story[/b][/h3]
The series shines in its storytelling and world-building. From Graham’s ascension to the throne in the first game to Alexander’s journey in [i]King’s Quest VI[/i], these games are steeped in fairy-tale lore and charm. The settings vary from enchanted forests to magical islands and cursed kingdoms, with each game introducing memorable characters.

Cedric the Owl from [i]King’s Quest V[/i] is infamous for his annoying voice, but even he adds a layer of nostalgia. The characters in [i]King’s Quest VI[/i], like the Winged Ones or the creepy Lord of the Dead, show how the series evolved into more nuanced storytelling.

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]Presentation[/b][/h3]
The early games were cutting-edge in their time but look rough now. However, the VGA updates for [i]King’s Quest I-IV[/i] still have a certain charm. By the time you get to [i]King’s Quest V and VI[/i], the graphics hold up surprisingly well, especially considering their age. The voice acting is hit-or-miss, with [i]Cedric the Owl[/i] being a love-it-or-hate-it situation.

The whimsical art style of [i]King’s Quest VII[/i] divides fans, but it fits the tone of the game. Meanwhile, [i]Mask of Eternity[/i]… well, it looks and plays like a very clunky 3D experiment.

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]Why Play It?[/b][/h3]
This collection is a history lesson in adventure gaming. The [i]King’s Quest[/i] series is legendary for a reason, and playing it today is like traveling back to the origins of the genre. Just be ready for some outdated mechanics, obscure puzzles, and lots of saving and reloading.

Despite its flaws, there’s a charm here that modern games can’t replicate. It’s a mix of fairy-tale whimsy, brutal challenge, and a feeling of genuine accomplishment when you solve a tough puzzle.

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]Annoyances[/b][/h3]
[list]
	[*][i]RNG Hell:[/i] Some puzzles rely on random chance, which feels infuriating, especially in [i]King’s Quest III[/i].
	[*][i]Pixel-Hunting:[/i] Missing a tiny detail can lock you out of progress.
	[*][i]Stairs:[/i] Seriously, the stairs are a menace. Sierra clearly hated us.
	[*][i]Presentation Gaps:[/i] While the stories and settings are timeless, the dated graphics and mechanics are harder to overlook in a genre that relies on immersion.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/h3]
[i]King’s Quest Collection[/i] is a love letter to a bygone era of gaming. It’s challenging, frustrating, and occasionally maddening, but it’s also magical, imaginative, and rewarding. If you’re a fan of classic adventure games or want to see where the genre got its roots, this collection is a must-have.

There was even a book that came with the game that was required for one puzzle, but just helped you be prepared for many others. The whole thing was told from vantage points that were always creative, like the camera being perched on a bookshelf when touring the local bookstore. It really left a lasting impression on me for the magic and imagination of entertainment.

Scifi adventure game.  You are a janitor aboard the Arcada, which is delivering a valuable planet-igniting device to a system that needs a new star.  Unfortunately, the ship has been boarded by hostiles and you, the apparent lone survivor, must save the day.  And then do it five more times.

Space Quest Collection is a series of six games: Space Quest 1 through Space Quest 6.  Each one has a relatively self-contained story; you don't have to complete, play or even know about the others to play any given one.  Spread across ten years, the collection represents advances in storytelling and production quality.

Space Quest 1 is low-tech, with 7-bit music and graphics to match.  By the time you get to Space Quest 6, you're at fairly detailed graphics, smooth motion and voice acting.  The leap is tremendous, but that doesn't mean there isn't worthwhile content in SQ1.  The games have the quirky humor Sierra is (was?) famous for, and it's always satisfying to work through the puzzles, obstacles and challenges to complete one.

Be advised that these are DosBox games, which means they were produced before Microsoft Windows was even a thing.  But I didn't run into any performance or glitch issues with them on either of two grades of machine, so they should be safe for any machine one can find today to run them on.

My nostalgia may be waxing here.  SQ1 was hot stuff when it came out in 1986; the average gamer born after that might not see the appeal.  But I got the collection through Humble Bundle, which, considering how many hours of story-driven game the whole collection represents, made it a helluva value.

This collection of 6 game is a nostalgic blast of classic Sierra adventure games, following the unlikely heroics of intergalactic janitor Roger Wilco. From killer robots to time-traveling sequels, each game delivers sharp humor, quirky puzzles, and wonderfully absurd sci-fi settings. While the early text-parser interface and occasional bugs can be frustrating, they’re part of the retro charm for fans of the era. The writing is consistently witty, filled with genre parodies and hilarious deaths that make trial-and-error oddly rewarding. It’s a barebones package with no extras, but the games themselves still hold up as cult comedy classics. If you can handle some old-school jank, this collection is absolutely worth exploring. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3513582095

The Space Quest Collection isn’t just a bundle of old games. It’s a glimpse into a time when adventure games could be clever, weird, frustrating, and deeply funny, all at once. I didn’t grow up thinking I’d ever root for a space janitor, but somehow Roger Wilco became one of those unlikely heroes I’ll never forget.

These games have a way of getting under your skin. Not because of cutting-edge graphics or gameplay innovation, but because they somehow make failure hilarious and success feel like surviving a Rube Goldberg death trap designed by a drunk comedian. You die a lot. Often in the dumbest ways possible. But every time, you reload, laugh a little, and try again.

What stands out to me most is how self-aware the writing is. It constantly pokes fun at sci-fi tropes, gaming conventions, and especially at Roger himself. He isn’t brave, smart, or particularly skilled. He’s just there, trying to mop up his life one mess at a time, and somehow saving the galaxy in the process. There’s something oddly relatable about that. Sometimes life hands you a plunger instead of a sword, and you do what you can.

The tone shifts from game to game. Some lean hard into slapstick, others have surprisingly dark undertones. But the heart of the series stays intact. The narrator’s sarcastic commentary adds an extra layer that feels like having a snarky friend beside you the whole time. It's not just gameplay. It's an experience that knows how absurd it is and leans into that with both boots.

Revisiting this collection feels like rummaging through a dusty old VHS shelf and finding something that still holds up. Not because it’s perfect, but because it’s sincere. It’s flawed, goofy, occasionally clunky, and exactly what makes it special.

I guess what I love most is that Space Quest doesn’t take itself seriously. And in a world that often takes everything far too seriously, that’s worth a lot.

Roger Wilco may not be the hero we asked for. But he’s the janitor we deserve.

Ho un aneddoto che fa parte della mia vita sin dal 1991, e dato che riguarda direttamente Space Quest 4 decido di scriverlo qua sotto, rubando qualche minuto a chi mai si troverà a leggere questa recensione:

In quel periodo i soldi scarseggiavano e, al contrario di oggi, il 99% di quel che giocavo era piratato; ecco arrivare la famigerata Copy Protection della Sierra! Comunque la carenza di soldi non vuole essere una scusa, solo la mia motivazione.

Per chi non sapesse, la copy protection Sierra funzionava in modo molto semplice  : nelle prime battute del gioco, veniva chiesto al giocatore un "qualcosa", che poteva essere un codice alfanumerico, un nome, una parola e queste info si trovavano solo nel maledetto manuale che, ovviamente, un pirata non aveva.
Ad esempio in SQ5 le coordinate per spostare la navicella si trovano solo sul manuale. 

Ultima informazione : all'epoca i giocatori che volessero ricevere aiuti per andare avanti con un gioco o consigli su come battere un particolare nemico scrivevano delle vere e proprie lettere alle riviste specializzate, come The Games Machine o Zzap!, le quali pubblicavano la lettera con tanto di nome, cognome ed indirizzo.

Io che ero bloccato alla copy protection di SQ4 mi sono battuto a tappeto svariate riviste per trovare qualche sfortunello, anch'esso alla ricerca di info per il medesimo gioco, e alla fine trovai un ragazzo dei dintorni di Ancona.. 

Mi recai in un centro specializzato in, beh, telefonate, pieno di cabine ed elenchi telefonici di tutta Italia. Ora il nome del ragazzo non compariva, ovviamente, per cui mi scrissi tutti i cognomi corrispondenti per quella città e, tornato a casa, cominciai a chiamare a casaccio questi numeri, spacciandomi per un suo amico; per fortuna i numeri da provare erano solo una dozzina !

Insomma alla fine trovai la nonna che mi diede il numero giusto ! Non si concluse bene perché il tizio, con giusta ragione, si rifiutò di aiutarmi ... ricorderò per sempre il disagio di quel povero ragazzo mentre parlava con uno sconosciuto che gli aveva dato la caccia !! Che ricordi
