While I enjoy 'The Club' quite a bit, but looking at this for most people I would give this a 'mixed' rating as you still have to manually fix some things yourself and most people don't want to do that nor should they. I am going to specifically look through the lenses of the game itself especially at the $3-4 range I got it on sale for, don't buy for $15 100%.

'Games For Windows Live' plagues this game and it might not have been to much of an issue since the service still actually works, but the version sold here on Steam is outdated meaning you will have to install a newer patch yourself, you could get Windows/Xbox achievements doing this and if the online wasn't dead you'd be able to play that as well, but if you don't want to deal with it like me then downloading XLiveless off [url=https://community.pcgamingwiki.com/files/file/576-xliveless/] PCGamingWiki [/url] and just dropping those DLLs in your main folder solves the issue instantaneously. Now you won't get the achievos, but you'd be stuck in singleplayer regardless so I didn't care, especially since they aren't Steam achievements anyway.

You will play as one of the 8 characters presented and you are brought into this tournament called 'The Club,' in which everybody competes in a plethora of locations trying to be #1 on the leaderboard gaining points through everyone's favorite activity murder. It's a lot like 'Twisted Metal,' force a bunch of guys into something with the chance of being able to not just win a prize, but also freedom..... for most of the cast at least. There isn't a whole lot here in terms of story, but this was developed second after gameplay and it shows with how short the cutscenes are and how little of them are here.

Gameplay is a straight up blast to play though. Matt Cavanagh, the lead designer had described the game as "a racing game with guns," and that's exactly what it is. For most of the rounds you will run as fast as you can from point A murdering goons and thugs while trying to keep your combo alive building up the highest score possible to point B escaping. It's simple, but it works and is very fun. There are 2 other types of rounds where you will stay in a spot and survive while the clock counts down, being strapped with a bomb that if you left the specific area for over 5 seconds causing the player to blow up, but the goal of gathering points is the same, the shooting is still competent enough for these to be fun, but not as fun as running through levels, these feel like an afterthought 100%. Any other mode only really adds timer to the main mechanic so it doesn't change much.

Running through these levels you will build up combos by killing enemies and shooting skull signs, you want to keep this building as much as you can to gather the most points possible, but you also have to change up the way you play. You will gain less points if you repeatedly kill enemies without ADS, but then you might gain more by ADS, or if you do an action (dodge roll) to get a "Death Roll," etc. While it doesn't need you to change it all the time to actually gain points, it does make you think about changing your playstyle just a bit. Skull signs are here just to simply keep combos going so they don't bleed out. Don't even go for secret skull signs unless there is an achievement for them as these don't continue your combo and don't give you additional points. The game will also present secret paths or secret rooms that may give you a secret skull sign, ammo, or health, but all these do is bleed your combo out so don't even take the risk unless you might need health or ammo, which is a gamble. These "off the beaten path" sections of levels also feel like an after though as why would you divert the player in an "against the clock" TPS, unless it was to punish the players, but even if you lose a combo points are easy to garner so it doesn't feel like a punishment more of an afterthought instead.

As far as the levels themselves go, I don't have to much of an opinion, besides the beaten paths that lead to dead ends in most levels the paths themselves are pretty linear. Albeit once you start going to like the halfway point they really start to feel cluttered which battles against the FOV itself, there isn't any setting for FOV so by cluttering debris all over the place also having screen crunch, it can sometimes take a second to differentiate things in a level. This doesn't make the game impossible by any means, I just want to point it out.

As stated above. $15 is a no go, but for $3-4 I can dig it. If you are uncomfortable going through modding/patching older PC games this is also a no, which not that a person should have to do this regardless, but at a certain price point I ignore it. I recommend it as it's a fun game that is obtained at a cheap price quite regularly, I also opted out of GFWL and used XLiveless instead so it also wasn't a hard time getting up and running. Moral of my core feeling is that while this game is a blast, it also feels full of afterthoughts that make the game feel on a "tech demo" basis, not that it takes away very much, but still.

[h1] The Club: An Arcade Shooter Ahead of Its Time?? [/h1]

[h3]*note*  I was able to get it working flawlessly on Steam Deck (Feb 2026)[/h3]

The Club feels like a game that released at the wrong time for me. Back then, I was more into story-driven games built around progression, so it never really clicked. I put a few hours into it when it first came out but didn’t fully understand or appreciate what it was trying to do. 

Revisiting it now, though, it’s [b]incredibly fun[/b] and somewhat underrated.

There’s no real 'story' here. Think of it purely as a third-person arcade shooter focused on speed, flow, and chasing high scores. It cuts straight to the chase of what makes video games fun. It’s all about quick, pick-up-and-play sessions driven by mechanics, momentum, and mastery.

Replayability comes from refining your runs and pushing for higher scores on each level. It’s also much more enjoyable on PC, where mouse aiming makes the gameplay feel more precise compared to the Xbox360 version.

At $3.99 on sale, it’s absolutely worth a try if you’re looking for something more 'arcadey' that you can jump into over a weekend.

TL;DR:
A Good and fun arcade shooter game, but a bad port because GFWL.

Summary:
Previously played on Xbox 360, THE CLUB is an arcade shooter, emphasis on what the dev called "a racing game with guns". You have at least a total 8 roster in this game, with two being unlocked as your progress the game. Each "Club" characters have their highs and low on their stats, which may feel unique to each play style.

PROS:
It's an arcade shooting, which the goal is to kill as many enemies and achieved a high amount of combo. The more the combo you earn, the more the points you'll achieved. It's simple. The idea was basically, here's a gun, have fun! If you missed out on an enemies or Skull Shot Signs, your combo will bleed, which will drain f@#ked your momentum.

CONS:
On the game sides, the Combo Bleed can dried up so fast, that you will lose momentum. And the Skull Shots can be very distracting once you faced too many enemies. It's not so bad, but it can get overwhelmed when you trying to achieved your best Score.

On the technical sides, the game suffers from GFWL, which broke the Steam Overlay, making you unable to take Screenshot or look up Guides during in-game. Someone even told me to use a cr4ck3d.exe to bypass the GFWL to Steam Overlay, which I have tried! And It didn't work, sadly.

It also has problems with Windows 11, that I tested it on my friends PC. Even using the Steam Community Guides and the Title Update 3 fix from PCGamingWiki doesn't seem to work. Some said it works for them, but I don't know, I guess my friend PCs are just different.

In addition to that, this game is a barebones PC port, straight up from the Xbox 360, which heavily prioritize it's Controller UI. You can play this with K+M and remap your keys, but only Xbox UI is primarily implemented in this game. Tough sh!t for K+M users I supposed, if they don't remember their Keybind.

The game is no longer maintained because the developer Bizarre Creations was acquired by Activision and later closed down by Bobby Kotick, because BLUR and 007 BloodStone underperformed. Which led the IP to be remain with SEGA and no longer maintained.

In-order for SEGA to update/remaster/remake this game, they need to have their in-game developer to do it, or outsourced it to external developers like General Arcade, Virtuos, QLOC or any Studios that are capable of porting the game to perfection.

VERDICT:
If there is a mixed reviews options, it would've been that for THE CLUB. Sure, it's a fun game, but because of GFWL issues, it's just a f@#k!n' mess for those who just wants to play the game Plug-and-play.

If you want to try this game, I highly recommend it, but only when it's on sale.

The Club is a fast-paced third-person shooter developed by Bizarre Creations and published by SEGA that set out to do something radically different from most shooters of its time. Released in 2008, it reimagined the genre as a high-octane, score-driven competition rather than a story-focused campaign. Instead of realism or tactical cover mechanics, the game borrows heavily from arcade design principles, transforming combat into a performance where speed, accuracy, and rhythm matter more than survival. Its world revolves around a deadly underground blood sport known simply as “The Club,” where elite combatants—each with unique backgrounds and motivations—compete in gladiatorial shooting events for the amusement of a secretive audience. There is no moral nuance or grand narrative here, only the raw spectacle of killing for points, presented with the same mechanical precision and intensity that characterized Bizarre Creations’ work on titles like Project Gotham Racing.

At its core, The Club is built around the concept of chaining kills to maintain momentum and build massive scores. Each enemy you take down contributes to your combo multiplier, but hesitate for even a few seconds, and your chain resets. This system forces players to treat combat as a continuous, flowing performance rather than a cautious firefight. Every level becomes a kind of race, demanding players memorize routes, anticipate enemy placements, and plan how to move efficiently from one kill to the next. It’s a design philosophy that feels more akin to a racing game than a traditional shooter—success depends on maintaining tempo, optimizing your “lap,” and achieving the highest possible score through precision and speed. The gunplay itself is tight and responsive, emphasizing quick reflexes and situational awareness. There’s a constant push-and-pull between aggression and control, as missing a shot or taking too long to reload can mean losing your entire combo streak and with it, your place on the leaderboard.

Structurally, the game offers several modes that build on its score-attack foundation. The main Tournament Mode lets you select from eight different characters, each with distinct attributes such as speed, stamina, and accuracy. These characters compete across a series of events set in varied environments—from abandoned prisons and derelict shipyards to crumbling cities and ruined mansions. The levels are compact but cleverly designed to promote fluid movement and multiple paths for experimentation. Outside the main campaign, Single Event and Gun Challenges allow players to refine their skills on specific maps, while the multiplayer component—both online and split-screen—was intended to extend replay value. Unfortunately, while the competitive elements were forward-thinking for their time, the lack of long-term progression and limited map variety ultimately restricted their staying power. Still, at its best, The Club captures the addictive, one-more-run appeal of a pure arcade experience, rewarding mastery over brute force.

Visually, The Club reflects the gritty sensibilities of its era. The environments are bleak and industrial, drenched in shades of gray and brown that fit the dystopian tone of the underground blood sport. While the graphics were technically competent for 2008, the character models and textures now show their age. The design of the arenas, however, is effective: they’re built like obstacle courses, with clear sightlines and looping layouts that encourage aggressive movement. The audio design complements the game’s frantic pace, with crisp gunfire, visceral impact sounds, and crowd-like ambient noise adding to the tension. The music, though somewhat understated, reinforces the rhythm of combat, building tempo as your kill chain grows. There’s an undeniable sense of intensity in the presentation, and when everything clicks—when you’re sprinting through corridors, blasting enemies in perfect sequence, and watching your combo counter soar—it delivers a rush that few shooters can replicate.

Where The Club falters is in its lack of depth beyond the scoring system. The concept is brilliant, but it leaves little room for variation once the initial thrill wears off. Enemy types repeat frequently, and the structure of most missions—race through, kill everyone, reach the exit—doesn’t evolve much over time. The narrative setup, while serviceable, barely exists beyond the initial premise; the competitors are introduced with stylish character bios, but their personalities and motives are never meaningfully explored. This minimalist approach works for players who only care about refining their technique, but those looking for story-driven progression or cinematic storytelling will likely find it unsatisfying. The repetition can also wear thin after extended play sessions, as the emphasis on scoring and speed leaves little incentive for exploration or experimentation outside of chasing higher leaderboard rankings.

Despite its flaws, The Club remains a fascinating and underappreciated experiment in game design. It dared to strip away the cinematic excess that dominated shooters of the late 2000s and instead focus entirely on mechanical mastery. It demands that players unlearn the habits of modern shooters—hiding behind cover, moving cautiously, conserving ammo—and embrace a mindset closer to classic arcade games like Time Crisis or even Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater. It’s all about performance, about finding the rhythm between movement and precision, and about turning something as violent as gunplay into a score-based dance. In that sense, The Club succeeds completely. Its pure, distilled gameplay loop makes it endlessly replayable for those who connect with its design philosophy.

In the end, The Club is both a product of its time and ahead of it. It’s raw, fast, and unapologetically arcade-like, standing apart from the cinematic realism of its contemporaries. Its stripped-down design won’t appeal to everyone—especially those who expect narrative depth or multiplayer longevity—but for players who value gameplay mastery, tight mechanics, and the adrenaline rush of perfect runs, it remains a unique gem in SEGA’s catalogue. Bizarre Creations took a risk creating a shooter that prioritized skill and style over spectacle, and while it never achieved mainstream success, its influence can still be felt in later score-driven games that celebrate precision and replayability. The Club may have faded into obscurity, but its relentless pace, clever design, and unapologetic devotion to arcade principles ensure that it remains one of the most intriguing curiosities in the history of third-person shooters.

En el año 2010 escribí lo siguiente en aquel blog de videojuegos que usted ya sabe: "The Club es, posiblemente, el juego más infravalorado de esta generación. [h1]Empire: Total War – 111/10. God Save the King. Unless I'm Playing as a Republic.[/h1]
Some games you remember for their gameplay. Others for the memories they gave you. Empire: Total War gave me both.

My godfather introduced me to this masterpiece. He was a proper Prussian commander: disciplined formations, calculated tactics, and an almost religious devotion to military order.
I preferred the Russian approach.
[b]NÁS MNOGO! URAAA! FOR THE TSAR![/b]
Naturally, he kicked my ass.

At first...

A month later, our battles became evenly matched. Eventually, I discovered the wonderful art of ambushes, flanking maneuvers, and French military ingenuity. Suddenly, his Prussian formations were being attacked by units appearing from forests, hills, and apparently my magician's hat.

He never quite understood where the hell I kept finding more soldiers.

Those memories alone make this game priceless to me.

[h2]An Empire Worth Building[/h2]
What I absolutely loved was the sheer scale and freedom.
I played practically every faction I could, experimenting with different strategies and rewriting history.

As France, I defended the Bourbon monarchy while trying to conquer every American colony and crush British colonial ambitions.
As Russia, I secured my European borders before turning my attention toward India.
As Great Britain, I decided the monarchy had enjoyed itself long enough, started a revolution, established a republic, and proceeded to spread democracy across the world.
[b]Congratulations! You are being liberated. Please do not resist.[/b]

The ability to reshape nations, change governments, research technologies, expand overseas, and build your own alternative history made every campaign feel different.

[h2]Gunpowder, Cavalry, and Glorious Naval Warfare[/h2]
The battles were spectacular.

I loved watching infantry formations exchange volleys, cavalry charge into enemy lines, and soldiers engage in beautifully animated close combat.

My preferred strategy was simple: research military technologies as quickly as possible, develop powerful infantry and cavalry, and let them do the talking.

Artillery? Occasionally.
A well-timed cavalry charge? Absolutely.

And the naval battles? Easily among my favorite features.
Massive ships of the line exchanging broadsides, maneuvering for position, and tearing each other apart with cannon fire. Capturing enemy vessels was especially satisfying. Why sink a perfectly good warship when you can add it to your own fleet?

The Spanish Santísima Trinidad was an absolute monster.
Even the battle AI could surprise me. Some engagements forced me to improvise, rethink my plans, and fight for every victory.

And then there were the Native American factions.
I arrived with money, soldiers, and diplomatic proposals.
They refused my gold and gave my army a considerably less diplomatic response.

Fair enough...

[h2]Diplomacy: Apparently Written by a Drunk Ambassador[/h2]
As much as I adore Empire, its diplomacy is easily one of its weakest features.

Negotiating reasonable agreements could be ridiculously frustrating. Enemy nations demanded absurd concessions, refused perfectly sensible offers, and behaved as though military reality simply didn't exist.

Until they had one province left.
Suddenly, everyone became remarkably cooperative.
[b]Amazing what losing an entire country does for your negotiating skills.[/b]

The pirates could also be incredibly annoying, and the limited variety of general and politician portraits became noticeable after countless campaigns.

These flaws deserve criticism, even if they never ruined my enjoyment.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Empire: Total War is one of those rare games that lets you create your own historical adventures on an enormous scale.

I preserved the Bourbons, expanded the Russian Empire toward India, overthrew the British Crown, and spread democracy at gunpoint.

I fought spectacular naval battles, improvised my way through unexpected defeats, and spent countless hours experimenting with different factions.

But above all, I'll remember those battles against my godfather.

He taught me how to play. Eventually, I taught him to check the forests before advancing.

[b]111/10 – The diplomacy was terrible, the pirates were annoying, and half my generals looked like the same man wearing a different hat.

I tried to buy peace with the Native Americans. They refused my gold and introduced me to a completely different kind of diplomacy.

God save the King. Unless I'm playing as a republic.[/b]

Total War, który był pierwszym takim spadkiem jakości w historii CA. Słabe AI, kiepskie bitwy.

Please disregard my current playtime, I have around 200 hours offline on this account and my first ever steam account (ironically this was my very first "steam game") has over 7,300 hours. It wouldn't be far fetched to say that this is, or is one of my favorite entries in the TW series. Yes, it is a relic of it's time, it's buggy, the UI can be ugly at times, the AI is some of the worst I've ever seen from the campaign map to battles, unit pathing is horrendous when running down routing units, or trying to charge units, or simply reforming in the chaos one two armies start clashing. It can be frustrating and at times you ask yourself why do you play this game. 

But you play it because it's a moment in time from a company that was truly swinging for the fences, you play it for it's scale, you play it to watch grand battles play out before you as an orchestra is providing this sweeping and uplifting motif, you play it for the graphics that have held up remarkably well over the years, you play it for it's actually in depth campaign mechanics and economic systems (for a TW game), you play it to fight through the age of enlightenment when mankind is beginning to throw off the shackles of Kings and Emperors. Yes, It's lacking a lot of the QoL that later games will receive, I'd say that Napoleon (the very next release after this) blows this out of the water in a vanilla gameplay experience. But I will die on the hill that Empire Total War is unmatched in it's scale and scope of the game, yes the WH games have a larger map due to merging, yes Shogun 2 is the tightest gameplay out of the series, yes Rome 2/1 & Medieval 2 are triumphs in their own right. But I don't think anything in the series can touch the scale that this game was going for. It maintains the grandiose empire building the era deserves, while avoiding the excessive bloat that WH has added. 

This is a review fueled by nostalgia and a yearning for times gone by, I can not emphasize enough that if you go in expecting a fully polished game you will be disappointed, if you're just wanting to install the game and nothing else, pick Shogun, Rome 2, or potentially Kingdoms, I'll include Napoleon as well (I have an immense amount of time in the WH trilogy as well, but I am leaving them out of this review as I feel the successes of those games have largely poisoned the direction that CA is headed as a company and can not in good faith recommend a game that will continue to kill the company that I grew up loving). 

If you are willing to embrace the jank, and eventually mods for the game, I can't recommend Empire enough. It has one of the most robust modding scenes in the series outside of potentially Medieval 2, the overhauls are excellent and crafted with care, and all target the common pain points that the vanilla experience will provide. If you're still unsure about it, wait for a sale, CA often holds franchise sales and the game becomes extremely cheap during those times

Overall, this is a genuinely enjoyable game. It has its flaws, and it definitely shows its age, but I had a great time playing through it. I'd recommend giving it a shot, especially if you're a fan of the franchises and it's on sale.

Recommended. Even with acid splash punishing clean kills, three bodies replay one conflict through tracker blips, heat vision and ceiling lunges over ruined pyramids.

Three bodies hold the same corridors through pulse fire, combat rifles, sentry lines and hacked bypasses behind flashlights. Motion trackers turn distant blips into early torchlight routing decisions long before contact. Cloak discipline rewards patient stalks with mines, smart discs, thrown sticks and trophy belts under alternate visions. Wall-ceiling traversal earns its keep when vent routes open into high-speed harvest lunges past faltering flamethrowers.

At shotgun distance, acid splash punishes clean kills and forces retreats. Capped reserves empty fast against erratic vectors, leaving point-blank bursts as the only answer inside the splash while unlimited pistols remove reasons to switch past escort holds. The torch cone costs steady hands for routing that acid splash punishes across three short campaigns.

I bought AVP 2000 and AVP 2010 together because I've always liked the movies but avp 2000 didn't click with me and I had low expectations going into avp 2010, however after spending 10 hours across 3 campaigns I'd say its more than worth it.

You get to play as a Marine, Xenomorph and Donald Trum- I mean Predator, All the 3 campaigns have something unique to offer as a Marine you are honestly free to choose what kind of playstyle suits you but as a Xenomorph I found a combination between aggressive and stealthy approach better and as for the Predator it leans heavily towards stealth with occasional moments where you can be aggressive.

The story is surprisingly not that bad either and all 3 campaigns take place in the same universe and are linked together just like how Half-Life 1 and it's expansions Opposing Force, Blue Shift and Decay take place at the same time in the same universe. Most of the time you'll revisit locations but it will change depending on who you're playing as so basically to really understand what's going on you need to play all 3 campaigns and its worth every second.

Then comes the weapons all good except the pulse rifle is annoying to use and needs a buff but other than that everything the marine uses is well balanced and you can carry 2 weapons of your choice at a time the ammo isn't scarce but not that abundant either the game deals with this by giving you the opportunity to switch weapons often though.

Then there is the xenomorph it isn't really loaded in the weapons department but it makes up for it by its other abilities like scaling walls and drawing enemies away to ambush them the options open up a lot of opportunities for you to play any way you want. Personally I like to distract the marines and use hit and run tactics when they are in groups or other times I would hide in the dark and latch on to an unsuspecting marine and pick them off one by one. I even go on the offensive if there's room to strike I think you get my point.

Now the predator.. He is one of the most fun characters to play with  he can use a cloaking shield to blend in with the environment, jump several feet away, has 2 energy powered weapons and 2 throwables which include a sawblade and something that resembles a spear and let me tell you these things do a lot of damage, the sawblade itself if it hits any limb chops it off immediately in most cases and the spear is OHKO for most enemies and then there is the mask itself you can use different vision modes to highlight and track enemies this really helps pick them apart in dense jungles and dark spaces.


Now as for the graphics I personally like the early 2010s feel of it, the character design, environment, weapons I don't have anything negative to say about them. Even the main menu UI itself evokes a feeling of nostalgia for me and that ambient sound itself embodies that "dark and gritty" vibe.

Anyway that's all I could gather because i just finished the game and wrote this review right away I apologise if I missed something but yeah AVP 2010 is one of the greatest fps games ever made. Certainly in top 50 if not 25.

[h1]TrackMania Nations Forever — Just One More Run[/h1]

[b]You know that feeling when you say "just one more try" and suddenly an hour has disappeared? Welcome to TrackMania.[/b]

This game is pure arcade racing fun. No complicated career, no endless progression grind, no pretending to be a professional racing driver. Just you, a ridiculous track, and the desperate hope that THIS time you won't fly off the road like a rocket with commitment issues.

The tracks are creative, the driving is fast, and chasing that perfect run is ridiculously addictive. You'll crash, restart, improve your time, and immediately convince yourself you can shave off another few milliseconds.

[b]And then you do it all over again. Because of course you do.[/b]

It's simple, it's fun, and it absolutely nails what an arcade racer should be: something you can jump into, enjoy immediately, and lose yourself in for hours and it's totally free.

[b]THE VERDICT[/b]

I had a blast. If you want straightforward, addictive arcade racing without unnecessary nonsense, TrackMania Nations Forever is an absolute classic.

[b]Just one more run. I promise.[/b]

Abysmal direction and broken progression systems that turn a battle of wits into an infuriating guessing game.

If you are thinking of picking up Sherlock Holmes: Nemesis, it is a massive step backward for Frogwares that trades genuine detective work for contrived design choices. While chasing a flamboyant gentleman thief across massive historical London locations sounds like a brilliant premise, the actual game execution is an unoptimized chore that actively disrespects the player's time.

Here is what you need to know before diving in:

• Horrific Navigation and Map: The navigation system and map layout are aggressively broken. The game will routinely demand that you locate a specific shop or historical destination on a precise street, only for you to completely overshoot it because street names are entirely absent from both the map interface and the physical in-game environments. You will spend hours mindlessly circling back and retracing your steps through poorly optimized corridors just trying to figure out where the game wants you to go.

• Artificial, Mindless Backtracking: Progression relies entirely on exhausting colossal environments like the British Museum or the National Gallery by running back and forth to trigger arbitrary flags. Instead of using Sherlock’s intellect to piece together a case, you are subjected to agonizingly slow errands—like hunting down four literal birds in a massive courtyard or spending 20 minutes finding a single book on a sea of unmarked bookshelves just to fetch a tiny snippet of context.

• Pedantic, Strict Riddle Parsing: The text-input mechanics and word-association puzzles are brutally unpolished. When you are finally asked to answer questions and present your findings to Watson, the game's text parser demands hyper-specific, exact wording. If you do not type the exact, singular word the developers intended—even if your deductive logic is 100% sound and factual—the entire game stalls your momentum completely.

• Absurd, Contrived Tasks: The actual narrative substance quickly devolves from high-stakes mental warfare into a total farce. Rather than executing brilliant forensic analysis, the game forces the world's greatest detective to complete utterly ludicrous, immersion-breaking chores. You will find your patience pushed to its absolute limit as you spend your time preparing a specific meal for a dog or tracking down a collection of missing dolls inside Buckingham Palace.

Final Verdict: A structurally flawed puzzle hunt that replaces brilliant investigation with artificial friction. If you don't want to deal with unmapped streets, pedantic text boxes, and running in circles for hours, save yourself the headache and skip this entry entirely.

Ansiklopedi bir oyun olsaydı... 

Sherlock holmes oyunları ile tanışmam Epic Games'in Crimes and Punishments'ı bedava vermesi ile olmuştu.  Kitap okuduğum zamanlarda bayılarak okuyordum bu seriyi. Dizisini falan da çok sevmiştim. Bu sebeple, sherlock holmes oyunlarını da seveceğimi düşünmüştüm. Ancak, biraz baktığımda Crimes and Punishments'tan önce hiç de azımsanmayacak sayıda (çoğu da eski yapımlar olan) Sherlock oyunları olduğunu gördüm.  Bu yüzden önce eskileri oynayıp, sonrasında modern olanlara geçmenin doğru olacağını düşündüm. The Secret of the Silver  Earring'i bugün oynanır seviyede bulmadığım için bir sonraki çıkış yapan oyun olan Sherlock Holmes: Nemesis'i denmeye karar verdim. Oyunun hikayesini ve dedektiflik tasarımını çok beğenmesem de beni sonuna kadar ekran başında tutmayı ve sonraki sherlock oyunları için hevesli bir şekilde bırakmayı başardı.  

Oyunda hoşuma giden ilk özellik, first person kamera modunun gelmesi oldu. Yapımcılar tek bir tuş ile eski yukardan bakmalı ile bu kamera modu arasında geçiş yapmamızı sağlamışlar.  First person modu, fps oyunlarındaki kadar kusursuz hissettirmese de gayet yeterli bir seviyede olmuş. Point and clicklere özgü kamera açısındansa bu benim hayli hayli tercih ettiğim bir değişim olmuş. İkinci sevdiğim unsur ise, Sherlock ve Watson betimlemeleri oldu. Kitapları okumam üzerinden uzun zaman geçtiği için tam hatırlayamıyorum ama aklımda kaldığı kdarıyla başarılı yansıtıldıklarını düşünüyorum. Diğer bir sevdiğim özelliği içerisinde bolca ansiklopedik bilgi bulundurması oldu. Eminim ki tarihe ve sanata düşkün olanlar için muazzam eğlecenli olmuştur bu kısımlar.  

Bütün bu olumlu özelliklere ek olarak güzel bir atmosfer yakalamayı da başarmışlar. İnsanı o zamanlara götüren bir hava, bugün bile sırıtmayan bir grafikle birleşince ortaya güzel bir eser çıkmış. Ancak tüm bu pozitif özelliklerin yanı sıra bazı kısımlar da can sıkmıyor değil. İlk olarak hikaye ve akışı beni çok sarmadı açıkcası, Arsene lupine'in mottosu daha iyi anlatılabilirdi bence.  Bir diğer eksi yön ise, bazı bulmacaların tam bir amele işi olması.  İnsanın zekasını ölçmekten ziyade oyun süresini uzatmak için yapıldıkları belli oluyor.  Özellikle British Museum kısmı gerçekten çok baydı beni. Oyunun diğer kısımlarındaki bulmacalar da böyle olunca haliyle kendinizi dedektif gibi hissedemiyorsunuz.   

Özetlemek gerekirse, bol bol "ötekileştirilen" French ve değerli İngiliz milliyetçiliği yapılan bu oyundaki eksiler Sherlock'un disguise'i gibi kalıyor. Evet, kötü duruyor ama sahip olduğu tüm iyi yönler göz önüne alınırsa bu kadar da olur diyorsunuz.

Sherlock Holmes: Nemesis — 9/10

Вот эта игра меня реально приятно удивила. В первую очередь графикой — я вообще не ожидал, что она мне настолько зайдёт. Да, сейчас она уже далеко не новая, но у неё есть какой-то свой охуенный визуальный стиль, который создаёт очень приятный вайб.

Особенно нравится сама атмосфера расследования: ходишь, осматриваешь места, ищешь всякие улики и постепенно пытаешься понять, что вообще происходит. Есть ощущение, будто реально оказался внутри какого-то старого детектива.

И вот именно из-за атмосферы мне хотелось продолжать играть. Даже когда не сразу понимаешь, что делать, всё равно интересно исследовать мир. Иногда правда сидишь и думаешь: «Блять, ну и как я должен был до этого додуматься?» 😂

Для меня Nemesis — это тот случай, когда игра не обязательно должна быть современной, чтобы выглядеть и ощущаться круто. Свой стиль у неё есть, и он мне очень понравился.

Dieses Zettelsuchen in der Bibliothek von diesen Museum ist besonders schlimm, da man das ca. zehnmal oder so macht. Das sind teilweise einfach keine guten Rätsel.
 
Wer errechnet das bitte wirklich ohne in die Lösung zu schauen? Für dieses Spiel braucht man auch etwas Allgemeinwissen. Ja natürlich. Zumindest ist mein Allgemeinwissen so hoch, das ich weiß, dass man einen Hund auf gar keinen Fall Schokolade geben sollte. 36*41? Kein Problem, das rechne ich täglich im Kopf. Errechnen und packen sie 16 Sardellen auf den Teller. Na sicher, warum nicht gleich 20 auf so nen Teller ist doch platz. Wollt ihr mich eigentlich komplett verarschen? Löse 5 Aufgaben und dann ist der letzte Zettel am Fuß der Statue, wo ich schon zehnmal vorbei gegangen bin. Vorher konnte ich diesen Zettel natürlich nicht finden.

老式推理爱好者的情怀盛宴，但入坑前请务必做好功课
作为同时吃福华和罗平设定的双厨，冲着两大侦探同台对决的设定入的手，Frogwares工作室对维多利亚时代伦敦的还原确实没得说，国家美术馆、伦敦塔这些标志性场景的细节直接把代入感拉满，探案的时候踩着石板路路过雾蒙蒙的泰晤士河，真的有种跟着福尔摩斯一起跑现场的感觉。解谜部分也对得起老牌推理游戏厂商的功底，足迹分析、物证拼合、密码破译的逻辑都很顺，最后白金汉宫的对决桥段，两位高智商角色的张力直接拉满，情怀党狂喜。
但必须说几个非常劝退的点，想要入手的朋友一定要提前掂量：
第一个最头疼的是到现在都没有官方中文补丁，整个游戏文本量巨大，大量维多利亚时期的英式书面表达、特定历史名词，甚至还有不少艺术类专业术语，我四六级飘过的水平，玩的时候基本三句就要切出去查词，解谜卡壳一半是因为没看懂线索描述，体验碎得一塌糊涂。
第二个是门槛真的不低，游戏里不少案件线索和维多利亚时期的历史背景深度绑定，还有很多涉及大英美术馆藏品、博物馆馆藏的相关知识，要是对那段历史和艺术藏品没点了解，有时候对着物证看十分钟都反应不过来关联点在哪，我中间卡关去翻攻略，才知道某个线索对应的是当时真实的社会事件，这种设计对不了解背景的玩家非常不友好。
如果你是硬核推理爱好者，愿意为了玩这个游戏提前补背景知识、对着词典啃文本，那它的内容质量绝对对得起你的付出；如果只是想轻松体验个探案故事，那这个上手难度大概率会让你玩得非常累。

There are two things to appreciate:
1. this game really tries a different approach compared to other ones from the series, mostly utilising a gameplay around riddles rather than "deduction" or just go-and-fetch tasks
2. all subsequent Frogware's games are better, meaning they constantly evolve

There are some examples of a ridiculousness of this one:
1. you need to attract a certain bird and you already know how, but you cannot collect needed objects until you find a quite obscure interactive point which gives you zero new information
2. you need to look at 4 paintings in a gallery and you know exactly which ones are they, but you cannot progress until you speak with a character who actually tells you nothing of importance 
3. there is a hammer you cannot take until you are tasked to find a specific key. hammer, key, really clear connection, right?

so the game tries to be clever but at the same time often looks so stupid that it is nauseating.

and I like the fact that the next game about Jack the Ripper borrows characters' models from this one in abundance, just replacing textures. yeah, that were the times when Frogware was really cheap.

Ich würde dieses Spiel weder besonders gut noch besonders schlecht nennen.

Ein bisschen Allgemeinwissen ist bei den Rätseln teilweise übrigens auch gefragt.

I love Frogwares Sherlock Games and you can definitely see that they've gotten better with age, the Ukrainians are on to something, but you need to reign in your expectations if you're coming from Crime & Punishment, Devil's Daughter, Chapter One etc.

This really is the bare-bones building blocks for what they would go on to develop in the future.  If you can forgive that you're going to have a good time, but if not please stay away you won't have fun.

There are so many reasons i don't recommend playing this game that i don't know where to start. So my overarching recommendation to you would be to take your 2 hour evaluation period seriously (for a potential refund) 

List of issues:
- Performance problems on larger maps (steady stuttering on the museum level for example)

- Maps are way too large (Find feather on ground in a football pitch)

- Lack of cohesion between puzzles (This picture has a animal in it so now go across the map and click the small corresponding animal statue)

- Punishes exploration (If you search around, even in your attempt to progress, you will frequently find that items you've already looked at you can now pick up and need to go back for)

Pros:
- Good humour dotted out, as if the developer said "This is drier than sand paper, have a boost"
- Controls are fine
- Level design is genuinely beautiful

Overall: The games biggest selling point has little to do with what it is marketed to be, if you like sherlock holmes, start with testament. That has its own problems, but is much more playable than this

It also does depend on the player. If you are willing to make this game a mini project, have a real life detective board and notepad, you will probably have a blast. As for me, gaming stays in the game.

Un jeu qui a du charme avec des énigmes de difficultés variées, on passe de puzzles très simples et à des intrigues tirées par les cheveux. Comme d'autres évaluations l'ont souligné, ce jeu laisse peu de place à l'initiative personnelle, il est par exemple obligatoire de passer par une série d'interactions afin que le personnage résolve une énigme alors que le joueur a déjà deviné la solution. [spoiler]Je pense notamment à l'énigme devant amener au British Museum où Sherlock Holmes doit obligatoirement demander au directeur de la galerie à quoi fait référence la ville de Sainte Catherine, même s'il a vu auparavant quatre portraits de Sainte Catherine d'Alexandrie dans la salle des œuvres italiennes.[/spoiler] On notera également une certaine redondance dans les énigmes, passant d'un poème à un autre, d'un livre à un autre, etc. Le gameplay ne se renouvelle pas beaucoup et on peut vite se lasser.

Le problème à mes yeux réside principalement dans l'intrigue de manière générale. Au départ, même si elle est un peu fantaisiste, elle tient relativement debout, mais cela va très rapidement changer. Le jeu n'ayant plus en tête que la mise en place d'énigmes dans tous les sens, peu de cas est fait de la vraisemblance : [spoiler]que Lupin ait eu le temps de mettre sans dessous la galerie d'art en une nuit, passe encore, mais qu'il ait eu le temps de laisser une tonne de messages codés dans le British Museum, au nez et à la barbe de la police qui surveille les lieux, allant jusqu'à graver une lettre sur une stèle égyptienne dans la salle même où quatre officiers surveillent la pierre de Rosette, le tout en trouvant le temps d'éplucher l'immense bibliothèque du musée sous les yeux de son conservateur, et sans se faire repérer par qui que ce soit, ça devient ridicule. Sans parler de la serrure dans les sous-sols de Buckingham qui ne s'ouvre que lorsque que vous faîtes correspondre deux expressions mathématiques en chiffres romains... dans quel monde une serrure pareille pourrait-elle être utile ?[/spoiler] Pour moi, le segment le plus éprouvant reste celui de [spoiler]Buckingham Palace[/spoiler] où vous devez effectuer toute une série de tâches secondaires et inintéressantes, afin d'obtenir qu'un personnage ultra caricatural, passant son temps à faire des allusions graveleuses et sexuelles sans intérêt, vous ouvre sa porte et vous lance sur une nouvelle série de tâches secondaires et inintéressantes afin que vous puissiez accéder au véritable objectif de Lupin, en l'occurrence [spoiler] la reine Victoria, qui voit surgir Lupin dans sa chambre avant de lui accorder un baiser parce que... scénario ? Et de le laisser s'enfuir par un passage secret parce que... scénario ?[/spoiler].

Certaines résolutions d'énigmes sont tellement alambiquées, certains objets très difficiles à trouver car n'apparaissant pas ou ne pouvant être sélectionnés qu'après une série d'interactions précise, je me suis retrouvée à consulter la soluce plus d'une fois. En fait, tous les éléments précédents m'ayant fait perdre goût au jeu au fur et à mesure de la partie, j'ai même terminé le jeu en la suivant à la lettre, juste pour le terminer. A decent game considering that it is from 2008. Graphics and environments are good, although the environments are extremely large for a find-the-object game. One interesting part of the game is that you are not in the sketchy streets of Whitechapel solving murders, but instead visiting the top sights of London, some of which are reproduced with amazing detail. 

This game is less focused on finding clues to figure out who committed a crime--because we know from the start who is the villain--and more focused on finding keys and other objects. There are multiple layers of "go fetch" such as when you need Object A from someone to do something, but first you have to help his brother find his lost cat, but to find the cat, you need to find some meat, and to get some meat, you have to do a favor for the butcher, etc...

One frustrating part of the game is that items or clues are not available in a location until you hit a progress point. A box that was not clickable when you first walked into a room is suddenly clickable after you speak to someone or otherwise hit a progress point in the game. It makes for a lot of backtracking.  

The puzzles are the weakest part of the game. Some puzzles literally require outside knowledge (such as English literature) and others require some pretty sophisticated math.  Other puzzles are just baffling in that you have no idea what you are supposed to do and there is no logic to them. The worst are the quizzes where you have to type in an answer to an obscure question, and the game is unforgiving.  

Another issue--solved in later games--is that you spend a lot of time figuring out "what the hell do I do next?".  There is no "objective" list telling you what you need to do, so you have to decipher it from dialogue, documents, etc. Sometimes you need to talk to someone that you've already talked to, or you need to select and object to make it active before speaking. Other times, you have to put your magnifying glass over a hidden footprint or other clue. 

Overall it was still a fun game to play and it has elements of greatness that we see in the more recent games.

(first of all, i am not someone familiar with puzzle games, nor i am familiar with frogwares' sherlock holmes games, but i AM familiar with arsène lupin in the "i pretty much grew up reading books about this guy and still read them to this day" way, so i think this review shouldn't be taken 100% seriously)

while playing this game, i finally understood how herlock sholmes felt in the entirety of "arsène lupin vs herlock sholmes", since arsène lupin here made me real fucking angry.

this game is old, so expect it to look old and run like an old game, in my experience, some of the door and items holmes could pick up would have some weird texture errors, like a door being fully black or it shining brightly like a diamond, but aside from that, the game ran quite smoothly! it didn't crash on me once, and i was happy since the game doesn't have an autosave feature... yes, there's no autosave, remember to save frequently.

two things that annoyed me were the fact that the game assumes you have knowledge on british landmarks and literature, in my case, i had little to no knowledge of the british! and that made me confused on where to go sometimes. the other thing was the cursor, it made me so mad that if i wanted to click on something (like a hint), i had to aim it a little below of where i wanted to click, which made some of the puzzles frustrating.

character-wise, i don't think it is accurate for lupin to spend half of his time (probably) giggling and writing riddles for holmes, neither it is accurate for holmes to waste his time running around and solving lupin's riddles. i did find it fun to receive lupin's riddles at first, but... after some time of doing the same thing over and over again it got boring.

lupin is also absent for the most game, just like in "arsène lupin vs herlock sholmes", and i must say, that made me really happy! buuuut i do understand how that can be disappointing for some, because his face is literally in the cover art, and we only see him for 3 or 4 cutscenes.

watson in this game is stupid, he makes stupid actions and says stupid things, i wonder if maurice leblanc was in charge of some of his dialogues? anyway, watson's portrayal here was strange, but this is a sherlock holmes game at the end of the day, not a watson one.

the ending was... dissapointing, to say without spoilers, it felt like frogwares didn't really know what to do for the ending, so they came up with a quick solution with a dialogue that felt really strange to read (especially in lupin's side).

overall, it feels a bit like a chore to play this, even if you're a fan of both holmes and lupin, but i don't think it's THAT bad of a game, just mediocre, play it if you have nothing to do, but don't expect a masterpiece.

Have played many hidden object games, detective games, CYOA text adventures and so on and I very much appreciate games allowing for some degree of inference or using visually / contextually obvious clues. This title wants you clicking on all possible triggers: for example measuting footprints in museum by rapidly flailing roulette across them frantically clicking on every activation point imaginable (measuring actual texture wasn't working).

Despite still feeling like the game I'm giving my honest attempt at playing, is not too far from barely working licensed product, stifled by technology of its time and quite possibly other constraints, there is something earning it a positive review. Specifically it is the following:
- first-person controls that have all necessary actions so you don't need frankly abhorrent third-person camera anymore;
- much better graphics, animation and dialogue;
- art gallery has fairly good representations of period-accurate real artworks with what I can assume are mostly correct informational snippets.

Art gallery alone gains this title a recommendation, even if gameplay itself is far from ideal.

A cryptic letter from notorious burglar Arsene Lupin challenges Sherlock Holmes to stop Lupin from stealing five items important to England, thus engaging Holmes in a bout of mental sparring against France's most eccentric gentleman-genius. National pride and Holmes' ego are at stake. This is the fourth title in the Frogwares franchise of Sherlock Holmes games; and stylistically it is the sequel to "Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened (2008)."

The story is implausible but also humorous, charming, and usually fun. The pacing falters however as Sherlock is forced to continuously revisit rooms within environments to find new clues or compile objects. This game often feels like a 'wild goose chase'--a premise the developers seemingly  acknowledge at the end with a sly wink when Arsene Lupin's true motive is revealed.

Frogwares's love for mathematics-based puzzles with complex (and often obscure) solutions becomes a frustrating slog: find the proper weight ratio for a combination of berries, seeds, and fish; correct an equation written in Roman numerals to make it true; count the revolutions of planets in a mechanical model and apply the numbers to a formula hinted in a verse; etc. Word puzzles are at times equally frustrating to decipher; a particular 'anagram' became confusing by having more letters than the solution. Fortunately, there is a system of sequential hints that will reveal solutions to players. There were a few puzzles however I still couldn't understand the logic even after I had fully revealed the answer.

Some progress relies on an assumed 'common knowledge' that the player may not have--a familiarity of London's landmarks, for example; or recognizing from clues a famous example of English literature. There is one quiz that Holmes must answer to progress further, and the solution is the name of a Sir Arthur Conan Doyle character that fans will know well--but is only referenced in passing in the game by an item found within a different level. Once again the hint system will bail the player out; but this specific challenge seems unfair if not unnecessary.

With certain puzzles excluded, the game is overall casual and fairly easy to navigate and solve with moderate trial-and-error exploration. There are some graphical glitches, however. Occasionally some object textures don't load or doors won't animate after they've been unlocked. The final chapter seems the most flawed, as animated and moveable objects randomly respawn in anachronistic placements. This impacted my ability to complete the last sequence of actions before Holmes confronts Lupin.

The game is long (I logged 22 hours to reach its conclusion) but I enjoyed the journey. Holmes is more likeable than in "The Awakened," his temperament here less condescending and snide. In "Nemesis" Holmes is focused and deliberate--similar to his portrayal in "The Case of the Silver Earring." Dr. Watson remains Holmes' steadfastly loyal friend and unwitting comic foil, fumbling through the case with good intentions but poor choices, but here he also has some agency. With "Nemesis" we see a dynamic between the two characters that is entertaining yet collegial.

Well... would there be a review option available between good and bad, I would have picked that one out. Such an option doesn't exist though and this game's way too well made for giving it a negative one. Therefore I will offer to you all now the pros and contras: 
* Great detective work, challenging puzzles and interesting environments.
* Loved the hand-painted looking backgrounds in the loading screens.
* There were a creepy scene in the story, which was really giving good horror-vibes!
* It's different from the original Dracula-story, therefore not just a 100% copy of Bram Stocker.
- Some puzzles were too hard and/or didn't feel right. I asked in the discussion forum how to solve the hieroglyphic one for example, but didn't get a response. So get used to keep a walkthrough next to you for solving this game.
- Dracula's looks seemed to have been more focused on horny, teenage Twilight fans, instead of real horror-lovers. Not even his eyes glowed unnatural red once. 
- The ending was really short and disappointing. Can't go in detail though without spoiling you all. Let's just say that it made zero sense, how the count could have survived this whole procedure (vampire or not, doesn't matter).

So... yeah honestly I can only recommend it to fans of vampires and detectives. And maybe while it's on discount.

[h2]Po stopách Draculy napříč gotickou Evropou[/h2]

Dracula: Origin je old-school 2D point-and-click adventura, ve které se vydáváte napříč Evropou, abyste v roli Van Helsinga zastavili hraběte Draculu v jeho plánu přivést zpět svou dávnou lásku – i za cenu zkázy celého světa.

Hra slouží jako prequel k Dracula: Love Kills a i když jsem se zpočátku obával, že půjde o Hidden Object hru jako u pokračoivání, naštěstí tomu tak není. Dostáváme zde plnohodnotnou adventuru s výrazným příběhem a klasickým pojetím žánru.

Temná atmosféra by se díky svému gritty vizuálnímu stylu dala krájet a fanoušci adventur typu Nibiru nebo Posel smrti si tu přijdou na své. Hra velmi dobře pracuje s pocitem neustálého ohrožení a gotickým nádechem prostředí.

Puzzly jsou navržené rozumně – vyžadují přemýšlení, ale nejde o nic vyloženě frustrujícího. Většinu času máte pocit, že řešení dává smysl v kontextu světa i příběhu.

Co ale hře nelze úplně odpustit, je její technický stav. První spuštění na systémech Windows 10/11 je celkem problematické a český překlad je místy tragický– u jednoho puzzlu jsou dokonce prohozené názvy položek, takže bez přepnutí do angličtiny nebo nahlédnutí do návodu se dál nedostanete. Samotný závěr hry mi pak přišel spíš slabší, ale to už si každý musí zhodnotit sám.

I přes tyto nedostatky má Dracula: Origin skvělý příběh, zábavnou hratelnost a silnou atmosféru odpovídající gotickému období, ve kterém se odehrává. Doporučit ji mohu všem milovníkům klasických point-and-click adventur.

Dracula: Origin, developed and published by Frogwares, is a richly atmospheric point-and-click adventure that reimagines Bram Stoker’s gothic tale through the perspective of the infamous vampire hunter, Professor Abraham Van Helsing. Set across a series of haunting locales—from the mist-covered streets of London to the crypts of Vienna and the cursed depths of Transylvania—the game weaves a story that feels both familiar and refreshing, bridging literary tradition with the studio’s trademark investigative approach. Known primarily for their Sherlock Holmes series, Frogwares brings a similar sense of methodical puzzle-solving and meticulous world-building to this dark supernatural narrative. The result is a game steeped in mystery, religion, and dread, where every puzzle and clue draws you deeper into the eternal conflict between faith and damnation.

The story unfolds as Van Helsing uncovers Dracula’s plan to reclaim his lost soul through forbidden rituals and ancient texts, a twisted quest that threatens to enslave innocent lives in the process. While the premise may sound straightforward, Frogwares adds depth through the structure of the investigation itself, encouraging players to think like a scholar and a detective rather than a traditional hero. The narrative is driven by research, deduction, and exploration rather than combat, and that slower pace fits perfectly with the genre. Each location is treated as a self-contained chapter, filled with hidden mechanisms, secret chambers, and cryptic writings. The narrative flow is linear but engrossing, gradually revealing the tragic humanity that still lingers beneath Dracula’s monstrous exterior and the obsessive zeal that fuels Van Helsing’s pursuit. This interplay between intellect and faith becomes the backbone of the experience, giving the game more weight than a simple retelling of Stoker’s story.

Visually, Dracula: Origin captures the spirit of gothic horror with striking precision. Every environment is designed to exude a sense of decay and foreboding, from candlelit cathedrals lined with ancient relics to desolate tombs where the dead seem only half-asleep. Frogwares’ use of detailed, pre-rendered backgrounds lends the game a painterly quality that reinforces its mood of slow, creeping dread. The 3D character models, though modest by modern standards, blend naturally into these static scenes, creating a cohesive visual style that feels timeless. The sound design is equally effective: subdued choral arrangements, low cello tones, and ambient echoes of footsteps or distant thunder create a persistent sense of unease. These sensory details elevate the experience, turning each location into a living embodiment of gothic melancholy. It is not a world of jump scares or overt horror, but one of quiet tension and spiritual decay—a mood that lingers long after the screen fades to black.

The core of Dracula: Origin lies in its puzzles, which range from logical conundrums to intricate object-based sequences. You’ll decode runic inscriptions, align symbols on ancient devices, and concoct potions using alchemical tools. Some puzzles are elegantly integrated into the world, making you feel like a genuine scholar unraveling lost knowledge, while others demand a degree of patience and trial-and-error that can test even seasoned adventure fans. The game occasionally suffers from the genre’s classic frustrations: pixel hunting, obscure item combinations, and leaps in logic that feel more arbitrary than intuitive. However, when the puzzles click, they create moments of genuine satisfaction, rewarding careful observation and intellectual persistence. Frogwares’ inclusion of a subtle hint system helps mitigate the more punishing moments, allowing players to highlight interactive objects without completely removing the challenge.

The pacing of the game mirrors its investigative tone. Dracula: Origin is not designed for speed or constant excitement; instead, it thrives on slow discovery and quiet triumphs. Each chapter builds tension gradually, culminating in moments of revelation or confrontation that feel earned rather than forced. The linear structure keeps the story focused, but it also means that exploration is largely confined to specific screens or environments. There’s little room for deviation or experimentation, which may frustrate players accustomed to open-ended design. Yet this constraint serves the story well—it preserves the momentum of Van Helsing’s investigation and allows Frogwares to maintain narrative control. The rhythm of alternating between searching, reading, and solving puzzles gives the game a deliberate cadence, one that feels fitting for a character as scholarly and methodical as Van Helsing himself.

Characterization in Dracula: Origin leans heavily into archetype but remains effective. Van Helsing is portrayed as a man of science and conviction, his faith both his weapon and his burden. His dialogue, while occasionally melodramatic, conveys a genuine sense of moral conflict. He is not merely chasing a monster but confronting the darkness within human ambition and belief. Dracula, meanwhile, is presented with tragic gravitas—a fallen figure whose search for redemption has twisted into obsession. Supporting characters, though less memorable, serve their purpose as intermediaries and foils to Van Helsing’s journey. The voice acting varies in quality; some performances carry the necessary gravitas, while others sound stiff or theatrical. Still, the overall presentation sustains the gothic tone admirably, and the narration helps ground the story’s supernatural elements in emotional realism.

From a technical perspective, Dracula: Origin shows its age but remains playable and visually appealing. The interface is intuitive, with point-and-click navigation that keeps the focus on puzzle-solving rather than micromanagement. The game runs smoothly on modern systems with minimal adjustment, and the crisp resolution of its artwork has aged well. The lack of dynamic camera movement or full 3D environments might seem dated, but it also preserves the painterly aesthetic that defines Frogwares’ early works. The attention to detail in every room, artifact, and document compensates for the static nature of the visuals, encouraging players to linger and absorb the atmosphere.

As a whole, Dracula: Origin stands as a quietly ambitious entry in the adventure genre, one that succeeds not through innovation but through craftsmanship and mood. It captures the timeless tension between faith and temptation, intellect and evil, weaving them together in a tale that honors its literary roots while carving out its own identity. Its pacing and design may not appeal to everyone—those seeking fast action or modern accessibility might find it slow or demanding—but for players drawn to gothic storytelling and cerebral challenges, it delivers a rewarding and memorable experience. Frogwares’ ability to fuse mystery with myth makes Dracula: Origin more than just another retelling of the Dracula legend; it becomes a meditation on obsession, redemption, and the eternal struggle between light and darkness.

Los jugadores exploran varios lugares, resuelven acertijos y recolectan objetos que les permiten progresar en una historia que combina elementos de terror y misterio. Dracula: Origin se destaca por su enfoque narrativo fuerte, ofreciendo una narrativa que sigue fielmente el lore del famoso vampiro, al tiempo que introduce nuevas tramas y giros, como la búsqueda de un antiguo manuscrito que podría devolver el alma a los vampiros. Visualmente, el juego presenta escenarios muy detallados pintados a mano que capturan la atmósfera gótica y sombría de finales del siglo XIX, con gráficos que, aunque no avanzados para su tiempo, aportan una estética coherente con el tema vampírico.

La jugabilidad se centra en la interacción con otros personajes y el examen de entornos estáticos en busca de pistas. Los jugadores deben usar el ingenio para resolver los enigmas, lo que a veces incluye la combinación de ítems en el inventario para desbloquear nuevas áreas o detalles de la trama. El desarrollo de personajes y la narrativa profunda son parte integral de la experiencia, ofreciendo un desafío intelectual más que un combate directo. La recepción crítica de Dracula: Origin fue mixta, con elogios hacia la fidelidad de la historia, las ilustraciones y el diseño de personajes, pero con críticas hacia algunos aspectos repetitivos de la jugabilidad y la falta de innovación en las mecánicas tradicionales de point-and-click.

Sin embargo, para los aficionados de los vampiros y las aventuras gráficas, el juego ofrece un tributo sólido a la mitología de Drácula y un viaje narrativo envolvente. En resumen, Dracula: Origin es una aventura cautivadora que invita a los jugadores a adentrarse en el mundo del vampiro más famoso de la literatura, con una riqueza narrativa y una ambientación que satisfará a los fanáticos del género y a aquellos interesados en los mitos vampíricos.

This game has one good thing going for it: the puzzles are truly excellent. Not too hard, no too easy, some really satisfying. But the rest of the game is all over the place. Voice acting is hit and miss, locations are usually really good, but the story is pretty nonsensical in a lot of respects. It starts off like a simple, detective-esque game, then it becomes very dark very fast (with things like [spoiler] on-screen cannibalism, burning someone alive and watching it decompose in front of you, seeing several dismembered dead bodies, and the aftermath of torture [/spoiler]; it definitely crossed more than a few lines for me), and yet it ends in an almost childish way, with an awful first cutscene for the final confrontation, and a desperate attempt at a cliffhanger for a sequel in a shorter, second cutscene). It also has a very weird mixture of christian lore and lovecraftian lore, which doesn't really make any sense (Lovecraft is all about cosmic horror, the feeling of dread and despair from being insignificant in a vast cosmos with beings far superior and knowledge that our mind couldn't even process; including a somewhat benevolent god who is "the god", and including other "gods" that are actually just "demons", even when being referenced as "gods", is nonsensical to say the least).
It definitely left me feeling disappointed more than a few times, and it overstayed its welcome for a few hours at the very least. I can't really recommend it.

I generally like games from Frogwares, but Dracula: Origin didn’t quite hit the mark for me. Despite its potential as a point-and-click adventure, I can only call it average at best.

The game is loosely based on Bram Stoker's Dracula, a story I absolutely love. This version just didn't work for me though. You play Van Helsing, traveling between different regions as you search for Dracula, but the story moves slowly and never really builds up much momentum. It creates a decent atmosphere with some nice environments, but overall it felt rather boring. The ending also comes out of nowhere and leaves things surprisingly open.

On top of that, the slow character animations annoyed me. You can’t run anywhere, which makes backtracking tedious.

Speaking of backtracking, it’s one of the game’s biggest issues. The game is highly linear, divided into separate chapters/regions, and you can’t revisit earlier areas. Sometimes it locks you in one place and forces you to examine everything before letting you move on. In the museum, for instance, I had to locate every item on the shelves and interact with them before the game would let me leave. You also frequently backtrack to the same places, sometimes two or three times, and yet there are also some screens that are empty and serve only as pathways to the next area. I liked that some screens can be accessed from different directions, offering a new angle of the same space with other items or details. 

On the puzzle side, the game fares better. The puzzles are logical, which fits this type of game, though a few were tricky enough that I used pen and paper to solve them. I appreciated the balance here; no overly wacky or nonsensical solutions like in other point-and-click games. Pixel hunting is present but manageable since you can reveal hotspots with the spacebar.

The voice acting is decent enough, though it's not perfect. I had issues with Van Helsing's delivery. He tends to overact or completely miss the tone the dialogue needs. At least the entire game is fully voiced, which is nice. Dialogue itself is fine but nothing remarkable. There’s also a lot of reading: letters, newspaper clippings, and other documents that you collect in a journal. The journal also neatly stores all the dialogues you’ve had, which can be useful for revisiting clues or refreshing your memory. 

It took me around 2-3 weeks (8 hours playtime) to finish; not because it was difficult, but because I kept putting it down to play something else. At least I didn’t encounter any bugs, and for the 0.99€ sale price, I can’t say I regret buying it.

Dracula Origins is a very odd point and click game. On one hand, the title? Complete misnomer. There is no origins in this. We start of extremely roughly in the middle of the Bram Stoker novel. Van Helsing, our player character, is trying to protect Mina and destroy a recently arrived Dracula. It proceeds to take several deviations from the novel, including a somewhat unexpected turn into an early 20th century American author's territory that I did not expect. (I try not to elaborate for spoilers). Its not too far out of left field to take me out of the game, but it is quite strange how much location hopping is in here rather than the original novel, which only had England and Transylvania as major settings. The tinge of other genre's of horror strangely works in this game when I think it would've been worse in other adaptations. 

Our flavor of Dracula for this evening feels very much like a combination of Sir Christopher Lee and the Dracula in Hugh Jackman Van Helsing movie. I do like the backstory they've chosen for him, illustrating that Dracula was just as monstrous as a man, as he is when he's a monster. He's not very redeemable but he's a fun antagonist. Van Helsing feels like a combination of Peter Cushing and Edward Van Sloan. It works for the narrative. 

The models look pretty decent still. They aren't going to win any awards, but they certainly had some care put into them and therefore unlike other games of this era do not look like a potato. The puzzles are challenging, and the point and click elements are well done. I will admit though, I did need to consult a guide once or twice while playing through.  The pacing is pretty good and it never feels like you are staying at the same location for too long. 

I say if its on sale, go for it. Its a nice, classically spooky game perfect for Halloween.

Esta magia supuestamente podría devolver la vida a las almas condenadas, pero Drácula no desea devolver a cualquier alma al azar, él desea traer a la vida a la mujer que amaba. Jonathan Harker que es presentado en el juego como un ex caza vampiro y discípulo de Van Helsing, advierte a su maestro sobre este movimiento de Drácula y los manuscritos.
Mina Murray, la prometida de jonathan Harker, y amiga de Van Helsing, es raptada por Drácula, Él cree que sería el cuerpo perfecto para albergar a su amada perdida. Broken origins, broken code: a masterclass in frustration.

If you are thinking of picking up this franchise-starter on a modern PC, save your sanity and skip it. While the developer would eventually go on to make some incredible detective titles, their very first entry is a fundamentally broken, frustrating mess that holds up poorly in absolutely every department.

Here is why you should avoid this historical relic:

• Nightmarish modern incompatibility: Out of the box, the game is virtually unplayable on a modern machine. You will be greeted with broken screen sizes, an uncooperative or hyper-sensitive cursor, and constant crashes every time you try to transition to a new level. To even get it running, you are forced to hunt down external third-party software like DxWnd, tweak profile settings, and run backend applications in the background just to navigate the main menu.

• Obnoxious pixel-hunting and moon logic: The puzzle design is aggressively anti-intuitive. Instead of utilizing clever deduction or observation, the gameplay drops you into a first-person perspective where you will spend hours pixel-hunting for tiny, blurry items hidden in grainy environments. Miss a single obscure object—like a near-impossible-to-see hairpin—and your progress is completely soft-locked until you look up an external guide.

• Grating audio and painful presentation: The technical presentation is completely agonizing. The sound design features ears-piercing, repetitive background tracks that abruptly cut off and restart, mixed alongside clipping audio. To make matters worse, the main character is saddled with an incredibly irritating nasal voice delivery that spouts obvious, silly remarks instead of actual brilliant insights.

• Massive narrative disconnect: For a detective game, it barely feels like a mystery story at all. Outside of the opening and closing cutscenes, the narrative completely vanishes. The entire middle of the game is just a series of survival-horror-style room escape traps that have zero bearing on the actual plot, plagued by clunky writing and bad grammar.

Final Verdict: Even when given away for free, this game demands too much troubleshooting and offers far too little enjoyment in return. It is an outdated chore that belongs in the past. Do yourself a favor, skip this broken origin story, and jump straight into the developer's vastly superior modern sequels instead.

Je voulais découvrir l'intégralité des Sherlock Holmes de Frogwares, en commençant par le premier épisode. L'expérience aura été courte.

Je précise d'emblée que je ne suis absolument pas rebuté par les vieux jeux. J'en pratique encore régulièrement et je sais apprécier leurs qualités malgré les contraintes techniques ou les conventions de leur époque.

Après avoir passé un temps considérable à faire fonctionner correctement la souris sous Windows avec DxWnd, j'ai enfin pu découvrir le jeu… et comprendre que les problèmes techniques n'étaient finalement pas les plus gênants.
