Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy is an old-fashioned detective adventure that combines an intriguing murder investigation with elaborate environmental puzzles and a distinctly unsettling atmosphere. Developed and published by Frogwares, the game places players in the role of the legendary detective as he investigates the suspicious death of an archaeologist inside an imposing Victorian mansion. Its mixture of Egyptian mythology, hidden secrets, and traditional point-and-click mechanics creates an interesting premise, although the experience is frequently undermined by frustrating puzzle design and outdated gameplay conventions. It is a title that demands considerable patience, rewarding curiosity occasionally while testing the player's tolerance for obscure solutions.

The investigation begins when Elisabeth Montcalfe seeks Holmes's assistance in uncovering the truth surrounding her father, Lord Montcalfe, whose apparent death is surrounded by unanswered questions. With Doctor Watson absent, Holmes must investigate the family's mysterious estate independently. What initially appears to be an ordinary inquiry gradually becomes a complicated search through concealed rooms, suspicious artifacts, and dangerous mechanisms. The Egyptian theme adds an intriguing supernatural dimension to the mystery, encouraging players to question whether the strange events have a rational explanation. Although the narrative establishes an effective sense of curiosity, its progression is frequently interrupted by puzzles that receive more attention than the characters or investigative revelations.

The mansion itself is arguably the game's greatest strength. Its elaborate interiors, atmospheric corridors, and unusual decorations establish a convincing location for a classic mystery. Every room seems capable of concealing another clue, creating a sense of anticipation whenever a new area becomes accessible. Egyptian artifacts provide visual variety while reinforcing the archaeological background of the central investigation. Despite the limited graphical sophistication, the environments retain a certain nostalgic appeal. Unfortunately, their static presentation and occasionally unclear interactive elements make exploration less intuitive than it should be, particularly when essential objects blend into the scenery.

Gameplay revolves around examining environments, collecting items, interpreting clues, and solving interconnected puzzles. Some challenges successfully encourage observation and experimentation, producing satisfying moments when their underlying logic becomes clear. Others are unnecessarily complicated, relying on obscure object interactions or solutions that feel disconnected from genuine detective reasoning. Instead of consistently allowing players to reconstruct events through evidence, the game frequently requires them to overcome mechanical obstacles. This distinction matters because solving arbitrary riddles does not always capture the intellectual satisfaction associated with Sherlock Holmes. Consequently, the gameplay alternates between engaging mental challenges and exhausting trial-and-error experimentation.

Navigation presents another substantial obstacle. The first-person perspective uses a traditional scene-based movement system that feels restrictive compared with modern adventure games. Moving between locations can become repetitive, especially when searching previously explored rooms for overlooked objects. The interface provides limited assistance, and identifying useful environmental details sometimes becomes more difficult than understanding the puzzles themselves. These limitations contribute to an uneven sense of progression, where the excitement of discovering new information can quickly disappear after prolonged periods of wandering without clear direction.

The audiovisual presentation delivers mixed results. The manor's decorative architecture, Egyptian relics, and shadowy interiors establish an atmosphere of isolation and unease, but the dated textures and limited visual detail diminish their impact. Music and ambient effects provide an appropriately mysterious background, while the voice performances are serviceable without being particularly memorable. The absence of Watson also removes the familiar exchanges that usually bring personality and humor to Holmes's investigations. Although the setting remains appealing, the presentation cannot fully compensate for the limited character interaction and inconsistent storytelling.

Technical compatibility is another concern. Despite its extremely modest hardware requirements, the game can encounter difficulties on modern computers, including display problems, awkward mouse behavior, and launch issues. Steam Deck compatibility is currently Unknown or Unverified, with no official Valve Verified or Playable designation established. Running it through Proton may be possible, but reliable performance and controller functionality are not guaranteed. Its mouse-focused interface may require trackpad controls, custom configurations, or additional troubleshooting. Players seeking a convenient handheld experience should approach it cautiously.

One positive consideration is that the game is available for free on Steam, allowing curious players to investigate its unusual design without a purchase. However, its Mostly Negative user reception reflects the considerable obstacles separating its promising concept from an enjoyable experience. Dedicated enthusiasts of classic adventure games may appreciate its demanding puzzles and historical significance within the Sherlock Holmes series, but newcomers will likely find its mechanics unnecessarily punishing. The experience is better appreciated as an interesting example of early detective adventure design than as a consistently entertaining mystery.

Ultimately, Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy succeeds in establishing an intriguing atmosphere but struggles to deliver the satisfying investigative experience its premise promises. Its mysterious estate, archaeological themes, and occasional clever puzzles provide genuine appeal, yet awkward navigation, inconsistent logic, technical inconveniences, and limited narrative development prevent it from reaching its potential. It remains worth exploring for patient retro gaming enthusiasts and dedicated Sherlock Holmes fans, although anyone expecting polished detective mechanics should temper their expectations.

An atmospheric but frustrating mystery adventure whose intriguing premise and nostalgic charm are overshadowed by cumbersome controls, uneven puzzles, and outdated technical execution.

First off: If you're trying to see what the fuss is about with Frogware Sherlock Holmes, DO NOT START HERE. The more modern games are miles above this one. I know this is the free one, but seriously just shuck out some cash for Crimes and Punishment or Chapter One. Save this one for later when you're just looking to keep the magic alive.

There is a guide in the discussion that explains how to make the game playable on current devices. I have absolutely no tech savvy and could still follow the instructions to get it to work. I ended up needing to rename a few more files than the guide mentioned before unloading the zipfile. Their tip on mouse speed is absolutely necessary. And I followed a commenters suggestion to change the game properties to 640x480. 

The game is very simple in design, but complex in puzzles. The puzzles are definitely more just a collection of Egypt themed puzzles than any deduction/mystery solving. The mystery story happens around you, but you do none of the crime solving (AGAIN this differs greatly from the other games which is why you should try one of the others first). Definitely needed to have the walkthrough handy to know where to find certain unmissable clues that we're nearly impossible to spot/decipher otherwise. Even with the properties tweaks, the game did still crash a few times, so take the advice of save often!

All said, out of thoroughness, I wanted to play this one to finish up the total of the Frogwares Holmes collection and I'm glad I did. I play for a brain teaser, not for the most stunning game play. It's an old game, I understood that going in. (Btw the voice acting isn't bad, you guys just don't like his voice. Actually, of the old games, I thought it was one of the better voice acted. I admit, it's mostly Sherlock talking to himself.)

I really wanted to like this game, and there is occasionally something to enjoy here, but to actually play through this game was a genuinely horrible experience.

The main thing holding it back in 2026 is the fact that it just does not run well on modern hardware. There are a few guides on Steam that can help getting it running and solve the mouse bug (fairly straightforward, but requires downloading a newer version of the DXWnd software the game needs and setting up a game profile in this programme), but in the end despite my best efforts to get it to run in fullscreen, I eventually ended up playing it in an 800x600 window, in which my mouse behaved very erratically (moving faster left and up than right and down, which was infuriating and disorienting and honestly made me almost travel sick; fine control for puzzles and even turning the view was nightmarishly difficult). Even then, it seems almost guaranteed to crash when loading the next chapter unless you skip the preceding cutscene with spacebar. It often crashes during other cutscenes as well, or when trying to load after getting a game over screen. It would often fail to launch after a crash unless I restarted Steam, or in some cases my whole computer.

In addition, the puzzles are generally poor. The first and second chapters I thought were okay, I was on board at that point and could work almost everything out by myself, but it only got more and more painful from there. The problem is that the majority of 'puzzles' are basically just finding some items lying around and working out where to place or use them. Some of these uses are intuitive; many are not. This is compounded by the fact that you often need to be near pixel-perfect in order to pick up items, most of which do not stand out from the environment at all and are not at all obvious as interactables. By the end of the game I was consulting a guide before I left each room just to check I'd found everything before moving on. Also, save regularly, not just because of the crashes, but because there are a few timed sections, one of which is extremely unforgiving and barely gives you enough time to resolve even if you already know the solution. 

The next major weakness is that there is a massive ludonarrative dissonance. The puzzles rarely have much bearing on the story, and in general it does not feel like a Sherlock Holmes story at all. The opening and ending cutscenes were the only bits that really felt like Holmes, with the rest of the game being more the kind of puzzles you'd expect from a survival horror game than the sort of wit/knowledge/observation-based deduction Holmes is famous for. The writing, dialogue, and documents throughout are also clunky, often featuring bad grammar (to the point that the actual intended meaning is sometimes hard to deduce) and occasional spelling errors.

This is not helped by the appalling and grating voice acting. Some reviews here seem to regard the voice acting as fun bad, and there is a small bit of that ('my manor is going to be blown up!'), but Holmes' voice acting is not fun, it is just painful. It is one of the most shockingly bad attempts at a British accent I have ever heard, but it is done entirely earnestly and in the most obnoxious tone ever. Lines are often repeated incessantly, such as in the final puzzle, where every one of the 5 or 6 items required to be placed prompts the same 'it's almost ready!' voice line. The actor who played Watson, who only appears in the final cutscene, was the only one I thought gave it a good shot (though again, his impression of a British accent left a lot to be desired).

I can imagine that I would have enjoyed this more if I played it as a child on my Windows 98 computer, where I would only have had to contend with the unintuitive gameplay, and (presumably) less of the crashing and nightmare-inducing mouse control issues. As it is though, it is a very hard sell.

I understand that anyone wanting to play this is probably in the same boat I was, wanting to start this franchise from the very beginning. However, I really think that this is a game that would be much better enjoyed through watching a longplay of it on YouTube. The story is barely there and I doubt it has any bearing whatsoever on later entries in the series. It is not a long game, but the technical issues and fiddly-ness of playing it on modern hardware drags it out a lot.

Ultimately, if you do want to play it, look for the guides on Steam about fixing DXWnd to resolve the mouse issues. You may be able to get it running fullscreen; I could not. Even when I did get it running in some semblance of fullscreen, I found it most stable just using the default settings (use x,y coordinates and 800x600), as mentioned above. Save often. I recommend keeping a guide handy, as some of the items required are damn near impossible to find unless you know what to look for and where (hairpin is the worst). Also, potential spoilers here, but one of the last puzzles is a nonogram. Use the white pieces for the background, the black ones for the main shape. I spent an hour on it the wrong way round and had to do it from scratch (there is a solution online if you just want to copy it and save yourself the pain).

Played this game way back in the day and only once, which is telling, lol.  I love the Frogwares Holmes series but this one is definitely an early attempt (it is the very first one), and it shows.  It is just feels jank AF and poorly implemented.  The voice acting is TERRIBLE, like most adventure games at the time had some pretty hit or miss VA, but this one is just beyond the pail, with Holmes sounding super nasally and whiny.  However, despite the dated appearance and heavily-pixelated backgrounds, I think the setting is very interesting--a secluded English mansion, full of ancient Egyptian artifacts, on the outskirts of London with an apparent mummy running around loose and the occupants of the house mysteriously vanished.  The mystery starts off rather intriguing but ultimately is a bit of a letdown, but not horrendously so.  The music is boring and repetitive and very "90s mystical synth," which feels out of place.  Actually a lot of this game feels both very outdated and ahead of its time for 2003.  The game feels very much like a 90s game similar to Myst but you've got almost-360-degree camera movement (which is VERY jank on today's hardware).  And the setting, ambience, and gameplay feels very much like the escape room genre of games very popular in the last few years (which I think are also heavily influenced by some of the same 90s adventure games).

Also, this game IS still playable on Windows 11 but you should follow one of the Steam guides and you must use the program DxWnd in order to get the game to run properly and mitigate some of the jank.  Also, you will likely need a guide as a fair amount of the puzzles are not designed well or just designed to be frustrating, like a lot of adventure games from the 90s were as well.

Overall, despite all the issues, I do find some charm in this game, mostly for its setting and ambience.  It does still feel, maybe not quite Holmes-ian, but still of the period.  The follow-up game, "Secret of the Silver Earring," is much more classic Holmes in my mind and actually begins the series to actually feel like piecing together and solving mysteries rather than just escape room puzzles.  

So I will recommend this game but only to die-hard adventure game fans, especially vintage ones, or those who really like the setting and are interested in playing all of the Frogwares Holmes games.

I had a great time with this game. It's nowhere near as bad as most of the reviews suggest. It's just a relic from a time when people didn't mind beating their heads against the wall for an hour before figuring something out. Setting the game up to run properly took about five minutes thanks to instructions in the community, and you can get around the crashes between levels by saving often and skipping the cutscene on the second try. 

There are definitively moments where you'll have to look up an answer online, but 90% of the puzzles in this game are solvable, and 80% are even intuitive to some degree. I suppose it's an upside that this was one of the few times I didn't feel bad for looking things up after I'd put in some effort, so it didn't ruin my experience. 

The atmosphere also holds up, especially in the first half. The writing is delightfully nonsensical, Sherlock's dry wit is amusing, and it wasn't until the end that I started to lose my patience, partially because it felt silly to spend an hour pixel hunting for a hairpin when the house is about to come down on top of you.

The story is bizarre, the voice acting is comical and some of the puzzles are random and have nothing to do with the story. Also, it seems to have absolutely nothing to do with the Sherlock Holmes universe. However, if you want to have a retro point and click puzzle game experience, and have a walkthrough handy to help find the nigh impossible items you need, it's worth a play. On the other hand, I can see that a bunch of people really won't enjoy this.

SHERLOCK HOLMES: THE MYSTERY OF THE MUMMY - компания FROGWARES делает лучшие игры по Шерлоку Холмсу, не уверен, что пройду старые части, но вот новые 100% 

Если вдруг выйдет так, что я пройду старых Шерлоков, тогда обновлю обзор!

С самого начала чувствуется атмосфера: туманный Лондон, таинственный особняк, и уже понятно - тут точно творится что то неладное. Играешь за Холмса, и это приятно: берёшь лупу, разглядываешь каждую мелочь, а в голове так и звучит его фирменный тон - «Элементарно, мой дорогой друг». Управление простое, не приходится мучиться с непонятными командами - взял предмет, посмотрел, записал в блокнот, и дальше в путь. Загадки в меру хитрые: пару раз застопоришься, почешешь затылок, а потом вдруг - бац! - и всё складывается в единую картину. Особенно радует, что нельзя просто тыкать во всё подряд: надо думать, сопоставлять факты, иначе застрянешь на полпути. Диалоги выдержаны в стиле эпохи - ни тебе современных шуточек, ни неуместной суеты, всё строго по канонам детектива. Визуально игра не блещет суперграфикой, но зато создаёт нужное настроение: тёмные коридоры, старинные вещицы, загадочные записки. Иногда ловишь себя на мысли, что слишком уж всё тихо - и тут вдруг скрипнет дверь или промелькнёт тень, и сердце ёкает. В целом, проект цепляет тем, что даёт почувствовать себя настоящим сыщиком: ни спешки, ни лишних эффектов, только логика, наблюдательность и щепотка мистики.

Игра, в которой вам потребуется чертовская сообразительность и отменная наблюдательность. Вместе с легендарным Шерлоком Холмсом и доктором Ватсоном вам нужно искать улики, изучать показания свидетелей и разгадывать очень непростые головоломки. Для работы с уликами в вашем распоряжении масса разнообразных приспособлений, начиная обычным увеличительным стеклом и заканчивая микроскопом. В Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy вас ждет незабываемое детективное расследование в компании со знаменитым сыщиком. Причем графика в игре действительно удивляет – отменно нарисованные локации, прекрасные модели персонажей и отличная анимация.

This game did not run on my Windows 10, but it worked perfect when I switched to Arch Linux.

Now for the review:

Just don't try it.
Really.

The game is not intuitive at all. The first level is fine, but beyond that, every puzzle just doesn't feel fair. 

I bet if Sherlock Holmes himself played this, he would also be lobotomized by every obscure object placement. Not to mention that every hidden object has like 10x10 pixel that you can't even notice upon your thousandth glance.

Also, unlike Resident Evil or any other functional puzzle game, this game doesn't distinguish interactable puzzles from display objects that you can observe. This create a gameplay where you wack a very specific item to every clickable object across every room and hallways. 

I'll give you an example:  There's a fork, which is on the hallway at the second level, that you can pick up. This fork is also like 10x10 pixel. Much like the subject of the mystery, I'd only recommend this game to those interested in some digital archeology. Even so, you will find yourself fighting to get through it's slim five levels, including updating the middleware needed to the run game, applying dozens of tweaks to it, editing script files to skip broken cutscenes that crash your game, and reloading anyway when the game still crashes. Playing this game is like trying to climb a ladder of dust, you can feel something when you reach out, but try to grip and it collapses under the pressure. That being said, I did enjoy the atmosphere and the artstyle. It's very interesting to see where the studio, Frogware, began and where they have gone since, and given it's free, it more than serves that purpose. It reminds me of Hitman: Codename 47 in that way, another game I've reviewed (many years ago), which is mostly interesting in the series which it produced. I played the old Hitman games in release order to get a sense of how the games improved, both technically and artistically, and I'm intending the same with the Sherlock games. The key difference will be that I was very familiar with the Hitman series before doing so, while I am a stranger to the Sherlock games. So far, this was a very rough start but I am looking forward to the games yet to come and will keep you posted.

For more specifics on this game, I found the first two levels to be the most enjoyable as you get to explore the mansion of an eccentric aristocrat and see his personality reflected in the manor, but the puzzles were obtuse and annoying, with lots of searching for items rather than solving problems. This reached an ugly peak in level 3, which has you shuffling around a wine cellar, dragging your mouse over 100+ bottles to find the five usable ones to insert in a puzzle that makes no sense in or out of game. Then, you contend with sudden timer that you are not told about, and which caused me to softlock myself and have to restart the game entirely. This is extra frustrating because there's a lot of notes in this section, so I was going very slow to read over everything and learn what I could about the story. (Save before you craft the torch in level 3!!!) What puzzles come after that are just irrating and tempermental, such as picking up a chair that you cannot put down, open your inventory, move or open the menu, until you find the specific section to click to place it. 

Level 4 simplifies the puzzles and tries to amp up the tension with more timed events, although mechanically it's just frustrating. I was starting to enjoy the cutscenes, the one with Parkey is a highlight, as all the previous ones were just Holmes fiddling with things, however, most of them crashed my game at least once or twice, and in extreme cases, as referenced above, I had to comment them out of the game's script entirely. Level 5 was more enjoyable in comparison, although it had a lot of cutscenes and so a lot of crashes, especially at the end. Revisting previous parts of the mansion, changed due to events, was very gratifying. Everything builds up to the longest cutscene in the game, where Sherlock explains a mystery that was indeed mysterious, in that I wondered where it went halfway through. The justification is hasty, poorly delivered through dodgy voiceacting, though to be fair to him, one fella voiced all the male characters, and talking to yourself for the big climatic finale can't be easy. (The single female character was voiced by an equally amateurish lady.)

TL;DR I feel bad being to it, but it's free and cool to see where the studio came from, and if you're like me, tweaking it to work actually was very satisfying. (More satisfying than anything in level 3. UGH) Controls, gameplay and story is poor, but the atmosphere is solid even if the music is very repetitive.

The game starts off quite well but from the 3rd and even more from the 4th level onwards, puzzles get very difficult, don't make any sense, even the supposed clues don't help and pixel hunting reaches extreme levels. There's some hardcore pixel hunting in early levels too but it's do-able whereas on later levels it's not bearable anymore. I got so pissed off with the game that I went through the entire last level (and some of the 4th level) with the help of an online walkthrough, I simply had no desire to even try and figure out puzzles anymore.

Do I recommend the game? No, not all, but do try it out if you're interested what are most negative reviews about.

Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy is a point-and-click adventure that answers the question:

> “What if we gave you Sherlock’s brain… but *none* of his patience?”

You’re invited to investigate a mysteriously abandoned mansion museum.
In practice, you will:

* Click on 3 pixels per second
* Solve 19th-century OSHA violations
* Develop a deep hatred of sarcophagi

---

### Pros:

* Peak early-2000s adventure energy: static pre-rendered rooms, weird camera angles, and puzzles designed by someone who’s never heard the phrase “too obscure.”
* Sherlock occasionally says something smug like, “Elementary,” after you solve a puzzle you brute-forced by randomly combining items for 10 minutes.
* Inventory full of extremely specific trash: broken rods, mysterious keys, clock hands, half a cog, some rope, one brick, emotional damage.
* Every room feels like an escape room built by a museum curator who *really* didn’t want visitors.

---

### Cons:

* Difficulty curve:

  * Tutorial: “Turn key, open door.”
  * 10 minutes later: “Align the ancient mechanism using a code hidden in a painting you didn’t realize was interactable.”
* Miss one tiny hotspot and you’ll spend 30 minutes walking in circles like a Victorian Roomba.
* The mummy isn’t even the scariest thing here – it’s the realization you’ve been stuck on the same lock for half an hour.
* Sherlock’s voice lines give “I’m judging you” energy every time you fail at basic observation. And he’s right.

---

### Peak Holmes Experience:

* Examining the same statue five times because *this* click might be the magic one.
* Picking up 12 useless objects and somehow missing the one item that actually matters.
* Solving a ridiculously convoluted mechanism, opening the door, and immediately saving because you know you’re not doing that again.
* Finishing a chapter and confidently saying, “If I lived back then, I could’ve been a detective,” while your browser history is 90% “sherlock mummy walkthrough part 3.”

---

7.5/10
It’s clunky, old, and occasionally unfair, but if you like classic janky puzzle adventures and being told you’re dumber than Sherlock Holmes, it’s beautiful.

Would click on every wall, insult the mummy’s interior design, and pretend I solved the puzzles without a guide again.

My friend bought us a Humble Bundle containing all of the Sherlock Holmes games from Frogwares. "Brilliant," I thought, for I always wanted to try those but never decided to actually do it. So, I visited the Wikipedia article about the series and found out that the first game in the series was "Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy" which wasn't in the bundle. A quick search revealed to me that the game is free on Steam. Red flags were immediately apparent. The reviews for the game are, as of writing this review, mostly negative, and reading them revealed to me that the game is very hard and that most of the people completed it with the help of a guide. Besides that, a technical guide needs to be followed in order to even get the game to work properly in the first place.

Since I am foolishly brave and prone to mental sadomasochism, despite all of those red flags, I decided to give it a try and experience the series in order. I had no idea how bad of an idea that was and how quickly what was supposed to be a relaxing Sunday experience would turn into a descent into the depths of hell.

After following a guide on how to make the game work properly on modern systems, I started my descent into madness. I was met with dated graphics, ominous music, and a pretty challenging first room of the game. You see, "Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy" is more of an escape room adventure game than what you imagine when somebody mentions a point & click adventure game and has more in common with the "Dracula" adventure game series from Microids+ than with your traditional point & click games.

The first room set the tone for the rest of the game. I immediately got a bit stuck and had to start sweating in order to understand what the game wanted from me. I don't think I'm exaggerating when I say that many would give up on this very first room. After the first room, I picked up the pace, and I managed to complete the first level and after that the second relatively quickly, though I did get stuck a bit on the second level (quite literally even, because the game crashed during the transition to the next level, so you have to skip the cutscene in order for it to load properly, which also happened for the transition to the fifth level and (I think) during the one to the fourth level).

The third level, however, is where things started to go downhill... Extreme cases of pixel hunting, even darker and more unpleasant environments, cryptic puzzle design, hints whose meaning gets lost in translation, and nonsensical puzzle solutions. It started getting bad. Really, really bad...

The fourth level—now this was where the game started breaking me. There was this secret door with 19 bricks around it you can press. At first I tried to work out the combination, then I revealed a hint—number 3. The only number with 3 digits known to me at that time from the letters found throughout the game didn't work, so you know what I did? I asked ChatGPT to list me all the possible combinations of 3 of those 19 bricks at a time. There were 900+ of those combinations, and I was so sure in my deduction that I went on to brute force the solution. Hours later, I finished trying all of them, to no success.

I started losing my mind on this puzzle. I asked for help from my friend (who I already asked to help me with the start of the third level, but there he just kept me company until I found the ridiculously hidden item I needed to progress), another friend, my mother, and my sister, but to no success. Finally, I asked my third friend for help, and after an hour, we worked out a solution.

My mental torture continued with the rest of the game. You see, this is not really a bad game. It was made by a small team on what was probably a miniscule budget, and it has that retro charm of old adventure games, at least in some places. It is clear that they tried to do the best they could with those limitations. All of the characters were voiced by just two voice actors!

However, what this game is, is badly designed. Very badly designed. The whole thing feels like you are playing one of those casual hidden object adventure games, but instead of the game being a breeze to get through, it's the complete opposite, because unlike those hidden object adventure games, here the game provides minimal help, and when it does provide help in the form of hints, it's very likely that it will confuse you more than it will help you. And when you aren't struggling with a particularly cryptic puzzle, you will be struggling with extreme pixel hunting. Some of those item placements are nefarious...

I got frustrated. I felt extreme anxiety. My biorhythm got messed up, I lost sleep, and I may end up getting sick—all because of this game. I simply refused to read a guide and instead relied mostly on my own patience and the help of my friends, when they could offer it, which was only that one time during the fourth level. Hey, even Sherlock had Watson! But yeah, my stubbornness got the best of me, and I refused to read guides even when things got that serious. Why? Pride! Oh, and I read an IGN review that clearly showed they completed the game. If they could do it, so could I (this gave me a bit of help with a mention of a hairpin at a particular place in the game, so I guess you could consider that as looking for external help, but since I was by that time familiar with the game's pixel hunting, I'm pretty sure I would have found it myself; it would have just taken me more time).

And that's what it all comes down to. Time. We have a limited amount of it, and when we play video games, we want to have fun. This game is for the most part the opposite of that. So, to conclude this lengthy review—"Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy" is a very unpleasant experience. It doesn't look good; its repetitive music, which plays on loop, will make you go mad; its cryptic puzzle design and pixel hunting will be your worst nightmare; the dopamine hits of advancing in the game are weak; and the sense of accomplishment after finally beating the game is barely existent. If anything, you feel relief from finally being done with it.

Yeah, I am aware that without this game the rest of the series wouldn't exist and that its massive success allowed the team to continue its work and existence, but let's face it, Frogwares as a team is aware that this game has aged like milk from 2002, and that's why it's free to play. I am thankful for its existence, but I really, really don't recommend it to anyone but the most hardcore genre fans who get high on this sort of stuff. Also, I can't stress this enough: if you are prone to overthinking, consider not playing this even if you like this kind of stuff; otherwise, you'll end up like me, with 27 hours of your life wasted on a game that on average takes less than 10 hours to beat...

While i would not usually review a game I have not finished, this will be an exception. I liked [i]Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments[/i] a lot so I wanted to play every games in the series by Frogwares in their release order - barring the hidden objects spin-off.

First, I ran this game without any issue on a Linux distribution. I was using Proton-Sarek 10.15 and there was no issues with the mouse so this review will not be tainted by any technical issues.

Even for a game released in 2002, the graphics are not good at all. Due to the low resolution, the painful pixel-hunting is even more frustrating due to the blurry backgrounds. You cannot Alt+Tab in the game.... Well you can but it is not consistent and there are no notes regarding clues in the in-game notebook, meaning you will either have to write them in a physical piece of paper or remember them.

The gameplay is just not interesting. I got bored after half an hour of pixel hunting and I must admit that it is the first time I rage-uninstalled a game due to this. The music, while good, is constantly looped which makes the whole experience grating.

One unintentional positive aspect of this game is the voice acting. It is not objectively good at all but it is so campy I cannot hate it.

I understand that this was clearly a low-budget game and I should not expect a lot since it was from 2002. However, while I can excuse some technical shortcomings due to the budget (hence why I did not mention the stiff animations of the cutscenes for this reasons since they are not a major part of the game and do not influence the playability), the game is just not engaging at all and even for a free game I felt that I just wasted my time. Fortunately, Frogwares has really improved its craft with the subsequent games. In fact, I feel bad for leaving a very negative review for a company who has done better later on and I started to play this game with an open mind. But objectively, this game just is not good at all. It's very bad.
According to the not-very-reliable Wikipedia page, this game sold 1 million copies by 2013. I think this is a bigger mystery than the one you need to solve in-game.

Some kind of wrapper/utility is used to run this old game from 2002, so Steam didn't track my time at all.  I brute forced the five minutes of recorded playtime required to post this review, but my real playtime was about five hours.

I decided to see if this game was worth playing, despite the horrific Steam review score.  Additional setup is required to even get this game to start without crashing, but it is at least a little playable.  The Dark Age of Adventure Gaming produced this game, and it has all the terrible elements you'd expect:

[list]
    [*]Conspicuously low budget
    [*]Grainy, ultra-low resolution visuals
    [*]Objects that are tiny and hidden in shadows
    [*]Unexpected or bizarre combinations/interactions
    [*]Interactive areas with absolutely no visual indications
    [*]New game mechanics appear with no notice or explanation
    [*]It's possible to fail/die
    [*]No feedback for many actions, either on success or failure
[/list]

I played many games with these attributes during the 2000s, the legit DARK AGES for the adventure genre.  I've done my dues.  So, when I got stuck on the very first puzzle in the very first room, I busted out a walkthrough.  That puzzle does NOT give the player enough information to fully solve it and guessing is REQUIRED.

The game has plenty of stumbling blocks that will stump all players, due to a lack of information on how to create the solution, or because necessary objects are hidden in shadows.  This is a game where you have to mouse over EVERYTHING.  The graphics are basic, but levels are still cluttered with objects and frickin ANYTHING could be an item you need to pick up.  That's bad enough, but even worse, each screen is a full 360° image!!!

This kind of gameplay is only bearable in the modern era if a walkthrough is on hand.  I tried to play as much as I could without one and I was able to get a little satisfaction.

Even with a walkthrough, I nearly gave up on the game.  Sliding tile puzzles have been my adventure game nemesis for 25 years, but I've learned to deal with them.  There are two of them in Mystery of the Mummy.  The puzzle that nearly killed my playthrough was the largest nonogram I have ever seen, at 31x31.  I usually enjoy nonograms, but with the horrible interface, the jerky mouse control, and the requirement to manually count squares, it was really unpleasant.  I decided to give up on this game.  Later, I changed my mind.  Eventually I got it after 30-40 minutes of tedious counting, I and was able to finish the game 15 minutes later.

Interestingly, I have a Sherlock Holmes nonogram game with better puzzles:
https://store.steampowered.com/app/1546340/Detective_Riddles__Sherlocks_Heritage/

I went through all this just to confirm that Mystery of the Mummy is not worth playing.  Forget about it.  Most adventure games from this era need to be shoveled into the dustbin of history, and Frogwares' first Sherlock Holmes game is no exception.

I did enjoy the voice acting of Holmes.  It's that stuffy, nasally English accent we associate with snooty, pompous aristocrats - and it's just funny to listen to.
As they say- it's busted, and probably not worth your time getting to work.

Я фанат книг і ігор про Шерлока, як і інших екранізацій, і мене дуже сильно здивував рейтинг цієї гри, і я був дуже неприємно здивований якістю людей, що залишили негативні відгуки. Така велика кількість людей не спромоглася подивитися системні вимоги, і побачити, що гра не підтримується навіть Windows 7, не те що сучасними системами? Я майже не знайшов адекватні рецензії про саму гру, виключно величезний хейт, від людей, які не знають про системні вимоги, і що старі ігри часто не працюють на сучасних пк, але це не привід знищувати їм оцінки. Вони як в тому мемі, 200 тисяч одноманітних коментів що гра не працює на моєму Windows 10\11, вже написані, ще мільйон на підході.

А тепер для тих хто хоче пограти, то ось по цьому гайду я фіксив мої проблеми з запуском: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2487592801] ОСЬ ЦЕ ПОСИЛАННЯ[/url]. Загалом, не дуже приємно почалося моє знайомство з цією грою, бо купа поганих відгуків одразу налаштували мене не дуже добре до напевно єдиної гри з усієї серії, в яку я ще не грав. Але саме гра насправді подарувала мені хороші враження. Тепер далі розповім нарешті про саму гру.

I've tried, time and time again, to get into these point-and click adventures (or how i prefer to call them: pixel hunting nightmares), but i think it's finally time to admit to myself that they're not for me, for the exact reason i already stated there. 

As desperately as i've wanted to get into that genre, because a lot of these games would probably have great stories, the so-called "gameplay" is just so primitive and beyond tedious. Can't do this, can't do that, so you'll end up clicking on every possible pixel until you find something by pure luck. I genuinely question if people actually find these games themselves fun, or just play them for the stories alone, because they certainly aren't very fun to play, but i guess to some they are then, i just tend to prefer some sensical gameplay instead of trying to figure out the most cryptic shit you could think of. 

That said, i think my dislike for these games essentially comes down to that, it seems the no. 1 rule of point-and-clicks is the more nonsensical something is, the more likely it is EXACTLY what you are supposed to do. Idk if that's the case with this Sherlock Holmes franchise in particular, but i just couldn't even get past the first quiz in this, so i gave up. I'll rather just go for the newer games, and hope the remake of this is gonna be more pleasant to play, which i have my doubts on too, because i'm not a fan of the generic Netflix design of the young Holmes in those games at all, and remakes are rarely better than the originals, but in this case i'm pretty sure that even if i won't enjoy that one too much, i'll at least enjoy it a little bit more than this, because from what i've seen it has some actually decent game mechanics, instead of this pixel hunting bs. 

Now... okay, i may have been harsh there, and i may also be too used to different kind of gameplay, who knows, i generally have an issue with the old PC games, same goes for all the old CRPGs, which i also so desperately want to like, because i am a huge fan of both RPGs and retro games, but my preferences are just in other genres of that, i suppose. 

With all that said, and my frustration out of the way, the tricky part is that i am, once again, not the right person to review this kind of game, because as anyone reading this probably already figured, i just don't like this type of gameplay in general, so if i could, i'd give this a "neutral" option. While i personally can't recommend it, simply because i just absolutely despise this kind of game design, i can still say if whoever is reading this right now is a fan of point-and-clicks, you might have a better time with it. 

Personally i've just had enough of these, and i need to stop wasting my money on them, even if they're on a tempting sale like this bundle was, because i basically never enjoy my time with them, as much as i try to lie to myself and think that "maybe this one will finally click", but no, it won't, because my issue is with the core mechanics of these games in itself. 

It's a shame, because while they at least remade this with different kind of gameplay and i can go for that, i was also really interested in the "Sherlock Holmes versus Jack the Ripper" entry, because i love this stuff based on true crime or mythos/folklore, but i can't force myself. I have so many games to play anyway that i won't waste more of my precious time with something i'm not really into, again, it's a shame, but it is what it is.

A great atmosphere completely ruined by a broken, aging engine.

If you are thinking of buying Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened (2008) on a modern PC, stay away. While the Lovecraft-meets-Sherlock story is incredibly cool, the Steam version is a technical nightmare that Frogwares has completely abandoned.

Here is why you should skip the 2008 original:

• Game-Breaking Save Bug: The game will randomly stop writing save data. You can lose hours of progress instantly, especially around the hospital and harbor chapters, forcing you to use third-party community save files just to finish.

• Modern Hardware Incompatibility: This game hates modern Windows and multi-core CPUs. Out of the box, it will crash, black screen, or give you Nvidia PhysX errors. You have to download fan patches (like the NTCore 4GB Patch) just to make it run.

• Frustrating "Moon Logic" Puzzles: Typical of 2000s adventure games, the puzzles suffer from massive difficulty spikes. You will constantly get stuck pixel-hunting for tiny, un-highlighted items on the floor.

• Jarring Lore Shift: If you are a Holmes purist, be warned. Watching the world's most rational detective deal with supernatural, reality-bending Cthulhu cosmic horror can feel incredibly out of character.

Final Verdict: Do not buy this version unless you love editing .ini files and troubleshooting legacy drivers. If you want to experience this story, buy the 2023 Remake instead. It actually works.

Окрема втіха це лавкрафтівська тематика, вплетена в історію Холмса органічно. Кумедно, бо паралельно граю в Call of Cthulhu, а нещодавно подивилась мультик 2026 року про кита, який бореться з Левіафаном. Коли Ктулху чи Левіафан перегукуються одразу в трьох творах підряд, один за одним, то це вже не збіг, а привід посміятись. Плюс я якраз читала твір Лавкрафта «Звір у печері», тож, як то кажуть, вся ним обліплена була.

А от загадки це випробування. Складні настільки, що мої власні тупняки мене дратували, тож десь 30% гри пройшла з гайдами, вирішила просто не страждати, коли логіка головоломки відмовлялась вкладатись у голові. Додає діч і те, що часом треба проклікувати об'єкти у строго визначеному порядку, хоча між собою вони майже не пов'язані, але це, як кажуть, специфіка жанру.

I started playing this game many years ago, then lost my save so I took quite a long break lol. Played the remake (liked it a lot!) and then finally came back to this one after playing the silver earring. Obviously this is the remastered version, however, even still I think it improves a lot upon the silver earring. You have the option of point and click and first person/more modern controls. Neither are bad, but if you want a slower experience, play point and click, and if you want a more smooth, swift experience, try first person. I did a little of both but eventually stuck with first person. Even though I love point and click games, the areas are very vast and make the point and click and SLOW experience. Outside of this, I think the gameplay overall is a lot smoother compared to silver earring, and there are no timed puzzles (thank you). Holmes and Watson are still entertaining and their VAs are very good and capture the characters well. The story is also awesome, and despite having already played the remake I found the original still quite gripping because there are some striking differences. It's very interesting to see the differences between our Sherlocks in this compared to 2023 LMAO. Ultimately, I think this one is worth your time, even if you've played the remake.

Much better entry than the previous games and much, much more entertaining than imaginary “duel of wits” with Arsen Lupin. In fact, this game is closest to being graded actually good (and my standards for such old titles are set accordingly). This time however I’m going to write longer review (that inevitably will be rewritten to be shorter, drier and more concise in a couple months).

Technically speaking game works and has third-person and first-person cameras. Quality of graphics is on par with early 2000s titles. Holmes and Watson act close enough to their literary counterparts. In theory, players can finish entire game in a couple hours, unless they’re stuck on something or find mismatch between guides and game items or action sequences. Rather good improvement conpared to other titles in series...

There are enough drawbacks too and while some are subjective, others are objective. For example oddly nauseating movement animation in first-person (no idea why to be honest) don’t make it the most enjoyable experience either, but may be fine otherwise. Gigantic almost empty environments requiring backtracking or investigation sequences where bets “research” tactic is random clicking are not that bad either (beats dungeons where you have to go back the same way you came in, literally).

Instead of asking how to solve this puzzle and progress further, more frequent line of questioning was that of spending time on the game at all. Instead of feeling like uncovering a mystery that may or may not be actually important in-universe, this turns into an exercise in tedium where one part is too easy, another too hard and the third makes you ask “what the F is that and why???”

You know what? I’m going to do the funny thing – recommend this title. Not that bad all things considered. Don’t wanna play anymore though.

[h2] Wer hätte gedacht, dass Sherlock Holmes nicht nur Verbrechen löst, sondern auch einen Lungenfacharzt braucht?  [/h2]

The Awakened ist ein mitreißendes Abenteuer, das manchmal so dramatisch ist, dass sogar die Musik ein eigenes Drama schreibt.

Watsons Unfähigkeit: Watson ist in diesem Spiel so hilfreich wie ein Regenschirm mit Löchern — nett gemeint, aber sobald’s drauf ankommt, läuft alles schief. Watson bleibt das wandelnde Schaufenster für „Wie man es nicht macht“ — stolpert, vergisst Hinweise und bringt Holmes öfter in Erklärungsnot als jeder Verdächtige. Man liebt ihn trotzdem: ohne Watson wäre Sherlock bloß ein einsamer Kerl mit großem Hut und noch größerem Ego.

Geschrei von Sherlock: Holmes grölt an manchen Stellen, als hätte er versehentlich eine Opernprobe im Wohnzimmer gestartet. Seine Lautstärke ist wie ein Gewitter in einer Bibliothek.. effektiv, aber niemand bedankt sich dafür. Manchmal klingt er weniger wie ein Gentleman-Detektiv und mehr wie ein Wecker, der schließlich kapituliert.

Dramatische Musik: Funktioniert überraschend gut... Spannung garantiert, Herzinfarkt optional.

Bugs: Ja, auch die besten Detektive kämpfen gegen pixelige Spukgestalten — das Spiel hat ein paar Macken. Besonders fies: Einmal konnte man nicht mehr speichern. Plötzlich steht man da, nach einer Stunde Spielzeit, und merkt: „Speichern? War das ein Vorschlag oder ein Mythos?“ Tipp: Speichert häufiger als Watson seine Lebensgeschichten erzählt.

Fazit: Trotz schreiender Deduktion, dramatischer Musik und Watsons ständiger Tollpatschigkeit bleibt The Awakened ein gutes und unterhaltsames Spiel. Es ist wie ein britischer Krimiabend: etwas überdreht, ein bisschen chaotisch, aber am Ende trotzdem unglaublich befriedigend — mit dem zusätzlichen Bonus, dass man zwischendurch lauthals lachen darf.

Bewertung: 6/10, weil Sherlock zwar die Welt retten kann, aber scheinbar nicht die Speicherfunktion.

It also crashes in third person view sometimes, so I played the game in first-person view. It should be quite enjoyable either way, though third-person is slightly easier since it restricts the volume of irrelevant objects you can look at.

As for the game itself, I have yet to finish it yet. If you are familiar with the Silver Earring, the previous game, then this game is significantly less "hardcore" than that. For most players, that is probably for the better. Still, there is plenty of mystery solving to be had. It is a fine game. Also has a built-in hint system (question mark at bottom of the inventory screen), so there should be no need to ever rely on an external walkthrough.

At times, the game has an issue with signalling what is interactable. Some items dont become interactable until you've passed some trigger. Definitely could've been improved how that's handled. For example, by leaving the objects examinable before the trigger.

Hervorragend:
- Story: Spannende Erzählung im Stil von Arthur Conan Doyle gepaart mit dem Universum von H. P. Lovecraft
- Easter Eggs: Durch das Spiel verteilt findet man subtile Anspielungen auf die vorherigen Spiele der Reihe, Details aus den Romanvorlagen und einen Kurzauftritt von Hercule Poirot. 

Positiv:
- Charaktere: Durch Wechsel der Erzählperspektive zwischen Holmes und Dr. Watson können beide ihre Stärken ausspielen. Da die Story aber wenig in London abläuft, fehlen bekannte Namen aus dem Scotland Yard
- Grafik: Erstmals in der Reihe kann man zwischen First- und Third-Person wechseln. Für ein Spiel, was mittlerweile "volljährig" ist, hat es sich einigermaßen gehalten.
- Gameplay: Der dritte Teil der Reihe verzichtet zum Glück auf die Timed-Events des Vorgängers sowie auf die Recaps am Ende eines Levels. Dafür gibt es mehr Rätsel im Adventure-Stil, zusammen mit ein paar Zahlen-Rätseln

Neutral:
- Technik: Das Arneson-Haus scheint anfällig für Bugs zu sein, die dafür sorgen, dass man nicht mehr weiter kommt. Hier hilft nur das Laden eines vorherigen Speicherpunktes. Davon abgesehen lief das Spiel aber flüssig und ohne Abstürze

📖Фанфік про Шерлока і тентаклі Лавкрафта😱

Вирішив, так би мовити, залізти глибше у старенькі ігри про Шерлока. "The Awakened (2008)" стала першою в списку, бо на неї зробили добротний ремейк + всі ігри до 2008 у мене не запускаються, а з бубнами я вже натанцювався, дякую! 
Що тоді, що і зараз - у керма українська студія "Frogwares", любителі детективних історій. 
Це третя частина у серії про Холмса, і водночас перша, де Шерлок потрапляє в хоррор-атмосферу по мотивам Лавкрафта😈.



За сюжетом ми маєм справу зі зниклим моряком, що на перший погляд здається звичайною історією, але нитки приводять у різні куточки світу, і окрім Лондона нас занесе у Швейцарію, Новий Орлеан і на Шотландський острів .
Хотів би росповісти про сюжет більше, про довбаних фанатиків, морського бога... Але не буду, бо якщо ви дійсно хочете побачити розгубленого Холмса де логіка "тріщіть" по швах, вам краще одразу перейти до ремейка😵‍💫.
https://store.steampowered.com/app/1949030

Але якщо ви все ще тут і дійсно хочете сюди залізти, вам потрібно знати, як воно...У 2025 році: 

✅Це детективна класика "point-and-click", де треба думати самому. Підказок нема, суто хардкор, або гугл вам в допомогу. (Доречі можна бігати від першої особи, мені це було зручніше, ніж клікатись з мишкою.)  
✅Атмосфера гри тривожна. Можливо, ви подумаєте, що це через графоній... Але ні...Коли будете у психлікарні - зрозумієте. І в загалом це було сильно й сміливо комбінувати жанри жахастика і детектива...Я знаю, що у нас вже є "The Sinking City", але на момент виходу "The Awakened" - це було дуже цікаво💀
✅Прикольні міні ігри, але деякі можуть здатись складними і ви полізете в інтернет та зрозумієте, що клепка в вашій голові не фурижить. (Так було зі мною... і з вами теж буде... не сумнівайтесь😅). У певні моменти нагадує "Nancy Drew" (Якщо ви в курсі🫡) 
 
❌Мене дратує механіка взаємодії. Поки не відкриєш всі активності, по сюжету не просунишся (А це може бути слід на околиці будинку, чи пляма крові десь на стіні і це ППЦ). Є ще момент, де треба здогадатись,  про що думає Шерлок, і прописати це вручну.... Якщо ви любите скіпати діалоги, то ви зайдете в ступор, бо під час цього етапу вине зможете переглянути історію діалогу, або інвентар з щоденником (Особисто потрапляв таку халепу і ліз в інтернет за інфою, бо не розумів, що від мене  хочуть😑)
❌Моменти, де гра каже одне, а робиш в результаті інше.
Один приклад: у Америці нам натякають, що треба обміняти стерлінги.

Archaic, trial-and-error progression and broken gameplay mechanics that turn a classic murder mystery into a frustrating technical headache.

If you are thinking of picking up Sherlock Holmes: The Silver Earring, it is a mechanically broken point-and-click entry that manages to ruin its authentic Victorian atmosphere with abysmal design choices. While the foundational premise of solving a high-profile mansion murder sounds like a classic Doyle adventure, the execution relies on archaic systems, terrible controls, and sudden gameplay shifts that feel outright malicious.

Here is what you need to know before diving in:

• Tank Controls in Water: Navigating the pre-rendered 3D environments is an absolute nightmare. The character pathfinding and collision detection are completely broken; clicking on a destination often results in Sherlock doing awkward, robotic spins or outright ignoring your commands. Trying to maneuver him into specific rooms or narrow corridors feels like trying to steer a shopping cart with broken wheels.

• Absurdly Unfair "Deadly" Puzzles: The game randomly abandons its traditional investigation style to throw you into atrocious, unprompted timed sequences. At one point, you are forced to run through a dark woodland maze on a strict time limit to fetch a bucket of water to put out a fire, with no clear indication of where the bucket even was. Combined with the sluggish character movement, these instances lead to instant, repetitive failure screens.

• Broken Logic Quizzes: At the end of each in-game day, you are locked into a mandatory, pedantic quiz before you can progress. You must answer a series of questions and tie them exactly to matching clues and journal entries. Because of terrible localizations and translation errors, the logic falls completely flat; the game will reject your perfectly accurate evidence simply because it wants a different, ambiguous journal entry that might not even show up properly in your menu.

• Trial-and-Error Stealth: One of the most infamously awful segments requires you to sneak past a guard dog at night. The dog essentially possesses x-ray vision, triggering an instant game-over from massive distances regardless of whether you are standing behind solid walls or environment assets. It forces you into a brutal cycle of quick-saving and reloading just to guess the exact, arbitrary path the developers expected you to walk.

Final Verdict: A structurally flawed puzzle hunt that replaces brilliant investigation with artificial friction. If you don't want to wrestle with clunky point-and-click navigation, unpolished logic tests, and immersion-breaking instant deaths, save yourself the headache and skip this entry entirely.

Tried to play this in 2026 — unsurprisingly, it hasn't aged well for modern displays. If you're on a current setup, expect these problems:

- The clickable hotspots don't line up with the objects they belong to. Your cursor has to sit noticeably away from an item to trigger it, and the offset gets worse toward the edges of the screen.
- Changing the resolution in the settings won't fix it — the misalignment comes from the game's internal coordinate maths, not the resolution itself.
- Because of that, some interactive elements are a real pain to click, and a few end up effectively unreachable.

There are workarounds, atleast according to some forums I stumbled upon but didn't try yet — forcing a 4:3 aspect ratio through your GPU control panel, or using a tool like DxWnd — I wasn't willing to install extra software or fight the game just to play it. Seems like a genuinely good storyline underneath, which is a shame. If Frogwares ever patched the aspect-ratio handling, it'd be worth another look.

I didn't quite plan on writing this review; but I wanted to add a little grain of salt to the varied rating this game has, as I've enjoyed it a good bit. 
For context, this isn't my first approach with the Frogwares Holmes' games. As of writing this, I've played through Crimes and Punishments, Devil's Daughter, Nemesis, Mystery of the Mummy (not thanks to the absolutely horrendous PC port) and Jack the Ripper, believing the latter to be the peak of the series. I've also read all classic Doyle stories about the detective pair; so I know what I'm talking about. 
This game is... tedious. Especially at the start there are a good deal of details you can very easily miss due to them being blended into the backgrounds, the controls are orthopedic at best (who the fuck thought was a good idea to do timed puzzles in such a game??? And there's two of them???), and the story can get feel very convoluted, making one get lost easily. 
Ah, but I did say I enjoyed it, didn't I? With all my frustrations about it, I found it quite fun. Investigating around, making theories on my own... the game itself does have positive things, too. Sherlock and Watson feel just like this script was wrote by Doyle himself; something all Frogwares games get right is their characterization. I really liked the graphic aspect too, although it may be because I found the old looks charming. Some of the puzzles are really good, too; I especially enjoyed the checkboard one. As I'm Spanish, I played this with the Spanish dub; quite a good one as well. The story, while convoluted, is generally interesting and it pays off quite well at the end. I really liked the long cutsenes as well, it felt just like seeing Holmes and Watson's shenanigans all over again. 
In general, this isn't the best work in regards of Holmes games. You aren't really missing out on anything big if you decide to skip it; but if you decide to play it, and take into account the old design choices, I think you'll find a charming little adventure inside.

[h1][b] Reseña de Sherlock Holmes: The Silver Earring[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Sherlock Holmes: The Silver Earring es una aventura clásica de apuntar y clic donde tu trabajo no es “sentirte detective”, sino serlo: revisar escenas, juntar pistas y comerte rompecabezas con cara de “esto en 2004 era normal, cállate”. Es misterio puro con vibra retro, de esos que no te llevan de la manita con un marcador gigante diciendo “PRESIONA AQUÍ PARA PENSAR”.

La propuesta es simple y (casi) elegante: investigar, deducir, avanzar. La primera impresión es la de un museo interactivo: encantador, un poco tieso, y con ese aroma a juego viejo que te da nostalgia… o alergia, según tu tolerancia al género Aventura.

[h2]Lo Elemental (y lo No Tan Elemental)[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Misterio y detectiveo bien al centro: si viniste a investigar, aquí se investiga.  
  Rompecabezas con intención: no todo es “clic a todo”, hay que pensar (a veces de más).  
  Apuntar y clic retro cumplidor: directo, sin inventar sistemas raros para “modernizarse”.  
  Buen sabor a época: se siente como aventura clásica, con su ritmo y su estilo.  

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Cero logros: Steam te mira y te dice “¿y tu dopamina artificial, campeón?”   
  Comunidad miniatura: 10 jugadores actuales; básicamente una reunión familiar silenciosa.  
  Retro… y se nota: si esperas comodidades modernas, este juego te responde con una pipa y un “no”.  
  Rejugabilidad limitada: una vez resuelto el misterio, el truco ya se vio (a menos que te guste sufrir igual dos veces).

[h2]Conclusión (Bueno)[/h2]
Sherlock Holmes: The Silver Earring es de esos juegos que no intentan caerte bien: te suelta el caso, te deja pensar y espera que estés a la altura. Si te gustan las aventuras de misterio y el apuntar y clic de toda la vida, aquí hay una experiencia competente, con rompecabezas que no piden permiso.

Ahora, seamos controversiales: no es “una joya olvidada”, es un juego correcto con edad encima. Y con 10 jugadores actuales, está más cerca de ser un club secreto que una plaza pública. Aun así, 647 recomendaciones totales sugieren que, para su nicho, el juego sí cumple lo que promete.

І це не тому, що загадки геніальні, просто логіка розробника іноді живе окремим життям.

Ще один біль - піксельхантинг, і тут, думаю, пояснювати нічого не треба. Але найбільше дратує те, що гра взагалі не попереджає про критичні моменти. Немає автозбереження, немає натяку, що зараз варто зберегтись. Прогавив - перепроходь від останнього сейву, навіть якщо це була ціла глава тому. Мені саме так і довелось втратити купу часу просто через те, що гра вирішила нічого не пояснювати.

Атмосфера не вразила, але й не розчарувала. Класичний Шерлок, класичний Лондон, очікуваний антураж. Сам Шерлок для мене був радше функціональним героєм, а не персонажем, до якого сильно прив’язуєшся. Зате діалоги між ним і Ватсоном - окрема насолода. Їхні перепалки, репліки, стиль спілкування - це той шматок гри, який тішив.

Попри всі недоліки, я не шкодую, що пройшла її. Вона складна, дратівлива, місцями нечесна до гравця, але саме в цьому є її дивний шарм. Ти відчуваєш себе детективом, який не просто дивиться катсцени, а продирається через купу дивної логіки, аби докопатися до істини.

Я б радила цю гру тим, хто любить старі квести, багато тексту, дивні загадки і детективи, де треба думати. Але якщо вам потрібен сучасний, інтуїтивний і комфортний геймплей - краще проходьте повз. Це не гра, це маленьке випробування на впертість.

Я не люблю користуватись гайдами і зазвичай впираюсь до останнього. Але тут чесно визнаю - без них я б не дійшла до фіналу. Тож усім, хто захоче пройти самостійно, бажаю сильних нервів, світлого розуму і вчасних сейвів!

I have very recently gone through the entirety of Frogwares Sherlock Holmes games in release order. In the grand scheme of the series I rank this as sixth (out of the ten main games) best in the series altogether. i do have a lot of affection for it however quite a few of the games released after this one are phenomenal 3d point and clicks in my opinion and it is not a discredit to this game that it does not rank as highly. I do think this would be a good starting point for a lot of people into the series considering I don't think anyone should play the previous game (Mystery of the Mummy) unless they can get it to run on old hardware and it does a good job of setting up gameplay expectations for the games after this.

I will say as a caveat that this game is a bit dated however I personally enjoy old 3d Point and Click jank but I do acknowledge that not everyone will be willing to put up with that frustration. I however rank this higher than a lot of other 3d Point and clicks of the time. There is a bit of Pixel searching where you drag the mouse back and forth over the scene many times to ensure you didn't miss anything but in general it will not let you advance through the game unless you have everything. There is one exception to that rule however I feel like one moment of being able to softlock yourself isn't that bad considering this is very early into Frogwares repertoire and it is a problem you never see again after this.

Just... don't forget to get the picture from sitting room on the first day.

In terms of gameplay it is a typical point and click. There however is one sneak scene that I did find frustrating and you will probably have to redo the same thing multiple times before getting through, I highly recommend looking up a video guide at this point just to see where and when to click and then still try a few times before getting it. 

It does however do a good job at making you feel as if you are solving a mystery, clues are sprinkled throughout the story and I found myself pondering over motives and the evidence. You will look at and run chemical tests to discover what things are. It really feels like you're investigating. At the end of each day you have to put together evidence to support your answers to questions in a quiz so it does keep you from getting too far off-track as I feel you would without a bit of a guiding hand. It felt satisfying to get to the end and figure out the crime. It doesn't feel as if I had simply watched Sherlock solve it but rather as if I had actually assisted in the conclusion which I feel is a distinction that a lot of Detective point and clicks games tend to miss.

I also feel like it would not be fair to mention that it did take a bit of effort to run without bugs, as I mentioned I ran through DXWnd to solve clicking glitches where it felt like my clicks did not register on the right space. It does run without it but it was with some frustration. For the best experience there is some troubleshooting required however it was considerably less than I had to do for the previous game and really, once I ran through DXWnd I had no problems. Just read through the discussions in the community tab and you should be able to fix any problems you have, 

In conclusion : decent 3d Point and Click for the time. Some PIxel Hunting but I personally didn't mind. Some troubleshooting needed but not as bad as some older games can have. Some frustrating gameplay mechanics but also some really good ones. If you can put up with some jank I feel like the story/deduction aspect makes up for the downsides. If you're a fan of Old Point and Clicks of the early 00's I would definitely recommend this one.

Clunkiness aside, I think the game did well enough with the investigative aspects and I was about to give it a favourable score until I got to the end. 

The story is too spread out with too many suspects and too many moving parts to offer a satisfying experience of solving the mystery on the player's side. Even if you can point in the right direction you don't have enough information to fill in the blanks -- especially when some of the details are unintentionally misleading and the revelations absurd.

"Secret of the Silver Earring" is the second game in the Frogwares Sherlock Holmes franchise. Consider this the real start of the series though, because it introduces the Sherlock Holmes character model and voice actor that will be used through the next three titles: "Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened," "Sherlock Holmes: Nemesis," and "Sherlock Holmes vs. Jack the Ripper." It is also the first game to include Dr. John Watson, and the first to show Holmes and Watson's apartment at 221 Baker Street. Although "Silver Earring" is the debut for a quadrilogy of Sherlock Holmes adventures, it is stylistically unique within the franchise.

"Silver Earring's" predecessor, "Mystery of the Mummy," was a first-person, point-and-click escape room game that uses anchor points to navigate around each room. The two games have very little in common beyond Holmes' items satchel and a phalanx of logic puzzles to solve.

"Silver Earring" is a third-person detective game. Holmes moves to the waypoints the player directs him to, which takes some getting used to but is quickly mastered. Much of the game requires interviewing an expanding list of witnesses; finding relevant documents; processing evidence; and deducing facts from all of the available clues. There is little action, although  Holmes will sometimes have to sprint to complete challenges. 

There are minor visual glitches that sometimes cause characters to not match the perspective of the scene. These don't affect gameplay, and while the graphical anomalies are sometimes jarring if not amusing when encountered, they don't affect gameplay.

The pacing is meticulous and formal, like a Victorian-era period piece on PBS Masterpiece Theater. The sleuthing requires digesting numerous testimonies and reading stacks of letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The mystery becomes convoluted with suspects and possible motives, and it takes an almost superhuman memory to keep track of it all. And in the end, deducing the right conclusion is a feat only Sherlock Holmes can accomplish.

This game has aged better than some of Frogwares' other titles, mechanically speaking. It's pretty fun, if straightforward, although some of the details of the final deduction are frankly impossible for the player to figure out on their own, which is probably why this game lets you see the ending cutscene even if you get the last quiz wrong.

Unlike some of the later titles, this is just one big convoluted case, so I'd advise playing through this in as few sittings as possible so you don't lose the thread of the plot.

Some people really despise the quiz mechanic, and I can imagine it's painful if you haven't got a clue which answer you got wrong, but these questions are really not that hard to think through. Just look up a guide if you're stuck.

Oh, and save often. The game doesn't crash, but it has a few obnoxious sections that can lead to a game over.

Po ograniu ostatnimi laty całkiem sporej ilości przygodówek, które albo utrzymane są w baśniowych klimatach, albo polegają na odnalezieniu jakiegoś starożytnego skarbu przy okazji zwiedzając pół świata miło jest zagrać w przygodówkę w której prowadzimy śledztwo, a tereny po których się poruszamy to głównie Londyn i jego okolice.

Szkoda, że zabrakło jakiegoś samouczka, który zapoznałby nas z możliwościami detektywa. Nie są one może jakieś skomplikowane, ale sami musimy się domyślić, iż w pewnych momentach trzeba skorzystać z lupy, probówki czy taśmy mierniczej, którą Holmes ma w ekwipunku. Śledztwo trwa pięć dni, a każdy z nich jest dość podobny. Na początku przesłuchujemy wszystkich w danej lokacji, zbieramy dowody. Gra wypuści nas wtedy gdy zbadamy wszystko, nie ma więc obaw, że gdzieś utkniemy, bo coś pominęliśmy. Później Sherlock Holmes i doktor Watson wracają na Baker Street 221b, gdzie dokładniej badają zebrane dowody np. korzystając z książek czy przeprowadzając proste testy w laboratorium. Na koniec musimy rozwiązać quiz składający się z kilku pytań odpowiadając Tak lub Nie, dodatkowo każdą podpowiedź musimy poprzeć odpowiednim dowodem. Ułatwieniem jest tutaj kolor ramki w której umieszczamy dowód. Niebieski dla przesłuchania, zielony dla dokumentów, listów i innej papierologii jaką znaleźliśmy, czerwony dla notatek Sherlocka, gdzie zamieszcza swoje spostrzeżenia odnośnie wartych uwagi rzeczy np. śladów butów czy różnych przedmiotów znalezionych w danym miejscu. Po udanym dobraniu zebranych dowodów i prawidłowych odpowiedziach na każde z pytań dany dzień się kończy i zwykle oglądamy cut-scenkę.

Zagadki są w miarę ciekawe, choć do niektórych przydałoby się jakieś dodatkowe naprowadzenie. Mało jest tutaj łączenia ze sobą przedmiotów w ekwipunku, jedynie czasem trzeba np. przeciąć coś nożem. Regularnie natomiast używamy wspomnianej lupy, probówki czy taśmy mierniczej na różnych obiektach. Czasem naturalnie zdarza się utknąć jeśli nie dostrzeżemy jakiegoś małego przedmiotu czy nie zbadamy mokrych śladów butów, które jakoś nie wyróżniają się zanadto. Kilka razy zdarzyło się też, iż jakiś przedmiot można było użyć dopiero w określonym momencie, więc choć go wcześniej zauważyłem to później nie zwracałem na niego uwagi skoro okazał się nieaktywny. Twórcy mogli też sobie podarować etap w lesie w którym można się zgubić i na dodatek jest tam czasówka, gdzie trzeba w tym labiryncie dość szybko się przemieszczać. Im bliżej końca tym fabuła prowadzona jest coraz bardziej pospiesznie. Sam tytułowy srebrny kolczyk pojawia się dopiero pod koniec gry. Cały czas miałem wrażenie, że detektyw wie więcej niż ja, mimo, iż się w niego wcielałem. Na koniec poza zwyczajowym quizem możemy rozwiązać dodatkowy quiz odpowiadając na pytania kto stał za poszczególnymi morderstwami, gdyż sir Bromsby nie jest jedyną ofiarą. W każdym przypadku mamy do wyboru chyba wszystkie postaci jakie pojawiły się w grze. Tego quizu nie trzeba rozwiązywać. Tak czy siak i tak oglądamy niemal 25-minutowy film w którym Sherlock Holmes szczegółowo wyjaśnia całą intrygę. Od słuchania tego aż mnie rozbolała głowa. Myślę, że zagadka mogłaby być mniej skomplikowana tak by gracz też mógł poczuć satysfakcję z jej rozwiązania.

Jeśli chodzi o działanie na Win10 to nie odnotowałem większych problemów. Jedynie zdarzają się babole graficzne z wyświetlaniem niektórych postaci zwłaszcza z oddali. Mamy wrażenie, że lewitują albo chodzą po ścianach. Zapewne ma to związek z rozdzielczością i błędnym nakładaniem się dwuwymiarowych teł z trójwymiarowymi postaciami. Nie przeszkadza to jednak w rozgrywce, trzeba się do tego przyzwyczaić. W grze usłyszymy utwory m.in. Dvořáka, Czajkowskiego, Griega czy Schumanna. Muzyka mogłaby być nieco bardziej różnorodna, bo jak siedzimy za długo w danej lokacji to może znużyć.

Po tych wszystkich przygodówkach rozgrywających się w fantastycznych światach jak The Longest Journey, Dreamfall, The Whispered World czy zwłaszcza po słabym Silence miło było zagrać w coś bardziej przyziemnego. Jest to pierwsza gra z serii ukończona w tym roku, lecz na pewno nie ostatnia. Sherlock Holmes: The Silver Earring to jedna z bardziej satysfakcjonujących przygodówek w jakie ostatnio grałem. Ma dokładnie to czego oczekuję od point&clicka. Już ostrzę sobie zęby na kolejne części.

If you are planning to play this, do consider a walkthrough.

But why then do I still recommend this game? It is because of the type of person who this kind of game appeals to in the first place. If you're even considering playing a 2004 adventure game, you already know to expect these things.
If we ignore these plagues of the time, what we are left with is the competent presentation of an excellent mystery. Though it's a tough one. Indeed, I could not fully figure it out myself, though the clues were all there. Had I sat with it longer, I most likely could have. But alas, I wanted to finish the game within a day. Though there were a couple times that the exact piece of evidence I was supposed to present was not so clear, despite me knowing the answer full well. Again, consider a walkthrough.
