Why can't a game ever bring up 'TRUE CRIME'? Why does it always have to be fictional? I don't get it. Do developers fear lawsuits? Are they not aware how big the 'True Crime' business industry already is? All they have to do is go down to a book store and read. Alas the closest I have played so far to 'True Crime' is 'L.A Noire' and they took a whole range of liberties with that one believe me. 

Mah-jong Investigations is developed by a company which disbanded in 2009 http://www.mobygames.com/company/zemnott-inc . The game is somewhat similar to 'Criminal Case' found on Facebook but take out the Hidden Object Games and replace them with Mah-jong solitaire and instead of watching the case play out entirely itself, here you have to do some very babyish deductive work.

For those that don't know this is 'Mah-jong solitaire' (mah-jong itself is a completely different game) its a puzzle game based on finding the same tile strategy. The goal is to match open pairs of identical tiles and remove them from the board, exposing the tiles under them for play. The game is finished when all pairs of tiles have been removed from the board or when there are no exposed pairs remaining.

This games biggest appeal is also its greatest flaw let me explain. You play as a detective whose ultimate goal is to raise yourself up 10 ranks in the 83rd precinct until you become a 'Deputy Commissioner'. Every time you’re presented with a case and a map with several locations of interest. Once you visit a location a mah-jong solitaire game is laid down and as you match up certain 'special tiles' they have a direct impact on your case and also offers you an extra mini game here and there.

Magnify Glass - Means often mundane information will be presented to you such as there was a country music cd found at the crime scene. Does this have any relevance to the case? No. So you just ignore it.

DNA Pattern - This tile means that some DNA evidence needs to be analysed and you can match up a person's DNA with the evidence found if you would like. It means that you have to play a Tetris style mini game using arrow keys which feels somewhat awkward and long especially if you are checking it out against the wrong person. DNA evidence may not be applicable against perp 1 but it could be applicable against perp 2 or the other half the dozen suspects standing in your queue of queries. So more often than not you will learn to ignore this option.

Police Car - Not sure if this tile is connected but eventually you have to play a minigame each case where the police car is trying to a catch a suspected culprit and you have to link up matching tiles flashed in a trail behind the speeding car or the car gets away. This is actually quite fun at first, but the further you rank up it starts to get ridiculous in speed and time requirements and you soon learn it has no real bearing to the ultimate outcome of your case so you just ignore and let the car just speed away.

Security Camera - Adds additional perpetrators of a crime to your case. Instead of just finding one guy you might now need to find 4. These tiles you can't ignore. The game will request you to find the perps whether you click on them or not.

Fingerprint - These tiles often reveal info more pertinent to your case such as 'perp 1 has blonde hair', problem is that you might have a dozen suspects in your line up with blonde hair, so more often than not you will just learn to ignore this.

Telephone - Not sure if this tile is linked up, but your forever answering the bleeding phone and having people tell you mundane info like 'Barry likes Westerns'. Seriously I'm in the middle of a police chase and someone has to phone up and tell me that. Can't I hire a secretary? Since people lie on the phone, you will learn to completely ignore this facet.

Interrogation - You can play a mini game on each suspect which requires you to play a memory match up game like you have 20 chance to find the pairs to 48 tiles. Basically ridiculously impossible odds and so you will learn to ignore this.

Alibi - Finally the only tile that has a definite bearing on your case. Each time you match up one of these it takes a suspect off your line up because they have revealed a iron clad alibi. Collect enough of these 4 mah-jong solitaire games should do it, you have enough people off your suspect list to work out who committed the crime.

The game with all its additional add-on is dressed up to look like it’s something more than just a mah-jong solitaire game which makes it appealing, but since all those add-ons really don't have a significant impact to your cases you’re really just left with the realization that just playing mah-jong solitaire is your best option if you want to quickly move through the ranks. After about 50 mah-jong solitaire games you start asking yourself will this ever end?

Hence the game’s greatest appeal it's mini games is also its greatest weakness since they have no true bearing and just begin to look like unnecessary clutter. The multiple perps behind this crime is Zemnott. You’re looking for a blonde haired person, a dark brown haired, a bald person, and one who wears glasses, most average build, one tall, and one short, most normal height. Ok now with that info go get them. Wait it seems the culprits made a getaway back in 2009 speeding furiously down the highway, angry customers who hate mah-jong solitaire should start pursuit. HOLD YOUR HORSES! This just in "BARRY LIKES WESTERNS!!!"

MIUS (ça va plus vite) qu'est ce que c'est ? C'est le mahjong solitaire de windows avec une couche d'enquête policière procédurale façon "qui est ce ?", aussi simple que ça.

Dans MIUS, une partie débute sur un crime généré de façon procédurale: quelqu'un (ou plusieurs personnes) fait quelque chose d'illégal et il va falloir le/les arrêter. Le jeu se passe dans une ville, et il y'a plusieurs endroits dans cette ville. Dans chacun, il y'aura des éléments d'enquête à trouver. Et beaucoup d'ordure à virer. 

Uns fois le crime généré, on choisi un endroit dans la ville.
Une fois dans l'endroit désigné, on a un tableau comme dans le mahjong de windows: une disposition aléatoire de pièces de mahjong qu'il va falloir éliminer en faisant des paires. 

Plusieurs sortes de tiles existent:
-les ordures => c'est en travers de ton chemin, il faut les virer et puis c'est tout
-les indices => taille du suspect, couleur de cheveux, sexe, hobby ...
-pouvoir spécial => permet de voir à travers les tiles pour situer où sont les indices 
-la recherche => c'est comme un indice sauf qu'il faudra attendre que le labo finisse son analyse pour savoir ce que tu as trouvé
-l'alibi => permet d'éliminer un personnage des suspects
-la caméra => un indice indirect sur le coupable (on a trouvé des CD de country => le suspect aime la country)

Et il va donc falloir faire des paires pour les éliminer du tableau/débloquer la fonction.

Une bonne idée: avec la pléthore de tiles sur le tableau, ce n'est pas toujours évident de faire une paire, alors il existe le sac. Le sac permet de prendre une tile et de la mettre de coté en attendant de trouver sa moitié. Mais attention, si je prends une tile ordure PUIS une tile indice, pour éliminer la tile ordure je dois d'abord éliminer la tile indice. Un peu de prévision dans ses mouvements est requis. 

Quand on manque d'indice il est possible d'interroger un suspect: pendant un temps limité on va jouer à un jeu de mémoire. Plusieurs tiles sont retournées, face cachées. Il va falloir faire des paires en les retournant une par une. Quand deux tiles sont retournées ET si elles ne forment pas une paire, elles se remettent face cachées, mais tu sais où elles sont ... à toi d'avoir de la mémoire. 

Chaque enquête dure 30 minutes, et il est possible de gagner un peu de temps en vidant complètement un tableau (des fois ça sert de triller toutes les ordures), et au final il y'a un décompte de points et un score, ce qui permet de nous faire grimper les échelons et devenir un gradé. 

Le jeu est très relaxant, tout choupi et très clair dans sa présentation, et j'ai beaucoup de plaisir à y jouer comme j'ai aussi eu beaucoup de plaisir à jouer à Sudokuball Detective (autre jeu casual d'enquête mêlé de jeu de société), parfait pour un après midi de glande, de petites cessions, pour occuper sa gamine ou amuser un adulte qui n'aime spécialement les jeux vidéo. ^^

You unearth clues by playing Mahjongg and use those to arrest criminals. Definitely not worth it for the full price, but on discount it's a fun Mahjongg game with a twist, especially if you enjoy the detective genre.

Absolutely excellent semi-casual game, gives a very good investigation feel and has decent variety.  Each case contains: 

*) Multiple locations to check out, each of which corresponds to a separate mahjong solitaire puzzle.  Solve slightly-easier mahjong to get clues.  Generally, more puzzles are available than you'll need, and you can try to solve the case at any point.
*) Use clues to identify suspects as perpetrators -- there's different kinds.  You can discover new suspects or find alibis that rule out old ones, you might learn facts about the suspects, or the perpetrator, and perpetrator facts are solid enough but vague enough that you actually have to think about it.  What is "average height"?  Obviously the 4'11" girl can go, but what about the 5'9" one?  It strikes a delicate balance.
*) Interrogate suspects for more clues -- which is a Memory minigame with yet more tiles.  Turn over tiles two at a time, trying to find matches.  The better you do, the more facts you get about that suspect -- or, they might even confess under pressure.
*) You have a phone, which occasionally gets anonymous tips or clues from the lab -- which tends to go off when you're busy doing something else, making it mildly (but not terribly) more difficult to concentrate on the puzzles.
*) Smooth and easy to use interface makes the logic puzzle segment a breeze to interact with, while the multiple suspects and the nature of the clues ("at least one suspect has bloodtype AB+" : if there's two suspects, you can't rule out other bloodtypes, but when one suspect has several suspicious traits...) keep things novel and interesting.

It fits a lot of genres I like together into one thing.  Casual puzzles, tacked together with just enough narrative to make each one have meaning and context, and enough variety and inter-relatedness to keep it interesting.
A+!

My only critique is that it could possibly use more suspect portraits, or be more careful about which one gets assigned where (double-chin lady probably shouldn't be described as having a light build, for example), but that's minor.

Let me begin by saying I've played this game in short intervals depending on my time from basically 2007 to now.
I ended up buying the game cheap from a Babbages back in the day at a mall, and I played it on my XP, so I've got a lot of experience in this game and how it works.

- The design is simple. That is why I play it. -

When I was a kid, I didn't want to play Rollercoaster Tycoon and instead prefered '3D games', but I couldn't afford the newest RC when it came out, so I got this instead. It's fun enough for £1 in the steam sale, surely. I can recommend to begin on a big-ish lot and work your way up. Basically, you begin with however big of a budget you need (starts at 10k, I believe), then you select your advertising preferences, ticket prices, and if you give away free tickets. You don't have to do these things, and can play without. These are limited choices, but it's easy for kids to understand. (And people like me, who just kinda wanna play a bit without actual commitment.)

If you play in sandbox mode, which is what I usually do, the game starts you in your empty lot, if you start with 10k, make it simple at first by choosing a cheap-mid range ride, ticket stand, a generator, a sitting area, bin, two food stalls - either food & drink and a ball game. Theres quite a few to choose from, I usually have one of each, starting with a regular soda stand and a burger one, then advancing onwards towards like Ice cream stand and BBQ chicken etc.

This can be your starting first day to make money. Before you begin your day, go to the menu and click maintence to make sure you have a janitor/repair man. He does everything, I usually get two in my first day. turn your speed to 1/2, close stuff, then repair all the items in your grounds before you start. This is a part of the game that is tedious and annoying, but it's fast enough and takes only a minute. Once you do that, make sure things are open (small stuff like tables and bins open automatically but rides you need to do manually) you can begin your day.

Days end around 10pm and you can start again the next day at 1/2 speed, adding more rides, food stalls, or whatever you need.

I usually start with my basics listed above, and then add onwards. Sometimes if my queue is too long for a ride on the first day, I'll buy another ride to fit in. Just watch your budget.

Hot Dish, developed by Zemnott and published by Ziggurat, is a classic casual cooking and time-management game that reflects the design sensibilities of late-2000s PC titles. Built around the fantasy of rising from an inexperienced line cook to a respected culinary professional, the game emphasizes speed, coordination, and rhythm rather than realism or narrative depth. Its structure is straightforward and intentionally accessible, aiming to deliver short, repeatable challenges that test how well players can juggle multiple tasks under pressure.

The core experience revolves around preparing dishes accurately and quickly in increasingly busy kitchens. Players begin in a modest restaurant environment, where the mechanics are introduced gradually through simple recipes and limited multitasking. As progress is made, new restaurants unlock, each themed around different cuisines and expectations, such as more refined or faster-paced kitchens. These new locations introduce more complex recipes and tighter timing windows, steadily increasing the difficulty without dramatically altering the core mechanics. This gradual escalation gives the game a steady sense of progression, even if the structure remains familiar throughout.

Gameplay is driven almost entirely by timing and coordination. Recipes require specific sequences of actions—selecting ingredients, combining them correctly, and completing preparation steps at the right moment. Managing multiple dishes simultaneously is where the challenge truly lies, as players must keep track of several cooking processes at once to ensure that everything is completed on time. Letting one dish overcook or missing a preparation window can cascade into failure when the kitchen becomes crowded with orders. This emphasis on multitasking gives Hot Dish its addictive quality, rewarding players who can maintain focus and develop a strong sense of rhythm.

To keep the experience from becoming entirely monotonous, the game introduces occasional modifiers and power-ups. These temporary boosts can provide brief relief during particularly hectic moments, such as slowing down time or improving cooking efficiency. There are also small diversions layered into the main loop, including moments where players must deal with cleanliness or inspections, which briefly shift attention away from cooking itself. While these additions are not deeply developed systems, they add just enough variation to break up the flow of constant food preparation.

Visually and technically, Hot Dish is unmistakably a product of its era. The graphics are simple and functional, prioritizing clarity over presentation. Ingredients, utensils, and cooking stations are easy to identify, which supports the fast-paced gameplay, but the overall look lacks personality or flair by modern standards. Animations are minimal, and the interface is utilitarian, designed to communicate information quickly rather than impress visually. Sound design follows a similar philosophy, offering basic audio cues that reinforce actions without drawing attention to themselves.

One of the game’s biggest strengths is its immediacy. There is little downtime between actions, and success depends almost entirely on player performance rather than long-term planning or character upgrades. This makes Hot Dish easy to pick up and play in short sessions, particularly appealing to players who enjoy casual challenges without the commitment of learning complex systems. However, this same simplicity can also limit its long-term appeal, as the lack of mechanical evolution may lead to repetition once the core loop is fully understood.

Player reception over time has reflected this divide. Those who enjoy traditional time-management and cooking games often appreciate Hot Dish for its straightforward challenge and nostalgic feel. Others find it dated and lacking in depth compared to more modern cooking simulators that offer richer progression, co-op play, or more expressive presentation. The experience largely depends on expectations: approached as a retro casual title, it delivers competent and occasionally satisfying gameplay; approached as a full-featured simulation, it can feel thin.

Ultimately, Hot Dish stands as a snapshot of an earlier era of casual PC gaming. It offers a focused, skill-based cooking experience built around multitasking and timing rather than storytelling or immersion. While it may not hold up as a genre-defining title today, it still provides a serviceable and sometimes engaging challenge for players who enjoy managing chaos in a virtual kitchen. For those with an appreciation for classic time-management games or a desire for a simple, no-frills cooking experience, Hot Dish remains a modest but recognizable entry in the genre.

First impression: Hot Dish is a decent casual time-management game.

Based on recipes, you cook several dishes simultaneously (the challenge is to finish them quickly and at the same time) and work your way through 3 restaurants and hence through 3 different types of cuisine. There's also some match-3 going on from time to time. The tasks are fairly complex for a time-management game right off the bat, because you have to coordinate the different dishes, but it's still easy to get into.

The game runs at 800x600, and I had trouble getting my stirring properly recognized: for some of the sub-tasks, there is also very little feedback if you did them well, or what you'd need to improve if any. It is also difficult to memorize recipes since you don't do them in order, but you basically have to because dishes need to be done at the same time.

This may be a great game to have on your phone or tablet while waiting at the restaurant, but it didn't really impress me much as a PC game.

This game is about cooking like every other cooking game, but have few points that make it different, mostly in a negative way :

[b]The cooking is not linear[/b]
This is somewhat a good addition and quite realistic. If you are cooking a fried rice it is logical if you are able to cut the fishes first, or cut the vegetables first, both should not matter. But both should be cut before frying them. Thus, this game does it quite correct in mixing between linear and progressive when cooking.

[b]Degradation of materials[/b]
This is very weird. If you finish a food too fast, you will lose the quality of "materials" and your food quality, despite excellent cooking, will be reduced to nothing. And to finish your food in their best quality, all foods should be finished at the same time, to prevent "loss of materials". Strangely, to keep the materials fresh, all you need to do is chop or grill it. Very illogical. Don't you have some freezer or fridge while you are waiting? Also, which restaurant produce three main course at the same time?

Also, there is no explanation on each dish on what process they should take to finish, so you can time it well. Let's say, dish A requires 8 steps, dish B requires 4 steps. So, what you are going to do is finish dish A 4 steps, then synchronize ending with dish B. But in this game, you rely on blind luck.

[b]Low quality graphics[/b]
Even Cooking Mama on Nintendo DS have better quality than this. If you simmer something, you don't "see" what is added. You don't really feel the vegetables that are put into the pan, or the sauce, or anything. The texture is very bad. I can go hungry after playing Cooking Mama on Nintendo DS, but not on this game. 

[b]No Progression[/b]

Dr. Daisy Pet Vet is a delightful veterinary-themed time-management game that combines animal care, fast-paced decision-making, and lighthearted humor into an accessible casual gaming experience. Developed by Zemnott and published by Ziggurat, the game follows Daisy, a newly graduated veterinarian who must complete five professional rotations to finish her residency. Instead of presenting complicated medical procedures or realistic veterinary simulations, it focuses on entertaining challenges that require players to diagnose illnesses, treat animals, and efficiently manage an increasingly demanding workload. Its cheerful atmosphere and straightforward mechanics make it particularly appealing to players who enjoy classic arcade-style management games.

The central premise revolves around helping Dr. Daisy establish herself as a capable veterinarian while traveling between different animal-care facilities. Her journey takes her through five distinct environments: a pet clinic, farm, bird sanctuary, sea park, and zoo. Each location introduces different animals and situations, creating a satisfying sense of professional advancement. Although the storyline is relatively simple, the changing environments provide enough variety to keep the experience engaging. The progression from treating ordinary household pets to handling exotic wildlife gives the adventure a charming sense of accomplishment.

Gameplay emphasizes speed, organization, and efficient multitasking. Players must guide Daisy through veterinary responsibilities while ensuring that animals receive the attention and treatment they require. The time-management mechanics encourage quick thinking, careful prioritization, and increasingly effective strategies as the workload becomes more demanding. What begins as a relatively relaxed experience gradually develops into a hectic series of challenges where maintaining efficiency becomes essential. This familiar gameplay structure should appeal to enthusiasts of restaurant-management and other service-oriented simulation games.

One of the game's most substantial features is its collection of 50 levels spread across five veterinary locations. This provides a respectable amount of content for a casual title, particularly when combined with the different environments and animal patients. Each stage contributes to the overall progression while encouraging players to improve their performance. However, the fundamental gameplay loop remains largely consistent throughout the adventure. Although this repetition can be satisfying for players who enjoy mastering established routines, those seeking constantly evolving mechanics may eventually find the experience somewhat predictable.

The inclusion of 30 different animals adds considerable personality to the adventure. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional veterinary patients, the game introduces a humorous assortment of creatures suffering from unusual medical conditions. Chickens develop chickenpox, bald eagles experience feather loss, cows struggle with lactose intolerance, and flamingos suffer from pink eye. These exaggerated illnesses highlight the game's playful approach to animal medicine and help distinguish it from more serious veterinary simulations. The amusing diagnoses also make the experience particularly approachable for younger audiences and players who appreciate whimsical humor.

Another appealing element is the variety of diagnostic devices, medical equipment, treatment contraptions, and unconventional cures incorporated into the veterinary activities. These tools reinforce the medical theme while giving players different responsibilities to manage. Upgrades are also available at individual locations, allowing improvements that can accelerate gameplay and personalize the facilities. Although the upgrade system does not offer the complexity of a dedicated business-management simulator, it introduces an additional sense of progression and rewards players for improving their efficiency.

Visually, Dr. Daisy Pet Vet embraces a colorful, cheerful presentation that complements its humorous subject matter. Its environments and animal characters prioritize clarity and accessibility over sophisticated graphical effects. This approach works well for a game centered on identifying patients and responding quickly to their needs. Nevertheless, the presentation feels noticeably dated compared with modern casual simulations. Players expecting detailed character animations, elaborate environments, or contemporary interface design may find its visual simplicity less impressive.

The game's greatest strength is its ability to transform ordinary veterinary responsibilities into entertaining time-management challenges. Its approachable mechanics make it easy to understand, while the increasing pace provides opportunities for players to develop better strategies. However, its limited narrative depth, repetitive activities, and relatively straightforward progression prevent it from offering the complexity found in more ambitious simulation games. The experience is best appreciated as a focused casual adventure rather than a realistic representation of veterinary practice.

From a technical standpoint, the game has exceptionally modest system requirements, making it theoretically suitable for low-powered computers. However, its reliance on older Windows technologies, including DirectX 9 and a listed Flash Player dependency, raises potential compatibility concerns with contemporary operating systems. These outdated requirements may necessitate troubleshooting, particularly for players using modern hardware. The game supports single-player gameplay and offers interface localization in several languages, including English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish.

Regarding Steam Deck compatibility, Dr. Daisy Pet Vet has an Unknown compatibility status, meaning it has not received an official Steam Deck Verified or Playable designation. Its lightweight graphics and relatively simple gameplay suggest that the hardware itself should not be a major obstacle. However, compatibility with Proton, older software dependencies, and possible control-mapping requirements remain uncertain. Players should therefore approach Steam Deck installation cautiously, as reliable functionality cannot be guaranteed without testing or additional configuration.

Overall, Dr. Daisy Pet Vet delivers an enjoyable combination of animal-themed humor, accessible time-management mechanics, and progressively demanding veterinary challenges. Its diverse collection of patients, five distinctive locations, and equipment upgrades provide a pleasant sense of variety and advancement. Although repetitive gameplay, dated presentation, and technical compatibility concerns limit its broader appeal, the game retains considerable charm for enthusiasts of traditional casual management experiences. It is particularly suitable for players seeking a relaxing yet occasionally hectic veterinary adventure without complicated systems or demanding controls.

The interesting thing about Dr. Daisy Pet Vet is not that it's attempting to be a top down business simulator/tycoon/tablet clicker game, but that it's a horrible tablet-port tier clicker game released in 2008, years before the massive influx of tablet games showed up and permanently lowered the general level of quality of video games by several orders of magnitude. 

Run a vet clinic, not by understanding animal care or anything, but by clicking mindlessly on the screen repeatedly with no real method or skill necessary.

First, a note: This game seems to have serious functionality issues in Windows 10. Or, at least it does on my system. No matter what compatibility setting I use, it still only runs for a short while before crashing. Fortunately though, I did play it a bit on my old Windows 8 computer, so the small amount of refresher time was enough to at least feel able to leave a fair review.

As far as the gameplay goes: it is a time management game. Unfortunately, it does it in the worst way. That is, while this is marketed as a veterinary game, the gameplay is literally just rapidly clicking as fast as you possibly can. You basically click the animal once to evaluate them, and then go to the medicine cabinet to get a syringe, then click the animal again to give them the shot. Sometimes there's a contagious disease that requires hand-washing or the need to go grab the x-ray machine to use on some patients, but even then, it's all just rapid clicking. This is a game that would have gained so much from the inclusion of mini-games or even just different diagnosis/treatment possibilities, or something. Plus, the "upgrades" are insufficient. You quickly get up to having six beds to make use of, spread across the room, but you can't move that far quickly enough to not make it seem more like a chore rather than fun in trying to reach the goal score.

Educational value-wise, I'd say there's really none, though it tries in some ways in-game to pretend otherwise. Granted, it isn't marketed as such in the store, so I can't fault it much for that. Though I would suggest that adding some real educational value would have helped the game a LOT - even if only by making it be a great game for kids.

The graphics and such are pretty much what one expects from such games, so I don't fault those. The main problem, really, is that it just doesn't take advantage of what it could have been.

你是否是最强车手？在计时赛模式（Time Trial mode）中，与全球车手比拼最快圈速
在内容丰富的生涯模式（Career mode）中，你将化身赛车车队老板：招募车手、签约赞助商、购置赛车，并对车辆进行调校与性能升级

[h1]Racing[/h1]

The "RPM Tuning" (original name of the game) refers to the game's main draw, which is the ability to customize your cars like crazy. Each car can be tweaked mechanically and aesthetically with all sorts of body kits, wheels, engines, exhaust systems, and such, all of which can be bought and placed on your car.

The actual racing doesn't do much to salvage the game. The one thing you can't complain about are the controls, which handle reasonably well. There are some issues with drifts spinning out, even when you aren't really traveling all that fast, and the collision detection is random, to say the least. But otherwise, the cars handle fine. The most obnoxious thing about races involves the blatantly obvious rubber-band artificial intelligence. It actually works both ways, though. If you're way behind, the game will let you catch up to your opponents.

As a result, the positive aspects have more weight overall than the negative aspects. But “RPM Tuning” is just as far away from been a masterpiece, as it's far away from being called a failure, so that we find ourselves pretty much in the middle of the field. 
[h3][hr][i]The PC version of 'RPM Tuning' offers some interesting ideas and it's fun for some short time, but ultimately lacks variety and a modern presentation. Only hardcore tuning fans should take a look.[/i][/hr][/h3]

Midnight Outlaw: 6 Hours to Sun Up, developed by Merscom and Babylon and published by Cosmi Valusoft, stands as a clear product of its time—born during the height of early-2000s street-racing enthusiasm, when neon-lit drag races, swaggering underground crews, and nitrous-fueled highway duels dominated gaming culture. Though now available on Steam, the game very much reflects its mid-2000s budget PC roots, presenting a dramatic, cinematic framing of illegal nighttime racing condensed into a single adrenaline-charged night. The premise is simple but effective: as an up-and-coming street racer seeking money, reputation, and machinery powerful enough to survive until sunrise, you must climb through a series of events, rival encounters, and story beats that stitch the racing together. The framing suggests high stakes and dangerous momentum, even if the execution rarely reaches that intensity.

Structurally, the game blends traditional circuit races, sprint challenges, police escapes, and quarter-mile drags. On paper, this variety should create a constantly shifting experience, but the repetition becomes noticeable early on. Track layouts and environments tend to reappear with slightly altered routes, creating a sense of déjà vu as you progress. Still, the core loop—race, earn cash, buy upgrades, race again—carries a familiar and comforting rhythm for players who enjoy progression-driven racers. The customization system, though limited by modern standards, attempts to emulate the era’s tuning culture, allowing changes to engines, nitrous systems, tires, and cosmetics. Watching a car gradually evolve into a more aggressive, faster machine remains one of the game’s more satisfying components, capturing a small slice of what made the genre so appealing during that decade.

However, the moment-to-moment driving reveals the game’s most persistent flaws. Vehicle physics are stiff and unwieldy, producing sliding, bouncing, or tank-like steering responses that lack weight or nuance. Instead of feeling like you’re controlling a highly tuned street machine, the cars often behave like unstable boxes careening across the asphalt. Collisions exacerbate this, triggering exaggerated flips, sudden losses of control, or a complete reset of race momentum. The sense of speed—a crucial component of any street racer—comes and goes, never consistently capturing the breathless thrill the premise promises. For some players, this unpredictability adds unintentional comedy; for others, it becomes a barrier to enjoyment. The controls were clearly designed for older PC setups, and without modern refinements, they struggle to meet contemporary expectations.

The presentation also reflects the technological limitations of the time. Environments are sparsely detailed, traffic density is low, lighting is flat compared to today’s standards, and textures often appear repetitive. Yet there is an earnest attempt to create atmosphere: distant city skylines, highway signage, industrial zones, and nighttime color palettes suggest a world that could have felt immersive with more development resources. The narrative, delivered through FMV-style cutscenes and stylized dialogue, aims to emulate the melodrama of street-racing movies, complete with betrayals, swaggering rivals, and a gritty sense of nocturnal rebellion. Though the acting and writing have aged into camp, they provide amusement and personality, making the game memorable in ways it may not have intended.

Technical performance introduces additional complications. Because the title was built for operating systems and hardware from two decades ago, modern compatibility is hit-or-miss. Many Steam users report crashes, audio issues, graphical glitches, or complete failure to launch without community fixes or compatibility tweaks. Even when running smoothly, the game’s optimization feels archaic—frame pacing can fluctuate, input responsiveness may lag, and repeated loading interruptions disrupt immersion. These issues may be manageable for patient retro gaming enthusiasts, but they understandably frustrate casual players who expect plug-and-play reliability.

Where Midnight Outlaw manages to retain value is as a curiosity—a preserved artifact of the era when the market was hungry for street-racing games and even lower-budget developers attempted bold entries into the genre. It captures the aesthetic trends, mechanical assumptions, and cultural fascinations of the period, and for some players, that alone is entertaining. The low price point helps soften expectations, allowing it to be experienced as a short nostalgic detour rather than a serious contender in racing game history. For collectors, genre historians, or those who vividly remember discount-rack PC racing games from the mid-2000s, it may even feel oddly comforting.

Ultimately, Midnight Outlaw: 6 Hours to Sun Up is a game defined by ambition outpacing execution. It aims for cinematic street-racing energy but lacks the mechanical polish, visual fidelity, or structural variety needed to fully deliver it. As a modern racing experience, it struggles to compete with virtually any contemporary title. But as a time capsule—flawed, scrappy, and unapologetically tied to its moment—it offers a kind of rough-edged charm. Enjoyment will hinge almost entirely on expectations: approach it as a retro curiosity with modest goals, and it may deliver a few hours of scrappy fun. Expect a gripping, polished racing experience, and sunrise will arrive long before satisfaction does.

This is my review of this game titled: Midnight Outlaw 6 Hours To Sunup.

Ok I want to start off by saying that I indeed bought this game on steam and when proceeded to download and install and launched I was quite surprised to find out that another game similar to this is named - Top Gear RPM Tuning and is exactly the same game. Now both games have issues working proper on modern day windows/systems (beware people) and mind the other reviews on here about this one because whatever issues it has with newer operating systems (as mentioned) they are very true. However I did get the game to work with no problems but you must jump thru hoops in order to do so, skipping the video intro sequence by pushing the "return key" on the keyboard is a essential action to do so then the game won't crash (most times) and setting compatibility modes are necessary. Now the biggest issue as far as running this game on the current hardware that I have "when actually playing it" is the maps graphics walls/structures/scenery seem to disappear at will, almost seems like the game is drawing the stuff on the map on the go? But again that alone is a sign of a very old game the way it was created. The way this is fixed as a quick solution is by hitting the cars nitro, as this lights up the screen and somehow that triggers the drawing of the game's graphics to render faster then the track and everything around you comes into full view again (for a couple of seconds) and then you must hit nitro again over and over each and everytime the graphics/track disappears just to rectify that problem. Aside from those issues mentioned above here is some good things about this game, surprisingly for how old this game really is it did recognize my Logitech wireless controller which I thought it would never be able to do. Also this is a fun street racing game to play, for its generation and considering back in the day it might have been impressive to look at at one point. If you see the screenshots and videos of this and you think it looks cool - Your not mistaken. Infact to be honest I actually played it (quick race mode) for a little while (despite all the problems mentioned above) and it did keep me entertained for the most part. Underneath all the huge unplayability factors is a nice little street racing game "that needs to updated majorly to fit today's standards" with lots of cool features to have fun with. Valusoft prob won't do any updates anytime soon with this game anymore since the company might have went belly up out of business a long time ago, and if someone had the time to fix it (as a personal project) they would have already done it by now a long time ago. But the problem is no one really cared about this game when it was abandoned so a lot of time would be put in to rectify all the above and I guess no one feels it is important enough to follow up on. Some of the creators that are still around are prob very aware of the universal issues with the different hardware and the game's compatibility issues with newer windows and such, but they do not feel its something they must do to try to make a competitor out of this with the current market of "newer" racing games with nicer graphics and gameplay that are relevant and available these days - I honestly don't blame them.      

What else is there to say?

The cars handle well with good comfortable arcade like style physics/controls. The maps are nice but a little bland for my taste. The music being played per race is catchy and pretty standard dance tracks (not sure if they are real dance tacks or just composed by a random person). Then there is the other cars you see your opponents driving that look powerful and fast enough to win by a landslide but the AI in this game proves that theory wrong. The amount of cars available in this game to drive are not a vast whole lot to choose from so its really up to you how you wanna tune them and that part I found really innovative though as there a are at least 3 or 4 different upgrades for each tier of car parts. Like I said there is a hidden gem here but only if someone has the time to find it and remodel this gem.

BTW: I do have RPM Tuning as well it is on Abandonware site for download. The only thing is the graphics glitches (mentioned above earlier) which I will try and see if I can tinker with that. With that all being said I really hope that one day someone can update this game to be working on newer hardware as intended but that day won't come. Leaving this game as it is with the graphics glitchy - it looks like the whole city got hit by an atomic bomb.

I won't recommend this to anyone to download just because the fact it has not been updated/formatted to work on modern systems and the price tag of this should be a lot lower if not, even free dare I say. Its a nice fun street racer game but really old and games that are this old should not have a heavy price tag on them just because of the universal compatibility issues alone.

[h1]Main review[/h1]
Runs on Windows 7 Pro 64-bit without needing any compatibility setting. Slight problem with the start-up flash screens; right side is cut off.

No Anti-Aliasing supported in-game, had to force it in Radeon Crimson driver setting. Not sure if it makes any difference. Runs smoothly at 60fps. Highest top 2 resolutions are 1280 x 1024 and 1280 x 768.

Seems to be glitchy with random crashes but rectified that by unloading unncessary processes and services. Will update later if random crashes still persist.

One cutcene encountered so far with missing sounds that maybe due to missing sound files.

Very similar to NFS Underground 2 except that there is no replay but the cutscenes are fully 3D rendered using game engine and with voice acting.

Cars are recognizable to real world models but only approximated. No dashboard view. Not as arcady as NFS series which is notorious for their strong autobrake under low throttle. Damage modelling cannot be turned off; dunno if it's only visual or have physics impact.

From the Main Menu there is Quick Race, Adventure and Tuning & Race modes. Adventure mode is subdivided into Tuning, Cars, Free Roam and Story modes. Haven't tried other modes yet except Free Roam and Adventure modes. In Free Roam there doesn't seem to be anything to do other than explore. I have not seen any hotspots like workshops or car showroom in Free Roam like in NFS Underground 2. Maybe because it's too early in the Adventure mode?

There is only one savegame where you can use autosave or manual save.

[b]Graphics[/b] look okay for its age but some building textures look horrible. You'll notice that especially in the cutscenes. Reflection and lighting effects are quite nice. Again they are similar to NFS underground 1 & 2, i think. There are several camera views during race but some aren't practical because they are placed in front and to the side making them risky to use while driving. The cameras can only be cycled with the Tab key and the default camera view is too close to rear end while its narrow FOV makes it a bit difficult to see what's up ahead going into corners. There is another slightly higher chase view which has marginally better FOV.

There are many race [b]music[/b] tracks but they are typical of hard driving rythmic music similar to most NFS 2 to 7 series. There is no media player control to select or deselect music tracks, it plays tracks at random exept in the menus in which only one track is looped. Thankfully the menu music is quite nice and not so monotonous.

Overall it's quite fun and there is a lot of depth to car customisation. The story mode is better than NFSU 2 because it uses  fully 3D animated characters within the game world with good voice acting. For the above reasons and the slighly better than NFS driving physics i give it 7/10. However the lack of replay brings it down 6.5/10.

This game turned out to be a hidden gem for me and a gateway to golden sweet nostalgia from the good old times. A majority of the content is so well done with a great passion for details but of course there are a few flaws as well.

✅ Timeless visual artstyle with a beautiful scenery and a lot of model creativity.
✅ The soundtrack is just wonderful, dreamy and atmospheric. A perfect fantasy fit.
✅ The entire vibe and mistery of the established game world and plot feels archaic in a very sweet way, but also deep and ancient and it pulled me a lot.
✅ The game takes a LOT of time in everything what youre doing and its one of the few where its actually a really good thing. Everything has animations, looting, skinning, taking a plant or lockpicking and and and and it rolls on your skill checks and in the whole picture its just so relaxing in a way i can hardly describe but its GOOD.
✅ Controls, systems and stats are quickly understandable even if you never play such games.
✅The followers and different archetypes that you gotta combine to get a good flow in combat are really interesting and motivational.
✅ Boss fights are fun and interesting and reward you with nice gear as well
✅ I love how every piece of gear is visible both on the characters as well in their little icons and theres a good bunch of unique gear and particular weapons with special effects that felt rewarding to find and mess with. So progression overall in levelups and skills, gear and economy..all of that really hooked me. Its simple but feels very satisfying.
✅ Rolls on dodge and parry got actual animations where characters block hits with their shields or weapons or dodge out of the way, dope detail! Sadly doesnt work for every enemy type.
✅ Multiple interesting maps and cities each with their own stories and vast handplaced details.
✅ There are a ton of small and funny sidequests that are very memorable and even if theyre super fetch like they still tell their own tale and rarely feel truly generic. These also pop up again and again in new "chapters" in already visited hub worlds. 
✅ The main plot is alright. Its not crazy and it falls of towards the end a lot but atleast the first half was a lot of fun. 

❌ Requires manual fixing to even get it to start today. In my case it was pretty simple just typing a code into the starting commands for the game launch and it was fine afterwards.
❌ While the overworlds are always handcrafted and particular pretty much the opposite goes for dungeons. Especially ferdok underground tunnels that you also find in multiple castles, ruins and graveyards ALWAYS look exactly the same and theyre waaaay too long and man it just feels tedious af. One of the worst parts of the game and its really not fun.
❌ The ending is really bad. Not directly by plot which is okay but the entire gameplay aspect behind it, firstup with some mindless puzzles that never occured before followed by a mountaintop with an endless hardcore mob spawner that you cant fight through, and instead being forced to just tank the wave to hit the spawner is very bad.
❌ The camera is pretty weird to control in a few situations and gets floaty af
❌ Most of the dialogue isnt voiced so you gotta read a lot

All in all i had a blast playing this game. I somehow never noticed its existence despite being literally what i was searching so desperately in the past few years being a oldschool rpg nostalgic dude. Its one of the best rpgs i have ever played despite its flaws and it has such a beautiful and immersive core. Really recommend anyone interested who is fine with doing a little research and how to get it to run.

Drakensang is a traditional party-based fantasy RPG that rewards patience, careful character development, and tactical thinking rather than fast reflexes. Developed by Radon Labs and published by DTP Entertainment, it is based on The Dark Eye tabletop role-playing system and adapts version 4.0 of its rules for a computer RPG. This tabletop foundation gives the game considerably more mechanical depth than its straightforward fantasy appearance might initially suggest. It is a game about understanding statistics, developing specialized characters, assembling a balanced group, and gradually mastering a fairly elaborate collection of interconnected systems.

Character development is easily one of the highlights. Instead of reducing progression to basic improvements in health, damage, and defense, Drakensang provides more than 40 spells, over 30 talents, and almost 40 special abilities. The expert character creation option gives experienced players additional freedom to customize their protagonist, while the broader selection of archetypes makes the system manageable for newcomers. Progression feels meaningful because talents are useful outside combat as well. Dialogue and other interactions can depend on character abilities, giving players a reason to develop social and utility skills instead of investing everything into combat statistics.

Adventuring revolves around a party containing up to four characters. Choosing companions with complementary strengths is important because individual characters naturally settle into different roles. A durable melee fighter can occupy dangerous opponents while another character attacks from range, provides magical assistance, or supports the group through specialized abilities. The system encourages players to think about the party as a complete unit rather than treating companions as disposable helpers following the protagonist.

Combat happens in real time but can be paused whenever tactical control is necessary. This feature is essential because encounters become much easier to manage when commands are issued carefully. Pausing gives you time to select targets, activate abilities, organize spellcasting, and reposition party members before allowing the battle to continue. It produces a deliberate style of combat where preparation and decision-making frequently matter more than rapid button presses. The animations and responsiveness naturally show their age, but the underlying tactical system remains engaging for players who appreciate classic CRPG combat.

Magic further expands the tactical possibilities. The large collection of spells combines with talents and special abilities to make characters feel increasingly specialized as the campaign progresses. Learning how these systems interact can initially be intimidating, especially for anyone unfamiliar with The Dark Eye. Drakensang does attempt to make the tabletop rules more accessible for a PC audience, but it still retains enough complexity to require experimentation. That learning process ultimately becomes part of the appeal, particularly for players who enjoy studying character sheets and optimizing their party.

The campaign offers numerous main and optional quests while taking players through a detailed interpretation of Aventuria. The story was created with involvement from original The Dark Eye authors, helping the adventure feel connected to the established setting rather than merely borrowing its name. Exploration introduces a mixture of familiar fantasy threats and stranger creatures from the tabletop universe, including ogres, linnorms, giant amoebas, undead mules, and other unusual enemies. This variety gives the setting its own personality even when the broader medieval fantasy presentation initially seems conventional.

Questing benefits considerably from the game's emphasis on character talents. Conversations are not completely separated from character progression, meaning certain skills can affect interactions and available approaches. This strengthens the role-playing component because building a character involves more than determining how efficiently enemies can be defeated. The abundance of main and side content also makes exploration worthwhile, particularly for players who prefer thoroughly investigating an RPG world instead of rushing through its central storyline.

Visually, Drakensang inevitably reveals its age. Character animation, environmental geometry, interface design, and visual effects come from a very different generation of PC gaming. Nevertheless, its colorful fantasy environments retain considerable charm. The third-person viewpoint helps provide a stronger sense of physically traveling through the world, while the varied environments give the lengthy campaign a welcome feeling of adventure. Artistic direction holds up better than the underlying technology, even though nobody should approach it expecting modern production standards.

Its age creates some practical disadvantages as well. Menus can feel cumbersome, the abundance of statistics may overwhelm inexperienced players, and some systems require more explanation than the game comfortably provides. Modern players accustomed to streamlined RPG interfaces may need several hours before everything becomes intuitive. The original PC requirements also reflect its 2009 release, so the hardware demands are extremely modest by current standards, although running an older Windows title can occasionally involve quirks on contemporary systems.

Steam Deck compatibility is an important limitation. Drakensang is officially categorized as Unsupported for Steam Deck. Players interested primarily in handheld play should therefore not assume a trouble-free experience. Even if unofficial configurations or compatibility-layer adjustments can sometimes produce different results, the official status remains Unsupported, making a conventional Windows PC the safer choice.

Drakensang ultimately succeeds because it commits strongly to being a traditional role-playing game. Its greatest strengths are its extensive character development, four-member party management, tactical pause-based battles, flexible magic system, talent-driven interactions, substantial quest content, and detailed adaptation of The Dark Eye. Its dated presentation and relatively demanding rules create a noticeable barrier to entry, but players willing to work through that learning curve will discover a substantial fantasy adventure with much more depth than its age might suggest.

Это максимально уютное олдскульное приключение, где ты будешь часто жать на тактическую паузу, раздавая команды своему отряду. Боёвка тут чистый рандом и математика. Здесь нужно следить за позициями, лечить каждую царапину и постоянно копаться в статах. Идеальный выбор, чтобы залипнуть на неделю, обложившись табличками характеристик и наслаждаясь ламповой атмосферой!

[i]Всем известно, у каждого «идиота» есть Мечта. Моя, например, - освоить электронное воплощение настольных ролевых систем, ибо в них лежит логичное развитие любимых мною «партиек». К сожалению, громогласное величие [u][url=store.steampowered.com/app/228280/Baldurs_Gate_Enhanced_Edition/]«Baldur's Gate»[/url][/u] и грандиозный масштаб [u][url=store.steampowered.com/curator/44272419-Owlcat-Games-Ltd./]творений «Owlcat Games»[/url][/u] пока внушают мне благоговейный ужас. Значит, начну с чего-то, ммм, попроще. После вдумчивого поиска я остановилась на данном проекте: симпатичная картинка, малоизученная Вселенная и неуловимое сходство с обожаемым [u][url=store.steampowered.com/app/47810/Dragon_Age_Origins__Ultimate_Edition/?l=russian&cc=de]«Dragon Age: Origins»[/url][/u] подкупили моментально. Будем надеяться, что выражение «Иди туда, где страшно, - именно там ты обретёшь силу»  правдиво хотя бы отчасти.[/i]

[b]Техническое исполнение:[/b] неважное. Для запуска на Win 10 придётся провернуть [u][url=steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=573860852]нехитрые манипуляции[/url][/u], которые, впрочем, не «вылечат» стабильные вылеты раз в 5-6 часов – сохраняйтесь почаще и обязательно чередуйте слоты. Если сохранения перестали загружаться, то [u][url=steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3625976876]отключите «HD-текстуры» в настройках игры[/url][/u].

[b]Графика:[/b] уютная. Исчезающее волшебство Сказки наконец-то побороло вездесущую (и уже вкрай осточертевшую) мрачность Средневековья. Вместо ожидаемого маршрута сквозь жуткие локации с повсеместной разрухой и стойким ароматом беспросветной хандры Художник проведёт дорогами необыкновенной красоты. Вольный ветер гоняет воздушные облака по бескрайнему небосводу и ласково приглаживает пышное разнотравье полей. Серебро водоёмов весело переливается под тёплыми лучами слепящего солнца. Безмятежное раздолье равнин опьяняет свободой, коварная теснота гор манит тайнами, а немногочисленные каменные города и бревенчатые селения гостеприимно распахивают двери. Даже заброшенные подземелья, хмурые пещеры, непроходимые болота и тенистые леса пронизаны светом и залиты красками. Заботливые руки украсили пейзажи всевозможными мелочами, обжили интерьеры предметами быта, грамотно расставили освещение и присыпали всё ненавязчивыми эффектами. Местное население, в свою очередь, может похвастаться приличной коллекцией лиц, впечатляющим ассортиментом выразительных фигур (низкорослые бородачи и полногрудые воительницы в наличии), обширным гардеробом времён немецкого феодализма, детализированным рыцарским вооружением, действительно запоминающимися ключевыми персонажами и неплохим разнообразием врагов. «Болванчики» активно жестикулируют в разговоре, реалистично изображают фехтование и беспощадно разносят деревянную тару в щепки, задорно разлетающиеся согласно примитивной физике. Лишь бедноватые во всех смыслах постановочные ролики на движке да штучные повторы сегментов окружения слегка портят сию чудесную картину.

[b]Звук:[/b] знакомый. Благородный оркестр, используя богатый набор инструментов — от классических труб, барабанов, скрипки, флейты и церковного хора до весьма экзотических бубна, колокола, арфы и испанской гитары, — создаёт чарующие композиции с очевидными источниками вдохновения. В неспешных мелодиях безошибочно угадываются памятные мотивы из «Гарри Поттера», «Героев Меча и Магии», «Властелина колец» и «Звёздных Войн». Торжественная, сдержанная, неунывающая, настороженная - музыка неизменно следует единому стилю и безупречно задаёт нужное настроение, так ни разу и не осмелившись эпично вырваться на передний план. Треки плавно перетекают друг в друга через затухание, а образовавшуюся тишину виртуозно вытесняет многоголосая среда. К неодушевлённому «ансамблю» органично присоединяется «пёстрый коллектив» живности: щебечущие пташки, стрекочущие насекомые, рычащие дикие твари и «вздыхающее» домашнее зверьё - тихо не бывает никогда. Актеры озвучания хорошо попадают в роли, наделяют речь в диалогах отличительными чертами и читаемыми эмоциями, но отчего-то полностью обходят вниманием беззвучные фоновые реплики. [u][url=www.zoneofgames.ru/games/drakensang_the_dark_eye/]Официальный перевод от «Нового диска»[/url][/u] добротный, едва заметные неточности встречаются всего пару раз.

[b]Сюжет:[/b] литературный. Здешний Автор проявил себя скорее как образцовый Писатель, чем изобретательный Сценарист. Вооружившись четкой структурой и чистым слогом, Он написал крепкий фэнтезийный роман, в котором ничего не раздражает и ничего не восхищает. Ладно скроенный мир умело, постепенно, лаконично раскрывается перед новичками и дружески похлопывает по плечу знатоков, не награждая за любознательность ни тех ни других. Все, от высокомерного аристократа с мудреным именем до последней безродной сволочи, охотно идут на контакт и выписывают бесконечно уважительные фразы, старательно избегая любого юмора или нравственной неоднозначности. Протагонист, на словах бывалый приключенец с насыщенным прошлым и выдающимися персональными качествами, на деле - стопроцентный дилетант во всех сферах, личные стремления которого бесцеремонно подменяют великой целью, навсегда низвергая так называемого Избранного до ранга безвольной пешки. Его союзники и противники - банальные типажи без какой-либо харизмы, внутренних конфликтов, нелегкой судьбы, грязных секретов или навязчивых идей. Шаблонные напарники сразу выкладывают исчерпывающую биографию, не меняются со временем и не желают близких отношений, продолжая быть надёжными попутчиками исключительно из соображений альтруизма, а плоские злодеи нисходят до общения безумно редко. Загодя «объезжая» интригующие задания, непростые выборы, непредвиденные последствия и эмоциональные моменты, приземленная история невозмутимо движется по протоптанной тропе к предсказуемому, бесцветному финалу. 

[b]Геймплей:[/b] увлекательный. Рой циферок заранее загнал меня на [u][url=aventuria.ru/]всеобъемлющий русифицированный фанатский сайт по «The Dark Eye»[/url][/u] с [u][url=aventuria.ru/load/doc/uebersetzung/pervoe_znakomstvo/63-1-0-1306]универсальной памяткой для старта[/url][/u]. Оказалось, то были напрасные волнения, ведь Разработчик, как и обещал, облёк оригинальные глубокие правила в доступную форму. Вступительное обучение, пусть и опускает некоторые тонкости, дает развернутые ответы на большинство вопросов, а в удобном интерфейсе легко ориентироваться. Самобытное устройство прогрессии очень интересно изучать и крайне трудно поломать, поскольку компьютерный «Мастер Подземелий» всегда предложит выгодное распределение очков и закроет глаза на маленькие «эксперименты». Возникшие пробелы в «образовании» уверенно заполнят полезные ремесла и многофункциональные компаньоны. Изготовление вещей требует грамотного распоряжения деньгами и материалами, не скатывается в жонглирование кучей ингредиентов и приносит ощутимые бонусы на выходе. Непохожие спутники займут пустующее место боевой единицы, торгового посредника или опытного ремесленника, и отметят значимые победы бурным ликованием. Динамичные битвы приветствуют тщательную подготовку и по-настоящему захватывают тактикой, увы, не балуя сменой условий, новыми механиками или подробной статистикой. Выбирайте из широкого арсенала с уникальными экземплярами, пробуйте себя в необязательных испытаниях, находите собственный подход к решению проблем - единственный уровень сложности прекрасно сбалансирован под разные способы прохождения.

[b]Онлайн:[/b] нет.

[b]Достижения:[/b] нет.

[b]Модификации и доп. контент:[/b] нет.

[b]Вывод:[/b] «Drakensang» - это редкий нынче представитель высокого европейского героического фэнтези и чрезвычайно комфортная точка входа во «взрослые» ролевые игры. Детище «Radon Labs» вряд ли задержится в памяти и сердце, но точно станет приятным путешествием по невероятно живописным декорациям и отличным интерактивным учебником для неискушенного игрока. Что же до меня: страхи поборола, бесценный опыт получила, оптимизмом заразилась. Следующий!

Drakensang fue mi primer RPG, por ello le tengo un especial cariño aunque trataré de ser objetivo en todos sus aspectos.

- [b]Punto 1: Accesibilidad[/b]
Para empezar, el juego no está disponible en castellano en la versión de Steam, y creo recordar que en GOG tampoco. Esto es un problema pues el juego cuenta, desde su lanzamiento, con una versión en español en la que participan actores de doblaje y voces muy reconocibles del cine para los españoles. Que Steam no haya querido añadir esta opción y que tengas que buscarla por internet e instalarla por tu cuenta es un problema. 

Otro problema es que el juego no tira bien en Windows 10. Ni tiene una versión Widescreen. Para jugar hoy en día, tendrás que recurrir a programas de terceros o a tocar los parámetros de lanzamiento. 

- [b]Punto 2: Jugabilidad[/b]
Drakensang usa un sistema por turnos en tercera persona, que se repite también en su segunda entrega: The River of Time. Este sistema bebe de juegos de rol y fantasía como Dungeons & Dragons, aunque Drakensang sigue un modelo propio que alcanzó cierta fama en Alemania, pero que hoy se encuentra obsoleto: The Dark Eye.

El juego funciona a base de tiradas de dados ya sea para combatir, para la curación, o para algunos diálogos. Puedes seguir todas estas tiradas en un pequeño menú que se abre en la esquina inferior izquierda de la pantalla, y que es muy útil para focalizar qué acciones funcionan mejor o el daño que hacen. 

La hoja de personaje es extensa y puede resultar abrumadora para los jugadores nuevos. Tienes una serie de habilidades sociales, mágicas, de combate y destrezas que, o vienen desbloqueadas de base, o tienes que aprender mediante los entrenadores que te proporciona el juego. Asimismo, algunos conjuros están bloqueados según la raza que seas. Por ejemplo, los humanos no pueden acceder a determinados conjuros élficos, y los enanos directamente no disponen de magia.

En este respecto, obtienes un determinado número de PA (puntos de aventura) conforme vas avanzando en la historia completando misiones, eliminando enemigos, y logrando tus objetivos. 

- [b]Punto 3: Historia y narrativa[/b]
Aquí es donde realmente brilla el juego. Partes de una premisa muy interesante que se enlaza con otras subtramas de Drakensang, aportando profundidad y riqueza a la historia. Como jugador, tienes una amplia variedad de misiones secundarias que complementan y expanden el universo de Aventuria. 

Durante tu aventura, te relaciones con una amplia variedad de personajes, pudiendo reclutar a algunos de ellos y emplear sus habilidades durante la batalla. Todos cuentan con un trasfondo que, en menor o mayor medida, sirve para conocerlos mejor. Estos personajes comentan en diferentes puntos de la historia, y puedes hablar con ellos para aprender más sobre su vida u opiniones. No obstante, este aspecto se siente pobre cuando lo comparas con otras entregas como Baldurs Gate 3, o la saga Dragon Age (antes de Veilguard). 

- [b]Punto 4: Inmersión[/b]
Más bien este punto podría llamarse "detalles", pero queda mejor aludir a lo inmersivo del juego. 

Los escenarios, si bien son interesantes en un primer momento, proporcionan poca interactividad más allá de recoger algunas plantas, abrir puertas, o cumplir ciertos objetivos. En este aspecto, lugares como Ferdok se sienten vacíos pese a estar rodeados de personas.

Las armas no pueden enfundarse. Esto parece una nimiedad, pero lo corrigieron en su segunda entrega. Ir apuntando con tu espada a todo lo que se mueve saca bastante de la inmersión. 

Cuando avanzas en la historia, accedes a diferentes lugares. La mayoría de estos lugares se vuelven inaccesibles una vez logras completar tus objetivos allí. He echado en falta volver a ciertos lugares, tras algunos sucesos de la trama, para ver cómo han cambiado las cosas. Sin embargo, el juego no te lo permite. 

El sistema de creación es simple. No hay mucho más que añadir en este aspecto.

----

En conclusión, es un buen juego que en su época se convirtió en un referente para miles de personas que probaban los videojuegos por primera vez, o que descubrían el rol. Sin embargo, el tiempo no ha sido bondadoso con él y hoy en día es fácil ver las carencias y fallos que en su día no lográbamos ver, o nos parecían aspectos positivos porque no teníamos con qué compararlo. 

Mi recomendación para ti es que, si quieres comprar este juego, espera a que esté de oferta (lo he llegado a ver por [b]1,99€[/b], como ahora que estoy escribiendo esta reseña), y sumérgete en él obviando la problemática anterior.

- Average main quests however some of the sidequests take the cake and could be their own main story in some games, like exploring Ardos murder and all the chainquests that link to it, also a lot of sidequests to keep you busy
- Great character class, skill and stat choices worthy of an CRPG and with it a lot of possibilites to tackle missions (through combat, sneaking, seducing, bartering and so on a lot of playstyle choices)
- Good amount of companions to choose from, sadly not all have their sidestories but a lot of dialogue is voice acted same for main NPCs, not winning any oscars but still good
- Great variety of itemization (many weapon, magic, armor and potion types to fit your playstyle)

Cons:
- Its an older game so on higher end pc and windows you might have problem running (i ran it on windows 10, i had to exit fullscreen always when the game started and in credits else it crashed, after that i could play in fullscreen normally, had to lower graphic settings to medium else it crashed midgame beacuse of memory leak, in mid settings it runs fine, if you have problems check steam guides/forums for solution)
- With no real fast travel or mounts a lot of time wasted trying to sell stuff in the big main city and reaching locations traveling on foot
- The combat is in real time with a pause function where you can issue commands which is good and works well, you can pause yourself with spacebar or when an enemy spots you for the first time, this is also good, problem is if enemies are not close together and are spread out, the first enemy spots you it pauses, you issue commands and unpause so combat begins, second enemy spots you it pauses... in the end it pauses 5 times or more in rapid succesion which is annoying, this only happens to spread out groups as tight groups spot you at same time

All in all a very solid CRPG and a hidden gem in my opinion worthy of a playthrough.

Story
The story is almost nonexistent so I made one to role play as my own. I took the role of a kid with a large supply of LSD going on a permanent trip and raising a dog at the same time. This seemed to fit in well with the rest of the game and the comic sans like text.
Gameplay
I was extremely disappointed in the gameplay. All that you do is move your mouse around and left click. I see what they were shooting for but they seriously need to add more gameplay elements to squeeze out more game time.
The feeding feature in the game is the most important element. If you feed your pet too much basic food their stomach will get fucked and they will become sick and you will have to blow all of your fucking cash on the little bitch. In real life I had to put my dog down when she became sick and the lack of realism really ripped me out of the game. You should be given the option to be able to pay the medical bills or put the dog down. 
Another thing you can do with your doggo is make it do tricks. This piece of the game was also a letdown for me. When the game's text notified me I had unlocked the roll over trick, I attempted to roll over but it then said I hadn't unlocked the ability. This mildly upset me until I grinded to unlock the roll over ability all over again. The ability you would be able to unlock after rolling over is glitched and you cannot unlock it. We may never know what that trick was without a trip into the game's .ini files.
Graphics/Performance
The graphics in this game were extremely underwhelming for the most part but the models created for the dogs were honestly on point. You are given a decent selection of puppers and an unlockable doggo labeled "special." I have not yet unlocked the special dog and will update my review if that happens.
The game is stuck, much like Conan the mighty pig and Dark Souls, at 30 frames per second. This demolishes any hopes of you going competitive in this game and you should look to higher tier titles like Golf With Your Friends for any such action.
Music
I usually give positive praise towards games for their nice soundtracks but this game's soundtrack in particular made me want to hang myself by the cord of my mouse. It does not fit in well with the gameplay on screen and actually gave me a headache, forcing me to stop for my own well-being. 
Overall
Pro(s):
•	Decent looking puppers
Con(s):
•	Ear bleeding music
•	Boring gameplay
•	Story takes a lot of imagination from a role player’s perspective 
•	30 FPS
•	Comic sans like text
•	Illusion of choice (Pay medical bills/ kill dog)
•	Glitched parts of the game that are unreachable
•	Boring gameplay
In my greatest attempt to be nice, only buy this game if you are either A) Brain dead or B) Emotionally detached from reality and need to escape to a virtual dog with minimal feedback and few negative responses to give yourself a much needed ego boost after getting your ass whipped by an alcoholic father.
Or if you want to get from 49 games on Steam to 50. Even then only buy it on sale.

Hunting Unlimited 2010 is part of a long-running series that tried to strike a balance between accessible, arcade-leaning hunting gameplay and the more deliberate pacing associated with traditional hunting sims. By the time this entry arrived, SCS Software had established a clear identity for the franchise: large outdoor environments, plenty of weapons and equipment, a substantial list of missions, and a free-form hunting mode meant to evoke the quiet, patient rhythm of real-world hunting. This installment follows that formula closely. It offers a straightforward experience that is easy to jump into, giving players immediate access to hunts without forcing them through complicated tutorials or overly technical mechanics. Its focus is on quantity, accessibility, and variety rather than simulation depth, and this defines much of its appeal as well as its limitations.

The game presents two primary ways to engage with its content. Challenge Mode provides dozens of structured missions, often with clear conditions such as tracking a specific animal, hitting certain score thresholds, or navigating timed scenarios. These missions introduce brief bursts of purpose and direction, functioning almost like mini-arena challenges in a first-person shooting gallery format. They keep the pace brisk and provide a sense of progress, even if the challenges start to feel repetitive once you have completed a few sets. Free Hunt Mode is more open-ended, inviting players to choose a region, equip their preferred weapon loadout, and step into the wilderness with no objective beyond seeking out game. When the mood is right, this mode offers a quiet, meditative experience—long walks through forests or plains, scanning the distance for movement, and savoring the occasional tension of lining up a careful shot.

Weapon variety is one of the game’s most enjoyable elements. Hunting Unlimited 2010 includes a broad assortment of rifles, shotguns, bows, and crossbows, along with accessories such as calls, scents, scopes, and binoculars. While the differences between weapons are not deeply simulated, they are distinct enough to encourage experimentation. Players can tailor loadouts to different kinds of prey, and trying out new combinations gives the early hours a sense of discovery. The inclusion of a slow-motion bullet cam, a feature carried over from earlier entries, adds a dramatic flair to successful hits, giving each carefully executed shot a moment of cinematic polish.

However, the game’s age becomes clear in its presentation and underlying systems. The environments, though geographically diverse, often look sparse and uniform, with repetitive textures and limited detail. Forests and plains feel open but empty, lacking the environmental richness that modern hunting games use to immerse players. Animal behavior, too, is basic. Prey tends to move in predictable loops or flee in simple patterns, making them feel more like mechanical targets than natural creatures reacting dynamically to sights, sounds, or wind direction. This simplicity can undermine the sense of realism and diminish the excitement of tracking, which is a core element of more advanced hunting simulations.

The pacing of hunts reflects these limitations. While hunting inherently involves waiting and observation, Hunting Unlimited 2010 often creates long stretches where very little happens—not because the player must be stealthy or thoughtful, but because the world lacks density and meaningful cues. It is not uncommon to wander for several minutes without finding any tracks, movement, or ambient activity. For some players, this quiet, low-pressure pacing may feel calming; for others, it comes across as dull or underdeveloped. Challenge Mode helps counterbalance the slower moments by injecting structure and variety, but once the missions begin to repeat familiar patterns, even that mode loses some of its momentum.

Technical factors also play a role in shaping the experience. The game’s low system requirements remain a positive point, especially for players with older or less powerful hardware. It runs smoothly even on modest systems and loads quickly due to its small footprint. On the other hand, being an older title means compatibility issues can surface on modern operating systems. Some players report crashes, input quirks, or other stability problems that can interrupt the experience, and with no active development or official updates, these issues are left to the community to troubleshoot.

Despite its shortcomings, Hunting Unlimited 2010 carries a certain nostalgic charm. It belongs to an era when hunting games were more common and tended to emphasize accessible fun rather than high-fidelity realism. For players who grew up with similar titles—or those who appreciate games that prioritize simplicity and straightforward enjoyment—it can still offer a pleasant, stress-free diversion. The mixture of weapon experimentation, mission variety, and open-ended exploration creates a gameplay loop that can be relaxing in short sessions.

Ultimately, Hunting Unlimited 2010 is best understood as a light and approachable hunting game rather than a meticulous simulation. Its strengths lie in its accessibility, its selection of gear, and its modest but enjoyable structure of challenges and free roaming. Its weaknesses—dated visuals, simplistic AI, repetitive pacing, and limited immersion—reflect its age and the modest ambitions of its design. For players seeking a casual hunting sandbox that requires little commitment and can be enjoyed in quiet moments, it remains a serviceable entry. For those who want depth, realism, or richly simulated ecosystems, it will fall short. Still, as a piece of early 2000s hunting game culture, it has a gentle appeal that persists in the right mindset.
