[h2]重玩经典的得与失[/h2]
在现在这个时代，愿意去玩十几年前，甚至几十年前经典游戏的做法我是十分鼓励的，而且好处多多。首先经典都是那些经过时间充分洗刷，褪去起初宣发造势的热度，真正靠质量被大家所记住的游戏。通过游玩它们能体会到经受住时间考验的独特之处，还能看到游戏业界多年来的发展脉络，体会到和当代游戏的不同之处。能在Steam上买到的这些经典大都价格十分便宜，有些在打折的时候甚至只要几块钱，而且几乎任何电脑都能以最高特效流畅运行。经过多年的更新和修补，一般现在售卖的都是问题最少的版本。即使不是的话，Steam站内一般也有获得最佳体验的解决方案。经典游戏没有中文的话，大都配有汉化组和玩家个人的汉化。玩家群体多年来积累出了完整的新手指南、攻略、彩蛋合集、百科、专业测评、剧情讲解、推荐视频等等，总能令你找到最需要，也最希望有共鸣的社区内容。

当然，有得就有失。老游戏在目前版本的Windows系统和硬件设备上运行是有可能存在问题的，即使能通过打补丁的方式解决，有问题就意味着体验门槛变高。如果恰好没有汉化补丁，门槛就更高了，还可能没有成就和云存档。经典游戏的画面水平一般都落后于目前的时代，如果总带着有色眼镜去看的话，会受不了相对过时的画面。一些游戏的设计会受到当时游戏的影响，部分机制在后来可能逐渐被摒弃，比如重复任务和地图上满屏的收集品。另外，有些游戏带有多人模式或者合作模式，时隔多年可能一个人都匹配不到，甚至服务器都没了。由于游戏较老，玩家群体远远少于热门大作，社区并不活跃，真想找到讨论的人也并不容易。如果不注意的话，一些剧情讲解和短测评可能会剧透，破坏游戏体验。

说了这么多，Steam上的这个版本如何呢？绝大部分系统上都可以正常游玩，但打完汉化补丁后，win11无法正常运行。我的另一台win10电脑可以正常用汉化，但不能使用耳机。汉化补丁提取自官方中文版，质量很高，繁体中文，部分翻译习惯和简中略有区别，比如名字翻译为《荣耀战场：地狱栈道》。简体中文的汉化也有，名字翻译为《手足兄弟联：兵临绝境》，只不过我没有找到，也就没法测试是否好用了。

[h2]当年看来惊人的技术力[/h2]
很多人会因为画面不佳的缘故拒绝体验曾经的经典游戏，不过这款18年前的作品至今看起来都非常出色。其特效和画质相比前两作大幅升级，从虚幻2转换到虚幻3，而且是我认为是虚幻3引擎早期表现得最好的作品之一。开头漂亮的荷兰乡村小镇关卡就是绝佳的例子，蓝天、绿草和风车搭配在一起非常养眼，简直就是一副风景画。开场动画里有对前两代部分场景的新引擎重制，诺曼底D-Day的跳伞依旧震撼，一开头的滑翔也是大场面了。游戏有着舒适的色调，电影感很强的渲染，其火焰和爆炸效果、光影、烟雾、反射、环境细节、人物面部表情和动作等都很出色。

游戏最令我震惊的是大量的破坏效果，不同高度的木栅栏、木桶、木桌椅、玻璃、沙袋等等全都可以破坏，甚至地面会留下清晰的弹坑。敌人如果躲在不牢靠的掩体后面，可以直接把掩体打碎。有一次为了实现我想要的攻击角度，我拿手雷把一人多高的栅栏炸出一个缺口，绕到了敌人后面发动奇袭。手雷和炮弹的破坏效果十分惊人，相当多的掩体可以破坏，而且经常会触发慢动作效果。敌人的胳膊和腿都可以炸掉（断面可见骨头），人可以被炸成两截，甚至脑袋都可以被炸掉一半。当时没有任何一款游戏做到这种人体破坏效果，哪怕《使命召唤5：战争世界》也比不上。游戏开头死掉的平民身上有弹孔，远距离爆头会触发爆头飙血慢镜，似乎脑袋上也有弹孔。本作中你可以指挥火箭筒小队，用他们来炸可破坏掩体或沙袋后的机枪小队特别爽，可以看到掩体和敌人一起被炸碎上天。有时场景中会有高处的机枪点，比如尖顶教堂的钟楼，指挥火箭筒炸掉的时候会触发脚本式的破坏效果，建筑会被完全破坏。我似乎是在《战地：叛逆连队2》和《战地3》中才再次见到这样的破坏效果。

游戏里还有很多小细节，比如医院关卡中拿到的M3上沾着血；玻璃在畸形透视和破坏效果上非常拟真；无论敌我，戴头盔时头盔可以被打掉。游戏第一关有绵羊士兵的彩蛋，它们会径直冲向德军爆炸，不知有没有受到《百战天虫》的影响。有一关里有激光枪和猫猫枪两把隐藏武器，可惜我照着视频打的时候怎么都试不出来。当然，不可忽视的是，游戏场景里可到达区域之外部分的制作还是比较粗糙的，能看出明显复制粘贴的痕迹。

[h2]开场空军基地长镜头解析[/h2]
整个剧情我不想从头到尾说一遍，但是开头的长镜头非常值得说。首先这是整个小队的介绍，玩家需要通过这场戏来认识人物，如果不是从初代玩过来的老玩家，就需要场外解析的帮助。另一点就是这场戏为整个游戏的好几个包袱埋足了线索，越看懂这场戏，越能把一切串起来。何况这段3分20秒的长镜头本身就有很多看点，比如其配音表演、场面调度、视角变换真的棒极了！下面开始，人名以繁体中文版为准（仅哈萨克改为哈索克），使用简中补丁的朋友根据读音判断吧。

长镜头从科特兰和道森的谈话开始入镜，但声音是从贝克和弗兰奇的谈话开始，这两条线索是着重刻画的。前一幕中，我们扮演玩医院教学关卡前，跟贝克对话的人一直被挡住脸。然而，如果你细心的话，不仅可以通过口音认出，还能通过头盔认出来。贝克小队的人数是13人，这不是个幸运数字，补充的新兵弗兰奇头盔上没有这个数字，是手写的，这个头盔同样出现在少女被枪杀的现场。一个环绕镜头和战友拍头的动作点出了他的外号「豆豆」，还展示了外套背后写的名字，这件衣服还会出现数次。通过他联络起了贝克和科瑞恩，贝克受弗兰奇之托让科瑞恩照看他，对方暗示他谎报年龄参军。这为科瑞恩的过度照顾、贝克的指责、以及两人关系决裂埋下了伏笔。

道森是个调任过来的士兵，迷信的他最感兴趣的是「诅咒之枪」这件事，后面详细聊。哈索克派喜欢爱玩笑的杰士伯去搞油漆，后来油漆拿来的时候，他们往吉普车引擎盖上写了小队阵亡名单，后面多次出现。由哈索克引向扑克牌帐篷，这里面有意大利裔歧视，弗莱尔指责帕多克出老千的冲突。这为后来弗莱尔阵亡铺垫他们之间的关系，还让大家熟悉后来被晋升的帕多克。当然，这条线做的最弱，后面很少再被提到，也就拿枪打车和阵亡反应那段了。小队中第一个死的马什全程没说话，走出帐篷的坎贝尔的脸看起来像极了裘德·洛，最后把镜头引向吉普车。众人提了几句麦克以后，贝克作为小队长给大家鼓舞士气，他说自己不做演讲，然而游戏结局正是以贝克的演讲结束的！

[h2]诅咒之枪[/h2]
这把M1911手枪从初代就开始铺垫了，跟贝克一起长大并参军的好友坦克手乔治·里斯纳最开始拿着这把枪。乔治死后（可惜他在3代只有个一闪而过的背面镜头），艾伦从他手里拿走了枪。艾伦、加内特和莱格特专门讨论过这把枪，《地狱公路》开场动画专门重制了这一段，加内特也碰了枪。不久后，艾伦和加内特都死了，戴索拉从死亡现场拿起了这把枪，但随后就放下了，最后莱格特把枪拿走了。戴索拉不久后在紫心小巷那里被德军飞机炸的不成人形。守卫30高地时，莱格特就是拿着这把枪射击时被炸死的。当然，并不是所有人的死都跟这把枪有关，比如死于狙击手的奥比等人。

在初代的删减片段中进一步详细展示了这把枪，乔治在宿舍里首次拿出来，他走出后让正在交谈的穆扎碰了这把枪。看了这一段，我们才能把D日在飞机上就被炸死的穆扎跟这一切联系起来。主创们在展示这一段的时候，还道出了这把枪的起源是贝克的父亲，他死的时候拿的就是这把枪。这一段也说明死亡手枪这件事并不是从三代开始的，而是从初代就被编剧作为重要线索开始铺设。三代开场动画中，还进一步展示了这把枪最初的归属，以及上面刻着游戏标题Brothers in Arms和For Matthew（麦特Matt是简称）。这把枪是他父亲专门给他的，但因为母亲的缘故，麦特不能拿，也因此这把枪作为遗物最后到了他最好的朋友乔治手上。

三代里这把枪一直都留在贝克的手里，哪怕他被炸到河里，丢了大部分武器装备，这把枪也一直陪伴着他，而他则安然无恙。同时，小队里与这把枪毫无关系的弗莱尔和弗兰奇还是死了，进一步说明了「诅咒之枪」迷信的真相。结局里贝克在演讲后把枪扔掉了，如果有续作的话，我猜大概率会有回顾这把枪落地/落水的镜头，不知道又会辗转到谁的手里。

[h2]出色的故事和演出[/h2]
除了上面说的开场长镜头和诅咒之枪，本作对故事是讲述也是很成熟的。开场通过重制前作的部分关键画面的方式，做成类似美剧的前情提要（要是真用虚幻3把前两作重制了多好）。开场的教学关实际是后期的事情，类似于初代先展示守卫30高地，然后再从跳伞开始讲，都用制造悬念的倒叙手法。游戏后期镜头质量下降，但仍然在水准之上。另外，游戏中大量的台词和镜头前后呼应，比如开场和结局的台词完全一样。特洛伊·贝克依旧为马修·贝克配音，其表演真的很棒，各种情绪都展示的很到位。配乐也极佳，有时我会停在主菜单，就专门为听那段配乐。各种长镜头、主观镜头和跟随镜头用的也很多，比如一开场镜头穿越云层和玻璃缓缓到达主角面前；攻占大桥和过河那段的几个主观长镜头的临场感非常强，像小「奥马哈海滩」，大场面气氛到位，过程还比较诙谐幽默。

哈索克作为二代主角镜头颇多，本作展示了他之前被打断手指的镜头。曾经同伴中牺牲的道尔和佩奇的名字写在吉普车上，他还把前者的徽章别在头盔上纪念。他似乎是队伍中唯一结了婚有孩子的，最令人动容的是他说不想再错过女儿生日了。他开吉普车的时候撞树上遭到科瑞恩嘲讽，跟贝克争论科尔之死值不值，在医院救下贝克，还为贝克的精神状态向麦克打报告，最终在与贝克争论精神和指挥问题时被迫击炮炸伤。幸而没死，但是再也无法走路，这让他在本作以半喜半忧的方式退场。除他之外，科瑞恩的镜头也挺多，我还一度想制作组会不会拿他作为新的第二主角做个类似二代的资料片。

此外，还想说一下本作的宣发问题，即「预告骗」。很多出现在预告片里的机制根本就没出现在游戏里，拿CG当实机糊弄人，而且坐火车、玩具商店那段基本上全都被删减了。正片里确实有玩具店，也就是尼古拉斯儿子逃进去的那个，但是没有额外镜头了，也没有遭到迫击炮轰炸。预告篇关卡也压根没出现，严重怀疑是专门为了演示而制作的关卡，需要配合走位并加了大量额外脚本演出。这种事并不是第一次发生，《进军30高地》的宣发期间，Randy Pitchford已经在2004年的E3展上进行过一次几乎一样的虚假宣传（实际不止这一个IP，还为此吃过官司）。

[h2]一度化身恐怖游戏[/h2]
游戏最恐怖的关卡莫过于医院那段，堪比正儿八经的恐怖游戏，吓退了不少年轻玩家。实际上，游戏从风和日丽的荷兰之行的初期就开始渲染恐怖氛围了。第一关中没有友军和平民死亡，贝克也没有任何幻觉；但是从第二关「五零辛克」开始先目睹了一名女孩被德军拖到谷仓里吊死，后看到给雪茄的牧师被炸死。此后，贝克一跟众人分开就开始出现幻觉。他见到不知真假的圆框眼镜就陷入到了过去的闪回之中。后来的科尔之死更是加重了悲剧氛围，本地联络人尼古拉斯的孩子失踪，让贝克想起了告别孩子上战场的战友哈索克。短暂的民众热闹欢迎，很快就被道森提起的过去，以及德军轰炸所终结，战友一个个死亡，贝克也愈加陷入自责和崩溃。

当他们返回遭到轰炸的城市时，队友发现了之前救下的小男孩尸体，不久后尸体的脸就会多次突然闪现，似乎学的是初代《极度恐慌》。医院关卡当然是把恐怖氛围贯彻的最为彻底的一关了，没有队友，灯光少，黑漆漆，阴森森；轮椅会动，不知是遭遇灵异，还是炮弹爆炸造成的；贝克所见会突然扭曲，灯光会依次熄灭。最恐怖的一个是钻墙洞的时候，阴森发绿的莱格特的鬼脸会在洞口外直接贴脸出现，让人吓得差点扔鼠标。临近结局，贝克的幻觉愈发强烈，死去的士兵会突然变成莱格特的样子。哪怕在众人陪伴下，他也能看到死去战友的鬼魂，甚至能跟莱格特对话，说的还有来有回的。被吓到的哈索克赶紧跟麦克报告，好在麦克对莱格特的行为知情，压下了这件事，后来谈论莱格特事件时一定程度上也减少了贝克的愧疚感。这些内容专为表现贝克的精神状态，类似《死亡空间》中艾萨克的幻觉，我还挺喜欢的。

[h2]继续借鉴《兄弟连》电视剧，但是还有《使命召唤》[/h2]
游戏这一部继续借鉴《兄弟连》，诺曼底之后自然就是市场花园行动了，罗伯特·辛克团长继续由电视剧里的演员扮演。两者都有新兵加入并且着重刻画，最像的部分就是荷兰民众的欢迎场面，简直一模一样。当然，游戏没有回英国的休整，没有对战虎式坦克，没有奇袭，没有渡河营救英军（但仍有营救英军任务）。游戏更偏向于战斗和战场，展示了更多荷兰当地风情。根据电视剧，接下来肯定就是比利时的巴斯通了，即突出部战役。贝克也说「I can handle snow」，这就是明示了，然而「未完待续」让玩家一等就是18年，而且看样子还要继续等下去。

游戏在各方面玩起来更像《使命召唤》了，抛弃了前两作的很多特点，加入了诸多偏向单人化而非小队化的设计。对我来说并不排斥，多了一个解开局面的选项有何不可，况且单人射击体验还不错。前两作的难度相当高，现在的玩家很可能已经接受不了了。首先取消的就是血条，主角可以呼吸回血，单人行动没了对血量的担忧。其次就是枪械晃动和后坐力大幅减弱，准度大幅提升。在掩体中会自动切换为类似《战争机器》的TPS，瞄准时等上几秒就可以让枪械完全没有不晃，让远处的敌人可以精准命中。游戏还有意将我们跟队友阻隔开，体验专门设计的单人关卡，常常要独自面对数十个敌人。

[h2]难度大幅下降，小队存在感也降低[/h2]
游戏难度相比前两作明显降低，敌人削弱，玩家加强，存档点增加。前作中的MG42是令人畏惧的存在，只要暴露就会迅速被打死，正面没有任何将其摧毁的机会，只有绕后一条路。然而，本作中的MG42会不时缩进掩体，而且开火准备时间长，几个短点射往往就可以把枪手轻松爆头。他们几乎成了敌军中最先被我识别出来并干掉的目标，没了压迫感。敌军炮兵主要都是88炮和单人火箭筒（似乎并不是铁拳），不再有会修正落点的迫击炮，前作中稍不注意就会被一发全带走。前作中即使绕后，拿着汤普森能否干掉敌军也未知，因为枪械准度低，先手情况下也可能被反杀，通常和小队一起行动胜算才高。在本作里，端着MP40绕后心里就不慌了，哪怕对方有四个人。贝克的火力也增强了，可以直接提着MG-42当冲锋枪用，还能部署在掩体上，200发弹容简直像作弊器。敌人的MP40非常好用，98K则基本可以当成狙击枪用了，导致我更喜欢捡德军武器用。

小队中多了火箭筒班组，简直是大杀器。敌人缩在掩体后不出来？一发炮弹全炸死。机枪组便于压制，也是个很好用的班组。队友死了？不要紧，下一个存档点就可以原地复活。不过，个人感觉队友的操控性下降，稍远一些的敌人无法攻击，必须强制靠近到一定距离。由于敌人增加，交替掩护进攻的策略也没那么好用了，即使被压制的敌人也会打死转移的小队，让我进一步倾向于靠自己完成任务。突击队变成了普通的火力班组，不再有冲锋选项，没法像前作一样面对绝境冒险冲破死局。我还经常会遇到敌我双方射上半天不死人的情况，往往还是需要你去解开僵局。坦克变成了单独操控的小关卡，不再可以指挥。由于无法放大视野，导致开炮像是打狙击，节奏很慢。

此外，我还遇到过队友不攻击的情况，可能是Bug，但似乎绝大多数人都碰到过。最搞笑的是，你带着小队用炸药炸88炮时，自己跑远了，但队友只会围在炮的旁边被炸死！？游戏在情报和史实拟真方面大幅缩水，每章只能解锁两三页市场花园行动和101空降师的作战情况，几乎没了具体的战斗记载、实地考察、地形地图，文献档案。指挥模式变成了手绘地图，看不到敌人部队番号。游戏不再像之前一样认真调研，几乎完全按照编剧的思路在做。比如营救尼古拉斯之子那里，完全是神剧风格：几十个装备精良的德军不间断射击，小孩反复转移掩体毫发无损，硬是让一名狙击手打得全军覆没。

[h2]为什么不出续作了？[/h2]
一句话就可以解释：《无主之地》系列这么赚钱，为什么还去延续一个市场前景不明的IP？《无主之地》出到4代，哪怕评价变成褒贬不一，依旧大赚特赚，自然集中主要精力专做这个IP。外界因素也能找到一些，比如业界二战游戏从10年代开始退潮，几乎没了大制作。包含单人战役的也就仅剩《使命召唤：二战》、《使命召唤：先锋》和《战地V》，且评价都不咋地。同时，业界转向服务型FPS，更加专注于多人体验。当然，主因一定还是在Gearbox内部，他们这些年也不是没做过《无主之地》之外的FPS。《永远的毁灭公爵》（2011）、《异形：殖民军》（2013）、《为战而生》（2016）……他们每出一款《无主之地》，就会再出一款糟糕的FPS。现在甚至要吃死无主之地，不做别的游戏了，疯狂推出各种DLC、新版本、合集、前传，连衍生游戏都出了两款了。

不过，Gearbox似乎从未忘记《兄弟连》系列，每隔几年Randy Pitchford就会跑出来说游戏正在开发，一直说到2020年代。比如20年说要开发《兄弟连》的电视剧；21年说正在开发另一款《兄弟连》游戏，但在游戏完成之前，不会透露任何消息；24年又说正在开发下一款《无主之地》和新的《兄弟连》。呸，4代在次年发售，《兄弟连》连个影都没有。Pitchford都说了十几年了，我是不信了，此人嘴里的话绝不能都信。2011年E3展上《兄弟连：狂暴4》的预告片居然会出现，就说明他们实际上已经放弃正经延续这个IP了。我都怀疑，哪怕《无主之地》在下一部迎来商业上的失败，他们依旧不会延续这个IP。所谓的开发中其实只是在「新建文件夹」，我们应该是永远见不到续作了，贝克和他的小队永远没有结局！

Art arda çıkan iki oyunun üstüne verilen arayla üçüncü oyun yeni nesile geçerek önceki oyunlarda olan eksikleri ekseriyetle gidermiş. Öncelikle oynanıştan başlayalım. Silah hakimiyetindeki gerçekçi olmayış durumu ve isabet oranının aşırı düşüklüğü düzeltilmiş. Bununla beraber hikaye açısından derinlik artırılmış. Genel olarak sürükleyici olsa da potansiyel tam olarak maalesef kullanılamamış. Yine de gayet güzel bir hikayeyle seriye devam ediyor.
Bölüm tasarımları ve diğer mekanikler de önceki oyunlara kıyasla güncellenmiş. Manga yönetimi ve taktik artık çok daha keyifli ve çeşitli. Grafikler dönemine göre çok güzel. Atmosfer kıtlığı da düzeltilmiş. Artık ağaçlar ve yeşillikten oluşan bölümler dışında bir çok farklı atmosferde oyunu deneyimleyebiliyorsunuz.
Eksiklerine gelecek olursak, oyun artık son çeyreğinde kendini tekrar ediyor ve size yeni bir şey sunmuyor. Bu noktada oyunu bitirme motivasyonu olarak elimizde maalesef sadece hikaye merakı kalıyor. Bunun dışında siper mekaniğinin gelmesiyle beraber oyun siz sipere girdiğinizde TPS moduna geçiyor. Bu elbette zorunlu bir tercih lakin bir oyun bence hem FPS hem TPS olmamalı. İkisinden birisi tercih edilerek yola devam edilmeli. Bu konudan şahsi olarak rahatsız olmamla beraber elbette sevenlerin de olduğunu düşünüyorum. Zaten oyun iki kısmı da güzel kotarıyor.

Oyunun birkaç bölümde size tank sürme mekaniğini vermesi çok güzel olmuş çünkü tank sürmek gayet keyifli ve akıcı. Hatta bu konuda Battlefield 1'in ilham noktası bile bu oyun olabilir.

Genel olarak serinin önceki oyunlarına göre çok daha akıcı ve keyifli bir iş ortaya konmuş. Kesinlikle devam etmesi istenecek kalitede işlerden biri lakin maalesef muhtelif sebeplerden devamı gelmemiş. Sağlık olsun.

Hell’s Highway is, in my opinion, the strongest entry in the entire series. Just like the second game, it delivers a solid, engaging story that is enjoyable to follow and gives the right amount of weight to both the action and the characters.
The gameplay also holds up very well. The firefights feel cinematic, the battlefields are packed with more cover, and squad management is much more satisfying thanks to noticeably improved AI. I also really appreciated how destructible the environments are, with cover and objects being torn apart by grenades or simple gunfire. It makes the world feel far more reactive, giving you the sense of moving through an actual battlefield rather than some World War II theme park built entirely out of reinforced concrete.

Overall, Hell’s Highway feels like a major step forward for the series. It is just a shame Ubisoft never really followed up on it with similar games, a remake, or a proper fourth entry. A pretty baffling choice, especially considering how much room this genre still has to offer.

This is an early tower defense game.  It's graphics were nothing to write home about when it was released, they still aren't.  The game itself falls in the "you will lose, how long can you hold out?" genera of TD games.

It’s like falling in love and having the time of your life, only to realize a few months in that it won’t last long-term.

This game is very unique, very beautiful, and constantly pushes you to experiment. It teaches creativity, lets you build your own approach, and delivers experiences you won’t find anywhere else. That phase alone makes it a must-play. But eventually, routine sets in. You start telling yourself each run is as fresh as the first, but the illusion fades. The game doesn’t evolve, and over time the systems begin to feel more limited than they first appeared.

Achievements offer little incentive, and the lack of meaningful meta progression makes the experience feel static once you understand it. You keep trying to make it work, until burnout hits and clarity follows.

You had an incredible time, but in the end you start to question whether it was worth the investment.
Then again, what is a game if not an experience? It might still work for you.

Harvest: Massive Encounter is such a simple yet extremely deep game. It's a survival game in the skin of an RTS.

You have 2 resources: circley-things and energy. You get circley-things by mining the rocks that are scattered around the map; and you get energy from solar panels. All buildings require a certain amount of each resource to construct and, once built, require a certain amount of energy to operate. Each game is split up into waves with enemies pouring in from all directions. The enemy's goal is to destroy all of your buildings, while your goal is just to survive as long as possible. As the game continues, each wave will be made up of different types of enemies in ever larger numbers.

I've spent a lot of time in this deceptively simple game; but I highly recommend it.
It starts off slow-- I wish they could accelerate the resource-gathering phase-- but once things get moving it stays tense and engaging for the rest of your in-game life.

Harvest: Massive Encounter is one of the first steam games I ever bought and one of the few I really regretted. In Harvest you have to micro manage the hell out of everything. There's really only like 3 towers with attacks. There's 0 story, no modding, no interesting scenarios, and for me, very little replayability once you get things figured out.

It does some interesting things and is pretty different from most other tower defense games, but I can't recommend this game to anyone because it has so little depth. The interesting: 1) power management, you have to supply energy to your mines and your towers or they will not work (Creeper World 3 has something like this and I've seen some warcraft 3 custom maps that do this.). This is one of the few places where Harvest shines. 2) chaining of lasers together to make bigger, more powerful weapons. You can end up with an extremely powerful laser weapon and balancing how big you build them vs how many targets you need to hit is the main way you manage your weapons in the game. 3) the creative mode lets you build your base however you like and spawn monsters or waves whenever you want.

Sadly, that's pretty much it. Managing your lasers and your power grid and building some missile weapons is pretty much all you have to work with. In a genre that has everything from poison towers to buffing towers to armor shredders and many other forms of defenses, this one brings very little interesting and new to experience. Once you've played a few hours and survived a couple of onslaughts, you've seen everything the game has to offer. Oh and if you are a tower defense enthusiast who likes mazing, you can forget that. There are no walls in this game, and once a bad guy touches one of your buildings, it's gone. The game is pretty unforgiving in the sense that if you start to lose bits of your base, you've pretty much lost all of your base. 

I would *only* recommend it if you are a TD enthusiast (you might find it interesting then) who doesn't mind having a game in their library that they might only ever sink 10 or 20 hours into, or a game developer (to see the unique things it does and the many ways it fails to live up to other games). But it really only has replayability if you are the kind of player that likes to play the same map over and over again to shoot for more efficient times, because that's essentially what the game has: one map (with 3 different skins) and that's it. I was terribly dissapointed in the game and still am, over half a decade later.Sadly, the developer never added anything to the game to give it replayability.

Games that I would recommend over this one:
Creeper World 3 - Arc Eternal (power grid, towers, much deeper gameplay, has a map editor and thousands of maps made by fans to extend gameplay for months or years. It's part tower defense, part real time strategy game (except you can pause) because you can move the towers. The replayability has made this my favorite game on steam since Space Pirates and Zombies (a space ship shooter, not in this genre).)
Gemcraft - Chasing Shadows ( tower defense game with clever upgrade system, something like a hundred maps to play with, and challenge modifiers to make maps as tough as you like. Probably the best pure tower defense game that exists)

Other tower defense worthy mentions: Fieldrunners 2 (great variety of towers, great presentation, good mazing), Sanctum, Sanctum 2, Defender's Quest, Valley of the Forgotten (Great Story!)

If you're a Linux user, don't bother with this game.  In my experience, while the store says it supports Linux, the game refuses to work on most Linux systems you'd ever use.  When you launch a game, a script runs that tries to detect if you have the right libraries installed to run the game, but it just doesn't like 64 bit systems.  The script "runs", but fails to install anything.  Oh, and it relies on apt-get, so good luck getting the script to work at all if you're on a non-Debian system.

Let's say you forget Steam entirely, run the game's executable directly.  NOPE!  If you have the right libraries installed, in my experience, the game will look for the 64-bit library names, meaning you've got a 32-bit game asking for 64-bit libraries.  That just doesn't work.

Why am I posting this as a review, rather than asking for help on the community hub?  Because this problem is not happening just to me, and it has happened throughout the near year I've owned this game.  The reason I have that hour of playtime for a game that supposedly doesn't work?  I accidentally installed a 32-bit version of Ubuntu when I decided to hop distros, so I played this while I waited for the 64-bit version to download.

TL;DR: I can't speak for anyone using Mac or Windows, but on Linux?  Go elsewhere.  There's a reason there is no system requirement tab for Linux.

The Wonderful End of The World is a game from a different era, created to satisfy a niche. Everyone loves Katamari Damacy, but back in 2008 it would take another 10 years for the franchise to properly be ported to the PC! The Wonderful End of The World is undeniably a different developer's take on this type of game, and so I was immediately curious to check it out.

Now the core gameplay of having to collect items roughly your size, growing, and rushing against time limits. Even the story is reminiscent - while ditching the Japanese absurdist humor Katamari is known for it, it had a similar narrative about saving the world via cramming a bunch of items together. The difference however is that you have a mannequin rather than a ball, and this makes moving around feel almost like a 3D platformer at times. In fact you can even jump in a certain hidden mode! I will admit despite my love of the Katamari franchise, I actually somewhat preferred The Wonderful End of The World's control scheme in most scenarios. It was simple, tight, and worked well.

The one problem I do have with this game however is the tight corridors in certain areas. Katamari does a lot more to make it so the player won't be stuck too easily, but being a smaller title, The Wonderful End of the World unfortunately doesn't have as many safeguards from players getting stuck or even put in outright unfair situations. This is most notorious in the level Cafe Internets, where the abundance of tables makes it very easy to be stuck and the cobra NPC had knocked me into objects, causing me to physically get stuck at times! I found most of the game fairly easy to progess in, with getting a higher rank being a fun challenge, but it becomes problematic when you realize you need an A rank for every stage to access the final level. While I was able to get the others in 5 tries max, Cafe Internets was noticiably more difficult due to the tightness of the level and took around 30 tries for an A rank. Rice Cake Parade wasn't nearly as much of a problem, but it does also deserve a mention because while the 2D graphics gimmick was cool for this level, it also made it more difficult to get a sense of the hitboxes in a 3D space.

All in all, I did really enjoy my time with this game, and would recommend that if you are curious to try a another develolpers' take on the katamari forumla, you check out The Wonderful End of The World.

A less polished eat 'em up than Feeding Frenzy 2, but one that I ended up finding a little more to appreciate nonetheless. The Wonderful End of the World is basically just, what if a Katamari game was made in Unity and had you controlling a standard character controller instead of a ball, and the answer is, it's still fun. This marks another game I decided to play in one session on a whim, a task made even funnier by the way there's an achievement for completely restarting the game upon completion and beating it all over again in a single sitting, but it's not like I had a bad time doing so either. In particular I'm charmed by the aesthetic of this, it feels extremely late 2000s indie in how slapdash and rough everything feels, albeit in a way that doesn't ever come across as actively frustrating.

I'm also fond of how they ensured that each level had a different feel to it, both gameplay wise and in its scenery, not really hitting any points of repetition, as even the stages with similar types of scenery would be structured in a way to feel very different. Whether it was by having hidden clusters of small objects or making things really sparse to ensure that every pickup felt significant, there was a constant sense of needing some semblance of routing, especially with how the scoring works in this compared to a standard Katamari. On a typical Katamari game, the strategy tends to be running through clusters of smaller objects as quickly as possible and then learning to pivot to the bigger stuff ASAP. Wonderful End of the World flips this idea into one that feels more focused on prioritisation, as every item is worth the same number of points, meaning that being thorough with those smaller objects before you get too big to be able to have them register as pickups is vital, lest you leave yourself in a position where you can no longer get the highest rank on that given level without restarting.

This especially came into play with the internet cafe level being such a tight game of optimisation to properly complete that it took me well over an hour to accomplish, making constant micro-adjustments to my pathing and inching slightly closer with each try. It's strange that it's one of the first levels in the game that has this sort of difficulty to it and that everything else is easier, but it doesn't really detract from how much fun that hour was, to the point where I wish the rest of the game would keep throwing similarly difficult challenges my way. Despite wishing that more of the game were as fun to me as that opening hour or so, this is still a perfectly good time, one that feels like a time capsule of this era of indie sensibilities, being perfectly content with putting together a rough execution of a cool idea and that being all it took for it to be a lovely time, even if it's very what you see is what you get.

[h1]One of its kind type of game[/h1]
[hr][/hr][i]People are talking about some bizarre katamari thing. I do not know what it is. Is this some sort of Japanese fish dish? The point being, what is the point of a game if it is on a platform on which nobody plays with? Thus this game has no competition. Backwards compactability is just one thing out of many why console peasants are incomparable to PC games.[/i][hr][/hr]
[h1]📋Did you knew?📋[/h1]
That this company, Dejobaan games brings you quality games for 75 years? I did not knew it to, but it is in the intro. In fact, there is a lot of cool stuff just before you start playing this game. Game has a fun intro song which ties into main character, you and what you are doing. It is wonderfully done song which is masterfully woven into this game.

[h1]💻Gameplay💻[/h1]
Game is simple. Eat smaller objects. Grow. Eat larger objects until you become the biggest. It is simple game where you have to find the most efficient route to grow the quickest. Game is fairly short, so it doesn't overstay its welcome with simple mechanics. It can take few tries to complete a level with highest score and some levels are notoriously difficult, but it is doable to achieve in half an hour the best score if you have one functioning brain.

[b][i]Improvements[/i][/b]
[olist]
[*]The only thing which I had missed are levels which allows you to scale a lot. It might be an engine limitation, but game is pretty limited in how much you can eat before completing entire level. You can't eat a lot of small objects when you scale out of control nor you can scale into ridiculous levels.

[*]Another issue which I had is that when you try to complete time based challenges, I did struggled with two things. As you grew, it was unclear if you can eat an object until you waste time coming to that object and bumping awkwardly back. Thus wasting your precious time and getting annoyed. It then reveals engine flaw as it hasn't any way of determining what you can eat. Only what developers wrote on text file. This arbitrary number often leads to you being unable to consume smaller objects and vice versa, being able to consume bigger objects a lot sooner than you would expect. 

[*]Also, as you grow bigger, you might end up bumping into massive objects which you cannot eat. Then you will awkwardly turn around and lose control for a second until animation is finished. It feels very annoying and can be frustrating. Game also slows down as you become bigger and traversal becomes frustrating as you are racing against the clock in a slow character trying to eat fewer and fewer objects which you might or might not be able to eat since you can't tell that just by looking at them.
[/olist]
[h1]📋The Appeal📋[/h1]
I played a demo for a bit long time ago and since then I wanted to come back to this game. I enjoyed game a lot back then, thought it to be original and full of soul, creativity. I found it fun and creative up to this day. Even if it is simple, one-man indie game by today's standards, what sets it apart is that you can see that developers clearly cared and they tried to make a fun game.

I did enjoyed growing mechanic. At first you start at someone's garden. As you eat small objects you gradually grow until you break out of a garden into an yard. You start consuming ever bigger objects until the house itself doesn't seem massive. Then you go on the rampage as last seconds is usually where you start scalling out of control, eating entire neighborhoods in a desperate attempt to just get a little higher score. You can feel growth of your character and shift of scale.

 This is something which a lot of game struggle when trying to implement scale. Armored Core, Planetary Anhilliation try to do scale. However they fail at it since they forget one simple thing. In order to get feeling of scale you need two things:
[list]
[*]A size comparison;
[*]A small world;
[/list]
These games fail at one or both of those aspects like every similar game which I saw. First of all, world in which you play must not scale with you. You won't feel big if you scale game's asset with character. Also you need to establish a size comparison. If your character is huge, you must have ordinary units small. This could be done by having one big unit and normal comparison units small. For example, you want to show how big tank is? You give player a normal infantry man which serves to establish scale. Then you bring a tank which is many times bigger. Most games fail at this, because:
[list]
[*]Tank is not up to scale;
[*]Environment is not up to scale;
[/list]
World around you will be made bigger. Thus, you will feel equally small. Even if you make environment small, it will create feeling of playing in a sandbox since everything else will be just as big. The Wonderful End of the World and Psychonauts and Dark Souls are the only games I know which did scale well. Even the fact that I have to bring up games which fail at scale is a reason why we should call out game designers as frauds and bring them back to programming. 

[h1]The Wonderful End[/h1]
There isn't much to say about this game. It is short. It is simple. It is well crafted where entire story leads to the last level when world actually ends. Achievements are also interactive, well one at least is. A simple game often avoids perils of more complex or longer games when some mechanic in them breaks. Thus it is just better to play this game than spend more time reviewing or reading reviews than it would take to complete a small an hour or two adventure.

[h1] AT A GLANCE [/h1]
[list]
[*][b] Game Name: [/b] The Wonderful End of the World
[*][b] Original Release: [/b] 2008-01-25
[*][b] Genre Tags: [/b] Casual, Logic, Puzzle
[*][b] Estimated Playtime (Campaign): [/b] 3-4 hours
[*][b] 100% Achievements Playtime: [/b] 3-4 hours
[*][b] DLC Required for 100% Achievements: [/b] No
[*][b] Multiplayer Aspect: [/b] None
[*][b] Replayability: [/b] Some
[*][b] Recommended To: [/b] Casual Gamers, Achievement Hunters
[/list]
[h1] REVIEW [/h1]
[b] The Wonderful End of the World [/b] is a casual, logic puzzle game. 
[h3] STORY [/h3]
The world is going to end but you will be able to save as much of it as you can carry.  While the setup is nothing more than a generic scene to then begin playing, it definitely helps set the tone of the game.
[h3] GAMEPLAY[/h3]
The game deals with collecting items, growing in size, and grabbing more items.  You start each map as a small puppet and eventually grow to an enormous size. The goal is to collect as many items/points before the timer reaches zero on each map. 
[h3] PLAYTIME [/h3]
The game isn’t that complicated. You may find you will need to replay some maps to get a good path down to get to the A+ rating on the board.  There are 12 maps to play, (and 2 secret puzzles.) Play time for this game is ~3-4 hours to complete all puzzles and get all achievements.
[h3] INFORMATION[/h3]
The game was part of a Steam event in April 2011, involving Portal’s GlaDoS, which had a specific DLC associated with it for the ARG event. This DLC is no longer available, but was incorporated into the main game by the developers.  If you see some accounts that have a “Wonderful End of the World Accessed Content.” DLC, that is what it was for. (To access the hidden maps, hold the U key while entering Arcadia, and press P while entering the Sugar Candy level.)
[h3] COMPLAINTS [/h3]
There is nothing specific to complain about for this game.
[h3] REPLAYABILITY [/h3]
The game has some replayability as the game does offer other play styles and has a fun atmosphere. I have found I come back to this game and enjoy it each time I do. 
[h3] RECOMMENDATION [/h3]
I recommend this game to anyone that likes casual or puzzle games or is an achievement hunter.

[h1] Touch My Katamari VS. Wonderful End of the World comparison: [/h1]

[b] Touch My Katamari (PSVita, 2012) [/b]
-Most levels are super barren with objects few and far between with barely any of the humorous object arrangement that gives the series so much character
-Most of the actually fun levels are locked behind DLC
-Two levels are taken from We Love Katamari, both of which were also reused in Katamari Forever
-Plot is basically the same as We Love Katamari
-You have to buy time attack and eternal mode with currency that you need to grind for
-Feels like a mobile game that was slightly upgraded and put on the PSVita
-Creepy 3D modeled version of the king that you have to look at all game
-Absolutely no relation to Valve's "Portal" series


[b] Wonderful End of the World (PC, 2008) [/b]
-Levels are actually fun to play and have character in how they're designed with some being very abstract and unique
-No DLC, you get everything the game has to offer with a single purchase
-Completely original levels 
-Completely original plot
-Timeless and exploration modes for levels are unlocked through playing the game normally
-Clearly made as a PC game through and through
-No extremely ugly and off-putting 3D models of The King of All Cosmos are present
-Has relation to Valve's "Portal" series (Secret companion cube level and potato sack bundle)


[b] Conclusion: The Wonderful End of the World is a better Katamari game than Touch my Katamari

AAAAaaaaAAaaaAAaa!!! is a game about falling. Back from an era when most popular indie games were quite experimental, this game is all about jumping from buildings and trying to land without breaking all your bones. Along the way, you can "kiss" different buildings (getting close to them) or "hug" them (staying close to them), this will give you points. As you progress, you'll also unlock a can of spray paint, which allows you to tag certain buildings, and the Flip-It glove, which allows you to give the thumbs up to your fans (or flip the bird to your haters). What's the point of all this? Points. There's also scoring plates spread through some of the levels, which grant you extra points, plus a few other special plates. After succesfully (or unsuccesfully) landing, you'll get a score depending on how well you did, and you'll also receive teeth, the game's currency, used to unlock more levels.

Visually, it has a quite distinct, and flashy style (maybe not recommended for people with photosensitivity), and the buildings, or polystructures, as the game calls them (because, I kid you not, it actually has a backstory!) are quite abstract. As for the soundtrack, it has some really nice tracks that pump up the adrenaline while playing.

I can say with certainty that this is an enjoyable game. It's weird, but it's got its charm, so I can recommend it.

[h1]Overview:[/h1]

"[i]AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity[/i]" is a base-jumping game where the player parachutes into a colorful world filled with lights, buildings, rings, and other random things while attempting to rack up as much points as possible. The player must perform specific tasks to earn these points which are all tallied up after they land successfully. The game itself doesn't have so much as a plot as it does a [i]lot[/i] of kind of short stories that act like audio books. After finishing a specific amount or certain levels, you'll hear these stories usually from someone named "Neban" (I may have spelt that wrong). Other stories can also be unlocked with "[i]teeth[/i]", a currency obtained from finishing levels and obtaining stars (based on your score) alongside other levels that are randomly scattered across a unique level selection screen. To be honest, the stories are kind of boring but try to come off as funny. Although a lot of games don't have this style of humor, it's unique and a fresh take on comedy but doesn't really do it too well. The game itself is extremely random in terms of context and the game and text will mention things about pigs, grandmas, knives, meditation and all sorts of random stuff. All sculpted into each of their own unique story, some can be funny, others boring and some even unsettling. All in all, "[i]AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity[/i]" has quite a lot of different things in it but most I kind of just brushed off as nothing really came to be entertaining for me. Overall, "[i]AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity[/i]" attempts to do a lot to keep the player amused, engaged, and entertained, but perhaps tried a little [i]too[/i] hard. The amount of '[i]content[/i]' in the game may be a bit overwhelming for some users and although I want to give the developers credit for coming up with so much stuff to put in the game, sometimes too much can be a detriment to the overall game.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]

Where to start... well for starters, all you really do is move around a level while falling and avoiding obstacles but also staying close enough to them that you'll give them '[i]hugs[/i]' and '[i]kisses[/i]', all to which give you points. That's the basic premise of the game. However, later on you'll be tasked to do other things such as gesturing spectators, slowing down time, vandalizing buildings and breaking score plates. The game itself feels very basic but later levels will soon start to overwhelm the player and honestly is a good challenge ([i]but maybe too good[/i]).

The objective of the game is to basically obtain '[i]5 stars[/i]' on every level to prove how awesome you are. This is done by accumulating a certain amount of points to earn these stars, each giving the player a certain amount of teeth which is again: the game's currency. Teeth play a huge role in the game and every level requires teeth to be unlocked. This however becomes an issue later on because levels start to cost too much teeth for you to save up without having to replay previous stages you've beaten. The worst part is that teeth can only be obtained in beaten levels if you're able to achieve the same star rating you already got when you beat it the first time. This becomes repetitive super quickly and I can understand the game wanting you to improve, but assuming you do it successfully, you're only rewarded with a measly 250 teeth. And some levels can cost up to 12 [b][i]thousand[/i][/b] teeth! There are plenty of levels in the game which is good, but 85% of them are boring and below average at best. Frankly it's a grind that shouldn't be there and honestly, it's almost impossible to obtain a 5 star rating on some levels. And some of the maximum rewards for achieving 5 stars don't even surpass the initial cost of said level which is just a slap in the face. There are very specific ways to play the level in order to achieve the best rating and since you're free to move wherever you wish, it could take forever to find the perfect route. To put it bluntly, the game forces you to grind for some of the later levels but makes it a very monotonous task.

The rest of the game isn't horrible or anything, there's actually quite a lot of random stuff, and a generous amount of levels. The issue is that the random stuff overwhelms the player because there's just too many things going on and the levels themselves eventually start to feel the same.

[h1]Controls:[/h1]

As I said, all you really do is move around and avoid obstacles. Some things in the level can alter how your run plays out such as bounce plates, plates that slow you down or speed you up, teleporters, and other unique objects that can help you maximize your score. These objects themselves are actually fine and can be super helpful at times. None of them feel awkward to use and very few times would they actually not be helpful. The only complaint I have is that the controls feel very slippery. Momentum lingers a little too long for my liking and I find just trying to stay in a straight line more difficult than it really should be. Just be on your toes if you do plan on playing this game because you will in fact glide quite a bit (even though you [i]are[/i] falling so that mechanic does make sense I suppose).

[h1]Graphics:[/h1]

Something definitely straight out of the mid 2000's. "[i]AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity[/i]" has somewhat of a unique art-style and is actually kind of amusing to look at. It's something that you definitely wouldn't see anywhere else. It's the kind of environment and world you would find in those walking simulators that have floating buildings and other-worldly stuff you would [i]never[/i] see in a normal game. It's actually quite refreshing and I like what they did with the layout for all their levels (from a visual standpoint, gameplay wise... is another story but I digress). The graphics themselves look like things you'll see in a game from early 2000 and aren't magnificent. The visual appeal really comes from the placement of everything rather than the actual detail each object has.

[h1]Audio:[/h1]

Also quite unique. The quality itself is actually pretty good for its time but also a bit laughable (but not in terms of comedic value). Mostly everything can be comprehended and are not muffled beyond belief which is good but most of the audio clips where people are talking sound very boring (although intentional) and is not entertaining regardless of its intention to sound like a deadbeat. Sound effects during play however are decent but pretty average as well.

[h1]Conclusion/TL;DR:[/h1]

"[i]AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity[/i]" is a mediocre base-jumping game with slippery controls and unique visuals. Avoid obstacles and perform other tricks to obtain points and currency to unlock other levels. Late game becomes grindy and the overall gameplay is underwhelming to say the least. This game is definitely for a select audience and it may or may not be fun for some. It unfortunately did not speak too well to me. For the price tag, you could do better.

review:
[h1]Overview:[/h1]
'[i]AaaaaAAaaaAAAaaAAAAaAAAAA!!! for the Awesome[/i]' is a first person free falling game and is a remastered title of the original game '[i]AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity[/i]' with 82 remastered levels from the original as well as 43 new levels, '[i]AaaaaAAaaaAAAaaAAAAaAAAAA!!! for the Awesome[/i]' offers a decent amount of additional content but the question is, is it fun?

This is the kind of game that doesn't follow a single plot but has a boat load of oddball stories that verge on the line of just barely being funny. The humor is definitely there but much of it is weak but can potentially trigger a chuckle or a smile at the very least. It's very much the same as the original game and doesn't quite hit it with me. There are quirky videos, dialogue and texts that spew nonsense and if you want a taste of what I mean, just take a peak at the achievements. They'll give you a pretty good idea of the vibe that the entire game kind of takes off from.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
Now as much as I want to appreciate the obscure sense of humor that the game delivers and how I kind of wish more games had this weird, self-aware style of humor, the gameplay is just something I can't really get behind. I just want to say that the concept really [i]did[/i] intrigue me. Even when playing the original game way back then, I honestly thought the game would be more fun than it turned out to be for me.

Don't get me wrong, the game [i]is[/i] kind of fun at the start. You didn't (and to an extent, still don't) see many games that adopt the core gameplay around base jumping and to be honest, I kind of see why. The idea seems exhilarating at first but it doesn't take long for the player to realize the repetition that follows. The game tries to offer a good amount of things to do during a free fall in an attempt to mix up the gameplay and give players more to do than just steering until they land but it falls flat.

Some of the extra things range from waving or cursing bystanders watching you, "kissing" buildings and other objects which just mean staying close to them as you pass by and breaking glass plates all while you avoid obstacles. Many levels require you to somewhat multitask as all these actions can work in tandem with each other which can prove to be pretty hard. The goal is to essentially rack up as many points as you can to hopefully meet an end-of-level criteria that based on your performance, rewards you with teeth which is the games currency used to purchase other levels and extra content.

So the structure is there, the progression is there, the content is there and the concept is there. So why don't I find the game very fun? I honestly can't put my finger on anything else besides the fact that the game is pretty much the same exact thing through and through. Although the developers introduced different mechanics and level layouts to try and keep things fresh, it still just feels the same. Sure some levels are harder and longer than others but everything just feels like carbon copies of one another.

When I play one level and beat it, even if I don't get the maximum reward, I never feel inclined or motivated to play it again unless I need extra teeth and have no other means to get it anywhere else which was rare. Despite level layouts differing majorly, it all still felt repetitive. Perhaps it has to do with the fact that everything just looks the same. There isn't any uniqueness to the level designs that pop out to me so the idea of playing over 100 levels that all follow the same visual style just doesn't sound fun.

[h1]Control:[/h1]
Much of the same coming from the last game. Controls are fine and feel responsive. Obviously being a game where you're free falling, momentum plays a large part in the game so movement flows fine and doesn't feel inconsistent to the point where the game feels unfair. That being said though, there really isn't much else to the game besides gliding around while pressing a couple of keys every now and then.

[h1]Graphics:[/h1]
Honestly, I don't mind it. For it's time, it really isn't bad but nowadays it's definitely dated. The backdrops are lower resolutions of images such as mountains, the Earth or a cityscape which don't look great and the actual level is the same industrial constructs some with bright lights attached to them. It gets old fast and despite the game having lots of lights and visual effects (which are also lackluster to say the least), everything just looks bland. It looks slightly better than the original game but honestly, there isn't much visual improvement.

[h1]Audio:[/h1]
Pretty unique in my opinion. There are tons of hyped up music that plays all throughout the game and during jumps which you'd imagine would make the game feel very thrilling but it doesn't really capture that feeling. Despite that, the music is still pretty cool and the dialogue as mentioned is humorous. Sound effects are fine too but is nothing special.

[h1]Conclusion/TL;DR:[/h1]
'[i]AaaaaAAaaaAAAaaAAAAaAAAAA!!! for the Awesome[/i]' is a first person base jumping game that is an upgraded version of the original game '[i]AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity[/i]'. AaaaaAAaaaAAAaaAAAAaAAAAA!!! for the Awesome is a genuinely fun arcade base-jumping game where you freefall through floating cityscapes, hugging buildings for points and nailing landings — simple mechanics that are surprisingly addictive. The witty one-liners and quirky humor (yes, you collect teeth) keep things light, and the blood-pumping soundtrack adds real energy to each dive. That said, the gameplay loop is fairly shallow, and I found myself burning through the novelty faster than I expected — it's more of a pick-up-and-play game than something you'll sink hours into. If you can grab it on sale for a couple bucks, it's absolutely worth it for an evening of quick, chaotic fun.

I'd recommend this game, with the caveat that it's probably worth closer to $5, especially this far from its release. The game is very simple and pleasant to spend a bit of time in, but there really isn't much more to the game than you see on the tin. You jump, you try to stay as close to objects as possible without hitting them, and then you try to stick the landing.

There are a few powerups you can unlock, such as the ability to flip off people protesting your antics, but there are really no fundamental changes to that, at least that I've seen while perusing the unlockables.

The game also suffers a bit from its age, especially in the realm of input compatibility. While controllers do technically work (and dual analog input is really handy for a precision movement game like this), none of the instructions, tutorials, or tooltips provide information for anything except mouse & keyboard, forcing one to figure out even simple things like how to deploy their parachute blades for themselves. (At least for my controller, B deployed the parachute blades, and the left and right triggers were a thumbs up or obscene gesture, respectively.)

Overall, this is fun for short play sessions - or maybe longer if you get really fixated on beating your previous high score - but it probably doesn't have the staying power to be worth full price, at least for me.

Aaaaaa! For the Awesome is a basejumping game. You jump off a building and fall, dodging obstacles, collecting points and interacting with the world, and hopefully land safely at the end. Each level is brief, but filled to the brim with adrenaline. I suspect it in no way resembles actual basejumping, but then, it doesn’t have to. It resembles an idealised form of basejumping, where the idea of almost certain death is something to be joked about, and where the point is never to land safely, but rather, to fall spectacularly. The player becomes a spectacle, and it’s fun.

As fun as the basejumping is, it’s the greater world that really gives Aaaa! For the Awesome its heart and soul. There are fragments of a greater story sprinkled throughout that tell a surreal narrative about why the player is jumping off a building and what the world beyond those buildings actually is. This narrative doesn’t actually matter for the fun of the game - basejumping is going to be fun, regardless of where it’s set - but it adds a character and a surrealness to the game that make it an infinitely more interesting experience.

Did I need to feel the sensation of bugs crawling on my skin in a game about jumping off buildings? No. Am I grateful that the game created it anyway? …I guess?

It’s this combination of surreal, colourful environments and cheeky humour that make Aaaa! For the Awesome special. As terrible as I was at the controls - and to be clear, this is not a game meant to be played on touchpad, nor did I expect it to be - I found myself with tears of laughter rolling down my face at the humour and audacity of the game. This is not a game that holds back in lampooning itself, the situations it contrives, or the player themselves. It is self-aware, and happy to invite the player to have a laugh alongside it. 

It is also, most importantly, just fun.

I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with this game. The intense gameplay keeps me hooked, always itching to perfect every level for that coveted 5-star rating. However, the game's repetitiveness becomes apparent after a while, with a lack of variety in the levels.

The challenge to nail down hugs, kisses and the "thread the needle" stunt feels inconsistent. It seems like the game struggles to accurately register every move, which can be frustrating. There are moments when flying through a tiny gap earns you points, while other times it doesn't register at all.

Graphically, the game is starting to show its age, but it still holds up reasonably well. Despite these drawbacks, the addictive nature of trying to conquer each level overshadows the issues, making it difficult to put down. If you can overlook the minor flaws, there's a satisfying thrill in the daring descents and precision required to master each stage.

I’ve set myself a 2021 challenge to finish the uncompleted games in my Steam library in alphabetical order and write a 500+ word review once done. My completion challenge for this game was to unlock all the levels and finish them – it took me just under five hours.

Starting the challenge early, and the first game anyone with it in their library will play in an A-Z challenge is AaaaaAAaaaAAAaaAAAAaAAAAA!!! (For the awesome). A game about base jumping while trying to not break your face on the way down. That’s not easy when you must fly close to things for points – flying near stuff for a long time gets hugs, flying near particular things gets kisses.

The game isn’t visually impressive, a collection of low polygon surfaces with bad textures, but it’s one of those games that proves you don’t need good graphics to have a good time. Once you’re speedily zipping round towers with the energetic soundtrack pumping you’re past caring about graphics. This game is fun.

Each level is short, satisfying, and point plates for more difficult routes, a glove that you can use to flip off or give thumbs up to passing protestors or fans, and a spray can that you can use to tag certain buildings test your twitch reflexes even further as you try to avoid yet another squishy landing. There’s a plot, of sorts, but I can’t say there’s much of an ending. That said, AaaaaAAaaaAAAaaAAAAaAAAAA!!! is an enjoyable experience and one I’d recommend for the gameplay alone.

A Great Warhammer 40K Game, But a Disappointing Sequel

Dawn of War II is an addictive tactical RTS with excellent squad-based combat, satisfying progression, fantastic voice acting and an outstanding soundtrack. The characters are memorable, the factions feel distinct, and the grimdark atmosphere is superb.

Unfortunately, the drastic departure from the original hurts its appeal as a Dawn of War sequel. The lack of base-building and tech trees, restrictive squad limits, repetitive missions and frustrating backtracking left me wanting more. I also experienced several crashes, which didn't help.

Despite its flaws, I thoroughly enjoyed the campaign and its tactical gameplay. It's a fantastic Warhammer 40,000 experience, even if it isn't quite the Dawn of War sequel I wanted.

Anniversary Edition includes both expansions, Chaos Rising can be launched directly from the base game but if you want to play 2nd expansion “Retribution” you install it separately from your Steam Library.

Disclaimer: Still haven't gotten to the Chaos Rising expansion; so I don't know what changes have been made. This short review is for the original DoW II and Retribution. I started with Retribution because I've played these games way back when they came out and my fondest memories were of that one. Also I'm sick of Space Marines. I will list what bothered me most, which is what's important for potential players. The positive stuff is mostly tied to the love of the IP, music & VA and some nostalgia. Also I have a personal weakness for the customization options + the way equipment works in this game in comparison to DoW 1. 

DoW II: Tried on Primarch (hardest difficulty) and learned something very quickly - this game doesn't play well when you are micromanaging. 

1. Pathfinding is mediocre, units and squads get intermingled and bump into each other constantly, so you have to micro-micro-manage individual squads like you are up for a hyper-intensive RTS competitive trophy. Stupid.

2. We're talking about a RTS game where your only resource management are the limited charges on  (some) abilities, and the temporal restrictions in the form of cooldowns. You do not build units or worry about tiers. So why is the ONLY aspect that's supposed to work without hindrance (the movement, quick response time to input, and pathfinding) so labor intensive I do not know. The game demands quick response times in certain engagements but some units have slow animations on abilities. Stupid-er. 

3. But the dumbest decision the devs have made (and should've been changed in this edition imo) is basically everything about how missions work outside of the missions themselves. That's confusing so let me explain: You get 1 deployment per day. Do well on that deployment and you may get up to 2 additional deployments (but most likely you'll manage only 1). To get an extra deployment you have to do extremely well in at least 2 of the 3 categories during a mission: Fury, Resilience, and Speed, with scorelines from 1 to 5 skulls. Foundries (special building you can permanently capture on maps) are also crucial to earn extra deployments down the line. Get 12 of these skulls (or maybe 10-11 + the bonus from captured foundries) - get an extra deployment. 

Fury is based on the % of enemies cleared on the mission's map. But it also may be based on what you had for breakfast, because you will sometimes clear a whole map and get 55%, meaning you've sacrificed Speed for Fury and didn't get the pay-off. What's supposed to be the easiest of the 3 is also the most unreliable. Poetic - but that doesn't make for rewarding gameplay, you absolute donuts. Resilience works fine; if the main guy in a squad is incapacitated you get 1 skull less. The same squad leader can be incapacitated multiple times during the same mission but you won't get penalized further unless another squad leader gets incapacitated. What doesn't work fine is that some bosses' attacks do such a steep, unavoidable amount of great damage at times that you might lose a crucial skull right at the end of a mission. And Speed is . . . annoying. The game doesn't lend itself to playing fast, especially on higher difficulties. Even on Recruit, the easiest, rushing will get your squads killed more often than not, or force a retreat and mandatory revives which will further hurt your score. The whole system is dumb.

4. Then there's Rippa Splitta's mission. This one deserves a point of its own. This mission is the actual reason I'm writing this review - to spit venom here instead of break my gaming equipment, or trying to find out where the devs live to send a Nurgle-based gift. Probably one of the worst starts to a mission in a game - your squads are dropped in the middle of the base, get under attack immediately, and somehow the spot where they are dropped is very prone to bugging your squads (especially Avitus) and rendering them immovable (to the point that they can't even turn to attack in the opposite direction). So now you are at 3/4 of your squad strength (probably worse as in my case Avitus uses anti-building and anti-vehicle), at the start of the mission, surrounded. So, just restart the mission, right? 

This leads to the biggest oversight and slap in the face for a player. You can't restart missions. If you exit a mission for any reason - that's counted as your deployment for the day. Tyranid infestation meters go up, incumbent missions get 1 less day to be completed. STUPID. 

Retribution: Is awesome. Play it.

A WH40k themed squad-based RTS, where you need to finish missions with a customized squad of yours, in different maps. There is a story with interesting plot twists and  story-wise expansion with the different factions ramming into the trouble that was already getting more prominent. 

The intense battles where the squad needs to be properly aligned to the battlefield, be it trenches or walls to hide behind, or for the sharpshooter to be hidden or positioned on top of a tower, adds the real charm of the squad-based RTS in here, since instead of less micro management done on a proper battalion or legion, now we have highly effective a small squad with more detailed gameplay required. Such as the force commander, the main character, highly customizable depending on the strategy and the squad structure deployed for every mission.

The DLCs bring more RP-related touches to the game, such as the character alignment to Chaos or the Emperor, deciding the fate of the hero is also a nice detail, knowing the inner-struggles of Space Marines against the Chaos with its charms of power and vengeance.

I strongly think that, especially after playing both, DoW2 is a good squel to the first game which was a masterpiece and a legend on it's own category. Knowing more about the squad as the story progresses, customizing them according to your needs or tactics, the main character being a power-fantasy element capable of changing the direction if the battle being led, add more fun to the game.

Shoot them.

Un monument du jeu vidéo qui accuse ses presque 30 ans visuellement, mais qui reste un classique incontournable si on accepte son côté exigeant.

Il faut remettre les choses dans leur contexte : Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee est un jeu qui a presque 30 ans. À l'époque, le 640x480 pré-rendu était magnifique, mais aujourd'hui sur nos écrans modernes, il faut être honnête, ça pique un peu les yeux.

Ce qu'il faut savoir avant de se lancer :

Une prise en charge manette "ok sans plus" : Le jeu est tout à fait jouable à la manette, mais l'adaptation PC accuse son âge. À titre personnel, j'ai pas mal galéré avant de trouver la bonne configuration de touches pour être vraiment à l'aise.

Une histoire sympa avec un vrai propos : Au-delà de son humour noir et de son univers industriel décalé, le scénario reste super prenant et porte une vraie critique écologique et anticapitaliste qui fonctionne toujours aussi bien.

Des timings impitoyables : C'est un jeu de plateforme/réflexion à l'ancienne. Certains passages demandent une précision millimétrée et ne pardonnent absolument aucune erreur de timing, ce qui peut vite mettre les nerfs à l'épreuve.

En bref : Un grand classique avec une vraie personnalité. Si vous arrivez à passer outre les graphismes d'époque, le réglage un peu capricieux de la manette et quelques séquences die & retry punitives, l'expérience vaut largement le coup.

I've been playing platformers since the late 90s, and returning to the original Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee is still an unmatched, atmospheric experience, provided you are willing to do a little bit of mandatory tweaking before you actually hit play. The game itself remains an absolute masterclass in cinematic puzzle platforming, dropping you into the grim, industrial nightmare of RuptureFarms with its signature of dark humor and the brilliant speak mechanics that were wildly innovative back in the day. However, to be completely objective, the vanilla Steam release is essentially a raw dump of the old 1997 PC port that runs terribly on modern systems. If you just download it and launch it natively, you will likely run into broken resolutions, awful framerate pacing, crashes, and modern controllers that simply refuse to work (which to me was the most important issue, coming from hundreds of hours on the PS1 version). The absolute only way to properly enjoy this classic today is to skip the first google results about abewin.exe workarounds and download the R.E.L.I.V.E. engine. This completely replaces the original executable, adding native resolution support for modern monitors, smoothing out the performance, and making your gamepad actually work without third party tools. Once you drop that essential engine replacement into your folder, you are good to go. If you have the patience for that clunky 90s design and take a couple of minutes to set up R.E.L.I.V.E., this original version easily remains the definitive way to experience Abe's journey today.

Un juego de plataformas bastante impresionante gracias a las varias mecánicas que se implementan en sus niveles (sombras, estructuras, enemigos, códigos, etc), con escenarios y una ambientación extraterrestre muy llamativos, junto a una banda sonora más que decente que ofrecen una experiencia de juego desafiante.

Si algo me quedó claro después de 20 horas, es que en Oddworld lo que más necesitas es [b]PACIENCIA[/b], el margen de error en este juego no te perdona y cualquier descuido resulta en una muerte instantánea gracias a caídas, obstáculos, enemigos de gatillo fácil o con una velocidad increíble, lo que te llevará a repetir toda una zona una y otra vez si no mantienes tu paciencia.....y cordura.

Una cosa que me gustó fueron la creatividad de los diseños tanto de los enemigos como de las otras criaturas que vemos en este mundo alienígena, la historia es simple, tratando de Abe´s, un esclavo Mudokon que tiene que salvar a su pueblo de volverse una fuente de alimento en las granjas. 

Para ello tendremos que atravesar variados niveles en busca del poder suficiente para contraatacar, en donde seremos capaces de salvar a 99 Mudokons (tarea difícil), dependiendo de la cantidad que rescatemos lograremos un final bueno (+50) o malo (-50).

Algo que si me molestó, es el tutorial que nos ofrecen, nose si me salte una zona o que pero algunas mecánicas muy importantes las tuve que aprender varias horas después por cuenta propia o el juego te las enseñaba mucho después. Ojo con los guardados y los CONTROLES, revisen su configuración y asignación, no es lo mismo agacharse con la X que con las flechas xd, y la importancia del canto para abrir portales y rescatar a tus amigos.

A pesar de eso y las incontables muertes que me sacaron de quicio, lo recomiendo, no solo para que sufran igual que yo sino porque es un juegazo de plataformas muy divertido y carismático para ser de 1997. Además de que está totalmente traducido al español, en cuánto a rendimiento no tuve problemas más allá de algunos crasheos ocasionales y que las cinemáticas se ven algo borrosas :p.

Mucha suerte si deciden probarlo, el ensayo y error serán su mejor amigo.

Abe's Oddysee is still a classic, but running it on a modern PC takes a bit of setup. Out of the box, my CPU fans blew like crazy and hit 75C because the 1997 engine runs an uncapped single-core loop that pushes one CPU core at full boost voltage, even on the main menu.

I spent a long time testing standard fixes like setting a global or program specific max frame rate in GPU software, or changing CPU affinity in Task Manager and researched other solutions but didn't bother trying riskier things with the registry, BIOS and so on. None of what I tried worked because they don't stop the internal code loop from maxing out that single core.

Here is what actually fixed everything for me:

1. Finding & Adding the Executable
Auto-scans in GPU software won't detect this game. You have to manually add AbeWin.exe to your NVIDIA graphics program settings as well as Windows Graphics Settings to force your dedicated GPU (if you have a CPU with integrated graphics) and apply other custom profile options. (However frame limiters won't work like I said earlier.)

2. Visual & Scaling Fixes
Right-click AbeWin.exe > Properties > Compatibility tab:

Check Disable fullscreen optimizations.

Click Change high DPI settings, check Override high DPI scaling behavior, and set it to Application.

In your GPU control panel or App, make sure the scaling device is your GPU, Override the Scaling Mode Set by Games and Programs is checked and lastly enable GPU Integer Scaling as the mode. On a 1440p monitor, this gives you a sharp 1920x1440 centered picture with clean black sidebars instead of a blurry stretched image that aspect ratio gives. For other resolutions, you'll have to research that because integer scaling needs to divide evenly to work best, but on a 2560x1440p display panel the math works out for integer scaling with this game; you can switch back to Aspect Ratio whenever for other games. 

3. Fixing the CPU Heat & Fan Noise
Go to Windows Control Panel > Hardware and Sound > Power Options > Create a Power Plan (left side of the window) > create a custom plan name at the bottom (I named mine "Old Games")  and save it with default options > Change Plan Settings > Change Advanced Power Settings > Processor Power Management > set Maximum Processor State to 95%. This turns off CPU Turbo Boost voltage spikes for any programs while the plan is on, dropping my CPU temps from 75C down to a completely silent 41C with zero performance loss. I made a desktop shortcut for Power Options to swap to this plan when playing old unoptimized games like this that lack normal support. 

Once those quick steps are done, the game runs quiet and cool and when you aren't playing this game you just switch back to your recommended or default profile you normally use.

Speaking of saving people, I somehow managed to beat the game while killing most of the people I was actually supposed to rescue. I would like to say this was intentional, but honestly, some of it was probably the controls fighting for my downfall. Sorry, Mudokons. I tried. Sort of.

Despite all the rage bait moments, I genuinely enjoyed the game. There is something satisfying about finally figuring out a section after failing it approximately 47 times.

Do I want to play it again right now? Absolutely not. Am I probably going to return to it eventually to get 100 percent completion? Unfortunately, yes. Apparently, I enjoy suffering.

A cinematic platformer in the vein of games like Prince of Persia, Another World and Flashback. Weirdly compelling subject matter and lore, but the game is way too finnicky and the controls can be too stiff. Part of this is the actual charm of the genre: everything becomes a little sequence of actions that have to be performed in order, sometimes very cleverly, to clear a level; however, missing a jump and losing 5 minutes of progress simply because the game decided that you were -1U next to the precise spot that you had to jump from to clear a gap, or having to reset from checkpoint by suicide because you have to carry 4 mudokons, one by one, to the ring, telling them to stay and then release them at the same time precisely in that order tends to get to you. There's also no screen scrolling; all of this is also by design and charming as well, but most players should look into the remake, which I'm willing to bet has a lot more QoL. But there's a je ne sais quoi about the OG.

Alright, so first off, be aware that this game doesn't have excellent game design. Infact, the game design is actually somewhat subpar. The game oftentimes doesn't tell you important things (i.e, there is a part of the stockyards level where you have to get a stone to throw to set off mines by hitting a bag while jumping. The game does not that you can get said stones that way, or that you need them), and the save system is quite bad, with you having to tediously do things over and over again if you die, and trust me, you WILL die a lot.

So, why am I recommending it?

Because it's oftentimes satysfying as HELL to get past a puzzle, and, most importantly of all...

The art.

This game's art is GREAT.

Scratch that, the game itself is ART!

Genuinely, I CANNOT stress this enough, I LOVE the way this game looks. The closest things to it I can think of are Badlands and (to some level) Half-Life 1. It feels like an alive, yet decaying world. Like an ecosystem growing over a manmade one. It feels like if nature and machinery were swapped, and various manmade constructs began growing out of the ground, only for nature and machinery to get swapped back, and have vines grow on top of them. I truly cannot describe just how it feels. There's also a remade version with better game design (New 'N' Tasty), but that one feels more generic and flat. 

Overall, if you're fine with having to check playthroughs from time to time, and generally having to play a difficult stealth/puzzle/platformer game, this is a MUST BUY!!!

I played this a lot as a child. Yeah, definitely not the demographic, but when I got older, I found the game has a rythm and flow. Gone are the frustrations I once struggled with. The game has a great story, courtesy of Lorne Lanning and Sherry McKenna. I adore the atmoaphere, but that's everything you've heard before.

My relationship with it is bittersweet. I love the game. I love everything about it (yeah, I'm a sap). The mod community is huge, and is celebrated by OWI themselves. Something I am very grarteful for. That alone puts this in a positive range, let alone the stellar work on this classic. Thing is, I used to do modding, and some fan edits on YouTube featuring other models from Munch's Oddysee etc, and i lost my YT channel over it. It is a bit harder to go back after so much was lost. However, that does not sully my views of the game too much. I heartily recxommend it to anyone, but with a warning: If you want to mod, do not link the mod on YouTube. They will terminate your channel, but if you just want to play the base game, then you will have lots of fun...and maybe the occasional cry of rage.

(The review does not include my hours recorded because I played the relive modded version of the game which you can learn about here: https://github.com/AliveTeam/alive_reversing)

It pains me to not finish this game, but it's awful checkpoint system and incredibly unfair puzzle design makes this very difficult to recommend in the modern day. The sequel, Abe's Exoddus, has quicksave functionality which makes the game much more enjoyable yet I would find Oddysee far less grating if there were checkpoints, say, after you completed one of the optional secret challenges or in the midpoint of a very long set of challenges. I think it is okay to have to re-do sections you have already completed if they are fast to re-do if you have mastered them already. In Oddysee there are plenty of puzzles where sections of them are extremely easy but time consuming to re-play like when Abe has to wait to hear the end of a combinations of whistles before being able to respond (you can't just whistle beforehand if you already know what buttons/keys to press in combination). On top of all of this, some of the puzzle design is clunky as hell with the solutions being very unintuitive and reliant on so much guess work that figuring them out often doesn't feel satisfying. It is a shame, because this game has so much going for it including the speech system, [precise platforming, the grimy and alien aesthetic, and still impressive PS1 pre-rendered backgrounds. I think I'm just going to play Exoddus because that one has all of the great stuff I am looking for with few of the downsides.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
✅ Recommended

A legendary classic and a very nostalgic game for me.

[h2]My history with the game[/h2]
I played Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee many times as a child.

I even had the PC CD version back then, and I spent a lot of hours with this game. It became one of those childhood games that stayed in my memory for years.

On Steam, I only played it for 16 minutes, but this review is mostly based on my older experience with the game.

I also played the remake on PlayStation 4, and because that version has better visuals, I probably will not return to this original 1997 version for a full playthrough again.

Still, this game means a lot to me.

It is my #45 game of all time.

[h2]Quick signals[/h2]
💸 Value: ✅ Worth it
🖥️ Requirements: ✅ Runs on almost anything
🎨 Graphics: ✅ Old and pixelated, but iconic
⏱️ Length: ✅ Around 6–10 hours
📖 Story: ✅ Memorable
🎮 Difficulty: ✅ Challenging
🐛 Bugs: ➖ No major issue in my short Steam revisit

[h2]What I liked[/h2]

* The atmosphere is unique and unforgettable.
* Abe is an iconic main character.
* The world, art style, sounds, and dark humor still have a special charm.
* For a 1997 game, it had a strong identity and creative design.
* It gave me many great memories as a child.
* Even today, it works as a reminder of how original and different older games could be.

[h2]What didn’t work for me[/h2]

* The original visuals are very old now.
* The pixelated look may be hard to enjoy for newer players.
* The remake is easier to recommend visually if someone wants a more modern version.
* I personally do not feel the need to replay the original fully anymore.

[h2]Is it an endless game? How long to beat?[/h2]
No, this is not an endless game.

It is a classic story-based puzzle platformer. A normal playthrough can take around 6–10 hours, depending on skill, patience, and how many Mudokons you try to save.

[h2]Who will love it[/h2]
Veterans of older PC and PlayStation games will probably appreciate it the most.

You may enjoy it if you like classic puzzle platformers, darker atmosphere, old-school difficulty, strange worlds, and games with a very unique personality.

[h2]Replay value[/h2]
Replay value is decent, especially for nostalgia or for players who want to save more Mudokons.

For me personally, the original is now mostly a great memory. I would rather replay the remake because of the improved visuals, but I still respect the original a lot.

[h2]Final note[/h2]
Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee is not a game I will probably replay fully in its original form again, but it is still very important to me.

It gave me many childhood memories, and because of that, I can easily recommend it.

Recommended, especially for veterans and players who still enjoy older pixelated classics.

I am a huge fan of the immediate sequel of this game, called Abe's Exoddus. Recently, I've taken the time to play through this first game, going into it with the knowledge that it's "the same game but shorter and with a few less mechanics".

I was wrong. 

Now I need to stress that this game is NOT atrocious by any means. The music, atmosphere, sound effects, characters designs, world building, etc. are masterclass and leagues ahead of today's games industry.

Sadly, Oddysee flops badly in the gameplay department. The challenges and puzzles involved in making progress through this game are really, really awful. The solutions often involve having to do the last thing you'd logically think of, such as jumping into a well that launches you back into the air from right next to it, instead of jumping into it from on high, with the game never explaining that there's a difference. In general, a lot of progress is done by first faffing about for several minutes, before coming up to a precision timing or other critical point, which can be easily failed, then you have to watch the game load for 3 seconds, Abe spawn for 3 seconds and then spend the several minutes faffing about just to get back to the critical point again.

I don't recommend getting this version as it has no emulation save states, which is something that you will need to make this game more bearable.

If you think this game sucks, I do highly, HIGHLY recommend not skipping Exoddus, as the puzzles and challenges are far better designed in that game.

extremely vibe based game with incredible artwork and heavy messaging that's fantastic to see, unfortunately it's brought down by what feels like a tutorial every screen for the entire first hour to then thrust you into the most obtuse puzzles known to mankind and no way to redo any situation where you may have messed up saving a mudokon. Like cool I need to save 100 of these guys but I'm just going to cut past the multiple screens of other mudokons if you're just going to tell me to go fuck myself after I let one die. 

It doesn't help that when it feels like it's picking up out of the factory in the dark wilderness that it then halts you with a situation in which the only 2 exits are guarded by patrolling enemies you can't sneak past. You're not given any objects to throw or any way to avoid them. I'm not sure if there's a secret mechanic the game wasn't telling me about or if I genuinely had to fiddle with the platforming mechanics to somehow cheat my way to the next screen, but there certainly isn't a way to sneak jump or anything. Eventually the game after already forcing me into situations where mudokons would die if I hadn't already played beforehand, has now forced me into a situation where I need to runback multiple screens, wait patiently for patrols just to try my luck at the same passageway where there's not really a way to sneak past save for one path where maybe I can grab a ledge and lean back off it to maybe keep them from seeing me when they get alerted. Even then every movement I've tried hasn't allowed the grab and attempting to jump then crawl down off to hang has gotten me shot.

I get if maybe the point is replayability, and of an era, but by the ps1 era it's just odd to see, especially when it already has rather hostile player mechanics with the prince of persia esque platforming, brutal runbacks, and a middle finger waiting for you if you don't save every single one of the mudokons.

I'd still maybe recommend the game since It's on sale for less than a dollar, and genuinely I really think the world, messaging and art is a fantastic strong point that's only helped by the aging display methods and graphics.

Note: download the R.E.L.I.V.E mod before you play this! The pc port was made quite a while ago and some stuff doesn't run, look, or play in general like it did back in 1997. This mod fixes that!

Legitimately one of my favorite games ever. Brilliant brilliant brilliant. It's hard without being too monotonous or cheap (though there are some gotchas lol). If you can get it working, play this instead, and if it's too hard for your liking (nothing wrong with that fyi), try New & Tasty.
