Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus reprend tout ce qui faisait le génie du premier épisode et passe la vitesse supérieure. Si vous avez aimé Abe's Oddysee, vous allez forcément adorer cette suite qui corrige les défauts de son aîné tout en multipliant les idées de gameplay.

Pourquoi il surpasse le premier :

Plus fin graphiquement : Sans révolutionner le moteur de l'époque, les décors gagnent nettement en finesse, en détails et en variété d'ambiances. L'univers industriel et mystique d'Oddworld n'a jamais été aussi immersif.

Plus de contenu et de possibilités : L'aventure est beaucoup plus généreuse et le GameSpeak s'enrichit énormément. On peut désormais donner des ordres à plusieurs Mudokons à la fois, gérer leurs émotions (colère, déprime, aveuglement) et même posséder de nouvelles créatures (Glukkons, Slogs, Scrabs, Paramites) ou... ses propres pets explosifs.

Beaucoup plus confortable à jouer : L'ajout majeur qui change tout, c'est enfin la possibilité de sauvegarder à tout moment (QuikSave). Fini la frustration de devoir refaire trois écrans entiers après une erreur de timing !

En bref : Une vraie bonne suite comme on aimerait en voir plus souvent. Elle garde toute l'âme et l'exigence de l'original tout en étant plus vaste et plus agréable à parcourir. Si vous avez accroché au premier, foncez les yeux fermés.

As with Oddysee, this game is a treat. It is well known that it had a rushed 9 development cycle, but that makes it more impressive. What you may not know is, despite the small time allocation, they still updated things. Watch the Security Eye animations in both games. They still found time to alter it.

I absolutely recommend this game. It's story is great, its visuals are fantistic and stand above the remake's. Voice work is fantastic. Though, I never knew why Abe sounded like he had a cold during this outing. (Must've got it in that trek from Monsaic to Necrum). 

As with its predeccesor, the modding community is huge. There are mods out there that take days to complete. Some are downright cruel, while others are works of art. Inspiration is not only enjoyed, but supported by OWI, and I think that, on its own makes this something special.

Call me an old sap, but I can't actually think of anything to criticize, given the rushed dev cycle. Sure, there are changes. The "enemy in next screen" piano is gone, though is still in the game files. All o Ya is a welcome addition. I think everyone's said that by now. If you REALLY want a nitpick, I would say that the Necrum Vault trials (Mudomo and Mudanchee) are filler. Beautiful, well designed filler. Abe should have the Weirdos' trust by now, but I guess those guys are stingy. But, it is so well made up for. New additions, gorgeous backdrops and level designs make those levels breeze by. Even moreso once you've slogged through the GBA version.

In conclusion, (and to stop me writing a novel) I would say, even if you haven't played Oddysee, you should play this. Yes, it comes in the Oddworld Classic pack, but if you want to get a feel for Abe's controls, this one instructs you a bit better. Yes, you may lose some context, but they actually have a dedicated recap just before you start the game. Before long, you'll know all the tricks, and be a pro in no time...says me who's been playing it for 20 odd years.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

A classic Oddworld game and another strong nostalgic memory from my childhood.

[h2]My history with the game[/h2]
I tried Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus on Steam for 12 minutes.

Just like Abe's Oddysee, I also played this game as a child. I had the original CD version and spent a lot of hours with it back then.

This Steam revisit was short, but the game still works as a strong nostalgic reminder of that time.

[h2]Quick signals[/h2]
💸 Value: ✅ Worth it for classic game fans
🖥️ Requirements: ✅ Runs on almost anything
🎨 Graphics: ✅ Old and pixelated, but iconic
⏱️ Length: ✅ Classic story-based game
📖 Story: ✅ Memorable Oddworld style
🎮 Difficulty: ✅ Old-school challenge
🐛 Bugs: ➖ No major issue in my short revisit

[h2]What I liked[/h2]

* It still has the classic Oddworld atmosphere.
* Abe is still a great and memorable character.
* The world, sounds, humor, and darker tone have a very unique identity.
* It brings back strong childhood memories for me.
* I am glad this original version is still available for players who want to return to it.
* For fans of older puzzle platformers, it still has historical value.

[h2]What didn’t work for me[/h2]

* The original visuals are obviously very old now.
* Newer players may find the pixelated look harder to enjoy.
* Since Soulstorm exists as a newer version, I personally prefer to play that instead.
* I do not really feel the need to fully replay the original today.

[h2]Is it an endless game? How long to beat?[/h2]
No, this is not an endless game.

It is a classic story-based puzzle platformer. The full playthrough length depends on your skill, patience, and how much extra saving and exploration you want to do.

[h2]Who will love it[/h2]
You will probably enjoy Abe's Exoddus if you like old-school puzzle platformers, classic PC games, darker atmosphere, strange worlds, and the original Oddworld style.

Veterans who played it back in the day will probably appreciate it the most.

[h2]Replay value[/h2]
Replay value is decent, especially for nostalgia or for players who want to experience the original version again.

For me personally, I am glad I can return to this classic, but I will probably play Soulstorm instead because of the improved graphics.

[h2]Final note[/h2]
Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus is another important childhood game for me.

I may not fully replay this original version today, but I still respect it and I am glad it is available on Steam.

Recommended, especially for nostalgic players and fans of older classics.

[h1][b] Reseña de Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus®[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus® es esa aventura 2D noventera que te invita a “salvar a todos” mientras el juego te responde: “claro, campeón… ahora pisa mal y muérete por quinta vez”. Controlas a Abe en una odisea de plataformas, sigilo y rompecabezas con humor negro, ciencia ficción rara y un mundo tan atmosférico como incómodo.

La propuesta es simple y cruel: avanzar pantallas resolviendo situaciones tipo “si mueves esto, explota aquello”, usando canto/posesión y mucha paciencia. Es una aventura en el sentido más clásico: exploración por pantallas, lógica a prueba de orgullo y un ritmo que alterna entre “qué inteligente me siento” y “por qué sigo aquí”.

Primera impresión en Steam hoy: es un clásico de culto con personalidad, pero también una cápsula del tiempo. Y como toda cápsula del tiempo… viene con bordes filosos.

[h2]Lo Glukkon y lo Mudokon[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
 Diseño 2D clásico con plataformas + rompecabezas que sí te hacen pensar   
 Ambientación tenebrosa y súper “años 90” (en el buen y el peor sentido)   
 Humor negro y comedia incómoda: el mundo es triste, pero se ríe de ti igual   
 Sigilo y tensión bien marcados: avanzar se siente como robarle la cartera a la muerte   
 Identidad de culto: raro, memorable y con personalidad propia   

Lo No Tan Bueno:
 Difícil y castigador: el juego ama tus errores más que tú a tus logros inexistentes   
 Cero logros en Steam: ni una palmadita digital por salvar mudokons   
 Retro de verdad: controles/flow con aroma a “así se hacía antes, aguántate”   
 Comunidad activa diminuta (2 jugadores): el club de fans está en horario reducido   
 Gore/oscuro: si esperas ternura, te equivocaste de planeta

[h2]Conclusión (Muy Bueno)[/h2]
Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus® sigue siendo una aventura con identidad, de esas que no piden permiso para ser raras. Su mezcla de plataformas, sigilo y rompecabezas funciona porque el mundo está diseñado para que te importe… y para que sufras un poquito por importar. Controversialmente: sí, es injusto a ratos; y precisamente por eso se siente tan “de la vieja escuela”.

Ahora, hablemos del elefante en la sala: 2 jugadores activos. Eso no significa que esté muerto; significa que este es un ritual para iniciados, no una fiesta. Aun así, 1450 recomendaciones no salen de la nada: el juego se ganó su lugar como clásico de culto por mérito, no por moda.

Si toleras lo retro y te gustan los rompecabezas con mala leche, vale la pena. Si necesitas recompensas modernas tipo logros y abrazos del sistema, aquí solo hay pantallas oscuras y consecuencias.

Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus is a remarkable sequel that builds upon the foundation of its predecessor while expanding both the scale and ambition of its darkly satirical universe. Developed and published by Oddworld Inhabitants, the game continues the story of Abe, an unlikely Mudokon hero who once saved his species from becoming corporate meat products. This time, the stakes feel more spiritual and existential. After experiencing a vision from ancestral spirits, Abe discovers that the oppressive Magog Cartel is desecrating sacred Mudokon burial grounds to harvest bones for the production of SoulStorm Brew, an addictive beverage used to control the enslaved population. The narrative weaves themes of exploitation, addiction, environmental destruction, and corporate greed into a surreal yet pointed allegory, delivered through grim industrial backdrops and dark humor that remains striking decades after release.

At its core, the game refines the cinematic 2D puzzle-platforming formula that defined the original. Movement is deliberate and weighty, with Abe able to run, crouch, roll, jump, sidestep, and cling to ledges with careful precision. Every screen presents a self-contained challenge filled with lethal hazards, from land mines and motion sensors to hostile creatures and armed guards. What makes the experience distinctive is its emphasis on problem-solving over combat. Abe is not a warrior; he is vulnerable and fragile, and survival depends on timing, observation, and ingenuity. Trial and error plays a significant role, as many traps must be learned through failure. While this design philosophy can feel punishing, it also fosters a sense of accomplishment when players finally navigate a sequence flawlessly.

One of the series’ most innovative mechanics, GameSpeak, returns in expanded form. Through simple vocal commands, Abe can communicate with fellow Mudokons, instructing them to follow, wait, or operate switches. These interactions transform the game from a solitary platformer into a rescue mission where responsibility weighs heavily on the player. Each Mudokon saved contributes to the overall ending, adding moral weight to every action. Possession, another defining feature, allows Abe to chant and take control of certain enemies, turning them into temporary tools for clearing paths or solving puzzles. In Exoddus, new abilities such as invisibility, healing, and emotional states that affect followers deepen the mechanical complexity, giving the sequel a more layered and experimental feel than its predecessor.

The world design is expansive and atmospheric, shifting between sacred catacombs, grim mines, industrial complexes, and the grotesque machinery of the SoulStorm Brewery. Pre-rendered backgrounds are richly detailed, combining organic decay with oppressive industrialization. The art direction creates a strong contrast between the natural and the mechanized, reinforcing the game’s environmental and anti-corporate themes. Character animations are expressive despite the 2D limitations, giving Abe and his fellow Mudokons personality through subtle gestures and reactions. The sound design further enhances immersion, with haunting ambient effects and unsettling mechanical noises echoing through corridors. Even moments of silence are purposeful, amplifying tension before a dangerous sequence.

Difficulty remains one of the defining aspects of the experience. The game demands patience, memory, and precision, often requiring players to memorize enemy patrol patterns or execute near-perfect timing to bypass obstacles. While modern design sensibilities might favor more forgiving checkpoints, the harshness here contributes to the identity of the game. Each safe Mudokon escort or successfully navigated trap feels earned rather than handed out. That said, the unforgiving nature may deter newcomers accustomed to smoother control schemes and more generous save systems. The pacing can also feel dense, with lengthy sections that test endurance as much as skill.

What truly elevates the experience is its tonal balance. The bleakness of forced labor, addiction, and environmental ruin is offset by absurd humor and satirical exaggeration. Corporate propaganda, grotesque executive characters, and exaggerated industrial branding create a biting critique of unchecked capitalism. Despite its cartoonish exterior, the game carries emotional undercurrents about freedom, identity, and spiritual heritage. Abe himself remains an endearing protagonist—timid, uncertain, yet persistently brave. His journey is less about heroics and more about resilience and responsibility, which lends the story a grounded emotional resonance beneath the surreal surface.

Even decades after its initial release, the game retains a unique charm that few platformers replicate. While technology and design philosophies have evolved, the blend of cinematic presentation, social commentary, and intricate puzzle design gives it a timeless quality. It may not offer the smooth accessibility or streamlined mechanics of contemporary titles, but it compensates with personality and depth. For players willing to embrace its deliberate pacing and demanding structure, it delivers a memorable adventure filled with tension, creativity, and moral stakes. In the broader landscape of classic platformers, it stands not just as a sequel, but as a defining chapter in a series that dared to combine sharp satire with challenging, methodical gameplay.

“Oddworld - Abe’s Exxoddus” is the 1998 sequel to the 2D side-scroller Jump ’n’ Run title “Oddyssey” from the year before. Generally received very positively by players and critics in 1997, the humorous adventures of the quirky character Abe are getting a major expansion in its yet sinister environment, directly connected to part 1. Considering mechanics and difficulty, the game has also received some significant adjustments which make it a better experience, though it’s still quite challenging and thus too challenging for children in my view. Story-wise, it’s pretty much the same: you control Abe and try to free as many fellow Mudokon workers from the clenches of the evil Glukkon factory bosses. Nevertheless, the second instalment has some inherent shortcomings preventing it from gaining an even higher rating. 

After about 21 hours play time in a completionist approach (rescuing all 300 workers), here’s my pros/cons list:

Pros: 
+ continuation of part 1
+ intro well done
+ maintaining same, great humour and alien slavery setting
+ great atmosphere
+ story well done
+ lots of smaller and bigger challenging riddles
+ much more detailed environment
+ on the more serious side, an even worse, more sinister and ruthless behaviour of company bosses without becoming overexaggerating, well incorporated into the overall inhumane industrial setting
+ really, they’re treating the Mudokons so badly (blinded ones and the tear collectors…) !
+ the quicksave option decreases the difficulty tremendously and makes the issue of “repeat whole sections” much more bearable, in other words much more forgiving than part 1
+ restart path option possible if you have made a mistake somewhere on the way
+ both quick save and permanent save keep the actual position of the character, what a great relief!
+ much more interaction with the environment and NPCs
+ more enemy variety, most of them really keeping you on your toes
+ possession of nearly everything in the levels is possible now
+ shorter secret levels which are usually less difficult than the main path (in part 1 it was the opposite)
+ higher task variety
+ this time even a vehicle to steer available
+ command several Mudokons at once
+ more varied levels with an abundance of sections
+ conclusion well done

Cons:
-	Engine-inherent issue of rolling screen change preventing some better timing of movements and reconnaissance of forward areas
-	Tasks and levels become very repetitive after first half of the game
-	Controls still a bit sluggish when you actually need to depend on them
-	Sometimes input errors coming from the engine (e.g. moving sideways instead of jumping up into a door or well)
-	Some level elements or enemy bodies actually have a strange size or rasterization resulting in the left or right third to be used, at least when considering the visuals, making it harder to time or guess the correct movements
-	Super stretched 2nd half of the game
-	Lots of level and asset recycling in 2nd half
-	Too many hubs making you branch off and come back again, at least for my taste
-	Rather sudden, rushed ending

Conclusion: 
Exxoddus is a much more refined, well-balanced game than its predecessor, especially when it comes to mechanics and difficulty. But the inherent shortcomings of the engine regarding screen change rolls and the slightly sluggish, unprecise as well as sometimes erroneous controls can still make it frustrating in various sections. Nevertheless, a much better experience than part 1.

This is a copy-paste of my review for Oddyssee.
Although they are separate games, they are very similar at core which is why the following applies for 99% of both games, and differences I've explicitly mentionned.
tl;dr: Exoddus is basically Oddyssee with a few more gameplay features/QOL features, and more content. Play Oddyssee first if possible, as it is simpler and shorter and Exoddus elaborates on it.

The 2D Oddworld games (Oddysee, Exoddus) are classics of their time.
They are essentially puzzle-platformer games.

Controls-wise, they kinda build upon the original Prince of Persia (1989) and the like, but improve the formula on multiple ways.
tl;dr: controls may feel oldschool to a modern gamer, but once understood are 100% precise.

Gameplay-wise, there is actually a lot to do despite this being at core a platform game.
Abe (main protagonist, of "Mudokon" species) sometimes will use speed (run from the dangers, quick enough), but most of the time will need wits to advance through the game.
His goal is to save his companions from certain death where he used to work, but to that end, he has got to acquire special powers by passing trials (more screens/puzzles) in two uncivilized regions, with equally dangerous traps and creatures.
The player can try to save all Mudokons (very difficult, as there are secret passages), save all he finds (easy enough), or save the least of them he can (are you trying to be mean on purpose or something ?).
The normal ending requires saving half of them and is easy enough to achieve.

So, Abe has got a set of basic platformer-character actions. He can walk, crouch, crouch-run, run, jump (forwards, or upwards, can grab a ledge), sneak (silent walk), etc. and can also manipulate levers, pulley-based elevators and a few other machines.
He can also grab and throw a few objects (rocks, meat balls, grenades).
Now, Abe can also:
- chant to take complete control of some creatures (one at a given time), or eventually command them to die.
- speak with fellow Mudokon characters (simple stuff like "hello", "follow me", "stop" etc.). Feature is called "GameSpeak".
Most creatures are agressive, except Mudokons. To save Mudokons, you basically have to speak and guide them a bit like the lemmings you have to save in Lemmings. Except hopefully orders are simpler, and Mudokons are not unstoppably suicidal. They will follow Abe to portals, through which they safely escape.
Creatures' AI in Oddworld is simple and goes like clockwork so that the gameplay is not ambiguous.

That's about all there is to it, but it allows for countless situations with little repetitivity.

Exoddus is the same at core, except that there are more news ways to solve puzzles. New creatures (and Abe can take control species he previously couldn't), new abilities.
A few QOL features as well. A few supplementary GameSpeak words for finer guidance, as well as a Quicksave (save at any moment, instead of checkpoints only) feature.

I did not talk of the scenario/story, because they oftentimes are secondary to me in games, but what we have here is above average expectations for a platformer game. Oddyssee/Exoddus feature simple but efficient stories (of the Miyazaki kind, short of better comparison) with a moderate use of FMV cutscenes, as well as multiple endings, as mentionned previously.

ps. be warned that the 2D Oddworld games are difficult, but mostly fair games. I haven't tried the new 2.5D Oddworld games (New'n Tasty / Soulstorm) but have heard that they unfortunately lack the precision-platforming of the oldies.
The original games are the good kind of old-school.
There have certainly been older and more recent attempts to put puzzles into platforming, but these games may very well be the finest out there, and the chanting + GameSpeak features make them truly unique and memorable.

I have sympathy for this underdog of the classic range. The first ever Oddworld game in 3D. Now, i'm not nostalgia-blinded. I know the environments are recycled. I know the story has problems. I know it's more for kids and things aren't as gritty, but it's still classic Oddworld. Abe seemns older and more battle-hardened. Much is competent, even if the sounds they gave him aren't perfect.

Speaking of sound. Yes, there are some sound bugs in this. A creator named Dee Dyne did make a fix. I believe he's still on Discord. It's been a while since I got that patch. (sorty if this is useless, I just know he's proud of it and that it did help with my recent playthroughs).

The visuals, i've seen people get mad at. Guys, it was 2001, and they had never done RealTime. They were designing for X-BOX. A whole different system to the PS1. It was gonna look rough, especially in the modern day. 

My biggest issue with it, is that the story is so seperate from the prior two games., Yes, it was technichally meant to be Game 2, with Exoddus being an expansion to Oddysee, but it feels a bit too seperate. Abe and the Sligs are just sort of there, with the Vykkers being more of a presence. At least, as characters. There are plenty of Sligs to gun down with their brand new laser guns. Oh, yes. Sligs have got lasers now, as do the Mudokons. The Muds even have their own Zapper defenses.

On that point, why in the name of Mudos did they remove the ability to take out chant supressors? They have zero collision. That was a major point in the first two games. Take out an orb or drone, then possess a Slig to complete a puzzle, or clear the path. Sure, levels like Stockyard Escape didn't allow it, but it meant you had to get crafty. It shifted the gameplay from Rupture 1, where you could use grenades on them and tear your way through. Here, it just feels like they exist. The Zappers aren't much better. The first lot just reset Sligs back to their spawn points, while the next lot only do something if you lure Sligs in. Not too bad, if you didn't already clear your path througth most of them to activate them. Great idea in concept, not so good in execution. Also, I love the regrowing land mines. Weird choice with no context, but it's so odd that I can't hate it. I think that sums up this game.

The end goal is amicable and very strong, but the tasks to get there paint our heroes as kinda evil. Needs must, i suppose. I won't lie to you though, the Golden Quarma ending still tears me up. It feels like you really did the absolute best thing, and are rewarded aptly. The bad ending...uhhh, well, let's just say it's the direct inverse of that. 

Look, some hate the dumbed down story of this game, and I can see its shortcomings, but once you've played the GBA version, you'll get a new appreciation for this version. That's a promise.

I do still recommend it, guys. Yeah, the achievements are broken, but that's not the game's fault. Take the game as a time capsule, back to an experiment that walked, so that Stranger could run.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
❌ Not Recommended

A 3D Oddworld game that simply did not work for me.

[h2]My history with the game[/h2]
I played Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee on Steam for 17 minutes.

This version is apparently a newer port from 2016, and I wanted to try it mainly because I have nostalgia for Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee.

This time, however, the game did not grab me at all.

[h2]Quick signals[/h2]
💸 Value: ❌ Not worth it for me
🖥️ Requirements: ✅ Easy to run
🎨 Graphics: ⚠️ Old 3D visuals
⏱️ Length: ➖ I stopped after 17 minutes
📖 Story: ➖ Did not hook me
🎮 Difficulty: ✅ Simple
🐛 Bugs: ➖ No major issue in my short playtime

[h2]What I liked[/h2]

* It is still connected to the Oddworld universe.
* You can play as Abe again.
* I understand that some fans may appreciate seeing Oddworld in 3D.

[h2]What didn’t work for me[/h2]

* The 3D gameplay did not feel interesting to me.
* Compared to Abe's Oddysee, it lost a lot of the charm I liked in the original.
* It felt boring by today's standards.
* Honestly, I think it would have felt boring to me even around the time it originally released.
* After only 17 minutes, I had no motivation to continue.

[h2]Is it an endless game? How long to beat?[/h2]
No, this is not an endless game.

I personally stopped after 17 minutes, so I cannot fairly judge the full length. My review is based only on this short Steam experience.

[h2]Who will love it[/h2]
Maybe dedicated Oddworld fans who want to try every game in the series will find something interesting here.

For casual players, or for people who mainly loved the older 2D Oddworld style, I do not think this is easy to recommend.

[h2]Replay value[/h2]
For me, replay value is none.

I tried it, but I do not want to continue or return to it.

[h2]Final note[/h2]
Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee may have its fans, but it is not for me.

I respect the Oddworld universe, and I still have strong nostalgia for Abe's Oddysee, but this 3D entry felt boring and uninteresting very quickly.

Not recommended.

The gameplay feels crude and unpolished. The platforming feels imprecise and overtly strict. The combat is button-mash trash, while the mechanics for controlling your army of NPCs are just a vastly worse version of Pikmin. The camera's extraordinarily slow movement acceleration makes any sort of fast-paced gameplay impossible. The camera's tendency to simply do as it pleases or sometimes outright ignore your inputs is a baffling choice by the developers that negatively affects the entire game. The way that characters must turn to face the exact direction that the left analog stick is held in before finally being allowed to move a full second after the initial input was made instantly ruins any fluidity this game could have ever had. The sound effects for Munch falling from too high and Abe drowning are shrill and so annoying that it's beyond my comprehension how the developers thought it was okay to leave as is; I would prefer a rusty nail on a chalkboard. I still am nostalgic for this game even 18 years after I first played it. However, after 100%-ing it, I've gotta say I'm beyond disappointed at how little it held up to my expectations. This is at best a very mediocre videogame. But the worst is yet to come. Because if playing this game by itself isn't enough of an issue. The absolutely nightmarish state of this PC port dwarfs any flaws this game has.

Upon launch the game always took up both my monitors and only showed 40% of the game's screen to me. Video settings are nonexistent. So you need to use the shortcut (Alt+Enter) to force the game into windowed mode. However, my keyboard has a shortcut (function+z) that puts it in Mac mode. This for some reason swaps the Windows and Alt keys. But it also doesn't register Alt as Alt because Mac has to be special and replaced Alt with the options key for some absurd reason. So I spent an hour and a half trying to find some 3rd-party program that auto-launches games in windowed mode before finally pulling up a keyboard press website that displays which keys are being pressed. While much of this scenario isn't the fault of the developers. The root of it is. This game always launches in an unplayable state and requires the player to waste time fixing it because the developer didn't care to do so themselves. Because of that, they will collectively waste hundreds, potentially thousands, of hours of human time that could have been spent having fun with a nostalgic game. Beyond that, the game randomly crashed about half a dozen times during my 2 playthroughs. As well as some absurd vertex stretching in level 22 that made the game pretty difficult to play.

But the fun hasn't ended yet, because certain achievements don't work on the default version of the game. Not just one or two either; five out of thirty-eight don't work. So I tried the original 2016 version in the hope I could unlock them there. Half the time it doesn't recognize arrow key inputs from my 60% keyboard, and all menus cannot be accessed by controller. Not only that. But somehow this original version bypasses the multiple layers of framerate limiter settings I have put on my PC. I refuse to let this ancient game run at 4,000 fps and utilize my entire GPU. So I go on yet another hunt to figure out how to fix all this crap. Until I finally come to a realization. The only reason I don't want to use Steam Achievement Manager to unlock achievements that I have already earned through gameplay. Is because I have too much pride as a completionist (cringe I know, but bear with me). Pride is the root of the other 6 deadly sins. So I said screw it and unlocked them with Steam Achievement Manager. I care more about my sanity and well-being than I do about getting a dumb program developed by a bunch of nimrods to actually function properly.

I'm taking an additional half point away for the absolutely abhorrent sound design and achievements not functioning properly. Adding it all together, this version of the game gets a big fat ZERO from me. What a disgrace of an application. Shame on you, Oddworld inhabitants.

Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee represents a significant turning point for the Oddworld series, marking its transition from meticulously staged 2D cinematic platforming into fully navigable 3D environments. Developed and published by Oddworld Inhabitants, the game continues the franchise’s tradition of blending dark satire, environmental commentary, and offbeat humor, but it does so through a noticeably different gameplay structure. Originally released in 2001 and later updated for modern systems on Steam, this installment carries both the ambition and the growing pains of early 3D design, making it a fascinating, if sometimes uneven, evolution of the Oddworld formula.

The narrative introduces a second playable protagonist alongside Abe: Munch, the last surviving Gabbit. While Abe’s people, the Mudokons, have long suffered under corporate exploitation, Munch’s species has been hunted nearly to extinction for their eggs, which are processed and sold as a delicacy known as “gabbiar.” The story once again revolves around corporate greed and industrial cruelty, but this time the stakes feel even more personal. Munch’s journey to reclaim the last of his species’ eggs intertwines with Abe’s ongoing resistance against the Glukkons, forming a dual-hero structure that defines the game’s design. Their partnership provides both mechanical variety and emotional grounding, as the survival of an entire species hinges on the player’s success.

Gameplay shifts dramatically from the tightly controlled, screen-by-screen precision of the earlier titles into open 3D spaces that encourage exploration. Players alternate between Abe and Munch, each with unique abilities that must be used in tandem to solve environmental puzzles. Abe retains his signature chanting ability, allowing him to possess enemies and command fellow Mudokons, while Munch brings aquatic mobility and the capacity to interact with specific machines and electrical devices. This dynamic creates a cooperative puzzle structure within a single-player experience, where success depends on switching between characters strategically. The concept is clever, and when it works, it delivers satisfying moments of coordination and problem-solving.

However, the move to 3D introduces both opportunity and friction. The environments are more expansive than anything previously seen in the series, featuring industrial complexes, natural waterways, and sprawling facilities filled with hazards. This added scale enhances the sense of place and reinforces the world’s oppressive industrial aesthetic. Yet early 3D camera systems and movement controls can feel less precise compared to the deliberate choreography of the 2D entries. Platforming occasionally loses the razor-sharp clarity that defined Abe’s earlier adventures, and navigation can sometimes feel cumbersome. These issues are not constant, but they are noticeable enough to shape the overall pacing and challenge.

The thematic identity of the series remains intact. The game continues its biting critique of consumerism and exploitation, delivered through grotesque corporate villains, exaggerated advertisements, and absurd product branding. The humor is still dark and satirical, balancing bleak subject matter with oddball charm. Munch himself brings a different tone to the narrative; where Abe often embodies quiet resilience and reluctant heroism, Munch’s vulnerability and determination add emotional variety. The dialogue and cutscenes lean more heavily into comedic timing than previous installments, sometimes sacrificing subtlety for accessibility, but they still reinforce the franchise’s distinctive personality.

Visually, the game captures the strange beauty of Oddworld through expressive character models and varied landscapes. While it lacks the pre-rendered detail of the earlier 2D titles, the real-time environments create a new sense of immersion. Industrial zones are cluttered with machinery and oppressive architecture, while natural areas offer brief contrasts of color and openness. The updated Steam version improves resolution and performance, smoothing out some technical limitations of the original release. Even so, certain textures and animations reveal the game’s early 2000s origins, reminding players of its place in the transitional era of 3D game development.

The difficulty curve is more forgiving than in the earlier Oddworld entries, but it still demands attention and patience. Combat plays a slightly larger role, with vending machines dispensing ammunition that can be used against enemies, adding a layer of light action to the formula. This shift makes the experience somewhat more accessible, though it also softens the tension that came from Abe’s near-total vulnerability in prior games. Escorting Mudokons remains a key objective, preserving the moral dimension of saving as many allies as possible to achieve a better ending.

Ultimately, the game stands as an ambitious experiment within the series. It may not possess the laser-focused precision or haunting minimalism of its 2D predecessors, but it compensates with expanded scale, dual-character mechanics, and a broader sense of exploration. For longtime fans, it offers a deeper look into Oddworld’s lore and a chance to see the franchise evolve beyond its original constraints. For newcomers, it provides an accessible entry point into a universe defined by satire, survival, and resistance. While imperfect in execution, it remains a distinctive and memorable chapter that demonstrates both the risks and rewards of creative reinvention.

Rating: 8/10

Я проходил две первые части серии, но новая часть свернула куда-то не туда.
Из 2D платформера со стелсом и секретами резко превратилась в какую-то аркаду с собирательством и детскими задачами.
Да, это что-то новое, но смотрится такой переход максимально странно.
Игралось бы, в принципе, неплохо, если бы не злоебучая камера - отрыжка неудачного переноса в 3Д. Иногда она любит взять такой ракурс, что заруинит вам игру. Да, мышкой можно повертеть и это немного исправляет ситуацию, но иногда мышка позволяет "влететь" в текстуры и наблюдать их изнутри, не помогая игровому процессу. Ну и да, удачи вам в прыжках с этой хуетой.

Сами уровни игры иногда настолько неинтуитивны, что без руководства игру просто не пройти. А полного руководства в видео - формате попросту не существует, только в текстовом, который ещё и перевести нужно.

Задумка разделения функций на двух персонажей была бы неплоха, если бы не было столько умений у каждого из них. Про некоторые ты забываешь (настолько редко их пользуешь) и иногда из-за этого ловишь полный затык в игре.

Сложность если поначалу ещё терпимая (а в опциях нет выбора!), то потом она просто доводит до нестерпимого гнева и мата. Признаюсь честно, я уже настолько заебался с этой игрой, что психанул на уровне со взрывчаткой и расставленными мехами вокруг, которые в тебя палят. Игра просто допинала мою психику. Поэтому считерил: нашёл сейвы, чтоб перемахнуть этот ебучий уровень.

Ну и отмечу, что Steam в своём репертуаре (а может и сами ленивые разрабы). Выкинуть в свой магазин игру родом из нулевых, без малейших апдейтов или улучшения графики. Ну и русский язык для слабаков, верно ведь ([i]сарказм[/i])?
Удачи тебе понять брифинг на английском и все ролики, для которых русификатора НЕ СУЩЕСТВУЕТ. Хорошо, хоть для текста есть русификатор, а то с некоторыми правилами в игре был бы полный затык.

Резюмирую: не прикасайтесь к этому говну, если не хотите сжечь себе нервные клетки. Для ознакомления и понимания задумки двух персонажей - можно пройти первые 5-6 уровней, далее никаких особых отличий нет.
Эта часть - худшая из серии Оддворлд, в которую я пока играл (3 первых части). Постараюсь пропить чай с мятой и забыть эту парашу побыстрей (всё равно потерянные 17 часов жизни мне никто не вернёт).
Это что угодно, но НЕ ИГРА.

[h1][b]🎮 Reseña de Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee es ese clásico raro que mezcla Acción, Aventura y un toque de Estrategia como si alguien hubiera tirado tres géneros en una licuadora… y sorprendentemente no explotó. Aquí alternas entre Abe y Munch para avanzar en plataformas 3D, resolver rompecabezas y sobrevivir a un mundo que parece diseñado por una corporación que odia la vida (y sí, es parte del chiste).

La propuesta es: “piensa antes de saltar”, “usa al personaje correcto”, y “manda a tus amiguitos a hacer el trabajo sucio”. Hay comedia negra, violencia caricaturesca y gore lo suficientemente incómodo para recordar que Oddworld siempre ha sido “divertido”, pero con un letrero de “esto en realidad es bastante cruel”.

Primera impresión en Steam: se siente como visitar un museo interactivo donde algunas piezas siguen brillando… y otras crujen cuando las miras. Un jugador, logros, cromos, y compatibilidad parcial con mando: lo mínimo para que tu biblioteca se sienta productiva mientras sufres con cariño.

[h2][Oddworld: Lo que te abraza y lo que te empuja al vacío][/h2]

Lo Bueno:
✅ Alternar entre Abe y Munch le da variedad real a la aventura y a los rompecabezas 🧠  
✅ Mezcla decente de plataformas 3D + acción + estrategia ligera: no es solo brincar por brincar 🎮  
✅ Humor oscuro y comedia absurda: el mundo es miserable, pero al menos se ríe de ti 🤡  
✅ Tiene logros (38) y cromos: dopamina legal para completaristas 🏆  
✅ Clásico con personalidad: no se siente genérico aunque tenga años encima 🧩  

Lo No Tan Bueno:
❌ Compatibilidad parcial con mando: o sea, “funciona… pero no te emociones” 🕹️  
❌ Es un juego de un solo jugador: si buscabas caos con amigos, aquí solo tienes tus pensamientos 😶  
❌ Plataformas en 3D de la vieja escuela: a veces el “salto” es una apuesta y tú eres el casino 🎲  
❌ Comunidad actual minúscula (3 jugadores): más solitario que tu lista de deseos en rebajas 🪦  
❌ La violencia/gore puede sentirse más incómoda que “divertida” según tu tolerancia 🩸

[h2]Conclusión (Bueno)[/h2]
Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee es “Bueno” porque se atreve a ser raro, cínico y con corazón… aunque a veces te lo entregue a golpes de plataforma 3D y controles que te recuerdan que esto viene de otra era. La mezcla de Acción, Aventura y Estrategia ligera se sostiene, especialmente cuando el juego te obliga a pensar y alternar habilidades en lugar de solo avanzar a lo bruto.

Ahora, lo controversial: este juego no te pide permiso para ser incómodo. Entre comedia, violencia y gore, te suelta una sonrisa y luego te hace cuestionar por qué te estás riendo. Y sí, en Steam hay 965 recomendaciones totales, lo cual sugiere que no estás solo en tu mal gusto… aunque irónicamente ahora mismo solo hay 3 jugadores activos, así que el club existe, pero se reúne en una cabina telefónica.

Si te gustan los clásicos con personalidad (y toleras sus mañas), vale la pena. Si tu estándar es “todo debe sentirse moderno y suave”, este Oddysee te va a parecer una excursión escolar obligatoria.

Si quieres una aventura en tercera persona con plataformas 3D, rompecabezas y humor negro marca Oddworld, entra sin miedo (pero con paciencia). Si buscas perfección técnica o comodidad moderna, mejor míralo como lo que es: un clásico “bueno” que no se disculpa por ser incómodo y peculiar.

[*] Lots of attention to detail for QoL stuff (most of the time)
[*] Multiple endings!
[/list]
[h2]Cons[/h2]
[list]
[*] Munch feels kinda useless most of the time. He can't do anything with Spooce and he's slower than Abe, so most of the time you want to be using Abe primarily. Plus, Abe has a possession ability while Munch has sonar, but sonar is able to be used so infrequently that it's basically worthless on most levels. For a character whose name is in the title, it's a pretty big letdown, though still result
[*] Possession ability is far too overpowered
[*] Saving the eggs is a tedious task simply because there's so many of them. Since this is only a mechanic in a few levels at the end, it's not a big problem
[*] The final few levels have some awkward sections
[/list]
[h3]Bugs[/h3]
[list]
[*] Most gamespeak options don't work, some cutscenes fail (but dont stop you from progressing)
[*] Looks normal and decent but might fall short in direct comparison to original
[*] Pathing can be bad on followers, resulting in them getting disconnected from your party if you're not paying attention
[/list]

Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath HD est sans doute l'épisode le plus atypique de la saga, et pourtant l'un des meilleurs. Injustement passé sous les radars lors de sa sortie originale, cette version HD lui rend enfin justice avec un lissage visuel très appréciable qui permet de redécouvrir son univers western-décalé dans d'excellentes conditions.

Pourquoi il vaut le coup :

Un gameplay malin et nerveux : Le mélange entre vue à la troisième personne pour l'exploration/baston et vue subjective pour le tir fonctionne à merveille. L'idée des munitions vivantes (petites créatures aux effets variés à capturer soi-même) apporte une vraie dimension tactique. Conseil : jouez impérativement à la manette, les sensations y sont bien meilleures qu'au clavier/souris.

Une vraie bonne histoire : L'ambiance de chasseur de primes solitaire fonctionne super bien, et le scénario réserve quelques rebondissements bien sentis qui collent parfaitement à l'ADN critique et décalé d'Oddworld.

Le seul bémol :

Une fin un peu expédiée : On sent qu'il a dû y avoir un problème de budget ou de temps sur la dernière ligne droite. Le rythme s'accélère brusquement dans le dernier tiers et le dénouement paraît un peu rushé par rapport au reste de l'aventure.

En bref : Un excellent Oddworld, original et ultra-attachant, qui mérite largement une seconde chance aujourd'hui malgré une conclusion un peu précipitée.

I liked it, because the bounty system is fun, the characters are memorable, and the world seems so out of place, all while not overstaying its welcome. 
I beat this game fairly quickly, and I'm kind of glad to have done it. The lack of controller support was not great, but the game is surprisingly good on Keyboard and mouse. I hated how dated some of the combat felt, but I gave the game grace, because I know this is an old game.

The story was not the strongest part of the game, and that is okay, too. Sometimes, I felt that the game really had you doing stuff, just to have to doing stuff. Not bad, but kind of lackluster. The comedy held me over, though.

Hopefully we get a sequel and the [spoiler] Steef [/spoiler] will make a grand return.

A distinctive action adventure combines third person exploration, bounty hunting, and first person shooting into a memorable and creative experience. The blend of genres feels natural throughout the journey, with each gameplay style supporting exploration, combat, and progression in meaningful ways. A unique world filled with unusual characters and locations helps create a setting that remains engaging from start to finish.

Bounty hunting provides a satisfying gameplay loop built around tracking targets, exploring large environments, and choosing effective strategies during encounters. Capturing targets alive often feels especially rewarding, encouraging careful planning and creative use of available tools rather than relying solely on direct combat. Mission variety helps maintain interest as new challenges and objectives continue to appear throughout the adventure.

One of the most creative aspects of the experience comes from the living ammunition system. Different creatures serve different functions, creating opportunities for experimentation during combat encounters. Weapon variety extends beyond simple firepower, encouraging tactical thinking and making encounters feel distinct. Resource gathering and ammunition management add another layer of depth without becoming cumbersome.

Storytelling gradually reveals a compelling narrative supported by memorable worldbuilding and strong character development. The journey evolves in unexpected ways, allowing exploration and gameplay to remain closely connected to the unfolding story. Environmental design contributes greatly to immersion, with every region offering a unique atmosphere and identity.

The visual upgrade enhances an already memorable adventure while preserving the qualities that made the original stand out. Creative gameplay systems, rewarding exploration, engaging bounty hunting mechanics, and a distinctive setting come together to create an experience that remains fresh even years after release. The overall result is a highly enjoyable adventure that successfully blends action, exploration, and storytelling into a unique and memorable package.

4K / 120fps / no screen tearing Self-Remaster Settings: 

Note I'm using an RTX 5070 for this, on Windows 11, fully updated Nvidia app and Gaming Ready drivers.

Get the app Borderless Gaming on Steam.
Get the Lossless Scaling app on Steam. 
The game crashes at 4k so in the popup for Settings before the game starts, set it to 1440p, Vsync OFF, Fullscreen OFF, Antialiasing OFF

Set monitor in Windows OS Settings to 120 hz
Nvidia Control Panel app: Display > Setup Gsync > Enabled for Windowed and Fullscreen mode

Run the game via Steam, it'll have the app bar at the top since its not Borderless. Alt+Tab to the Borderless app, find Strangers Wrath in the list, right click and choose Make Borderless. Now the app is running in a forced borderless window mode, no menu bar.

You can then start the Lossless Scaling app. Make sure Frame Gen is set to OFF.

In the Scaling section, set it to LS1. 
Rendering: Sync Mode: VSYNC
Gsync Support: ON
Draw FPS: ON (this is the overlay in the upper left corner of the game)
Click the Scale button in the upper right and Alt-Tab to the game

The main menu is a video background running at 30 fps, so load into a saved game to get into the game engine to see the real FPS. If you don't see the 120 / 120 overlay, Alt-tab to the LS app and then back. You may have to choose Unscale and then Scale again in the LS app, then Alt-Tab to the game again.

Once you see 120 / 120 in the upper left, you've confirmed its running at 120 solid, with the 1440p upscaled to 4k if you monitor is 4k. I had screen tearing issues if the LS app Rendering didn't have Vsync enabled. You can't use the game Vsync or the Scaling app won't work right and thus you can't boost the 1440p to 4k. The Nvidia Control Panel Vsync option didn't work either. Having the LS app do the Vsync eliminated screen tearing finally.

Make sure your settings match mine and you'll have butter smooth gameplay at 4K/120 with no screen tearing, upscaled from 1440p. I can finally play through this game and have it looking smooth and sharp, thanks to AI helping me work through the tech issues to get it running far better than the 480p/30 OG Xbox console version released early 2005.

Also, yes the game is good, not amazing but definitely worth a few bucks on sale, especially with the 4K/120 working great now.

OddWorld: Stranger's Wrath is a game that tries to do invoke feelings of playing a hybrid of Ratchet & Clank and Conker's Bad Fur Day and unfortunately can't seem to find it's identity. For the first 60% of the game you spend time going into 3 different towns which act as little hubs to begin bounties, with each area having about 4-5 bounties. There is also a general store which allows you to purchase ammo and occasionally upgrades. suddenly after completing the last bounty in the 3rd (and last) town the story and gameplay take a sudden shift in direction. You're no longer collecting bounties and now set on an adventure to hunt down some big bad boss and the game suddenly becomes super linear. The story feels a bit convoluted with the final cutscene "twist" not even have much emotional depth because the sudden main antagonist of the game had basically ZERO deposition to explain the motivation behind why he is doing what he is doing. I could get over all that because the real attractive part of this game is cool combat and ammo type system; BUT its all ruined by the final quarter of the game spiking difficulty by stripping you of all your upgrades from the first portion and then giving you 3-4 different armors which in my opinion never made me feel like I was any more tanky than the previous suit. The REAL crime is just how buggy this game is. the worst offender is for some reason after you discover what the Stranger is I had a bug where if I tried moving from a stand still in 3rd person mode the Stranger would just stand there or spin in a circle, the only way I could get my directional inputs to matter was to get momentum first by either swapping into 1st person mode and then switching out after taking some steps, jumping, or attacking, This lead to some very frustrating moments and deaths because I would try to go take cover only to have the bug render me stuck in place while getting beamed by the enemies. The next bug required me to dig into an obscure forum because there is a section at the end where you are timed to run to the final boss' office while avoiding dying to snipers and gunners only to make it to the end and the Stranger not running through the door in the cutscene and you getting locked out of the next area, and since that section was the MOST frustrating one for me with a LOT of deaths it turns out you have to quickly skip the 3 second cutscene to teleport you behind the door or suffer the consequence of trying to make that run all over again. [h2]Verdict[/h2]
✅ Recommended, but mostly for nostalgic players

An okay Oddworld spin-off that I respect more than I personally want to keep playing.

[h2]My history with the game[/h2]
I played Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath HD on Steam for 33 minutes.

I did not play this game back when it originally released, so I do not have nostalgia for it. I mainly tried it because I wanted to explore more games from the Oddworld series.

After trying it, I can say it is okay, but it is not something that grabbed me enough to continue.

[h2]Quick signals[/h2]
💸 Value: ✅ Worth trying on sale
🖥️ Requirements: ✅ Easy to run
🎨 Graphics: ⚠️ Old, but acceptable in HD
⏱️ Length: ➖ I stopped after 33 minutes
📖 Story: ➖ Did not hook me quickly
🎮 Difficulty: ✅ Simple to understand
🐛 Bugs: ⚠️ Launcher issue with anti-aliasing

[h2]Technical note[/h2]
The game did not launch for me when anti-aliasing was enabled in the setup launcher.

If the game does not start, try turning anti-aliasing off.

I also set the maximum FPS to 60, but in-game my monitor still showed 144 FPS.

[h2]What I liked[/h2]

* It is an interesting and different take on the Oddworld universe.
* The idea of mixing first-person and third-person gameplay is unique.
* The HD version makes the game look playable enough today.
* I can understand why nostalgic players or older fans may still enjoy it.
* It is not a bad game, just not really for me.

[h2]What didn’t work for me[/h2]

* The game did not hook me during my short playtime.
* I cannot imagine myself finishing it.
* Without nostalgia, it feels more like an okayish older game than something I personally need to continue.
* The launcher issue with anti-aliasing is annoying.
* The FPS setting also did not seem to work properly for me.

[h2]Is it an endless game? How long to beat?[/h2]
No, this is not an endless game.

I personally stopped after 33 minutes, so I cannot fairly judge the full length. This review is based only on my short Steam experience.

[h2]Who will love it[/h2]
You may enjoy Stranger's Wrath HD if you played it back in the day, have nostalgia for it, or like older action-adventure games with unusual mechanics.

It may also be worth trying if you are a big Oddworld fan and want to experience something different from the main Abe games.

[h2]Replay value[/h2]
For me, replay value is very low.

I tried it, I respect it, but I do not feel any motivation to continue or replay it.

[h2]Final note[/h2]
Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath HD is an okay game, and I can recommend it to the right audience.

For nostalgic players, it may still be a fun return. For me personally, without nostalgia, it did not grab me enough to keep playing.

Recommended, but mainly for fans and nostalgic players.

Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath (2005) was a very underdog game even upon its original release in 2005. Critically lauded, but a commercial failure that publisher Electronic Arts saw fit to basically shadow drop only on the original Xbox right as the Xbox 360 launched, the game was basically stillborn from lack of marketing and the choice to release it on only one then-current console with no next-gen console or PC versions. Only 600,000 copies were sold in total; by the time the game made the rounds in magazines garnering critical praise, people learned about the game too late, as it was already sold out, and EA wouldn't print more. 

As for the game itself. Stranger's Wrath is the most interesting combination of 3rd person platforming and 1st person shooting, merging something like Rare's Banjo-Kazooie with a zany Oddworld take on the 2000's FPS phenomenon kicked off by games like Halo: Combat Evolved. You seamlessly switch between both perspectives with a button press on the fly, and have combat options in both modes, using melee attacks similar to Banjo or even Crash Bandicoot in 3rd person, while then having your crossbow in 1st person to handle action that way. Damage is handled with a "self-heal" mechanic you engage manually, transferring stamina back to your health bar.

The star of the show besides the "Stranger" himself is the "live" ammunition you have on that crossbow. With both primary and alt fire modes each housing a different critter that serves as your ammo, you have things like "zapflies" for regular shooting, "chppunks" as distraction ammo, "bolomites" to wrap up enemies, and so on. The primary objective is to "bag" bounties, which involves incapacitating enemies then sucking them up with a vacuum cleaner of sorts; alive is best for the most "moolah", but dead also works if you happen to kill them, and same goes for bosses. Upgrades for money, and you can both "hunt" and purchase your ammo as you go.

The story is full of crude humor and some of the most memorable dialog you can imagine, while also being somehow deep, moving, and epic. Seriously, you will laugh and even possibly cry if you make it to the game's unforgettable ending, which plays out both like a tragedy and a redemption at the same time; we really didn't deserve games this good back then, and now we barely get things that qualify as games from the same publishers. The game has a classic three-part arc, with the first giving you the basic feel for the world, the second opening up to be a bit non-linear, and the third leaning more heavily into the FPS mechanics as the action intensifies.

The only real problem here are the technical issues the PC port of this game suffers from, based on the 2012 HD Remaster originally a Playstation 3 exclusive. Graphically this doesn't do much to the original 2005 Xbox presentation aside from increase onscreen object count (especially with foliage and grass), and overall render resolution. You DON'T want to run the game in 4K, and probably want to disable fullscreen optimizations too. Some people may need to use Windows 7 compatibility mode too, depending on their hardware. 

Steam says controllers aren't supported, but that's not true, you just have to disable Steam input and use the game's launcher to select and configure a compatible Xinput controller. Yeah, this means you Playstation controller users may not be able to use a gamepad without a custom Xinput wrapper, but for everyone else, controllers work just fine so long as you configure your buttons before launching the game for the first time. Other than that, this is still a fun, quirky game that has a surprising amount of depth and character development, and the last Oddworld game directly developed by Oddworld Inhabitants with a wholly-original story.

One of the most unique FPS games I've ever played.

What makes it unique is that the ammo of your guns is various sorts of animals which you often have to hunt down. There is only one gun, but you can shoot two different types of ammo at the same time. There are some stealth elements too, but they are mostly poor and hard to perform.

The game changes what it tries to be multiple times. The first third of the game is linear bounty hunting. The 2nd half of the game give you more space and freedom, you can choose from various bounties in any order and you have this big area unlike the linear design before. The last third of the game is linear again, although the rest of the game is plain combat battlefield sections. The stealth is completely gone in that last third. For me, personally, that last act was the weakest third of the game, it's not terrible, but it's pretty mediocre. Such a letdown after the very strong first two thirds.

Some additional problems I have with the game is that for one, the difficulty spikes are insane. There are sections where you play for two hours straight and it's very easy, you do not die once, and then there's some place where you die maybe 10-20 times. Boss Battles are also hit and miss. I got to admit that every single boss battle is unique and original. Some are superb, but others are annoying and unfair. The game is also quite glitchy, a few times I thought I broke the game and was only able to beat it because of physics or found some other ways around it. For instance, there is one place where you must speak with a chicken to proceed. But for some reason, he was in the water floating, and when he is in the water you cannot talk with him. Luckily, due to the game's physics you can swim into him and he will slowly move. So, I managed to get him back to the solid surface, and he was standing again, and I could finally talk to him. In some other game, me swimming into a character would probably not move them from the spot, so I was very lucky.

Overall, a great game, but could have been so much better, especially the final levels.

7 Wonders II is a match-3 game which is fairly basic on the surface, but has some interesting twists. The main objective is to construct the 7 Wonders [spoiler](Stonehenge/Colosseum/Great Wall/Taj Mahal/Angkor Wat/Shwedagon Pagoda/Moai Statues)[/spoiler] and optionally an extra hidden Wonder [spoiler](Machu Picchu)[/spoiler]. To make that happen you have to create building blocks, which you do by matching the specific block type that represents that particular wonder. The more blocks of that type you match, the more building blocks you make and the faster you can build the wonder.

To finish each stage and collect the building blocks, you have to complete 2 objectives: clear all background squares by matching their blocks; and move the main block to the last row so that the workers can collect it. After you've done both, the stage ends and you can place your building blocks in the wonder. There is a time limit, and if the time runs out before you complete the stage, you lose 1 life and have to try again. There is also a 3rd objective, this one is optional but necessary if you want to unlock the 8th wonder: [spoiler]On each stage there is a special background square with a border, if you match the square with blocks of that color, a piece of a map will drop. With enough pieces, a secret stage will begin where you need to complete a puzzle in a finite number of moves - thankfully you can backtrack the moves as much as you want as long as the timer don't run out. If you complete this secret stage in all the 7 wonders, you will unlock the hidden one.[/spoiler]

To help finish the stages, powerups will appear each time you match 4 or more blocks together. There are 3 types of powerups, and the type shown depends on the match pattern (e.g. 4 or more blocks matched in the same row summons the ice powerup). You also have a bonus power that you can use at will, but has to recharge once used. This power is especially useful to bring the main block to the last row.

Overall, I had fun playing the game. It took me 6 hours to beat, the difficulty felt very easy at the first 4 or 5 wonders and spiked hard on the last ones. I even lost a life and had several close calls on the last stages, so beating the game kinda feels like a fair challenge, especially with all the 8 wonders unlocked [spoiler](I ended up with all 8 unlocked, rank Keeper of the Forgotten Knowledge with 1,364,679 points for reference)[/spoiler]. If you're a fan of match-3 games or can only game in small intervals, you should probably give this game a try.


[h1]The Good[/h1]
+ Music, SFX and art are blend very well with the gameplay
+ The difficulty felt well balanced, becoming harder near the end but not oppressive
+ Some "secrets" in the game to spice things up [spoiler](8th Wonder - Machu Picchu)[/spoiler]
+ 12 options of bonuses gives some extra decision making [spoiler](my favorites are destroyer and cluster bomb)[/spoiler]


[h1]The Neutral[/h1]
* The leaderboard seems to be hardcoded into the game, not real players
* Probably works better as a mobile game to play on a quick break


[h1]The Bad[/h1]
- The game shows its age sometimes, the resolution options are limited and the hardware cursor option don't work well in my setup
- The gameplay becomes kinda repetitive after a while, each new wonder don't bring any meaningful extra twists to the table
- Lack of strategic depth
- No achievements

A fun little puzzle game to play when you have nothing to do.

The game is very relaxing and not that stressful, that said that means the game is also very easy and not much of a challenge.
 
The gameplay is simple, match tiles in the same color and remove all the obstacles under the tiles. When you have removed all obstacles, you continue to the next stage until the game is done. When you complete a section of stages you get to build some wonders of the world and get a history lesson about them. You can ofc. Skip these lessons if you aren’t interested.

During the game you´ll get powerups to help you win. These powerups are extremely overpowered which is why the game is as easy as it is. So, if you are looking for a relaxing game that is not hard to complete look no further.

All that being said, there is a lot of games in the "7 wonders" series and this is not the best one. I would rather recommend “Treasures of Seven” which have more fun mechanics to work with and more challenging levels. In the end don´t buy all the games in the series as they are very similar, and therefore not worth collecting. Get the one that sounds most fun to you mechanic wise and stick with that one.

[h1] LIVE RISING 2.5 [/h1]

“Luxor: Amun Rising” is one of those expansions that doesn’t try to reinvent the wheel—it sticks to the tried-and-true formula of the first game and fine-tunes it. This time, players won’t face Set himself, but the Princes of Megiddo, whose countless minions come in endless chains of colorful spheres. We still have our trusty winged shooter, and the goal is clear: don’t let the balls reach the pyramid.[eos]

The game feels noticeably bigger: 88 levels give about an hour more gameplay than the original. Full credit to the designers at MumboJumbo—the ball movement patterns are much more original and challenging. The early stages are a joy because they don’t repeat, and even though levels start to repeat in the second half (like in the first game), new elements introduced closer to the finale keep things interesting. Visually, the game serves as a bridge to full 3D, confidently shifting to a 2.5D format with a redesigned map and funnier illustrations.

A big new feature is the addition of difficulty levels (Easy, Medium, Expert), letting you either chill with a YouTube video or go for a real challenge, racking up 30+ million points per playthrough. But the real star of 'Amun Rising' is the new Scorpio bonus. This defender moves along the track toward the chain and can clear a large part of the tail or even wipe out leftover balls all on its own. It’s a super powerful tool that adds a lot of energy to the gameplay (though unfortunately it’ll be noticeably nerfed in future editions).

The soundtrack in this installment has become more pleasant and less heavy, which just makes the meditative vibe even better.

Even without some modern conveniences and wide-screen resolution, 'Luxor: Amun Rising' is still a top-notch example of the genre. It’s a solid, honest casual game that nails its purpose — entertaining the player and giving that satisfying feeling every time a chain pops.

Luxor: Amun Rising, developed by MumboJumbo and published by Accelerate Games, builds directly on the foundation of the original Luxor, refining its mechanics and expanding its content without straying from the formula that defined the series. It feels like a natural progression rather than a reinvention, taking what worked in the first game and enhancing it with smoother gameplay, a larger campaign, and small but meaningful improvements that make the experience more polished overall.

The core gameplay remains centered on controlling a horizontal launcher that fires colored spheres into an advancing chain. The objective is unchanged: create matches to eliminate segments before they reach the pyramid. What continues to make this system engaging is the balance between immediate reactions and forward planning. Players must constantly read the movement of the chain, anticipate future positions, and place shots with precision to trigger chain reactions. These cascading eliminations are especially satisfying, offering moments where careful setup leads to large-scale success. Compared to the original, the pacing feels slightly more fluid, with improved responsiveness that makes each action feel more deliberate and controlled.

One of the most noticeable differences in Amun Rising is the increase in content. The game features a significantly larger number of levels, each gradually introducing more complex patterns, faster speeds, and additional colors that raise the difficulty. Early stages provide a gentle learning curve, but the challenge ramps up steadily, requiring sharper reflexes and better decision-making as players progress. While this escalation keeps the experience engaging, it largely relies on intensifying existing mechanics rather than introducing entirely new ones. As a result, the gameplay evolves in difficulty more than in variety, which can make later stages feel like extensions of earlier ones rather than entirely new challenges.

Power-ups continue to play a central role in shaping the experience, offering tools that help manage increasingly demanding situations. Abilities such as slowing the chain, reversing its direction, or clearing large sections provide moments of relief during more intense levels. The game introduces a few new power-ups and refines how they are presented, making them feel more integrated into the flow of gameplay. These additions do not drastically change the core mechanics, but they enhance the pacing and give players more options when dealing with difficult scenarios.

In addition to the main campaign, the game includes alternative modes that offer different ways to engage with its systems. Survival-style challenges, for example, test how long players can endure under constant pressure, emphasizing consistency and endurance rather than progression. These modes add variety and extend replayability, though they still rely on the same core mechanics, meaning they feel more like variations than entirely new experiences.

Visually, Luxor: Amun Rising maintains the Egyptian theme of its predecessor while presenting it with slightly improved detail and variety. The environments feature a mix of temples, ruins, and desert landscapes that provide a more cohesive sense of place. While the graphics remain relatively simple, they are clear and functional, ensuring that players can easily track the movement of spheres even during fast-paced moments. The soundtrack complements this with energetic and thematic music that reinforces the sense of urgency as levels become more challenging.

Despite its improvements, the game is still constrained by the limitations of its design. The reliance on a single core mechanic means that repetition becomes more noticeable over time, particularly during longer play sessions. While the increased number of levels and additional features help extend the experience, they do not fully address the lack of fundamental variation. Additionally, the randomness of incoming spheres can occasionally influence outcomes, leading to moments where success feels less dependent on skill and more on chance.

Even so, Luxor: Amun Rising succeeds in delivering a refined and highly enjoyable puzzle experience. Its strength lies in its ability to take a proven formula and enhance it without overcomplicating it, resulting in a game that is both accessible and engaging. It is particularly effective in shorter sessions, where its quick levels and satisfying mechanics encourage continued play.

In the end, Luxor: Amun Rising stands as a strong sequel that improves upon the original in meaningful but measured ways. It offers more content, smoother gameplay, and a slightly more polished presentation, all while staying true to the core identity of the series. While it does not introduce groundbreaking changes, it delivers a solid and addictive experience that fans of the genre will appreciate.

A standalone expansion pack to the original Luxor. I have many of the same issues with this one as well, but there are some improvements. 

Just like the original game, Luxor: Amun Rising is priced at $9.99 and doesn't work outside of the box, requiring a different .exe file to be downloaded from a 3rd party and placed into the game's folder. The sketchy ball accuracy has returned as well, likely because both games run on the same engine. The standard shooting speed is still a little too slow, however this is not as much of a problem anymore as I will explain in a moment. 

Now for the improvements:
1) Difficulty selection has been added, with three difficulties to choose from. While not as preferable as a simple practice mode, this addition does allow for players to practice harder levels at a lower difficulty so they don't waste all of their lives on one stage when trying to complete the game on a harder difficulty. This fact alone diminishes the annoyance of the slow shooting speed, since practicing on Easy difficulty will quickly improve a player's ability to make shots when they matter most on harder difficulties. 
2) The addition of a new power-up, the Scorpion, has huge implications for the flow of the game. The Scorpion is essentially a "get out of jail free" card if you are about to lose in a stage. It gives a few seconds of breathing room as you refocus. Easily the best addition to the game. 

Aside from this, the rest of the game is about as good as the original Luxor. Solid and consistent Ancient Egyptian theme, with sounds and music that compliment the design. The gameplay is still simple and addicting overall. Players can also use this game to practice for the original Luxor as well, since the games are extremely similar in mechanics. 

However, I still have a hard time recommending Amun Rising over newer entries in the series. Starting in Luxor 2, we see huge changes in gameplay flow and many improvements to the overall feel of the games. I would recommend waiting for a big sale or just skipping ahead to Luxor 2.

Luxor Amun Rising is an Egyptian style Zuma game by Mumbo Jumbo that is unfortunately disappointing on a couple of levels. The most obvious is that fullscreen is not supported and you are limited to a very small 800x600 window on the screen. While there is a fullscreen option, it does not stretch the image and simply blackboxes the main content. Secondly, the Steam Overlay is not supported so you cannot screenshot your high scores. I would recommend that most puzzle gamers and definitely the mainstream audience give this game a pass.

'Luxor 2' is a classic Egyptian-themed casual action-puzzle game where players shoot colored spheres to create match-three chains and destroy advancing marble tracks before they reach the pyramids

This is my FAVORITE 'LUXOR' GAME ever! It's in fact my favorite marble-shooter game ever, yeah, I'm not a Team 'Zuma', I love 'Luxor' more, especially 'Luxor 2', but I still like 'Zuma', too, don't get the wrong idea. It's nostalgic, simple, and incredibly addictive. There's a great stage variety, and satisfying power-ups. 'Luxor 2' also introduced 3D levels (they're basically movies behind/under the marbles and PC, but still, for its time they were AAA level 3D designs), better physics, better controls, better maps, better story (the last "Set's Temple" map is a 'Papyrus' cartoon level evil Set; I love when media portrays Set really evil, not some strong guy), and MOST IMPORTANTLY, the thing that made 'Luxor 2' the pinnacle of the franchise, LIFETIME STATISTICS! The devs went all the way OCD-friendly mode and added statistics for literally anything: how many marbles you destroyed for each color, how many power-ups you took, how many wins/losses you got for each map, how many times you completed story mode for each difficulty, how many global points you earned, and etc., and etc. If I knew this day will come, I would've kept my save file from early 2000s.

One of my problems with this game is that the devs abandoned it and didn't renew the files for newer systems; since Flash was discontinued, so did these retro games that were based on Flash. Another one is that the devs abandoned this game, too: they didn't implement Steam Cloud feature for this game, so if you want to keep your stats forever, you'll need to move your save file between your PCs. Surprisingly, 'Rockstar' is also lazy when it comes to this, they also don't have Steam Cloud for any of their games (from the very first 'GTA' till 'GTA V'), which is weird, because 'GTA' games was always popular because of their extremely detailed statistics; it really would be cool to save those stats forever.

EDIT (26.10.2026): Although, I don't remember this being a case when I played it as a kid, but it seems the devs mixed up stats for marbles destroyed for orange and turquoise. Another reason I am adding this info because I don't forget it in the future, when I return to this game and look at my lifetime stats.

[b]TL;DR: a promising sequel that turns into a frustrating RNG casino, with technical issues making things even worse[/b]

Luxor 2 is a pretty interesting sequel on paper, with more challenging levels, different difficulty settings, and several new game modes. Alongside Adventure, there are also Survival and Practice modes. The game even has badges, which don't really offer much beyond tracking your progress, but they're a nice little addition anyway.

Unfortunately, not all these additions make the experience better. Some level layouts are difficult to read, making it hard to predict where the orbs will go on your first attempt. The extra modes don't add much to the experience for me, either.

My biggest problem, however, is Expert difficulty, especially after stages 8–9. Some levels are extremely small, the orbs move ridiculously fast, and you're dealing with as many as [b]nine[/b] different colors. There's a difference between making a game challenging and making it frustrating. When the playing field is this cramped and the orbs move this quickly, your ability to plan ahead feels increasingly limited.

At that point, the game turns into a fckn casino where you're basically praying to God for a favorable arrangement of orbs and the right bonuses. Power-ups like lightning strikes, fireballs, the Speedball buff, and even the new Net buff often feel practically useless in the later stages. When you're already struggling to survive, getting one of these instead of something actually useful feels like a wasted opportunity, especially when the right power-up could save your entire run.

Even if you get lucky with the right bonuses and orb combinations, just one mistake can cost you the entire level. And with a limited number of lives, losing too many times means having to restart the entire stage. Combined with the heavy reliance on luck, this makes repeated attempts feel unnecessarily frustrating.

The technical side doesn't help, either. Luxor 2 feels noticeably less smooth than the original on my setup. Windowed mode is particularly unpleasant on my 144 Hz monitor, while fullscreen feels better. The heavier visual effects can also make an already chaotic screen harder to read, especially during intense moments. I've also experienced occasional unexpected closures.

Compatibility is another issue worth considering before buying. This is an old game originally designed for much older versions of Windows, and getting it to run on modern systems can require additional work.

I don't mind a difficult game. What bothers me is when the difficulty feels less like a test of skill and more like a test of patience and luck. Luxor 2 has some interesting ideas, but its frustrating balance and technical issues make it difficult for me to recommend.
