There’s not much to get excited about in Luxor 2. Basically, it’s the same casual game, just with some new textures and a couple of colors—turquoise and orange for the balls. The new stuff includes a dagger bonus and ball recoloring, while the good old scorpion bonus from Amun Rising got noticeably nerfed, which can sometimes make tense situations even tougher. Levels are now kind of 3D with little background animations, but it’s nothing to write home about. There are three different difficulty modes, plus survival and practice, but that doesn’t really save things.

The bonus levels where you can only use daggers are super annoying. You end up mindlessly clicking, making your finger super tired, and you don’t really get anything from it—just farming points. In-game achievements are pretty meaningless too, just cold numbers that don’t make you want to keep playing. No real rewards, no useful Steam stuff, and no in-game trophy graphics here.

The main problem with the game is the completely broken balance. In 'Expert' mode, the balls fly everywhere, making it almost impossible to build a proper long chain like in the first two games. The aim is off: the ball often goes nowhere near where you're aiming, so you can't really plan your shots when catapulting. I ended up dropping the game at level 10-4 because I wasn't in the mood to waste time on wonky aim, awful sounds, and no balance. This game in the series is definitely D-tier.

Luxor 2, developed by MumboJumbo and published by Accelerate Games, takes the foundation established by the original Luxor and expands it into a larger, more content-heavy experience without straying far from its core identity. It is very much a sequel in the traditional sense—more levels, more power-ups, and a slightly refined presentation—rather than a bold reinvention. For players familiar with the first game, it feels immediately recognizable, offering the same addictive marble-shooting mechanics while gradually increasing the scale and intensity.

The gameplay remains centered on controlling a horizontal launcher that fires colored spheres into an advancing chain. Matching groups of three or more clears segments of the chain, and the objective is to prevent it from reaching its endpoint. This formula is simple but effective, relying on a balance of quick reflexes and forward planning. Players must constantly evaluate the movement of the chain, anticipate future openings, and position their shots carefully to create chain reactions. These cascading matches are one of the most satisfying aspects of the game, rewarding precision and strategic thinking in equal measure.

Where Luxor 2 differentiates itself is in the sheer volume of content and the way it escalates its challenge. The campaign is significantly larger, featuring a wide range of levels that introduce faster speeds, more complex paths, and additional colors that increase the difficulty of forming matches. Rather than introducing entirely new mechanics, the game builds on its existing systems by intensifying them, pushing players to refine their skills and adapt to increasingly demanding scenarios. This approach keeps the experience engaging, though it also means that the gameplay evolves more in difficulty than in variety.

Power-ups play a key role in maintaining the game’s pacing and excitement. Various abilities allow players to slow down the chain, destroy large sections of marbles, or unleash powerful attacks that can turn the tide in difficult moments. These tools add a layer of unpredictability and provide moments of relief during more intense stages. While they do not fundamentally change the structure of the game, they help break up the rhythm and introduce bursts of action that keep the experience from feeling too uniform.

The game also includes multiple modes beyond the main campaign, such as survival challenges that test endurance and skill under increasing pressure. These modes offer alternative ways to engage with the mechanics, though they largely rely on the same core gameplay loop. As a result, they extend the game’s lifespan without significantly altering the overall experience. Players who enjoy mastering the system and chasing higher scores will find value here, but those looking for new mechanics may find the variety limited.

Visually, Luxor 2 continues the Egyptian theme established in the original, with temples, hieroglyphs, and desert-inspired environments forming the backdrop for each level. The presentation is colorful and functional, ensuring that players can easily track the movement of marbles and identify targets. However, it does not introduce significant visual innovation, and over time the environments can begin to feel repetitive. The audio design complements the gameplay with consistent, thematic music, though it serves more as background support than a standout feature.

One of the game’s most noticeable drawbacks is its tendency toward repetition. While the increased number of levels provides a sense of scale, many stages share similar layouts and patterns, which can reduce the feeling of discovery. The challenge becomes more about endurance and precision than adapting to new ideas, and this can make longer play sessions feel somewhat monotonous. Additionally, while skill is a major factor in success, there are moments where the randomness of incoming marbles can influence outcomes, occasionally leading to frustration.

Despite these limitations, Luxor 2 remains an engaging and accessible puzzle game that excels in delivering short, satisfying bursts of gameplay. Its straightforward mechanics make it easy to pick up, while its increasing difficulty provides enough challenge to keep players invested. The game’s strength lies in its consistency—it knows what it is trying to do and executes that vision effectively, even if it does not push the formula in new directions.

In the end, Luxor 2 is a reliable sequel that builds on the strengths of its predecessor while offering more content and slightly refined gameplay. It may not introduce groundbreaking changes, but it delivers a polished and enjoyable experience for fans of the genre. For those who appreciate its simple yet addictive design, it offers plenty of opportunities to test skill and chase higher scores, even if its repetitive nature limits its long-term appeal.

Luxor 2 has some improvements over the original, mainly in graphical presentation and the hit-detection on the spheres when you shoot them. There are new features too, such as an endless mode and a practice mode to help hone in your sphere matching skills. There is also an adequately detailed performance tracker and in-game milestones for completionist's sake. However, it is still hard to recommend the game because of the following issues: 

1) For most players, the game will not run out of the box and will require a fan-made patch to run properly. 

2) Despite the improvements to ball-accuracy, about half of the game's levels negate it by introducing too many twists, turns, and tunnels that only make shooting more frustrating than ever. Some of the worst map designs I've ever seen. It's not a skill issue, since the accuracy problems occur only in the twists and turns. Its difficult to explain in writing, but even in less than 10 hours of play I have encountered the strangest accuracy problems when trying to slot in spheres as they are making a twist or a turn in their pathway. Most of the time they will slot up to two spots out of place when these circumstances are met. Don't get me wrong, the maps are pretty to look at, but if half of them only allow adequate shooting conditions for less than half of the sphere's track, then what was the point of improving the ball accuracy problems from the original Luxor? 

3) There is a strange issue with the swapping mechanic. By clicking the right mouse button, you can swap between two spheres that you can shoot. Too many times I have clicked the right mouse button to swap to the second sphere only to end up shooting the first one. It has caused me many losses and it is unacceptable. Even the first games did not have this issue. I don't know what went wrong here or why it happens. 

Luxor 2 is a good improvement, but the map design really drags everything back down. Its still not good enough to recommend at full price. Wait for a sale or buy the HD remaster.

The targeting arrow is incorrect as it doesn't truly indicate where an orb will go. For example, on a corner, you can move your mouse to certain angles and the targeting arrow will show that you can shoot somewhat up a line of orbs (as if to shoot through them) to make a match with that color, but it won't and it will hit the first orb on the corner, breaking your combo. If points are important, I had a severe bug where I was playing the bonus level after stage 4 and my power went out. After booting the game up some time later, I was on stage 5-1 and I had 0 points.

[*] Очень душная.. Уровни длятся слишком долго. Успеваешь постареть пока один уровень пройдёшь. 
[*] Долгий КД (cooldown) между выстрелами. Бесит нереально. Даже когда шарики максимально близко. 
[*] Очень странный алгоритм выбора шаров для броска: вначале это вроде полный рандом, но когда жук навозный подкатывает шары к пирамидке, игра берёт цвета шаров самых близких к этой пирамидке. Но! В самый ответственный момент начинается дичь, и цвета шаров берутся откуда-то из середины, вообще не в тему.  
[*] Тоже самое применимо и к рандому самих сфер. Чем дальше в лес, тем злее дятлы. Всё больше шариков в разнобой, даже парами не ходят. Как комбить - непонятно, когда скорость их качения очень быстрая, аж в глазах рябить начинает.
[*] Дизайн уровней (траектории) рисовал какой-то наркоман. Объяснить цензурно не берусь, поиграете хотя бы до 9 уровня и сами всё поймёте. Очень часто получается, что шарик кинуть некуда, т.к. везде не тот цвет, и ты ждёшь пока цепочка с нужным цветом выкатится из тени или из под другой цепочки. Геймдизайн отвратительный. 
[*] "13 впечатляющих бонусных раундов в конце каждой стадии" - того кто их придумал ждёт отдельный котел в царстве Аида. Вот в Luxor Evolved бонусные уровни действительно бонусные, в них приятно играть. А здесь... Пока один жук навозный катит шарики - то в целом норм. Можно играть и даже комбить. Когда сразу два жука навозных катят шары: это пздц. Скорость очень высокая, шаров много на экране, начинается рябь в глазах, ни о какой тактике и речи быть не может. Ты просто максимально быстро спамишь ЛКМ. Хотите приблизить артрит сустава указательного пальца и угробить мыш - эти уровни для вас. Лично я их пропускаю, когда появляются два навозных жука одновременно. 
[*] звуковое сопровождение. Собственно, сами звуки норм. Вопрос исключительно к музыке. Композиций три штуки на всю игру. Заглавная в меню, другая одна и та же для всех уровней. Но слышать чаще вы будете третью - тревожную. Это когда сферы близко к пирамидке. А близко к пирамидке они будут чаще, чем всегда, поэтому эта тревожная музыка начнет вас гипнотизировать и заставлять разбить мыш с монитором. Благо, музон легко отключается в меню, в фоне ставится свой jungle/dnb и игра становится на порядок веселее. Но! Проклятый долгий КД и античеловечный рандом будут сбивать весь ваш ритм. 
[/list]

[h1]Новая волна? Дайте с текущей разобраться![/h1]
На этот раз MumboJumbo приготовила подарочек в виде Luxor 2 - новой версии игры жанра 3 в ряд. Рассмотрим в подробностях все эти моменты:

[h1]Преимущества:[/h1]
[h1]Геймплей[/h1]
Геймплейно игра не поменялась: мы находимся внизу, двигаемся и уничтожаем волны шаров, которые скарабеи пытаются провести до пирамиды. При нескольких цепочках/комбо подряд ловим бонусы. Однако есть новвоведения, о них далее.

[h1]Новвоведения[/h1]
Игра не обошлась без них. Помимо обновлённого движка, механики и новых уровней - не оставили без внимания и бонусы с шарами. Из бонусов появились: перекрасить определённый участок шаров (куда вы кинете бонус), шторм, который уничтожает несколько соло-шариков в случайном порядке, и палка (палочка-выручалочка или называйте как хотите) - попадаете в шар и в тот, который попали - исчезает с поля. Шарики же теперь бывают оранжевые и голубые. Есть ещё одно новвоведение, но о нём ниже.

[h1]Уровни сложности[/h1]
Также, как и в Amun Rising - игра предлагает на выбор 3 уровня сложности. И на этот раз они более чем оправданы - Эксперт здесь даёт жару в прямом смысле. Потенциал этой сложности расскрывается начиная с 10й главы, а особенно это заметно в 12 главе, где вы наверняка рано или поздно потеряете жизнь.
Ниже демонстрация одного их самых сложных уровней игры:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mc_4B8cLsdA
Причём, 14-4 чуть-чуть легче вариации 12-9 - там шары немного быстрее идут и лично у меня ушло более 100 попыток пройти 12-9.
По окончанию кампании, игра предложит вам перейти на более высокий уровень сложности с текущем кол-вом жизней и очков. А вот если вы прошли игру на эксперте, то игра вам предложит пройти испытания Хоруса - 25 уровней этих испытаний на ещё более высокой сложности (куда хлеще эксперта). Сможете ли вы их осилить?

[h1]Разрешение[/h1]
Ура, наконец-то можно поставить разрешение какое нам нужно. Только 16:9 не ждите - в видео, продемонстрированном выше, показано как игра будет выглядеть в фулл-скрине (то бишь исключительно 4:3).

[h1]Достижения[/h1]
Их нет. Но они здесь и не нужны. Игра предоставляет достаточную сложность, чтобы обходиться без них. 

[h1]Недостатки:[/h1]
[h1]Решение проблемы с запуском игры[/h1]
Основная часть отзывов в стиме по этой игре состоит из: "у меня не запускается игра". Дело в том, что когда разработчики выпустили эту игру в стим - они по ошибке exe файлу дали неправильное имя. Из-за чего игра не работает, хотя если залезть в настройки и запустить в режиме совместимости - она идёт.
Решается эта проблема довольно просто: Luxor2.exe переименовывайте в Luxor2_x86.exe и врубаете совместимость с XP SP3 (отдельная благодарность автору [url=http://steamcommunity.com/app/15920/discussions/0/350533172704450223/]этой[/url] темы) и вуаля - игра работает.

[h1]Оверлей стима[/h1]
К сожалению, даже если вы решите проблему с запуском - вы не сможете использовать оверлей, а соответственно - и поделать те же скриншоты.

[h1]Итог:[/h1]
Порт Luxor: Pharaoh's Challenge, который я прошёл энное время ранее - был настолько упрощен.. уровни там были абсолютно те же, а вот бонусы имели слишком большой эффект. Здесь этого всего нет и у меня было удовольствие проходить данную игру. Хотя испытания Хоруса здесь уже исключительно на любителя, ибо в них игра наказывает за ошибки и шары там парами никогда не ходят + скорость. 

[h1]Вердикт:[/h1]
Для новичков рекомендуется сначала пройти предыдущие части, ибо здесь даже на лёгком не всегда простенько будет, а затем можно приступать к этой. Любителям и остальным - несомненно рекомендую.

'Luxor 3' is a classic Egyptian-themed marble-shooter puzzle game where you play as a reincarnated scarab battling the god Set to free trapped god essences by matching colored spheres before they reach the pyramids.

I remember playing it only for 30 mins when it came out, because back then the games were working through subscription system, and I didn't have money to buy them (I mean, back then we all pirated games). Back then I really wanted to play this game (it had new scarabs, power-up upgrades, and etc.), because it was a continuation of my favorite game, 'Luxor 2'. However, after finally buying it on Steam and playing, I realized this game doesn't really live up to the glory of 'Luxor 2'.

What I really love about this game is that it's somewhere between 'Luxor 2', when 'Luxor' was great, and newer installments, when 'Luxor' went downhill; so basically, this is the last good 'Luxor' game in the franchise. I really love "Crossing the Nile" mode, I could play it all day long. 'Luxor 3' also has statistics, but compared to 'Luxor 2', it diminished a lot: like there's no stats for each marble destroy, for each level wins/losses, for each power-up, and etc., there're only stats for each difficulty completed, global points, accuracy, and etc., that's all. Not much, but I'm still glad they didn't totally abandon the lifetime statistics. Also, I believe (I may be wrong) 'Luxor 3' uses real 3D maps. By "real" I mean not movies of 3D maps behind/under the marbles and PC, but the 3D map really exists on our screens. Graphics-wise, 'Luxor 3' is an upgrade.

Thanks God, this one doesn't rely on Flash, so this will work on newer systems, but this game has so many flaws that I can't really recommend it, but I have to.  Let's start with the obvious one: I really hate the crosshair, this must be the worst crosshair in any game I've ever played in my entire life, or even in gaming history; it's really weird, your second marble/shot is shown in a dot, but your first marble/shot over it in a shape like upside down "U". I swear, I have 99% accuracy in 'Luxor 2', and I almost always get 100% accuracy, except a few times when I'm in a hurry, or just miss, or in some maps where you have more chance of missing due to the layout, but in 'Luxor 3', I get 100% accuracy 50/50; that crosshair is confusing as hell. Why would you put first marble on a upside down U-shaped part of the crosshair when literally every crosshair in literally every game uses center dot for the main shot? Maybe if you never held a mouse in your hand, you'll have better time using this crosshair, but for anyone with legacy skill of FPS games, this crosshair will make their experience of this game uncomfortable. Speaking of uncomfortable, the physics in 'Luxor 3' is bad, and I mean it: you shoot a marble at a certain angle, where you know in 'Luxor 2 it would land there, but here it lands near it, ruining the marble train. Multicolored marble and recoloring power-ups (forgot their official names) have similar designs, I've missed good opportunities because of them many times than I would like to admit; it would be cool if the devs just used better design. Bonus levels are fun and chaotic, but getting 100% accuracy on them almost impossible (I know you don't even need to get 100% accuracy on them, because there's no such achievement for it in 'Luxor 3' unlike 'Luxor 2', but still). Also, don't like how marble train attaches itself when you break its middle part, this also confuses veteran players if they came from earlier 'Luxor' titles. Another problem is that the devs abandoned this game, too: they didn't implement Steam Cloud feature for this game, so if you want to keep your stats forever, you'll need to move your save file between your PCs. Surprisingly, 'Rockstar' is also lazy when it comes to this, they also don't have Steam Cloud for any of their games (from the very first 'GTA' till 'GTA V'), which is weird, because 'GTA' games was always popular because of their extremely detailed statistics; it really would be cool to save those stats forever.

In conclusion: 'Luxor 3' is a good gameif you are a fan of 'Luxor 2', and want to experience another 'Luxor' game, but 'Luxor 3' has TERRIBLE UX, I would say it lacks UX at all.

Classic game to destress

Luxor 3, developed by MumboJumbo and published by Accelerate Games, takes the established marble-shooter formula of the series and expands it into one of its most content-rich and feature-complete entries. Rather than attempting to radically change the core gameplay, it focuses on refining and extending what already works, offering a larger campaign, more modes, and additional progression systems that give the experience a greater sense of depth. It feels less like a reinvention and more like a culmination of ideas introduced in earlier titles, presented in a more polished and expansive form.

The central gameplay remains immediately recognizable. Players control a horizontal launcher that fires colored spheres into a moving chain, aiming to create matches that eliminate sections before they reach their endpoint. This mechanic continues to strike a balance between accessibility and challenge, allowing players to quickly understand the basics while still demanding precision and foresight as difficulty increases. Success depends not only on reaction speed but also on the ability to anticipate how the chain will shift, creating opportunities for chain reactions that can clear large portions of the board. These cascading moments remain one of the most satisfying aspects of the game, rewarding careful planning and execution.

What distinguishes Luxor 3 is the scale of its content and the variety of ways it presents its core mechanics. The main adventure mode spans a large number of levels, each introducing variations in layout, speed, and complexity that gradually push players to refine their skills. While the fundamental gameplay does not change significantly, the diversity in stage design helps maintain engagement over a longer period. In addition to the main campaign, the game includes multiple alternative modes that offer different challenges, such as endurance-based survival scenarios or more controlled puzzle-style encounters. These modes provide a welcome change of pace and help extend the game’s replayability, even if they rely on the same underlying systems.

The introduction of a more developed progression system adds another layer to the experience. Players can collect in-game currency and items that allow them to unlock and upgrade power-ups, giving a sense of growth that was less pronounced in earlier entries. These power-ups play a crucial role during gameplay, offering abilities that can slow down the advancing chain, reverse its movement, or clear large sections instantly. The ability to enhance these tools over time encourages players to revisit levels and improve their performance, adding a subtle but meaningful incentive for continued play.

Visually, the game continues the series’ Egyptian theme, presenting environments filled with stylized temples, hieroglyphic patterns, and desert-inspired imagery. While the presentation is not particularly advanced, it is clean and functional, ensuring that players can easily track the movement of spheres and focus on the action. The visual clarity becomes especially important during more intense moments, where multiple elements are in motion simultaneously. The soundtrack complements this with energetic and thematic compositions that reinforce the sense of urgency as levels become more challenging.

Despite its expanded content and refined systems, Luxor 3 still faces some of the same limitations as its predecessors. The reliance on a single core mechanic means that, over time, the experience can begin to feel repetitive, particularly during longer play sessions. While the variety of modes and level designs helps mitigate this to some extent, the game rarely introduces entirely new ideas that significantly change how it is played. Additionally, the randomness of incoming spheres can occasionally influence outcomes, creating moments where success feels less controlled than intended.

Even with these drawbacks, Luxor 3 remains a highly engaging and accessible puzzle experience that builds effectively on the strengths of the series. It offers a substantial amount of content, a satisfying gameplay loop, and enough variation to keep players invested for extended periods. The game’s focus on refinement rather than reinvention results in a polished and cohesive experience that delivers exactly what fans expect, while still providing enough additions to feel worthwhile.

In the end, Luxor 3 stands as one of the most complete entries in the franchise, offering a well-rounded and content-rich take on the marble-shooter formula. It may not push the genre in new directions, but it executes its design with confidence and consistency, making it a strong choice for players who enjoy straightforward yet challenging puzzle gameplay.

Dieses Spiel habe ich bereits einige Monate im Besitz. Das Spiel hat meine Kindheit stark geprägt, da es eins meiner ersten Videospiele überhaupt war. Damals schon als besseres "Zuma" bekannt, besaß ich dieses Game bereits als CD Spiel. Als ich es dementsprechend vor einigen Monaten auf Steam gesehen hatte, musste ich es einfach wiederhaben. Nun ja, was soll ich sagen, das Game hat sich halt null verändert und ist genau so cool wie damals.

Das Spiel "Luxor 3" wurde vom Entwicklerstudio "MumboJumbo" entwickelt und wurde bereits 2007 veröffentlicht. Es handelt sich hier um ein kleines Geschicklichkeits- sowie Gelegenheitsspiel, bei dem man verschieden farbige Kugeln auf eine schlangenartige Aneinanderreihung von weiteren Farbkugeln schießen muss, um diese dann zum Platzen zu kriegen. Verloren hat man, wenn man die "Schlangen" nicht rechtzeitig getötet bekommt und sie Ihr Ziel auf der vorgegebenen Route erreichen. Um einen jeweiligen Teil der Schlange zu zerstören, müssen immer mindestens 3 Kugeln derselben Farbe nebeneinander sein. Zusätzlich gibt es aller Hand Powerups, wie eine "Explosionskugel" oder einen "Blitz" die/der jeweils einen beträchtlichen Teil der Schlangen zerstören kann. Diese Powerups können übrigens auch im Shop verbessert werden, um diese noch effektiver zu gestalten. Ebenso können auch visuelle sowie soundtechnische Änderungen dort gekauft werden. Zwischen den einzelnen Level hat man je nachdem, ob man in einer bestimmten Stage alle 4 Figuren eingesammelt hat, noch ein Bonuslevel, um seinen persönlichen Punktescore zusätzlich zu erhöhen. So spielt man dann Level für Level, Stage für Stage, bis man das Game mit einem neuen Gesamtscore abgeschlossen hat. Was ich an dem Spiel sehr cool finde ist die grafische Aufmachung der einzelnen Level, welche zwar 3D Optik verwenden, jedoch an sich in 2D angezeigt werden. Dadurch entsteht eine gewisse Tiefe in den eigentlich statischen Bildern. Das Gameplay wird allgemein mit beruhigenden Klängen begleitet. Die einzelnen Level wurden gut, durchdacht designet und geben dem Spieler die gewisse Abwechslung. Leider hat das Spiel keine Errungenschaften und kostet rund 10€ auf Steam.

An sich ist das Spiel nicht schlecht und ich werde es definitiv weiter empfehlen, aber den Preis von rund 10€ finde ich etwas zu hoch. Wartet lieber auf einen Rabatt. Macht euch einfach ein eigenes Bild davon. Müsst ihr wissen.

Luxor 3 is the third game in the Luxor game series. A match-3 type arcade game with a hybrid twist, the objects that are being matched are moving along a track. An addictive, fun experience that appeals to all audiences. A lengthy campaign (around 120 levels), a puzzle mode, and free play to sate your ball-blasting thirst. The story is simple, Egyptian gods have come to you to restore their power and artifacts that have been robbed from them by Set. There is multiple level types throughout the story. The normal mode consists of a number of "trains" or segments of orbs traveling down the pathways to the end. After destroying the last one, you win the level. Defender Is a unique path with a ton of statues blocking your shots, but otherwise the same. Puzzle gives you limited shots and some random segments to destroy to challenge your efficiency and logic puzzle solving. Crossing the Nile levels features "trains" moving left and right to absorb your shots. A small train lies on the opposite side of the Nile that you need to destroy to win. Survival levels challenge you to survive endless segments for a limited amount of time.

          What sets this one apart from the first two games is the enhanced graphics, new story, upgradable power-ups, and more levels and types. I played this title an insane amount of time when I was younger and enjoyed this one the most out of the series.

Back in 2009 I bought Luxor 3 as Christmas Presents for my friends, cause I liked the game myself. Now over a decade later, I've played the game through for the third time, and I still loved to play it! I thought it was about time I wrote a review for this game. 
(Non-technical review under the dots)

As we change equipment through the years, my first problem I encountered when starting Luxor 3, was the resolution of the game. The maximum resolution was only at 1920*1440, and it messed up my icons on my desktop. I checked the Internet, and it seems that all you gotta do is to 

Go to : C:\ProgramData\MumboJumbo\Luxor 3
Open file "GameVars.txt" with Notepad or your text editor of choice.
(kudos to Steam user Yaan1s)

As soon as I put in RenderMaxAspect to 2.5 and Width/Height to 2560*1440p, the resolution in options were put in there (4k too), when the maximum resolution by default only gave 1920*1440, which also messed up all my icons on the desktop. After rearranging my icons again, and testing some more, it did not move my icons ever again...

(Right click desktop -> Show -> "alligning icons automaticly" and "allign icons to grid". Might take a few restarts before Windows 10 resets and saves the icons placed)

Edit: Aw heck! The icons changed again, after restart. I hope it's just the game, and not gonna remain like this.


I was finally ready to the place, with the correct resolution this time (4k was also available now), and I could finally start the game.

The music can be a bit repetitive, and the SFX sound is a bit loud, so a good advice is to go with it for a while, and play the game, then turn the music off completly, and keep the sound to maximum 20-25%, then play your own music (you can still hear the game sounds pretty well anyway). Works great really!

...

Okay, so the game is based on Egyptian gods, and there is a story you follow. The point of the game is to get 3 balls of the same colour together, and so they will vanish, and you can go to the next balls, until you finish the level. As I said earlier music and sounds can be a bit repetitive, but the graphics are really amazing, and the story brings it all together, together with the possibillity to buy and upgrade stuff, that helps you out in the game.

I would recommend playing on Normal difficulty. The 2nd one. For most this will be challenging in a way that you are kept busy most of the time, but you are also able to complete _most_ levels fairly easy. There are even (ingame) achievements, if you wanna spend even more time on the game.

I enjoyed the game in my entire third playthrough as I have done earlier, but I am not a very big fan of the puzzle levels in Luxor 3. I wanted to be kept busy, and not having think too much about how to solve this and that.

Well, obviously I will recommend this game. I did play some of the earlier Luxors even before buying Luxor 3 a long time ago, but I think this one is the best.

[b]Cons[/b]
- Dated
- Annoying minigames
- Repetitive

[h1]Overview[/h1]
Little Farm is a simple arcade puzzle game that's pretty old at this point and did not age well. Each level consists of different shaped square grids with new levels giving you more weirdly shaped fields making things more difficult. To pass a level you need to draw squares of matching crops to harvest them and fill the waiting trucks before the timer runs out. There are about 80 levels in total and even though each level is different the gameplay does get pretty repetitive. Playing through levels also gain you money that can be spent in the shop for upgrades to make things easier. There are also bonus rounds that are minigames and these give you extra cash but are kind of annoying to do. You won't really need to hoard money since you'll end up with way more than you need even after buying all upgrades in the shop.
The graphics and music are nothing special but they aren't bad in any way, it's good enough for what it is.
If you don't mind or are looking for a simple casual arcade style puzzle game then this might fit the bill. It's good to play in small bouts, maybe just a few levels each session to not burn out from the repetitive gameplay.

Given how many casual games are out there, I can't imagine that the casual-game marketplace has less competitive pressure than the AAA-titles do.  So I must conclude that the casual marketplace just isn't as picky or discerning as the more "hardcore gamer" market is, because few casual developers seem to bother striving for excellence; they develop their games to the point of being "okay," call it a day, and publish.

[i]Little Farm[/i] is yet another drop in that vast ocean of "okay" casual games.  The graphics are clear, cheerful and cartoonish.  The music loop gets a bit irksome over time, but is not offensively bad.  The gameplay concept is understandable, and reasonably interesting, involving trying to find the largest rectangular configuration of four same-coloured squares on a grid.  It's not a unique gameplay concept, but it's not nearly so overdone as "Bejeweled" or "Farmville" clones.  The use of a farming theme, conversely, is about as overdone as it can be in casual gaming.

There's an upgrade store, but while the upgrades make you more succesful, they don't make any real change to how the game is played.  Play well, and you'll have every item from the store bought by the time you've completed half the levels.  There is an "oil drilling" element to the game, which acts as nothing but a random drawing of bonus cash.  Bonus levels offer a form of gameplay that differs from the core levels, which would add some variety, if it were not for the fact that the bonus levels are both easy and mindless.

Bottom line: [i]Little Farm[/i] avoids a thumbs-down only because it has no serious flaws, but it has no virtues, either.  It's a bland, forgettable, generic piece of shovelware.  It will fill an empty hour as well as the next casual game, but there are many better games out there that you should really consider first.

这是一款体量很轻的休闲小游戏（不管是游戏文件大小还是游戏内容），现在来说的话，放到手机上更为合适些。
游戏的核心玩法很简单：
    就是通过鼠标指针框选一个矩形，当满足四角均为同一种农作物的时候，便可消去所框选的所有农作物。随即这些作物会被自动装车带走。如此反复，完成关卡给定的装满若干辆容积不同的卡车的任务。

游戏的难点在于：
    需要有一定的耐心和观察力，否则很快便会觉得无聊或者找不到可消去的作物。同时还会有暴雨、害虫、乌鸦等天敌随机出现，妨碍你的作物收获。
    商店的物品乍一看很贵，但是到了后期就会发现，这为数不多的几种商品会很快会被玩家买光，以至于到了游戏最后几个stage都不再有新的东西可以入手，显得比较乏味了。而余下的就是有为了通关而不断地与害虫、兔子以及时间条作斗争。

毕竟是08年的游戏，而今天的玩家大多见多识广，此类游戏的套路怕是很难入发法眼了。或许放到手机上用来消磨时间还会有市场啊吧。

一款操作简单的益智小游戏
1.规则：
在指定的时间内，用鼠标围起农田，使得围起来的范围内的四个角对应作物类型一样（比如都是番茄）
即可收货该范围内的所有作物
和停在农田前的卡车上一样标记的作物会填充到卡车进度上，进度完成后切换到下一辆卡车
其他的作物，如果你有建造仓库（初中期），对应的作物则会放入仓库
否则会被丢弃掉
所有卡车进度条全部填充完毕后就算胜利
2.随着关卡解锁，会出现新的关卡要素
①出现瓢虫，一段时间后该块作物会枯萎，直到被收获掉才恢复生长作物（此时不能作为顶点四个角）
②出现暴雨，一段时间后该片土地会进水，会永久绝收
③万能作物，可以作为任意作物进行匹配
④兔子，需要被点击多次，一段时间不处理会把植物吃到，同样要被收获后才恢复生长作物
3.出售作物获得的金钱可以用来升级，比如建造仓库，建造水泵、喷洒农药的飞机、收集雨水的水塔、以及购买更高级的种子（可以卖更多的钱）等等
4.每完成一定的关卡，会出现一些其他小游戏
主要有：
①收集完场地内的所有植物，规则同普通关卡，只不过已收货的土地不会再次生长出作物
②点击右侧水车集水，然后浇到没有成熟的作物上直到成熟收获
③用杀虫剂杀死飞来的瓢虫，但不要伤害蝴蝶，直到全部作物成熟

游戏质量整体来说还算一般
只不过价格36感觉偏高，已有的这些游戏性，心里价格在12-18左右
真个游戏的市场差不多5、6个小时，但玩了2、3个小时候基本上就腻了

Un puzzle game qui aurait sa place sur une tablette ou sur facebook, on reprend le thème très aimé de la ferme pour le décliner dans la gestion de champs. Les niveaux s'enchainent avec des champs de diverses formes, et le but est globalement toujours le même, remplir l'afflux permanent de camions qui viennent chercher vos légumes avec le bon type de légume avant qu'ils arrivent au bout de votre route. Pour les remplir, il s'agit simplement de trouver des carrés dont le 4 coins sont tous le même légume afin de récolter tous les légumes de ce type contenus dans le carré (et de provoquer la repousse immédiate de nouveaux légumes à leur place). 
 
Le jeu vient avec son lot d'upgrades et d'évolution de gameplay pour essayer de renouveler un peu l'interet, peu à peu des insectes viendront manger vos plantes (mais vous avez de l'insecticide), des orages viendront ruiner vos champs (vous avez un seau), des corbeaux manger vos trucs (vous avez des filets), si l'ensemble ajoute de nouvelles actions on a pas vraiment l'impression de progresser en achetant les upgrades, le tout étant calculé pour que vous puissiez les acheter au moment où un nouveau fléau s'abat sur votre ferme. 
 
De toute façon vous vous en foutez, pour vous faire de la maille vous aurez rapidement l'opportunité d'installer des puits de pétrole sur vos fermes du passé qui se chargeront de vous fournir tous les dollars nécessaires à l'achat de toutes les upgrades. Luxor, developed by MumboJumbo and published by Accelerate Games, stands as one of the foundational entries in the marble-shooter puzzle genre, delivering a straightforward yet highly addictive gameplay loop that has proven remarkably enduring. Set against a stylized ancient Egyptian backdrop, the game frames its action within a mythological struggle, placing the player in the role of a defender tasked with stopping advancing forces tied to the god Set. While the story itself is minimal and largely serves as context, it gives the game a sense of thematic cohesion that elevates it beyond a purely abstract puzzle experience.

The gameplay is built around a simple but effective mechanic: players control a winged launcher that fires colored spheres at a moving chain of marbles. By matching three or more of the same color, sections of the chain are eliminated, and the goal is to clear the entire sequence before it reaches its endpoint. What makes this system engaging is the way it blends quick reactions with forward planning. Players must constantly assess the movement of the chain, anticipate where shots will land, and create opportunities for chain reactions that can clear large portions of the screen. This balance between immediacy and strategy is what gives the game its lasting appeal.

As the game progresses, it steadily increases in difficulty, introducing faster-moving chains, more complex paths, and a greater variety of colors. This escalation ensures that players are continually challenged, requiring sharper timing and more precise decision-making. Power-ups are integrated into the experience to help manage this growing difficulty, offering temporary advantages such as slowing the chain, clearing sections of marbles, or enhancing the player’s firing capabilities. These elements add a layer of variety and provide moments of relief during more intense stages, helping to keep the gameplay from becoming overwhelming.

The campaign is structured as a series of levels that gradually build on one another, creating a sense of progression as players advance through increasingly demanding challenges. While the variety in track layouts and pacing helps maintain engagement, the core mechanics remain largely unchanged throughout. This consistency is both a strength and a limitation. On one hand, it ensures a reliable and cohesive experience; on the other, it means that the game rarely introduces new ideas once the player has mastered its fundamentals. Over longer play sessions, this can lead to a feeling of repetition, as the challenge shifts from learning new mechanics to refining existing skills.

Visually, Luxor embraces its Egyptian theme through stylized environments, decorative elements, and a color palette that evokes ancient iconography. While the graphics are relatively simple by modern standards, they are clear and functional, allowing players to easily track the movement of marbles and focus on gameplay. The soundtrack complements this presentation with energetic and thematic music that reinforces the sense of urgency, particularly during more intense moments when the chain is close to reaching its endpoint.

Despite its strengths, the game does have some limitations. The reliance on a single core mechanic means that long-term depth is somewhat limited, and players seeking a more varied or evolving experience may find it lacking. Additionally, while skill plays a significant role, there are moments where the randomness of incoming marbles can influence outcomes, occasionally making success feel less controlled than it could be. These elements do not detract significantly from the overall experience, but they do highlight the boundaries of the game’s design.

In the end, Luxor succeeds as a classic example of accessible, skill-based puzzle design. It offers a gameplay loop that is easy to learn, satisfying to master, and well-suited for both short sessions and extended play. While it may not have the complexity or variety of more modern titles, its simplicity is part of its charm, allowing it to remain engaging even years after its release. It is a game that understands its strengths and delivers a focused experience built around them.

Rating: 7/10

[h1] Luxor (anciently — Thebes) is a city in Upper Egypt, on the east bank of the Nile. It's the main city of the province with the same name. [/h1]

The first Luxor game is a classic and a benchmark of the casual game genre. Even compared to the legendary Zuma, Luxor has its own charm, although the competitor might have slightly nicer graphics and sound. Right now, the game doesn’t have the highest approval rating on Steam, but that’s mostly due to users complaining because they can’t run a twenty-year-old game on Windows 11. In reality, you just need to install a simple patch that’s freely available in Steam guides, and the game works perfectly.

That said, the game runs faster in windowed mode than fullscreen — so if you go for the fullscreen option, be ready for black bars.

The gameplay is pretty standard: you shoot balls, match them by color, and grab falling bonuses so the balls don’t reach the endpoint. There are 14 stages in total, each with around 5-6 levels on average (not counting the last 14th stage, which has a single unique level for the whole game). The difficulty ramps up in a clear way: every roughly third of the game, a new ball color shows up and the chain speed spikes. If you run out of lives, you have to start over from the beginning of the current stage. With enough skill, it’s totally possible to finish the game without dying at all. For many, this is a childhood game — some, like me, first played it when we were little, so the nostalgic vibes here are super strong.

Of course, the game has its flaws. It feels a bit long because there aren’t many original levels — almost all the variety of locations is gone by the fourth stage, and after that it’s just repetition at a faster pace. There aren’t many situations in the game, you can’t choose the difficulty or a specific level manually (that only gets fixed in the second part), and there’s no clear story or dialogues like in Zuma. And at the end of the day, it’s the same melody across all levels — the music isn’t totally cringy, but it’s pretty sparse.

Despite the monotony, it’s still a great way to kill some time. The game doesn’t try to be complicated or deep; it just works as a solid time-killer. If you want to get nostalgic or just pop some balls, Luxor is definitely worth checking out.

Luxor (the series) is definitely one of my favorite games of all time. It is like Zuma, but with an Ancient Egyptian touch and I'm all for it. As a kid I was so in love with the game and the weird but interesting hieroglyphs in it, that my whole obsession for Ancient Egypt culture started to grow and flourish. 

Today, as someone who already learned a bit of hieroglyphs, I'm again surprised by the dedication of the developers cuz some of the hieroglyphs are actually correctly used, and some paintings actually align with real relics. The majority of the "text" are unreadable cuz the writing orders are completely chaotic, but I can see that they have at least studied the Gardinar's list of Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs. Back when I was a kid, I used to think game developers would never go this far cuz they're "just making games"... but now, MumboJumbo is just like all the other indie game developers we know today. They are great artists who clearly enjoyed making these little games.

A clear drawback of this game would be the repetition of maps. Every stage has the same maps and sometimes a new one designed for this particular stage (which is nice). It can get boring at times, but again this is a zuma game what do you want. Still a good game.

Luxor is a match 3 arcade game with a twist - the  orbs move on a path. The goal is to shoot colored balls at the "trains" or segments moving along the path and match all of the balls before it reaches the end. More and more segments are required to complete the level with more colors being introduced, and the segment getting a farther head start incrementally ramps up the difficulty. Rinse and repeat for the 100 or so levels then the glory of the Egyptians gods will be restored.

The graphics look fine and the UI functions as intended.
The audio gives proper feedback and has a nice thematic sountrack.
No bugs were encountered in my playthrough, but a few complaints. Later Luxor games offer more power-ups with awesome, unique abilities, which this game sorely needs. The "catch up" mechanic of the segments seems to be very weird or unfair at times when making numerous match chains.

Overall, an addictive and good time killing experience for anyone. Also, yes, I am aware that many can not play the game. The game doesn't work as intended with new hardware, but an easily to comprehend patch exists for many of the Luxor games

Aside from the game normally being priced at $9.99 and being difficult to get running on modern computers, Luxor has a few other issues I feel are worth mentioning: 
1) There is no difficulty selection, and by extension, no way for players to practice difficult levels. 
2) The hit-detection on the balls seem a little sketchy. They sometimes don't slot into where you shot them at. I have not noticed this issue in other marble-shooter games I have played. 
3) The default shooting speed feels a little too slow for the pace the game sets after stage 3. This makes catching the speed power-ups a necessity. This issue is compounded by the lack of a practice mode I mentioned above. 

Despite this the game is still mostly enjoyable, with an attractive and consistent Ancient Egyptian-themed art style complimented by appropriate sound design and music, as well as simple and addicting game play. 

Wait for the game to go on a big sale, or just play the newer entries in the series. The newer Luxor games have difficulty selection, better ball accuracy, and are easier to get running on your PC.

Никогда не играл в эту игру в детстве, в отличие от напрашивающейся для сравнения Зумы. Купил для маман как времяубивалку, а заодно решил и сам проверить реакцию в столь незамысловатой аркаде. 

Что сказать? В принципе, мне понравилось шарoёbuться, довольно релаксирующая затея, особенно, если на фоне поставить документалку, аудиокнигу или музыку. Так просто играть надоест, но в купе с прослушиванием чего-либо на фоне — отличная разрядка.

И так как игра вышла позже Зумы и явно была ею вдохновлена, я не могу не провести сравнение и аналогию. Да что говорить, тут даже количество этапов идентичное Зуме (13 этапов), так что первоисточник видно невооруженным взглядом. Поэтому сразу отвечу на вопрос. Игра [u]слабее[/u] чем [b]Zuma[/b]. Пусть тут и вроде бы больше бонусов, например, и даже больше локаций, но тут нет главного — челленджа. Вся игра пролетает, в отличие от вдохновителя, налегке, — практический никакой задачи, никакой сложности и хардкора. Лишь буквально несколько самых последних уровней это предоставляют, но в целом за всю игру я просто чиллил, кидая шарики. Возможно, сыграло то, что перед этим я как раз прошёл ту самую Лягушку, поэтому, пресыщенный сложностью, эту игру не ощущал абсолютно. Но порадовало, что в целом формат игры чуть отличается, и ты будучи неведомой крылатой херней можешь двигаться только снизу по горизонтали. Это, в принципе, как и добавление новых и местами необычных бонусов, создаёт отличительный геймплей.

Что же по явным минусам? А то, что, чёрт побери, эта игра ни в какую не хочет запускаться на Windows 10. Будьте готовы к тому, что придётся пошаманить — лично мне пришлось качать патч. Я, конечно, люблю порой задачки, но явно не в этом смысле. Ну и облачного сохранения тоже нет, беда.

Got this in a bundle, but this is bad. This is a very bad hidden objects game. First, the resolution is fixed to 1024x768. Second, some objects are unidentifyable. Even after the hint function pointed them out to me, I felt that it would have been impossible to find them, that is how 'well' the game hid the object. The game has a 'relaxed' mode, but I could see any difference when using it. Perhaps it reduced the number of objects?
There are some variations to the theme, you find object, you compare scenes, you find items that belong to a certain category, but in that last one I ended up clicking items until one of them was identified as a kitchen item. Don't know what that was because of the poor graphics.

The game has a unique take on the 'Hidden Object' genre, framing it under the concept of a gameshow. It appears interesting at first yes, but unfortunately, squanders its potential.

You are assigned a vacation destination at first, which sets the overall theme of that playthrough. You then spin the wheel which determines the prize value of each found item for that round, with finding items consecutively and being the first to find the item before your competitors awarding more money (the game's equivalent of points). Aside from the HOG scenes, you do have a small selection of gameshow-style minigames, which sells the gameshow vibe pretty well. Except, there is literally no point in collecting the cash. The cash you win from completing rounds in the gameshow is just a gimmicky stand-in for the arbitrary point/score system you find in games. This defeats the whole premise of the game of the gameshow concept of competition, and by extension, a superficial time limit to make decisions.

The HOG aspect is your box-standard scenes; nothing special. However, given the age of the game, the graphics aren't particularly great and playing on a widescreen monitor exacerbates the problem. Most of the item outlines are very grainy and looks stretched out, making it particularly hard to identify them sometimes. And unless you prefer to strain your eyes to play in Windowed mode which does alleviate the problem, you may find the HOG scenes to be quite frustrating sometimes.

Also, while there are different destinations to play for, the gameplay is more or less the same. It just changes the backgrounds of the HOG and affects some of the minigames like the trivia one, since they ask fun facts about the vacation destination. Essentially, once you've played through one destination, you've more or less played what the game can offer, unless you want to try out the minigames you didn't get a chance to play or are a completionist by nature. One destination takes you less than 30 minutes from start to end and it gets repetitive and dull quickly.

An interesting hidden object game concept

So, you find objects.  And sometimes you play minigames that are related to finding objects.  That's true of every HOG out there.  But here, instead of wrapping it in a story to add a bit of narrative interest, it's framed in the conceit of a game show, where performance is rewarded by greater winnings -- in other words, a point-based score system with a dollar sign stuck in front of it.  But since the points are meaningless, there's no real incentive to strive for more of them -- or even to care how many you have acquired.  Which makes the entire set of "game show" elements -- the "Wheel of Fortune" wheel, the smarmy host, and so forth -- just an aggravating waste of time between HOG scenes.  The HOG scenes aren't even very good.  There's nothing here worth recommending.  If the cheesy game show aesthetic amuses you, try the "You Don't Know Jack" series instead.

Discovery! A Seek & Find Adventure is an unusual spin on hidden object games, where instead of some kind of story driven adventure, it's posed as a travel-themed game show where you go through rounds against AI competitors to win more money than they do, and win a "pretend" ticket to whatever destination came up on the wheel. 

While the idea is novel, it doesn't hit the mark.   The hidden objects are rarely related to the topical country selected for the round.  Other issues, the objects are weirdly sized and weirdly positioned (some just hanging in the sky).   Although there's no real "rules" for hidden object games, it's just weird finding a slice of pizza bigger than 20 men sitting on the Sydney opera house.  Also, fixed resolution and 4:3 aspect ratio make this unacceptable for PC.

Juego de objetos ocultos que te ubica como concursante de un show de concursos (ni idea quien vería algo así)  que se queda en una sola temporada por falta de consistencia y calidad.

PROS
-Variedad de Mecánicas: Entre cada ronda de objetos ocultos se accede mediante ruleta a 1 de 4 minijuegos que le dan algo de diversidad. 
-Sonido: Sin ser destacable, a menos hacen loop de forma correcta, es acorde a cada locación y no distrae. Los diálogos del presentador (que no afectan en nada si te los saltas y son los únicos diálogos en el juego) son energéticos sin caer en ser fastidiosos.

NEUTRO
Logros: el juego tiene logros internos, pero no están coordinados con steam ni parece que vaya a hacerlo. En neutro porque se que a mucha gente le interesan un pepino los logros en steam

CONTRAS
-Resolución fija. Solo se puede cambiar de pantalla completa a modo ventana.
-Calidad de imagen: La calidad de los objetos a encontrar varia demasiado, de fotos super nítidas a imágenes casi pixeladas y descoloridas, lo que afecta la presentación y en ocasiones a la identificación de dichos objetos en el juego.
-Y los rivales apa?!:  Participas en un programa de concursos contra 2 rivales, pero igual podrías participar tu solo porque rara vez ofrecen competencia. En la ronda de objetos ocultos rara vez se acercan a tu puntaje, y en los minijuegos ni siquiera participan, lo que hace completamente anecdotico que estén ahí. Si la IA del juego te llega a ganar mas de 1 round, tal vez ya necesitas lentes (o nuevos lentes). Los únicos que medio ponen presión son los gurus al final del juego, principalmente los últimos 2, no demasiado, pero al menos te presionan un poco.

CONCLUSION
Dale una oportunidad si eres asiduo de este tipo de juegos y si o si tienes que jugarlos todos cual si fueran pokemons, o si acaso te lo ganaste en un sorteo como yo. No ofrece nada superior a otros juegos del genero y para los que no les gusta este genero les resultara tedioso y aburrido despues del segundo programa.

TLDR: Low quality gameshow style hidden object. Pretend like you win prizes as only excuse to get dumped in postcard scenes flooded with small items to find.

This game has a lot of issues, between the abusive use of color reshades, the complete lack of proprotions, the use of object to obstruct parts of other objects and the occasional modes where no hints are provided there is a lot of frustration to be had. The A.I. opponents represent no threat and serve as a very weak narrative vehicle to motivate you to go forward. Winning fake vacations is not exciting either. All you get for your trouble of going through the same country postcards three times to finish the match is the opportunity to then play that country in standalone mode.

The objects have all the qualities of having been randomly placed but they are not. Loading the same postcard twice will place the objects in the same locations they were before.

There is the occasional memory card game, spotting 7 differences but they are derivative and arguably poorly implemented

Given the sheer overabundance of much better polished hidden object games that either throw in better narrative, better atmosphere, better setting, cleaner art or more interesting puzzles this falls at the bottom of the barrel fairly hard. Removed permanently into hidden library of deleted titles for declutter.

Look, we are simple folk.

When I say "we", I mean of course my brethren, the Hidden Object Game people (or "hog people" for short).

We don't ask for much, just pretty-ish environments in which we can look around for misc. objects from a laundry list (such as: manacles, a whip, candles, an Xbox One console, heavy-duty plastic tarps, a wooden horse, tax forms, a ball gag) to click on. And that's enough to content us, really.

Sadly the art in this is pretty abysmal. Objects are resized in a way that does not make sense relative to each other; likewise, objects are fuzzy that should be in focus and conversely. The photos that the art is sourced from are pretty ugly/dull, and garish colour filters are applied liberally to make matters worse.

I understand that this was done in an effort to make the object hunting a bit more challenging, but the combined "eyesore power" of all these techniques used at the same time is just too much.

There's a game show conceit in [i]Discovery! A Seek and Find Adventure[/i], and that's at least a novel way to frame the different environments. They bungled the meat of the game though, letting us hog people down.

숨은 그림 찾기 게임. 세계 각지를 테마로 하며, 퀴즈 대회 식으로 AI와 경쟁한다. 제 나름대로 여러 방식의 게임 진행도 도입해놓았다. 예를 들면, 찾아야할 사물 목록에 따라 그대로 찾는 고전 방식 외에, '사무용품 찾기' 등의 주제별 사물 찾기같은 것이 있다. 

 이 게임의 구매는 별로 추천하지 않는데, 우선 배경과 사물의 사진이 꽤나 이질적이기 때문에 별로 조화롭지 않기 때문이다. 그냥 JPG 파일을 곳곳에 심어둔 느낌이 든다. 좀 어렵게 하기 위해서 배경의 색에 묻히도록 조화를 시켰다든가 하는 방식은 썼지만 별로 달갑지는 않다. 

 실수에 패널티가 없기 때문에 처음엔 집중해서 사물을 찾으려하지만 플레이어는 금세 학습하게 된다. 아무데나 마구 클릭해도 괜찮기 때문에 굳이 공들여 찾을 필요가 없다. 각 나라를 테마로 잡는 사진들이나 바뀔 뿐 판에 박힌 진행은 장르의 특성상 어쩔 수 없기 때문에 지루해지고, 무성의한 플레이에도 별다른 제약이 없어서 더 흥미를 잃기 쉬워진다. 

 AI가 그다지 똑똑하지 못하다는 것 역시도 긴장감을 떨어뜨리는 중요한 요인이다. 경쟁을 위해 심어놓은 AI가 너무나 잘해도 플레이어는 좌절감을 느껴서 재미를 잃겠지만, 너무 못하면 존재의 의미가 없어지기 때문이다. 플레이어가 스테이지를 마무리할 때까지도 1~2개의 사물을 찾고 있는 광경은 한숨이 나온다. 물론 스테이지를 거듭할수록 AI는 더 강해질 것이다. 하지만 그 정도의 스테이지에 도달하기 전에 이미 플레이어는 게임에 흥미를 잃고 떠날 것이다. 

 Steam에 보기 드문 '숨은 그림 찾기' 게임이지만 별로 훌륭하지는 않다. 하나의 쓸모가 있다면 명절 때 어린 조카들이 쳐들어왔을 때 얌전히 잡아둘 역할을 혹시나 할지도 모른다는 점이다. 하지만 요즘 재미난 모바일 게임에 익숙해진 아이들이 이 게임에 매력을 느낄지는 미지수이다.

This is another one of those games that I really wish that there were a neutral rating for. It is not a bad game, but it has flaws that left me torn, and ultimately opting not to recommend it. For one, there is not much real playing time involved here, at all (though it does at least try to implement true replayability via mini games and different game modes, though over the course of the game one tends to start to learn where things are in the scenes). My total time playing it reflects a great deal of replaying after needing to restore everything on my computer, as I wanted to know what happens in the end of the game, out of simple curiousity. My assessment:

At first, the game show idea is compelling. What could be better than adding in some AI opponents to race against in a hidden object search? Yet, in this game all of your opponents were apparently dropped on their heads as children. Repeatedly. Then, even though you unlock new opponents as you progress, their level of challenge doesn't go up any. So wide is the margin with just casual play that you could pretty much put on a blindfold and play the main levels without an issue when it comes to winning against your opponents. The exception to this comes only after the main levels are completed and you play in the tournament of champions, when the level of challenge presented by the opponents seems to jump up a bit more toward what you might be expecting (or, at least what I was expecting). But, at that point, whether you'll even care anymore is anyone's guess.

The graphics and naming of objects are also a bit iffy. That is to say, while I definitely wasn't expecting much, the hidden object scenes are quite annoying to work with compared to many such games due to the almost choppy nature of the graphics (this is hard to explain, but if you look closely at the blown-up screen shots you should somewhat see what I mean) as well as the fact that items are not always named and/or depicted clearly. Something will look more like one thing while being called something else, for instance, or will be depicted in an unfamiliar fashion, thus requiring a hint or dumb luck to find.

Overall, it is an excellent original concept for a hidden object game, but it ultimately fell just a bit short of my expectations. As I said above, I'd give it a neutral rating if I could, but as I can't, I also find I cannot bring myself to recommend it.

After playing three Artifex Mundi games, I thought that I would lay off reviewing hidden object games, since I clearly don’t like them. Well, I’ve reconsidered. I don’t dislike these puzzles on principle, so there should be a way to present them to me that I enjoy. I want to see if there’s a hidden object game I can recommend, so let the griping continue! Or maybe not? Is Samantha Swift worth my time?

What I can say for sure is, despite the lower production value, I prefer Hidden Roses of Athena to all of the Artifex Mundi games I’ve played simply because it didn’t waste my time. Each area has a hidden object challenge, and once you’ve found every object, you never have to revisit it. I didn’t have to backtrack through long, winding paths across multiple areas to find any puzzles; a puzzle will take up two rooms or multiple rooms around a single hub at most. This was also the shortest HOG I’ve played, comprising eight locations with less than ten puzzles per location. No half-baked side stories, just eight short levels. Unlike Artifex Mundi, where I was begging for the games to end, Samantha Swift not only kept things short, but briskly paced as well.  It even had a superior hint system, including an object scanner and limited but plentiful instant hints instead of unlimited hints that take ages to recharge.

So can I recommend Samantha Swift and the Hidden Roses of Athena? Not really. Though the simplicity is a breath of fresh air, it doesn’t make up for lack of substance. The game is beyond easy; I had about 25 hints left after completion, and what little thought the puzzles required often had Samantha jumping in with an unsolicited hint.  Maybe they were trying to compensate by making the clicker annoyingly precise.  If I’m two pixels off or within some inner negative space, the click should catch the object.

Again, I prefer this straightforward approach to chasing after a glowing arrow in the Artifex Mundiverse, but these duct tape approaches to guiding players show an inability to make naturally intuitive gameplay.  A lot of old adventure games are unintuitive, but some of them have engaging narratives, clever writing, or a fascinating world. This one doesn’t. I zoned out whenever Buddy McGuy was telling me my mission objective. Did I miss the thrilling adventure? Did Samantha’s rival do anything? Was there any significance to the roses outside of being MacGuffins? It's empty storytelling like this that cultivates a dead environment.  It is at times livened up by a few bright colors and fun puzzles, but mostly just feels like a mediocre picture book.  The game's trivial weirdness is more memorable than its main plot.  Why is gold used as a distraction by making noise instead of being valuable?  Why is a paperweight (which could look like anything) a hidden object and why is it used to break glass?  Why is the Japanese object that is clearly a shamisen called "instrument?"

I should keep things in perspective. This isn’t a terrible game; I came out of it a lot happier than I had with similar games, and I think someone who knows what they’re getting into buying this on sale will be reasonably satisfied. I maintain, however, that this genre has potential, maybe not in spades, but enough that is clearly being squandered by developers focusing on accessibility over innovation.

This is a very old game which doesn't have some of the gameplay conveniences that later Hidden Object games implemented (nor does it have any of the point & clicking activity, it's 95% hidden objects, yet it's not bothersome, I guess I was in the mood for some quiet clicking.)

Still, this Indy/Lara wannabe is pretty fun, and I really enjoyed her adventures and embraced the silliness and cliché quests. Yes, I have a hard time believing Sam would be able to infiltrate the Louvre museum at night and not meet a single watchman. That she'd find a secret place below the museum and would think it's okay to steal from it. That she'd receive help from locals in Tibet to steal a national treasure. That she'd find countless places that reportedly hadn't been visited in centuries, and yet managed to find modern items on her hidden object hunt. I'm pretty sure the Mayans didn't invent the microwave oven. (There's no microwave oven in the game, but you get my drift.)
(Spoilers following in the next paragraph, although the story is so obvious you won't mind)
..That someone would open their museum in a volcano (?) and actually call it 'Payne Museum'. That someone would steal back items from that museum, and mark their origin as 'Payne Museum' instead of, I don't know, 'Greece' for the Scepter of Zeus. 'Hey, guys, we stole from them alright, but they stole from us first!'
And finally, that Athena herself would find Sam worthy of yielding her shield and be deemed a hero, even though she kept stealing for her museum.

But despite all of that, it was fun, fun and fun, and I'll definitely play the other games in the series.

Note that some of the hitboxes for objects aren't exactly very forgiving. Also, I appreciated that Sam commented in speech bubbles from time to time, but if you're doing a click frenzy, they'll be dismissed immediately. I only realized near the end that you can repeat her last bubble by clicking her face... (Now that's a hint I'm giving you!)
And the resolution is really low. 800x600, I think..? You can either play fullscreen, which, meh, or launch in a window, and use the Windows key and +/- signs to manually increase the window size with the magnifier tool.

[h1][b] Overview[/b] [/h1]
Samantha Swift and the Hidden Roses of Athena is quite the long title. It is psychological horror as well as a hidden object adventure game. I love my fair share of hidden object puzzle games; The Secret Order series as well as the Nightmare From the Deep series were both astoundingly good games. But this, this is something else. I played as little as I could bare before uninstalling every last trace of this from my computer. Why? It’s pretty damn nigh malware.

[h1][b] Components[/b] [/h1]

[b]Visuals[/b] - The visuals style is cartoony and bright. Vibrant graphics are usually nice, but in this case the visual quality is horrendous. The background scenery is simply subpar, but the findable objects are of such poor quality that they contrast against everything else. They stick out like a sore thumb. In hidden object games, the graphic quality needs to be consistent, especially between objects and the background. When they don’t seamlessly blend, it ends up being an eyesore à la this game. Maybe this game is just old, but it shouldn’t be looking 30 years old. Ever heard of Crysis? Believe it or not, Crysis came out before this game did. The resolution is eye-bleedingly bad and age is simply no excuse. Heck, Toonstruck (my first ever casual adventure game) has better graphics, and it’s over a decade older than this!

[b]Audio[/b] - I skipped all the cutscenes because I wanted to get right into the gameplay. So I can’t say much for the voice acting. The sound effects and music weren’t really noticeable, which means they weren’t great, but it also means they weren’t bad.

[b]Gameplay[/b] - It pretty much plays like a standard hidden object game, with nothing unique or special about it. It lacks any originality or challenge in the gameplay aspect, though fans of casual adventure games probably won’t mind.

[b]Story[/b] - The story seems to be overly clichéd and silly, but at least it progresses a bit.

[b]Functionality[/b] - My goodness. I’ve played dozens of games with a resolution of 800x600 or less, my most memorable being the best sh’mup of all time: Jets N Guns (with a resolution of a mere 640x480!). Yet somehow, this game is 800x600 and manages to look like 200x150. That’s not even the bad bit: upon launching this game it changed my DESKTOP RESOLUTION to 800x600. WHAT!? As if the stupid game wasn’t bad enough, it decides to MESS WITH YOUR COMPUTER WITHOUT PERMISSION. Now my entire screen is all zoomed in, and the game itself is minimised and won’t even launch properly. I struggle to navigate my computer to fix this horrendous resolution, but upon changing it back to 1920x1080, NOTHING HAPPENS. Not only does this game DESTROY YOUR ENTIRE COMPUTER’S RESOLUTION, it feels the need to PERMANENTLY LOCK IT AGAINST MY WILL, while the game is running. If this isn’t malware then I don’t know what is.

[b]UX[/b] - Menus aren’t the best but they can be navigated fine, and the game is really easy and simple to play. 

[b]Miscellaneous[/b] - I simply do not appreciate games messing with my desktop resolution for no reason. This game runs at 800x600, BUT DON’T FORCE MY ENTIRE COMPUTER TO THIS ABOMINATION OF A RESOLUTION. Thank you.

[h1][b]Valuation[/b][/h1]

[b]Longevity/replayability[/b] - It seems to contain at least a few hours of gameplay. Whether or not you can persevere... well I can’t predict.

[b]Support[/b] - Non-existent. No patches. No fixes. Many people in reviews and forums complaining about the game not launching, or the game completely breaking after launching a second time, and not a single fix has ever occurred.

[b]Is it worth the money?[/b] $10 is a bit much for a piece of broken malware.

[h1][b] Highlights [/b] [/h1]
[list]
[*] The audio and story are the least bad attributes but they are by no means positive
[/list]
[h1][b] Downsides [/b] [/h1]
[list]
[*] Desecration of my PC
[*] Awful graphics
[*] Abundance of technical issues
[*] Worse in every way compared to games released decades prior
[/list]

[h1] [b]Conclusion[/b] [/h1]

Likeable characters (though their backstory is limited to a few notes in the game menu), nice artstyle (especially with light effects and animations during hidden objects search sections) and enough variety from puzzles to keep you engaged till the end, though it would have benefited it more had the game been longer or had some endgame features been unlocked for replayability like in some other games from this developer.

I wouldn't recommend this at full price, but definitely worth getting on a sale or from a bundle.

[h1]Short version: 64%[/h1]
Hidden Roses of Athena is an old hidden object game with a cute visual style and a typical Saturday morning cartoon treasure hunt adventure storyline.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
I’ll be blunt: the existence of this game on Steam is a mystery to me. Samantha Swift and the Hidden Roses of Athena is the first entry in a hidden object game series that started in late 2008—an age where hidden object games were a lot different from the ones we know nowadays. Additionally, the publisher released it here five years later, with a price tag that would have been atrocious back then, let alone today.

Still, if we look past all of these, we find a cute little ancient HOG under the 800×600-pixel exterior. Hidden Roses of Athena is your typical cartoonish treasure hunt adventure, where we accompany an archaeologist on a trip all around the globe, looking for the titular roses of Athena. The story is cute and the hidden object scenes are surprisingly good for their time, so, in the end, it is a game one can have much fun with—if they can get it at a reasonable price and do not mind the ancient graphics.

The HO scenes, and puzzles, are rarely challenging and the game seems to be aimed at a younger market than this old man!

If you don't mind the graphic style, that it's fairly short, and that there is no voice acting, just text, then you might get a couple of hours entertainment out of it, more if you play with kids, but the price is a negative. The game is too expensive for what it is. Try to pick it up in bundle or sale. (There are also lots of reports of problems running the game under Windows 8 and Windows 10. Решил добавить к своему рациону прохождений нечто казуальное, чему можно уделить 10-15 минут и выйти, продолжив в любой момент.

Жанр “3 в ряд” простой и понятный, особо не меняется. Я уже проходил 7 Wonders of the Ancient World, потому что была игрой детства. Оказывается, серия довольно большая. Treasures of Seven предлагает тот же самый геймплей, но с одним большим отличием.

Фишка игры в том, что мы можем переворачивать поле с камушками, как кубик. С каждым поворотом мы меняем правило выпадения новых камушков, так как перспектива меняется. Вам также нужно очистить каждую клетку, чтобы человечки внизу уровня смогли построить архитектурное чудо. 

В конце каждого раунда необходимо провести по полю большой камень с изображением цифры 7. Для этого на поле нарисован пунктир. Понадобится много раз крутить экран, чтобы камень продолжал падать от наших “матчей”. Идея прикольная и разбавляет игровой процесс. Иногда будут мешать порталы, которые могут вернуть нас почти в начало. На последних уровнях финиш может быть под замком, для открытия нужно сделать совпадение определённым цветом.

Камушки вновь красивущие, мне они очень нравятся. Появились новые цвета. Только синий цвет показался слишком кислотным, глаза от него побаливали. Если соберёте больше 3 камушков, то получите привычные бонусы по типу аое атак по вертикали и горизонтали (с новой функцией переворачивания что угодно может трансформироваться из горизонтали в вертикаль и наоборот). И снова есть особый бонус, который даётся за использование других, разрушает случайные клетки. Также иногда появляется бонусная цель, требующая за короткое время сделать “матч” конкретного цвета. В награду ненадолго заморозится время. В любом случае, времени для прохождения тут достаточно, идёт оно неспешно.

Времени даже слишком много выделяется. Даже при больших затупах его хватает с огромной лихвой. Даже ваши внуки успеют допройти, если вы вдруг умрёте за монитором.

Теперь появилась отдельная кнопка замены камушков, если вы не видите ближайших совпадений. Вещь удобная, а откатывается путём новых “матчей”. Если доска слишком причудливая, то вы часто будете видеть уведомление, что ходов совсем не осталось, поменяется расположение автоматически.

Само название говорит о 7 Чудесах, а уровней тут 10! Нелогично получается. Интересных мест не очень много. Запомнились только Пизанская Башня и Сергиев Посад. 

Игру есть за что ругать. Она слишком затянута, начиная от большого количества уровней, заканчивая их длительностью. В Ancient World уровни пролетались быстро и незаметно. В Treasures of Seven они тягучие, к тому же в конце всегда надо опускать этот камень. Всё это превращается в слишком затянутую жвачку, от которой устаёшь. Хотя игра задумана для того, чтобы отдыхать в ней, отключать мозг.

Внешний вид симпатичный, но поддержку широких экранов так и не завезли. На уровнях даже есть смена дня и ночи.

Музыка нормальная. Звуки камушков, как всегда, чудесные.

Сюжет тут только в истории построек. Локализации нет. Если владеете английским, то можете ознакомиться.

Игра средняя, но предлагает уникальную идею с переворачиваем поля. Она портится затянутостью, но всё равно было приятно поиграть в очередной “3 в ряд”. Однако, эта игра заставляет меня сделать паузу в этом жанре.

Плюсы:
- красивые камушки и их звук
- уникальная механика переворачивания поля
- удобно поиграть в любое время 10-15 минут
- приятный визуал

Минусы:
- отсутствие поддержки широких мониторов
- затянутость уровней
- слишком просто, времени на уровень выделяется так много, что ваши внуки успеют допройти

Decent match-3 with a twist, but also a bit of a grind

7 Wonders: Treasures of Seven is a cozy little match-three puzzler with a gimmick that actually works: rotating the board to guide the key to the lock. It adds a nice layer of planning on top of the usual “match colorful gems and watch stuff explode” formula. When it clicks, it’s satisfying to set up chains, rotate at the right moment, and watch the path open up exactly as you intended.

That said, it also feels quite repetitive after a while. The basic loop doesn’t really evolve much, and the game leans heavily on doing the same type of level again and again with slightly higher requirements. It’s the kind of puzzle game that’s relaxing in short sessions but starts to drag if you play for too long.

Presentation is fine: music is harmless background noise, visuals are dated but readable, and performance is solid. No major bugs, no crashes, it just works. It’s also very easy to run on basically any modern machine.

If you enjoy classic casual match-three games and want something light to zone out with for a bit, this is a reasonable choice. If you’re looking for depth, variety, or modern production values, this will probably feel more like a nostalgic time-killer than a must-play.

7 Wonders: Treasures of Seven attempts to build upon its predecessor's foundation but ultimately ends up stripping away much of what made 7 Wonders II a more enjoyable and mechanically satisfying experience. While the visual presentation has improved - with cleaner animations and updated graphics - the gameplay feels shallower, slower and noticeably less engaging.

One of the few mechanical additions is the ability to rotate the board, which allows for some satisfying plays and small tactical considerations. However, this feature alone cannot compensate for the lack of depth in the game's core design. The new maze navigation mechanic, centered around guiding a keystone through a series of paths, is clearly positioned as the primary innovation. Unfortunately, it falls flat. Rather than adding complexity or variety, it introduces a layer of forced interaction that is tedious and breaks the flow of play.

Challenge is virtually nonexistent. The time meter is so forgiving that it rarely reaches even a third of its total duration, even during casual play. And if a player takes too long to make a move, the game highlights one automatically. This severely undercuts any sense of urgency or strategic pacing. In contrast, 7 Wonders II offered a more balanced difficulty curve, along with rechargeable powers that added both utility and variety to each level, all of which are notably absent here.

Each wonder feels visually distinct but mechanically identical. After a few levels, the gameplay becomes repetitive, with minimal strategic variation and no new mechanics introduced. I couldn't bring myself to finish the game, after about 3 hours of gameplay I've had enough, and that's quite rare.

Overall, 7 Wonders: Treasures of Seven fails to refine the formula that defined its predecessor. It's not offensively bad - just slow, unchallenging, and ultimately forgettable. Unless you're an old geezer looking for a low-challenge match-3 experience to fill short breaks, there's little reason to recommend it. 7 Wonders II remains the superior game by far.

Interested? Let me tell you about it! Inside this version of 7 Wonders, you get to build nine structures in total, which you'll complete at the same time you work on building an outer cube and an inner cube which holds a compass. That is because once you earn the things you're supposed to, you get to move a cube along a pathway to reach each level's lock! The art/graphics are nice and simple, but beautiful. I've always enjoyed their details in this series, even if they're "outdated" as some people would say.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good match-3, a puzzle, or just learning about some historic buildings!
