Precipice of Darkness, Episode One, officially titled Penny Arcade Adventures: On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode One, is a narrative-driven role-playing adventure developed and published by Hothead Games. Released as the first entry in an episodic series inspired by the popular Penny Arcade webcomic, the game blends elements of classic RPGs with point-and-click adventure mechanics and a strong emphasis on humor and storytelling. Rather than focusing purely on traditional role-playing systems, the game aims to recreate the comedic tone and quirky world of the webcomic while introducing players to a strange alternate version of the early twentieth century filled with supernatural threats, bizarre inventions, and eccentric characters.

The story takes place in the fictional city of New Arcadia, a stylized 1920s setting where technology, mysticism, and oddities coexist in unusual ways. Players begin as an ordinary citizen whose quiet suburban life is abruptly disrupted when a massive mechanical robot destroys their home. Shortly afterward, the protagonist meets Tycho Brahe and Johnathan Gabriel—commonly known as Tycho and Gabe—two eccentric detectives who investigate the bizarre and often dangerous mysteries that plague the city. What begins as a personal misfortune quickly evolves into a larger investigation involving strange machines, cult activity, and ominous forces operating beneath the surface of New Arcadia. The narrative moves quickly between comedic absurdity and darker supernatural themes, creating a unique tone that reflects the style of the original webcomic.

Gameplay combines exploration, puzzle-solving, and turn-based combat in a hybrid format that borrows ideas from both adventure games and RPGs. As players explore different areas of the city, they interact with objects, examine environments, and engage in conversations that advance the storyline. These exploration segments often involve simple puzzles or humorous encounters that highlight the personality of the characters. Many interactive moments trigger comedic dialogue exchanges between the protagonist, Gabe, and Tycho, reinforcing the playful and sarcastic tone that fans of the webcomic will immediately recognize.

Combat encounters introduce the RPG side of the experience. Battles occur against a wide variety of unusual enemies, including malfunctioning machines, sinister cultists, and bizarre creatures that inhabit the city. The combat system uses a turn-based structure where players select attacks, use items, and activate special abilities. One of the game’s notable mechanics is a timing-based system that rewards careful attention during battles. Successfully pressing buttons at the right moment can increase damage dealt or reduce incoming attacks, adding a small element of skill to what would otherwise be a standard turn-based system. While the combat mechanics are not overly complex, they provide enough variety to keep encounters engaging throughout the game’s relatively short runtime.

The visual presentation of Precipice of Darkness, Episode One is heavily influenced by the comic that inspired it. Characters are stylized with exaggerated proportions and expressive animations that reflect the cartoonish humor of the source material. Cutscenes often resemble comic panels, reinforcing the connection to the Penny Arcade universe while giving the game a distinctive identity. The world of New Arcadia itself is filled with imaginative details, combining retro industrial technology with supernatural elements to create a setting that feels both humorous and mysterious.

A major strength of the game lies in its writing and dialogue. The script captures the sarcastic and often absurd humor that defines the Penny Arcade brand. Characters frequently deliver witty remarks, sarcastic observations, and unexpected comedic moments during both story sequences and exploration segments. Even mundane interactions can lead to humorous exchanges, making the dialogue a central part of the overall experience. Players who enjoy character-driven storytelling and comedic writing will likely find the narrative one of the most entertaining aspects of the game.

Because this installment serves as the opening chapter of an episodic series, its story focuses largely on introducing the world and establishing the main characters rather than delivering a fully self-contained narrative. The game’s main campaign can typically be completed within a few hours, and while it resolves some immediate plot points, it leaves several mysteries unresolved in preparation for later episodes. This episodic structure means that the experience sometimes feels more like a prologue than a complete RPG adventure.

Despite its relatively modest length and straightforward mechanics, the game succeeds in delivering a memorable and entertaining experience. The combination of humorous storytelling, stylized visuals, and light RPG gameplay creates a distinctive identity that separates it from more traditional fantasy role-playing games. Instead of epic battles or massive open worlds, the focus remains on quirky characters, strange mysteries, and comedic moments that drive the story forward.

Overall, Precipice of Darkness, Episode One is an unusual RPG-adventure hybrid that prioritizes personality and humor over mechanical complexity. While its episodic format and short length may leave some players wanting more depth, the game successfully introduces a bizarre and entertaining world filled with memorable characters and strange encounters. For fans of the Penny Arcade webcomic or players looking for a humorous narrative-driven RPG experience, it offers a charming and distinctive start to the series.

On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness is a surprisingly charming little RPG that I had a blast with — the Penny Arcade humor lands well if you appreciate that brand of absurdist, slightly crude wit, and there's something genuinely delightful about beating up mimes and hobos with a rake in a Lovecraftian 1920s setting. The combat system keeps things engaging with its active-time mechanics and QTE special moves for blocking and combos, which adds a satisfying layer of skill beyond just issuing commands. It's short — I wrapped it up in around 7 hours — but that brevity works in its favor; it never outstays its welcome or devolves into a grind, especially since enemies are finite and stay dead. If you're not already a Penny Arcade fan, some of the humor might not click, but the comic-book art style and tight combat are enjoyable on their own merits. Recommended, especially at a sale price.

I've heard of the webcomic Penny Arcade, which this game is based on, and have read a few at some time, but can't remember anything about them, so I went into this game blind. The setting seemed fun and the graphics are nice, but it wasn't what I expected, for better or worse. I didn't expect a character generator that is fairly detailed, even if it's far from what Bethesda have in their games. I was quite pleased with my creation, all the same.

There is some voice acting by a narrator here and there, but it's mostly just text, which is a bit of a bummer to me (I prefer fully voiced characters), even if the text is fun to read. The humor is sometimes random, sometimes simple or mildly vulgar. I personally enjoyed it, but it's not for everyone. The plot revolves around giant robots and HP Lovecraft-like ancient, dark gods.  

I thought this was gonna be turn-based (like it says on the tags), i.e. where you can take your time to look over your options and then make a plan for each character, but the combat is real-time and all your abilities/attacks are on a timer. This makes things more hectic and at the start I was a bit stressed, because I hadn't taken a good look at what the different items did or how to tell them apart in the heat of the moment ("oh, so the throwable green bottles reduce the enemies' defense, but the pink bottles reduces their damage"). 

Once I got that sorted out it got a lot easier, but I still haven't figured out/mastered everything you can do (when to block, how to counterattack and team attack) and I can't be bothered to find out either, because the game isn't that good and you don't need to master every aspect to win every battle, fortunately. Also, if I had seen that the game had a manual before beating it, that might have answered some questions, but nowhere in-game did I see any mention of a manual and how many games come with manuals these days anyway.

I played on the easiest difficulty, because the combat in games of this kind (great source material, rich in lore and character) usually seems like an afterthought. Some people don't mind that if everything else is great, but bad combat most often equals bad gaming experience for me. That's not the case here, but it still isn't great. Some attacks from enemies do very low damage and then the next one takes off half of your max health pool. It's also good that there are only three bosses, because it takes quite a while to wear down their massive health bars. I do like that there are several combat options available, items for offense and defense as well as healing and even supporting characters that you can occasionally call in for help. You get these items by smashing containers around the areas and they respawn if you go to another area and then come back. Sometimes the containers are empty or contain an item that you can't carry any more of, but if you lack an item, you can just keep on smashing until you find it.   

I started playing this game now, knowing that I could finish it in time for the Summer Sale, where I'll probably pick up the second episode if it's on sale. If it's not discounted enough or at all, then I can wait. While the game is fun, it's not that good that I absolutely must play the second episode soon to see what happens next.

I love Penny Arcade, or, at least, I love the 2000s era of the webcomic, before they got really big. It was wild, and free and weird, just like the Internet was in those days. The joked about everything and anything, all from a perspective of gamers, and that resonated with me.

These games (I'm going to copy the review, or parts of it, to all four episodes) are not exactly that, but they evoke the same emotions and atmosphere, with a healthy dose of Lovecraftian horror.

Episodes 1 and 2 are very light RPG games, with real time combat and a neat 3D visual style. Episode 3 is a straight up JRPG, while Episode 4 is a JRPG/Pokemon kind of game.

All four games follow the same story, which starts off like a fairly classic Lovecraftian RPG in Episodes 1 and 2, but transforms into something much much weirder in 3, and especially 4. The ending of Episode 4 is completely worth it, and I was very happy after I played through all the games.

The massive change of visual style between the first two and last two episodes can put some people off, but it didn't really bother me.

Ultimately, this whole series is something I would recommend to PA webcomic fans, but also to people who are looking for a fresh dose of weirdness, even if they never heard of the comic. The story, setting and characters are just perfect, whereas the gameplay is a secondary concern.

I ended up playing 'On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode One', after playing Episode 3.   That may not have done this game any favours, as it's a very different game (developed by a different studio) to the 3rd game.   While the 3rd game is a Final Fantasy style game, this is much more like a 3D Point and click game with RPG combat, and the overtures towards that design do weaken the game a little bit.

Graphically, this definitely reminds of Grim-Fandango and Discworld Noir, and that similarity continues into the feel of moving around the world.  The issue is that this style of motion and interaction can feel quite slow and plodding - particularly when moving from crate to bin to crate in order to loot for inventory items through an irritatingly slow animation.   Combat meanwhile (which you'll do a lot of) is instead true to the JRPG formula - with a time-based recharge for 3 tiers of action:  firstly, the inventory (stat buffs/nerfs, healing and some damage items), then basic attack and finally special attacks.   This leads to some tense late game moments while balancing when to act and when to wait, waiting for a character to unlock their top tier attack, and hoping that you can survive that long without needing to use an item.
 
On that note, healing is not necessarily an essential part of combat, nor the usual reason to act early.  Each enemy attack is telegraphed and a brief 'block' sign pops up as the attack hits.   If you press within the window then you can get one of four outcomes: a perfect block with counterattack, a good block, a partial block and a failed block.   Late game enemies have aggressively short time periods on those block windows, and i couldn't reliably get blocks for some enemies because of that, but ironically, by the late game, the bigger issue is that some enemy attacks apply stat nerfs to you too.   It can be frustrating getting a character ready for their ultimate only to find that you fail a block and their attack stat is quartered, though you can sacrifice another player's attack to provide a buff to the character (only one buff/nerf can be active at a time).

Overall though, that challenge (and occasional frustration when things don't work out) is what makes the gameplay here.  The story, while present, is a little thin on the ground for much of the game, told primarily in cutscenes at key events, and some conversation, and the way the story is handled definitely feels like it belongs in that brief burst of Episodic games we saw in the mid 2000's:   While a story is wrapped up within Episode 1, it clearly leaves lots of open items for later Episodes (and while Episode 3 isn't a direct continuance due to the change of developer, the events of Episode 1 are clearly directly relevant to the story there, even if not critical knowledge).

Overall, i recommend Episode 1, but with caution that I consider the third game to be superior.   However since this isn't a bad experience (nor particularly long at 6 hours for my run), it's worth playing through to get the complete story experience that the guys at Penny Arcade intended.

This is Hothead games attempt to make an episodic real time rpg where you play yourself in an goofy steampunky world of Penny Arcade's design. Slated as a four episode romp, only two episodes were released/worked on by Hothead. I say "worked on" because the first episode contains a teaser of episode 2 that touches on the high notes where Episode 2 just has a simple animated character as the teaser; heavily suggesting they didn't actually do much work on 3. 

"Episodic" gaming was a trend in the early 2010's attempted by many and never pulled off well. Even Telltale eventually tired out it's audiences by refusing to add new gameplay mechanics to it's series. Essentially they would make a game engine with a story that spanned multiple episodes, where things you did in one episode would be remembered later. The problem is so much time went into creating new levels and tracking down voiceactors that the actual "Game" part of it tended to be extremely simple. 

How this is reflected here is that between Episodes 1 and 2 almost nothing is carried over except specific items. The character abandon all their old weapons at the end of E1 and you start right fresh again for E2. There are no choices to be made, and the secrets that do exist are not all that important. 

How the game works is you have a team of characters with rapidly filling up action buttons you can use to do attacks and special moves. All the special moves make use of QTE minigames and if you ace the minigame you do max damage. There's also a mechanic where if you do full damage with a special attack on an enemy to kill them you get a tiny bit more damage. At first the fights go by quickly, later they take forever.

Episode 1 can be thought of as "The Good One" because it's funny, has amazing enemy designs, and has a good flow to it. You chase a big robot across the city, fight mimes, and eventually kill a god.

An amazing opening adventure that I've replayed 4 times over the years. Great writing and direction mixed with dark humour, sarcasm and idiocy makes this game such a pleasure to play. Highly recommended no matter what kind of games you're into!

This is not normally the kind of game I would play, but since it came bundled with the DeathSpank games, I decided to give it a try.

On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness (Episode One) is a turn-based game (I take exception to people applying the "RPG" label to it - there is practically no character or skill progression, beyond a handful of equipment upgrades), in which your avatar teams up with a band of detectives after some misfortune to take down a god. Throughout your journey, you will fight various enemies on your quest for vengeance. ultimately culminating in a mighty showdown with a god and setting the scene nicely for the following games in the series.

The combat itself is fairly straightforward, but be warned -  you need to become proficient at blocking, if not outright mastering it. There will be many situations where you find yourself totally outnumbered and blocking (or even better, counterattacking) will be your path to victory. Combat itself always begins with an initiative roll, but I am not sure what factors in this game influence it, or how it is decided, but it can also make a big difference if you roll highest and have the opportunity to get the first shot in. It will require good use of combinations, as well as strategic choices of which enemy to focus on, in order to ultimately prevail. The combat does get a little monotonous eventually, but it should still keep you entertained while you beat them into submission for the sake of story.

DISCLAIMER: The humour is an acquired taste - some will like it, some will not. I would suggest a little research first; if this type of humour is annoying for you, steer clear of this game as the entire experience is laden with it.

Recommended for Penny Arcade fans, and for those looking for something a little different.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#228 out of 558)... it's time for On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness: Episode One.

I used to think the Penny Arcade webcomic was hilarious. Then I grew up and realized that I had been mistaken. The tie-in game, however, remains relatively entertaining, as it relies only partially on the often very forced humor of the comic, and is oriented more towards Lovecraftian parody. And when it comes to parody games, I'd say it's one of the better ones out there. The simple 3D art style doesn't look great, but it gets the job done and provides sufficient grounding the the adventure, allowing the characters to feel as though they genuinely belong and the world. More importantly, it allows the characters to convey the appropriate emotions nonverbally--which, sadly, cannot be said for the latter entries in the series.

If you're looking for a compelling story, you won't find it here: you won't even find a completed story. What you will find is a fun, affectionate parody with some silly visuals. If you're fond of the webcomic, you'll very likely enjoy the game; and if you're not so fond of the webcomic, well, there's still a good chance you'll enjoy it.

Note: also played on Sony Playstation 3

Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two, officially titled Penny Arcade Adventures: On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two, continues the episodic RPG-adventure series created by Hothead Games and based on the popular Penny Arcade webcomic. Serving as a direct follow-up to the first episode, the game builds upon its predecessor’s combination of comedic storytelling, adventure-style exploration, and turn-based RPG combat. While it retains the same distinctive tone and characters, Episode Two expands the narrative, introduces new locations and enemies, and refines several gameplay elements, offering a more polished continuation of the bizarre detective story unfolding in the city of New Arcadia.

The story resumes shortly after the events of the first episode, with the player character continuing to work alongside Tycho Brahe and Johnathan Gabriel—better known as Tycho and Gabe—as part of their eccentric detective agency. The trio remains entangled in a strange conspiracy involving mechanical creatures known as the Fruit Fuckers and the mysterious forces behind their creation. What initially appears to be a series of bizarre technological incidents gradually reveals deeper connections to supernatural elements and secret organizations operating throughout the city. As the investigation progresses, the characters encounter cultists, inventors, and other unusual figures who help uncover new layers of the growing mystery. The narrative continues to balance absurd humor with darker undertones involving ancient powers and unsettling forces lurking beneath the city’s surface.

Gameplay once again combines exploration and puzzle-solving with RPG-style combat encounters. As players travel through different areas of New Arcadia, they examine objects, gather items, and interact with characters to move the story forward. Many of these interactions involve light puzzles or item-based tasks that require players to pay attention to environmental details. These segments serve not only to advance the plot but also to deliver some of the game’s funniest moments, as dialogue between the characters often turns simple tasks into elaborate comedic exchanges. The writing plays a major role in keeping exploration engaging, as nearly every interaction offers some form of witty commentary or unexpected humor.

Combat remains turn-based but introduces a few refinements compared to the first episode. During battles, players control the protagonist along with Gabe and Tycho as they face off against a variety of strange enemies ranging from mechanical monstrosities to cultist followers. Each character possesses unique abilities and attacks that can be used strategically depending on the situation. A timing-based mechanic adds a small layer of skill to combat, allowing players to increase damage or mitigate incoming attacks by pressing buttons at the right moment. As the characters gain experience, they unlock new abilities and equipment that improve their effectiveness in battle, giving the RPG progression system a greater sense of development as the story advances.

The visual presentation maintains the stylized aesthetic established in the first episode. Character models retain their exaggerated proportions and cartoon-like expressions, reflecting the artistic style of the original webcomic. The environments of New Arcadia continue to blend elements of 1920s industrial design with strange technological inventions and supernatural imagery. Cutscenes frequently appear in comic panel form, reinforcing the connection to the series’ origins while giving narrative sequences a distinctive visual flair. Although the graphics themselves are relatively simple by modern standards, the consistent art direction helps give the game a unique identity that stands apart from more traditional RPG settings.

One of the strongest aspects of Episode Two is the continued development of the characters and their relationships. The interactions between Gabe and Tycho remain central to the game’s humor, with Tycho’s sarcastic, intellectual demeanor often clashing with Gabe’s impulsive and energetic personality. The player character also becomes more integrated into the group dynamic, contributing to the detective agency’s investigations while reacting to the increasingly absurd situations they encounter. As the story unfolds, certain plot elements hint at deeper personal motivations and hidden histories among the characters, adding a bit more narrative depth to the otherwise comedic adventure.

Despite these improvements, the episodic format still limits the overall scope of the experience. Like the first installment, Episode Two is relatively short and can usually be completed within a few hours. While it advances the overarching story and introduces several memorable moments, it does not fully resolve the central mystery, instead setting the stage for further developments in later episodes. Players hoping for a large-scale RPG adventure may find the limited length somewhat disappointing, though the concise pacing helps keep the narrative focused and entertaining throughout.

Overall, Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two successfully expands on the foundation laid by the first episode, delivering a stronger sense of story progression while refining the combat and exploration mechanics. The game’s greatest strengths lie in its sharp writing, quirky characters, and distinctive setting that blends comedic absurdity with elements of supernatural mystery. Although its short runtime and episodic nature prevent it from feeling like a fully complete RPG experience, it remains an enjoyable and memorable continuation of the series for players who appreciate humorous narrative-driven games.

I love Penny Arcade, or, at least, I love the 2000s era of the webcomic, before they got really big. It was wild, and free and weird, just like the Internet was in those days. The joked about everything and anything, all from a perspective of gamers, and that resonated with me.

These games (I'm going to copy the review, or parts of it, to all four episodes) are not exactly that, but they evoke the same emotions and atmosphere, with a healthy dose of Lovecraftian horror.

Episodes 1 and 2 are very light RPG games, with real time combat and a neat 3D visual style. Episode 3 is a straight up JRPG, while Episode 4 is a JRPG/Pokemon kind of game.

All four games follow the same story, which starts off like a fairly classic Lovecraftian RPG in Episodes 1 and 2, but transforms into something much much weirder in 3, and especially 4. The ending of Episode 4 is completely worth it, and I was very happy after I played through all the games.

The massive change of visual style between the first two and last two episodes can put some people off, but it didn't really bother me.

Ultimately, this whole series is something I would recommend to PA webcomic fans, but also to people who are looking for a fresh dose of weirdness, even if they never heard of the comic. The story, setting and characters are just perfect, whereas the gameplay is a secondary concern.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

[b][u]Runden- KS mit Actioneinlagen[/u][/b]

Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two hat wie der Vorgänger ein semi [b]Runden-KS[/b] mit ATB (active Time Battle)-Leiste, in dem die Helden und Gegner sich gegenseitig dabei abwechseln, der Gegenseite eins auf die Mütze zu geben. Jeder Charakter hat drei [b]ATB-Leisten[/b], die unterschiedlich schnell aufgeladen werden. Eine für Items, eine für normale Angriffe, und eine für [b]Spezialattacken[/b]. Letztere initiieren immer eine QTE(Quick Time Event) Sequenz, bei der es darum geht, bestimmte Tasten zur richtigen Zeit zu drücken. Je besser man abschneidet, desto besser das Endergebnis. Bei einem perfekten Ergebnis erledien Gegner außerdem einen Statuseffekt.Mit einer perfekt aussgeführten Spezialattacke gefällte Wiedersacher geben außerdem einen dauerhaften Bonus auf den verursachten Schaden des betreffenden Charakters. Ähnlich geht es beim Blocken von Gegnerischen Attacken zu. Das richtige Timing verringert den erlittenen Schaden und verhindert ärgerliche Statuseffekte.

[b][u]Schlauchlevel mit wiederauffüllenden Kisten[/u][/b]

Die [b]Schauplätze[/b] von Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two können alle über die Weltkarte erreicht werden. Die Level sind im Grunde ziemlich geradlinig und sowas wie Abzweigungen gibt es nur eher selten mal. Relativ oft kann man am Wegesrand stehende Behälter zertrümmern, und für diesen Akt von Vandalismus einige Gegenstände bekommen, die beim Verlassen der Schauplätze nachgefüllt werden. Gelegentlich stehen mal ein paar Gegner im Weg, die aber anders als Items nicht wieder auftauchen. 

[b][u]Frustfrei ist das Dasein[/u][/b]

Wie im ersten Teil auch gibt es nicht wirklich sowas wie ein Game Over. Wird man von einem Widersacher mal in den Boden gestampft, erwacht man an einem Punkt kurz vor dem letzten Kampf wieder zum leben. Hinzu kommt, dass man nach jedem Kampf komplett geheilt wird. Items liegen quasi auf der Straße und das Level-Cap (30) kann man locker erreichen, auch wenn man nicht jeden Gegner mitnimmt. 

[b][u]Knobeleien für zwischendurch[/u][/b]

Die Minispiele und Rätsel in Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two sind zwar nie bockschwer aber mit unter etwas kniffelig. Ohne hier zu viel zu verraten, sag ich mal, dass man kein Superhirn sein muss und jedes Rätsel gut schaffbar ist.

[b][u]Meckern auf hohem Niveau[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] Ich habe offen gestanden keine Ahnung, wie ich den letzten Boss gefällt habe. Alle paar Kampfrunden heilt der sich komplett und selbst mit Geschwindigkeits-D-Buff habe ich dem nicht mal die hälfte seiner HP runtergekloppt, bevor der sich regeneriert hat, aber irgend wann isser dann einfach kollabiert. 

[*] Gegner werden mit der Zeit irgend wie eher leichter als schwerer, weil ich gerade zu Beginn ein paar Probleme mit dem QTE hatte
[/list]

[h1]Schwierigkeitsgrad[/h1]

Das Spiel ist auf drei Schwierigkeitsgraden spielbar. Leicht, Mittel und Schwer. Wobei die eigentliche Schwierigkeit vom Koordinationsvermögen des Spielers abhängt, da QTEs eine große Rolle in Kämpfen spielen.  

[h1]Soundtrack, Grafik, Steuerung[/h1]

Der Soundtrack ist recht gut gemacht und eigentlich immer passend umgesetzt. 
Die Grafik basiert im Erkundungsmodus und im KS auf Renderoptik, die zwar ihren Zweck erfüllt, aber eben nicht wirklich hochwertig ist. Zwischensequenzen und die meisten Dialoge werden in einem comicartigen Grafikstil dargestellt, welcher sehr gut gemacht ist und den Charakter des Spiels gut wiedergibt. 
Für die Steuerung werden Maus und Tastatur verwendet

Much of my review for the first episode applies to Episode 2 - except with some critical changes, most of which are not to the better.   
Firstly the Quick-Time-Events for the special attacks are a little harder (especially on the top tier attacks), which in itself is fine, but the game does encourage you to use them for kills in order to maximise your damage. 
Secondly, more of the enemies are resistant to either your special attacks, or to specific characters - making much more of combat a tedious waiting game (while in Episode 1 you might want for the devastating final attack, in Episode 2 you wait for an ability to inflict any real damage...).
Thirdly, the nature of the episodic game means that the characters you built development from the first game are lost.  The game is perfectly playable either as a sequel (with imported character) or as a straight new game (without), but in order to ensure that both states are possible, the game replaces all characters weapons and effectively wipes the slate clean in stats.

These changes are a crying shame, as the story from the first episode continues, develops, and I think is told in a slightly tighter way in Episode 2.  Better yet, items you collected in the first game become useful during the course of this one (presumably available irrespective of whether you loaded an Episode 1 save), and the combined games do tell a great tale.

Unfortunately, I'm writing this fresh after finishing the game, and the  final change is a doozy:
The final boss is disappointing to say the least.  Without spoiling it, both games lead you to expect an epic final battle here,  and you start it in a standard epic RPG boss fight style (in much the same way as the first episode's final bossfight).  However, after you deal about 10% damage, the game says 'no that would be boring, here's a simple 3 button puzzle instead'.  It's frustrating because i went out of my way in the last few fights to ensure I had maximum damage on my characters (via collecting the damage boost from finishing enemies with special attacks) and all my weapons were levelled, only to be effectively railroaded into a near-cutscene ending.  What really makes it upsetting is that the intent is good - mixing up the final boss combat is a genuinely good idea, and there's intermediate bosses earlier on for whom this works well, but the resulting fight is frankly boring - it's literally just 'guess the right order for these three buttons' with about 20 attempts (more if you've mastered blocking).

Were this the last game in the series, I'd probably be upset, but (seeing as i played the 3rd game before 1 and 2) I know that the story continues and the gameplay in at least the 3rd game is significantly improved.    Fortunately though, the clear weaknesses of the first 2 games were understood and recognised, and did not translate into the subsequent game (it may have played into the decision to change developers and style of game for the latter two parts, or it might just be coincidence, but either way the result is much improved).

Overall, as with Episode 1, the game is good, and the story it is telling is interesting, witty and enjoyable.   I just wish that these first two episodes were a bit higher paced, and that they could have matched the brilliance of the 3rd episode that followed.
Recommended if you want to follow the saga: while Episode 3 didn't NEED these two episodes to follow, they certainly help.  In isolation though (and absent the wider story arc), this isn't anything too special, and i'm not sure I'd strongly recommend it on its own merits, certainly not ahead of Episode 3, or for context, even Episode 1.

This is Hothead games attempt to make an episodic real time rpg where you play yourself in an goofy steampunky world of Penny Arcade's design. Slated as a four episode romp, only two episodes were released/worked on by Hothead. I say "worked on" because the first episode contains a teaser of episode 2 that touches on the high notes where Episode 2 just has a simple animated character as the teaser; heavily suggesting they didn't actually do much work on 3. 

"Episodic" gaming was a trend in the early 2010's attempted by many and never pulled off well. Even Telltale eventually tired out it's audiences by refusing to add new gameplay mechanics to it's series. Essentially they would make a game engine with a story that spanned multiple episodes, where things you did in one episode would be remembered later. The problem is so much time went into creating new levels and tracking down voiceactors that the actual "Game" part of it tended to be extremely simple. 

How this is reflected here is that between Episodes 1 and 2 almost nothing is carried over except specific items. The character abandon all their old weapons at the end of E1 and you start right fresh again for E2. There are no choices to be made, and the secrets that do exist are not all that important. 

How the game works is you have a team of characters with rapidly filling up action buttons you can use to do attacks and special moves. All the special moves make use of QTE minigames and if you ace the minigame you do max damage. There's also a mechanic where if you do full damage with a special attack on an enemy to kill them you get a tiny bit more damage. At first the fights go by quickly, later they take forever.

Episode 2 is the bad one of the two. Almost nothing you did in episode 1 carries over, everybody uses new weapons, different attacks, and the fruit f**kers are only sort of involved despite this being a wrap up to that storyline. It's more of the same, there are 4-6 mobs of enemies you have to track down and kill over and over and over again until you finally unlock the last area. The big inclusion here though is that some fights have scripted events like enemies fleeing or standing at an INVINCIBLE BACK ROW where they can hit you but nothing can hit them. Enemies in this game are A L W A Y S attacking, to the point where when there is one enemy remaining they seem to never stop moving. 

To top it all off, one of the quests involves giving you a key that will be used in E3 and we will NEVER know what's inside it.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#229 out of 558)... it's time for On The Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness: Episode Two.

I used to think the Penny Arcade webcomic was hilarious. Then I grew up and realized that I had been mistaken. The tie-in game, however, remains relatively entertaining, as it relies only partially on the often very forced humor of the comic, and is oriented more towards Lovecraftian parody. And when it comes to parody games, I'd say it's one of the better ones out there. The simple 3D art style doesn't look great, but it gets the job done and provides sufficient grounding the the adventure, allowing the characters to feel as though they genuinely belong and the world. More importantly, it allows the characters to convey the appropriate emotions nonverbally--which, sadly, cannot be said for the latter entries in the series.

If you're looking for a compelling story, you won't find it here: you won't even find a completed story. Episode Two picks up where the first game left off, and ends on a similarly incomplete note. It's a bit disappointing, but given that the story hardly takes itself very seriously, it's forgivable. If you can overlook that, what you'll find is a fun, affectionate parody with some silly visuals. If you're fond of the webcomic, you'll very likely enjoy the game; and if you're not so fond of the webcomic, well, there's still a good chance you'll enjoy it.

Note: also played on Sony Playstation 3.

The four titles in the Rain-Slick series are distilled gaming joy and are some of my all-time favourite games. They are short and simple and basically perfect, everything about them makes my brain happy. I love RPGs, of any sort, but I especially heart jrpgs and turn-based RPG's. Throw in some additional stuff going on during battles like bonus inputs and I'm over the moon. 

All four Rainslick, despite changing dev house halfway through, manage to carry a flavour of gameplay clear through to the end. They are a special kind of special that the early(-ish) Penny-Arcade writing and artwork just meshed beautifully with the chosen game world weirdness and lovingly designed gameplay to make two titles that are gorgeous cartoon romps through what is possibly my all-time favourite game aesthetic and two titles that sum JRPG and Penny-Arcade more perfectly than any math has ever known. That there will never be any more of them because the artist from Penny-Arcade did not enjoy being involved in the game making process is somewhere between hobo heartbreak and a proper kick to the wombats.

Much like the Kingdom Rush titles I have purchased them in every way on every system for everyone I know because while they are not triple-A event games that took nine figures and years of hundreds of people's lives to craft, they are as close to perfect chunks of gaming as I've ever found. They are not Michelin Star feats of feast and glorious plated palated perfection, they are 50 cent box mac and cheese or three buck street tacos that will win no prizes but are exactly what you want.  Your favourite food doesn't necessarily have to be the best highest quality most beautifully prepared meal you've ever had, it just has to make you happier than the rest of the field.  And nothing makes me a happier gamer than the utter joy I get from some unique JRPG gameplay wrapped up in a weird world of mimes, cosmic horrors, and nieces that are equal parts adorable and Tony Stark. 

Too Long, Didn't Read:  A small perfect chunk of RPG happiness right up there with all the Kingdom Rush games and the original Plants vs Zombies for pure fun times to have had by all.  I've bought and rebought on each platform for every RPG lover in my life, and if I could push a big ol' magic button to get four more Penny-Arcade RPG's at the super low cost of the P-A artist being devoured by pelicans the world would be some sixty hours happier whilst finding itself one party-pooper short.  And the button would keep getting pressed just in case alternate timeline payments are also acceptable.

Greetings Everyone!  It’s time for round 2!  Specifically the game “On a Rain Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two” which is the sequel to well…the first one and you are here to read a review.  So what do we have here?  Eh, the continuation of an RPG that comes straight from Penny Arcade, which should be enough to buy it immediately, but is the game itself good?

Home Wrecker:   The game starts off more or less the same way it begun previously and in most games that might be annoying but I found it humorous at least.  This is much like the rest of the game, more of the same.  If you liked the original you will enjoy this and probably don’t need to read this review to begin with.

Call Me Kratos:  The game seems to have learned a bit from the original, it keeps the graphics and sound effects but the enemies are a bit more dynamic (though the bosses can be a bit easier) and the abilities you unlock are interesting as well.  You ultimately get part two of the first game polished a bit with additional options and some interesting storyline.  You aren’t going to have jaw dropping inspiring events but you may find a perpetual smirk on your face as you are murdering millionaires or baking pies.

Die Robots:  One annoyance of the game is that there seems to be a lot more ‘back in forth’ by that I mean that you are required to go back and forth between zones to accomplish stuff, I do not know if this was to pad game time (doubtful as the game is short unashamedly) or just a design that wasn’t thought through thoroughly.  You also get more of the same as far as targeting issues and I did notice that the game’s enemies seem to heal a lot more, this never caused severe issues but I did find it annoying from time to time.

This isn’t an epic 99 hour RPG but it is an enjoyable tromp down memory lane and an interesting story told from one of my favorite comic strips.  If you don’t already have this game you really should grab it if you are a fan of parody, RPGs or Penny Arcade.  But, while you decide I’m going to start into the third game, enjoy!

I have pretty mixed feelings about this series. On the one hand, I greatly enjoyed Episode One and Two. The comic book style is quite endearing, and plot is pretty interesting. Humor is on point, as can be expected from Penny Arcade as a whole.

However, the fact that the developer and overall style of Episode Three and Four changed makes me want to caution new players from diving into this world. I could not bring myself to finish Three, as the enjoyment died off entirely. The latter half of the series looks like it was made in RPG maker, which by itself isn't a drawback, but is pretty stock combat/features with no flair. The storytelling/humor seems to have left the series entirely but that point.

One and Two are definitely still worth playing, even if you don't plan to play the rest, but it seems pretty hit or miss as to whether people enjoy the latter two. You've been warned.

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
[b]On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two[/b] is not as challenging as the first game, but it continues the narrative and tradition of the first. It boasts solidly designed and enjoyable RPG elements, with a light and hilarious story.  This is a good pick-up for any casual RPG fans out there looking for some lighthearted fun.

Like the first game, technically, this is a parody game— but to be honest it plays better than many modern “real” RPGs that are emerging from the indie realm.  It plays like an old-school, turnbased-combat RPG, complete with leveling-up elements and a mild form of gear upgrading.  The gameplay is definitely fun and the RPG elements will keep you addicted to the progression.  You will find yourself striving to reach that next milestone of development as you play through the hilarious campaign.

[b]On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode Two[/b] is a [i]Penny Arcade[/i] game. The story is fun and funny; it doesn’t take itself too seriously.  It is very lighthearted and the game is packed with hilarious and immature humor.  The characters are likeable, and cartoonish.  The art style is charming and fits the atmosphere of the game perfectly.  It all comes together as a very comic-like production.

This is a good second chapter to the first game.  There is really nothing drastically different in this one compared to the first, but that’s not really a bad thing because the first was pretty good.  As they say: “if it ain’t broke…”

I strongly recommend playing both [i]Episode One[/i] and [i]Episode Two[/i] in order and together, as they are more two parts to a whole than they are two separate games.

When I was a child, my father played this game near release, and the faint glimpses of what I'd seen on the Xbox 360 enamored me for years upon years until I finally found it on Steam. As I concluded my search, I encountered some truly distinctive art direction, such as a rolling world camera I've only experienced with this game, as well as a cartoonish open world reminiscent of Diablo, and tongue-in-cheek humor that hit 85% of the time. The environment of this game was equally as impressive, with detailed terrain, creatures, and flora thoughtfully placed throughout. The one problem I had with this game, though, was that the bosses were far less fleshed out, with many of them able to be killed easily unlike the areas they were placed in.

100%ing this game was relatively easy and enjoyable, but the achievement where you had to get to level 20 was aggravating to grind when I had already completed every objective besides the final boss.

Проходил DeathSpank несколько раз ещё в детстве со старых дисков, и вот наконец-то добрался до неё в Steam, закрыв на все 100% достижений. Несмотря на то, что игра вышла ещё в октябре 2010 года от студии Hothead Games (при участии легендарного Рона Гилберта) и издательства Electronic Arts, сегодня она играется всё так же бодро и дарит массу удовольствия.

О чём игра?

Мы играем за гротескного героя по имени Смертошлёп (DeathSpank) - самопровозглашённого «Вершителя Правосудия, Победителя Зла и Героя Угнетённых». Его главная цель - найти загадочный «Артефакт», попутно сокрушая орды монстров, спасая сирот и выполняя десятки совершенно безумных поручений.   

Плюсы, за которые игру стоит взять:

Гениальная пародия на жанр: Формально перед нами классический изометрический слэшер и экшен-RPG с тоннами разноцветного лута. Но по факту - это едкая и очень смешная сатира, высмеивающая все штампы фэнтези и ролевых игр: от пафосных диалогов до абсурдных квестов.   

Смесь диаблоида и классического квеста: Здесь не нужно бездумно гриндить. Между боями мы общаемся с яркими NPC и решаем забавные головоломки с комбинированием предметов из инвентаря в духе старых point-and-click адвенчур.

Необычный визуальный стиль: Мир игры крутится под ногами героя словно цилиндр, а все декорации (леса, замки, подземелья) сделаны в виде плоских картонных фигурок из книжки-раскладушки. Смотрится самобытно даже спустя годы.

Короткая и не душная: Огромная редкость для жанра - игра не растянута на сотню часов унылого фарма. Она компактная, проходится на одном дыхании, а все ачивки выбиваются легко и с удовольствием.Итог:Если вы устали от гигантских мрачных RPG и хотите весёлого, динамичного приключения на пару вечеров с отличным юмором - смело берите, классика проверку временем прошла!

Recommended. A relentlessly funny action-RPG where a dim-witted hero chases an Artifact and rescues orphans from a singing tyrant, and nearly every quest, item name and conversation exists to land a joke.

The quest slate exceeds a hundred (the giving tree's retail requests, stone soup, a wizard's chimaera recipes), the Justice meter rewards weapon chaining, out-houses double as fast travel and checkpoints, and the prong-anator 3000 forging cutscene alone justifies the run. Roughly eight and a half hours to 100%.

Late-game damage spikes swing wildly and unlearnably, the final boss's three-second stun and full health-regen punish forgetting his weakness, the tin can recycling quest grinds randomised drops for trivial reward, and enemies occasionally freeze or refuse damage. A standard skeleton elevated purely by committing to the comedy.

[h1][i]“Never pay more than 20 bucks for a computer game.”[/i]
~Guybrush Threepwood[/h1]

Even though I was in my 20s already, I still managed to make one heck of a lot of good memories in the 2000s. Of that specific kind you may call nostalgic. I mean, come on. Internet just stopped being all about those ugly “home pages” (remember those?) full of unholy [b]GIF[/b] images and exploded with things like [b]Flash[/b]-powered cartoons and webcomics. Online entertainment is taken for granted nowadays, but back in the day it was something fresh, something new. The fact that we were able to get indie content online for free? It was mind-blowing. Also, yes. [b]Xbox 360[/b] just came out. Watching [b]Happy Tree Friends[/b], reading [b]Penny Arcade[/b] and playing [b]Gears of War[/b], that's what it was all about. Like I said, lots and lots of great memories. In order to fully understand [b]DeathSpank[/b], though, it's important for us to travel much further back in time. To the times when I was just a little kid.

[b]Maniac Mansion[/b]. Released in 1987, it was a quirky horror-comedy adventure that quickly became one of the most beloved games in the genre. Who made it? [b]Ron Gilbert[/b]. It was he who wrote it, it was he who directed it and yes, he coded it too ([b]Maniac Mansion[/b] was [i]the[/i] game that gave us [b]SCUMM[/b]). Soon after, [b]Ron[/b] made [b]Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade[/b] and after that... Yeah. [b]Monkey Island[/b]. And again, he acted as both writer and director. Now, if you ever played at least one of those games, you know that [b]Ron[/b] has a very specific kind of humor. Almost one of a kind. And since his [b]LucasArts[/b] times were long over (and so were his times in [b]Humongous[/b] and [b]Cavedog[/b]), he just fooled around, making things online. One of which was that [b]Flash[/b] cartoon that had a character called [b]DeathSpank[/b].

The idea was to create an over-the-top character who was absolutely, completely absurd. In order to fight stereotype, of course. And the result... was so strangely charming that [b]Ron[/b], his friend [b]Clayton Kauzlaric[/b] (who worked with him at the time) and everybody around them instantly fell in love with it. One thing led to another, but since [b]Penny Arcade Adventures: On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness[/b] already proved that web content can be turned into a video game ([b]Ron[/b] actually helped to make that game as a consultant) and be successful, well, here we are. [b]DeathSpank: The Video Game[/b].

What exactly did we get? Well, [b]Ron[/b] described his project as “[b]Monkey Island[/b] meets [b]Diablo[/b]”. Because that's... essentially what it was. Naturally, one should not expect anything complicated here. Pretty much everything in this game is simplified on purpose. The whole idea was not just to make a funny [b]Diablo[/b] clone, but to make it dumb. You hit things and they die. No classes to choose from, no points to spend (stats go up automatically on level up), no builds to worry about... It's a parody, remember? Doesn't sound like a lot fun, though. That's probably why publishers weren't that excited and [b]Ron[/b] had some pretty hard time convincing them (his time with [b]Penny Arcade[/b] helped again here). I mean, parodies can be fun in things like cartoons and comics, but in video games? Like I said, it didn't sound like a purposely dumbed-down game is a good idea.

Worry not, though. [b]DeathSpank[/b] did have an ace up his sleeve. The thing is – what we have here is one of those juicy little [b]Xbox LIVE[/b] co-op games. Just press the button on the second controller and here we are – [b]DeathSpank[/b] is joined by his trusty companion [b]Sparkles the Wizard[/b]. Yes, [b]Sparkles[/b]. [b]The Wizard[/b]. Because... [i]justice[/i]. And also bacon. [i]Anyway[/i], [b]DeathSpank[/b] is one of them co-op oriented games. And while fully playable in single-player, it's in co-op where it really shines. Just because what looks like a tiny little world map and a very lacking length (you can easily finish the whole game in one sitting), in co-op becomes “just the right size”.

What's even better is that [b]DeathSpank[/b] is not just about [b]Diablo[/b]. It's also about [b]Monkey Island[/b], remember? They did try to make quests here a bit more tricky than usual and while there was a risk in that (overly complicated quests can ruin all the fun, especially in co-op), they almost succeeded. “Almost” because there [i]are[/i] some quests that need slightly more polish, but thanks to the fortune cookies mechanics, which was designed to give you hints up to the “no, seriously, dude, go there and do that, it's that simple!” point, it actually worked. In other words, it's no [b]Uru[/b] here (remember that “puzzle” in [b]Uru[/b] that wanted us to stand still and do nothing for ten bloody minutes?). So yeah, it's... Quite a thing, really.

Looks charming too. I mean, sure, those [b]Flash[/b]-like cutscenes are only [b]720p[/b], while the graphics itself are anything but high end (again, it was an [b]Xbox LIVE[/b] game, designed for limited download speed at the time), but it came with its own signature style, which, years later was imitated in popular games like [b]Don't Starve[/b]. So... is [b]DeathSpank[/b] one of them forgotten gems? Kinda, yeah. But not without “buts”.

The problem with [b]DeathSpank[/b] is that pretty much everything here is kinda... flat. Nothing it does, it does with a bang. Jokes, for example, are fun, but not hysterical. They'll make you smile for sure (especially if you enjoyed [b]Ron Gilbert[/b]'s previous works), but they'll rarely (if at all) make you [i]laugh[/i] (as long as we're not talking about [b]Michael Dobson[/b], who voiced the lead character — [b]Michael[/b] is downright hilarious and his voice will stay with you long after you'll uninstall the game). Gameplay? It sure works. The game is fun to play, but you'll also feel like you'll be fine without it. Like, there's no “five more minutes!” element here. And when you're done (another bad thing about [b]DeathSpank[/b] is that it ends with a cliffhanger and no, it's not an element of a parody, they just didn't have enough time to finish everything they'd planned and therefore decided to split the game in two)? You won't feel like you need more.

Still, [b]DeathSpank[/b] is totally worth catching up with if you've somehow missed it back in the day. Not only is it one of those games that captured the mood of the time (make sure to listen to [b]Crazy Frog[/b] songs in the background for the full effect), it also aged surprisingly well. Sure, sure, [b]720p[/b] cutscenes and UI won't look good, controls won't be as smooth as in modern alternatives, while there are some rough edges related to the PC version specifically (in order to play alone with the gamepad, for example, you'll need to change settings accordingly, otherwise you'll end up starting a co-op game instead since the gamepad is tied to the second player by default), but the thing is – [b]DeathSpank[/b] is a very... relaxing experience.

That's its strongest point. It doesn't ask anything from you. It allows you to just sit back and have simple fun. The game just doesn't take itself too seriously. Heck, even the in-built leaderboards are not about how good you are, they're about things like how many chickens you've killed. Yes, [i]chickens[/i]. Because why the heck not, right? So yeah, if we'll judge [b]DeathSpank[/b] by our usual standards and start asking it to do certain things? It's obviously lacking. In pretty much everything. It's not one of those games you buy for $999.999. Flat soda, remember? You don't buy it for the price of the real deal. But just for fun? It's totally a thing. Flat soda is still sweet and let's be honest, we all need some sweets now and then. That's just this game's philosophy. Not to try too hard and be funny. Exactly why it never became obsolete. And the best of all? It's below 20 bucks.

Как написал один человек в обсуждениях, «играл в DeathSpank 3 часа в детстве и до сих пор не могу забыть. Это всё, что вам нужно знать об игре». И это правда.

DeathSpank — простенький линейный хак-энд-слэш без особых претензий. Бегаешь, кликаешь врагов, ставишь галочку «Автоматически надевать лучшую броню» и ни о чём не думаешь. Управление сделано довольно приятно, учитывая, что это порт: удобно переключаться между наборами оружия, можно как бегать на WASD, так и просто щёлкать мышкой, всё довольно отзывчиво и бодро работает. Игра сама по себе не сложная (на нормале, по крайней мере), а если где-то и сталкиваешься со слишком сильным монстром, то, скорее всего, игра и не предполагает, что ты должен победить его прямо сейчас. 
Однако то, за что чаще всего запоминают DeathSpank в плане геймлпея — это загадки. DS часто называют смесью Дьябло и Monkey Island — и это правда. Тут довольно много взаимодействия с инвентарём, текстовых квестов в диалоге и прочих нажиманий рубильников. Сложность, правда, идёт, в основном, не из самих загадок, а от того, что игра не очень хорошо учит в себя играть: так никто не пояснит, что правый клик на объект позволяет применить к нему что-то из инвентаря, а правый клик на предмет уже в инвентаре его выкинет (что полезно в довольно известном затыке с колесом и термитами). Да, до этого быстро доходишь методом тыка, но, каюсь, что сейчас, что на выходе игры лазил в интернет искать, как в одном из первых квестов кинуть наковальню в колодец. Система печенек с предсказаниями, буквально объясняющая решение квеста вплоть до географического положения нужных элементов, тут, увы не помогает.

Ну а второе, за что игру помнят до сих пор — это юмор. DeathSpank — клишированная героическая история, поданная с шутками а-ля Монти Пайтон или Т. Пратчетт. Особенно тут выделяются диалоги: они прекрасно озвучены — особенно главный герой — и строятся по принципу импровизации, где каждая последующая реплика развивает предыдущую, а не пытается её оспорить. И весь этот абсурд с лепреконами-мафиози и королевским курьером которому в работе нравится всё, кроме, собственно, доставки посылок, представлен игроку с максимально серьёзным лицом. Например, сам главный герой — хаотично добрый рыцарь без страха и упрёка (с парой странных хобби, но это опустим) в фиолетовых Плавках Добродетели, путешествующий по миру через систему сельских туалетов (подробности перемещения сам Дэтспанк предпочитает не уточнять) и исполняющий любые просьбы страждущих, даже если это суп из камней с куриными лапками. Ну а концовка, плавно подводящая к сеттингу и событиям продолжения, мне запомнилась ещё с первого прохождения, вместе с парой особо заковыристых (плохо объяснённых, ага) квестов. 
Где-то тут ещё можно похвалить прекрасную рисованную графику в стиле диорамы и западающую в память музыку и звуковые эффекты (перестук при открытии нового туалета, скажем), но вы и сами всё видите.

Конечно, есть и минусы. Даже для 9 часов с небольшим для 100% прохождения со всеми ачивками игра всё же ощущается ну вот немножко затянутой. Не в последнюю очередь в этом виновен набор лута: да, броников и оружия в игре много, но-о-о-о лучшие из них ты получаешь уже к середине игры, и всё разнообразие на этом моменте заканчивается, хотя игра и продолжает тебя одаривать новыми сетами одёжки — они просто хуже того, что ты уже купил. Местный ааналог ульты, когда ты можешь объединить два оружия для получения какого-то особого эффекта, здесь, скорее, поиграться, чем реально помогает где-то — ты либо сильнее врагов всю игру, либо должен пробежать мимо особо сильных и вернуться потом. Да и в конце начинается совсем уж лишний бэктрекинг и knowledge check «А помнишь, где ты видел персонажа А и объект В 4 часа назад?», без которого бы, да, игра была короче, но и не наскучивала бы под конец.

Однако даже при всём этом DeathSpank очень затягивает, проходится за два вечера в режиме «ладно, ещё одну локацию зачищу и хватит», и не особо утомляет. Прекрасный артефакт из прошлого, которому стоит уделить внимание и из-за ненапряжного геймплея, и из-за хорошей презентации.
P. S. На Win11 работает без нареканий и поддерживает 16:9 без каких-либо танцев с бубном.

[h3] “Greetings, DeathSpank!” [/h3]
Replaying it this time, I finally realized what I truly love about [i] DeathSpank [/i]. It’s not just the surface-level dark humor, but its way of expression—one where deconstruction comes before content. It uses a straight-faced heroic narrative to carry utterly absurd, everyday nonsense, turning meaning itself into the punchline.

In this game, quests can be ridiculous, the hero can be foolish, and morality can feel arbitrary. Imagine mixing grand, epic hero dialogue with mundane, idiotic chatter—[i] DeathSpank [/i] pulls this off brilliantly. It’s like a solemn knight from a classic chivalric tale suddenly starts spouting trash talk, or delivers something incredibly stupid with ceremonial gravitas. That contrast isn’t just black humor—it rises to a kind of “formalistic humor,” where the structure itself becomes the joke.

That said, from a gameplay perspective, it’s relatively thin. At its core, it plays like an old-school ARPG in the vein of [i] Diablo [/i], but without much system depth. By the mid-to-late game, repetition sets in, and it’s easy to feel fatigued or bored. There’s also a slight sense that it starts strong but doesn’t quite stick the landing. These shortcomings are worth pointing out.

Even so, its strengths far outweigh its flaws. What makes [i] DeathSpank [/i] special is how it constantly deconstructs things that are usually treated with gravity—“quests,” “heroism,” “morality”—without hollowing out the experience itself. You’re still progressing, still making choices, still invested; you just gradually realize that none of it needs to be taken all that seriously.

In a way, it’s not really telling a story about an absurd world—it’s gently reminding us that meaning might be constructed, even illusory, but the experience is real. There’s a touch of mild existentialism in that idea, and I find it genuinely appealing.

Imagine Monkey Island as an action RPG rather than a point-and-click game, but also a bit worse. I feel mixed about this, given I'm replaying it after playing it back in 2011 or so. It plays fine on a modern PC, and I haven't had any problems with controls or crashing. I think a lot of issues are more quality of life problems and comparing this to later games, which I seem to recall did a better job of skill management. The story is also funny at times and a great demonstration of voice actor ability, but it becomes grating and a lot of the humor doesn't really work. You can only listen to Deathspank be an obnoxious asshole about women so much, or at least see it as a dialogue option, understand he's meant to be an obnoxious pastiche of a generic white male fantasy hero, plus a ton of dick and masturbation jokes (and maybe one anti-union joke, which, huh?), so many times before it becomes droll. The actors do a phenomenal job, and there are many quite elaborate and silly moments in this. I just started skipping through dialogue after a while because of how frustrating running back and forth trying to figure out where I was going was.

It's extremely hard to figure out where quests are located, and you get a very limited number of fortune cookies for largely useless hints, some of which include things like, "The item is in front of [building you don't know the location of]", involving either meticulously combing through the entire map or just googling a guide. A related issue is that the map is often quite useless, as you can only see an overview of sections of it you're not in, rather than zoom in and out as you please, and when you're looking at the Outhouse map, you can't see where, say, quest markers are, so you have to arbitrarily click and hope you remember where the largely unremarkable map locations are. The only notable locations are Pluckmuckle, Von Prong's castle, and the Enchanted Forest, which cover only a small portion of the map, and are difficult in themselves to navigate.

The one gameplay issue I had was using items in your inventory (e.g., the whistles). They required a lot of clicking to get Deathspank to register them. The other one is the limited inventory and inventory management problem. You get so much stuff, it's annoying to have to decide what to leave behind or just sell. Buying anything other than quest items and maybe potions is largely pointless, so it's not that big a deal, but you have a lot of stuff and some things, like nature weapons, are necessary for hurting certain enemies, so you don't want to trash anything but your highest level gear. It took me ages to find a crossbow with actually decent damage, so if I'd trashed the one I had, I'd have been out of luck for most of the game when dealing with ranged enemies. Another problem is that initially, and from what I remember playing this the first time, low level enemies would stop bothering you once you got high enough of a level. This worked for a time, but after like my third play session, vanished entirely. Even gray enemies would go after me if I wandered too close to them.

It's a relatively easy RPG for folks who want that sort of thing, with an art style that hasn't aged but won't be everyone's cup of tea. I still love the spinning sword and wished there was a higher level one than the 800 damage one. It's the best weapon in the game, after the really nice crossbow. If you want to play more of this, all three of these games are on Steam, the third just isn't called "Deathspank": look for "The Baconing". I can't say I recommend that, given I remember it being the worst of the three, but they're all here if you want to play them.

DeathSpank thrives on an exuberant mix of irreverent humor, comic-book style presentation, and hack-and-slash action, forming a quirky adventure that feels as much like a cartoon romp as it does an action RPG. At the center of it all is the self-important, loudmouthed, justice-obsessed hero DeathSpank, a character whose exaggerated bravado is matched only by the absurdity of the world around him. The game wastes no time establishing a tone that blends fantasy parody with comedic self-awareness, inviting players into a realm where every quest, character, and encounter leans boldly into silliness. From the outset, it becomes clear that the narrative is less about epic stakes and more about enjoying the ride — and it’s this playful philosophy that powers much of the game’s appeal.

In terms of gameplay, DeathSpank draws heavily from action-RPG traditions, offering fast-paced combat built around swinging weapons, unleashing special attacks, swapping gear, and slashing through hordes of bizarre creatures wandering the countryside. The mechanics are deliberately straightforward: each weapon type offers slight variations, enemies scale in predictable ways, and exploration revolves around discovering loot, killing monsters, and completing a steady stream of quests. Rather than trying to reinvent or deeply complicate the genre, the game aims for accessibility and rhythm — the pleasure comes from mowing through enemies, chaining attacks, filling the Justice Meter to unleash powerful moves, and gathering heaps of increasingly silly loot that keeps the momentum going. This simplicity makes the game easy to slip into, especially for those who enjoy a light, arcade-like loop.

Quests play a major part in shaping the game’s personality. Though many follow familiar structures — retrieving items, slaying certain enemies, escorting characters, or solving small puzzles — they are consistently infused with humor. NPCs deliver lines with a wink, objectives often take unexpected comedic turns, and even mundane tasks are framed in exaggerated, theatrical fashion. This levity helps soften the repetitiveness that inherently comes with completing dozens of small tasks. In many ways, the quests exist less as tests of strategic thinking and more as vehicles for comedy, encouraging players to enjoy the absurd vignettes scattered across the landscape. The tone is whimsical without losing coherence, and the writing maintains a steady stream of charm throughout the campaign.

The world, though not sprawling by modern RPG standards, is crafted with visual flair. The crisp, stylized art direction blends hand-drawn elements with bold color palettes, giving each region a storybook sensibility. This aesthetic suits the game’s comedic approach, helping environments feel lively and expressive even when their gameplay roles are simple. Whether wandering through whimsical forests, eerie graveyards, or eccentric villages, players are greeted with a playful sense of personality that ties the world together. Coupled with fitting sound design and character animations that accentuate movement and humor, the overall presentation remains one of the title’s strongest attributes.

However, the simplicity that helps DeathSpank remain approachable also introduces its biggest limitations. Combat, for instance, while fun in short bursts, lacks depth and variety. The loop rarely evolves in surprising ways: after the first few hours, players will have seen most of its tricks. Enemies, though amusing in concept, often require similar strategies, and weapon upgrades rarely change the underlying flow of battle. The game’s structure — filled with fetch quests, routine mobs, and familiar loops — can eventually feel repetitive for players seeking richer systems, strategic complexity, or deeper progression. What you see early on is largely what you get until the end.

Despite those weaknesses, DeathSpank remains an enjoyable experience for the audience it targets. It isn’t trying to be a sprawling RPG epic or a mechanically intricate action game. Instead, it delivers a humorous, fast-paced journey filled with eccentric characters, silly quests, and lighthearted combat that prioritizes fun over depth. Its charm lies in its willingness to commit fully to its comedic tone, embracing parody and absurdity without hesitation. For players wanting a brief, amusing escape — something colorful, energetic, and uncomplicated — DeathSpank provides a satisfying and memorable adventure. It may not offer longevity or deep systems, but as a vibrant and humorous hack-and-slash romp, it more than fulfills its mission.

Deathspank overall is a very fun hack and slash RPG in the vein of Torchlight or Diablo, but with a parodic and tongue-in-cheek tone. This is one of those games that seems to partially hang its hat on its humor and is one of those rare cases that actually gets a lot more hits than misses, I many times found myself laughing out loud at some of the references or funny puns during the dialogue. You'll meet many colorful characters along the way, on Deathspanks quest to recover The Artifact. The game features loads of sidequests and a fun combat system that will require blocking, timing and reflexes to succeed. The game can be pretty challenging and isn't one where you can turn off your brain and succeed (at least on normal difficulty). The art style and sound design are also very stylized, it almost felt like a Maxwell Atoms Billy and Mandy alternate universe to me, in the very best sense of the comparison.

I do have a few gripes about the game, it seems that at some points there are difficulty spikes that seem unfair, or occasionally getting hit by a swarm of enemies you're not familiar with only to be exploded in one hit, I think there would have been a slightly better way to streamline the mobs to gradually work the player up. However, this can be mitigated by doing a slight amount of grinding and upgrading your armor and weapons with better stuff. I also found some of the quests and goals to be cryptic to find and had to look up solutions, even when using the fortune cookie hint system which is helpful. The game in my opinion would have done well implementing a waypoint system, as so many times quests will involve visiting many different locations and the twisting paths of the map can quickly become mazelike and you'll spend too much time wandering figuring out how to get back to where you needed to be, a simple waypoint system would have mitigated any and all of that frustration and wasted backtracking.

Overall despite being a bit rough in some areas the game is a very satisfying hack and slash game with some modest customization elements and a lot of fun and laughs to be had. It's a shortish experience, I got about 100% completion in slightly over 10 hours, not the longest game but definitely good bang for your buck. On sale for $3 it's a total steal but even $15 is a pretty reasonable price for the amount of fun I had. Check this out if you want an  RPG thats a bit different and dark or if you love the moreish gameplay loop of games like Torchlight or even Champions of Norrath, you should have a blast!

Deathspank – игра, которая высмеивает жанр ролевых игр, культуру американского общества, и берёт самое лучшее из игр серии Diablo. За те 10 часов, которые уйдут у игрока на полное прохождение, игра не успевает надоесть, оставляя после себя приятное послевкусие и неожиданный финал, который полностью ломает представление о мире игры.
Звуки электронной гитары будут сопровождать игрока по картонному, вымышленному и карикатурному миру средневековья, от одного чудаковато-то задания к другому. Чего только стоит задание с нахождением пропавших сирот и помещением их в мешок, или помощи местному Индиане Джоунсу с зачисткой пещер, в которые он сам не может пойти из-за боязни узких пространств, темноты и пауков.
Снаряжение, что герой будет находить на протяжении всей игры выглядит красиво и эстетично, как если бы его комплекты продавались отдельно в виде дополнений, в лучших традициях тех же Electronic Arts. В мире также полно оружия с разными характеристиками, начиная с мечей, жезлов, арбалетов и заканчивая каким-нибудь молотом, который не наносит урон демонам, но, в буквальном смысле, выбивает из них дерьмо.
“Мультяшность” мира DeathSpank позволила ему хорошо сохраниться в наше время. Каждая локация имеет свой тон повествования. Перемещение между которыми происходит через деревенские сортиры.
Настоятельно рекомендую проходить игру на английском языке, не используя кривой русификатор от команды ZoG Forum Team, из-за которого теряется львиная доля юмора, что есть в диалогах, и использовать контроллер для более комфортного прохождения.

It's a pretty simple game: you go around and slash and hack everything on your way, sometimes stopping to talk with random people, cause they may have a quest for you. Nothing fancy, just the basics of any game that's ever existed. The world isn't very fancy as well: it's a nice mix of generic landscapes with some bizarre additions here and there, to spice the things up.

What does stand out are the dialogues. They are full of light-hearted humor and random references told by weird characters with weird views and requests. If you have read Terry Pratchett - you will find DeathSpank's world somewhat similar to the Discworld in terms of how likewise the folk of those worlds is in their absurdity. It's a funny mix of ill logic with fairly reasonable statements, although unexpected, somehow being perceived as a norm. Moreover, the names, descriptions and even signs receive the same bizarre treatment. And of course, just as every good joke, they have some connections to the everyday real world occasions.

The only questionable part of the game is combat: even though it's very simple, it's also weirdly balanced. In the beginning you crush everything, then, for a short amount of time, everything crushes you, and then you again come on top, destroying every poor creature that dares to stand on your way. The blocking system greately contributes to that: it allows to block all damage for short amount of time, but there is no real way to fight back unharmed if you are surrounded, because multiple enemies together attack faster than character can swing his weapon and hide behind the shield again. And there will be lots of multiple enemies hitting you at the same time. Thankfully, soon enough nothing will really bother you due to how fast leveling goes.

Overall, DeathSpank is a very chill game. Its simplicity allows for the relaxed playthrough when you just want to calmly spend your time, and the omnipresent humor let's you truly enjoy such experience, captivating and stimulating to continue playing. It's a game that just wants to be a game, not a great all-consuming experience that desires to take away all your time and energy, or to encourage you to contemplate about deep and difficult topics.

Recommended. A joke-dense action-RPG sequel that swaps fantasy for a wartime comedy lens (Nazi-era orcs, undead potatoes, POW escapes) and layers guns onto the hack-and-slash loop, keeping the formula fresh.

Pistols, bazookas, flamethrowers and a laser gun give fights a spatial dimension the melee original lacked, dozens of multi-stage quests (cannons, mating glands, mailbags, bacon rocks) sustain the absurdity, and named gear sets (Spartan, Greatest Generation, Terrible Lizard) churn the upgrades.

Fast travel arrives too late, so the first half is backtracking across large maps, gun-wielding enemies hit far harder and more accurately than the melee mobs, fortune-cookie hints mislead as often as they guide, and the X Island treasure hunt pays out sixteen dollars. The comedy never sags, and the wartime twist makes it the series entry that stands apart.
