It's been a while since I last played a DeathSpank game, and even still I hadn't forgotten it. The irreverent, often nonsensical and somewhat meta humour and interesting art style leave a lasting impression, at least on me, and going back into DeathSpank was a touch nostalgic, as well as interesting.

That said, I may have good memories, but there are a few things that concern me about this title. The difficulty is all over the place - in the beginning, enemies are regually higher levels than you are and sport some very frustrating kits (flamethrower troops, exploding robots, ect.) which makes getting going a little on the rough side, and will likely cost you a few deaths. After that, the difficulty evens out a touch apart from noticeable spikes (the invincible Undead Commanders and skirting around the giant electric tower) until you reach the desert town, whereupon I started to get significantly overlevelled - to the point where mobs started to become green and grey instead of orange and red levels, and aside from choosing to tackle the frost DLC at it's level, I didn't experience any real difficulty once I reached that point, which leaves the pinnacle of difficulty being reached at about 25% of the way through the game. Armour is largely just a health booster, other equipment barring weapons is also just basic stat boosting, and levelling rewards are still mediocre as they were before. I also feel the combat is a little... wonky, due to how tricky it can be to melee some enemies due to odd hitboxes, or how dangerous enemies can just be spawned in to annihilate you if you pick the wrong quest or wander into the wrong cave. 

That aside, though, there's plenty to like. DeathSpank's sense of humour and meta awareness proved to be a fun distraction, and DeathSpank (the protagonist) has a wonderfully stupid personality, which leads to a lot of amusing moments - the bumbling idiot hero cliche isn't used much, and that's a shame because it lends itself well to a lot of fun dialogue. The actual plot is a little dry, and doesn't contain a lot of *particually* interesting moments, but that might be the story beats not landing for me, since the encounters with bosses and NPC dialogue tend to be at least a little amusing. I'm also very fond of the artstyle and the visual presentation of the world and gear you acquire - DeathSpank's artstyle has let the game age much better than a lot of similar games from it's time period, and I think that'll continue to occur as time goes by.

There aren't a lot of games out there that remind me of DeathSpank, and I've played quite a few titles in my time, which speaks to the game's somewhat unique presentation and styling. While I think too many games like it would diminish all of them, I have to say, I'm glad some do exist. For every serious, intense and meaningful game with important characters and complex world building, it's good to have a few irreverent, lighthearted titles that put on a good show. DeathSpank is one such title - and I'd say that it's worth the money and the time, though I would recommend playing the first one first as some of the story beats might not land as well if it isn't fresh in your mind.

Прямое продолжение первой части (буквально: изначально DeathSpank и Thongs of Virtue были одной игрой, но из-за каких-то ограничений цифровых магазинов тех лет её пришлось поделить надвое), так что играть рекомендуется сразу же после неё.

Игра начинается прямо с концовки оригинала: ДэзСпанк из клишированного фентези-сеттинга внезапно попадет на столь же клишированные поля Второй Мировой — и в плен, сбегает оттуда благодаря искусству боя на картофелечистках и вместе с рыжей рыцаршей Сэнди и бесстрашным (и тоже клишированным) генералом подготавливает атаку на Северный Полюс, где обосновался скоррапченный Плавками Благодетели Санта Клаус. Попутно герой без страха и упрёка пройдётся ещё по паре неожиданных сеттингов, которые я, впрочем, спойлерить не буду. 
Собственно, из-за смены обстановки появляется первое отличие от оригинала (которых тут не очень много, справедливости ради) — сильный упор на огнестрел. Если в первой части арбалеты были очень ситуативные и больше подходили для раскидывания шушеры на 10 уровней ниже героя при посещении уже изученных локаций, то тут всякие пистолеты и пулемёты могут порой быть гораздо более выгодным решением, чем меч. Усилилось и влияние стихийных бонусов и уязвимостей: в первой части я вообще не обращал внимания на все эти цветные пометочки, тут же местами без изучения слабостей врага будет туго.
В целом, ToV ощутимо сложнее, чем оригинал. Аптечки будут улетать быстро, еду реально появился смысл покупать, чтобы экономить зелья лечения, а местами враги даже чуть ниже по уровню, чем ДэзСпанк, могут очень сильно потрепать. Стало больше противников на 5-10 уровней выше в несюжетных ситуациях, рассчитанных на то, что ты к ним вернёшься позже (чаще всего это либо квестовые негодяи, либо охранники каких-то сокровищ) — ну либо будешь бегать вокруг и тыкать стихийным оружием, к которому враг уязвим. Умирать приходилось сильно чаще, чем в первой части. Впрочем, благодаря DLC с бонусным лутом и новыми наборами брони, уже где-то с 17-18 уровня можно бодро скакнуть до 21-го и обзавестись объективно лучшим сетом брони и оружием в игре, после чего герою никто уже ничего не сможет противопоставить. К счастью, в отличие от DeathSpank, произойдёт это к концу прохождения, а не в середине. 
Немного изменился подход к квестам: появилась небольшая вариативность в некоторых из них, а внимательный игрок, который не ленится поговорить со всеми и обо всём, сможет ослабить сюжетных боссов, отобрав у них пару атак или натравив их же подручных. Квесты в целом стали чуть ближе к квестам как жанру по своей презентации и подходу, так что местами придётся мозгами пошевелить (либо пофармить печеньки с предсказаниями, дающие подсказки). Есть и пара паззлов, но особо о них сказать нечего. 
ОСТ и графика не изменились с первой части, всё ещё бодренько, есть такой Неверхудовский вайб в саундтреке, а стиль диорамы метко используется для презентации новых локаций. А, ну и морская тема очень понравилась, бодренько так звучит!

И, казалось бы, стало просто лучше, но-о-о-о... Во-первых, ToS дико багованный, тогда как оригинал работал без нареканий. NPC спавнятся друг в друге; музыка иногда путается, играть боевую тему или мирную; появились вылеты ([spoiler]бластер пришельцев[/spoiler] — это вообще лотерея: любой выстрел может привести к зависанию и вылету); один раз даже словил странный баг с зависанием сохранения игры, который не только намертво повесил компьютер до хард ребута, но и каким-то образом сломал сюжетную (!) непропускаемую (!!) ачивку, которую пришлось открывать сторонними средствами (ну, вы понимаете), поскольку сейв таки сработал — но уже после момента, где ачивку дают. Так что если у вас зависла надпись Saving — постарайтесь тут же через диспетчер задач закрыть игру, пока не зависло вообще всё.
Во-вторых, квесты хоть частично и стали интереснее, но большинство сайд-квестов — абсолютно унылый бэктрекинг, даже хуже первой части. Причём местами это даже не подаётся как шутка над устоями жанра: тебя могут просто трижды послать в одно и то же место, но с разными целями (хотя решением всегда будет просто всех убить). Из-за этого середины игры сильно провисает по динамике, запирая игрока в паре небольших локаций (не напрямую, но без их прохождения сюжет и часть сайдов дальше не продвинешь). 
Ну и в-третьих, юмора стало как будто меньше, а на одной deadpan-подаче диалогов 20 часов первой и второй части не вывезешь. Всё ещё есть искренне смешные моменты и забавные визуальные решения, но раскиданы они сильно дальше друг от друга, чем в оригинале. Плюс часть гэгов просто перекочевала из первой части: всё тот же помешанный на навозе фермер и его семейные проблемы, всё тот же исследователь пещер, одетый в Индиану Джонса, который перечисляет длинный лист своих фобий, та же куча отсылок на The Monkey Island. Слабенько, увы.

Однако в сумме это всё ещё весьма приятная игра, дико аддитивная и харизматичная. Если играли в первую часть, то нет никаких причин не сыграть во вторую. Если не играли в первую... то почему?

[h3] “Goodbye, DeathSpank.” [/h3]
Let’s get straight to it: this isn’t a bad game. Back in its day, it even felt pretty distinctive. But as a sequel to [i] DeathSpank [/i], it falls short. My “Not Recommended” isn’t coming from spite—it’s coming from a very real sense of regret. [i] This could have been so much better [/i].

I genuinely liked the original [i] DeathSpank [/i]. It was a remarkably [i] pure [/i] experience: low-budget ARPG mechanics paired with dense, deconstructive humor. It didn’t try to tell some grand story or build an elaborate world. Instead, it leaned into a straight-faced knightly tone while constantly delivering mundane nonsense and absurd logic, creating a sharp and deliberate contrast. The humor wasn’t forced—it grew organically from the structure itself, even carrying a faint touch of gentle existentialism. And importantly, it knew when to stop. At around 10 hours, it wrapped up [i] right before [/i] the gameplay wore thin—which made all the difference.

With [i] Thongs of Virtue [/i], that balance starts to unravel.

The most obvious issue is a mismatch between [b] scope, gameplay, and content [/b]. The mechanics barely evolve—it’s still a very shallow ARPG system—but the game’s length is artificially stretched, padded with a large number of repetitive side quests. Fetch quests, grinding, backtracking—you name it. These make up a huge portion of the experience, and they lack both variety and thoughtful design. The result? You’re forced to spend far too long in a system that was only ever suited for short bursts. The first game ended [i] before [/i] it got boring. This one keeps going [i] long after [/i] it already has. The mid-to-late game experience can be summed up in one word: a slog.

Worse still is the shift in narrative direction. The original was light on story, prioritizing deconstruction—often, things were funnier [i] because [/i] they weren’t explained. The sequel, however, suddenly pushes a heavier focus on plot, worldbuilding, and lore (the whole “Thongs” concept, for instance). That’s not inherently a bad move—but the game simply doesn’t have the narrative chops to support it. There’s more information, but not more clarity. Instead, it feels like you’re being dragged along: the story speeds up, while your understanding lags behind. This kind of [b] overloaded density [/b] actively undermines the breezy, freeform feel that made the original work.

The humor also takes a noticeable hit. In the first game, the jokes came from contextual dissonance—they felt natural. Here, it often feels like the game is [i] trying [/i] to be funny. There’s more randomness, but worse timing. Many jokes don’t land as clever—they come off as forced, or just plain confusing. It shifts from “I can’t believe I’m laughing at this” to “Are you trying to make me laugh right now?”

Side quests are another major weak point. Most of them lack any standalone narrative value, mechanical variation, or emotional payoff. They feel blatantly [b] canned [/b]—content not designed to enrich the experience, but simply to pad out playtime. And once you realize that, the game’s entire sense of momentum collapses. What’s left is just the urge to [i] finish it and uninstall [/i].

To sum it up: the problem with [i] Thongs of Virtue [/i] isn’t that it got worse—it’s that it got [b] heavier without getting stronger [/b]. It tries to expand a light, sharp deconstructive comedy into a longer, more complex RPG, but its gameplay depth, narrative ability, and content design simply aren’t equipped to support that ambition. As a result, flaws that were once easy to overlook become impossible to ignore over the extended runtime.

So, would I recommend it? I’d recommend playing the original [i] DeathSpank [/i]—it’s tight, stylish, and knows exactly what it is. But [i] Thongs of Virtue [/i]?

[i] Unfortunately, I can’t recommend it [/i].

Sometimes, stopping at “just right” is a kind of discipline that’s far rarer than it should be.

DeathSpank: Thongs of Virtue is a delightfully absurd action-RPG from Hothead Games, published by Electronic Arts, and it continues the outlandish adventures of the self-proclaimed hero of justice, DeathSpank. Picking up immediately after the events of the first game, the sequel wastes no time throwing you back into a world where heroic bravado, zany humor, and over-the-top situations collide. What distinguishes Thongs of Virtue right away is its commitment to expanding the universe beyond the fairy-tale fantasy backdrop of the original. Instead, the sequel blends multiple genres and time periods into a single chaotic road trip: one moment you’re battling demons in fantasy forests, and the next you’re mowing down enemies on a war-torn battlefield, sailing with pirates, or facing robotic monstrosities and alien abominations. This genre fusion gives the game an unpredictable, comedic charm and reinforces the series’ identity as a satire of RPG traditions.

At the heart of the experience is the combat system, which retains the accessible hack-and-slash gameplay of the first game while adding a wider arsenal to keep encounters lively. Instead of limiting you to swords, maces, and crossbows, Thongs of Virtue opens the door to modern firearms such as pistols, shotguns, machine guns, and even RPGs. These weapons coexist with magical staves and melee gear, allowing you to mix ranged and close-combat strategies freely. The quick-swap weapon wheel makes it easy to experiment mid-fight, and the returning “Justice” meter rewards steady offensive pressure with powerful area-clearing abilities. Combat is fast, flashy, and humorous rather than tactically deep, and it works best when embraced as part of the game’s exaggerated tone. While it can grow repetitive over long sessions, the variety of environments and bizarre enemies does help keep things feeling fresh.

Narratively, Thongs of Virtue embraces comedic storytelling without apology. You’re tasked with tracking down six mystical thongs—relics meant to maintain world harmony but corrupted by their wearers, who are now powerful, deranged bosses. This absurd quest structure sets the stage for jokes, puns, and affectionate mockery of fantasy and sci-fi conventions. The dialogue is written with a playful rhythm reminiscent of classic LucasArts adventure games, and Ron Gilbert’s influence is obvious in the dry wit, eccentric characters, and the willingness to be unapologetically silly. Even routine side quests become entertaining thanks to the humor baked into NPC personalities and quest descriptions. These writing strengths help compensate for the formulaic nature of some tasks, making even fetch quests amusing through charm and attitude.

The visual style remains consistent with the first game’s “pop-up storybook” aesthetic, using bold outlines, vibrant colors, and layered landscapes that give environments a handcrafted feel. Each region has distinct thematic flavor, from icy northern outposts to industrial war zones, and the exaggerated character animations reinforce the game’s comedic identity. While the technical polish might not rival modern action-RPGs, the cartoonish presentation suits the game’s tone perfectly. Voice acting is another standout, with DeathSpank’s booming, overconfident delivery anchoring the humor and supporting characters adding personality throughout the journey.

Despite its strengths, the game does inherit some weaknesses from its predecessor. The overall structure mirrors the first game closely—so closely, in fact, that players who finished the original shortly before playing the sequel may feel they’re experiencing a larger expansion pack rather than a fully distinct installment. The sidekick co-op feature also returns with limited functionality, offering casual support without much depth or agency for the second player. Additionally, combat simplicity and occasional backtracking can make the pace drag in certain segments. Yet these issues rarely diminish the game’s charm; rather, they highlight that Thongs of Virtue is best enjoyed in bursts, with an appreciation for humor over tightly engineered mechanics.

As a whole, DeathSpank: Thongs of Virtue succeeds by leaning confidently into its strengths: irreverent humor, colorful variety, and a gleefully chaotic world that refuses to take itself seriously. It expands the scope of the original while preserving the personality that made the first game memorable. For players seeking a polished, strategic action-RPG, this may feel too light and too silly. But for anyone craving a quirky adventure packed with jokes, outlandish characters, and satisfying, fast-paced action, Thongs of Virtue delivers an experience that is both entertaining and unmistakably unique.

[h1]DeathSpank: Thongs of Virtue – A Hidden Gem Worth Revisiting[/h1]
[h2]A Childhood Classic Full of Charm[/h2]
DeathSpank: Thongs of Virtue was one of those games from my childhood that left a strange but unforgettable impression. It’s quirky, colorful, and totally bizarre—in the best way. Coming back to it years later feels like finding an old comic book you loved as a kid. The humor, the cartoonish art style, and the ridiculous dialogue all hit the same notes they did back then. For anyone who played it growing up, it's a nostalgic ride full of laughs and strange memories.

[h2]Don’t Judge It Too Quickly – It Has Its Own Flavor[/h2]
At first glance, it might look like just another hack-and-slash RPG with silly jokes, but if you don’t judge it too quickly, there’s a surprising amount to enjoy. The game doesn’t try to be something it’s not. It leans fully into its weird world, over-the-top weapons, and absurd characters. And once you accept that it’s supposed to be weird and lighthearted, it becomes much more enjoyable. If you're willing to give it a chance, you’ll probably find yourself smiling more than you expect.

[h2]A Simple Story That Works[/h2]
The story isn’t complex, and that’s okay. Sometimes it’s nice to play something where you don’t have to keep track of ten plotlines and a thousand lore entries. The goal is straightforward: help DeathSpank collect the legendary Thongs of Virtue while battling ridiculous enemies and doing favors for equally ridiculous NPCs. It may be silly, but there’s something relaxing about a game that just lets you have fun and follow a goofy but focused storyline from beginning to end.

[h2]Fun Combat and Progression[/h2]
The gameplay is easy to pick up, with satisfying combat and a good mix of weapons, armor, and upgrades to play around with. You’ll find everything from machine guns to swords to chicken cannons (yes, really), and the gear you collect often adds to the humor of the game. The balance between action and exploration is solid, and the side quests, though often silly, are fun to complete. It’s a game you can enjoy without stress—perfect after a long day or when you just want something light and entertaining.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
DeathSpank: Thongs of Virtue may not be the most polished or serious RPG, but that’s not what it’s trying to be. It’s a lighthearted, cartoonish adventure that isn’t afraid to be weird—and that’s exactly why it stands out. For those of us who played it growing up, it's a funny and nostalgic journey. And for new players, it’s a great reminder that sometimes, a simple and silly game is all you need to have a good time. Give it a try—you might be surprised how much fun you’ll have.

I called the original DeathSpank "a thoroughly mediocre action RPG that takes after Diablo but never manages to be all that entertaining", and while some of my complaints 100% apply to the sequel, the significantly increased difficulty meant I actually had fun with Thongs of Virtue.

My gripe with the itemization remains the same as the original game, so I'll just repeat it here: "Probably my biggest mechanical issue with the game is the itemization - there's no randomly generated loot, and almost all items are just straight upgrades that require higher levels to equip. The only exception to these are the weapons which allow you to use your Justice Meter, which also have tiered upgrades, but deciding which of them to use is actually slightly interesting - though I found the spinning swords to be the best of them by far, to the point where I didn't really use the others much." In this game, at least, the stores were much more useful, as you actually had the money to purchase things sometimes, like potions, refills of your consumable weapons, and very occasionally equipment upgrades.

Due to being significantly harder than the original DeathSpank, Thongs of Virtue was also much less simple, since you need to use the variety of consumable ranged weapons, potions, and other items in order to get through the many tough fights in the game. Figuring out which ones to use when will turn an annoyingly hard fight into a cakewalk, which I enjoyed.

As far the humor... I said this about the original: "The parody elements were occasionally amusing, but frequently fell flat for me - that you're going on a set of stupid fetch quests isn't made any better by the game calling attention to how stupid the fetch quests are, for instance. It's one of my gripes about parody RPGs in general, that they frequently seem to think that it excuses replicating bad game design for the sake of parody. Some of the more puzzle-like quests were amusing, however, and weren't something I was used to in this type of game." and I'd stick with it, but somehow the humor hit better for me in 2025 than 2015. Can't really explain why, just my tastes probably changed.

So again, DeathSpank: Thongs of Virtue is the kind of game I would mostly suggest trying if you think its style of humor would appeal to you. It doesn't really stack up well without that, though Thongs of Virtue is in all ways a significantly better game than the original, and I will recommend it as a result.

A good sequel, it continues the humorous storytelling and still has witty dialogue and clever jokes. It has more varied environments, like a battlefield, a pirate beach, a haunted forest, a desert, etc., making the world more interesting. There are also a lot more quests, a lot more secrets, and more to explore, but this extra content can feel bloated at times as there are a lot of similar quests, just in different locations. The weapons have been expanded, adding shotguns, rifles, bazookas and even grenades. The combat is similar to the first title, which is fine, but could've used some innovation as it feels more of the same even with the addition of firearms. The quests are still full of twists and great writing. There's still local co-op, making slogging through some of the more tedious content a lot more fun. My biggest complaint is that there are some random difficulty spikes throughout the game and at times you'll just die because you were not prepared well enough and you get swarmed by enemies; so you kinda have to grind a bit and try to over-level the zones and also stock up on items constantly.

On the whole, it's still a funny hack-n-slash RPG that builds upon the first game while also adding new features and expanding the world.

TL;DR: If you want more DeathSpank and can put up with much higher difficulty and a less interesting world, this game is for you. This is more of a mid-recommendation than a full one, details follow.

The Baconing is the third game in the DeathSpank series and the only one not involving the original creative director Ron Gilbert (who also famously created Monkey Island). The previous 2 entries were light-hearted comedy action RPGs with a unique setting combining anachronistic elements, acerbic humour and a solid (if repetitive) gameplay formula. The fun loop from the previous games consisted of a crazily over-the-top bumbling fool of a main character (DeathSpank) who quests to help people (sometimes unwittingly doing the contrary) while chasing ridiculous Macguffins. Gear would drop from enemies as you explore the world where new themed locations would regularly come up to advance the plot. The latter was simple but fun and the first game especially nailed the addictive just one more quest gameplay. The second game was harder and had a bloated number of sidequests but still fun while completing the original plot with multiple endings. This third game however suffers significantly from the departure of the originals' creative director.

The Baconing replaces the occasionally dark yet goofy world of the previous games with consistently drab environments and misses the mark immensely when it comes to the writing. DeathSpank is actively evil several times instead of mostly bungling his way around and the characters are almost all bad in some way. The themed locations lack the cheerfulness of the previous games and the plot isn't even properly resolved by the end of the game which promises DLC and sequels that never came. Thankfully, the proper ending in the second entry helps reduce the sting. It's easy to write off the simple plot of the previous games but this entry proves that there's a deceptive depth to that apparent simplicity as they balanced fun with social commentary instead of going post-apocalyptic and openly grim with forced comedy like this one. The voice acting is surprisingly lacking for some prominent characters although the main character and several side characters are great. The music is fine although mostly recycled, as is much of the gear and models. The gameplay is also lacking in innovation but more of the same wouldn't be an issue with the fun core loop of this series, except this entry has a big issue: difficulty.

The game's difficulty is significantly ramped up and at seems like it was more balanced for co-op (I played solo). It's easy to die in most battles and the difficulty spikes are even more annoying than in the second game. The game seems to want to encourage more tactical gameplay but doesn't adjust the other mechanics to help with that. Switching equipment and potions should have been easier to negotiate the harder, more varied mobs but the controls are as limited as the previous entries (where the game was properly tuned for that) and it makes the ability to mix and match annoying as you need to switch loadout mid-battle from a menu. When you get used to it, the steady feeling of progress from the better previous entries returns somewhat but that is also sometimes stymied by irritatingly long segments without checkpoints. The game's balance doesn't seem like it was given enough time to cook and it should have spent longer in development.

I know this may seem like a non-recommendation but despite these many flaws, the fact is this game still provides more DeathSpank gameplay. The relatively short length (about 12 hours) and getting to play some more as DeathSpank still has a fun factor for fans. Fans of the series hankering for more can somewhat enjoy this. Anyone else though, play the first 2 games and ignore this one. I'm tenuously recommending this as I like the series but this game did test my patience several times.

The main selling point is the humor, but that's very subjective and ymmv. The actual gameplay is kinda terrible, so I can't really recommend it as a game in of itself.

The gameplay is just a very lightweight action-adventure of the style of Diablo or Titan Quest, but without the depth or character building that make those so good. Instead, it's replaced with a melee build with a mostly non-working shield who only attacks enemies you explicitly click on (while the rest of the horde murders you). In other words, there's no auto-attacking at all, so you just sit there spam clicking and trying to shield until you probably die anyway, and then have to walk back to where you died. Death feels cheap, but rather than this feeling kind of like a superpower, it instead just feels like a nuisance.

Really, the comedy is the whole selling point of the game. Some obviously love it, as the positive reviews show. For me, well... The first time I played it, I recall really enjoying it. It's a very irreverent sort of humor with a egotistical a**hole hero as the main character. My most recent attempt at playing it, though... The humor just felt rather stale. I think the problem might be that this sort of parody hero has been done to death at this point, deconstructed and reconstructed, and so it's lost a lot of the originality that existed when it first came out.

Not as relevant to me personally, but the graphics are also pretty rough. This is pretty unsurprising given the age of the game, and a lot of the backgrounds still hold up pretty well, but this then clashes with the mobs that look like something out of early World of Warcraft, still more polygon than mesh.

So should you get this? Eh. It's pretty cheap, but the game play is lousy. Really, it all depends on whether the humor clicks for you or not - as well as whether you're willing to throw yourself against waves of enemies over and over to finish an area and move to the next. Personally, I would skip this and go for another game unless you already know you're a fan of the humor - such as playing previous Deathspank games or watching a let's play or something.

Chaotisch, aber nach kurzer Eingewöhnung sehr zu genießen.

The Baconing erinnert an eine Mischung aus Diablo und Borderlands. Der Humor und die Story sind völlig hanebüchen. Nichts und niemand nehmen sich hier ernst. Der Hauptcharakter ist ne Mischung aus Rambo und einem männlichen Stereotyp nach dem anderen. Sämtliche NPCs, Gegner und sogar die Waffen/Items sind purer Quatsch. Alles schreibt nach "We dont give a f*ck".

Die Steuerung ist in Ordnung, krankt aber sehr daran, dass die Taste zum nur Angreifen / nicht bewegen irgendwie nie funktioniert, egal auf was man sie legt. 

Die Kamera ist mit das Schlimmste. Zwar kann man klassisch rein- und rauszoomen, aber nie weit genug. Das führt dazu, dass man häufig, vor allem wenn man nach Süden laufen muss, die Gegner nicht sieht, bevor sie Aggro haben. 

Das Kampfsystem ist auch... interessant. Vor allem der manische Zwang, dass man nach jedem Kampf sein Leben erneuern muss. Die Tränke dafür sind aber auf 5 limitiert, obwohl sie oft droppen. Essen stapelt sich unendlich, hat aber nur über Zeit Heilung, die bei JEDER Taste vorzeitig abgebrochen wird. Außerdem gibt es ständig neues Essen, je nach Level. 

Das Skillsystem, wenn man es so nennen will, ist sehr rudimentär und man versteht nicht, was davon gut/schlecht ist. Man kann z.B. "Sidekicks" besser machen, hat aber nie irgendwelche davon (das ist wohl nur per DLC möglich).

Das Waffensystem und die Rüstungen werden permanent erneuert. Alle 5-15 Minuten findet man etwas Besseres, das das Alte sofort ersetzt. Auf Wunsch übernimmt die Maschine das sogar automatisch, damit man nicht mal mehr wechseln muss. Das Alte kann sofort kleingehäckselt werden.

Geld ist in dem Spiel völliger Quatsch. Erst ganz am Ende könnte es passieren, dass man mal Tränke oder Superorbs aufstocken will. Ansonsten läuft man irgendwann mit 100k, 300k in der Tasche rum und weiß nicht wieso. Ich habe nie ein Item beim "Waffenhändler" gefunden, das besser war als meine angelegten. Und auch der "Essenshändler" ist völliger Quatsch. 

Fernkampf/Nahkampf sind auch nicht sehr ausgewogen. Wenn man kann, kann man alle Gegner entspannt wegsnipen oder mit Granaten hochjagen. 

Ein paar der anderen Items sind ebenfalls sehr mächtig / spaßig. 

QoL-technisch hätten mehr als 4 Item-Slots dem Spiel gut getan. Einer ist immer für Heiltränke besetzt, der 2. meistens für Essen. Bleiben 2. Es gibt so viele Tränke und Wurfpfeile und Granaten, dass man häufig gar nichts mehr tragen kann, so selten kommt man dazu diese zu nutzen. Gleichzeitig habe ich mich sicher 20x mit Granaten und aufgeladener Fernkampfwaffe selbst gekillt, wenn die Gegner zu nah herankommen.

Tode sind in "The Baconing" relativ entspannt. Man verliert zwar Geld, kann das aber bei der Leiche wieder einsammeln. Eher nervig, dass man sich erst mal vollheilen muss. 

Die Möglichkeit, über die "Klo-Teleporter" über die ganze Karte zu reisen, ist sehr gut. Weniger gut: Manche Klos in Dungeons sind "out of order" und irgendwie nur für Tode innerorts da...

Das Spiel an sich hat mir gut gefallen. 5 "Questitems", die wir an 5 Abschnitte der Karte bringen müssen. Alle sind thematisch unterteilt, bieten kleinere Nebenquests und diverse Rätsel. Bis auf das "Brückenrätsel" direkt am Anfang waren die meisten eher leicht. Die "Hinweise" in den Glückskeksen können manchmal sehr helfen, manchmal beantworten aber auch 3/3 eher wenig, was du wissen willst (WO!).

Fazit: The Baconing ist mit 10 Stunden rundum gelungen. Die Abschnitte, das fixe Autosave und manual Save System bieten viele Möglichkeiten für Pausen zwischendurch. Der Humor ist eigen. Gelacht und geschmunzelt habe ich selten, zumal das Spiel auch nur auf Englisch ging, aber es hat mich auch nicht weiter gestört. Das Kampfsystem ist ein wenig "Arbeit", viele Mikro-Unterbrechungen, viele (dumme, selbstverschuldete) Tode etc. Trotzdem macht es einfach wahnsinnig Laune. Du hast ein klares Ziel von Beginn an, bekommst am Ende einen Endbosskampf und das wars dann auch. Wer Lust hat, kann sich im "Hardcore" oder "Insane"-Mode vergnügen, aber inhaltlich dürfte man nach einem Durchlauf alles gesehen haben.

This is a hard one to recommend for me.  I would preface this by saying that only fans of the previous games should apply for this adventure.  There are critics that say the writing isn't as good or that it is juvenile.  I'm not sure I believe it's as bad as they say, though there is entire quest dealing with juvenile phrasing.  The voice acting for the most part is just as good as the previous two games and the humor worked for me more than it didn't.

As for the issues... there are plenty.  First, alt-tabbing tends to cause the game to completely crash, which is something the first game did only once for me and the second a couple of times.  This one, it was widespread.  The difficulty feels way higher as well.  The mechanic of shield bashing and reflecting projectiles is good in concept, but it seems that the designers looked at that benefit they gave you and then proceeded to make the enemies more numerous and of higher levels than they were previously.  To that end, the enemy levels feel arbitrary at times.  In the first Deathspank, once I was at a certain level, I could bowl over lesser enemies (even sending their bodies flying with a simple hit).  In this game, if there is a group of 4 projectile enemies that are 2 levels weaker than you, you have a great chance of getting killed if you're not very careful in how you approach the battle.  In the first Deathspank, I didn't die very often and when I did, it felt like it was something I might have been able to prevent.  In Thongs of Virtue, I died more often, but it still had an air of something I might have been able to prevent if I was better skilled.  In The Baconing, I would die several times in each section and felt there were plenty of cheap, unavoidable situations where the only way I could progress was to throw myself at a group of enemies and hope I'd take one or two of them out before dying so I would have less of them to go through when I came back to that area.  It made a lot of the combat very irritating.  Some of the fetch quests are a bit redundant and in one, the guy giving it to you even tells you that there is a boring way of doing it, so why don't you steal the items you need.  After that, he then proceeds to tell you how you STILL have to do a boring fetch quest to make this supposedly quicker method work.  

For some reason, they decided to remove the ability to simply drop items on the ground as well as removing the stash that you had in the previous 2 (and oddly, making the amounts you'd get for grinding inventory items down to a mere fraction of what you got before).  One could say it makes things more immediate, forcing you to use what you have, but I liked saving things I wasn't using in case I ran into trouble later on.  Example: you'll often find grenades.  In the previous games, I wouldn't use them very often, but I would hoard them in my stash just in case.  I would eventually find some tough enemy that I could use some help with and then go back to the stash for that help.  In this game, you have to use what you have and that is it.  The co-op character (I only used Sparkles this time out) is hit or miss as well.  Plenty of times, we'd hammer the button to heal and he wouldn't do anything at all, which resulted in plenty of lost lives on its own.  It seems like enemies would target the co-op player a bit less often than before, which was nice, but since they can take damage and you share a common health bar, you can still get to a point where you can run into trouble fast and then the next errant hit kills you, even if you weren't taking much damage prior.  The reflecting mechanic is nice in theory and it does work, but it would have been much nicer if it didn't need to be held in quite as long before activating.  It makes blocking a shot easy enough but reflecting some of the faster projectiles requires you to take that first blocked hit while you wait for the charge to complete (and some rare enemies practically require reflected shots to be killed, so hopefully you can master that ability early on).  

Each area is self contained and you will rarely need to go back to a previous section once you have moved on (unless you want to do some of the achievements such as completing the arena that you find early on).  They have their own fun identity and enemies and the NPC's are often fun to listen to (and it's fun to see characters from previous games show up in some capacity).  The overall storybook presentation is just as much fun as it was before and each area looks very nice.

This was a game that I definitely had some fun with, but it was the first of the series in which I was actually looking forward to finishing it so it could be uninstalled and not touched again.  While that sounds like a damning indictment, it's more because I liked the other ones so much.  The Baconing has its fun moments but they are nearly overshadowed by the many issues I have detailed above (it also doesn't help that it ends on a potential cliffhanger that seems like it will never be resolved since this game came out so long ago).  If you liked the first two games, give this a try or look at videos first to see if it will work for you but definitely do not start on this one as it is the hardest by far.  Start with the first one and get a feel for the way it plays and judge from there.

What it is: 3rd person adventure game with mild RPG elements. 

I'm going to start this review with this: As a "game" this isn't great. That is in the sense of game play. The combat is bad. The targeting is cumbersome, there's no "weight" to any of your attacks, every creature does an absolutely disgusting amount of damage, and your shield is basically cardboard if you don't get a perfectly timed block. There were countless times I died because the enemies aggro'd me behind a barrier/wall and swarmed me, I'd kill an archer only for a phantom bolt to hit me afterwards, and I'd want to attack one thing and the targeting system would switch it to something else right before I fire. I hate the game part of The Baconing

Now, with that being said, I liked the rest. The story is stupid, but the humor is solid. The game is fairly meta and takes jabs at tropes within the genre. There's a lot for pop culture junkies to get a chuckle at and occasionally I laughed out loud from a few things. The end of the story is the weakest part. There's no payoff and the later characters are all pretty derogatory. However, it's a fun adventure and doesn't take long to beat. 

Give it a go, if you find it on sale

The Baconing is (almost certainly) the final game in the DeathSpank series. Following on from Thongs of Virtue, The Baconing [spoiler]has you travelling the game world on a mission to defeat the AntiSpank and destroy the five thongs so painstakingly gathered in the previous game.[/spoiler]

The gameplay itself is basically identical to the previous two games, but the focus on combat is more pronounced – while you can go through the game quite simply on normal difficulty, playing on Insane will likely be a frustrating experience; you will need to rely heavily on the block and reflect mechanics, and you will find yourself growing increasingly frustrated when heavily outnumbered. The majority of the obstacles are not insurmountable, but it does detract somewhat from the enjoyment. Local co-op does make an appearance once again however, which may help to lessen the difficulty curve.

As in the prior game however, I did encounter some game breaking bugs, where the game would simply crash upon encountering a random enemy or something of the sort. I managed to get around it by simply avoiding those enemies entirely, but as the game is no longer maintained, bear this in mind – it may cause frustration if you are unfortunate enough to experience it. Additionally, I would also suggest backing up your saves regularly, just in case.

If you enjoyed the previous two games, you will still get some mileage out of this instalment. If the other titles in the series were not your cup of tea, best to avoid this one as it is practically more of the same.

Jeu de rôle couloir issue de la saga Deathspank, The Baconing est doté d’un humour (made in Ron Gilbert) qui fait mouche. La performance est d’autant plus réussie qu’il saura même satisfaire les anglophobes dont je fais partie (sur ce type de jeu en particulier).

Mélange original entre RPG et beat them all, le titre est accessible et drôle. Les experts préféreront la combinaison souris/clavier pour une visée plus précise, mais j’ai pu faire le 100% à l’aide ma manette Xbox sans difficulté.
Les voix/sons/musiques sont bien amenées et collent avec le ton léger de l’aventure, notre ami Deathspank étant le pivot de cette étrange alchimie. Un bémol sur l’impact inexistant des coups que l’on porte, au corps à corps en particulier.

Graphiquement c’est un peu fouillis mais original, ce qui pourrait définir l’ensemble du jeu finalement.
Menus simples et efficaces, co-op locale et succès globalement bien pensés, sauvegarde Cloud et patch FR disponibles.
Il ne manque au titre que des cartes Steam, la coopération en ligne et un réel boost de vitesse pour notre héros (pas mal de backtracking hélas).

13 euros pour un titre de 2011 c’est un peu cher, mais le jeu est rafraîchissant + satisfaisant. Je le recommande sans difficulté.

Sok játékkal játszottam már az évek során, van jobb rosszabb de általában abba amibe ténylegesen is pénzt fektetek nem igazán szoktam csalódni. És így voltam ezzel a The Baconing-nél is. Már a trailer és a képek alapján is sejtettem hogy bizony ez egy humor bomba lesz, ésss igen az is lett. De nem akárhogy.

Maga a megjelenése a játéknak is megér egy misét. Mert hogy Spanktopia egy rajzolt kicsit rajzfilmes enyhén cell shaded beütést kapott. Amit megtekertek azzal hogy a terep és a karakterek 3D-sek. De minden más inkább 2D-s. Pontosabban kicsit ilyan mintha egy díszlet lenne az egész, vagy egy kihajtogatható könyv. Ez egy igen furcsa, de még is megkapó megjelenést ad az egésznek. Látszik a kreatív gondolkozás ilyen téren, amit abszolút díjazok.
A hangeffektek teljesen rendben vannak, a soundtrack is elmegy egynek, bár egy idő után idegesítő lehet kicsit, amit egyébként a főszereplő is meg meg jegyez néha, így kicsit Deadpool-os beütése van a dolgnak ilyen szempontból.

Játékmenet terén igazából sok új nincs a nap alatt. A storeban RPG címkével van feltüntetve, én inkább azt mondanám rá hogy egy H&S. Fix kamera nézet van, a karaktert bill-el vagy egérrel is lehet irányitani. Rajtunk áll igazából. A szokásos dolgok megvannak, potion-ok (amiknek a limitje 5 db de hogy miért fogalmam sincs), HP feltöltő ételek, fegyverek, páncélok, stb. Az inventory szerintem kicsit kusza lett, de annyira nem zavart, hogy ne tudjam megszokni. Lehetett volna rajta dolgozni még egy kicsit.
Aztán természetesen van fejlődési rendszer is, ami 20 szintben kimerül, de ez kb. lefedi a teljes játékidőt is úgy hogy teljesen korrekt. Szintenként passzív skill-eket kapunk, amit annyira nem fogunk észre venni, de van ilyen is. Ami még plusz az az hogy akár Co-op-ban is lehet játszani.
A harcrendszer egyszerű nagyon, pajzzsal lehet védekezni illetve a lövedékeket vissza ütni, a többivel megy csapkodni vagy lővöldözni. Ami plusz az a charge attack, egy adott idő után (sikeres találatok után töltödik fel) bizonyos fegyvereknél lehet egy erősebb támadást használni. Ami talán csak probléma az az ellenfelek hitbox-a. Annyira precízre sikeredtek hogy könnyen megesik az hogy azt hiszed rákattintasz, közben pedig nem és így sokszor előfordulhat az hogy ahelyett hogy támadni a dicső DeathSpank, inkább átmegy egy másik helyre.
Az ellenfelek kellően változatosak, és viccesek is. Természetesen totál elnagyoltak, akárcsak a bossok. De ez ne zavarjon senkit sem, itt ennek így kellett lennie.

De mivel több ez a játék mint a többi H&S? Kapunk egy olyan sztorit ami ugyan rém egyszerű (és mondjuk egy az egyben kifigurázza a Gyűrűk Úrát), de még is szorakoztató. És nem is a cél az érdekes, hiszen már az elején lehet tudni, hogy a jó? fog győzni. Itt inkább az oda vezető út, a párbeszédek a karakterek közzöt, az idétlen helyzetek azok amik zseniállisá teszik az egészet. Amit lehet kifiguráz a játék, a hercegnőktől kezdve a kalózokon át az UFO-kig mindent. Mindenből viccet csinál, amiből csak lehet. Ha ez még nem elég sokszor a DeathSpank is kikacsint a játéból, kicsit olyan mintha tudná hogy ő egy játékban van. Ezt kicsit nehezebb észre venni, de van amikor csipkelődik. Pl. van egy megjegyzése a vége felé, hogy ide most illett volna a Rocky zenéje (nem biztos hogy ezt a filmet mondta, de egy filmcímet), de sajnos nem volt keret rá. Zseniállis. Maga a karakter egyébként egy antihős. Azt hiszi hogy jót cselekszik, de nem feltétlen. A jó érdekében kb. feldúl mindent. Pl. élteti a zsarnokokat és a korrupciót.
Ami meg bonusz az az irdatlan sok kikacsintás más játékokra, valós személyekre, a film és zene iparra. Ahogy ezt összerakták így egy az egyben az valami zseniális.

Összeségében egy nagyon korrektűl összerakott, élvezetes, vicces, pörgős játékot kapunk. Ami játékidőben nagyjából középmezőnyben van a maga 12 órájával. Ebbe minden küldetés benne van ami csak a játékban van, úgy hogy ennél rövdebb idő alatt is végig lehet pörgetni. Nyilván nem hibátlan a játék, pl. 1-2 mechanika lehetne jobb is, pl. az étel használata. Vagy az inventory lehetne kevésbé kusza. De ennek ellenére egy abszolút szerethető játékot kapunk, ami nem tökéletes ugyan de élvezhető. Nos Tanga pusztitásra fel barátaim!

'Unstoppable Gorg' is a brilliantly inventive take on the tower defense genre, replacing static paths with a dynamic system of orbital rings. The game’s standout feature is the ability to rotate these orbits around celestial bodies, forcing players to constantly reposition their defenses to intercept incoming enemy waves. This mechanic adds a layer of spatial strategy and kinetic energy that is rarely seen in the genre, transforming what could have been a passive experience into an active, high-stakes tactical puzzle. The 1950s "B-movie" sci-fi aesthetic is executed with incredible charm, using live-action FMV sequences and retro visual effects that give the entire project a unique and cohesive personality.

The game excels at balancing its nostalgic presentation with deep, challenging gameplay that rewards foresight and quick thinking. As players progress, the introduction of varied satellite types and increasingly complex orbital layouts ensures that the strategy remains fresh and demanding. Furthermore, the physics-based elements—such as using orbits to shield vulnerable structures or redirecting fire—provide a satisfying sense of control over the chaotic battlefield. For fans of strategy games, 'Unstoppable Gorg' stands out as a polished and highly original title that successfully subverts genre expectations while delivering a delightful tribute to classic science fiction.

Unstoppable Gorg, developed and published by Futuremark, is a clever and stylish reimagining of the tower defense genre that blends retro science fiction aesthetics with inventive gameplay mechanics. It immediately sets itself apart through its distinctive 1950s-inspired presentation, capturing the spirit of old black-and-white alien invasion films with campy humor, practical effects, and grainy film textures. The game opens like a forgotten B-movie, complete with overacted live-action cutscenes featuring rubber aliens, cardboard spaceships, and dramatic narration. This theatrical tone gives Unstoppable Gorg an identity that feels both nostalgic and refreshing, turning what could have been a standard defense title into a quirky homage to mid-century sci-fi cinema. The charm of its presentation goes beyond visual novelty—it establishes an atmosphere of lighthearted absurdity that contrasts beautifully with the surprisingly challenging strategy beneath.

At its core, Unstoppable Gorg retains the traditional foundation of the tower defense genre: waves of enemies approach, and the player must strategically deploy defensive units to protect a central structure. What makes the game unique is how it redefines spatial control. Instead of building towers on fixed grids or along predetermined paths, you position satellites along rotating orbital rings that encircle your base. These satellites function as your turrets, generators, and support modules, and you can rotate entire orbits to reposition them dynamically during battle. This means that defense isn’t just about placement but also about timing and movement. The constant rotation introduces an element of real-time strategy—anticipating enemy trajectories, adjusting defenses on the fly, and managing the flow of resources all require quick thinking and precision. It’s a brilliant twist that transforms what could have been a static experience into something fluid and tactile.

Each type of satellite fulfills a different tactical role. Some generate energy, which acts as your currency for deploying and upgrading defenses; others specialize in direct attacks, long-range sniping, or slowing enemy craft. There are also defensive satellites that can repair or shield your base, forcing you to balance offense and support systems carefully. The orbital mechanic ensures that positioning always matters—one poorly timed rotation can expose your defenses or leave key sectors vulnerable. This sense of constant motion adds tension and excitement to the familiar tower defense rhythm, demanding awareness and adaptability. Even after several missions, the novelty of turning orbits and watching your satellites realign never fades, giving every encounter a satisfying sense of control and chaos.

The campaign structure is straightforward but engaging, presented as a series of escalating missions across the solar system. The story, while intentionally absurd, maintains the campy energy that defines the game’s tone. Between missions, you’re treated to delightful full-motion video segments that look like they were lifted from vintage sci-fi serials. The over-the-top dialogue and theatrical acting lend personality to a genre that often relies purely on mechanics. Each new planet introduces new enemy types and strategic wrinkles—shielded ships, faster fighters, or large capital vessels that demand different configurations of your orbiting defenses. The difficulty ramps up quickly, and later stages require precise rotations and careful energy management to survive. Though the curve can feel unforgiving, the challenge makes victories deeply satisfying.

Aesthetically, Unstoppable Gorg is one of the most distinctive tower defense games ever made. The combination of black-and-white live-action sequences, stylized comic-book art, and the clean design of its orbital interface creates a perfect balance between nostalgia and functionality. The soundtrack reinforces the retro mood with a mix of space-age orchestration and pulpy sci-fi motifs that could easily fit in a 1950s adventure serial. Sound effects are crisp and deliberate—the whir of rotating satellites and the thump of alien ships exploding create a satisfying rhythm to each battle. The visual clarity of the orbital system also makes it easy to track the chaos, ensuring that even when the screen fills with ships and projectiles, the action remains readable and engaging.

While the game’s creative approach and presentation are impressive, it’s not without flaws. The fixed number of build positions on each orbital ring can make some battles feel restrictive, especially when compared to the freedom of movement in other strategy titles. The steep difficulty curve in the later stages may frustrate players who prefer a slower or more forgiving pace, as success often depends on trial and error. Some critics also noted that while the rotating orbit mechanic is innovative, it can occasionally feel clunky or disorienting in the heat of battle. However, these shortcomings are balanced by the game’s strong sense of identity and mechanical depth. For players who appreciate learning through repetition and strategy refinement, the challenge becomes part of its enduring appeal.

Beyond the main campaign, Unstoppable Gorg offers additional modes that extend its replayability. The Challenge and Arcade modes provide opportunities to refine your tactics or chase high scores, giving the experience longevity beyond the story missions. The variety of satellites and upgrade paths ensures that different play styles can emerge—some players may prefer aggressive, offense-heavy setups, while others lean on defensive fortifications and support systems. This flexibility encourages experimentation, making each session feel distinct. The satisfaction of perfectly aligning your orbits and repelling a wave of enemies is immense, and the moment when a chaotic battle suddenly clicks into harmony captures the essence of what makes the game so rewarding.

Unstoppable Gorg stands as a testament to how creative presentation and thoughtful mechanics can revitalize a familiar genre. It manages to be both a love letter to the absurd optimism of 1950s science fiction and a genuinely clever strategic experience. Its combination of humor, charm, and depth ensures that it’s more than just a novelty—it’s a well-designed, challenging, and memorable game that still feels fresh years after its release. For fans of tower defense games seeking something different, or for anyone who grew up loving campy alien movies, Unstoppable Gorg is a delightful surprise. It’s not just about defending a base—it’s about orchestrating a cosmic ballet of spinning defenses and gleefully embracing the chaos of an interstellar B-movie brought to life.

For my personal taste, it was a good & neat little game, one of my favorites, at least in the TD & Sci-Fi genres, which I generally don't really like too much.

The Towers are put on orbits you can spin on a given trajectory, making it an interesting and sometimes tactical mixture of static and mobile defenses.

It can be pretty hard though, even on the lower of the 4 difficulties and story mode, but challenges which add additional negative handicaps to the already challenging story missions, especially, as well as Arcade Mode after LVL 50, when mother ships are just flying all over the place, not respecting your little 'Invincible' (Which brings me to the next point: the encyclopedia is a nice little bonus). I might not even call it hard, though it wasn't easy, as trial & error principle may be more accurate, since if you figure out which satellites to use in which locations at what times it becomes easy enough, it just may take you several attempts and fails to find each mission's sweet spot.

Additional Cons:
- not all of the satellite types are really useful
- the Arcade mode is not customizable (different options would have been nice, etc.)
- there is no 'movie gallery' to watch all the video clips, + therefor an Encyclopedia though

The FMV parody sequences of 50s cheaply made Sci-Fi Movies are nice, but short and rather few, as a matter of fact after you win the last mission, which isn't even as hard as some of the ones before it, IMO, the game just ends, would have been really nice to get a final one minute FMV end sequence of brave space captain Adam rescuing Ms. Universe Arielle from the stopped Gorg menace.

The Soundtrack, background music are nice and suit the sci-fi setting well,
the Audio Effects (attacking, UFOs being destroyed, not having enough money to build etc.) are pretty good as well, though could have used even more variations as is already given.
The (only) British Voice Dub catches the atmosphere well (Subtitles I think are also only in English, just Menu, Mission select etc. is available in other languages I think).
Together with a little Starship Troopers Anti-Specieist Propaganda and some Marsian Alien Mars Attacks! flair (I just watched the movie for the multiplth time after many years and it goes well with the game, obviously ^^).

Also props to having a Demo so we can try out the game for free before spending money on it, which is how I came to buy it, since I liked the Demo gameplay and that you even added achievements to the Demo (Also props for making watch the credits an achievement), which not many Devs take the time to do.

Would have been nice to play some other games by Futuremark, something tells me I would have enjoyed them as well, unfortunately though only 3 were ever made and the other 2 are now unplayable, this being the last obtainable and playable one, before they shuttered or sold their gaming branch and also got acquired by UL to focus solely on benchmarking software. Would also have enjoyed some Steam Trading Cards and Points Shop items for this title.

Something tells me the leaderboard with points was either bugged at some point or cheated, or arcade points counted for others, but they didn't for me towards my total score.

The only similar games I played when it comes to the mix of genres, not the setting, is the early Plants vs. Zombies games, which are also a mix of Tower Defense and light-hearted comedy and I enjoyed as well. Though I found another title on steam called Fortified which is also a 3rd person shooter & TD mix and a parody of Alien Sci-Fi, which I hope to try out one of these days and will hopefully like as much as this one.

I'd even buy this title and recommend it to others for full price instead of waiting until it goes on sale, which I don't often do.

Anyways, good luck stopping the Gorg and not getting deceived by the Brainriders or de-mooned by the sunbots on your way to dangerous Planet X.

It’s a pretty fun tower defense game. What sets it apart is that your “towers” are actually automated defense satellites which are orbiting around planets! There’s a constant stream of alien invaders that have to be dealt with, but you can change the orbit of your satellites in order to maximize the effectiveness of your defenses. You just have to be careful, because moving one of your satellites will usually affect the location of several other satellites too, and you don’t want to leave any gaps in your defenses! 

The game has three modes: [b]Story[/b], [b]Challenge[/b], and [b]Arcade[/b]. [b]Story mode[/b] takes you on a 21 mission journey through the solar system as you try to fight off the “Unstoppable Gorg” alien invasion. It has a great kitschy 1950s sci-fi theme! Watching my protagonist get threatened by a silly-looking “Sunbot” alien brought a smile to my face; this is parody at its finest! It’s not often that you see a tower defense game with an entertaining story and fun visuals, so I have to give the developers props for that. [b]Challenge mode[/b] has 21 missions similar to Story mode, but with extra mission parameters. For example, in one mission the enemies might move with extra speed, while in another mission some of your satellites might now be locked in a set orbit, unable to be moved. In [b]Arcade mode[/b] you try to survive for as long as possible against increasingly tough attackers. I made it to Wave 75 before finally giving up. 

There is a large variety of enemies to fight, and you’ll constantly be changing tactics to deal with new threats. For example, one enemy type has a short-range suppression field, so any of your satellites that are nearby are rendered unable to fire. So only long-range attacks will be effective. Another enemy type is a bomber that will occasionally fire missiles towards your main base. But you can intercept the missiles with firepower from the right kind of satellites, or simply block the missiles by changing the orbit of your satellites and using them as an impromptu shield.

The player will gradually gain access to a large arsenal of satellites and bombs in order to fight the Gorg invasion. There is some standard tower defense economy management, as some satellites will generate income, allowing you to buy other satellites. You’ll need to strike the right balance between bolstering your economy and increasing your defenses. I found most of the satellites to be useful, but there are few stinkers. One is a “webber” satellite that slows down nearby aliens, but not enough to justify its cost. My favorite satellite creates an energy beam which links to other nearby satellites. Any alien crossing through the energy beam takes heavy damage, and complex beam-based defense grids are possible, which is pretty cool.

Pretty much every mission has a gimmick or twist to it, which you’ll have to figure out in order to progress. And this takes us to the greatest strength and greatest weakness of the gameplay. On the upside, the player is constantly forced to change tactics depending on the mission. The tactics that brought victory in the last mission will often not work in the next mission. So you never fall into the trap of just building the same satellites over and over, or having the same build order over and over. You are constantly forced to think and adapt to succeed. The downside to this is evident from most of the negative Steam reviews this game has acquired, which complain that the difficulty is too hard or that trial and error gameplay is bad. To be clear, in this game you will play a mission, lose the mission, then probably make several more attempts before finally beating it. Even on the easiest difficulty level, beating a mission on the first try will be rare. So, players who dislike having to rely on “[i]a priori[/i]” knowledge to win will not be a fan of the gameplay. On the harder difficulty levels, speedy micromanagement is necessary to win, which may also be off-putting to some people. As for myself, I played through all three game modes on the easiest difficulty level, and then replayed some of my favorite missions on harder difficulties. This gave me about ten hours’ worth of fun entertainment, which, considering the game’s low cost, is a pretty good deal. If you like innovative tower defense games, this one is worth a try!

Unstoppable Gorg is a tower defense game that utilized the standard mechanics, but also a lot of 50's 60's scifi with the UFOs and Flash Gordon (tm) type design for nostalgic look. Unfortunately, the game is extremely difficult, even on easy, even for veterans of tower defense, and the economy was emphasized to a much greater degree than bounty which made for a weird game balance. 

Basically, you need to build defenses for Earth when a fleet of alien UFOs invade. Simple enough. THe trick however, is instead of relying on bounties for each enemy killed, you have to instead place "generators" (solar satellites) to generate money before you can buy the satellites to place in orbit. There is bounty for kills, but they are so miniscule the mission would be over (and you lost) by the time you killed enough to build a turret. For example, killing a small UFO has a bounty of $2. When it costs $100 to build a simple Vulcan turret, and even a Vulcan turret cannot stop a medium UFO even after 2 passes, it's pretty obvious what they want you to build, esp. when selling such structures yields 35% return only. So winning comes down to timing: build what you need at the last second, and build moneymakers immediately, but the timing can only be found through experimentation. Yet how many times can you play a tower defense game? 

That's why this game never really quite got the receptive it hoped, compared to all the other tower defense games.

[h1]1950年代製作のSF作品にインスパイアされた
衛星周回タワーディフェンス[/h1]


日本語なし
英語は平易、ムービー中に字幕表示可能

久しぶりに遊びなおしたら改めて面白いと感じましたのでレビュー。
もう少し最近のゲームかと思っていたんですが2012年リリースでしたか、そうですか…。


[u]・前書き[/u]
1950年代に製作されたＳF作品を強くイメージ、オマージュして作られた本作。当時の私はトレイラーとスクリーンショットに妙に惹かれて購入したのを覚えています。直感に従った買い物だったわけですが、世界観やストーリーは期待通りの出来で、意外にも変則的なタワーディフェンスとして良く出来ており、遊び終わったあとも強く記憶に残る作品として私の中で隠れた名作としての評価を確立。この度改めて遊びなおしてみたところ思い出補正抜きにしても面白いと思いましたので、レビューを書いてみることにしました。

以下、評価点だったり気に入った点だったり


[u] ・ユーモアあふれるレトロなB級SF [/u]
古い作品ゆえに本作のストアページからトレイラームービーが消えていました。同じものがYoutubeにアップロードされていますので、まずはこちらをチェックしてみましょう。
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a0LrA4KY9_Y&ab_channel=ULBenchmarks
（動画紹介文に作中に登場するエイリアン衣装の製作過程を撮影した写真へのリンクあり、こちらも面白い）

トレイラーで使用されているモノクロなムービー、レトロな特撮作品に見られる独特の質感のメカニック、能天気さえ感じられるBGMなどなど、これらを見て笑顔になったあなたなら本作を十二分に楽しめる素養があります。

大雑把に世界観を説明すると、宇宙へと進出した人類がその過程で侵略性の爬虫類型エイリアンであるGorgに遭遇したのを皮切りに、人類の精神を侵す脳みそエイリアンMind Rider、金色金属の体を持つSunbotとも遭遇、戦争に発展するというもの。人類の存亡がかかった危機的な状況なはずなんですが、トレイラーでも使われている妙に陽気なメインバトルBGMや、大仰なファンファーレとともに流れる作中のニュースなど、プレイヤーに微塵も危機を感じさせません。
また、ダイナミックな動きで演説する姿を映した動画メッセージをよこしてくる各種族の頭領もキャラクターが立っており、うさん臭さと愛嬌たっぷり。英語がわからなくても語気とその身振りで大体何を言っているかわかります。特にSunbotの頭領であるRadiant Beemはそのポンコツロボットな外見や作中で果たす役割のおかげで、すっかり気に入ってしまいました。
トレイラーで一部が見られる1950年代の特撮を再現したムービーも数は少なめですが、ふわふわした動きのメカニックなど力が入った出来で、見ていて思わず笑みがこぼれてしまいます。
ストーリーは単純明快、全体的にカラッとした明るい世界観で進行していきます。小難しいことなんて考えずに娯楽として楽しめる方向へと全力で舵を切った作風、こういうのもいいですよね。
ここまで書いて気づきましたが、これ結構なバカゲーじゃな？

作中の登場人物や各種の衛星について捕捉説明がされているエンサイクロペディアも用意されており、開発のこだわりを感じます。作者が楽しんで作ったことが伝わってきてこちらも好印象。


[u] ・衛星をぐるぐる周回させて敵を迎え撃て！ [/u]
もう一つの核である、タワーディフェンス部分も合格点をあげられる出来。

守るべき対象である宇宙船や惑星の周りに配置された衛星の軌道を表した輪っか、ここにいくつか用意されている特定のポイント上に資金製造、迎撃、補助といった各種の衛星を配置していくのですが、この輪っかを回転させることで配置した衛星の位置を移動可能な点が本作の特色として挙げられます。この要素を活かすために全体的に配置できる衛星の数は少なめに設定されているため、可視化されている敵の進行ルートに合わせて輪っかを回転させ、臨機応変に対応させていくことが攻略のカギ。回転させている最中でも各衛星は機能するので、最大の火力を持った衛星をタフな敵に張り付かせて攻撃を集中させるといったこともできます。反面、オーソドックスなタワーディフェンスでは猛威をふるう周囲の敵の動きを遅くする機能を持つ衛星の使い勝手が若干悪かったり、攻撃対象の細かい選定が出来ないなどの若干癖のある挙動も見られますので、このジャンルに慣れている方でも少し考え方を切り替える必要があるでしょう。

難易度は4段階。ゲーム中特定の条件を満たすことで得られるメダルを獲得していくことがやりこみ要素として挙げられます。全体的に難しすぎず易しすぎずといったバランスで、攻略していく楽しさは十分。比較的余裕のあるステージ設計となっている場面も多く、使用する衛星の選択などの点でプレイヤーの好みも反映させられます。ただ、特定のチャレンジ（5.1）だけはこのゲームらしからぬ異様にシビアな操作タイミングと精度を求められ、実績全解除の最大の壁となっています。ここだけはバランス調整に失敗している感があって悪印象。

ステージの数としては、ストーリーモードが21面、パズル的な要素が強まったチャレンジモードが21面用意されています。タワーディフェンスとしてはステージクリアに主眼を置いており、ハイスコアを目指す作りにはなっていません。一応、どこまで敵のwaveを防いでハイスコアを伸ばせるかの耐久戦となるアーケードモードも別にありますけどね。プレイ時間はどの難易度に挑戦するか、メダル取得を目指すかで若干変わってきますが、1周を通してのプレイで10時間かからないくらいになるかと思います。ステージクリアごとに使用できる衛星は増えていきますし、ランダムで飛来しぶつかった対象にダメージを与える隕石や、常に回転し続ける衛星軌道の輪といったギミックも登場。価格帯も考えると飽きや中だるみを感じない程度のちょうど良い長さではないでしょうか。



[h1]世界観とゲームシステムの両方が上手く嚙み合った隠れた良作[/h1]
私としては世間にもっと評価されてもおかしくない作品だと思いますし、以上の要素をブラッシュアップした続編も出てほしいななんて考えているのですが、さすがに10年も経ったら期待はできませんよねぇ…。

I rate the game Unstoppable Gorg 3.5/5. A pretty good tower defense game with a silly 1950’s B movie (or perhaps TV show) aesthetic.

Beyond its silly style, what sets Unstoppable Gorg apart from other tower defense games is actually a fairly simple little gimmick; instead of taking place on a planet’s surface, defense towers take the form of satellites which are placed into different orbits around planets, space stations or a ship (depending on which level is being played) and must occasionally be rotated into position as each battle progresses to get them within firing range of enemies (don’t worry though, they aim themselves when an enemy is within their firing range). While this situation may sound complex, it really isn’t. The game’s design is actually incredibly simplistic. Despite being set in outer space, all the tactical gameplay really takes place in only two dimensions. That’s right, as with most standard tower defense games, this is essentially a 2D game. 

While not the best tower defense game in existence, Unstoppable Gorg is certainly not bad and is only mildly frustrating if played on the easiest difficulty. If you want added frustration for no good reason, there are a few higher difficulties also. There’s also an endless arcade mode to play around with. The best tower defense game I’ve ever played was Defense Grid: The Awakening, especially if you include all of its many add-ons (and its sequel felt almost like an add-on also) but if you’ve already played Defense Grid and you want even more tower defense gameplay I’d recommend giving Unstoppable Gorg a try, particularly if you can get it for CHEAP. Also, if silly 1950’s sci-fi B movie stuff makes you laugh, the intentionally hokey movie scenes shown in Unstoppable Gorg’s story mode makes this game worth a play through anyhow.

+Standard variety of enemies and satellite (tower) types.

+Really funny, cool 1950s styled movie scenes and aesthetic.

+No major bugs.

+Adequate sound and every single sound conveys a meaning.

+Fairly good level design and some fun mission situations before the story mode ends.

+Despite actually being a fairly short game the story mode didn’t feel either too long or too short. It includes a total of 21 missions/battles.

+/-Mediocre graphics (at best) but this means the game should run well on pretty much any kind of computer.

+/-As is standard in most tower defense games, some levels required a bit of trial and error puzzle gameplay wherein you may have to fail a mission several times before learning how to survive but on the easiest difficulty this never got very frustrating. The levels and enemies are never total push-overs in terms of difficulty and there will be some somewhat anxious and challenging battles here and there. There will definitely be times when you will feel as though you do not have enough resources to survive but figuring out how to best use very limited resources is usually a major component of this type of game.

-Confusing satellite graphics can make it hard to tell what kind of satellite you are looking at.

-Controls for rotating satellite orbits can be confusing and seemingly unresponsive at times. The satellites must be clicked on and drug in a circle along the path of their orbit to rotate them.

-Some satellite types don’t seem to have much of an effect on battles or battle conditions. For example, the satellites which increase the firing range of other satellites don’t really seem to have much of an effect, certainly not enough to justify their resource cost. Other satellite types are amazing and become totally vital (like the repair satellites). This means that some satellites will be used constantly in the game and others will almost never be used.

-Fairly short game lasting a little over 6 hours. Only 21 story mode missions. There are other game modes and several difficulties but once the story mode is completed they feel pointless.

-No ability to alter the plot. No alternate endings. No actual plot-related choices to make. No allies to acquire or decide between. The plot ends with an intentionally silly cliff-hanger. The huge amount of destruction you end up bringing down on the enemies may make you feel like an A-hole and the second half of this game’s plot reminded me, unpleasantly, of Ender’s Game (the book). Not a feel-good ending.

-No ability to easily replay all of the game’s movie scenes (including the mission completed movie scenes) makes it impossible to fully show this game's funny scenes to others.

-The entire game has just two songs, both of which get repetitive quickly.

-Limited camera controls which allow you to zoom in and out but you cannot rotate the view (but you can still see everything anyhow if you zoom out).

Toi qui aimes les [i]tower defense[/i]. Toi qui en as trop fait mais en veux encore, toi qui ne sais plus où donner de la tête. Toi qui as écumé les mers, toi qui as protégé les pyramides, défendu les châteaux et piégé mille fois tout ce qu'il est possible de piéger. Toi qui ne comptes plus les tours et encore moins leurs obus, toi qui as écrasé des millions d'insectes et repoussé des hordes entières de chevaliers noirs, toi qui cherches un nouvel os à ronger, l'heure est venue d'enfin faire franchir à [i]Unstoppable Gorg[/i] le fossé qui sépare ta [i]wishlist[/i] de ta bibliothèque.

 [i]Unstoppable Gorg[/i] a plusieurs qualités. Son [i]gameplay[/i], déjà, nous propose de défendre des planètes et des vaisseaux en plaçant des satellites en orbite. Il est possible de provoquer la rotation des anneaux et donc de déplacer les systèmes de défense qui s'y trouvent, mais à la seule condition de faire pivoter tout le cercle d'un coup. Déplacer une tour signifie donc faire bouger toutes celles qui se trouvent sur le même alignement. Une idée maline mise à l'épreuve par des vagues d'ennemis toujours plus vicieuses. Aussi, son ambiance de science-fiction retro va beaucoup plus loin que les seuls ennemis et les pièges censés les arrêter : l'interface mais aussi des scènes cinématiques qui nous rappellent les vieux films américains sans couleurs, ceux-là mêmes dont les effets spéciaux préhistoriques leur donnaient tant de charme, nous plongent dans une parodie de film de science-fiction. On entendrait presque le souffle sous le déguisement du type déguisé en casserole de l'espace. Et cela, [i]Unstoppable Gorg[/i] parvient parfaitement à le reconstituer.

Une bonne pioche pourvu qu'on se sente obligé d'aller fouiller dans ce rayon si particulier des jeux de défense de tour.

It is a neat little tower defense game.  It treats space as a 2-dimensional thing instead of a 3-dimensional thing by having this space station or what have you in the center.  You set up satellites in various rings with set placement locations and move those rings around so that your satellites can defend against waves of aliens.  The religious fanatic robots from the sun with ships that look like cars from the 1950s, the brain monsters from Venus, and the classic flying saucers of the titular Gorg are your foes, coming in from changing directions with varied units.  
If it sounds sort of bizarre that is because the whole thing has a neat B-movie from the 1950s aesthetic.  Complete with hammy cutscenes between missions that look like old movie reels.  (Soundtrack, appearance of all units, etc. all fit that too)  Campaign mode goes through a B-movie with you as the hero defending against the aliens from destroying various space stations around the Earth and other worlds in the solar system.  Not that directly funny but certainly fun in both gameplay and story.

The game can be challenging (even on lower difficulty settings) without being abusive.  The way to defend against the aliens requires you to think things out, plan ahead, not just wing it.  You'll lose sometimes and have to try a different strategy.  
An underrated gem.  And now I sound like an advertiser hocking it.  But seriously, you'll probably like it.

A pretty simple tower defense game where you place towers in orbits around your base and then move the towers around to adapt to enemies.

There are 21 campaign levels with multiple difficulties and unlockable 'challenge levels' which seem to be the same level but with extra restrictions (like certain orbits are locked or you can't build certain satellites).

What was more interesting to me were the cutscenes. It has the vibe of an old black-and-white B movie mixed with old war propaganda. It's cheesy with stereotypical roles: The male hero with model wife/girlfriend(?), enemy humanoid aliens (guy in costume), female alien enemy seductress, enemy humanoid robot (guy in costume). The simple story isn't really compelling but the effort put into the film made it interesting to watch (plus I don't watch old movies so there's a novelty factor).

Worth a look if you're fine with an obscure (you don't really know how much damage things do) tower defense and like the idea of watching old film.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] I enjoyed the film that was on most missions but not every mission has film to watch, sometimes it's just a newspaper.
[*] I would like a button to replay the film (or a scene replay section in the main menu). Currently you can only see stuff by replaying the missions.
[*] It's nice that clearing objectives on a harder difficulty also counts for easier difficulties
[*] Like a lot of games it doesn't tell you the numbers so it's a hassle to figure out if something is good/optimal or not.
[*] Waves should only start when you've placed a satellite.
[*] It would be nice to be able to hide the UI to see satellite placement options before picking your satellites. It would also be nice to see enemy routes.
[*] I would have liked a 1/2 speed mode for hectic situations.
[*] Why does shift skip the cutscenes?
[*] Sweeper should probably say 'All Damage' or Both or Physical & Energy.
[/list]
