Mata Hari is a 3D rendered 2D point and click adventure game where you guide the eponymous spy through various dangerous missions.

There's worse ideas for video games, but the problem here is that despite the 2008 launch date, the developers chose not to add any widescreen support, so the game falls below standards for contemporary PC gaming.  I can't recommend it.

This game would have been waaaaaay better with fast travel.  The problem is that it takes a couple of minutes to go from location to location due to having to go through the dialogue options to get where you want to go and the slow walking from one end of the screen to the ticket booth, not including the map mini-game which I actually enjoyed.  For a point and click game that requires you to go back and forth between cities constantly, it will drive you crazy and unfuns the game.  

Most of the game is dialogue puzzles; doing the right conversation topics.  The conversations require you to drag a button onto the character even though you are talking to that character. That's just bad UI. The puzzles go from 0 to 100 real quick.

The game is easy generally, but does require some pixel hunting which is another big thumbs down IMO.

The voice acting is cardboard, especially the main character.  

I did enjoy the atmosphere and story, but bad gameplay mechanics, bad voice acting, and tedious travel make this a big thumbs down.  Add in fast travel and easier to navigate dialogue UI  (why try to reinvent the wheel with tile/button dragging, all you created was a square) and the game would improve immensely.

Interessante avventura. Gli autori, con precedente esperienza in case di produzione di videogiochi non proprio da poco, come per esempio la Lucas, hanno voluto cimentarsi nella produzione che tratta di un argomento 'difficile', cioè della vita di Mata Hari. Difficile perché si devono impiantare le tecniche ed i modi propri delle avventure nel panorama della vita una sedicente spia, realmente vissuta. 
Nel fare questo hanno optato per un tono abbastanza leggero, anche se la protagonista è vissuta durante la terribile e tragica Grande Guerra e la sua vita ha avuto un epilogo efferato. L'avventura si lascia giocare, cerca di proporre enigmi in tema, certamente non ricorrendo alla furtività come nei giochi di azione. Molti storceranno il naso davanti ai minigiochi, peraltro saltabili, ma lo fanno a torto. L'opera è ben recitata, ANCHE IN ITALIANO. se si recupera la patch (ormai sono arrivato alla convinzione che Steam prenda dei soldi per non includere MAI le traduzioni italiane). La colonna sonora e la grafica sono adatte all'ambiente storico. Ci sono finali multipli in base a come ci siamo comportati complessivamente nel gioco ed in base anche alla nostra bravura in prove facoltative, come per esempio il recupero di segreti non necessari al proseguimento dell'avventura. Un'altra prova facoltativa è la danza: gli autori infatti hanno ben pensato che la nostra Mata digitale, come la sua controparte reale, non potesse esimersi dall'esibirsi in spettacoli coreografici, da svolgersi secondo le modalità dei giochi di ritmo musicale che ben conosciamo.
(Appendice semiseria: ho visto foto della vera Mata Hari, e nessuna mi ha fatto venire voglia, come dire, di frequentarla. Certo che gli uomini una volta dovevano essere proprio alla canna del gas ... Per essere seri: i canoni della bellezza credo siano molto dipendenti dai periodi storici, e poi molto del fascino dipende dalla personalità, non trasmissibile tramite le foto)

[/quote]

[b]THE CASE FOR[/b]
Based on the real historical figure, you play as the famous exotic dancer/courtesan/spy. You engage with the game world not by shooting and punching but by dancing, seducing, investigating, solving puzzles and avoiding the law and enemy agents, the kind of variety and originality that mainstream games still struggle to even get close to more than 10 years later.

[b]THE CASE AGAINST[/b]
It's shocking that with such a fascinating premise, they still managed to make a surprisingly dull game. Maybe they assumed that by using real life people they wouldn't have to put any work into making them interesting, because the game does not make the most basic efforts to introduce, let alone make us want to get to know any of its characters. Mata herself is completely one-note throughout the whole game, and the supporting characters are virtually indistinguishable from one another. The events that unfold throughout the story are supposed to be a big deal, but everything happens off screen and nothing seems to affect the protagonist at all. Neither her victories nor her failures seem to have any impact, and the consequences of her actions are barely mentioned in passing in consistently dispassionate dialogue. The game skips ahead several years in between episodes, and you're left wondering why they even bothered, because the only thing that seems to change in the game world is the color of Mata's dress. Even the settings, which are probably the best realized aspect of the game, are not affected in the least. The story is supposed to expand all throughout Europe, but the game ends up feeling pretty claustrophobic, as there's very little to explore, you get to see all of its locations pretty early on, and you end up spending most of the time jumping between the same four locations anyway. 

[b]THE VERDICT[/b] 
For all its flaws, I'm not recommending against playing it. It's pretty short and it's worth at least going through it once, but it's best to go in with very, [i]very[/i] low expectations.

[b]Un [i]point&click[/i] pour incarner Mata Hari dans une aventure librement inspirée de la vie réelle de la célèbre danseuse et espionne.[/b]


Après quelques apparitions sur scène dans des spectacles qui ont enthousiasmé le public, celle qui se présente sous le nom de Mata Hari se rend à une soirée dans l'espoir d'y rencontrer un imprésario qui l'aiderait à lancer sa carrière artistique. Du coup, elle va s'engager également comme espionne puis même agent double.
Ainsi commence le jeu pour un scénario mélangeant vérité officielle et fiction, qui prend parfois des libertés avec la chronologie des événements ou fait apparaître d'autres personnages historiques parmi les pnj (dont Marie Curie).



[b][u]J'ai aimé :[/u][/b]
[b]++ l'héroïne : [/b]Le jeu doit beaucoup à son héroïne et à la réputation de la vraie Mata Hari. 
Raconter sa vie est un sujet idéal de roman et l'histoire qu'on vit ici est relativement réelle, rehaussée encore par la présence d'autres personnages historiques, mais sans doute que le scénario de 4 petits chapitres est un peu court.

[b]++ l'écriture : [/b]Les dialogues sont relativement bien écrits et c'est pas si courant dans ce genre de jeu.

[b]++ le doublage : [/b]Le doublage français est de bonne qualité, spécialement celui de Mata Hari.

[b]+ le système de dialogues : [/b]J'ai aimé son originalité à base de choix d'icônes qu'on retrouve autant dans les conversations que dans l'inventaire.

[b]+ l'ambiance : [/b]On retrouve bien l'atmosphère de cette période d'avant 1ère Guerre Mondiale, notamment grâce à la musique adéquate. Chaque lieu bénéficie de petites animations dans le décor mais manque de personnalité et d'espace (presque réduit à un écran unique).

[b]+ le gameplay : [/b]Il est intuitif et la progression est naturellement fluide (en-dehors des mini-jeux) car le jeu a plutôt bien vieilli de manière générale. Il faut compter entre 7 et 9h pour terminer la partie.

[b]+ les graphismes : [/b]C'est visuellement plutôt agréable mais si c'est incontestablement daté techniquement parlant.

[b]+ le prix : [/b]Un tout petit prix qui rend ce jeu accessible même en-dehors des soldes.



[b][u]J'ai moins aimé :[/u][/b]
[b]-- le manque de difficulté : [/b]Les [i]point&click[/i] dans lesquels on est trop ralentis par des énigmes absurdes à la difficulté excessive sont rageants mais quand ils sont trop faciles, c'est pas forcément mieux. Ici, on a souvent une seule chose à faire à la fois et on est beaucoup aidé par le journal et même les pnj. Ca tourne presque au jeu trop casual accessible aux enfants dans le gameplay alors que l'essentiel du propos reste le plus souvent résolument sérieux et mature.

[b]-- les mini-jeux : [/b]Quelques mini-jeux variés et originaux, je dis pas non mais quand ils sont inintéressants et trop répétitifs, ça devient un réel défaut. Alors on peut les passer la plupart du temps mais sinon vous allez oeuvrer dans la séduction, la chorégraphie, le trafic ferroviaire et les réparations électriques.

[b]-- les aller-retours : [/b]Voilà un défaut classique des jeux du genre mais alors qu'au début en se prend à rêver aux voyages à travers l'Europe, les destinations sont finalement peu nombreuses et surtout les trajets aller-retours sont vraiment trop nombreux et peu agréables.

[b]- l'animation : [/b]Ca fait partie des limites techniques des graphismes avec les incrustations des éléments animés alors que l'animations des corps est pourtant très correcte mais dès qu'il y a interaction, avec un objet par exemple, c'est un peu trop limité.

[b]- l'incohérence : [/b]Souvent petites mais bien présentes dans plusieurs situations, ce qui nuit à l'immersion dans l'histoire.

[b]- la danse : [/b]Le mini-jeu de danse est déjà pénible mais alors que sont ridicules les esquisses de mouvements chorégraphiés par Mata Hari et que sont ridicules les réactions enthousiastes du manager. Dommage que l'aspect danse soit si mal traité dans ce jeu.

[b]- les scores : [/b]Il y a un système  de score pour diverses activités et ça n'a aucun intérêt.




Ce jeu est un classique du [i]point&click[/i] de son époque mais il est passé à côté sur trop d'aspects pour devenir la référence qu'il aurait pu être.
Pourtant l'histoire romanesque d'une aventurière sexy pendant une période troublée de l'Histoire avait tout pour faire un grand jeu. Le joueur se retrouve pourtant rapidement englué dans quelque chose de lourd, ennuyant et répétitif qui frise en plus souvent le ridicule. Dommage.

On peut cependant recommander le jeu aux amateurs de [i]point&click[/i] classiques qui n'ont pas peur de se frotter à des oeuvres un peu anciennes.

Pour les autres, on dira que ce n'est pas un titre incontournable ni du genre ni de son époque et que cette Mata Hari reste finalement assez sage.



J'attribue néanmoins le pouce bleu.
En attendant que Mata Hari revienne un jour dans un meilleur jeu.

Very nice adventure about famous dancer and very likely a spy Mata Hari. At the beginning she wishes to get a patron for her dancing career, but she also get captured into web of spies from which she can't never leave. Remaining story follows her life in the background of forthcoming World War.

Through the game you will notice few references on the historical situations, which was very nice! In addition to standard adventure "point and click" mechanics there are some mini-games. Traveling via railway - as a spy you need to avoid enemy spies so you have to choose your way carefully, also you have an option to skip this completely, but you won't get any points to improve your spying skill. Dancing - first you need to find an inspiration for a new dance, only then you can perform - when Mata Hari starts her dance, you will see four circles and flying notes, you need to catch them in the middle to get best score, if they get outside you get minus points, you have limit which you need to achieve otherwise you fail, according to your skill you get the money. In some cases the notes were flying really fast and it was hard to catch them properly with a mouse, would be better if it was suited for a keyboard, but still with some practice it was doable (I think you can skip it, but I am not sure as I have not used it). I got the best score with just few of them and still was able to manage the highest possible cash. When you have found all of the inspiration, you can choose whatever dance you want and make your fortune on the easiest = slowest one. ;) Not really a mini-game, but you have at your disposal the art of seduction. You have to choose the right seduction on the right type of man. Well, I have always succeeded on my second try, that probably mean that I wouldn't be a good spy. X) Besides the clues and info you need for the main story you can find some other information that can uncover more secrets. These are optional, but completing them will improve your spying skill greatly.

I have enjoyed playing Mata Hari, it reminded me of old adventure games. It has such nostalgic touch to it.

Story:
Ihr schlüpft in die Rolle der aufkommenden niederländischen Tänzerin Mata Hari und werdet in Paris als Spionin angeheuert. Ihr versalzt manche Beziehung, andere versüßt ihr, bis schließlich eure Tarnung auffliegt, und ihr zur Doppel- bzw. Mehrfach-Spionin werdet. In der Hoffnung den Krieg abzuwenden verkauft ihr Informationen und sabotiert hochinteressante Entwicklungen der Zeit (!!). Es soll alternative Enden geben. Lässt sich der Krieg abwenden?

Gameplay:
Das Spiel brüstet sich vorallem mit den Waffen der Frau, was zunächst sehr vielversprechend und innovativ klingt. Ob das aber eine so tolle neue Innovation ist? Zunächst beginnt das Spiel auf einer Party, wo man mit Lügen Zwietracht säht (was sehr viel lustiger ist, als man(n) erwartet, wenn man eine gewisse saboteurische Ader hat ). Man lernt den "Umgang" mit Männern und folgt ihnen sogar ins Schlafzimmer. Insgesamt ist das Game sehr dialoglastig. Eigentlich reicht es aus, sich stupide durchzuklicken, bis man bekommt was man will. Knackt man einen Mann nicht sofort, schlägt sich das nur in der Bewertung (die für den Spielverlauf komplett unwichtig ist) nieder. Um Handlungen oder Gespräche durchzuführen, zieht man ein Inventarsymbol auf die gewünschte Person (etwas gewöhnungsbedürftig). Es gibt leider viele Mini-Games, die sich ständig wiederholen und dem klassischen Adventuristen den letzten Nerv rauben. Den Entwicklern sei dank, gibt es einen Panik-Button, der ein Spiel sofort (erfolgreich) beendet.
Die Spieldauer liegt real bei ca. 5 Stunden, bei versprochenen 20 (!!). Vielleicht kommt man auf 10, wenn man jedes Mini-Game mitnimmt. Wäre das Spiel nicht so umständlich, wäre die Spielzeit um einiges kürzer. Um beispielsweise von einer Großstadt in die andere mit dem Zug zu kommen, klickt man sich durchs Taxi, den Fahrkartenschalter, um dann ein Mini-Game zu bestehen... Und man muss wirklich ständig umherreisen.

Die Rätsel:
Im großen und ganzen sehr unterschiedlich und einfallsreich. Dank Panik-Button kommt selten Frustration auf. Manchmal sind die "Rätsel" aber richtig dumm. z.B. ihr seid in Spanien, wollt ein Telefon anzapfen, euch fehlt aber ein Hörer. Also macht ihr euch auf nach Berlin, weil es dort ein öffentliches Telefon gibt, was wohl keiner vermisst (!?!). Mit dem gestohlenen Hörer bewaffnet, könnt ihr zurück in Spanien dem immer noch laufenden Gespräch lauschen. Die Spanier haben wohl echtes Sabbelwasser getrunken. Nebenbei quatscht ihr euch durch die endlosen Dialoge mit Bahnpersonal und Taxifahrern...

Die Atmosphäre:
Die Graphik ist sehr schön gelungen. Zwar sieht alles gezeichnet, comichaft und weniger 3D aus, aber dadurch kommen die Städte sehr malerisch zur Geltung. Zeitlich top getroffen mit beispielsweise Preußischen Flaggen in Berlin und einer immer passend gekleideten Mata Hari hat man das Gefühl in eine andere Zeit einzutauchen. Die Vertonung ist auch ziemlich makellos und der Sound selten störend (nur beim Tanzen, aber das liegt an der Art Mini-Game).

Fazit: Das Game hat wohl seine Höhen und Tiefen. Super interessante Ansatzpunkte in Spionage und selbstbestimmtem Informationsfluss, die z.T. gut aufgegriffen wurden, doch leider durch eine sehr starke Linearität bis hin zur Stupidität/Langeweile spielerisch verdorben worden sind. Insgesamt eine überzeugende Zeitreise mit zeitspezifischen sehr einfallsreichen Rätseln, die allerdings neben manchen einfallslosen Mini-Games lächerlich herüberkommen.

Норм.

Revivez les trépidantes péripéties de la Célèbre Mata hari, et découvrez les somptueuses rues de Paris, Berlin, Monaco et d'autres villes encore, au moment de la première guerre mondiale.

S'il est vrai que la belle époque est très bien reproduite dans cette aventure point and clic, que les doublages Français sont aussi très bien interprétés, on se heurte dès les premières minutes de jeu à certaines incohérences, à un gameplay lourd et redondant, et à un scénario dont le script semblerait par moments être tout droit sortit d'une mauvaise sitcom à la Française.

J'avais envie de recommander positivement ce jeu, j'en avais réellement l'intention, mais plus j'ai progressé dans l'histoire, plus je m'en suis éloignée à cause de ce gameplay... J'en suis arrivée à cette conclusion finale : ce jeu est chiant !

Pour ceux qui ont envie de l'acheter en ayant lu d'autres évaluations plus positives que la mienne, je vous conseillerai de stopper ici votre lecture, car ce qui va suivre pourrait contenir de potentiels "spoils".

Ce jeu se découpe en 4 chapitres, dès le premier chapitre je m'y suis ennuyée et j'ai eu du mal à accrocher, en effet je n'ai pas trouvé fort intéressant le fait de devoir faire un brin de causette avec tous les personnages présents dans l'environnement...

Tout au long de l'histoire, j'ai trouvé certaines répliques très cliché et l'une d'elle m'a fait pouffer de rire, je ne sais pas ce que vous en penserez, mais cette phrase m'a semblé tellement ridicule : "allez dire à cet idiot qu'il est idiot" que je n'ai pu m'empêcher de la relever et la noter ici.

J'ai noté aussi par endroits, certaines incohérences comme par exemple le fait de demander à un artiste de vous peindre un portrait au fusain, après avoir acquiescé celui-ci s'exécute mais en tenant toujours son pinceau et sa palette de gouaches dans les mains...

Autre chose et non des moindres, que vous pourrez constater du début à la fin : tous les personnages semblent avoir été comme contaminés par un mystérieux virus qui a sérieusement altéré leur mémoire immédiate !!! 
Exemple : vous parlez à un personnage, il répond à vos questions normalement mais vous retournez lui parler quelques secondes après et tel un amnésique, il vous répond "je ne vous connait pas" Ou alors ce foutu portier à qui vous devrez montrer 10 000 fois votre laissez-passer à chaque fois que vous voulez entrer dans ce club... c'est usant !

Il y a une phase aussi où vous devrez trouver de l'inspiration pour améliorer vos enchainement en matière de danse, ça m'a également fait beaucoup rire lorsque le spectateur s'esclaffait d'un gratifiant "fabuleux !" alors que Mata nous sort un pauvre déhanché à droite, un à gauche pour finir par un "majestueux" levé de bras au ciel, cela n'avait absolument rien de fabuleux croyez moi (rires).

Mata Hari ou plutôt "le perpétuel voyage de Mata Hari" aurait été un titre beaucoup plus adéquate car il résumerai plus clairement le gameplay et les objectifs de ce jeu !

Arrivés au chapitre 2 vous aurez de nombreux allez retours à faire entre plusieurs villes, cela se reproduira de façon perpétuelle jusqu'à la fin du jeu. En gros et sans trop exagérer, vous passerez au moins 70% de votre temps de jeu à cliquer sur le taxi, à arpenter toutes les gares et à avancer sur cette carte que vous finirez par maudire.

De ce fait, vous serez tellement exaspéré par ces voyages que vous finirez pour vous détacher de toute immersion, si immersion vous avez pu ressentir...

J'arrive à la fin du jeu, mais j'ai du quitter la partie avant terme tellement j'ai ressenti un ras le bol.
Il y a plusieurs fin à découvrir et franchement là j'ai envie de crier, de m'arracher les cheveux et l'idée même de rejouer le jeu depuis le début pour tenter une fin différente me donne une grosse poussée de boutons, je sent l'allergie monter en moi, je vais faire un oedème de qinck et m'étouffer rien que d'y penser. 

NON, NON et NON !!!! Je n'ai plus envie d'y rejouer !!!!!

In consideration of the calibre of game that Mata Hari is--a small, budget PC game of the type that were rife before the adventure game resurgence--I'll try to as fair as I can in order to afford the game the credit it deserves. However, if it's an abbreviated version one wishes, Mata Hari is not worth the time it would require to play it, as it simply doesn't do anything to single itself from the middling crowd.

Taking as its protagonist the real-life historical character of Mata Hari, the game superimposes her onto a decidedly tepid and uneventful series of adventures that culminate in a competent, if not memorable, ending. It speaks to the lack of individuality and creativity that developers decided on needlessly including characters that are barely, ever-so-thinly related to your character in any concievable way: you'll be chumming it up with Marie Curie, playfully engaging with the inspiration for the Mercedes brand, and meeting and impersonating the chemist Fritz Harber. Mata Hari was already an intriguing character that indeed did engage in some spycraft, and many of the persons she engages with are historically accurate, but it befuddles me why the game goes out of its way to feature unnecessary historical figures. The concievable and readily offered explanation is that the game itself is boring; amidst the backdrop of pre-WWI Europe espionage and infamous Bohemian indulgence, there just isn't a whole lot there. It's a shallow, easy game that augments its simple playtime by including a number of mini-games--all of which you'll be doing multiple times--that aren't particularly fun--and are often tedious. Perhaps the point that all the mini-games can be skipped speaks for their perceived value, as someone must have realised just how quickly they'd grow dull. 

Positively speaking, the game has some universally competent voice-acting, and somewhat faithfully portrays the sensuality of its character, even it does occasionally stray with its excessive, giddy frivolity. It's a precarious act trying to depict a character like Mata Hari in a video game without bleeding into sexist territory, which the game arguably does as Mata Hari carelessly sleeps around and eschews no qualms about flirting, but ultimately the historical character of Mata Hari mostly justifies the game's portrayal.      

Mata Hari is sugary, colourful cereal drowned in skim milk: set during an politically-charged epoch and portraying an sensual, lurid historical figure, the game fails to do more to define itself and instead relies on gimmicks and meaningless interactions.

Do hry lze doinstalovat [url=https://prekladyher.eu/preklady/mata-hari.88/]české titulky[/url] s úplnou diakritikou.

[h1]JAK SE HRAJE[/h1]
Hra "MATA HARI" se ukládá pouze manuálně, když neprobíhá rozhovor nebo minihra. Mata Hari je dnes světoznámou špionkou a hráč, který za ni hraje, s ní prožije čtyři kapitoly. Pohyb mezi lokacemi této adventury je řešen několika způsoby. První klasický je pohyb chůzí, druhý je pomocí taxi přesunem na známou lokaci v rámci města a třetí je vlakem. Cesta vlakem je řešena jako minihra. Jde o tahovou minihru s pohybem po zastávkách, kdy hrdinku pronásledují jiní špioni a ona se musí dostat do cíle, aniž by ji špioni dostihli. Za úspěšnou cestu je hrdinka odměněna body. Mata Hari byla sice špionkou, ale veřejnosti byla známá především jako tanečnice. A tanec je další minihrou této adventury. Zde stačí myší najíždět do čtyř kroužků ve chvíli, když do některého přijede nota. Čím blíže je nota prostředku kroužku, tím více bodu. Čím úspěšnější vystoupení, tím více peněz. Rozhovory jsou nedílnou součástí většiny adventur a tady tomu není jinak. Rozhovory jsou řešeny přesouváním ikonek, které zastupují nějakou větu. Takže když se chcete zeptat na auto, vyberete ikonku auta. Tímto způsobem jsou rozhovory velice intuitivní. Mezi minihry by se dala zařadit ještě mikrohra v rámci rozhovoru. Mata Hari se nebojí použít své ženské zbraně a sváděním mužů dosáhnout toho co chce ona. Nepodařená manipulace nemá fatální následek a tak hráč může dle libosti zkoušet, co na kterého muže platí. Lokace hry jsou pěkné a vynikají svým živým ztvárněním. Některé z nich se v průběhu hry i několikrát změní. Animace postav je přirozená a hlavní hrdinka během hry vystřídá několik různorodých oblečení. Ovládání postavy je přesné a funguje zde i přeskočení chůze dvojklikem a přerušení věty pravým tlačítkem. Mezerníkem lze zobrazit všechny aktivní prvky lokace. Ovšem jsou zde dvě výjimky. První je při hledání inspirace pro tanec a druhá výjimka jsou tajné dokumenty, jejichž sbíráním hrdinka získává špionážní body. Body z cest vlakem, body ze sbírání tajných dokumentů a peníze za tanec ve finále ovlivní epilog celé hry.

Beyond that however, everything falls apart. Do go play Black Mirror 2 and 3 though (optionally the first one, for background, it's from a different studio and annoying to play though). They're awesome and show how much this small studio learned in the interval.

Defense Grid The Awakening ist ein Science-Fiction Tower-Defense-Spiel, bei dem der Spieler als einsamer Stratege ganze Horden von Aliens davon abhalten muss, Energiekerne aus einem oder mehreren  Orten auf der isometrischen  3D-Karte zu stehlen und abzutransportieren. 

Unterstützung gibt dabei das hochgeladene, sehr redselige Bewusstsein eines Veteranen vorhergehender Konflikte. Seine gut geschriebenen Texte sind dann auch die einzigen Storyfragmente, denn Intro oder Outro gibt es keines. Aber es gibt Medaillen, wenn man keine Kerne verliert und möglichst wenig Türme baut. Das ganze System ist jedoch so undurchsichtig, dass es wenig Freude macht, auf allen Levels die Goldmedaille anzustreben. 

Meist hat man ohnehin genug zu tun, seine knappen Ressourcen in die verschiedenen Türme zu stecken und diese, vom billigen MG-Turm bis zu zeitverzerrenden Feldgeneratoren oder Flugabwehrraketen, an strategisch passenden Punkten zu platzieren. Im Idealfall laufen die diversen Alientypen gewaltige Umwege und spazieren schnurstracks in Reichweite der Türme. Das Ganze ist sehr flüssig spielbar, super mit der Maus zu steuern und macht unglaublich Spaß. Wird man einmal überrumpelt, weil etwa überraschenderweise bestimmte Gegner auftauchen, die man (noch) nicht erwartet hatte, hilft nur, den Level neu zu starten. 

Etwas Auswendiglernen ist also notwendig. Dennoch eine Empfehlung von mir, da das Spiel auch recht preiswert ist.

[h1]No envejeció nada mal...[/h1]

Recuerdo mi primer acercamiento al título en su día en el Xbox 360 por el 2009-10, y darle cientos de horas, para sacar el oro/platino de scores y los retos que son muchísimos, y en esta ocasión tiene todos los DLC's de manera asequible y barata, de los mejores tower defense existentes.

[h2]>A Grandes Rasgos:[/h2]
Pues... este titulito es un tower defense, en el que luchamos contra alienígenas que buscan llevarse las "pilas" de nuestro núcleo, si se llevan todas es game over, y el objetivo es sobrevivir cierto número de oleadas que va incrementando conforme se avanza la historia, así como las torres disponibles que tenemos y los enemigos que varían, en su momento fue de los mejores exponentes del género, aunque hoy en día el 2 es mejor por obvias razones, pese a ello la campaña y mapitas que casi llegan al centenar lo hacen una obra de notar, al menos si te gusta el género.

[h2]>De que va la historia:[/h2]
Pues... ya la dije, pero la reitero, no tiene mucha ciencia; aliens buscan eliminar nuestro núcleo de poder, como somos una IA debemos de defender el mismo para ayudar a la población civil, eso se entiende, que tampoco sobreabunda, haciéndolo más un título arcade-casual y divertido.

[h3]>Lo Bueno:[/h3]
+20 niveles de historia, más los retos y variantes, sin problema da mucha rejugabilidad (60 variantes) y eso solo historia, que los DLC's dan otro tanto y poco más de niveles más complejos y sus retos y variantes; si se busca algo longevo de buen precio es una opción.
+Como es norma en el género, es muy divertido el gestionar el posicionamiento de las torres.
+Logros relativamente fáciles, jugando.
+La cantidad de torres es decente.
+Tanto banda sonora como efectos de sonido cumple.

[h3]>Lo malo:[/h3]
-Que el "port" envejeció un poco mal; si tienes windows 11, tal vez se te trabe iniciándolo, a lo que la única solución que encontré fue cambiarle el archivo config y ponerle FALSE en el valor de FULLSCREEN, ya dentro del juego le puedes cambiar la resolución, sin embargo, debes de hacer siempre ese cambio al archivo antes de jugar o se queda trabada la pantalla.

[h2]>Resumiendo:[/h2]
Pues... si el "port" no tuviera errores, sería el mejor exponente del género en la plataforma: 9/10, sin embargo, la falta de atención de los developers y plataforma, para tener al punto y jugables todos los juegos, le quitan un poquito de calidad 8/10, al menos es jugable, y desgraciadamente no todos pueden ser gog, y realmente preocuparse por sus consumidores y la cultura de los videojueguitos.

Dicho lo anterior, si te gusta el género y lo ves en descuento es un imperdible y jugable a la fecha, con maromas técnicas.

One of the major sins I feel that's in this game is the time for construction / upgrade ... instead of towers being click and they pop up, it's click ... and then you wait ... for a while ... until they pop up.  The same is true with upgrades ... you have to time upgrades so that they're happening when a wave isn't slipping by while you're doing much needed upgrades.

An older game, but the interface felt dated at the time as I remember ... it feels a bit clunky to have both the point of interaction (where you want to build / upgrade) locked to the visual area (that is, I'd like to be able to, say, have my camera in one place while my cursor is in another) ... and it makes selecting towers / upgrades also difficult because it sort of puts it in a side menu that is only reactive to the mouse movement.  (I'm guessing it was designed for a platform OTHER than PC because it certainly doesn't feel like it was designed for PC)

It's okay, the graphics work out, but you're always so far out from units that you can't really appreciate how they look or easily distinguish them from one another ... they're generic aliens.

Defense Grid: The Awakening es un tower defense sólido y muy bien diseñado, pero también extremadamente exigente si decides ir a por el 100 %.

A nivel jugable, el juego cumple muy bien. Hay mapas que realmente te hacen pensar y planificar, especialmente si buscas optimizar rutas y conseguir las mejores puntuaciones. Sin embargo, también es cierto que existe cierta repetición en la base jugable, algo habitual en el género, pero que aquí se nota con el tiempo.

La dificultad es uno de sus rasgos más marcados. En muchos momentos puede resultar frustrante, y si solo quieres jugar, hay estrategias bastante dominantes (como abusar de ciertas torres). Pero si decides completarlo al máximo, el nivel de exigencia sube muchísimo.

El mayor problema viene precisamente con los logros. Conseguir el 100 % es una tarea larga, exigente y, en ocasiones, desesperante. Tener que repetir niveles una y otra vez para conseguir el oro puede llegar a saturar, alargando la experiencia muchísimo más de lo esperado.

A nivel visual, el juego se ve bien, aunque se echa en falta una cámara más flexible. El apartado sonoro cumple, con una música agradable y efectos que acompañan correctamente la acción.

Los contenidos adicionales y expansiones están bien trabajados, con guiños interesantes como los mapas inspirados en Portal, que aportan variedad y un plus para quienes quieran más.

En resumen, un tower defense muy recomendable si te gusta el género y disfrutas de los desafíos exigentes. Eso sí, si vas a por el 100 %, prepárate para una experiencia larga y bastante dura.

[h1] REVIEW [/h1]
[b] Mayhem Intergalactic [/b] is a turn-based, strategy game.  
[h3] STORY [/h3]
There is no story, background, or setup to the game.
[h3] GAMEPLAY[/h3]
The game plays much like a simple version of a board game. Every turn you choose to move and attack a planet or stay and defend. You upgrade a factory on any of the planets you own to continue generating new ships. Ships build every 2 turns on your planets. The goal is to own all of the planets
[h3] PLAYTIME [/h3]
The game is mildly difficult at the start of the map, as there is a factor of RNG that occurs, much like dice rolls in RISK do. Play time is ~3-5 hours to get all achievements.  Some achievements are very grind intensive. Additionally there are some multiplayer achievements that will require you to know or have another account to play against (and win 100 games).
[h3] INFORMATION [/h3]
The multiplayer achievements will be hard as close to no one is playing the game. (I played this game when it was first released to get all the achievements so I cannot confirm if they unlock in local multiplayer or not.)
[h3] COMPLAINTS [/h3]
There is nothing specific to complain about for this game.
[h3] REPLAYABILITY [/h3]
The game has replayability as it is a game you can load up and play a quick start game at any time, and these game matches can take as little as 15 minutes
[h3] RECOMMENDATION [/h3]
I recommend the game to anyone who is an achievement hunter or anyone looking for an old school computer board game like experience. Due to the age of the game and need for other players this is not a game I would recommend unless on a discount, or on a planned purchase event with a friend.

While the devs describe this game as a 'streamlined take on the classic "4x" genre', that's a bit of an overstatement. It's pretty much just a straight line. There realy isn't much to do other than build up an fleet and try to overwhelm everything as you expand outward. Other than your ships, the only resource to manage is upgrading factories on planets so they will build more ships each turn. This does forfit any ship building for that planet that turn and the only limit is that you can only upgrade one factory per turn & a particular factory cannot be upgraded on consecutive turns.

The main negative of this game is that there is no online community anymore, meaning that there are 3 achievements that will be impossible to earn without help from friends who also own this game.

So why do I recommend it? Because sometimes simple is fun. It's easy to generate a small map and have a quick game that you can finish in under 15 minutes or pull up a huge one for an 8 player last-man-standing war that can last a while. If you either allow the adaptive AI to level up as you win games (or raise it manually), eventually your opponents will put up a decent fight. If they get to be too much, you can always knock it down a bit to make it challenging and fun for you the player (and turn off adaptive AI). Without any real online play I don't think I'd pay full price, but if you can catch it on good sale it worth a few bucks for a quick and simple strategy fix.

Mayhem Intergalactic is a fun update to a classic game type. To win, a player must eliminate all enemy starships and planets. Planets produce starships, which can be sent to other planets to conquer or bolster defenses. The tricky part is that space travel can take multiple turns. Two fleets might pass one another on long voyages, leaving an undefended planet for attackers to conquer while the planet that fleet departed from gets demolished by the enemy fleet that just left the planet they attacked. If it sounds confusing, it can be odd to try to outthink your opponents to attack them but defend your own holdings, but there's no tech tree or micromanagement to handle. This is one of those simple yet complex fun to play games. The graphics are decent, the music and sound are good, and its mechanics, controls, and help are solid. Mayhem Intergalactic's well worth a few bucks for a bit of mental exercise.

Despite being released several years ago, this game is still a very original puzzle-platformer and it still has not lost its spark. The concept is simple and has been used countless times since then: use the environment to progress through the levels. In this case, rotation is the key. The puzzle aspect of each level is very attainable once you get used to the physics of the game. Additionally, new interesting mechanics are introduced as you advance through the levels, which is always welcome and prevents the game from becoming repetitive. I wish these mechanics were exploited more, to be honest. 

The paper-collage artwork is definitely unique and gives the game a very special personality, although the novelty wears off quickly. Maybe adding a little more variety, such as other elements to interact with or use, wouldn’t have hurt.
The sound effects, though, are another story. Although the self made sounds seemed an intriguing idea at first, they became annoying too fast for me. The crunching sound heard every time the character dies (which is quite often) is currently stuck in my head.

What I struggle with the most is how the fall damage and the momentum gained with rotations are designed. I’m not really sure if this is to prevent the player from finding an easy workaround in the levels, but both elements are far too punishing. There are some instances where a jump / rotation would definitely cause a death, but surprisingly the character is still alive. Move a few inches away, and in a very similar situation, the character is torn to pieces. This unpredictability is simply frustrating.

Although the game could’ve been a bit more polished in some areas, it is still an enjoyable experience. Plus, several bonus levels and challenge modes can be unlocked. I might attempt to play them later on, but they seem intended for people with a set of skills and patience that I definitely lack.

Puzzle platformer with a unique paper cutout artstyle, and one of three games (the other two being VVVVVV, and Gravity Rush) with gravity direction changing mechanics where I actually like what that mechanic adds to the game.

I finish incredibly few games from bundles, I just like trying them out, and supporting indie devs, but this was one of the very few I actually played all the way through, and picked up as a gift for a few friends I thought would enjoy.

An unusual indie platformer built around one strong core mechanic: rotating the entire world around your character. You can change the direction of gravity, which makes familiar platforming situations work in unexpected ways. A wall can become the floor, the ceiling can turn into the path forward, and a simple jump can become a small puzzle about momentum, timing, and fall distance.

The gameplay is mostly about careful movement, spatial puzzle-solving, and knowing when to rotate the world at the right moment. At times the game demands precision and can be a bit frustrating, especially when a bad rotation or fall forces you to replay a section. Still, the main idea is implemented well, and the levels gradually find different ways to use the mechanic instead of relying on the same trick over and over.

The visual style is also worth mentioning. The game looks like an animated paper collage, with torn edges, cut-out textures, and slightly surreal backgrounds. It is not just a decorative choice, but an important part of the atmosphere. The world feels strange, fragile, and a little abstract, which fits very well with the constant disruption of normal gravity.

Overall, "And Yet It Moves" is a very distinctive and memorable platformer. A good choice for players who enjoy experimental indie games, unusual puzzles, and visual styles that stand apart from the usual look.

And Yet It Moves gradually finds its footing with the rotation mechanic in the same way the player does. At times though, the game’s rough nature gets in the way of your enjoyment, your standard jumping already a bit weak but some gimmicks can be a bit unruly to wrangle if you don’t do them perfectly on your first attempt. The game gets more creative the deeper you get into it, but it’s certainly held back by how often your failures arise from little issues in how the game handles the way you and other objects move.

(DO NOT 100% THIS GAME, YOU WILL NOT ENJOY IT, JUST DO A CASUAL PLAYTHROUGH.) There is so much I want to say about this game, but then my review willl be too long. I will try to keep this brief. I have a love-hate relationship with And Yet It Moves. I'll start with the good parts. The artstyle of this game is timeless, and is the one part of the game that doesn't feel dated. If you ever wanted to play an Eric Carle book ( The man who Illustrated The Hungry Catterpillar) then this game is for you! The sound effects of this game are also funny, my personal favorites are the monkey sounds in chapter two (which is just the developers of this game making monkey sounds, lol), and the iconic/uniconic sound of falling in a black hole (just a dude whistling.) The soundtrack is original and cool-sounding, with all the sound effects and songs being composed only with the voices of humans. I have a soft spot for this game, so I didn't really notice or care about the flaws/bugs on my casual playthroughs, but GOOD LORD MAN, the mechanics of this game are inconsistent as Hell. The game tells you slopes don't kill you if you land on them, then there are perfect looking slopes that sometimes kill you and sometimes don't kill you. Sometimes you die from fall damage, sometimes you don't! THERE'S NO RHYME OR REASON!!! (There is also a bug where sometimes you boot up the game and your mouse cursor disappears, really weird.) And if you decide to get all gold badges for this game, it'll make you want to RIP ALL YOUR HAIR OUT INDIVIDUALLY.  There are three badges to get for each mode (Limited Rotations, Survival, and Time Trial.) Limited rotations is just beating a level in as little rotations as possible, (the game is about rotating the world,) Survival is just trying to get through a world without dying, and Time Trial*. *Time trial is the hardest of the three, which is just you needing to beat a level under a pre-made time limit, and some of these pre-made time limits are complete HORSESHIT on some levels, some are fairly easy to complete, and others require amazing percision to perform, but if you put a lot of elbow grease into it, it's only incredibly obnoxious and exhausting and insane. That's ignoring the last four levels. After beating the epilogue level, you unlock four hard final levels. These levels are fine to do on a normal playthrough, and honestly, the first two are easy to 100%, third is really annoying but doable, and the last level is seriously EVIL. The Chase is unironically the most bullshit level to ever get all the badges on. You need to complete an incredibly hard level on a strict time limit, while also needing to wrestle with the annoying inconsistent mechanics. You will die so many times on this level. You will start to feel hatred for the developers for this challenge, you will begin to go insane from the silence of the no music in these final four levels and the sounds of enemies chasing you. It requires insane luck, yes there's some skill to it, but it's mostly luck. It's too long to explain, just know it's like being teleported to the deepest layer of Hell where it's all frozen and cold, which is what you'll feel after you 100% this level. I decided to 100% this level first for some reason, and every subsequent level after that felt so much easier it's insane, and I'm glad I did it this way. Every other badge is Super Weenie Hut Jr's compared to this shit. If any of you out there are interested in buying this game, DO NOT SEEK OUT TO FULLY COMPLETE I HAVE TO REITERATE ON THIS. The developers genuinely dropped the ball hard on how they went about this Crazy achievement. I felt so much anger everytime this game kicked me in the nuts, but I kept going. It feels gratifying finally completing the last level and the whole game for that matter, but it just isn't worth it. It requires too much luck with the inconsistent engine this game runs off for it to be worth it. This review ended up being long, but whatever. I do recommend this game to people, it's short, but I feel like it's memorable. It is the first game this studio has ever made, after all, just don't 100% it. if you do feel like 100% this game, come to me, I'll be glad to help.

J'ai connu [b] And Yet It Moves [/b] grâce à sa démo sur le WiiWare qui était sortie à l'époque. Ça faisait au moins 10 ans que j'y avais pas joué, et je me suis dit sur le coup de la nostalgie que j'allais l'acheter.
Quelle erreur !

Autant certains niveaux je m'en souviens et ils sont funs, autant d'autres c'est juste du die and retry en boucle, des mécaniques chiantes, et beaucoup de bugs à en croire que le jeu n'a pas été testé après sa sortie en 2009.

Passé les niveaux sur le thème de la jungle, bien que la plupart étaient déjà chiants et certaines mécaniques incompréhensibles si tu regardes pas de vidéo walkthrough, le reste c'est juste difficile et heureusement que y avait ces niveaux sur la démo car sinon j'aurai pété un câble à l'époque je pense.

D'ailleurs la version WiiWare est beaucoup plus maniable concernant l'inclinaison dans les niveaux, le jeu se met en pause et tu peux vraiment choisir l'inclinaison comme tu le veux, puis relâcher quand t'es prêt. On dirait que le jeu a pas été conçu pour être joué sur PC, l'inclinaison est instantanée et très limitée (seulement 4 angles possibles), rendant certains niveaux plus difficiles que sur Wii.

Et concernant les sauvegardes, je trouve idiot que les checkpoints dans les niveaux ne sauvegardent pas la partie. Y a une fois j'étais à la fin d'un niveau et le labyrinthe était trop casse-tête, donc je suis parti me coucher, le lendemain en reprenant la partie j'étais au tout début du niveau, m'obligeant à recommencer les 20 minutes que j'ai perdues la veille. Ou alors quand un niveau est littéralement injouable à cause de bugs qui n'ont jamais été patchés, relancer le jeu oblige donc à tout se retaper et on a même pas la certitude que cette fois ça va fonctionner quand on sera arrivé à la partie qui était buguée.

Bref, je pense que j'aurais dû me contenter de la démo, je soupçonne même que les niveaux chiants du jeu n'ont pas été inclus dans la démo pour justement garder les seuls niveaux funs et intéressants du jeu. Dégueulasse comme marketing, et très déçu de mon achat. Comme quoi la nostalgie peut souvent être trompeuse.

《重力世界》是一款解谜平台跳跃游戏，背景设定在一个由撕碎的纸张构成的独特世界。在这个纸片拼贴世界里，你可以跳跃、奔跑，而最重要的能力是：旋转整个世界。学习运用旋转带来的物理效果，来破解途中遇到的各种棘手机关与难题。
你也可以在不同关卡中与时间赛跑，挑战自己的最快纪录。你的闯关过程会被记录为 “幽灵回放”，你可以将它与成绩一同上传至全球在线排行榜。你还能下载其他玩家的幽灵回放，与朋友和来自世界各地的陌生人比拼，看看谁能找到最快的通关路线。
在备受好评的原型版发布后，我们为你带来《重力世界》完整版本，包含三大风格唯美的场景与大量全新挑战。
进阶平台跳跃：除了跳跃与奔跑，你还能以 90 度为单位旋转整个世界。
17 个风格独特的关卡：在超凡的纸片拼贴世界中展开烧脑解谜，拥有三大不同场景，搭配手工制作的音效与音乐，让世界生动鲜活。
速通模式：你可以在每个关卡与时间或已记录的幽灵回放竞速，也可以在整个场景中进行马拉松式连续闯关。
在线排行榜与可分享的幽灵回放：挑战好友与全球玩家，冲击高分榜，精进你的旋转操控技巧。

And Yet It Moves is a distinctive indie puzzle-platformer that stands as an early example of how a single, well-executed idea can redefine an entire gameplay experience. Developed and published by Broken Rules, the game takes familiar platforming fundamentals—running, jumping, avoiding hazards—and reframes them through a deceptively radical mechanic: the ability to rotate the entire world. Rather than merely controlling a character within a static environment, players are asked to think spatially, treating the level itself as a manipulable object whose orientation directly determines gravity, momentum, and survival.

From the first moments, the game establishes its unusual identity through its visual presentation. Everything appears to be constructed from layered paper cutouts, rough sketches, and collage-like textures, giving the impression that the world has been assembled by hand rather than rendered digitally. This aesthetic choice is more than cosmetic; it reinforces the experimental, playful tone of the game and helps players accept the strange logic of a world that can be spun on its axis at any time. The fragile look of the protagonist—who literally tears apart when crushed or dropped from too great a height—further ties the visual style into the mechanics, making failure feel thematically consistent rather than merely punitive.

The core mechanic of rotating the world is what truly defines And Yet It Moves. With a simple input, the entire level can be turned in 90-degree increments, instantly changing which surfaces function as floors, walls, or ceilings. Gravity always pulls downward relative to the screen, so every rotation becomes a deliberate act of problem-solving. Obstacles that seem impossible when approached traditionally often become trivial once the world is reoriented, and safe ground can instantly become a deadly drop if rotated carelessly. This constant recontextualization of space forces players to abandon conventional platforming instincts and instead think in terms of geometry, timing, and cause-and-effect.

Level design is tightly built around teaching and expanding this idea without overwhelming the player. Early stages act as gentle tutorials, introducing rotation in safe environments where experimentation is encouraged. As the game progresses, new hazards such as falling rocks, crushing walls, spikes, and fire are layered in, demanding more precise rotations and quicker reactions. Mistakes are frequent, but the checkpoint system is forgiving, ensuring that failure serves as a learning tool rather than a source of frustration. The rhythm of trial, error, and discovery becomes the backbone of the experience.

Although the game lacks a traditional narrative, there is a subtle sense of progression conveyed through atmosphere and structure. Environments gradually evolve from claustrophobic caves into more abstract and open spaces, giving the impression of a journey without explicitly telling a story. Music and sound design play a quiet but effective role here, supporting the surreal tone without drawing attention away from the puzzles themselves. The absence of dialogue or exposition allows players to focus entirely on interaction and interpretation, letting the mechanics speak for themselves.

One of the most common criticisms of And Yet It Moves is its relatively short length. Once players fully grasp the rotation mechanic, the game does not dramatically expand or subvert it with additional systems, meaning the experience can feel brief for those seeking long-term depth or replayability. Some players may also find the physics occasionally unforgiving, especially in later sections where precise timing is required and a single misjudged rotation can result in instant failure. However, these moments rarely feel unfair, as the rules of the world remain consistent throughout.

Ultimately, And Yet It Moves endures because of its confidence and restraint. It does not attempt to pad its runtime with unnecessary features or dilute its identity with unrelated mechanics. Instead, it commits fully to a single, elegant idea and explores it thoroughly within a compact framework. For fans of puzzle-platformers who enjoy games that challenge spatial reasoning and reward creative thinking, it remains a memorable and influential title. Even years after its release, its core concept still feels fresh, serving as a reminder that innovation in games often comes not from complexity, but from seeing familiar ideas from an entirely new angle.

This mostly generic platformer has an interesting aesthetic and a fun gimmick that is tired now but I understand was somewhat ahead of its time, but the best descriptor I can give it is "annoying." The background ambience is annoying, so I turned that off. The sound effects are also annoying - very repetitive and insistent with no variation - but they give important gameplay cues. The player character's jumps are largely useless, as the true "jumping" you're supposed to do is achieved by rotating the world. Fine. But then you're contending with the absolutely unforgiving - and inconsistent - fall damage. Annoying.

There are times when a fall will kill you seemingly just because, and other falls that should be fatal but aren't because that is what the game wants you to do. You're *supposed* to be able to break your fall safely on sloped surfaces, but even the slope used to introduces this mechanic only works a fraction of the time. Every movement demands exact and mysterious precision that the graphics make hard to perceive and the controls mostly don't allow. You die. You die. You die. All while the entire vibe of the game appears to want to be relaxing.

I hope you enjoy jumping on bamboo poles. I spent the significant majority of my playtime trying to time my jumps in the nth of a second allowed to increase the jump distance a fraction of an inch. Missing that miniscule window of time means, more often than not, having to start over.

The puzzles all felt bland and lacked the "aha!" moment of figuring it out. Truly, the most puzzling part was figuring out which corner to try to fling the character towards, because whatever next platform was outside the view of the screen...

Also, I did encounter a game-breaking glitch in which a swing that was required to get from point A to B simply blipped out of existence and wouldn't come back. It wasn't stuck anywhere, it just disappeared while I was looking at it. There's no option to reset a checkpoint, so I just had to throw that run. Which was annoying, especially because it was after I had finally cleared a bunch of the aforementioned tedious bamboo poles.

Started as a computer science project of the Vienna University of Technology in 2007, And Yet It Moves is an innovative platform/puzzle game made by an independent developer. There is no real story in the game; as a nameless character, the goal is to traverse levels from a start to an endpoint. Jumping is the only move the protagonist has, but that is not all that can be done. At any time, the level the protagonist is in can be spun by 90° or 180°, causing time to freeze for a brief moment, and gravity to resume after the rotation has been completed. Spinning the screen has physical consequences, since gravity always points downwards, and rotating the level does not impact neither the momentum of the protagonist nor that of any other objects in the level. Falling from too high, though, kills the protagonist, so endlessly spinning a level to reach the end is not an option. Other obstacles like fires or black holes can also kill the protagonist. There are no lives, though, and a series of well-placed checkpoints make the challenges manageable; each checkpoint also clearly indicates in which direction the next one is, making navigation easy. And Yet It Moves has really stylish and unique visuals; the levels resemble a paper collage and even the main character is just a cutout pencil line-drawing on white paper. The soundtrack is mostly composed of ambient noises and amazingly performed beat-boxing. There are only 17 levels, making the game short, yet excellently paced. All things considered, And Yet It Moves is a very solid indie platform/puzzle game, worth the time it takes to finish it.

And Yet It Moves é um jogo de puzzle de plataforma no qual você pode rotacionar o mundo, assim alterando a gravidade, para passar de obstáculos e chegar no final de suas várias fases. Eu acho que ele é um jogo com uma mecânica inventiva pra época, e que faz um trabalho decente em usar ela de maneiras interessantes ao longo de sua duração, mas que não envelheceu tão bem quando comparado com seus contemporâneos do meio independente, assim como com as experiências que esse meio consegue nos proporcionar hoje em dia.

Meu maior problema com ele foi que suas mecânicas se baseiam em física, e em muitos momentos achei seus sistemas bem instáveis, são bem menos confiáveis do que se esperaria - seja a gravidade acelerando do nada, ou um trampolim que te mata ao invés de te dar um impulso. Eu vi que na época o jogo foi lançado para o Nintendo Wii e permitia nele uma liberdade muito maior de movimentação, com o jogador definindo o grau de rotação do mundo, enquanto nessa versão aqui a rotação está limitada à ângulos de 90 graus, o que dá muito menos precisão para o jogador. Eu também senti falta de qualquer tipo de narrativa ou objetivo além de chegar no final de cada fase, eu sinto que senti falta de algo a mais para me manter investido além de sua mecânica.

Dito isso, ainda estou recomendando And Yet It Moves: por mais que suas falhas tenham impedido ele de ter se mantido tão popular quanto Braid ou Limbo no decorrer dos anos, eu ainda acho que a originalidade de sua mecânica principal e a frequente diversidade e surpresa de momentos de seus níveis criam uma experiência que vale a pena ser jogada pelo menos uma vez para quem é fã do gênero. Eu especificamente só não acho que valha a pena pra quem deseja fazer 100% dele, eu mesmo desisti de ganhar de seus vários modos bônus depois de me frustrar com suas fases extras bem injustas.

(Observação: 7 horas do meu tempo de jogo foram tentando pegar uma conquista de jogar o jogo por 3h30min sem parar, como não veio na segunda tentativa desisti, então meu tempo real de jogo ficaria em torno de 7 ou 8 horas.)

[h1]The most unique puzzle-platformer of all time. 8.3/10.[/h1]Ah, [i]And Yet It Moves[/i] – I remember when I had first heard about this game: on the Wii, as featured in an issue of the (now-defunct) magazine, [i]Nintendo Power.[/i] That was ages ago, of course, but I had gotten the game prior to the Wii Shop Channel's close. This was when I had had no source of income—having been just a kid at the time—so I had had to ask my parents for a Wii Shop points card. And it was worth it, [spoiler]although I had never actually beaten the game until I decided to play it again on here[/spoiler].

From the preview screenshots for this game, one can tell that this game has a “paper”-esque aesthetic. [spoiler]And the unnamed protagonist is about as delicate as that – I died so many times from fall damage alone.[/spoiler] Running through the environment and rotating the world to change the direction of gravity, the goal is (literally) a goal—a piece of paper with a cut-out outline of the protagonist—which, upon entering, leads to the next level, until the final goal, [spoiler]the end credits, which, itself, is a playable level; after which, the game officially ends.[/spoiler] Avoid obstacles and traps, [i]et voilà:[/i] that's the game. Sound easy? It's not. [spoiler]It's, like, medium-difficulty or so.[/spoiler]

In addition to the aesthetic and gameplay, the [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xabYn35ngaY]aleatoric[/url] soundtrack is worth noting.

Broken down, I would say I'd rate [i]And Yet It Moves[/i] thus:[list][*][b]Aesthetic: 8.1/10.[/b][*][b]Graphics Quality: 6.7/10.[/b][*][b]Sound: 7.1/10.[/b][*][b]Gameplay: 9.1/10,[/b] although it was admittedly a little short.[/list][b]Overall, then, I'd rate this game as an 8.3/10.[/b]

And Yet It Moves is a physics-based puzzle game that challenges the player to manipulate the orientation of the environment around the protagonist, similar to a marble labyrinth. The game features a distinctive art style that resembles torn paper collage, creating a contrast between the realistic physics and the abstract visuals. The protagonist can also jump and interact with some objects, adding more variety and complexity to the gameplay. The game offers a novel and engaging experience that deserves attention.

The 15 years old code standards make the default resolution in this game...tiny, not adapting to our screen, so switching between the game ad anything else will lag and change the desktop organisation. 

It's not the worst racing game, but it's not among the best.
The graphics are still cute, the items are fun... it's not expensive, it was made with love. 
That all the positive things I can say. 

No tutorial about the different "game modes". Not knowing the rules, expect to loose very often at first. 
My first experience was a tag game on a tiny arena where everyone (AI?) was confuse and kept faling undner the map. 

There is no upgrades for the kart, and by default, it's difficult to control and slow.
But we can customize the style.

The circutits are lovely!
We can choose a list of curcuits to play like in a shampionship. But not the order in which they will be played - unless that is a bug I'm encountering. 

There UI doesn't have any accessibility settings (small font).
The menus lack fuctionalities like disabling all tracks, or ading all tracks.
For a 15 years old solo dev game, it's not bad. But it might be more logical to give it free. 

There is an obligatory warmup, I think it's a way to get used to the circuits, instead of the flying video we get of the whole track. But that warmup only let us test the first part of the track, we can't knwo whater to expect after that. 

The circuits are lovely, 
the tiny cars and pilots are cute, 
the animations and the sounds are good.

Personally, I liked the idea, but the result lacks polish. 
I can't recommand buying it, or even keeping it in your livrary today though. 

If a remake came, with 
- adpatative graphics that doesn't change our screen resolution, 
- accessibility / difficulty settings, 
- car upgrades that are more than just visuals, 
- more ways to handle the list of tracks (grouped into tabs by theme / game mods), 
- and a tutorial for each game mode, 

I'd like to give it a positive eval, then.

Zero Gear, developed and published by Brian Cronin, is a lively and physics-driven kart racing game that emphasizes fun, chaos, and creativity over strict competition. It’s a project that captures the energy of classic kart racers while injecting a unique indie sensibility, trading polished realism for unpredictability and personality. Released in 2010, it quickly established itself as a hidden gem for players who value multiplayer mayhem, accessible controls, and moments of spontaneous laughter. Unlike many kart games that follow a rigid structure, Zero Gear embraces the unexpected; its combination of customizable vehicles, exaggerated physics, and wild weapons ensures that no two races ever unfold the same way.

At first glance, Zero Gear presents itself with charming simplicity. The visuals are bright and cartoonish, evoking the spirit of older arcade titles rather than modern graphical fidelity. Every kart and driver is customizable, from the shape and color of the car to the look of the characters themselves, giving the game a lighthearted personality that fits perfectly with its tone. The environments are varied, featuring more than a dozen imaginative maps that range from whimsical racetracks to arenas built for chaotic mini-games. Despite its minimalist art style, the presentation has aged gracefully thanks to its clean design and deliberate embrace of a playful, timeless aesthetic. The soundtrack and sound effects enhance this energy with upbeat tunes and slapstick crashes that remind players not to take the competition too seriously.

Gameplay is where Zero Gear truly shines. Its physics engine drives the experience, meaning every bump, jump, and crash feels dynamic and unpredictable. The controls are intuitive—easy to learn yet difficult to master—giving players the freedom to experiment with movement and stunts. Power-ups add another layer of madness, turning every race into a balance between skill and sheer luck. Rockets, speed boosts, and traps litter the tracks, creating constant tension as positions change in the blink of an eye. What separates Zero Gear from more conventional kart racers is the way its physics often become part of the fun rather than a barrier to it. Players can launch themselves off ramps, spin through the air, or send rivals tumbling across the map with a well-placed hit. It’s chaotic, yes, but in the best way—where the messiness itself becomes part of the entertainment.

Multiplayer is the heart of the experience and the reason Zero Gear earned its devoted following. The game supports up to eight players in online matches or local sessions, and it thrives in these shared environments. Whether you’re racing competitively, playing tag, scoring goals, or simply causing havoc, the unpredictable physics and weapon mechanics create countless laugh-out-loud moments. Each mode has its own flavor: Race mode delivers traditional karting excitement, Goal mode functions almost like a soccer match with cars, and Tag turns the game into a playground of pursuit and escape. Playing with friends transforms the experience into something akin to a digital party—one where victory feels less important than the sheer joy of the ride. Even when chaos reigns and the results feel unfair, the humor and spontaneity keep frustration at bay.

For all its charm, Zero Gear’s strengths also reveal its limits. The game’s content is modest, with a small number of maps and modes that can feel repetitive over time. Its single-player experience is minimal, serving more as a practice ground than a true campaign, and without a consistent online community, it can be challenging to find active multiplayer matches. The physics, while entertaining, can occasionally work against precision driving, leading to unpredictable crashes or misjudged landings that break the flow of competition. Yet these imperfections are part of what give Zero Gear its identity—it’s not a finely tuned simulation but rather a celebration of chaos, unpredictability, and playful experimentation.

Despite these drawbacks, Zero Gear endures as a cult favorite because it captures something many games lose in pursuit of complexity: pure, unfiltered fun. It’s easy to jump into, quick to understand, and endlessly amusing in the right company. The game’s balance of simplicity and unpredictability gives it an appeal similar to classic couch multiplayer titles—perfect for short bursts of laughter-filled gameplay with friends. Its price point and lightweight design make it an easy recommendation for anyone seeking an accessible multiplayer experience that doesn’t demand commitment or mastery to enjoy.

In the end, Zero Gear is a reminder that the essence of a good racing game doesn’t lie solely in realism or polish but in energy, creativity, and shared enjoyment. It’s a game that revels in its imperfections, turning every mistake, crash, and absurd moment into a story worth remembering. Whether you’re competing seriously or just goofing around with friends, its charm lies in the thrill of unpredictability and the humor that comes from it. For an indie title built on such a simple concept, it delivers a surprising amount of joy—and though time has passed since its release, its spirited blend of physics-based chaos and lighthearted design continues to hold a special place among multiplayer racing fans.

Rating: 7/10

[h1]Overview[/h1] 
[list] 
[*]Racing game for kids. Additional game modes such as Tag, Sports and Slots.
[*]Get 100% achievements within 5 minutes (see the tips section below).
[/list] 
  
[h1]Gameplay ★★☆☆☆[/h1] 
[list] 
[*]The cars go fast... but yet they don’t cross the speed limit. By this I mean that acceleration is too fast, steering turns too much, and driving ends up chaotic due to the lack of control. But yet, there is no thrill of speeding when you jam down on the booster. You get reminded that you are driving a toy car. The devs left out all the visual tricks that could create the illusion of speed.  
[*]The gameplay is actually fun. Game modes are unique. Dropping toy cars down a pachinko machine and watching them bounce around till they drop into the score buckets below is strange but creative.
[*]And there are the sports modes. I wonder if this game could have been an inspiration for Rocket League. You get to play Soccer, Rugby, Ice Hockey and Basketball. Collect power-ups on the field which give you moves such as giant boxing glove punch, summon tornado, mine drop, and more!
[*]The problem with the otherwise fun sports modes is that the ball hitbox is weird, and the abovementioned car handling issues make it frustrating to play.
[*]Going back to the racing mode, the free speed boost for players lagging behind while the 1st guy gets almost nothing is so unfair. This is a game design choice prevalent in other racing games too. The idea is to increase player interaction for a more exciting game, but throws skill out of the window.
[/list] 
  
[h1]Art & Graphics ★☆☆☆☆[/h1] 
[list] 
[*]Graphics is bad. Though released in 2010, normal maps and global illumnination already exist at that point. No excuses for terrible lighting and texturing.
[*]Art style is a mess. The devs can’t decide whether they want a toys racing game or a life-size racing game with actual cars.
[*]The same cars end up going through makeshift tracks constructed from cereal boxes and stationery, to stadiums with cheering crowds, to freefalling down pachinko machines.
[*]And oh my, the color palettes. Those outdoor tracks that follow real world colors are fine, such as the wild west ones. But the others are just pure rainbow disco, and it’s not a compliment. I seriously wonder how those highly-saturated triadic color schemes got approved. A literal kid made it. A literal kid!
[/list] 
  
[h1]Music & Sounds ★★★☆☆[/h1] 
[list] 
[*]Goovy and sometimes funky soundtrack lightens up the mood. Suitable for kids.
[/list] 
  
[h1]Plot & Characters ☆☆☆☆☆ 0/5[/h1] 
[list] 
[*]Not even a toy story?
[/list] 
  
[h1]Controls & Interface ★☆☆☆☆[/h1] 
[list] 
[*]The game desperately needs a rear view mirror. It is ridiculous that a game that lets you shoot weapons backwards doesn’t allow you to see behind.
[*]And yet switches to back view when reversing? The perspective change is so disorienting. No racing game does it except this one.
[*]Lastly, MB2 mouse-look isn’t working. I suspect that this might be how the devs intended players to look behind, but it’s broken. 
[/list] 
  
[h1]Verdict [/h1] 
[quote]
Kid: Mom, can we get Rocket League? 
Mom: But darling, we have Rocket League at home!
Rocket League at home: (Zero Gear)

Play this for a quick 100% perfect game. Otherwise, play Rocket League instead.

I love this game! As with all Kart racers, it isn't about perfect physics simulation, but fun and charm, and this game delivers in spades!
It takes a little getting used to, because once you are in the air you cannot steer (unlike most Kart games), but you *CAN* still turn your wheels, so you have to pay attention, because if you try to turn left in the air, when you land your wheels will be facing left and will suddenly bite as you land.

While there are your standard race tracks where you shoot each other with fun weapons, my favorite game modes are not the races.
One game mode has you playing Soccer, and it's basically like a Kart version of Rocket League. It's hilariously fun in a group!
Another mode is kind of like Plinko from the Price is Right. You drive off a ramp, fling yourself down a hole, and try to land on something good. Any time you are touching a peg, you can try to jump and redirect your movement, but other than that it's down to gravity to see what you'll score.
Lastly, there is a Skiiball mode where you drive off a ramp and try to land in one of the holes worth points.

It's great clean fun to play with friends or kids, and you can buy a 4-pack cheaply.
Huge recommendation from me!

A PC Kart racer done right! I honestly wish this would get a sequel.
It's better than a lot of AAA Kart Racers, and this is from an Indie studio!

The handling of this game is in the grippy side (Think F1 Race Stars) instead of the drifty side (MK and CTR), but honestly that just works well considering physics is what it's all about.

Maps are pretty well thought out, I really like the variety of them too.
There's a lot of gamemodes besides the traditional racing, there's soccer, american football, tag, basketball, a pachinko machine mode and a skee-ball mode.

Customization is similar to Modnation Racers, however it's not as mad or as varied with the customization as MR.

This could be one of the only kart racers I actually prefer using keyboard and mouse instead of a controller, mostly because it does take good use of free-aim with the power-ups. (Controller support is not very good here either so lol)

Unfortunately it didn't age aswell as someone would expect, the collision physics aren't that good and you'll run out of tracks faster than you think, there's also no split-screen so that should be put into consideration.
 it's still really fun to play, but there's literally nobody online in this game so you'll have to bring a friend or two, you can play with bots and they ain't all that bad.
I can't stop thinking of the possibilities of what this could be if we had a sequel with workshop support..

Buy it when discounted, maybe a four pack.

Silent Hill: Homecoming es un juego que amamos porque somos fans de los juegos de Silent Hill.
La historia es de Alex Shepherd, un soldado que regresa a su pueblo, Shepherd's Glen, y lo encuentra todo abandonado, con niebla y lleno de monstruos. Su hermano menor, Joshua, desapareció y su mamá está en un estado raro, así que Alex tiene que ir a buscarlo y en el camino termina entrando a Silent Hill para descubrir qué pasó realmente con su familia y con el pueblo.
Sí, las dinámicas de pelea de este juego son un poco incómodas, se siente más pesado que otros Silent Hill, con combos, esquivas y el cuchillo, el hacha y la pistola, pero te acostumbras y al final se disfruta.
Lo que sigue habiendo son personajes y enemigos épicos, los monstruos con diseños bien perturbadores, las enfermeras, los Smog, los Lurker y los jefes que te ponen los pelos de punta. Y el ambiente, la niebla, el Otro Mundo, los sonidos, todo eso sigue siendo puro Silent Hill.
Es un buen juego, lo jugué hace un buen y ya ni me acuerdo de todos los detalles de la historia, pero si eres fan de Silent Hill, es un juego que tienes que jugar, porque sigue teniendo ese terror y esa historia oscura que tanto nos gusta. 9/10.

[h2]Families and Sacrifices[/h2]

I'm going to drop a hot take here: I actually enjoyed this game.

I mean, before I started playing it, I installed the Unknownproject's patch, that was recommended, and a mod to fix the sound. I know this patch unlocks the framerate, supports higher resolutions, fixes bugs and crashes, enhances the controls, among other things. Thanks to this patch, I didn't experience any issues in-game.

One of the other reasons I might've enjoyed this game is that, in fact, this is the first Silent Hill I've ever played, because I had it sitting in my Steam library for years, so it was time to pick it up (and my girlfriend wanted me to play it, too). The knowledge I have about Silent Hill comes from the first two movies, the fan-made maps for Left 4 Dead 2 (from Steam Workshop), and a little bit about the story of the first two games. Don't worry, I plan to play the other Silent Hill games available for PC eventually.

The only thing I had more difficulty in this game, other than a very few confusing puzzles, was the combat system. The combat is a little dogshit, yes, but I eventually got the hang of it.

Combat aside, I enjoyed most of the game's stuff, especially the soundtrack. The soundtrack is excellent, from the main menu to the credits. I saw that the genius behind the music is Akira Yamaoka, and he worked on every single Silent Hill game, plus a few other horror games, so I can see that he never fails.

The ambiance is sinister and well done, I found it eerie and haunting, with its typical and remarkable fog. The soundtrack enhances it too, along with the background sounds, like the monsters walking nearby and approaching us, or even the screams echoing from afar.

Now, regarding the story, I also enjoyed it. It has quite a few plot twists, and clearly, everything is not what it seems. There are many plot points that might confuse you too, but the questions eventually get answered, whether by advancing in the story, or even by reading the documents that can be found around (about what happened in Shepherd's Glen, the founding families of the town, the whole rituals thing, and the Order).

There's another thing that I found out after I finished the game: the game has five different endings. It all depends on three choices you make throughout the game: [spoiler]whether you choose to kill Alex's mother, whether you choose to forgive Alex's father, and whether you choose to save Wheeler.[/spoiler]

I got the ending where Alex [spoiler]wakes up in the psychiatric hospital, as if the entire story happened in his head. His dad did say before that Alex was never a military soldier, and that he was sent to a mental hospital, so that makes sense. Plus, he wakes up in the room 206, and I found memos that mention a patient in room 206 "scheduled to undergo a trans-orbital lobotomy tomorrow." I assume this is, indeed, Alex.[/spoiler]

Overall, I don't understand the hate for this game. Maybe to Silent Hill fans it's shit, maybe people didn't like the gameplay or even the story, or it's simply because the port isn't well made (although the patch I mentioned before enhances the game's quality of life). Maybe the game isn't that good at all, but I'm reviewing it based on my experience and my enjoyment.
