As noted on my other reviews for Company of Heroes I had major issues with this game last time I tried to play it on a modern PC. Random frame rate drops and you can't rebind keys which is a major annoyance. As such I can't recommend it.

Histoire :

Tales of Valor est la deuxième extension de Company of Heroes. Contrairement au jeu de base, elle ne propose pas une longue campagne unique, mais trois mini-campagnes inspirées de faits historiques de la Seconde Guerre mondiale.

Tu y incarnes successivement :
Les Tigers de Michael Wittmann.
Les parachutistes américains de la Falaise de la Poche de Falaise.
Les Britanniques lors de la libération de la ville de Caen.
Chaque campagne raconte une histoire différente et apporte une vision variée du conflit. Elles sont courtes mais bien mises en scène.
👉 On passe rapidement d'une mission à l'autre… mais au moins, on ne s'ennuie jamais.

Gameplay :

Le gameplay reste celui qui a fait la réputation de Company of Heroes :
Gestion des couverts
Contrôle des points stratégiques
Destruction dynamique des bâtiments
Positionnement tactique des unités

L'extension ajoute également plusieurs nouveautés :
Direct Fire Control : possibilité de contrôler directement un véhicule ou un canon.
Nouvelles unités pour toutes les factions.
Nouveaux modes de jeu.
Nouvelles cartes multijoueurs.

Le contrôle direct apporte un petit vent de fraîcheur, même s'il reste assez anecdotique comparé au gameplay classique.

👉 Prendre directement le contrôle d'un Tigre est grisant… jusqu'à ce que trois canons antichars te rappellent que tu n'es pas invincible.

Graphismes & ambiance :

Toujours aussi solide.
Le moteur graphique continue d'offrir :
Des explosions spectaculaires
Des bâtiments entièrement destructibles
Une excellente ambiance sonore
Même aujourd'hui, les combats restent particulièrement immersifs.

Difficulté :

Moyenne.
Les campagnes sont un peu plus accessibles que certaines missions du jeu de base, mais quelques objectifs demandent tout de même une bonne maîtrise des mécaniques.
Le mode multijoueur reste évidemment beaucoup plus exigeant.

Durée de vie :

Trois campagnes : 8 à 12 heures
Nouveaux modes de jeu : 5 à 10 heures

Points positifs :

✔ Trois campagnes variées
✔ Contrôle direct des véhicules intéressant
✔ Toujours aussi immersif
✔ Excellente réalisation sonore
✔ Bonne rejouabilité grâce aux nouveaux modes

Points négatifs :

✖ Campagnes assez courtes
✖ Peu de nouveautés majeures par rapport à Opposing Fronts
✖ Contrôle direct parfois gadget

Verdict :

Company of Heroes: Tales of Valor est une bonne extension qui enrichit encore le contenu du jeu sans révolutionner la formule. Les trois campagnes sont agréables à parcourir, les nouveaux modes apportent un peu de variété et le gameplay reste une référence du RTS.
👉 Moins indispensable que Opposing Fronts, mais un excellent complément pour les fans de Company of Heroes.
👉 Et tu découvriras qu'un char Tigre est extrêmement impressionnant… jusqu'au moment où toute l'artillerie ennemie décide que tu es devenu la priorité numéro un 😄

Bewertung: Empfohlen (für Fans der alten Schule)

Tales of Valor ist eine Erweiterung aus dem Jahr 2009, die drei kurze Kampagnen und ein paar neue Multiplayer-Modi zum Original hinzufügt.

Auch nach über 15 Jahren merkt man deutlich, dass das Spiel aus einer anderen Ära stammt die Grafik ist für damalige Verhältnisse immer noch beeindruckend, aber natürlich nicht mehr mit heutigen Standards vergleichbar.

Die drei Heldengeschichten sind atmosphärisch inszeniert und bieten in jeweils rund 90 Minuten intensive Gefechte. Besonders das direkte Panzerfeuer und die neuen Modi (wie das kooperative Operation Stonewall) bringen frischen Wind ins Geschehen.

Das Kern-Gameplay von Company of Heroes bleibt bis heute eines der taktisch tiefsten und befriedigendsten im RTS-Bereich.

Allerdings zeigt das Alter des Add-ons klare Grenzen: Die Kampagnen sind sehr kurz, neue Einheiten und Inhalte halten sich stark in Grenzen, und insgesamt fühlt sich das Paket eher wie eine kleine Ergänzung als wie eine vollwertige Erweiterung an. Für Neueinsteiger 2026 ist es kein guter Einstiegspunkt hier sollte man zuerst das Hauptspiel und Opposing Fronts spielen.

Fazit:
Ein solides Add-on aus 2009, das langjährigen Fans auch heute noch ein paar schöne Stunden bietet, vor allem im Multiplayer. Wer die klassische Company of Heroes-Ära schätzt, macht mit Tales of Valor nichts falsch. Bei aktuellen Preisen eine faire Ergänzung für die Sammlung.

7.5/10 – Gute, aber spürbar betagte Ergänzung zu einem echten RTS-Klassiker.

Company of Heroes: Tales of Valor is a compelling real-time strategy expansion that builds upon the foundation laid by the original Company of Heroes, delivering an intense and immersive World War II experience with a focus on tactical combat and narrative-driven missions. Developed by Relic Entertainment, this standalone expansion offers new campaigns, units, and game modes that enrich the original game’s formula, appealing to both longtime fans and newcomers who appreciate strategy games rooted in historical settings. Its blend of challenging gameplay, detailed environments, and authentic wartime atmosphere makes Tales of Valor a worthy addition to the Company of Heroes series.

One of the key strengths of Tales of Valor lies in its diverse and engaging single-player campaigns. Unlike the broader strategic scope of the original game, this expansion delivers tightly crafted mission scenarios that emphasize intense tactical engagements. Each campaign introduces unique storylines focusing on specific battles or units, such as the deadly “Tiger Ace” missions or the harrowing “Falaise Pocket” scenario, providing varied perspectives on the brutal realities of war. The missions are well-designed to encourage thoughtful use of cover, flanking maneuvers, and combined arms tactics, requiring players to adapt quickly to evolving battlefield conditions and enemy tactics.

The expansion also introduces several new units and vehicles that add depth and variety to combat. From heavily armored tanks to specialized infantry squads, these new additions diversify the tactical options available and encourage players to experiment with different strategies. The improved AI responsiveness and unit behaviors further enhance the challenge, making enemy forces feel more dynamic and realistic. The multiplayer component benefits from these enhancements as well, offering fresh maps and game modes that encourage cooperative play and competitive matches, extending the game’s replayability and community engagement.

Visually, Company of Heroes: Tales of Valor maintains the high standards set by its predecessor, with detailed and destructible environments that contribute significantly to gameplay and immersion. The game’s dynamic battlefields, where terrain can be altered by artillery strikes and tank fire, demand careful positioning and use of cover, adding a layer of realism and strategic depth. The sound design complements the visuals effectively, with authentic weapon sounds, explosions, and voice acting that bring the tension and chaos of war to life. The cinematic cutscenes and mission briefings also help to immerse players in the narrative, reinforcing the stakes of each operation.

One of the expansion’s notable features is the addition of three distinct game modes: “Assault,” “Stonewall,” and “Panzerkrieg.” Each mode offers unique gameplay mechanics and objectives, refreshing the standard RTS formula. “Assault” focuses on fast-paced offensive operations where players must capture and hold objectives under constant pressure. “Stonewall” challenges players to hold defensive positions against waves of enemies, emphasizing endurance and strategic placement of units. “Panzerkrieg” offers a more armored-focused experience, where players command tank-heavy forces in direct combat. These modes provide variety and cater to different player preferences, ensuring that the expansion remains engaging beyond the campaign missions.

While Tales of Valor offers a rich and enjoyable experience, it does have some limitations. The campaign’s shorter length compared to the original game may leave some players wanting more, and the narrative, though effective, is less expansive than in the base title. Additionally, some players might find the learning curve steep if they are new to the series, as the game demands careful micro-management and strategic foresight. However, for those familiar with Company of Heroes or fans of RTS games in general, these challenges contribute to the game’s rewarding and tactical gameplay.

In conclusion, Company of Heroes: Tales of Valor stands as a robust and engaging expansion that complements the original game with new content, varied game modes, and challenging missions. Its attention to tactical detail, combined with authentic World War II atmosphere and dynamic battlefields, provides a deeply satisfying strategy experience. Whether you’re revisiting the franchise or discovering it for the first time, Tales of Valor delivers intense combat scenarios and meaningful strategic depth that make it a valuable addition to any RTS enthusiast’s library.

Short Review: 
4.3/10

Lengthy Review:
Usually I tend to do the whole good bad & ugly schtick but this game is just bad, I saw a review claiming people who called this game had blind nostalgia for Red Faction 1 and that couldn't be any farther from the truth, and my reason for saying this is because Red Faction 2 is nothing like the first game or even the games that came after 2, and this is coming from a new fan who just bought the entire franchise and has played through it, the dialogue, gunplay, map design, and destruction are all terrible, while visually it looks better than Red Faction 1, it's also not even set on mars. and has the most unserious over the top sounding voice acting it sounds almost cliche and intentional, the entire game plays like a fictional videogame you would see some dude playing in a early 2000's movie. It's genuinely so bad I only played for 13 minutes, didn't even make it past the 2nd level, and decided to uninstall, because it feels too linear, with scripted destruction that's not actually physics based, In red faction 1 I could take out 2 ends of a bridge and the middle would collapse, or I could blow tunnels through walls, but in RF2 you can take like a shaving out of the wall, and blowing up structures is scripted instead of dynamic, the only "dynamic" destruction is for stuff that's mandatory like if you needed to blow up an area around a door or a room to get in, either way this feels less like a red faction game and more like a generic early 2000's shooter.

The only reason this game gets even a 4 is because it launches fine on my system (for others I hear it crashes because of too much Vram so you may need a 3rd party fix, but to be fair the first game also requires this)
it has widescreen support, and it doesn't have any gamebreaking bugs off the bat, basically a 4 because the game works and functions, but that's about where the good ends.

My advice? Go play Red Faction 1, then skip Red Faction 2 and go straight to playing Red Faction Guerilla
because this game is a waste of your time, unless you're one of the few rare people who enjoy it anyways despite it's flaws and how different it is from every other Red Faction title.

Ein interessanter Fall, denn das Spiel schlägt unerwartet in alle Richtungen aus. Als Kind fand ich den zweiten Teil eigentlich cooler, kannte ihn aber nur aus irgendwelchen Testberichten. Als ich mich jetzt zuletzt nochmal informiert habe, schien der Tenor zu sein, dass alle den zweiten Teil total schlecht finden.

Jetzt habe ich es gespielt und muss sagen: Ich verstehe die Tests und das negative Feedback, aber unterm Strich ist es ziemlich gut. Das Hauptproblem ist schlichtweg, dass sich Teil 2 absolut wie ein Konsolenspiel anfühlt – akute Konsoleritis, sozusagen: Plötzlich hast du ein riesiges Fadenkreuz, die Munitionsanzeige ist gigantisch, die Level haben gefühlt alle fünf Meter einen Ladebildschirm und generell herrscht dieses klobige Design mit unscharfen Texturen. Alles wirkt sehr überbetont. Der erste Teil sah in einigen Bereichen tatsächlich besser aus.... Kennt ihr noch diesen speziellen, kantigen, detailarmen, aber super scharfen und präzisen Look von PC-Shootern aus den 2000ern, wie dem ersten Call of Duty oder RtCW? Den hatte Red Faction 1. Der zweite Teil sieht dagegen einfach nur unscharf weichgezeichnet und knubbelig aus.

Trotz dieser ganzen Konsolen-Krankheiten spielt es sich erstaunlich gut. Die Animationen sind schön, es gibt viel Abwechslung und – was eher selten ist – sogar richtig gute Fahrzeugsequenzen. (Man fährt halt nicht selber..)

Und dann ist da die große Zerstörungs-Frage: Ist das System in Teil 2 nun besser oder schlechter? Viele sagen schlechter, aber mir kommt es paradoxerweise viel besser vor. Aber dann habe ich mal genau darauf geachtet, und siehe da: Technisch gesehen ist die Zerstörung zwar irrelevanter und simpler geworden, aber für den Spielfluss ist sie grandios integriert. Dauernd geht etwas zu Bruch, man reißt Wände ein, zerstört Gegenstände und ballert sich sprichwörtlich seinen eigenen Weg frei.
Aus rein technischer Sicht ist Teil 2 aber tatsächlich billiger! Wenn man ein Loch in die Mauer schießt, ist das effektiv nur eine Wand, die als gezieltes Hindernis im Weg stand. Im ersten Teil konnte man noch richtig in die Felswand ballern und sich einen endlosen Tunnel graben – und zwar so lange, bis die komplette Munition leer war, noch bevor man das Ende der Map erreicht hat. Das geht im zweiten Teil gar nicht mehr - da gibt es keine einzige Stelle, an der man sich wirklich irgendwo eingraben kann. Es sind immer nur offensichtliche Hindernisse, die man zerlegt.

Ich verstehe also, warum die Engine oft als schlechter bewertet wird. Aber ganz nüchtern betrachtet: Im ersten Teil musstest du im gesamten Spiel viermal überhaupt eine Wand einreißen. Im zweiten Teil ballerst du dich pausenlos durch Wände, fährst durch Gebäude und schießt dir Löcher in den Boden, um in den Keller zu kommen. Auch wenn der Traum vom grenzenlosen Tunnelbau vorbei ist, macht Red Faction 2 beim Thema Zerstörung für den Spieler letztlich den besseren Job.

Wow all I can say is just wow.. what happened to this franchise already?

Red Faction 2 is probably one of the weirdest sequels I've ever played for any game. I'm not sure you can even call this a sequel because it so loosely ties into the first game you can skip it and play this one and miss nothing.

The game has you playing as a new character named Alias who is part of some group of other super soldiers or something, honestly the dialogue and the cutscenes were directed so poorly it was honestly hard to understand what was going on. You work your way through some levels until you finally decide its time to kill some dictator dude and then BAM we're at the climax of the game. The rag tag team separates and you gotta get revenge. If theres anything I noticed with volition games is that they are mostly always about getting revenge on those who wronged you. After some boring fights you finally get revenge and beat them. 

My first initial thoughts are I'm very disappointed with the way red faction is portrayed in this game. Sure they weren't portrayed any better in the first game since they are useless but here they are even more useless and used as nothing but fodder for the enemy. I also feel bad for the leader where he just gets slapped around then popped by one of your ex members. Honestly you could call these people something else and I'd honestly believe you. It reminds me alot of what happened to the saints in the Saints Row reboot.

This game plays like one of those TV show games you see one of the character playing and you'd think its a fake game. The art direction this time gives it this fake plasticy feel and Idk it feels more like a video game? I guess thats the best way I can put it. I honestly didn't like the art style they went with and even playing in wide screen at full res it still looks very off.

The gunplay this time doesn't feel as satisfying as RF1. The guns have this weird floaty feeling and your kit this time around feels very bloated. You have so many weapons but not enough enemies to use them on.  The enemies you do get to fight, some of them are ridiculously bullet spongy. You'll be sitting there shooting and they don't go down. There's is like a total of 3 weapons you'll use more then the others. Also I can't believe how they massacred my boy the rail gun. It feels like a cheap toy and its not as good as it was in RF1.

Also F THAT final boss fight. Holy this boss fight was super tedious and annoying to get through. Also this is one of those games without skippable cutscenes so you'll be seeing that final cutscene plenty of times if you die which will happen because not only is the final boss a massive bullet sponge he has two phases and one will insta kill you if you stay still even for a second! It also doesn't have subtitles so have fun trying to figure out what they are saying when you have explosions going off on screen or the sound of a gun going off.

I also didn't care for any of the characters. When they betrayed me I felt nothing because our team building and bonding happened off screen and before the game even happens so when it happens I was like "Oh well time to get em I guess".  I guess the only cool one is Jason Statham but that's because he's cool and has an awesome voice.

I'm not sure what happened but the writing in this game is terrible. The levels also suck and are extremely boring to look at. Sure RF1 also had alot of boring maps but atleast the characters and the story were better in that game. It also doesn't help this game doesn't have any damn checkpoints. It has a save system which is USELESS! It doesn't save where you left off it just restarts the WHOLE DAMN LEVEL WHEN YOU DIE!

The performance was also really good on Linux. Luckily this time you don't need any mods, just set your resolution and get to playing. All cutscenes except for 1 work but I'm pretty sure thats a bug because I was looking online and there's mods to fix it. It could also be an FPS problem but honestly this game is so forgettable that I couldn't careless if I missed a cutscene or couldn't see or hear what they were saying.

This game also has like 4 different endings which I will not be bothering to unlock because I won't be playing this turd ever again. You can beat it in one sitting. I only have the time I do in it because they patted out the ending of the game like they did RF1 and made the final boss extremely tedious to fight.

All in all I'm giving RF2 a 3/10 🍕 slices and the reason I rate it so highly is because I really enjoyed RF1 and this abomination is part of the same franchise. If this were a different game franchise I would have it like a 2. This game is NOT dad certified and its NOT worth your time. Only play this if you're a completionist like me or if you really wanna kill 3/4 hours of your life doing something mind numbing but honestly just use the money you'd spend on this game and go get a pack of gum or an Arizona or hell even a cup noodle. You'll enjoy that way more. Let's hope the rest of the series is better.

A principios de la década de los dos mil, el género de disparos en primera persona estaba experimentando una revolución madura gracias a títulos que cuidaban la narrativa y la ambientación, dejando a esta propuesta en una tierra de nadie bastante insípida.

El gran atractivo del juego seguía siendo la destrucción del entorno, pero el diseño de niveles no sabe qué hacer con él. Mientras que contemporáneos de la época como Halo: Combat Evolved expandían los horizontes con escenarios abiertos y una inteligencia artificial brillante, o TimeSplitters 2 perfeccionaba el frenetismo del disparo arcade con un carisma arrollador, aquí nos encontramos atrapados en pasillos grises con pasajes excesivamente guionizados. Romper paredes resulta divertido durante los primeros minutos, pero pronto queda claro que es un truco de magia limitado que no aporta una verdadera libertad táctica ni rivaliza con la solidez jugable de sus competidores directos.

La campaña principal sufre además de una brevedad alarmante y una preocupante falta de ritmo. El intento de introducir un escuadrón de compañeros con habilidades específicas se siente plano debido a un plantel de personajes arquetípicos y sin alma, incapaces de replicar la inmersión narrativa que años antes ya había estandarizado el primer Half-Life o System Shock. El resultado final es un producto sumamente plano que se deja jugar, pero que palidece ante la edad de oro del género que se estaba gestando a su alrededor, quedando relegado a ser una simple nota a pie de página de su época.

If you really love Red Faction 1 but haven't played II you're probably going to be disappointed. It seems Volition completely misread fan feedback and enthusiasm about RF1 and inexplicably went a very different direction with this sequel. When I picked this game up for PS2 back in the day I hoped for a continuation of RF1's story, more or better RF1 style gameplay, and more geo-mod fun. Story wise this game borrows one macguffin from RF1 but is otherwise completely unrelated and the game takes place on Earth. The gunplay feels about the same as RF1 with some variations. RF II actually pulls back on the geomod tech that made RF1 unique and it's barely used in the campaign. 

If you liked RF1's multiplayer you're out of luck here as Volition inexplicably decided to not include online MP on RF II.

All that said, I do like RF II. I've spent hours speed running it and I think it's kinda a charming microcosm of its time. The story and dialogue is cheesy on purpose as it's meant to be a satire to the typical action shlock that was popular in the early 00's. Moreover some of the story beats are meant to reference the U.S.'s conflict in Iraq which was a new issue when this game was being developed. I can only really recommend this game as a picture of its time and if you don't appreciate generic early 00's shooters or culture I can't really see anyone enjoying this as a first playthrough in 2026. At this point Volition is dead and the series IP is owned by a third party unlikely to ever revisit what made Red Faction special. Buyer beware- know what you're getting into. 

The game is also missing a lot of the creature comforts, bug fixes, and visual fidelity made possible for RF1 by dedicated community modders. There is a launcher being worked on that fixed most issues but it is not public at the moment as far as I know. If you're interested, check the FactionFiles discord (invite link is on factionfiles .com).

[h1]Red Faction II — ★☆☆☆☆[/h1]

[b]RF II[/b] оказалась одной из тех игр, которые лучше сохранились в воспоминаниях, чем в реальности. Перепройдя её в 2026 году, я искренне удивился тому, насколько иначе она воспринимается спустя годы. Возможно, дело в моральном и техническом устаревании, но сегодня игра выглядит крайне посредственно даже по меркам своего времени.

🔹Одной из ключевых особенностей [i]RF II[/i] является разрушаемость окружения, однако этот элемент используется настолько редко, что быстро перестаёт восприниматься как важная часть игрового процесса. За всё прохождение я лишь несколько раз столкнулся с ситуациями, где разрушение объектов действительно имело какое-либо значение.

🔹Сюжет также не смог удержать моё внимание. История развивается предсказуемо, персонажи пытаются казаться интересными и проработанными, но на деле выглядят довольно поверхностно и не вызывают особого интереса. В результате происходящее на экране довольно быстро начинает восприниматься как череда однообразных перестрелок без заметного развития.

🔸Впрочем, есть и положительный момент: игра проходится достаточно быстро. Кампания не успевает сильно утомить, а финальный босс хотя бы пытается предложить игроку какой-то вызов на фоне остальной игры.

После перепрохождения мне сложно рекомендовать [i]RF II[/i] тем, кто не испытывает к ней ностальгии. Сегодня игра может представлять интерес разве что для тех, кто хочет познакомиться со старыми шутерами начала 2000-х. Лично для меня она осталась довольно посредственной попыткой повторить популярные идеи своего времени, не предложив ничего по-настоящему запоминающегося, кроме частичной разрушаемости окружения.

[hr]

[b]RF II[/b] turned out to be one of those games that are better preserved in memories than in reality. Having replayed it in 2026, I was genuinely surprised at how differently it feels after all these years. Perhaps it’s due to moral and technical obsolescence, but today the game looks extremely mediocre even by the standards of its time.

🔹One of the key features of [i]RF II[/i] is environmental destructibility, yet this element is used so rarely that it quickly stops feeling like an important part of the gameplay. Throughout the entire playthrough, I only encountered a few situations where destroying objects actually mattered.

🔹The story also failed to hold my attention. The plot develops predictably, the characters try to seem interesting and well-developed, but in reality come across as fairly shallow and fail to evoke much interest. As a result, what happens on screen quickly starts to feel like a series of monotonous shootouts with little noticeable progression.

🔸That said, there is a positive aspect: the game is fairly short. The campaign doesn’t have time to become too tiresome, and the final boss at least tries to offer the player some challenge compared to the rest of the game.

After replaying it, I find it hard to recommend [i]RF II[/i] to anyone who doesn’t feel nostalgic about it. Today, the game might only be of interest to those who want to get acquainted with old shooters from the early 2000s. Personally, it remains a rather mediocre attempt to replicate the popular ideas of its time, offering nothing truly memorable except for partial environmental destructibility.

I played this game more than 20 years ago (that much I remember), but I didn't remember much - not how long I played it or if I finished it (I think back then I didn't). Just that you couldn't destroy as much as in the first game of this franchise and that I didn't like it as much.
I recently (yesterday) started playing the game again and finished today (admittedly: with cheats). The game is a mess.  In most parts of the game, enemies keep respawning again and again, which artificially raises the difficulty and forces you to constantly move on. On the other side the objectives and the direction to go are so poorly telegraphed even though the game feels much more linear than the previous game. The shooting and running is so monotonous and, as you can barely destroy any surroundings anymore, some tactical aspects are just missing.
The story? Feels very chaotic and poorly told. You, the hero of the story, are a soldier of the evil dictator and only turn on him, because he turns on you. Very heroic. You mustn’t shoot civilians (that mostly seem to be collaborators without guns in my point of view…) or your karma goes down (no idea how it was measured). I killed quite a lot of them (because I couldn’t care less and also disliked them) but still got the “you are the good guy” ending (I was the hero and became the military advisor). Supposedly there are 4 endings, I have no idea how hard you have to try to kill civilians to get a worse ending…
The graphics look less appealing to my eye than in Red Faction I.
The cherry on top: you can’t really save where you want anymore. You can save/will have to start at the last checkpoint. Want to skip at least the irritating dialogue/cut scene that started at the checkpoint? Tough look, I didn’t see how that was possible. My guess is: the game development was rushed. That is how it feels. Similar to Blood 2 (which is better in my opinion – and that says something).

I am a big fan of the original Red Faction. I have beaten it at least 15 times since 2001 and prefer to play on the highest Impossible difficulty which is quite challeging and interesting. When RF2 originally released I tried it in on a friend'd PC once and didn't like it. Especially because of the lack of quick saves which I use constantly in RF1. After that I completed Guerilla and Armageddon once but never touched RF2 again. Only heard some of its reputation.

Recently I finished RF1 again and decided I want to experience RF2 at last. And this was one of the games I regret to have played and wasted the time of my life on. Played on Hard difficulty, lowered it to Easy only for the final boss because I didn't want to waste more time on this game.

What little I liked:

* Some rare sections of the game are a bit atmospheric and I even liked them. Especially Alone In The Dark episode through to the subway station which reminded me a bit about RF1 ventilation systems and caves.
* Some civilian characters like hobos are hilarious and I laughed at their comments.
* The dev genuinely put some work into explosion physics. NPC models behavior when they die is surprisingly good.
* Night vision. If it was a thing RF1 sometimes desperately needed - it was flashlight or this. I actually liked the implementation with visual lags. But disliked the amount of time you need to use it to see anything at all.

What I actively disliked:

* Salvaged and butchered amazing original music by Dan Wentz. Many tracks are reused or re-edited to the worse versions. Only the main menu theme with Sopot's voiceover is a bit catchy and I enjoyed it.
* HORRIFIC graphics and style. The original RF still looks great to this day. I can even compare it to Half-Life 2 a bit in this aspect. But RF2 is a plastic toy console trash compared to it. It is objectively bad.
* HORRIFIC weapons with no impact at all. The only little upside is NICW which allows you to use grenades. It was a weapon I used most of the game. Compared to RF1 weapons it's a pain to watch and use.
* Damned UNSKIPPABLE and UGLIEST cutscenes at every major section start or boss fight. It's an insult to players.
* Some sections are ridiculously tough on Hard difficulty. Like the underwater one before entering the Nano Base. I lost about 10 attempts to survive constant submarine attacks.
* Sections with infinite enemy waves. I just hate this thing everywhere. But here it's especially bad because of the lack of quick saves. You need to progress the level for these waves to stop.
* Stupid invisible walls and closed doors which open automatically only after you complete some objective.
* The vehicles feel way worse than in RF1 and they were added only to brag about "our game has X types of vehicles".
* The plot and voice acting in RF1 were also quite lame. But here they are just pathetic. No way the devs themselves took it seriously.

Overall, this game is just a boring ugly console shooting range with tons of weak enemies and bad shooting. One of the worst examples of butchering the existing series. Actively DO NOT RECOMMEND to buy it and waste your time. Choose the original RF, Guerilla or even Armageddon. They are all way better.

[h1]Red Faction II. A Rebelião Perde o Fôlego[/h1]

[h2]1. Da revolta marciana à guerra sem rosto[/h2]

Lançado em 2002, Red Faction II tentou expandir o universo da franquia com mais ação, personagens e um enredo “épico”, mas o que nasceu como uma história sobre opressão e resistência, em Marte, virou um shooter militar genérico na Terra, agora, o jogador encarna Alias, um supersoldado bio-modificado a serviço de um governo corrupto que logo se volta contra ele, o tema da rebelião ainda existe, mas sem o peso simbólico do primeiro, não há mais o mineiro comum lutando contra a corporação, e sim um exército de clones lutando contra outro.

A Volition tentou dar um ar cinematográfico à série, mas acabou apagando o que tornava o primeiro especial, o senso de isolamento, a ficção científica suja e o tom político que ecoava Total Recall e Outland, aqui, sobra barulho, mas falta propósito.

[b]“Em Marte, Parker lutava por liberdade, na Terra, Alias luta por roteiro.”[/b]

[h2]2. Geo-Mod 2.0. O mito que se perdeu[/h2]

O Geo-Mod Engine, orgulho do primeiro jogo, retorna, mas como uma sombra do que foi, a destruição ainda existe, mas agora é limitada, contida e previsível, o jogador só pode destruir certas paredes e objetos pré-definidos, uma ironia cruel para uma franquia que nasceu da ideia de liberdade.

O impacto emocional do Geo-Mod sumiu, antes, explodir uma parede era um ato de rebeldia, uma declaração contra o sistema, agora, é apenas parte de uma sequência de ação roteirizada, sem qualquer significado narrativo, a Volition parecia tentar seguir o padrão de FPS do início dos anos 2000, mais lineares, mais “cinematográficos” e, com isso, abriu mão do que fazia Red Faction ser Red Faction.

[b]“Quando a destruição vira decoração, o mundo para de reagir.”[/b]

[h2]3. O caos sem contexto[/h2]

Os combates são mais intensos e variados, com veículos e explosões maiores, mas perdem em identidade, Red Faction II tenta compensar a falta de profundidade com pirotecnia, você controla tanques, torres e lança-granadas, mas tudo parece passageiro, sem impacto real.

Os inimigos são genéricos, os companheiros são caricaturas, e o ritmo apressado não deixa o jogador respirar, a narrativa pula de missão em missão sem estrutura, como se quisesse apenas gritar mais alto que o anterior e quanto mais grita, menos ouvimos.

A ironia é que o jogo busca ser mais humano, com diálogos e personagens dublados por nomes famosos como Lance Henriksen e Jason Statham, mas nenhum deles tem tempo de existir.
É ação sem alma, ruído sem emoção.

[b]“Red Faction II fala alto, mas não tem nada a dizer.”[/b]

[h2]4. Entre Marte e Terra. O que se perdeu no caminho[/h2]

Comparar Red Faction com Red Faction II é quase comparar ideologia com espetáculo, o primeiro era político, sujo, claustrofóbico, o segundo é patriótico, polido e superficial.

A troca de Marte pela Terra é mais simbólica do que parece, sai o cenário inóspito e alienante, entra a cidade genérica de uma distopia militar qualquer, sai o mineiro que luta por sobrevivência, entra o supersoldado que luta por comando e sai a revolução, entra a guerra.

A Volition parecia querer alcançar o público de Halo e Medal of Honor, mas no processo, sacrificou o DNA narrativo da série, o Geo-Mod virou truque, a crítica virou patriotismo, e o jogador deixou de ser o rebelde para virar apenas mais um soldado.

[b]“A chama da rebelião não se apaga com balas, mas com a perda de propósito.”[/b]

5. O visual sem identidade

Tecnicamente, o jogo é sólido, texturas nítidas, modelos detalhados e cenários urbanos mais amplos que o original, mas artisticamente, é vazio, as minas vermelhas e corredores industriais do primeiro jogo transmitiam opressão e atmosfera, aqui, tudo é metálico, repetitivo e sem alma, os ambientes da cidade de EDF parecem genéricos, intercambiáveis, sem o menor senso de lugar, nada lembra Marte, nada ecoa o isolamento, e o design de fases é linear até o limite, você segue por corredores que explodem e fecham atrás de você, o oposto do que o Geo-Mod prometia um ano antes.

[b]“Red Faction II é bonito por fora, mas oco por dentro, uma concha metálica sem coração.”[/b]

[h2]6. A crítica e o público: o silêncio após o estrondo[/h2]

Na época, Red Faction II recebeu avaliações mornas, a crítica reconheceu a boa ação e os gráficos competentes, mas lamentou a perda da destruição livre e da atmosfera política do original, os fãs, então, dividiram-se, alguns gostaram da velocidade e das armas, mas muitos sentiram que o jogo havia traído suas próprias origens.

O tempo foi impiedoso, hoje, o segundo jogo é lembrado como o elo mais fraco da sériem um experimento que tentou ser blockbuster e perdeu o espírito cult do original, enquanto Red Faction é estudado como marco técnico, Red Faction II é uma nota de rodapé, a sequência que esqueceu o manifesto que a inspirou.

[h2]7. Um legado enfraquecido e a perda do impacto[/h2]

Enquanto o primeiro Red Faction foi lembrado por sua ambição e por tentar mudar as regras do gênero FPS com a destruição geomod, Red Faction II parece ter perdido o rumo e, junto dele, boa parte da relevância conquistada, o jogo soa como uma sequência feita às pressas, sem confiança em seu próprio potencial, a ausência de um enredo envolvente e a superficialidade dos personagens demonstram um afastamento do que tornava o original tão intrigante, a tecnologia de destruição, que antes era o coração do projeto, aqui é tratada quase como um detalhe, um recurso secundário que raramente serve a algo além de breves momentos de espetáculo vazio.

A sensação é a de que a franquia trocou inovação por conveniência, e identidade por clichês, o peso político e a tensão social do primeiro título, com sua luta de mineiros contra corporações opressoras, foram substituídos por um patriotismo artificial e genérico, mais próximo de um jogo de ação descartável do início dos anos 2000 do que de uma continuação legítima, Red Faction II não apenas falha em evoluir a série, como parece retroceder, apagando o que havia de mais único em seu antecessor.

No fim, o legado do jogo é o de uma oportunidade desperdiçada, uma continuação que teve todos os recursos técnicos para se destacar, mas nenhuma visão criativa para realmente marcar seu tempo.

[h2]8. Conclusão. A revolução domesticada[/h2]

Red Faction II não é um jogo ruim, é um jogo sem alma, ele troca liberdade por controle, ideologia por espetáculo e coragem por conveniência, no processo, transforma uma franquia promissora em mais um produto da era dos FPS genéricos.

O que era grito virou eco.
O que era manifesto virou manual.
O que era revolução virou rotina.

E quando a destruição deixa de libertar, resta apenas o silêncio metálico de uma rebelião esquecida.

Red Faction II is a bold yet uneven sequel that attempts to expand the foundations of its predecessor while taking the series in a more militarized, Earth-bound direction. Developed by Volition and published by Deep Silver, it moves the action away from the Martian rebellion of the original Red Faction and into a dystopian near-future Earth ruled by the authoritarian Commonwealth government. The player assumes the role of Alias, a demolitions expert and member of an elite group of genetically enhanced soldiers, each with their own specialties. After helping the Chancellor gain power through warfare, the team is betrayed and forced to turn against their former master, launching a campaign of revenge and liberation. The story sets the stage for a fast-paced, high-intensity first-person shooter that blends political intrigue, science fiction, and explosive action in typical early-2000s fashion.

Gameplay in Red Faction II is designed around quick reflexes, heavy weaponry, and spectacle. The game’s signature feature remains its use of the Geo-Mod engine, which allows for limited environmental destruction—walls, pillars, and structures can be blasted apart to expose new paths or eliminate cover. While this system was revolutionary in the first Red Faction, its implementation in the sequel feels more restrained. Instead of open-ended destruction and experimentation, the destructible environments are largely scripted and confined to certain areas, giving the gameplay a more linear, corridor-based structure. Even so, watching walls crumble and terrain deform under heavy fire remains satisfying, and the destruction still gives combat a tangible sense of impact. The arsenal is diverse and satisfying to wield: machine guns, shotguns, rocket launchers, railguns, and dual-wieldable pistols all pack punch and variety. The combat’s pacing and responsiveness make firefights intense, even if they sometimes lack the strategic flexibility of more modern shooters.

Vehicle segments punctuate the campaign, adding variety through short sequences of piloting tanks, submarines, and battle mechs. These interludes succeed in breaking up the on-foot combat while emphasizing scale and power. The inclusion of squad members during certain missions adds a cinematic flair, with each teammate’s abilities contributing to the chaos, but these characters are not deeply developed. The campaign’s brevity—lasting only about five to six hours—underscores its focus on action rather than narrative depth. The story’s tone oscillates between pulpy science fiction and grim militarism, but it never lingers long enough to explore the moral complexity of rebellion or loyalty. Still, the game attempts to add replay value through its “Heroism” rating system, rewarding players for completing objectives and sparing civilians, subtly encouraging thoughtful play amid the destruction.

Visually, Red Faction II captures the gritty aesthetic of early 2000s shooters with its metallic corridors, industrial ruins, and flickering neon lights. The environments, though repetitive at times, are well-lit and atmospheric, conveying the oppressive mood of the Commonwealth’s regime. Explosions and particle effects still look impressive given the game’s age, and the destructible scenery provides dynamic visual feedback during combat. Character models, on the other hand, show their age with stiff animations and limited expressiveness, but their designs—particularly the armored soldiers and mechanical enemies—maintain a rugged appeal. The sound design complements the visuals well, with booming weapon effects and a militaristic score that heightens tension. Voice acting, featuring recognizable talent like Lance Henriksen, adds gravitas to the dialogue, though the writing itself remains serviceable rather than memorable.

One of the game’s enduring strengths is its sense of momentum. Red Faction II wastes little time between set pieces, pushing players through collapsing buildings, enemy convoys, and massive firefights with minimal downtime. It delivers a visceral rhythm that captures the thrill of large-scale rebellion, even when its mechanics show limitations. The multiplayer mode, originally designed for split-screen play, reinforces the game’s arcade-like appeal, offering fast matches with customizable bots and explosive weapon options. Although it lacks the online capabilities and sophistication of later shooters, it still provides nostalgic fun for fans of couch co-op and local competition.

Despite its strengths, Red Faction II ultimately falls short of the revolutionary promise of its name. The first game’s spirit of experimentation and freedom gives way to a more conventional action experience, prioritizing cinematic pacing over systemic depth. The restricted use of the Geo-Mod technology and the campaign’s linear design limit the creativity that once defined the series. Yet, viewed through the lens of its time, it remains an enjoyable and technically impressive shooter, marked by its explosive gameplay and confident presentation. It captures a transitional moment in FPS history—bridging the experimentation of the late 1990s with the cinematic direction that would dominate the 2000s.

Red Faction II may not have achieved the lasting acclaim of its predecessor or later entries in the series, but it stands as a solid example of early-2000s action design. It delivers satisfying combat, memorable destruction, and a pulpy sense of rebellion that still resonates for those who appreciate its era’s straightforward energy. While its narrative ambition exceeds its execution and its mechanics feel restrained compared to what came before, the game’s raw enthusiasm and tactile gunplay make it a worthy, if imperfect, successor. For players seeking a nostalgic, explosive journey into a world of revolution and ruin, Red Faction II remains an entertaining and atmospheric ride.

For the longest time, I had heard that Red Faction 2 is the black sheep of the series. I was told by people that the game is so bad that it's a stain on the legacy of the series. I was personally not impressed with Red Faction 1 at all, so I was wondering maybe people's higher opinion of that game was a factor in making such claims about the sequel. Therefore, I decided to try Red Faction 2 by myself and see how it fares...

[h2]Ladies and Gentlemen, Red Faction 2 [i][b]IS INDEED THAT BAD[/b][/i].[/h2]
I have only spent less than an hour with this game, and I still wish I had a way to get that time back and spend it on something else instead. I don't know how, but Red Faction 2 is a major backwards leap in terms of quality compared to the first Red Faction. Sure, I had major problems with that game as well, but I still put 4 times more time in Red Faction 1 compared to this game.
Red Faction 2 offers quite possibly the most boring shooting experience I have ever seen in a first person shooter. Every gun except for your grenade launcher feels like a peashooter, thanks to the usage of incredibly weak shooting sounds, insufficient amounts of recoil after firing, and the enemies barely reacting to being shot with a gun.
The game also makes the exact same mistake as the first game by introducing a game mode that basically kills all the fun, just after you finish the very first level. After you finish the first level, you are immediately forced to do a turret section for the entirety of the next level. The game will take you through the exact same areas over and over again, having you constantly shoot at ships and enemies that appear around you, for seemingly no reason other than prolonging the playtime as much as it can. And when you finish this level, the next level will also be a turret section for its entirety! Am I supposed to have fun like this?

But it's not like the other levels that feature traditional FPS shooting are any better. In fact, they are even worse!
The levels in Red Faction 2 are completely linear, with the environmental destruction that was introduced in the first game being mostly used as a decoration. And whenever you try to use it to actually open up paths, you might find yourself stuck on a small piece of geometry and being unable to move forward unless you make that hole bigger, even if you should totally be able to pass. And the enemy encounters? Oh boy...
Red Faction 2's idea of enemy encounters is having them endlessly pouring into the level until you find the way to get to the next part of it. The enemies basically NEVER stop arriving on the levels, constantly swarm you from literally every direction and get in the way of level exploration. This especially becomes a problem when you get to the train station, as the enemies in this level are small, explosive robots that are placed everywhere and chase you around with very high speed. So you cannot simply run away from them either.

And all I have been talking about so far, are stuff from the first hour of the game! It was at this point that I stopped playing and decided to use my time to do other things. If this was what I had to endure in the beginning, I dread what I would have ran into if I continued playing. Thus, I do not recommend anyone to try this game.


[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
A deeply flawed and problematic FPS that has somehow managed to end up being inferior to its predecessor by making all sorts of wrong game design decisions. Do yourself a favor & never try to play it.

Одна из лучших космических аркад, в которую мне удалось сыграть ещё будучи школьником. С одной стороны у нас тут поделие под Японские игрища того времени. С другой же стороны, под личиной Японской  аркады скрывается достаточно глубокая Британская космическая леталка с менеджментом, добычей ресурсов, исследованиями-производством, конструированием кораблей и войной за ресурсы. 

Сюжет простой. На дворе 23 век. Человечество, которое уже давно рассекает по солнечной системе на космических кораблях, в какой то момент решило, что нехрен сидеть в стартовой локации - надо начать прыгать меж звёздами. Германия подогнала под это дело свежесобранный сверхсветовой двигатель на основе чёрных нор, кротовых дыр и прочих варп-технологий. Америка под это дело собрала космический исследовательский фрегат в виде блюдца, на котором и установили Немецкий двигатель. А возглавила всю эту экспериментальную экспедицию представительница космических войск из Японии, вместе с командой экспертов из разных стран. 

И вот корабль уже летит на точку, где и должен будет произойти пробный прыжок. Экипаж в анабиозе. корабль на автопилоте в сопровождении боевых крейсеров. И тут внезапно движок врубается раньше времени и грёбанная тарелка тэпается в варп, попутно забрав с собой все сопровождающие суда. И спустя время варп выплёвывает эту посуду в неизвестном секторе вселенной, да ещё и в окружении недружественной расы, которая прописывает всей команде пздулей, а заодно и тащит движок. 

И вот с этого момента и начинается игра. Тарелка без двигателя, пропавший экипаж, ограниченные ресурсы, невозможность вернуться обратно. И мы во всём этом...нет, не капитан - единственный выживший пилот на каком-то маленьком челночке размером с гроб. Задача - сберечь тарелку-базу, найти пропавший экипаж и двигатель, вломить напавшим инопланетянам. И главное - вернуться домой. Что для этого надо делать? 

1) Исследовать неизвестный сектор вселенной. Место, в котором мы оказались, поделено на 5 секторов, каждый из которых представляет собой с десяток зон. Наша база-тарелка, будучи межпространственным кораблём, по умолчанию находится в варпе, откуда и способна перемещаться между локациями, дабы потом материализоваться в одной из них.   

2) Добывать ресурсы. Во всех основных локациях игры находятся скопления астероидов, которые можно ломать выстрелами, дабы собирать с них 3 вида минералов - желтый, фиолетовый и зеленый. У корабля есть предел грузового отсека. У тарелочной базы - предел хранения каждого из типов минералов. Собираем минералы, тащим на базу, а затем повторяем пока локация не опустеет.

3) Разрабатывать технологии и производить технику. Научный отдел на корабле разрабатывает улучшенные версии техники для корабля и базы. Производственный - производит уже изученное. На всё это требуются ресурсы в виде минералов, а также доступный обслуживающий персонал (изначально их 5, но потом, при нахождении и спасении выживших, его число растёт). 

И главное - время. Каждый прыжок между локациями в варпе  - это один условный ход, который при желании можно и не делать, пропустив его. Внутри же локации время течёт как обычно - чем больше находишься, тем больше оно проходит. Каждая разработка и производство требует определенного времени, в зависимости от количества людей, отданных на проект. 

4) Конструировать корабли. Каждый корабль состоит из сетки на подобие инвентаря из Диабло, в пределах которой и нужно выставить все его компоненты, дабы на нём можно было летать: 
-двигатель для перемещения, 
-генератор для того, чтобы всё оборудование работало, 
-Тяговый луч, чтобы тащить на борт вещи (ресурсы, выживших, вражеское оборудование)
-Отсеки и батареи для расширения характеристик корабля.
-Щиты для отражения атак.
-Ну и оружие для нападения и обороны, а также майнинга ресурсов. Оружия в целом не так много - Лазеры, ракеты, дроны, бомбы и т.д. Всего штук 6 видов. Но и этого за глаза хватает.

Всё это приходится не просто устанавливать, а заниматься менеджментом пространства корабля. Начальные типы кораблей не способны вместить в себя более громоздкие типы движков, генераторов и оружия. А более продвинутые типы хоть и имеют больше места, но поставят перед игроком уже другие задачи. Например если всё оборудование корабля запитывается слабым генератором, то при перерасходе энергии корабль может реально перестать стрелять каким-либо оружием, либо же отказаться включить ускорение. Ну а если на мощный корабль установлен слабый движок, то возникнет превышение массы и корабль будет двигаться в пространстве с божьей помощью. Ну а если во время боя отрубится щит, то...мои соболезнования.

5) Оснащать базу. Тарелка "Эгида-1" - это не только твоя база и способ передвижения. При попадании на локацию она останется в ней, дабы забирать у тебя найденный хабар, чинить, пополнять твой боезапас да и в целом будет защищать тебя от врагов, имея свой запас прочности. И учитывая, что урон в игре можно получить банально столкнувшись с астероидом, будет очень хорошим решением оснастить базу оружием. Для этого у неё имеется 4 места под малые турели и одно в центре для тяжелого лазера. Это даст возможность базе самой отбиваться от врагов на локациях. И учитывая, что Эгида-1 способна сама прилететь к тебе через любые астероиды по первому требованию, ничто не мешает оснастить часть её гнёзд тяговыми лучами для сбора минералов, а главный лазер заменить дрелью, чтобы тарелка не ломала ресурсы при разбивании астероидов. 

6) Отбиваться от врагов. Само собой, враги тоже не будут ждать, пока ты летаешь по сектору и качаешься. Каждый из 5ти секторов находится во власти вражеской космической станции на подобии нашей тарелки, которая является боссом этого сектора. Пока этот босс жив и в локациях сектора есть ресурсы, он будет создавать баржи-сборщии, которые уже сами будут, также как и ты, летать по локациям и опустошать их. 

И пока они это делают, сектор будет всё сильнее и сильнее наполняться врагами, концентрация которых будет указываться на карте сектора красными пятнами разных размеров. Эти пятна тоже могут перемещаться по локациям. А задетектив наше блюдце, дадут клич по всем соседним секторам, что уже через пару шагов созовёт в точку дислокации Эгиды-1 флотилию, которая сама вытащит тарелку на локацию. И уже там игроку предстоит воевать буквально с десятками кораблей, пока у базы заряжается варп-движок. 

7) И всё это ради сюжета. Да, в игре он есть. Причём существует и лор, и даже диалоги между персонажами. С каждым пройденным сектором мы получаем крупицу подробностей того, что тут происходит. Почему это место не выпускает тех, кто в него попал? Что за две расы, которые попали сюда ещё до нас? И был ли преждевременный прыжок Эгиды-1 случайностью? 

И само собой, игра не может без минусов. Однако обусловлены они не корявостью игрового дизайна, а корявостью её релиза в стиме:

1) Игра 2003 года. На тот момент перемещение на стрелочках с поворотом вместо смещения в стороны было ещё актуально. И если кнопки можно поменять, то вот смещения в игре нет - придётся поворачиваться. Благо хоть в игре у каждого объекта есть физика и инерция. А значит смещение легко заменит возможность разогнаться и начать валить боком.

2) Сам релиз в Стиме - это один большой косяк. Мало того, что в стим-версии отсутствует официальная русская локализация с ПРОФЕССИОНАЛЬНОЙ озвучкой артистами РФ (Учёного так вообще озвучил Пожаров), так ещё и треки музыкального сопровождения игры пожевали еbучие шакалы. В итоге править все эти косяки фанаты вынуждены своими же руками. Спасибо что хоть ачивки добавили. 

3) И да, в игре нет возможности поставить разрешение экрана выше 800х600. ВООБЩЕ!

В целом, я более чем рекомендую эту игру. Это классика, которой всё же удалось сохранить свою актуальность даже в наши современные 2к26. Ну а если ты фанат эстетики Y2K, то местное техно на музыке игры - для тебя.

I started playing Starscape over a decade ago, over a holiday break, and for one reason or another it got abandoned mid way through (Zone 3 i think), however it lingered in the back of my mind as being fun, a bit simplistic, and definitely worth finishing.    So, in 2022, in the spirit of defeating the backlog, this indie game got another shot. 

In 2022 though, Starscape is achingly dated, though it severely dated even back in 2011 (having been released in 2003).   The resolution is limited at 800x600 (yes, 4x3) and the steam fps counter was resolutely stuck at 22fps throughout.   These issues don't matter too much though, as the art style is pleasingly retro, with a cartoony grace that a higher resolution would wash away the human touch.   The game-play, a cross between asteroids and space war, with a minor crafting element, is enjoyable, if a bit samey over the 20 hrs or so to finish the game, though it has to be said, that there is a frankly outrageous difficulty curve in the last third of the game.

The story is somewhat generic: advanced earth spaceship gets lost, has to defeat aliens and escape back home, and though told through text boxes, it's not too in your face, while providing a clear motivation for continuing, and there's more here if you're willing to go looking for it.  Similarly sound effects and music are serviceable, nothing amazing, and harking back to the halcyon days when the game was released, you might well want to pop on a podcast (or, more appropriately, some mp3's) in the background.

But despite the minor gripes above, I still recommend this game, even in 2022.   Perhaps even more so now, than I might have done in 2011; as hand-held gaming PC's like the Steam Deck, and the Aya Neo are finally making the dream of a reasonably powerful gaming PC on the go a reality.   In that world, a game like Starscape, with its 'fight and mine your way through one more node' mentality is the perfect thing to play in short bursts.

Недостатки в виде устаревания игры (версия в Стиме — 2.9, но разработчик так и не добавляет современные разрешения экрана, локализатор выпустил игру в версии 1.6, пару мелких патчей, и, как водится, пропал с концами) не могут перевесить достоинства игры. Игра не очень оригинальна по жанру, но получилась необъяснимо привлекательной в сочетании аркадных полетов со сбором ресурсов, наличия пусть не хитрого, но хорошего сюжета, приятной игровой графики и интересной графики игровых меню с персонажами, не очень разнообразного, но довольно динамичного музыкального оформления. Звук терпящей бедствие станции «Эгида» (Aegis) просто шедеврален: услышав его, невозможно не выполнить своего предназначения — отбить ее у врага. К достоинствам можно отнести простую, но эффективную экономическую систему. Добываемые ресурсы тратятся на исследование и строительство линейно во времени, пока игрок находится в рейде (можно пропустить некоторый условный отрезок времени без отправки в рейд, находясь на станции), приостанавливаясь в отсутствие ресурсов. Как только станция вновь получает необходимые ресурсы, приостановленное исследование или строительство возобновляется. Вражеские флагманские корабли в стиле классических скроллеров вполне разнообразны и монументальны, но при этом, в отличие о скроллеров, мощь их вооружения не направлена в одну сторону, а распространяется радиально во все стороны игрового экрана. Довольно сложно и интересно, их не слишком много (по одному в каждом из 5 секторов Сетки), в самый раз, как, впрочем, и в целом всего игрового разнообразия (типов кораблей, их оборудования и вооружения). Есть и немного разнообразия в виде сюжетных заданий, погонь за космическими баржами, странными и опасными нодами Сетки. В общем, игра много лет нравится, она способна увлекать не хуже «Космических рейнджеров» (но проще и короче, для меня это скорее преимущество) и оставляет надежду на осовремененное продолжение.

Starscape is a curious fusion of an arcade and a turn-based strategy game. The arcade component is in total domination, but as long as it is not backed by strategic advancements, it tends to become overwhelmingly hard.

The main feature of the game is addictive gameplay. Despite the simple idea ("collect resources to become stronger, but watch your back and take offensive actions to collect intelligence") the gameplay is extremely immersive. The whole stroy takes ~12 hours (or less on low difficulty levels) to complete. The storyline is not bad, but not too bristling with events.

From purely technical point of view, the game mechanics is trivial: the more resources you collect, the more powerful you get; and few things can prevent you from collecting resources. Whenever you save a game, it is always easy to load and avoid any serious danger you get into. It is possible to think of circumstances resulting in 100% death, but I have never encountered such a coincidence in practice. The only thing the enemies can do is substantially delay your advance. 

[b]SUMMARY:[/b] plot is simple, but intriguing, graphics is nice, strategy is straightforward. But there is something in this game that makes it addictive and immersive. An insight into this game is highly recommended. Slightly overpriced (for a reason).

Killed some time with this back in college, but it's pretty meh.  Collect resources, upgrade your mothership and your fightercraft, research and build...but the mechanics don't come together, it feels shallow, the interface is a pain, and it doesn't do bigger than 800x600.  The concept isn't flawed, it's just too small: the mechanics would have been fine in a shorter game, a flash game, that kind of thing, but stretched out to full-game length it suffers.  This game doesn't need a strategic map, but you have to slog through it anyway.  Worst of all is that it caps what you're allowed to research pretty aggressively, so early in the game you're sitting on max levels of resources that you can't spend.  Way to identify the fun part of the game and then kick it like a puppy, guys.

I still have fond memories of this game though, mainly from one night when I heard the starbase alarm going off, said "Hey wait my mothership is still at full health", and realized it was my next door neighbor playing at full volume.

Verdict:  Go play Tyrian instead.  That's what you really wanted anyway.

This is actually a really fun game at first, when you are first upgrading and manipulating your ship.  You can make missile boats, blaster-based ships, you get option drones to fire when you shoot, and so on.  Mining is actually somewhat interesting to fool around with early on. 

It, however, gets repetitive, starting with mining, and then upgrading, and finally the combat.  The final ship components cause all end-game ships to look the same, and the final boss has a stupid mechanic which requires you to either have a way more responsive ship than the game gives you, or to angle a shot in a way that gives you a generally unsatisfying win because you didn't do the high-agility maneuvers that it feels like you should do.  It caps the game off with not even allowing you to have a solid victory in the final "cutscene."

Overall, a good 75% of a game marred by an overly repetitive final zone.  If you don't mind this, and the late 90s graphics, go ahead and get it! Sometimes things don't simply go as planned, especially when it comes to experimental Dimension Drives that use the barely contained power of an artificial black hole.
Now the space station known as the Aegis has ended up in an alien dimension with most of its crew missing and a huge chunk of its technology database stolen by a hostile alien race.
Now it is up to you and what little crew that remains onboard the Aegis to try and find the missing crew while also rediscovering technology to give the space station better defenses as well as better weapons and gadgets for your own ship and even new hulls that can hold more and such.
Of course you will need to gather minerals in order to build and research anything, of which there are thankfully plenty of asteroids floating about that may or may not contain the minerals you need in order to improve your arsenal.
Sometimes the aliens will show up all of a sudden while you're gathering minerals and they might have a capital class ship with them that will be holding equipment that you can use on both your ship and the Aegis, of course these ships are much tougher then the smaller fighters and drones so you might want to be extremely cautious in how you approach them.
If you're the type of player who likes to build up a mighty arsenal by doing research and such while also doing mining and stopping an evil alien race, then this is something for you.
Even without the underlying story of fighting aliens, it's surprisingly fun to just shoot at asteroids and collect minerals.

Lots of semi-interesting characters with a less than vomit-inducing plot? Not great, but it could be worse.

So... what's not to love? Why's this a thumbs down vote?

Well... here's the rub: the handling on your ships is very realistic, but it's slow and clunky. I'm alright with that, normally. It requires some planning of momentum and some good piloting to be competent, and that's fine.

The problem is that the boss battles aren't designed for the controls nor the physics of the game. They assume perfect, pristine, pin-point keyboard turning in rapid order. I'm fine with that if the interface made such a realistic possibility. Unfortunately, starscape's boss battles are like waltzing into the olympics' figure skating event wearing cross country skiis.

It doesn't matter how good you are, the controls simply flat out SUCK for trying to fight the bosses, and player skill seriously only has a very small amount to do with it. Someone with godlike reflexes could theoretically get through in a few tries, but most of your boss battles involve being expected to start moving out of the way before a boss even begins to box you in, without knowing when or where that attack will come from. If your ship were even remotely possible to be set up to cope with that, great, but it's not.

Keyboard turning and physics-based thrust maneuvering simply doesn't work for the style of bosses that Starscape throws at you.

The rest of the game is fun and fine, a few minor nitpicks here and there, but it's good overall... but the act-ending bosses are mandatory, and they suck HARD. I don't mean "it's difficult", I mean it in the sense of "this is one of the worst design decisions I've ever seen anyone ever make... did they even play test this to see if it was fun?".

Any fun you get from the game will be sucked dry as soon as you're stuck in a boss battle, and since the controls and interface flat out aren't up to the task of fighting the bosses, it's going to make you pull your hair out over it. I highly advise staying the hell away from Starscape just in general. Unless you're a masochist, then go right ahead.

Anyway, to stress it again, there's a difference between "difficult" and "bad design and poor UI/controls". Having a piss poor interface does not equate to "difficulty", it just equates to being BAD.




Final Verdict:

Not worth it, even if it's on sale for $1. You'll probably break a keyboard that cost more than $1, even if you don't have a history of such, and are a pretty mellow person normally. While the game has lots of really good points to it, and does a lot of stuff very well, it's flaws are gamebreaking. When you put more effort into fighting the game's interface than you do fighting the boss, the game's a bust.


Score: About 35%. It has some really good stuff, but the flaws are devastating and overpower any potential the game had.

Any of you grow up playing SubSpace? That old online top-down space shooter, that could have been the first MMO? (lots of players per server, 'till the very end, and that game was OLD - the days of dial-up. Beat that.) Well, this game feels a bit similar to that and Asteroids - fly around in a spaceship, blow up asteroids, and like in SubSpace, collect stuff to make your ship cooler. But in this, you collect minerals from the asteroids and enemy capital ships with a tractor beam, and you can only hold so much before you have to drop it off in the hangar. To actually make stuff out of it, you have to do some R&D - research better stuff, then actually build it. Both actions take minerals, and there's only so many minerals per area. And they don't come back. Thankfully we have a dangerous zone with infinite resources. *gulp* Oh, and this will play on pretty much anything. Woo!

Starscape is a very pleasant combination of Asteroids with a plot and some other gameplay types: a bit of adventure, a bit of tactics, a lot of fun.  You shoot asteroids to get resources (you need them to build parts or repair your fighter or base); all the while you're under attack by all sorts of enemy types.  You can research new parts -- fighter hulls, engines, shields, weapons, batteries -- which you then need resources to build.

Time is paused while you are in your base station, so you can choose what manpower to allocate to research or building, and you can arrange parts onto fighter hulls to try new tactics.  However, stuff doesn't progress until you get back out into the action.  And don't take too much damage out there or you'll use up the resources you need for building new toys, and have to go get more.  This is so fun!

I had fun with it though.  I haven't found anything like it since.

All the while, you're having to fend off and defeat the alien threat.

Have fun.

Has so far proven to be somewhat unstable on winblows 7 though. Still works well enough, but it's prone to crashing more often than I'd like. Frequent saves rrecommended.

80/100 - I just discovered this game is based on the old genre of ISOMETRIC PLATFORM, with classics such as Batman (1986), Head Over Heels (1987), SOLSTICE (1990), so the platforming is intentionally designed to be frustrating, slow, complicated (at least for the general standard) and yet fun.

Puzzles are a mix of precision and logic, only 2 rooms took me half an hour to solve with hard logic. The turn based combat is simplistic but it works properly as a hacking mechanic, try to not spend too much time grinding XP on those, its not necessary even on hard mode. Story? I didn't care about it honestly.

I remember playing this game forever ago, and then putting it down because there was some kind of glitch that made it near impossible to save one of the characters near the end.

Figured I'd give it another shot to at least *finish* the game, and somehow it's more frustrating than it was when I first played.

You know what's bad? Isometric platforming. You know what's worse? Isometric platforming with a slippery character. You know what's hell? Isometric platforming *block pushing puzzles* with a slippery character. 

And then there's the JRPG aspect of it, which, while interesting in theory, isn't very well balanced. If you don't go out of  your way to grind early on, one of your characters is more or less screwed into never getting past level 1 because downed party members don't gain EXP, and all EXP gained during the JRPG section is... reset? I tried grinding at this current point in the game, but it's at a point where she gets downed in two hits by basic enemies. 

So, well. I can't say I recommend this playing experience. If you like having to fight your character to perform even basic tasks efficiently and don't mind having to restart from the beginning when you inevitably don't attempt to fight every battle available to you, then be my guest.

Seems fairly retro by today's standards but still a good game that has some very light Mega Man Battle Network type exploration and battles. The platformer is a little unfairly difficult, and puzzles are okay, but I had fun with this one.

[h1] Blast from the past! [/h1]
A simple, yet nice mix of izometrical puzzle-platformer exploration and JRPG combat. The puzzles are pretty cool, couple of them even me scratch my head for and hour or so. The hacking part (which are the game's "combat") and all the management around it while not being very deep, still provide enough variety for the duration of a playthrough. There sure is a story in this game, but it is quite far from being the main driver for you to play. Barely there, yet still charming.

Although, i have to mention one thing. I wouldn't have played this game if it wasn't for my childhood. ("Transformers" magazines, anyone?) I felt very nostalgic about this title, so when i have stumbled upon a video on it and saw the original title of the game, it was pretty much a matter of time till i'd play through the entire thing. And now i'm done! To my big surprise, i ended up getting quite involved to the JRPG aspect of Mr. Robot, even tho i don't really play this kind of games. I also vividly remember being overwhelmed by it as a child and liking the puzzle-platformer part a lot more. Kinda funny... 

So, yeah, these are my impressions. The last thing i should mention is that the game is pretty easy on "normal". It does include the high difficulty option, but i haven't tried it. Oh, and the mouse & keyboard controls are probably the weakest part of the entire game. Hope you don't mind using arrow keys, heh. And if you have any troubles with the "Enter" key multiclicking - use Ctrl instead. Fills the same functions.

Thanks for the childhood, Mr. Robot!

Still as fun as it was in childhood. A bit easier now especially that I know English and games much better than when I was a kid but still difficult enough to be challenging in a fun way.

This is a game I first downloaded the demo for from ArcadeTown, when that was still a thing. I for the life of me couldn't figure out how I was supposed to find it, until one day I found it on a whim and found out it was on Steam(!!).

Mr. Robot is an unusual, imaginative blend of genres that reflects the ambition and inventive spirit of mid-2000s indie development. Created and published by Moonpod, it casts you as Asimov, a humble service robot aboard the massive colony ship Eidolon. When the ship’s systems begin to fail and the human passengers in cryostasis are placed in jeopardy, Asimov becomes an unlikely hero—navigating malfunctioning corridors, hostile machines, and corrupted digital systems in a desperate attempt to uncover what has gone wrong. The setup is simple but engaging, setting the stage for a journey that is equal parts physical exploration and virtual infiltration, wrapped in a moody, atmospheric sci-fi presentation.

At its core, Mr. Robot is a hybrid game composed of two distinct but interconnected parts. The first is a 3D isometric puzzle-platformer, where you guide Asimov through boxed-in rooms filled with hazards, moving platforms, switches, electrified panels, and environmental puzzles. These sections evoke the feel of classic puzzle adventures: precision movement, timed switches, crate manipulation, and hazard navigation form the backbone of progression. The isometric view gives the game a distinct identity but also adds a layer of challenge, as judging height and distance becomes essential for avoiding pitfalls. Much of the tension lies not in enemies but in the ship itself, with environmental dangers presenting as much threat as any antagonist.

The second component is the hacking mode—a turn-based RPG system that engages whenever Asimov interfaces with computer terminals or digital locks. Here, the game transforms completely: instead of platforming, you command a team of “ghost” programs that battle corrupted data defenses. These sequences are visually abstract and mechanically different, involving stat upgrades, skill choices, and careful selection of attacks or support actions. The duality between the two modes is striking, but it allows the game to flex different muscles. Physical sections reward dexterity and attention, while hacking battles demand a more methodical, strategic mindset. As progression continues, the connection between the two becomes more meaningful, with success in one influencing your capabilities in the other.

This unusual structure helps Mr. Robot stand out, but it is also what creates some of its roughest edges. The isometric platforming, while clever, occasionally suffers from perspective difficulties. Depth and elevation can be tricky to read, leading to misjudged jumps or unintended falls. Some puzzles require relentless trial and error, and repeated failure in the later stages can make progress feel slow or punishing. Conversely, the hacking system—while charming in its retro RPG inspirations—may feel shallow to players expecting deeper customization or more complex enemy behavior. Battles rely on straightforward turn-based mechanics, and once you establish a reliable approach, the sense of danger tends to fade.

What bolsters the experience is the strong atmosphere. The Eidolon feels like a living, deteriorating environment: dim corridors hum with failing machinery, automated systems behave unpredictably, and background audio reinforces the sense of isolation. The visual design mixes industrial metallic interiors with glowing monitors, data lines, and sterile maintenance spaces, creating a believable vision of a massive starship on the brink of catastrophe. The tone is more somber than comedic, and as the narrative evolves, there is a growing sense of unease that complements the gameplay loop of delving deeper into the ship’s problems.

Yet the game’s pacing can be uneven. Early sections do an admirable job of introducing systems and teaching puzzle mechanics, but as the adventure grows more complex, the flow can slow noticeably. The alternation between platforming and hacking is intriguing but sometimes disrupts rhythm, especially when long platforming sequences are abruptly followed by extended digital battles. Navigation can also become confusing, with the in-game map offering limited clarity on multi-room layouts or long-term objectives, occasionally leaving players wandering until they stumble upon the next correct path.

Despite these flaws, Mr. Robot maintains a loyal fanbase for good reason. It is a game with personality—quirky, earnest, and unafraid to take creative risks. It may not be polished to a mirror shine, but its commitment to blending genres and telling a small-scale sci-fi story gives it a distinctive charm. Asimov himself, with his modest role and unexpectedly heroic journey, adds emotional grounding to the otherwise mechanical world. For players willing to embrace its quirks, the game rewards persistence with clever puzzle design, atmospheric tension, and the satisfaction of unraveling a digital mystery piece by piece.

Ultimately, Mr. Robot is a project defined by ambition: a puzzle-platformer with RPG layers, a sci-fi story told through both physical and virtual conflict, and an indie game unafraid to experiment. It is uneven in execution but rich in ideas, offering an experience that stands apart from the formulaic tendencies of many modern titles. For players seeking something different—something that challenges both reflexes and strategy while delivering a memorable atmosphere—Mr. Robot remains a unique and worthwhile journey through a troubled starship and the circuits of a small but determined hero.

Rating: 7/10
