[h1] 이도 저도 아닌 평작 혹은 졸작[/h1] 

바이오하자드 5는 흔히 4편의 액션을 강화한 작품이라고 평한다. 다만 필자는 그 생각에 크게 반대한다. 5는 4가 구축한 액션을 제대로 계승하지도 못한 평작 혹은 망작의 수준이다.

우선 4편의 매력적 요소는 단순한 액션도 있지만, 무엇보다도 플레이어가 상황에 따라 다양한 대처 전략을 구사하고, 결과를 직접 체감 할 수 있다는 점에 있었다. 지형지물을 이용하기, 적을 유인해서 일망타진하기, 무기 케이스에 적절히 물품을 배치하는 등 플레이어의 경험에 따른 판단이 명확히 반영 되었다.

다만 5는 그렇지 않다. 플레이어의 대처 전략에 수시로 제약을 걸고, 그 결과도 영 시원치 못하다.

[h2]1. 게임 디자인과 레벨 디자인이 심하게 잘못되었다.[/h2]

챕터를 연속해서 진행해도 차질이 없을 정도가 게임의 방향성이 아니었던 듯 하다. 그런 점에서 챕터 시작마다 정비와 구매 시간을 준 것 같다. 다만 그 시간에 할 수 있는 행동이 매우 제한적이고 탄약 (유탄류 제외) 을 무엇보다 직접적으로 구매 할 수 없다. 적이 강한 화력과 물량으로 밀고 오는 성향이 강한 5에서 이는 매우 부정적인 요소로 작용해 플레이 시 어려움과 깊은 빡침을 유도한다. 무엇보다도 4와 완전히 같은 게임 조작법을 채택한 채로, 해당 조작법의 장단점을 고려하지 않은 채로 전장을 시가지와 총격전으로 바꿔버린 점도 그러하다.

챕터 분량도 지극히 임의적이며, 탄 소모가 많은 레벨 디자인이 연속적으로 반복되는 등, 중간에 쉬며 재정비하는 챕터를 주지 않는 경우가 종종 있다. 이는 앞에서 언급 한 리스타트를 통한 재정비를 유도하긴 하나 이 경우에는 게스트는 정상적으로 클리어 했다고 인정 되지 않는 기가 막힌 버그가 존재한다.

9칸의 제한된 인벤토리는 플레이어의 자유로운 플레이를 저하시킨다. 플레이에 기본적인 물품을 최소한으로 챙겨도 칸이 부족한 상황이 여러 번 생긴다. 이는 게임의 난이도를 올리는 동시에, 플레이어의 유동적 플레이를 크게 저해한다.

유탄 발사기를 얻고 난 이후부터는 탄에 따른 약점을 지닌 몹들이 등장한다. 하지만 이를 초회차인 유저들이 하나 하나를 파악 후 대응하기는 힘든 편이다. 이는 자연스럽게 다른 탄환의 낭비로 이어지고, 결과적으로 장기적 플레이 시 큰 부담 요소이자 플레이 시 어려움으로 작용한다.

[h2]2. 스토리의 질이 떨어진다.[/h2]
바이오하자드 시리즈가 6편 전까지는 B급 노선을 탄 작품인 것은 맞으나, 그 정서를 무리하게 스토리에 이식하려 하니 괴상하고 납득하기 힘든 상황이 여러 번 연출 된다. 짜장 엑셀라를 피하는 과정 컷신은 한심할 정도로 짜칠 정도이며, 질을 구한다고 혼자 크리스가 뛰어든다는 것부터 너무 무리이고, 그걸 본 쉐바가 갑자기 동참하겠다고 하는 것도 개연성이 없다. 게다가, 이때 까지의 메인 빌런이자 최종 보스인 웨스커를 짜장면 사부로 만들어버리고 허무하게 보낸 것 또한 큰 비판 포인트이다.

[h2]결론[/h2]
바이오하자드 5의 가장 큰 문제는 4편의 장점을 발전시키고 새로운 호평 요소를 넣기보다는, 액션의 규모와 시각적 화려함만을 키우는 데 집중하면서 기존 시스템과 새로운 전투 환경 사이의 균형을 제대로 잡지 못했다는 점이다.

전략적 자율성은 줄어들었고, 자원 관리는 불합리해졌으며, 레벨 디자인과 서사 역시 충분한 완성도를 보여 주지 못했다. 액션의 규모가 커졌다는 사실 만으로 전작보다 발전한 작품이라고 평가하기는 어렵다.

그런 점에서 필자는 바이오하자드 5를 4편의 액션을 강화한 후속작이라기보다는, 4편이 구축한 재미의 본질을 상당 부분 놓쳐 버린 작품이라고 평가하고 싶다.

Resident Evil 5 es un juegazo, aquí regresa el personaje Chris Redfield pero ahora están en África.
Chris va a África junto con su nueva compañera Sheva Alomar para investigar un brote de un nuevo virus que está convirtiendo a la gente en Majini, que ya no son zombies lentos, son zombies que corren, que gritan, que usan armas y que te persiguen en manada. Y donde aparece el épico personaje de Wesker nuevamente como villano, Wesker es el mejor villano de toda la saga, con sus lentes oscuros, su velocidad sobrehumana y sus peleas contra Chris que son legendarias.
Es un juego para jugar en cooperativo con un amigo, se disfruta muchísimo, con jefes gigantes, puzzles, persecuciones y mucha acción.
Si te gusta la acción y Resident Evil, este es obligado. 9/100.

Зашли с другом в кооп почистить зад африканским зомби, но в первой же серьезной стычке эта толпа сделала всё в точности наоборот. Сожгли мутанта в огромной печи и поплыли дальше: гоняли на лодке, вычищали аборигенов, позаимствовали у них пару яиц и благополучно их схавали прямо на ходу. А от местных загадок с зеркалами и лучами свету мне до сих пор кошмары снятся.

Дальше пришли к папочке Вескеру. Он красиво дал Крису пару раз по лицу, поуклонялся от пуль в стиле «Матрицы» и оставил нас разгребать тему с Джилл, у которой на груди висела «электро-блоха». Я скорее себе пассатижами зуб вырву, чем аккуратно сдеру с нее эту хрень! В итоге кое-как её отклеили и пошли зачищать огромный корабль.

Вескер красиво улетел на самолете, перед этим выдав Крису еще одну порцию мотивационных лещей. Мы минут 20 тупо пытались нанести ему хоть какой-то физический или моральный урон, пока до нас не дошло, что ему нужно тупо вколоть вирус. Ну а финалочка в вулкане — это вообще жестко: под конец игры патроны можно было по пальцам пересчитать, но мы всё-таки красиво улетели на вертолете. Без Вескера, естественно.

10/10, зашли поиграть в кооп — отжали яйца у аборигенов и поставили укол суперзлодею.

Chris Redfield goes to Africa to stop a bioterrorist threat, but quickly discovers that his biggest enemy isn't the infected — it's the local economy of ammunition. He teams up with Sheva, punches things that probably shouldn't be punchable, and eventually meets Albert Wesker, a man whose fashion sense is as questionable as his plans for humanity. Wesker is so ridiculously confident that you almost feel bad for him. Almost. He also seems to believe that sunglasses are a perfectly reasonable accessory for a world-ending crisis. A true businessman: always dressed for success, even when the world is about to explode.

The co-op/partner gameplay — and Sheva's character along with it — was actually a pleasant surprise. It's unpolished, but certainly not as bad as people make it out to be.

What troubled me were the latter two points: the departure from survival horror — something I deeply wish to see corrected in an eventual remake — and [spoiler] Jill, one of the franchise's original protagonists alongside Chris, being reduced to a brainwashed character. Unfortunately, this seems unlikely to change, as Capcom never seems to give its female characters the attention they deserve. [/spoiler]

Recomiendo este juego para aquellos amantes de los juegos como Grand Theft Auto, Amantes de la música y Seguidores de la cultura retro desde los videojuegos y lo vintage, donde estos ultimos se lo van a gozar con cada pieza de juego que se ofrece en esta historia.

Long story short: Driver: Parallel Lines is in every aspect an average game for its time. That‘s also the reason I don‘t recommend it: it‘s too generic, the plot is extremely flat, and all the mechanics like shooting and driving can also be summarized as average at best.

If you want Driver because of a good story, good shooting mechanics or good driving, I strongly recommend getting other games from that era. On the other hand, if you want to experience the - as far as I know - only game that actually shows you New York from two different eras - 1978 and 2006, respectively -, I recommend to check this Driver out, especially on sale. It‘s also the only aspect there it does a good job, in my opinion.


Long review:
Without spoilering too much, you won‘t experience significant character development or even some background stories. I won‘t necessarily call the story „bad“, but if you want to play Driver because of a good story and maybe even think about something like GTA IV, just no. GTA IV‘s story is like five standard deviations more interesting, polished and shows actually very good character development. This game does not. Still, like I said: It‘s not written in a bad manner, it just lacks any substantial depth: I would bet that the screenplay for the story didn‘t surpass ten pages.

Regarding the shooting mechanics: They do their job, and especially the shooting aspect is, in my opinion, acceptable for the time the game was released. The same I said above applies here: You won‘t play the game because of the shooting mechanics. They‘re dull, sometimes even whack. I think the mechanics can be perfectly summarized with one sentence: The game doesn‘t register head shots. Yep, you need to empty your magazine for one enemy.

Followed by the driving mechanics: It‘s okay, the driving feels organic and not that frustrating. The 2006 cars feel the same like the 1978 cars, even if the franchise is called „Driver“, you also won‘t play the game purely for the driving mechanics. The same I said above applies here: Get - even an old! - Need for Speed title, get Midnight Club, if you want a game focusing on actual good driving. This game won‘t offer even the slightest of the experience actual racing games would offer.

Last, but not least, and probably the only aspect where the game shines, is the map, the atmosphere, and, especially, the switch between 1978 and 2006 New York. Yes, New York feels atmospheric and the game regarding this aged well. Both New Yorks have their own era-typical feel, music and design. This 'dichotomy' of two different New Yorks may be unique in the world of gaming, and for exactly that, Driver offers an interesting, or at least unique, experience in exploring two different eras of an iconic city.

Like I said in the introduction: The only thing Driver does well and unique is the map and era design. For every other aspect of the game, there are tons of better games out there, even from the era the game was released back then.

# Análise: Driver: Parallel Lines (2006)

Esse aqui é, com certeza, o melhor jogo da franquia *Driver*. O que esse jogo fez ao misturar duas épocas totalmente diferentes na mesma cidade é algo fantástico. Eu joguei muito esse game e a forma como ele divide a ambientação é sensacional. É mais um baita clássico que, se você achar em uma promoção na Steam, compensa demais comprar para ter na biblioteca, mesmo sabendo que vai sentir o peso da idade dele.

### 1. A Genialidade das Duas Épocas e o Plot Twist

O maior acerto do jogo é a sua estrutura narrativa dividida em duas eras: a Nova York clássica e estilosa da década de 70 e a cidade moderna dos anos 2000. Você começa como o TK, um motorista de fuga jovem e marrento nos anos 70, e a história segue aquela pegada meio filme de "Sessão da Tarde", mas com um *plot twist* f*** pra caralho no meio.

O protagonista é traído, vai preso e, quando sai da cadeia 28 anos depois, nos anos 2000, o mundo mudou completamente. Essa virada te dá uma motivação muito maior para seguir até o final do jogo e buscar vingança contra a antiga gangue. É animal ver a diferença visual, a mudança nas músicas e o contraste cultural entre as duas eras.

### 2. Uma Nova York Gigante e Densa para o PS2

Para a época em que foi lançado, rodando originalmente no PlayStation 2 e no primeiro Xbox, os gráficos eram muito fodas. A recriação de Nova York é extremamente grande e impressionante para as limitações daquele hardware. Não sei se tem algum outro jogo de PS2 que consiga entregar uma Nova York com aquela densidade de trânsito, pedestres e tamanho de mapa. A transição estética dos carros de uma época para a outra foi muito bem-feita, mudando os modelos antigos e quadrados dos anos 70 pelos veículos modernos e velozes dos anos 2000.

### 3. A Física Clássica dos Carros e o Sistema de Tiro

A franquia *Driver* sempre foi focada na pilotagem, e a física dos carros e o sistema de batidas até hoje são muito bons e divertidos. Os carros têm peso, derrapam de um jeito gostoso de controlar e os acidentes são bem plásticos.

O forte da saga nunca foi a troca de tiros a pé — que inclusive quase destruiu o *Driv3r* (Driver 3) —, mas aqui em *Parallel Lines* eles conseguiram ajustar a mecânica. O tiroteio não é o ponto mais alto do jogo, mas passa longe de ser ruim; ele é legal, funcional e a troca de tiros funciona muito bem no meio das missões de ação, sem quebrar o ritmo da gameplay.

### Conclusão

*Driver: Parallel Lines* foi o jogo que salvou a honra da franquia ao entregar uma jogabilidade de corrida excelente, uma ambientação histórica f*** e uma trama de vingança que te prende do início ao fim. Claro que, por ser um jogo bem antigo, você vai sentir o peso da idade nos comandos a pé e em algumas texturas. Mas pela nostalgia, pela física animal dos carros e pela experiência única de ver Nova York mudar no tempo, ele vale super a pena. Se aparecer em uma promoção barata na Steam, compensa demais levar!

Driver: Parallel Lines is straight up underrated as hell.

The 70s side of the game? pure gold. The music, the dirty New York vibe, the cars, the clothes, even the way the city feels, it all comes together perfectly. [b]Driver Parallel Lines is a large open world action game set in New York City focussed on driving and vehicular activities/combat over on foot exploration & movement.[/b] The world & activities are simple & reflective of the genre during the 6th generation yet it has an evolving world that highlights two eras in New York that should be experienced for the $2 on sale price.

[i]Furthermore it remains the only available Driver game on the Steam Market.[/i]

The story is a simple yet undercooked revenge tale that takes place in 1978 before everything changes in a timeskip to 2006. The two Eras hold Vehicles, Objectives, Aesthetics & Mood reflective of their time & despite the change of weaponry the gunplay remains janky with wide bloom & autolock aiming.

[h3]Overview[/h3]
The story spans 2 Eras, the 1970's when you’re a young overconfident high ego upstart & the mid 2000's when you're an aged vengeful ex-con. You start in the 70's before fast forwarding into the 2000's halfway through the game; a change that brings a welcome breath of air into the experience with the introduction of faster cars, inflated income and increased action & grit. The city layout, buildings, interface & player visuals also change according to the active Era. 

Parallel Lines is vehicle centric despite having on foot gameplay/combat; nearly all activities involve your vehicle and are balanced for such engagement. You cannot run while on foot so you're incentivised to get the closest vehicle to continue. Vehicular combat & Driving take the forefront of the action (as the series’ name implies) with driveby shooting integrated into the vehicle combat model, although the engagement is restricted to forward contact. The vehicles in the 70’s have a weighted float to their control while the 2000’s are a hybrid of lightweight & cinderblocks; whilst certain vehicle types ebb & flow between the two depending on their class: Industrial, Muscle, Sports, Race, Motorcycle etc.

[h3]Important & Quick Note Bullet Points[/h3]
[list][*]This title is functional with Gamepads but they must be selected in the options menu via keyboard input before they can be used.

[*]The gameworld takes place in New York City with New Jersey, Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens & Manhattan all playable areas.

[*]The start of the game (1987) is slow, goofy & extremely cartoony; fitting for a nostalgic view of the era & the full of himself main character TK.

[*]Police are present with a twin bounty system and appear on nearly every second corner leading to frequent engagements & getaway runs from them during travels to mission objectives or free roam.

[*]Fast Travel is available but restricted to garages, the safe house & visible mission objectives. Using FT helps you circumvent long travels between locations and avoid the police if you get exhausted from their chases. It is perfect for the early game when you don’t have fast cars and have limited funds to upgrade your cars at the garage with Nitrous, engine, handling & cosmetics.

[*]The controls are janky with odd decisions such as double tapping acceleration (trigger) to activate boost

[*]Shooting has an instant lock on reticle with wide weapon bloom dependent on range from the target. Vehicle gunplay only targets in front of you with no rear view controls incentivising 180* turns.

[*]Vehicle controls are reflective of their class & build; heavy vehicles will be weighed down in corners requiring slow or lifted entries while light vehicles can enter fast, leave faster and possibly flip if inclines & declines are involved.

[*]Traffic Density is controllable via an options slider making the streets & driving experience butter smooth, tense or borderline undrivable depending on your preference.

[*]Draw Distance is low and as a result at High Speeds there are major texture pop-ins that affect the immersion.

[*]The tutorial & stylized font in my experience was hard to read & understand clearly upon introduction and the associated tutorial is quite basic yet dragged out. 
[/list]

[h3]Police[/h3]
Police are present throughout the open-world and missions & utilize a twin bounty system that allocates a separate wanted level to player character & vehicle based on witnessed criminal activity. Police will engage a pursuit if you enter their field of vision while wanted however interactions will vary depending on if your vehicle &/or character are wanted.

If the player character has a wanted level you will enter pursuit while on foot however if you’re in a vehicle that lacks a wanted level, the police will take their time to identify you while in their field of vision, allowing for swift avoidance and removal from detection. If spotted during this state both the player character & vehicle will gain/maintain wanted status.

However if your vehicle has a wanted level you will enter a pursuit upon FOV entry no matter the circumstances but your player character will not gain a wanted level until they exit the vehicle within the Police FOV. As such you can exit a vehicle while in the evade state and swap to a new undetected vehicle to leave the area without further engagement.

Police are ruthless when in a slow vehicle, exacerbated by a full traffic density setting in the options menu, creating tense getaway engagements. However as you progress & earn funds by completing side-activities & potentially gaining Perfect Driver Bonuses (extra $10,000 in 1978, $100,000 in 2006) to upgrade your vehicles in the garage or if you gain race cars by coming first in Circuit Races, your engagements with the police are insignificant as you speed out of their FOV and evade pursuit just as fast as it starts.

[h3]Main Story, Timeskip & changing elements[/h3]
Parallel Lines' main story is a simple revenge story after the lead becomes expendable in a successful kidnapping. It takes 9 hours to complete with a few mandatory side missions included and is the driving force behind the era change.

The story is told through era changing mission briefs & CGI cutscenes that hold up fairly well 20 years later with the exception of the exaggerated movement animations (also seen in engine) that may as well mimic a chafed Cowboy or Doflamingo from One Piece. 

Halfway through the game you'll reach an unnotified point of no return that will fast track the world to 2006, with the only way of returning to the 70’s being a menu extra feature unlockable upon the story’s conclusion (the same for replaying missions).

[h3]Side Content & Era differences[/h3]
Similar to the age distinct vehicles, themes, cityscape, buildings & weapons; the two Era’s also have a few different side missions discoverable through exploration & map markers.

Parallel Lines followed in the 2000’s footsteps of displaying main missions on the map alongside a select few side missions before hiding the remaining content across the world for the player to discover in their travels between the former marked missions.

[b]The revealed side content include:[/b][/list]
[*]Circuit Races at 3 designed racetracks (Hunts Point, La Guardia & New Jersey) each having three difficulty choices (Easy, Medium & Hard).
[*]3 Steal to Order Tow Truck vehicle pick-up & delivery tasks.
[*]Street Races with 3 unique race layouts per region. 9 unique layouts per era for a total of 16 unique street races.
[*]3 Loan Shark shakedowns (1978)
[*]3 Hitman target takedowns. (2006)[/list]
[list][b]Discoverable content:[/b]
[*]Taxi Pick-up/Delivery Jobs
[*]Robbery Getaways
[*]Demolition Derby (1978)
[*]Vehicle Delivery
[*]Police Evasion Speedrun
[*]Checkpoint Races
[*]2 Grand Prix[/list]

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
I believe D:PL is worth a playthrough for those who enjoy driving games & open world cities as the game offers a quality amount for its age. It is $3.73AUD during sales and that's great given its contemporaries have long since been delisted or remastered for x4 the price.

[h1][b] Reseña de Tom Clancy's EndWar™[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Tom Clancy's EndWar™ es estrategia militar con vibra de “Tercera Guerra Mundial para dummies tácticos”, donde mueves unidades, capturas puntos y haces microgestión lo justo para sentirte general… sin necesitar un doctorado en hojas de Excel. Su propuesta más llamativa: dar órdenes por [b]control de voz[/b], como si estuvieras en una sala de mando… o peleándote con tu micrófono en plena madrugada.

La primera impresión es clara: esto quiere ser una estrategia más accesible y “cinemática” que un festival de números. La campaña en solitario cumple como tour guiado por el caos geopolítico, y el multijugador existe… en teoría. En la práctica, con [b]14 jugadores actuales[/b], a veces te toca jugar “EndWar: Búsqueda de Partida Simulator”.

[h2]Reporte de Inteligencia: Lo que Domina vs Lo que se Desmorona[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Control de voz: idea arriesgada y muy temática, te hace sentir comandante (cuando coopera).  
  Enfoque táctico militar: el ritmo y las órdenes por escuadrones se sienten más “operación” que “granja de recursos”.  
  Un jugador sólido: si vienes por campaña/escenarios, hay material para entretener sin depender de nadie.  
  Multijugador incluido: cuando aparece gente, la tensión táctica se pone sabrosa.  
  Accesible dentro del género: estrategia sin ahogarte en menús infinitos.

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Comunidad bajísima (14 jugadores): el multijugador puede sentirse como un museo… pero sin guía.  
  0 logros: Steam te mira y dice “¿te divertiste? pues imagínatelo, porque no te lo voy a registrar”.  
  Control de voz no es para todos: si no tienes buen micro/entorno, prepárate para que tu “ataca” suene a “abraza”.  
  Profundidad limitada para veteranos de estrategia: los más puristas van a decir que esto es “estrategia con rueditas”.  
  Multijugador dependiente de la hora y la suerte: sin masa crítica, el matchmaking es un acto de fe.

[h2]Conclusión (Bueno)[/h2]
Tom Clancy's EndWar™ es como ese experimento raro que salió bien… a medias: una estrategia táctica con identidad, que apostó por el control de voz cuando eso sonaba futurista y hoy suena a “ojalá tu micrófono no sea una papa”. En solitario se deja jugar y cumple, y su enfoque militar está bien logrado.

El problema controversial (y realista) es que el multijugador, que era parte del alma del asunto, hoy vive con respiración asistida: [b]14 jugadores actuales[/b]. Aun así, el juego tiene [b]987 recomendaciones[/b], lo que sugiere que mucha gente sí le encontró el gusto, especialmente por su propuesta distinta dentro de estrategia. Vale la pena si vienes por la campaña y la curiosidad del mando por voz; si vienes por online competitivo constante… mejor reza, agenda con amigos o acepta la soledad táctica.

几乎没有派系差异。各派系兵种都一样，说是老美无人机厉害，大鹅装甲牛逼，欧洲人薄皮速度快，但是真没射程和视野优势明显，也是相当符合近现代战争规律了。

Великолепная игра на стыке жанров RTS и тактики. Практически варгейм для начинающих.
Игра построена на специализации каждого вида юнитов и умении противопоставить действиям врага правильную контрмеру. Видите вертолеты? Эффективны будут БТР. Против БТР нужны танки, пехота окопалась в здании — нужна артиллерия.
В игре решительно не работает тактика закидывания врага «топовыми» юнитами, так как даже сильный в одной ситуации юнит оказывается бесполезным в другой. Игра постоянно заставляет балансировать между войсками, которые нужны для реализации твоей стратегии, и войсками, которые требуются как контрмера стратегии противника. Ты не можешь быть сильным везде — в результате на карте постоянно происходит передвижение и ротация состава армии.
Прибавьте к этому ещё и влияние рельефа, географии разных карт, заставляющих распределять армию по флангам и продумывать безопасные пути переброски войск, — и получите один из самых необычных экспериментов в жанре. Мне даже жаль, что такой подход к RTS не стал мейнстримным.
Из по-настоящему серьезных минусов могу выделить разве что фактическое отсутствие сюжета, который можно описать тремя предложениями и по сути полностью раскрывается в самом начале. По прохождении кампании ничего нового вы, увы, не узнаете — вам просто покажут флаг выбранной вами стороны и поздравят с победой.

Score: 6.5/10

EndWar is built around a handful of bold ideas, some of which were genuinely forward-thinking for 2008. Unfortunately, many of those ideas either clash with one another or work poorly on PC, resulting in a game that is interesting to engage with, but often frustrating to actually play.

Camera and Core Concept

The defining feature of EndWar is its camera system, which is glued to individual units rather than providing a traditional top-down RTS view. In theory, this creates a sense of immediacy and battlefield immersion. In practice, it becomes one of the game’s biggest problems.

You fight the camera almost as often as the enemy. While you can zoom in and out, there is effectively no reason to use anything other than the maximum zoomed-out view. The closer perspectives actively obscure useful information.

The camera also behaves erratically. It can be difficult or impossible to frame all units in a squad, especially fast-moving gunships. Infantry moving through forests often cause the camera to zoom or clip unpredictably. Terrain occlusion is inconsistent, leading to situations where geometry blocks your view but still accepts movement orders.

The game might have benefited from going all-in on its camera concept; A fully committed first-person or unit-mounted perspective, such as helmet cams for infantry or gun cams for aircraft, would at least have been coherent. As implemented, the system sits awkwardly between tactical overview and cinematic immersion.

Controls and Input

EndWar was designed around voice commands, such as “Unit One, capture Alpha” or “Unit Two, attack hostile one.” On PC, this system is functionally useless. Issuing commands via voice is slower than clicking, less precise, and provides no real advantage.

Keyboard controls are poorly mapped and unintuitive. After well over 100 hours with the PC version, I never found a reason to use them. The mouse ends up doing nearly all the work.

Feedback is also unreliable. Units occasionally move in ways I did not intend or remember ordering. Selecting enemy units can be finicky, especially small, fast targets like helicopters. Environmental geometry often interferes with input. A slight misclick on a treeline can send units into a forest instead of the intended open ground, sometimes because the trees were visually occluded but still interactive.

It is clear the control scheme was better suited to the original console releases on Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3. On PC, it feels compromised and awkward.

Graphics and Presentation

EndWar has solid production values, typical of a late-2000s AAA release. Visually, it is firmly rooted in the era’s “brown and bloom” aesthetic. The heavy use of bloom and halation can make certain levels, particularly ice maps at specific angles, genuinely hard to look at.

Motion blur is excessive, cannot be disabled, and is one of the worst offenders. It is especially noticeable when switching between distant units, where the image smears so aggressively that it becomes disorienting and briefly unreadable. At times it is outright nauseating.

Textures are low resolution and blurry, which is more noticeable here than in many strategy games because the camera allows you to zoom very close to units. This becomes particularly apparent when compared to **World in Conflict**, which released a year earlier and holds up significantly better in terms of visual clarity and presentation.

Audio

The music is competent but generic, blending into the background rather than standing out. Voice acting, however, is excellent and arguably the strongest part of the presentation. Unit chatter is well performed and provides genuinely useful gameplay information, such as critical unit status or enemy deployments.

A notable omission is the lack of subtitles. There are no subtitles for cutscenes or spoken audio, which is a problem both for accessibility and for following the story.

Story and Single-Player Structure

The premise is solid and, in hindsight, fairly prescient. The execution is not.

The “Prelude to War” campaign, which is the most narrative-driven portion of the game, is essentially an extended tutorial. The main World War III mode is effectively the multiplayer structure repurposed for single-player.

There are cutscenes and news-style briefings in the WW3 and Theater of War modes, but they are sparse and largely disconnected from gameplay. They do not meaningfully affect missions or outcomes. Again, the comparison to World in Conflict is unfavorable. That game delivered a much stronger narrative presentation within a similar geopolitical framework.

Strategy Layer and Progression

Not everything falls flat. The RPG-like progression system for units is a smart way to add long-term investment and variety. Veteran units matter, and losing them carries weight.

The Theater of War and WW3 modes are the core of the experience and remain the most interesting part of the game. The persistent global map, shifting frontlines, and territory control give the campaign a sense of continuity. In WW3 mode, your individual performance contributes to your faction’s success or failure over a given period, which is a compelling idea.

The online component has reportedly been revived by the community, notably through IceColdSnake’s group, though details must be sought externally due to platform restrictions.

Final Thoughts

EndWar is best described as an interesting but compromised experiment. Its standout ideas were refined and executed far more effectively in later titles like Wargame and WARNO.

If you approach it with the right mindset and accept its limitations, there is still fun to be had, particularly in the Theater of War modes. That said, it is difficult to recommend without caveats. For most players, better and more polished alternatives exist.

A solid 6.5 out of 10.

A classic game I enjoyed quite a bit as a kid. Unfortunately, its voice command system is absolute garbage on modern systems. Success depends heavily on micro, but when I have misrecognized units traveling halfway across the map to achieve an objective a squad already on station could have secured... Endwar becomes a real cluster. It's a total washup whether asking your infantry to move to a transport will mean they embark or just stand there wasting valuable seconds. 

It also doesn't help that my advisor won't refer to enemy units by their designation. She unhelpfully announces "Check east quadrant: eyes on KH-65 'Howler' gunships," but doesn't say "Check east quadrant: KH-65 'Howler' gunships DESIGNATED HOSTILE ONE," so I can immediately call out and vector a counter. I instead have to visually verify the hostile myself to get its unit number, which is slow as can be with the sluggish camera controls.

Meanwhile, the AI suffers none of this input drawback and responds flawlessly. It can act at the speed of light, whereas you are trying to get your arbitrarily fixed camera out of the bushes or down from staring at a poorly-rendered cloud overhead.

Sure, you can play the whole game with KBM, but that defeats its central gimmick. It won't help either with ass backwards pathing (tanks can't fricking REVERSE), no clear indication that your units are under attack (transports blowing up despite taking no visible projectiles from an enemy I can't verify I'm out of range from), and ridiculous tacticool animations that can't be cancelled every time you want to enter or exit a vehicle or a structure. Your arty will creep forward to engage a foe that's already in range (a real sin of most strategy games, ngl), while your speedy warcrimes dispenser on wheels will do donuts instead of bugging out and get blatted by the enemy's always accurate artillery. (You have to manually spot and call in your arty; it doesn't auto-attack anything in range.)

The way abilities are designed in this game also drives me nuts. It's just an insta-delete of one of your four squad elements as soon as you make contact with no available countermeasures short of ECMing the whole enemy formation (and then they just spam the ability once they come back online). It feels like a low blow every time. You just roll your eyes and accept it's inevitable you won't get out of an engagement without sustaining losses.

The latter is especially conspicuous in how the campaign is scaled. "Oh cool, I can upgrade my tanks to microwave their shells to make them spicy," you say. Lies. It's actually more optimal to bank your upgrade currency because the AI will gain access to similar upgrades (read: insta-delete abilities) that will turn a 13-turn campaign into a 26-turn campaign. (As you keep eking out C-level victories while the rest of Grand Europa can't fight for nuggets, I guess.) Meanwhile, you can fire your unique rocket salvos or whatever from three separate units into a target and not even dent its armor. Go figure. Winning swiftly means barely getting to play with any of the cool toys, which deeply disappoints me.

Faction balance is also fucked. The EFEC is supposed to be fast: that's its only gimmick; you're supposed to out-maneuver the foe. But the Spetnaz Guards are seemingly just as fast and tanky as can be. Moreover, there are game modes where you *have* to confront such stronger enemies head on (instead of quickly capping your way to victory), but see my above comments about how micromanagement is borked, such that you can't swiftly and cleanly disengage without losses.

Oh, yeah, you also can't Alt-F4 out of the game, nor skip title cards and such. Irritating when I just want to quickly reload the battle I'm losing because all my reinforcements were literally airdropped in the alley between a building and an indestructible fence.

Tom Clancy’s EndWar is that game I use to get obsessively into alongside ChromeHounds and other games you just remembered just now because we’re talking about them. 

Set in an alternate timeline back when Ubisoft was sort of cool, Tom Clancy’s EndWar is an amalgamation of all the plots from other TC games of the time period like Ghost Recon: Advanced Warfighter and Splinter Cell: Double Agent but everything went wrong and now World War 3 actually happens.

In the distant future of 2020, an American and European backed anti-missile orbital network called SLAMS is introduced to the world, basically nullifying the risk of full scale nuclear war. Soon after, the three big players of the world are attacked by a mysterious Terrorist organization. One misunderstanding leads to another, there’s some fingers pointed, some trigger fingers get too hot, and now you’re fighting in World War III. 

On the bright side, WW3 looks really, REALLY cool. 

Originally released in 2008, EndWar was a pretty big deal for those types of people that liked to play interesting multiplayer games. A console RTS primarily, the game had you command your own army from either the US Joint Strike Force, the European Union Enforcer Corp, and the Russian Federation Spetsnaz Guard Brigade. Each one has their own strengths and weaknesses. 

The US JSF use a mix of powered armor skeletons and cool UAV technology to support their smaller but more elite infantry. The SGB hit you with the big guns and the big tanks, and the European Union gets to your control point before you can neener neener. 

It basically comes down to how you want to play the game or what faction you’re more jingoistic for. When I was younger I always played the EUEC because I thought they had cool laser guns. 

EndWar’s big thing was the Theater of War mode, a multiplayer mode where you chose a faction and stuck to it for the duration of a war, which was basically Risk but you’re the little soldier guy the players roll dice over. You choose a map that represents an uplink sector and then you fight players from the opposite faction in a war to take said map for your faction. 
Winning battles means you gained more credits and more experience for your soldiers, which carried over from one battle to another. You could actually permanently kill an enemy and remove that battalion from any future wars, forcing the other player to spend the credits on amping up a new unit. 

Yes, it was a Dick move. Yes, I did it every chance I got. This is war, son. 

As the battle went on and became more dire, you had a thing called Defcon 1, which was basically you’re go ahead to just blow up the other guy with a WMD. Since Nukes are off the table, each faction had their own big blow up button, the Russians used Thermobaric missiles, the EU had a space laser, and the Yanks liked to just hit you with a rod from god from orbit. 

I like that idea, hey we’re not allowed to use nuclear weapons anymore, better just break the earth’s crust instead. 

How the game plays is that you see your units from either a tactical map or from a third person like camera focused on whatever unit you have selected. From there, you can command the unit to move somewhere via mouse and keyboard as well as attack and defend sectors. But the big draw was the voice commands, EndWar relies heavily on map awareness and your abilities to command units via your own voice.

You say something like “Unit 1, attack hostile 1” or “Unit 2 capture zone B” stuff like that. Back in the day I remember having a lot of problems with it, but I’m guessing just how far voice technology has come, I never had a problem with it afterwards, I could even dish out multiple orders in one go now. Its a game that really profited with age, especially with its gimmick. 

Combat is actually pretty exciting. Large rounds and explosions are booming and violent, there’s no real gore but everything blows up good. Infantry can also use cover and are really well animated during movement and fights. 

Its a Rock Paper Scissors affair, you need to keep a consistent army to deal with the enemy force. Infantry can capture points, tanks blow up light vehicles, helicopters blow up tanks, light vehicles and AA can blow up helicopters, stuff like that.

Wow, this sounds like a lot of fun, Meta games aren’t really a thing with a lot of multiplayer games these day, we’re not really going back to the Mech Assault 2 and EndWar days. So what happened?

Well, nobody bought it. From what I understand, sales were horrible even back in 2008. It had a solid playerbase, you’ll always get someone interested when you say the words “Online war”. But it wasn’t worth keeping around apparently, according to Ubisoft, and a sequel was canceled in 2010. 

The game’s official servers shut down in 2016, and I think all kinds of online support finally ended in 2022 or so, so I don’t know if you can still do just regular player matches. So now you only have single player to work with.

You have two modes outside of bot matches. Prelude to War is a series of missions where you play as all three factions and fend off terrorists as well as one another later one. Prelude leads to WW3, which is a map painter mode that’s LIKE Theater of War, but you’re conquering areas faster and a Mexican guy isn’t explaining to me how to properly make Tacos at 3 AM in 2009. 

I don’t know if there’s private servers or some kind of community for it, I hope there is. EndWar is a neat game, its one of the stronger 7/10 games out there. The presentation is nice and I liked the control and voice gimmicks. It goes on sale for, like, 2 dollars sometimes, so you can just play around with it for a bit before moving on.

Its really a shame, I used to be such a big fan of the Tom Clancy license. I used to breath the worlds of Splinter Cell, Ghost Recon, and Rainbow Six back in the day, as well as the other TC spin off games like this and HAWX. It was all a shared universe, with a good chunk of the games crossing over in one way or another (You fly escort for Ghost Recon during the Mexican Civil War in HAWX and get to see them overhead in Advanced Warfighter 2, cool stuff like that.) 

EndWar isn’t the last game in that particular timeline, there are more after it, I know Wildlands and Breakpoint still talk about the stuff that happened in earlier GR games and Scott Mitchells, who’s your commanding officer if you play the Americans in EndWar, shows up still. But it was a very interesting series of games back in the day.

EndWar itself gets 7 perma-killed units out of 10. I’d say it was an 8 if the multiplayer was still around. But I’m going to be honest, even back in the day it was sort of hard to get a game going.
A shame, really.

Is EndWar better than (insert strategy title here)? Probably not.

Is EndWar revolutionary or did it push the RTT genre forward? Eh, maybe back in '08-'09?

Is EndWar unique? [b]Absolutely.[/b] Even now nearly 16 years later. And in my mind that alone is worthy of praise.

EndWar by Tom Clancy is a sci-fi Real Time Tactical game taking place in the distant future of 2020. Strategic nuclear warfare has been rendered non viable by new anti-ballistics technology and a globe-spanning ECM network. With the nukes collecting dust, the price of oil skyrocketing, and the US moving ahead in their domination of space, global tensions rise to a breaking point, leading into World War III. The war to End all War.

You command a battalion of Special Forces from one of 3 superpowers - the United States, the European Federation, and the Russian Federation. Each have fundamentally similar units with varying stats and special abilities. You choose your battalion based on its unit composition, and gradually upgrade it with credits you earn in battles. WWIII unfolds on a turn-based map, where you select from a few operations depending on where your nation is attacking and defending that week, how you perform in battle influences the outcome of other battles.

On the tactical level, EndWar sees you deploy platoons from your battalion in several objective-based modes. Battles are fast and furious, fought around 15 minutes on average. Unlike nearly every other RTS, EndWar locks your camera view to one of your units at a time. Your view floats above them and you generally see what they see, though you still have access to a minimap (and a diegetic SITREP view if your CV is on the battlefield). This forces you to think more about positioning and rely on your instincts for battlefield awareness, but also means your camera is usually at the center of the action. You don't miss out on anything cool your units are doing unlike some modern RTS games that offer full strategic zoom.

You select from just 7 unit types, the 3 most commonly used vehicle units adhere to a rock-paper-scissors balancing (though occasionally altered via the unit special abilities), while infantry and artillery act as wildcard units rewarding careful positioning. As units score kills they earn experience, making them more effective and allowing them to benefit from higher-level upgrades if you've bought them.

Of course, veterancy implies survival, which is never guaranteed. Units fight using a combination of 'shields' (representing their countermeasures/survival training) that are weak but regenerate quickly out of combat, and a larger static health pool that cannot be replenished. This gives you a small window time to react when your unit runs into trouble (which the game gives audible warning for), by retreating them from a fight to regain shields, or evacuate from the battle entirely so you can call in a fresh replacement. A unit will also be evacuated by air if it is knocked-out by losing most of its health, rendering it helpless in the meantime, during which it (or its evacuation helicopter) can be finished off. Units that survive retain any experience earned, while killed units are reset to the lowest experience level.

The overall strategic concepts in EndWar are straightforward and simplified compared to similar games. Battles are won by capturing/destroying objectives or enemy units. There is no resource-gathering mechanic: points for deploying units are rewarded regularly based on scenario conditions and how many objectives you hold, and most units cost the same. Support abilities can also be purchased with these points, provided you've upgraded your captured Uplinks, which can damage units, stun them, or call NPC units onto the battlefield to assist. Beyond this, each side gets a superweapon they can use starting when the battle reaches a decisive point (usually capturing more than half the objectives), giving the losing player a chance to use their WMD to regain the advantage - at the cost of the winning player getting a retaliatory WMD when they do.

So, it's a fairly straightforward game at face value, with simplified mechanics, some interesting yet limited depth, and various twists but nothing that hasn't been seen in other RTS games. What makes EndWar special?

Presentation, focus, attention to detail, and a few really cool features.

Units in EndWar feel very lively. Infantry move slowly on foot, need to physically enter/exit transports and structures with choreographed animations that take a few seconds, and slip into any cover available in a believable fashion. Vehicles, for all their sci-fi elements, are clearly based on real-world designs or hypothetical technologies (even if they aren't realistically simulated). They also move and maneuver at believable speeds, can run over some obstacles or wreckage, and track their targets, while every weapon system they're equipped with is fully animated. Everything you call onto the battlefield is carried there by transport aircraft, which land and deploy them - riflemen can even forward deploy at higher veteran levels to any point on the battlefield this way. The aesthetics and background information hold a generous dose of lore and personality that clearly sets each faction apart and reflects its nation's ethos. Everything just feels believable and thought out, aside from some clipping/path-finding issues that occasionally surface.

Voice acting is universally great, from your individual unit types to your battlefield advisors, and each has a vast array of contextual dialogue that immediately gives you feedback on their status even if they aren't onscreen. But what really changes EndWar is that you can [i]talk back[/i] to your units, via the ingame voice commands! This is a feature that is core to the game's identity, you can simply tell your units (or support abilities) what to do, and where, and the game will handle all the rest. While the voice recognition can be hit-or-miss depending on your microphone and voice, EndWar to this day has the best voice commands of any strategy game I can think of. Music is also on point, with a rarely-seen feature (in this genre anyway) that the music's tempo actively changes with the pace of the battle!

The upgrade system and overlying strategy layer between missions is compelling and makes your battalion feel all the more like "your dudes" in ways that few other RTS games do. You get invested in your special units that survive multiple battles, carry you through holdouts, and benefit from your hard-earned credits, and you genuinely feel something when they get killed off.

The game also had multiplayer, including what was once a persistent online campaign. Support for it ended. I am uncertain of the state of it in the present, but I would guess Ubisoft doesn't give a damn. I have seen groups/communities that still play EndWar, so that might be worth seeking out.

All in all, EndWar is a highly memorable RTS/RTT title that, for the price of only a few bucks on sale, is absolutely worth playing through at least once. The only real negatives I have against the game aside from the potentially grizzly state of multiplayer: the lack of controller support (should've been a no-brainer to include from the console version), the low unit variety, some issues with pathfinding, the AI being brainless at times, and the fact that some features just seem to have way more potential than the game actually squeezes out of them (like, imagine if you could side-grade your units into new types, apply unit-specific cosmetics or upgrades to further make your best guys stand out; or imagine if the strategic layer had more depth). There's still nothing like EndWar to this very day, much less anything that I could call a spiritual succession (World in Conflict is about the closest I can think of). You should pick it up if you're a fan of the genre, if only because we never know wen Ubislop will disappear it from the Steam store.

# **R.U.S.E.™ — A Brilliant World War II Strategy Experience**

**Rating: 9/10 — Highly Recommended**

R.U.S.E.™ is one of the most distinctive real-time strategy games set during World War II. It combines large-scale military operations, tactical deception, resource management, and strategic planning into an experience where victory depends on more than simply building the largest army.

**Story and Campaign:**

The campaign follows American officer Joe Sheridan through a series of World War II military operations. Players participate in battles across the European theater, completing objectives that require careful planning, effective leadership, and tactical adaptability. Although the story is not particularly character-driven, it provides an engaging framework for the strategic gameplay.

**Gameplay and Strategy:**

The gameplay revolves around building military infrastructure, producing units, managing resources, and commanding forces across expansive battlefields. Infantry, tanks, artillery, aircraft, and anti-tank units each serve different purposes, making combined-arms warfare essential.

Players must carefully balance offense and defense while protecting their infrastructure and exploiting weaknesses in enemy positions. Rushing into battle without proper preparation can quickly lead to defeat.

**Deception Mechanics:**

The game's defining feature is its deception system. Players can use misinformation, camouflage, reconnaissance, and fake offensives to manipulate enemy decisions.

A convincing decoy attack can draw enemy forces away from an important position, allowing your real offensive to succeed elsewhere. This creates a psychological dimension rarely explored so thoroughly in strategy games.

Success depends not only on understanding the battlefield but also on anticipating what your opponent believes is happening.

**Battlefield Design and Atmosphere:**

R.U.S.E. features expansive maps that encourage flanking maneuvers, defensive planning, and coordinated military operations. Its distinctive tabletop presentation makes battles resemble miniature military war rooms, reinforcing the feeling of commanding an entire army.

The combination of detailed terrain, moving formations, and large-scale engagements creates a memorable military atmosphere.

**Graphics and Sound Design:**

Although its graphics show their age, the game's visual presentation remains distinctive. Its zoom system allows players to switch between individual units and the wider battlefield, making it easier to appreciate the scale of operations.

The sounds of artillery, aircraft, engines, and gunfire complement the military atmosphere, while the soundtrack reinforces the tension of commanding forces during wartime.

**Multiplayer and Replayability:**

Multiplayer offers considerable strategic depth because human opponents can adapt their tactics and use deception unpredictably. Different maps, unit compositions, and approaches to warfare encourage experimentation and replayability.

However, the game's age means players should verify current multiplayer availability before purchasing specifically for online matches.

**Technical Performance and Weaknesses:**

R.U.S.E. has several limitations, including aging graphics, occasional repetitive encounters, and a learning curve that may frustrate newcomers. Its campaign is enjoyable but does not offer particularly deep character development.

Modern purchasing and online accessibility can also be challenging, depending on the platform and edition.

Nevertheless, these weaknesses do not diminish the originality of its strategic mechanics.

**Final Verdict:**

R.U.S.E.™ is an excellent strategy game that distinguishes itself through military deception, tactical planning, resource management, and large-scale World War II battles.

Its greatest strength is making intelligence and misinformation essential parts of warfare. Victory comes from understanding your opponent, concealing your intentions, and choosing the right moment to strike.

If you enjoy World War II history, military strategy, combined-arms warfare, and games that reward clever planning over mindless aggression, R.U.S.E.™ is highly recommended.

# R.U.S.E. — A WWII Strategy Classic That Still Stands Out

**Recommended**

R.U.S.E. is one of those strategy games that deserves far more attention. Instead of simply throwing as many tanks as possible at the enemy, it makes you think, plan ahead, gather intelligence, and use deception to outsmart your opponent. That's what makes it so satisfying.

The biggest strength of R.U.S.E. is its unique gameplay. The battlefield is large, the units feel different from one another, and every decision matters. You can build up your forces, establish defensive lines, launch a surprise attack, or trick your opponent into wasting valuable resources. The deception system is still one of the coolest ideas I've seen in an RTS game.

I also love the way the game presents the battlefield. The zooming camera makes it feel like you're looking at a giant military planning table, and being able to move between the big picture and individual units makes commanding an army enjoyable. There is something satisfying about watching a carefully planned operation come together.

Of course, the game isn't perfect. Some mechanics take time to learn, the AI can be inconsistent, and the controls can occasionally feel awkward when you're trying to select individual units in a crowded battlefield. New players may also need some time to understand the economy, unit counters, and deception mechanics.

Even with those issues, R.U.S.E. offers something that many modern strategy games are missing: the feeling that you're actually commanding an army, not just clicking on units and hoping for the best.

**Pros**
- Unique deception and psychological warfare mechanics.
- Large battlefields and a satisfying strategic zoom.
- A wide variety of WWII units and tactics.
- Rewarding defensive planning, reconnaissance, and flanking maneuvers.
- Plenty of strategic possibilities against human opponents and AI.

**Cons**
- A learning curve for new players.
- Unit selection and crowded formations can be frustrating.
- AI behavior can be inconsistent.
- Some mechanics and presentation show the game's age.

**Final verdict:** R.U.S.E. remains a memorable WWII RTS with an identity of its own. If you enjoy military strategy, outsmarting your opponent, and planning operations rather than relying on brute force, this game is absolutely worth playing. I hope it continues to receive support and improvements, because the core idea is still excellent.

**Recommended.** A true strategy game where deception can be just as powerful as firepower.

It’s an excellent game. I give 8/10 to Company of Heroes 1 and 8.5/10 to Sudden strike 4 and well I give 10/10 to RUSE.
The only game where I like Battles skirmish more than the campaign. You can play as 1939 or 1942 or 1945. All the three periods have different techniques.  In 1942 where you have anti-tank guns, in 1945 you also have prototype weapons.
	USA is very good, because you can produce units at very low cost than another nation. For some reason Russia is a bit costly, but their Planes are mighty. France is the strongest, and Long Range 90 mm Anti-tank position of Italy is very enjoyable. Japan has been added in this steam version.
	While you can plan when zoom out, the game also gives excellent view of the fight of the units when you zoom in. When enemy tanks are rushing at you, your anti-tank guns hidden in the grass attacks it with surprise attack and you can enjoy that destruction right in front of you. Well positioned hidden anti-tank guns can even destroy the mighty Tiger tank when accompanied with your Recon unit.
	Strategy and planning is very important in RUSE. If you think that you can win battle by producing more Aircraft planes, enemy will have a strong response by producing many Anti-aircraft Guns. You will definitely enjoy with anti-tank positions by destroying enemy tanks from a long distance, even before it can fire. But they may attack that positions from a distance through STUG or Assault gun. So you should have produced Bomber plane well before to finish this STUG or Assault gun to defend your anti-tank positions. And till that time, you can use the tactic and use RUSE The camouflage net which hides your anti-tank positions.
	If you play as Germany, like Russia it is also costly for producing some units. But Germany’s Tiger Tank is unmatchable in 1942 in battles. Interestingly the range of fire of Tiger Tank is almost equal to advanced anti-tank gun. Just 3 to 4 Tiger Tank and it will dominant the area. Let enemy send waves of tanks and other things but it will destroy it from a long distance, with a laughing dialogue which is really amusing. 
	The difference between other strategy game and Ruse is that where the other games may have very large map, and you cannot seem to be enjoying with that, in RUSE you feel that you are in control of all the plans and strategy. In RUSE you can execute your ideas, make adaptable changes to counter enemy tactics and all things are in your hand. And you can see all the destruction and result in front of you and enjoy. So I give this game RUSE 10/10 rating.
	I will advocate and eagerly wait for RUSE 2.And I Will definitely purchase it if RUSE 2 is released.

这是一款很特别的RTS游戏（Eugen的风格），节奏偏慢但玩起来并不轻松（反而经常让我急得跳脚）。在游戏中你可以使用各种诡计欺骗对手，瞬间改变战局，所以虽然游戏中没有同时代其他RTS中常见的战争迷雾系统，但侦察单位比以往任何时候都更加重要。自洽的兵种克制关系让每种单位都能发挥自己的用处，几乎不存在上场率低的问题。当然尽管机制很独特，剧情还是逃脱不了那个年代大家喜闻乐见的苏黑情节……
RTS这一经典的游戏品类在现如今已然有些水土不服了。现在大家更需要一个能够轻松释放压力的出口，而不是这种劳累，增压，费脑，且容易产生挫败感的体验，再加上RTS玩家对特定产品的黏性相当之高——帝国时代4已经出了，很多人还在玩帝国时代2，红警2，星际2……这种属于老顽固的游戏产品在可预见的未来大概率会越来越少，但至少现在我还能在这里流几滴时代的眼泪。

Um FPS do Velho Oeste, com toques de novela mexicana. 

Sobre o Plot do jogo, não é nada de especial, é sólido sim, mas fica-se pelo "Bom", talvez um pouquinho mais. É uma Prequel do 1º jogo, onde ficamos a conhecer melhor a família disfuncional dos irmãos McCall, iremos sempre jogar ou com o Ray ou com o Thomas. Bons protagonistas juntamente com o irmão mais novo. O restante das personagens, beira tudo a mediocridade, apenas cumprem a sua função para a história. Novamente, apesar de ter um ou outro momento, o plot vai ficar sempre num 7/10, talvez até 7.5/10.

Sobre a gameplay, como estava a dizer, sim, há duas personagens jogáveis: o Ray e o Thomas. De forma geral, é um FPS padrão, com armas que eram utilizadas no Velho Oeste. A única coisa a apontar é mesmo a mecânica de cover, que é estranha, pois trata-se de um sistema automático que não funciona da melhor forma. Outra mecânica padrão é o «Modo Concentração», que desbloqueias após matar uma certa quantidade de inimigos. Ao ativares o modo, o jogo desacelera e terás de selecionar os inimigos que estão no ecrã durante alguns segundos; os que forem selecionados são mortos instantaneamente pela tua personagem (há uma diferença na execução deste modo para cada personagem). A seleção é feita somente com o rato.
Agora, o diferencial deste jogo é mesmo a gameplay dos dois protagonistas. No início de cada nível, irás escolher ou o Ray ou o Thomas.
O Ray é uma espécie de tank; aguenta mais tiros, é letal a curto alcance e atira dinamite (que faz a função das granadas, já que estamos no século XIX). No entanto, não consegue alcançar sítios mais altos como o Thomas consegue. No seu «Modo Concentração», basta passar o rato por cima dos inimigos: quantas mais vezes passares por cima de um inimigo, mais disparos ele irá sofrer. As armas de eleição são os dois revólveres e a shotgun.
O Thomas já entra na categoria de sniper e assassino. É mais frágil, tem uma corda que lhe permite subir para locais mais altos e, de certa forma, consegue fazer parkour, embora seja um parkour limitado. No seu Modo Concentração, ele aponta automaticamente para um inimigo; no entanto, tens de clicar no rato para disparar. Quanto mais rápido fores, mais inimigos morrem. As armas de eleição são o arco e flecha, rifle de longo alcance e as facas, que servem para matar silenciosamente.
Durante o jogo, além de poderes apanhar o dinheiro, as munições e as armas dos inimigos, podes comprar munições e armas melhores nas lojas que vão aparecendo ao longo da aventura.
Sobre os inimigos, não notei grande inteligência: basicamente, vão para cover, avançam e assim sucessivamente. Não há propriamente classes ou tipos diferentes de inimigos.
Há secções do jogo que são uma espécie de mundo aberto (muito limitado), onde podes fazer missões secundárias que te dão dinheiro para gastar nas tais lojas.
Por último, ao longo dos níveis terás os «duelos». É como vês nos filmes de western: dois homens a olharem-se para ver quem dispara primeiro. Durante os duelos, vais ter de mover a tua personagem de acordo com os movimentos do inimigo e manter a mão da tua personagem o mais próxima possível da pistola para, quando o sino tocar, conseguires puxar da arma a tempo. Nesse momento, terás de apertar o gatilho no momento certo; caso contrário, é Game Over. Ao princípio parece difícil, mas não é; só que, às vezes, torna-se um pouco chato por causa da movimentação do inimigo
No jogo é possível montar a cavalo. Em ambientes abertos, a movimentação funciona bem; já em ambientes fechados, é má e com erros (bugs).

A soundtrack é razoável, esperava mais, uma vez que os westerns costumam ter grandes sons. Basicamente, são músicas de western genéricas

A ambientação do jogo é ótima: os níveis variam entre aldeias, quintas, florestas, fortes e o deserto, estando tudo muito bem feito. Sentes realmente que estás num western.

Para quem os procura, o jogo tem secrets.

Não joguei o multiplayer por isso nao vou opinar sobre o mesmo.

Levei umas 6 horas e meia para completar a campanha.
Ao preço a que o jogo está, vale a pena comprar — e em promoção, nem se fala. Para quem gosta do género ou deste tipo de gameplay, ou simplesmente quer um joguito para passar uma tarde, vale bem a pena

Nota final - 7.5/10

[b]Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood[/b] is an impressive game for its time, especially considering it was released in 2009. However, it has aged rather poorly, and some of its gameplay mechanics make the experience feel unnecessarily clunky.

The gameplay feels quite different from the previous game, particularly in terms of pacing, which is noticeably slower. It's a shame that the game is relatively short, because there is potential here, but the overall experience is held back by its mechanics. Gunslinger, released afterwards, does a much better job in this regard, with considerably more refined gameplay mechanics.

The technical issues also make the experience frustrating. The game crashes frequently, particularly when using Alt+Tab. I couldn't reliably switch to another window and return to the game without risking a crash. I also recall having problems with mouse sensitivity, although I'm not entirely certain. These issues make it difficult to enjoy the game on a modern system without looking for fixes and workarounds.

For a 2009 release, the game is genuinely impressive, but its clunky mechanics, technical problems and poor compatibility with modern multitasking make it difficult to recommend. There are better ways to experience the series, particularly with Gunslinger.

At times, while playing through the campaign, I wished the game had a little more grit or offered set pieces similar to those in the first game. That's not to say there aren't any breathtaking views here, but they're few and far between. What's the point of having better graphics if you can't manage to leave me as flabbergasted as you did in the first game?

They removed so many things that made the original great, like the stealth sections, the platforming, and those quieter moments when you could simply catch your breath and take in the beauty of the world around you. They changed a few things, but very few of those changes were for the better.

The lasso system works better this time around, but it looks so janky compared to the first game. Shooting the bow feels completely off, and the Mexican standoff mechanic doesn't work particularly well either. I mean, I was still getting killed during the final mission because the whole system feels so janky and poorly designed.

There are also a handful of missions set in semi-open environments where you can take on side quests. Unfortunately, these side activities boil down to doing exactly what you do throughout the entire game: shooting people. And that's pretty much it.

I wasn't expecting much when I saw that the game had a romantic interest, but somehow they still managed to mess it up. Marisa is introduced as a strong, independent woman, only to be turned into a damsel in distress mere seconds later. It's as if the moment the main characters lay eyes on her, all her strength and independence magically disappear. You'll spend most of the game having to rescue her. Her only real purpose is to serve as an object of desire, provide some information, and occasionally become the objective of a mission.

People can say this is a product of its time all they want, but Mirror's Edge, Bayonetta, Tomb Raider: Underworld, and WET all came out around the same time, so beat it.

After all that, you're probably wondering why I still recommend this game. Well, the truth is that, despite all its shortcomings, this game is a lot like one of those yearly Call of Duty campaigns. You play through it, have some fun, and then forget about it shortly afterward.

The main characters are also genuinely interesting, and despite the story being clichéd as hell, the dialogue is pretty awesome. It's also nice to finally find out what happened before the cult classic that was the first game.

This is the first sequel to the immersive western game '[b]Call Of Juarez[/b]'.  If you played that game, then you will be quite comfortable here, as this game is exactly more-of-the-same of what the first game had ([i]choice of 2 playable main characters, combat mechanics, keyboard controls, graphics, etc[/i]).  For reference, I've included my '[b]Call Of Juarez[/b]' review at the bottom.

Although this game itself is a sequel, the story is a prequel.  It starts about 18 to 20 years before the events in the first game.  In the first game, you played as either Ray McCall ([i]known then as Reverend Ray[/i]), or Billy Candle ([i]Thomas McCall's step-son[/i]).  In this game, you play as either Ray McCall, or his brother Thomas McCall.  They are Confederate soldiers in the Civil War around 1864.

Then they hear that a well-known Union commander, General Sherman, is marching through Georgia to the sea and burning down everything in his path.  They quickly realize that their family homestead is in General Sherman's path.  Thus, they desert the Confederate army to go save their mother, their younger brother William, and their home.  Their commanding officer, Colonel Barnsby, swears that after the war is over he will personally hunt them down and see them hang high for being deserters.

The brothers arrive one day late, finding their home with lots of damage and their mother dead.  They get William and head west, vowing to return one day to reclaim their land and rebuild their home.  They are both angry men now, liking liquor, women, and trouble a little too much.  Ray & Thomas seem to leave a trail of bodies everywhere that they go, so eventually the Pinkertons are on their trail.

([i]FYI, in real life, the Pinkerton Company was founded in the early 1850's, and was the largest private law enforcement company in the world from the 1870's to the 1890's.[/i])  Their brother William is a reverend who constantly lectures them about their evil ways, and pleads with them to change.  To escape the Pinkertons, Ray & Thomas cross the border into Mexico, as many wild west outlaws did.

Once there, they hear that the legendary gold of Juarez is actually real, and decide that getting ahold of that gold would provide them the financial means to finally go back to Georgia, rebuild their home, and settle down.  Of course, things don't go as planned.  They end up tangling with regular townfolk, local law enforcement, random outlaws, Mexican bandits, and 3 different Native American tribes.

In addition, throw into the mix a powerful force which is capable of tearing 2 brothers apart...  a sexy woman that both of them are lusting over.  The plot of the first game was good, but this one is better.  Personally, I think this one would have made a great movie.  Like the first one, this game also has 15 episodes, and also has slightly different skill sets between the 2 playable characters of Ray & Thomas.

You must play as Ray for Chapter #1, and must play as Thomas for Chapter #2.  Then you can choose which character to play from Chapters #3 to #13.  In Chapter #14 you will play as both, and for Chapter #15 you again can choose who to play.  The quick-draw duels are still a problem to get through, and several forum posts complain the game does not launch with newer computers and video cards.

Personally, the game randomly crashed on me once, but that was the only glitch of any kind that I experienced.  The graphics still look mostly okay in 2026, but are a little on the janky side in some places.  There are no trading cards, no achievements, and no Point Shop items.  The game menu still has an option for multi-player, but apparently the official servers have not had support for 10 years or so.

There are also menu options to download extra maps and extra missions, but I don't know if those work or not.  I did not bother to try them.  There are 4 difficulty levels available, but you must beat the game once to unlock the hardest difficulty.  I again enjoyed both the story and the gameplay, but was again disappointed in the length of the game.  It was a little shorter than the first game was.

For most people, the game should only take 8 to 10 hours to complete, depending on your shooting skills and pace of exploration.  It could take several hours longer if you want to torture yourself by going out of your way to try to find the 89 "[i]secrets[/i]".  There is no reward for finding them though, so I did not bother to go out of my way.  I just found the ones which were on, or close to, the main path.

Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood est un jeu de tir à la première personne développé par Techland et édité par Techland Publishing, sorti en juin 2009.

Le joueur incarne Ray et Thomas McCall, deux frères ayant combattu dans les rangs confédérés. Après avoir déserté pour protéger leur famille, ils se retrouvent impliqués dans une aventure qui les conduit des États-Unis jusqu'au Mexique, à la recherche d'un mystérieux trésor. Leur jeune frère William les accompagne également dans cette quête.

L'histoire repose essentiellement sur les relations entre les trois frères. Ray et Thomas possèdent des personnalités très différentes, ce qui donne lieu à de nombreux conflits et à une évolution intéressante de leurs relations. Le scénario mêle vengeance, trahison, rivalités et recherche de rédemption, tout en s'appuyant sur les grands thèmes du western.

L'un des principaux intérêts du jeu réside justement dans cette ambiance. Les paysages désertiques, les villages mexicains, les canyons et les villes de l'Ouest américain offrent une représentation particulièrement réussie du Far West. La direction artistique contribue à l'immersion et donne au jeu une certaine identité.

La jouabilité constitue également l'une des grandes réussites de Bound in Blood. Le joueur peut contrôler Ray ou Thomas au cours de certaines missions, chacun disposant de compétences et d'un arsenal différents. Ray privilégie une approche directe et brutale. Il utilise notamment deux revolvers, de la dynamite et des armes particulièrement puissantes à courte distance. Thomas adopte quant à lui une approche plus discrète et précise, avec des fusils, un arc et un lasso permettant d'atteindre certaines positions en hauteur. Cette complémentarité apporte une certaine variété aux missions. Les deux frères ne se jouent pas de la même manière et encouragent le joueur à adapter son approche selon les situations.

Le jeu propose également plusieurs mécaniques particulièrement intéressantes. Les affrontements peuvent être ponctués de séquences de concentration permettant de ralentir le temps et d'éliminer plusieurs ennemis rapidement. Les duels constituent également un élément important de l'expérience, avec des affrontements en face-à-face où le joueur doit dégainer au bon moment. Les combats restent globalement efficaces et proposent une bonne variété de situations. Les séquences à cheval, les affrontements contre des groupes d'ennemis et les passages utilisant des mitrailleuses ou des canons permettent de varier le rythme de la campagne.

Le principal défaut du jeu vient cependant de sa structure très linéaire. Les missions imposent généralement une progression précise et laissent peu de liberté au joueur. Les nombreux événements scriptés renforcent l'aspect cinématographique de l'aventure, mais peuvent parfois donner l'impression de suivre un scénario trop dirigiste.

La campagne reste également relativement courte. L'histoire peut être terminée en quelques heures, même si la possibilité d'incarner les deux frères et de découvrir différentes approches permet d'encourager une certaine rejouabilité.

Le scénario constitue néanmoins un véritable point fort. Contrairement à certains jeux de tir de cette époque, Bound in Blood ne se contente pas d'enchaîner les affrontements. L'histoire des frères McCall possède une véritable progression et propose plusieurs moments particulièrement marquants.

Techniquement, le jeu reste convaincant pour une production de 2009. Les environnements sont variés et les paysages possèdent une identité visuelle. Certaines textures et animations ont naturellement vieilli, mais l'ensemble conserve un certain charme grâce à sa direction artistique.

La bande-son et les doublages participent également à l'ambiance du jeu. Les musiques accompagnent efficacement les affrontements et les séquences narratives, tandis que les dialogues renforcent la personnalité des différents personnages.

[h1]Succès Steam[/h1]

Le jeu ne propose pas de succès Steam à débloquer.

[h1]Pour résumer[/h1]

✔️[u]Points positifs :[/u]

*Une excellente ambiance de western.
*Un scénario intéressant centré sur les frères McCall.
*Des personnages principaux bien développés.
*Une complémentarité efficace entre Ray et Thomas.
*Des approches de combat différentes selon le personnage.
*Des duels particulièrement réussis.
*Une bonne variété de situations et de missions.
*Des environnements variés entre les États-Unis et le Mexique.
*Une direction artistique qui conserve son charme.
*Une bande-son et des doublages efficaces.

❌[u]Points négatifs :[/u]

*Une campagne relativement courte.
*Une structure linéaire.
*Des missions parfois trop scriptées.
*Une liberté d'exploration limitée.
*Certaines mécaniques peuvent devenir répétitives.
*Une intelligence artificielle irrégulière.
*Une rejouabilité limitée malgré la complémentarité des deux frères.

[h2]📝📢Giriş📢📝[/h2]

Türklerin favori yapımcısı, Dying Light'ı geliştiren adamların elinden çıkan bu oyun; 2009 yılında çıkmış bir western temalı FPS oyunu.

Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood; ikinci Call of Juarez olmasına rağmen aslında ilk oyunun öncesinde geçiyor. Ama hemen öncesi gibi değil. Yıllar öncesinde ilk oyundaki Ray'i Ray yapan olayları öğreniyoruz. Yani ilk oyunu oynamadım diye aşırı endişelenmenize gerek yok.

İlk oyundaki gibi oldukça çizgisel ilerleyen bir FPS oyunu bu da. Artık dümdüz gidip biten oyunların azaldığı devirde, bu durumdan yakınanlar için ilaç gibi gelecektir. Hele ki western de seviyorsa.

İnternette oyun için Türkçe yama buldum. Kendim uğraşmadım ama ingilizceniz yeterli değilse sizin bunun için uğraşmanızı öneririm. Oyunu ortalama 8-9 saatte bitirebilirsiniz. Önerim en yüksek zorlukta oynamanızdır.

[h2]📖🎭Hikâye ve Atmosfer🎭📖[/h2]

Amerikan iç savaşının ortasında başlıyor oyunumuz. Ray ve Thomas adında iki kardeş cephede savunma yapıp cepheyi savunmayı başarırlar. Ama komutandan geri çekilme emri gelir. Ray ve Thomas geri çekilirlerse sahip oldukları evin ve ailelerinin düşmanlar tarafından saldırıya uğrayacağını anlayıp ordudan firar edip evlerini savunmaya giderler. 

Eve gittiklerinde fazla sayıda düşmanla karşılaşırlar ve onları temizlerler. Ama bu çatışma esnasında anneleri ölmüş ve ellerinde sadece rahip olmaya çalışan en küçük kardeşleriyle yıkık dökük bir ev kalmıştır. Ray ve Thomas firar ettikleri için ordu tarafından kovalanacaklarını biliyorlar ve bundan dolayı ileride evlerini tekrar inşa edeceklerine yemin ederek Meksika'ya kaçıyorlar. 

İşte oyunda da Amerika'nın o dönemine yakından bakıyor, bu 3 kardeşin savaş sonucu ne kadar değiştiklerini görüyor, evlerini geri inşa etmeye çabalamalarına, kadınlarla ilişkilerine ve en önemlisi de birbirleriyle aralarındaki ilişkilere yaşadıkları olaylarla birlikte eşlik ediyoruz.

Oyun hakkında daha fazla söylediğim her şey spoiler'a dönebilir, o yüzden daha fazla anlatmayacağım bile. Hatta fazlasıyla anlattım. Özet geçmek gerekirse senaryo western temasını içimizde hissettiren, ileride ne olacağını az biraz tahmin etsek de nasıl olacağı hakkında fikir yürüttüğümüz, oldukça kaliteli bir yapım. 

RPG ögeleri bulunmayan bir yapım. Herhangi bir karar vermiyoruz. Finali de belli. Sonunu değiştiremiyoruz.

Oyun tamamıyla lineer. Çoğu zaman açıklıklarda geziyor olsak da o çizgisellik hala hissediliyor. Bazı görevlerin arasına güncel Call of Duty'lerde bulunan açık dünyalı bölümlerden koymuşlar. Konulmasının asıl sebebi biraz süre uzatmak ve sana kullanmak için para kazandırmak. Yaptığın özel bir şey de yok burada. Belirli yerlere gidip oradaki düşmanları temizliyorsun sadece.

Bu oyunu güzel yapan en önemli olay ilkindeki gibi yazımı ve karakterleri. Gerçekten özenli bir hikaye anlattığını hissediyorsun. Aslında basit bir hikaye olsa da bunu güzelce sana yansıtmayı başarıyorlar. Karakterler de oldukça ilgi çekici ve orjinaller.

Oyun oldukça basit bir shooter aslında. Tabanca ve tüfekler ana silahlarımız. Ray ile oynarken 2 tane tabancayı aynı anda kullanabiliyor, Thomas'ın aksine dinamit kullanabiliyoruz. Aynı zamanda zamanı yavaşlatıp iki yandan silahın namlusunun hareket ettiği, o sürede de düşmanları vurmaya çalıştığımız bir ultimiz bile var. Bu ilk oyundaki Ray'in özelliğinin aynısı. Thomas ise tek tabanca kullanabiliyor ve otomatik nişan alınan ama her vuruşu senin sıktığın bir ulti sistemine sahip. Aynı zamanda bir tüfek, yay ve fırlatma bıçağı kullanabiliyor. Stealth yapabilesi bir karakter olsa da oyunun bunu çok desteklemediği aşikar. Thomas, Ray'in aksine kement kullanabiliyor ama oyunda aktif kullanabileceğimiz bir utility değil.
