Pour ceux qui aiment les jeux à la "bejeweled", le côté RPG en plus. Du "puzzle quest", quoi...mais en un peu plus travaillé niveau "background", je dirais. Une histoire somme toute plutôt classique dans un monde "medieval-fantasy" on l'on combat surtout des bestioles (invoquées ou sauvages) avec ses propres bestioles (oui, vous êtes une sorte de mage-invocateur...il n'y a pas de sous-métier, hein...). Les mécanismes sont cependant un peu obscurs malgré le tutorial...par exemple, mon impression est que le level des creatures qu'on contrôle est quasi-inutile: lvl 1 contre lvl 1, on gagne, puis avec sa même bestiole avec 6 ou 7 niveaux de plus que l'IA on peut perdre contre le même adversaire (pourtant toujours lvl 1, lui)....pas très clair tout ça. 
A part ça, que du classique: système d'affinité élémentales, combat de boss, de "mid-boss", quelques objets à utiliser lors des combats, combos (qu'on realise des fois au pif, du coup) des "gils" à gagner (oui oui, des "gils"...square-enix oblige...), le deplacement sur les maps se fait par clic de souris pour avancer d'une "case" (mais n'est pas très pratique et ça ne répond pas toujours bien), sur des chemins balisés mais relativement travaillés pour un jeu de ce type (avec des trésors, des "autels" pour restaurer les pv des creatures...)...bref on a une map vue de dessus qui bien qu'assez basique est plus agréable que de se deplacer sur des cases en tant que telles ou des lignes. 
Pas vraiment d' (voire aucune) animations que ce soit aux niveaux des creatures durant les combats ou des persos lors des échanges verbaux (...moi ça me gêne pas, mais certains pourraient trouver ça "cheap"...ceci dit, je connais pas beaucoup de jeu de ce type qui animent leurs persos...bref...). 
On peut se lancer sur une map avec trois bebêtes max dans la besace, et on choisit laquelle lancer en combat à chaque rencontre.  On peut changer son équipe une fois sur la map générale, histoire de se construire un trio adapté aux types d'elements rencontrés dans chaque map de combat (à condition d'avoir débloqué les dites créatures avec des objets specifique qu'on troive sur les maps de combats).
Je n'ai pas suffisamment d'heure de jeu pour évaluer la profondeur du scénar, mais c'est du square-enix (les musiques de combat me rappellent un peu les FFVII ou VIII, d'ailleurs...) donc peut-être l'objet d'une edit, car je sais pas mais comme dans la serie des FF, ca sent les rebondissements et les coups de théâtre...donc à voir...
Voilà, en esperant vous avoir aidé un peu quand même...

An odd teamup of Popcap and Square Enix trying their own hand at Puzzle Quest gameplay. Maybe they would have had something more successful if it weren't for the odd design decisions
[list]
[*] You have to pay currency any time you swap monsters on your team. This discourages experimentation and it doesn't help that a lot of the monsters are bottom-tier useless in your hands due to slow play styles or only countering one specific enemy type.
[*] Currency does not buy items. No on Xbox 360 they wanted to get you to buy a DLC pack with 10 of each item. No such DLC exists on PC, so the items you find in chests are seemingly all you get. Chests also don't respawn on any map I explored, so there's a finite amount for a normal playthrough. I'm fine with it limiting the number of times I can 'meat nuke' a boss, but the magic mirror is way too important especially after the halfway point...
[*] Said halfway point introduces a new mechanic, every twist you do that doesn't result in a match counts as you having twisted twice. It was way too easy without this mechanic, but after it's brought in it feels like a lot of the fun has been scrubbed from the game. If the enemy places an attack in the bottom-left corner (by default you can only twist clockwise), it's almost impossible to remove it in time. Instead gameplay devolves into saving your own attacks to camp the enemy's, which contributes to severely limiting which monsters are viable.
[*] The story feels like an awful stageplay. Laska could have been written out entirely and most maps boil down to 'chase after this person then split apart so you can chase down someone else'. The mastermind was pathetic and they don't even bother to scroll the credits when you beat him. Instead you get some more party chatter then back to the map.
[/list]

If you like Puzzle Quest, don't play this and stick to Puzzle Quest.

The UI really did not age well and the game crashes constantly if played in Full Screen.  

You can only "twist" (ie. rotate 4 gems) clockwise unless you use a consumable item to rotate counterclockwise once.  This limiting factor plus the fact that you eventually get penalised for any move you make which does not cause a match make for some questionable game play.  This is compounded by the abilities of monsters you face, some of which will replace gems with rocks or lock gems making your moves extremely limited.

The game also has this weird Pokemon aspect to it where you build a beast roster with different gem affinities and abilities of which you choose any 3 at once to go battle.  Their level is tied to yours but each beast has a level cap which seems like it was added just to force you to find more Beasts with higher level caps.

Popcaps und Square Enix ... zwei Studios die eigentlich nichts verbindet. Die einen kochen digitales Crack in Form von Handygames, die anderen erzählen bombastische Legenden und packen zwangsweise ein wenig Gameplay dazwischen.

Meine Theorie ist das beide Studius sich irgendwann an ner Bar getroffen haben, kräftig gesoffen und am nächsten morgen peinlich berührt neben einander aufwachten. 9 Monate Später kam Gyromancer.

Ein Match-3-Game dessen einziges Alleinstellungsmerkmal ist das man nicht 2 Perlen vertauscht sondern 4 Perlen dreht. Dazu noch Artwork, Musik und Story von Square Enix draufgesetzt und fertig ist das Game. 

Die Musik ist für diese Art von Spiel Bombastisch, das Artwork gut gezeichnet aber kaum bewegt (Auf der Karte bewegen wir uns als unanimierter Sprite, in den Storysequenzen sind geht die Animation nicht über gelegentliches Links-Rechts-Wackeln und ein paar Effekte wie Blutspritzer hinaus).

Die Story selbst ist typisch Japanisch darin das die eine tiefe Hintergrundstory hat, die nirgends erzählt wird. Oberflächlich sind wir ein unsterblicher Magier der nach dem Mord an ein paar Adligen den Rebellen in einen magischen Wald folgt um ggf. den Erben zu finden und zu retten. Dieser Wald verschließt sich allerdings alle paar Jahre um den neuen Herscher des Waldes zu ermitteln und in dieser Zeit wachsen die Bewohner zu Alptraumhafter Größe und hauen sich im Kayu-Style die Hucke voll.

Man bildet vor dem Betreten der Map ein Team aus 3 eigenen Monstern die einen dann durch die Kämpfe begleiten. Diese Monster gibts es nochmal in verschiedenen "Ausbaustufen" und in 6 Elementen / Farben a 2 Monstern (sprich 2 Rote, 2 Blaue etc.). Jedes Monster hat einen unterschiedlichen Spielstil und manipuliert das Spielbrett auf unterschiedliche Weise. Während der Feuerdrache sehr schnell sehr viele Angriffe auflädt die (wenn man sie sammelt) in einem explosiven Schlagwirbel den Gegner zerfetzen baut der Baumgeist sich eine große Regeneration auf und vergiftet den Gegner, so das dieser langsam verendet während der Baum sich stetig hochheilt. Die Unterschiedlichen Styles der Monster sorgen für reichlich Abwechslung und interessante Matchups. Einige Elemente haben dazu noch Vorteile gegenüber anderen und und und... insgesamt gibt es zwar "nur" 12 Standard-Monster (Mit je 3 Ausbaustufen) und zum Ende des Spiels nochmal 6 Ultimative-Monster. Aber allein die Teamauswahl ist für ein Pop-Caps game überraschend komplex.

Die Kämpfe finden im im Match-3 Modus statt, wobei, wie eingangs erwähnt, die Perlen nicht getauscht sondern gedreht werden. Wenn man jetzt eine Perlenkombo vervollständigt laden sich die Angriffe des eigenen und des gewählten Monsters auf. Dies geschieht schneller wenn man Kombinationen in der "Farbe" des jeweligen Monsters bildet, wobei die Farben für die jeweiligen Elemente des Monsters stehen, Rot für Feuer, Blau für Wasser, Gelb für Blitz usw. . Wenn ein Angriff aufgeladen ist überträgt er sich auf eine Perle auf dem Spielbrett und explodiert wenn man eine Kombination mit dieser Perle bildet, bzw. bei Gegnern (da der Gegner keine Züge bekommt) nachdem ein Timer abläuft. Sollte man eine gegnerische Perle vor Ablauf des Timers mit einer Kombo vom Feld nehmen ist der gegnerische Angriff somit pariert. Sein eigenes Puzzlegeschick hat somit direkte Auswirkungen auf den Kampf.

This is not a bad game, exactly.  And I got 15 hours of fun out of it...until things got annoying.  Here's the rundown:

The Good:
The actual match-3 battle gameplay is just fine.  Different than PuzzleQuest, but fun.
The monster and character portraits are high quality.
The monster collection mechanic is also just fine.

The meh:
There are a lot of other mechanics that aren't clearly introduced.
The complicating mechanics that are later introduced (that basically discourage moves that don't immediately result in a match) aren't really that much fun.
Music is fine, but more variation would have helped.
How do monsters get experience?  How does my level affect anything? I'm still a little confused.

The bad:
The story and dialog are a load of pretentious nonsense.
I'm fine with grinding. Ask anyone. But there comes a level where the bottleneck battle is 20 levels higher than your monsters, even if you've been grinding up till that point. Ain't nobody got time for that.
The special combo level (where you have to make a chain reaction that makes five matches) is very annoying. I've spent 20 minutes trying to get through it before giving up.

The verdict:
A great game (for about 15 hours) that eventually gets ground into the dirt by the necessity for grinding and overly difficult 'bonus' levels. Worth it if it goes on heavy discount. If not, not so much.
Gets old quickly and has a multitude of pacing problems which causes it to become a slog.

This is one of those ones where you want to give it both a thumbs up and a thumbs down. The actual game play is good, marred only by a sudden difficulty spike a third of the way through the game. The story - especially the writing - is awful.

The game is a collaboration between Square Enix and Popcap who seem to have both seen the cross-over hit Puzzlequest and decided they wanted a piece of the action. The core game is Bejewelled Twist with some extra running around mazes. You have different beasts to use in the matches and the affect how often special gems appear and what abilities they trigger. It does keep you on your toes strategy-wise. The main criticism of the game-play is that the rules suddenly change after four levels in a rather significant way. It does not make it easier. To be fair, without the change the game would get stale before the end, but its introduction is done poorly.

The packaging around the game-play is pitiful. The story is nonsense and the writing is terrible. I'm pretty sure the good guys were spending most of the time trying to suppress a popular uprising so the ruling classes could maintain their privilege. On top of this the art work (all static) looks like a cheap knock-off of the art from old dungeons and dragons books. The hero and heroine are eternally stuck in dramatic poses without any context.

I should add that the graphics are stuck at 720p. This was standard for Popcap games of the era, they didn't target people with the latest gaming rigs. What graphics options there are can be turned up to the maximum on any computer of the past decade (possibly two). Since most people will have been playing at at least 1080p it will be noticeable, but you get used to it.

Einer der schlimmsten Grinder, die man sich ausdenken kann. Langweilig, heftiges RNG und ein Spielspaß raubendes "Fehlerelement", dazu keinerlei taktische Freiheiten. Ein rundum böses Spiel, das SpielerInnen leider durch ein sehr interessantes, "casual"-wirkendes Konzept einlullt und wie eine Spinne einfängt. 

Ganz ehrlich: Die ersten Stunden kann man mit Gyromancer viel Spaß haben. Man kann sogar leicht und beschwingt durch schon geschaffte Abschnitte gehen, um zu versuchen alle "Erfolge" zu farmen oder einfach nur sein Level zu steigern. Man kann dabei leicht über einen Daumen hoch nachdenken. Aber dann...

Was ist Gyromancer? Es ist:
1. Eine Fantasy-Geschichte, die sehr oberflächlich ist, aber mit schönen 2D-Charakteren für eine gewisse "Dranbleiben"-Stimmung sorgt. 
2. Ein ewiggleicher Kampf: 1 Monster vs. 1 Monster. Wer zuerst auf 0 HP ist, verliert. Wir haben stets 3 Monster im Köcher, nicht mehr, nicht weniger. Alle Monster haben Maxlevel, sollten also regelmäßig durch Stärkere ausgetauscht werden. Außerdem gibt es, wie bei Pokemon und Co. Stärken und Schwächen nach dem Schere-Stein-Papier (+ einiges mehr) Prinzip.
Wir wählen also vor jedem Kampf eines unserer 3 Monster mit möglichst Pfeil nach oben (Vorteil), Nichts (neutral) oder, zur Not, Pfeil nach unten (Nachteil) und natürlich möglichst viel HP. Die Kämpfe entscheiden sich aber nicht durch Mana oder Fähigkeiten, sondern durch
3. das Bejeweled/CandyCrush etc. 3. Element des Spiels. Wir bilden Reihen mit 3+ gleichen Farben in waagerechter oder senkrechter Richtung. Haben wir 1 unserer max. 3 Fähigkeiten "aufgeladen", erscheint zufällig ein "verstärkter" Stein. Lösen wir diesen aus, gibt es einen Effekt (meistens Schaden) auf den Gegner. Dieser operiert exakt identisch, mit einem Unterschied: Er muss nichts fertigstellen, sondern aktiviert seine Fähigkeiten einfach über Zeit und unsere "Drehungen". Es erscheint ein Totenkopf-markierter Gegnerstein. Wir haben dann x-Züge, um diesen in eine 3+-Reihe zu bringen oder anders zu zerstören. Gelingt das nicht, löst er aus und der Gegner macht Schaden oder einen Effekt. 

Anfangs ist das Spiel fair und handzahm. Die Gegner sind level 1, 2, 3, so wie wir. Wir leveln sehr schnell und unsere Monster werden stärker. Schnell kriegen wir "neue Monster" und schaffen, Story betreffend, einen Abschnitt nach dem anderen.

Aber dann schlägt das Spiel GNADENLOS zurück. 

Auf einmal wird, aus dem Nichts, eine neue Strafe eingeführt. Jedes "unnötige Drehen" kostet Extra-Speed für Gegner-Fähigkeiten. Der Witz: Das Spiel macht es unmöglich, diese Drehungen zu vermeiden.

Aber es wird noch viel, viel besser:

Fast kein Monster verfügt über "Heilung". Auch unsere 4 "Hilfsgegenstände" können das nicht. Diese sind zwar nützlich, aber stark limitiert. Selbst mit 30.000 Gold können wir nirgendwo "einkaufen". Wir können uns also entweder in den ersten Abschnitten zu Tode farmen oder damit leben, dass die Gegenstände kaum eine Hilfe sind (weil immer aus).
Es gibt manchmal in Leveln "Heilungsschreine", aber diese sind einmalig und heilen nur anteilig, nie voll. 

Sind wir besiegt oder zu low, müssen wir das Level verlassen. Konsequenz: Voller Reset. Alle Monster wieder auf 100%, alle wieder da, alle Absperrungen etc. --> Der Grind kennt keine Gnade.

Auf Abschnitt 6, schon 10+ Stunden im Spiel, zahlreiche Abschnitte im Bereich 1-4 MEHRFACH gesäubert, auf Level 30+ gegrindet, warten plötzlich LEVEL 50 (!) Monster an unpassierbaren Abschnitten. Selbst mit VOLLEM LEBEN, Monster mit Vorteil (Pfeil nach oben) und "Durchbruch" (eine Art Super-Booster), werden wir in der Pfeife geraucht. Der Gegner, obwohl seine Fähigkeiten kaum Schadenspunkte machen sollten UND er einen verrückten Self-Heal hat, spawnt alle 5-6 Drehungen 5-6 Totenköpfe gleichzeitig. Es ist, und das meine ich völlig ernst, UNMÖGLICH (oder zumindest zu 99%), diese zu entschärfen. Folge: Rausch-artige Schadenskanonade, die du höchstens 2 Runden überlebst. 

Was will das Spiel hier von dir? Das du stundenlang Level 50 grindest? Das man irgendein spezielles Monster nur dafür braucht? Ich weiß es nicht. 

Das Spiel hat keinen Schwierigkeitsgrad. Du kannst nicht mal eben "auf leicht" stellen. Man wird, so tief im Spiel, einfach knallhart daran gehindert die Story zu Ende zu spielen. Keine Rede von den "Endleveln" wie "Rivels Probe", wo man nur noch lauter 50+ Monstern begegnet oder an Steinen Prüfungen wie "Kombo 5+", "Kettenlevel 5" etc. machen soll. 

Am Schlimmsten ist das verdammte Zufallselement. Der RNG-Faktor ist zum Kotzen. Mal spawnt eine deiner verstärkten Fähigkeiten auf einem Stein, der WEIT UND BREIT keine gleichen Farben hat. Mal spawnt er in der tiefsten Ecke. Und die Totenkopf-Gegner genauso. Mal kann man easy mit 1-2 Drehungen die Steine "entschärfen", mal weiß man schon den Moment des Spawns: Selbst in 7 Zügen finde ich dafür keine Verbindung. Konsequenz: Man kann nur noch Schadensbegrenzung betreiben, weiß aber genau: Ich krieg gleich schön Schaden. 

Warum kann man diese Items nicht einfach endlos einsetzen? Wenigstens ein Refill nach jedem Kampf? Oder ein Händler dafür?
Warum wird es überhaupt so schwer bis unmöglich gemacht, dass man die Drehrichtung verändert oder Dots entfernt?
Warum ist Heilung so schwer bis gar nicht zu bekommen?
Was soll das Element der "Strafe für unnötiges Drehen"? Es ist nichts anderes als ein kranker KI-Buff, der den Spieler massiv einschränkt und jeden Spaß, jedes Knobeln und Ausprobieren nimmt.
Warum kann man wenigstens die Story nicht ohne mega-Hustle abschließen und dann später diesen "Bonus-Content" auf Level 50+ machen, wenn man Bock hat (oder nicht...)?

Ich hatte schon nach ca. 2 Stunden überlegt, ob ich das Spiel wieder aufhöre, weil es einfach wirklich WENIG bietet. Es ist immer Monster vs. Monster, EXP-Grind und eben die Steinchen drehen. Aber der Story zuliebe wollte ich es doch durchziehen. Jetzt, nach 11 Stunden ernsthaften Versuchens, bereue ich meine Entscheidung. Das Spiel sagt mir dreist: Spiel einfach noch 10 Stunden, dann bist du Level 40-50 und kannst (vielleicht) Abschnitt 7 oder 8 erreichen. 

Du kannst mich mal am ***** lecken, Gyromancer! Selbst Grinds in Diablo, WoW oder anderen Spielen fühlen sich nicht so grenzdebil wie hier an.

Fazit: FINGER WEG, wenn ihr nach Anschauen der Trailer oder nach einer halben Stunde nicht merkt, dass ihr dieses Klötzchen-Drehen abgöttisch toll findet. Dieses Spiel wird SEHR SCHWER und ist ein mieser GRIND.

I almost want to recommend this game, since the dialogue is VERY campy and silly, and knowing Square Enix, that aspect was definitely not intentional, which frankly makes it even funnier. However, no amount of goofy facsimiles of medieval speech patterns can save this game's terrible gameplay.

In the beginning, it's not that bad, albeit a bit weird. It has similar gameplay to Bejeweled Twist, but instead of earning special gems from matching 4 or 5 gems in a row, they're earned by filling a bar on the HUD that corresponds to your beast's color identity. There's also a Pokemon-esque type matchup chart, but it's not relevant very often. Your special gems can be matched to deal damage to the enemy, and the enemy's special gems are treated like time bombs from Twist: they count down from an arbitrary number each time you make a move, and when they expire, their effect deals damage to you.

It's a very strange system, no doubt inspired by the surging popularity of Puzzle Quest at the time of the game's development. However, every other aspect of the game seems to clash with this battle system.

- Battles can take a VERY long time, especially against enemies with high health or fast-filling bars. Add in the fact that each level only has two or three enemy types, and you'll quickly get REALLY sick of certain enemies.

- Nearly every level contains monster dens that churn out the same type of enemy, each of which must be battled along a linear path in order to fight another boss monster inside the den in order to destroy it. At least the enemies spawned from the den disappear after you kill it.

- The game has a very irritating sense of how to make battles challenging, From the most recent two bosses that I faced, the former had a mechanic that let them run from battle without placing a gem on the field to do so, forcing you to replay the same battle on a strict timer over and over until you whittled down their health. The latter instantly placed a gem on the field with a 3-turn timer, forcing me to take unavoidable damage, and this ability also has a short cooldown, so it kept churning out short timers constantly throughout the fight. I can only imagine what the later bosses are like.

- Something that I had to discover for myself (since the reviews conveniently left this detail out) is that when a certain story event triggers, the game is irreversibly changed so that making an "idle spin" (a move that doesn't actively match gems) incurs a penalty. Whenever you make an idle spin, enemy action bars are filled dramatically, and timers count down an additional time. This feels HORRIBLE to deal with, since you often have to make idle spins to avoid taking damage, and certain abilities that already felt unreliable and clunky now feel even worse, since you have to constantly match gems to avoid the penalty. In addition, there's no algorithm like in Zen Mode of normal Bejeweled that guarantees matches will appear. There's a fairly good chance (especially in longer battles) that you are forced to either take a penalty or use one of your consumable items.

- On a different note, the music is not good. It's very by-the-book fantasy music, and it almost sounds like stock music. There's also almost no variation in the battle music. One track for normal enemies, one track for "dangerous" enemies, one track for bosses, and presumably one track for the final boss. It's mind-numbing to have to listen to the same track over and over and over again.

Overall, this game is funny to watch, but horrid to play. I doubt any streamers have played this game, but that's probably the best way to experience this one, rather than spend your hard-earned Gil on this strange little satchel of gems.

I found Gyromancer to be a very enjoyable puzzle-RPG hybrid. I was intimidated by some of the reviews here, which said that the game has horrible performance issues. Well, by some strange miracle, Gyromancer fortunately ran well on my PC, with no crashes and no deleted data. Please note however that this was just my experience, so people could still encounter technical problems on their computers. 

Two quick notes about performance. Firstly, the game has an uncapped framerate, and while it did not tax my graphics card all that much, the game might increase the temperature significantly on certain computers. Some cards are more vulnerable than others, so if you have had problems with games with unlimited FPS in the past, do take into account that this game also has uncapped FPS and might cause some fuss. The second thing worth mentioning is that, while the game did not delete save game data while I played it, IT DELETED IT ENTIRELY WHEN I UNINSTALLED. I was aware this might happen, so I only uninstalled the game AFTER i beat the final boss. So please be aware that uninstalling or modifying the game in any way might cause you to lose progress. It really sucks that such a thing happens in the first place, but as long as you take certain steps and avoid doing certain things, you will not encounter many problems.

I am saying all this because, despite the technical hiccups you might experience, Gyromancer is undeniably fun and I say it is worth sticking with it despite the problems. Fighting monsters is very addictive, even if it gets a bit repetitive near the end. The game does punish idle moves later in the story, but this is not as crippling as some people have suggested, and you will actually get used to it and learn to think more strategically. There are very few attacks that you cannot avoid, even with the idle moves penalty. 

The game is very grind heavy, which I found is a double edged sword. On one hand, it can be frustrating, such as the final boss, which required me to grind almost three hours in order to be strong enough to beat him. It is essential (heck, even the help menu in the game says it) that you should always be at least a couple of levels over your opponent. The final boss was a bit frustrating because it has two forms you have to beat, although, if you beat the first form and then come back, you will only have to deal with the second form, so in the end it was fair, even if a bit frustrating. 

On the other hand, it is very satisfying to level up, because enemies, as far as I could tell, DO NOT have level scaling. Which means that if you have trouble beating an enemy, all you have to do is level up, come back and crush the son of a b***h! While I consider Puzzle Quest to be the better game, this is one area where Gyromancer is superior to PQ. 

There are a few other minor flaws (such as how you find so few items, and once you use them up they are gone), but overall, Gyromancer is still one of the best puzzle-RPGs out there, and it deserves at least a try if you're a fan of the genre.

Weirder than seeing PopCap's logo following Square Enix's one is to behold the aggressive breed born from such unlikely partnership.

Gyromancer is somewhat oppressive in many levels: characters art pieces can be surprisingly wicked, the plot is dark and gory, and the gameplay--as far as gem-match puzzles go--aim to constrain the player instead of encourage creative problem solving. In fact, even simple actions as spinning gems counter clock-wise (something that could be intuitively pulled off with a right click of the mouse) cost an item, and must be executed sparingly. As it piles up towards the end, some concepts communicate badly and puzzles manage to become even cryptic, an unthinkable feature for an apparently casual setup.

But it still hooks. Finding, unlocking and training gorgeous beasts proves to be rewarding--and so does simply following the classic-yet-nicely-told story. To the point it's easy to take "twisting gems" for granted and end taking the game more seriously than it has any rights to be.

Gyromancer succeeds by not only dressing PopCap's stuff in a beautiful coat of paint, but also by adding meaning to mundane gameplay mechanics.

小学时接触的，现在已经大学了。最近发现steam上有这玩意，又重温了一下。
个人感觉游戏的模式让人眼前一亮，消除进行战斗虽然不是独一无二的想法，但是将消除的特点完美融入战斗系统是很赞的。这也直接使得游戏规则与操作十分简单。本人大概打了全流程7，8遍了（之前都是下的盗版），大部分战斗都可以无伤无空转完成，正努力把每一关的分数刷上万。这个游戏的核心玩法算是高效的消除。这要求玩家在尽可能短的步数内做到连锁，瓦解或者联击以及特殊颜色宝石的消除。因此游戏消除的时间毫无限制。游戏的立绘与音乐都很赞，能力宝石的特效也算是加分项。
美中不足的地方也有不少，其一就是游戏元素太单调，各种族魔兽的不同阶段改动太少。再就是后期游戏趣味降低，如果不慎把等级练的太高，就会很没意思。魔林消也很鸡肋（连消等级到五之后接着消满一圈槽造成极大伤害），因为一般消到等级五就已经结束战斗了。不同魔兽的强度不平衡，例如实战里瑞舍夫与古代龙的实力几乎碾压所有未突破的魔兽，在刷分中蚂蚁与枭也强于绝大多数魔兽，至于敌人，除非是跨越十级以上的战斗（可以做到），一般来说不存在极具挑战性的敌人。（当然，如果你在猎物丛林里先杀死螳螂恶魔，那么你将在跨20余级对原始真菌的战斗中大大提升水平（被虐））
虽然这玩意应该凉了也大概不会有什么人买，不过确实算是美好的回忆，期待一下肯定不存在的续作吧~

This is an old game, and honestly, there’s not much to say about it anymore. Even among older strategy games, it doesn’t really stand out.

Visually, everything blends together. Buildings look too similar, and it’s often unclear what is what. It takes extra effort just to understand what’s happening on the map.

The mechanics also feel a bit odd. Units don’t always behave clearly — some stop working for no obvious reason. The “radius” system makes things feel less logical compared to other strategy games where roads define movement.

Overall, it’s okay for casual play, but compared to other strategy games, it feels very basic and unremarkable.

Классический градостроительный-исторический симулятор детства, при этом, с исторической точки зрения, сделанный весьма качественно, в той степени, на сколько это вообще необходимо для геймплея, закладываемого этой замечательной игрой.

Imperium Romanum - казуальная градостроительная стратегия, которая больше всего придется по вкусу НЕ тем кто ищет в играх достоверность и аутентичность, а тем кто любит размеренно залипать на живущих своей жизнью человечков (каждый работник, его текущие занятия и потребности честно и довольно подробно визуализируются игрой).

Экономическая модель своей простотой и лаконичностью очень похожа на Stronghold, однако у нее нюанс: у всех (!) зданий ограниченный радиус действия. Другими словами если в Stronghold вы могли поставить пару лесопилок на другом конце карты и забыть о них, то в Imperium Romanum близ удаленных месторождений ископаемых придется основывать дополнительные деревни с главным зданием в центре и полноценной городской инфраструктурой вокруг: начиная с домов, акведуков, школ и рынков в начале, и заканчивая храмами, академиями и театрами на поздних этапах развития.

Из интересного: в Imperium Romanum есть гендерное разделение труда. Мужчины здесь как правило работают в мастерских и занимаются тяжелым производством: это лесопилки, шахты и разнообразные мастерские (пекари, мясники и кузницы, охрана правопорядка и пр.). Тогда как женщины работают преимущественно на фермах, прядильнях, рынках и изредка на торговых аванпостах.

Ну и конечно еще есть рабы, которые обязательно поднимут бунт, стоит только их немного перегрузить работой. Поэтому важно не раскидывать здания одной производственной цепочки далеко друг от друга.

На удивление - вся эта тема неплохо сбалансирована, и после того как вы разберетесь в CORE-механике головной боли при отстройке города не создает.

Боевая часть по сравнению со Stronghold очень сильно упрощена, и скорее является очередным экономическим вызовом игроку типа "построй достаточно стабильную экономику что бы содержать армию прежде чем твой город сожгут", чем чем-то самостоятельным (за исключением дополнительной кампании "Гражданская война Цезаря", где нужно выживать и побеждать против численно превосходящего противника, вот это занятно).

Now it's very charming and has that early 2000s handcrafted game feel to it that I miss from that era of gaming, but after 2 hours I've built a fully self-sustainable city on a hard difficulty map and there wasn't much left for me to do.

The city management is skin deep and once you get a hang of basic resources and food you are never in danger of failing. You don't even need to keep your citizens happy so long as you have enough prefects to break up riots.

The barbarian AI can be easily tricked by building a single tower on their road which will cause them to siege it giving you time to prepare.

With all that being said, it is still a charming game and I'd recommend giving it a try at least once, especially if it's on sale.

Europa Universalis: Rome is an interesting piece of Paradox history, but unfortunately it is much easier to appreciate as a historical curiosity than to actually enjoy as a grand strategy game today.

The premise is excellent. The game covers one of the most interesting periods in ancient history, when Rome was transforming from a regional republic into a Mediterranean superpower. You can play as Rome, Carthage, Egypt, Macedon, the Seleucids, various Greek states, tribal nations, and many other powers. On paper, this is exactly the kind of historical sandbox Paradox should be good at.

The problem is that the game feels extremely limited compared with later Paradox titles.

The character system is supposed to be one of the game's defining features, but it never reaches the depth or personality of what Paradox eventually achieved with Crusader Kings. Characters have traits, positions, loyalties, and relationships, but they rarely feel like fully developed political actors. They are mostly another set of statistics and modifiers to manage rather than people who generate memorable stories.

This is especially disappointing in a game about the Roman Republic, where internal political struggles, ambitious generals, rival families, corruption, and personal alliances should be central to the experience.

The political system is similarly underdeveloped. There are republics, monarchies, tribes, diplomacy, alliances, claims, and internal politics, but the mechanics rarely combine into the kind of dynamic political sandbox you might expect.

The military system is functional but fairly basic. Wars are important, obviously, but warfare can become repetitive very quickly. There isn't enough tactical depth to make individual campaigns particularly memorable, and once you understand the basic mechanics, military expansion can feel more like a routine process than a major strategic challenge.

Diplomacy is another weak point. The ancient Mediterranean was full of shifting alliances, rivalries, betrayals, client states, dynastic politics, and competing spheres of influence. Europa Universalis: Rome provides diplomatic tools, but they don't generate enough complexity to recreate that kind of environment convincingly.

The economy and province management are also quite limited. There are resources, trade, buildings, population, taxation, and other systems, but they don't provide the level of economic decision-making found in later Paradox games.

And then there is the interface.

This is an old Paradox game, and it shows. The UI is dated, information can be difficult to find, tooltips are not always sufficient, and managing a large empire becomes increasingly cumbersome. Modern Paradox players accustomed to Crusader Kings III or Europa Universalis IV will immediately notice how much the design has evolved.

The biggest problem is that the game often feels like an early prototype for ideas that Paradox would later develop much further.

You can see the foundations of several familiar Paradox concepts here: character relationships, political factions, population management, diplomacy, warfare, trade, and large-scale historical simulation. But almost all of them feel less developed than their later counterparts.

The Gold Edition does provide the additional content associated with the game's expansions, but that does not solve the fundamental problem. The underlying systems themselves are simply too limited and dated to compete with later Paradox grand strategy games.

That said, there is still something interesting here for dedicated Paradox fans.

If you want to see how Paradox approached the ancient world before Imperator: Rome, or you are particularly interested in obscure historical strategy games, Europa Universalis: Rome has some value as a historical artifact.

But as a standalone grand strategy game, it is difficult to recommend today.

**The ancient setting is fantastic, the historical scope is impressive, and there are some genuinely interesting ideas here. Unfortunately, the shallow character mechanics, basic diplomacy, repetitive warfare, limited economic systems, and extremely dated interface prevent the game from reaching its potential.**

It feels less like a finished version of the ancient-world Paradox formula and more like an early experiment that later games would learn from.

**Interesting historical curiosity, but too dated and mechanically limited for me to recommend. Not Recommended.**

I recently decided to give a chance to this game and I was greatly impressed actually, so I decided to write a review for those who do not know if the game is worth to play.
In summary, this is a really solid 2000's strategy game. For veteran Paradox grand strategy players who played CK2 and 3 and Europa Universalis 3 and 4, this game would be very familiar. It is overall a very simplified version of EU4 with some elements from Crusader Kings, which in my opinion it is ideal for new players and newcomers to this series of games, if you can accept the older graphics and UI and also a far less polished version of a grand strategy title.
The game works overall as a board game, where each player takes control of a country, at any date from 270 to 30 BCE (the rise of Rome and the conquest of the Mediterranean). You manage the politics, warfare, trade and diplomacy in way slower and a far more simplified way than most Paradox games. It is a more casual strategy board-like game, yet very enjoyable today for a 2008 title. 
Even if the game has a modern sequel in Imperator:Rome, it is still a solid choice and worth the price to enjoy the early 2000's aesthetycs in a classic old strategy game.

As a long-time admirer of Paradox Interactive’s grand strategy games, Europa Universalis: Rome – Gold Edition caught my attention not just for its setting, but for the sheer potential baked into its premise. Set in the twilight of the Roman Republic, it promises a detailed sandbox for historical drama, military conquest, and political intrigue. And for those who can get past its rougher edges, it mostly delivers.

At its best, this game evokes the spirit of ancient statecraft better than most. You don’t just command armies and paint the map your color — you must also manage senates, appease aristocrats, and keep ambitious generals from turning on the Republic. The character system is robust, especially for its time. Every statesman, general, and governor comes with traits and ambitions that influence both gameplay and storytelling. Watching internal politics unfold, sometimes in ways that disrupt your grand plans, gives the game a living, breathing quality that makes each campaign feel distinct.

The Gold Edition includes the "Vae Victis" expansion, which sharpens many of the original game's duller mechanics. The addition of a more involved political system adds an extra layer of depth, making governing your realm as engaging — if not more so — than the warfare. Ruling over Carthage, Egypt, or one of the minor Hellenistic states becomes a rewarding experience of juggling personal ambitions, balancing party influence, and navigating unpredictable internal power struggles.

However, Europa Universalis: Rome shows its age, and not always gracefully. The user interface, while serviceable, is dated and often obtuse. Important information is hidden behind too many menus, and the learning curve, even for those familiar with other Paradox titles, can be needlessly steep. The lack of clear tooltips and guidance is frustrating, especially when trying to understand how certain mechanics work — or why something suddenly broke down in your government.

Warfare, while functional, lacks the strategic flair found in later titles. Battles feel more about numbers than tactics, and supply, terrain, or unit variety don't matter as much as they should in a game with historical aspirations. Naval combat, too, feels like an afterthought, which is disappointing considering how vital sea power was in the Mediterranean world.

The AI has moments of brilliance — usually in domestic politics — but on the battlefield or diplomacy screen, it tends to falter. Enemy states can behave irrationally, and diplomacy often boils down to either brute force or patience, without much room for creativity. Bugs and crashes have mostly been ironed out over the years, but the game still lacks some quality-of-life improvements that modern grand strategy fans might take for granted.

Despite these flaws, there’s something oddly captivating about this title. Its blend of personal politics, ancient geopolitics, and unique flavor events makes for a deeply immersive experience — once you get past the rough exterior. It’s a game that demands effort, but it often rewards that investment with memorable moments that few others can offer.

Pros:
Deep character and political systems create compelling internal narratives

Wide variety of playable factions, each with unique challenges

"Vae Victis" expansion enhances gameplay with needed depth

Immersive historical setting rarely explored in grand strategy

Cons:
Dated UI and steep learning curve hinder accessibility

Warfare lacks depth and strategic nuance

Diplomacy and AI behavior can feel simplistic or erratic

Visuals and mechanics feel aged compared to newer Paradox titles

Final Rating: 7/10
Europa Universalis: Rome – Gold Edition is a flawed gem. It won’t appeal to everyone, but for those who appreciate detailed political mechanics and are willing to wrestle with its aging framework, it remains a rewarding — and rare — dive into ancient world strategy.

I've been enjoying the game so far. It doesn't look great by today's standard but the game is deeper than some might think. I also like that there isn't any mana system. The option to zoom and rotate is great. I also like the city-view option.

[b]The Negatives[/b]

Terrible treaty AI: The AI will basically just take random territory it controls during a war leading to border gore. A bigger issue however is that the AI likes to permanently occupy larger countries and never make peace. 

Civil Wars: The rebel faction just gets a bunch of random provinces for their rebellion. This just makes civil wars tedious and worse, Its bad strategy because preparing and adapting them is just pure luck. 

Populists: Its a bit ridiculous that they can win elections despite low popularity and few seats. This kinda undermines the whole point of managing the senate. Its not game breaking but you're punished with a changed national idea if you get a populist in power. You'll basically just have to occasionally arrest nobody senators who somehow find themselves next in line for the Consulship. 

Casus Belli: Its hard to find excuses for war. You gotta either wait for border incidents or spam assassins. 

Lack of factions: Not really a bad thing but the northern tribes are basically unplayable and the monarchies are boring. Stick to Rome and Carthage. 

Buggy: The game crashes and installing mods is actually pretty difficult. The patches needed to run most mods are hidden inside obscure threads on the Paradox forums and were apparently not made with Steam in mine. 


[b]The Positives[/b]

Generals: The game knows what its trying to be. The difference between a 9 general and 10 general  is thousands of deaths and this means that you'll have to do everything in their your power to get incredible generals infront of your armies. Most good generals will earn a following of soldiers who are loyal to them instead of the state and will tend to be ambitious. These generals will want promotions, triumphs and bribes and if they're especially ambitious they'll even start a civil war. Another nuanced mechanic is that units who are loyal to a general will fight better under that general so you have to try and balance your generals popularity with their threat to the status quo.  

Senate: The senate isn't perfect but managing it is focus of the game rather than an annoying side attraction. You get bonuses depending on which faction is in charge and get punished harshly with a changed national idea and negative modifiers if the populists get in. The senate is not a boring side attraction, its a den of intrigue and fun for those who like to autistically micromanage things. You want to switch which faction is in charge depending on your needs. 

Barbarians: Germania and Spain are made up of colonial provinces that spawn hoards. These hoards lack organization and equipment but their numbers and occasional brilliant generals make them a threat. As Rome you basically need to garrison the north because its unpredictable. You need to build forts and set up buffer states as at any moment a giant hoard that's actually a threat could spawn. The northern tribes are playable but they obviously only exist just to be made into buffer states by the player as they lack any mechanics or way to actually resist the barbarians. 

Less Mana: You can't instantly convert provinces culture or religion with some magical points. This means you have to actually manage your empire and deal with diverse populations. This means the game actually has a late game instead of a boring slog of steam rolling. Much of your great army will be resisting the barbarians and guarding against rebellions. You'll have to rely on a smaller corp of elite units with good generals to continue painting the map. That means you can't neglect the senate or stop managing your generals. 
This may seem like a minor detail but makes the late game fun. 

Chance: Battles come down to terrain, army makeup, modifiers (based on laws/government), numbers and generals. There aren't too many ways to game the system. You will get destroyed if you pick bad generals or attack across rivers but luck might be on your side and you might win despite your poor choices. However,  the luck of the dice roll can also undermine even the greatest of generals. This randomness is lacking in newer Paradox games and its sad because chance adds a layer of depth to strategy games. 

Challenge: Even Rome is going to have a hard time in the early game. Macedon, Epirus and Carthage all have generals that are actually good, much larger fleets and access to cavalry and even elephants. The challenge extends into the late game as more land means more governors, generals and influential senators to manage. You may also find yourself with less manpower in the late game as your  population of small landowners is replaced by a society of slaves and citizens who want bread and circus. Its a game with problems but its also a game that avoids all of the problems of a modern Paradox title.

With Imperator's release imminent, there's no reason to play EU:Rome, except to understand the systems in Imperator by looking at their ancestor, which is why I've bothered to play it.

Compared to regular Europa Universalis, EU:Rome is a strange beast. It incorporates some of the character focus of Crusader Kings, and a little of the economic management of Victoria, while adding a little of it's own flavor to the mix. The problem is, that since this game came out well before Crusader Kings 2 (which imo revolutionized Paradox games) it's playability is extremely hampered by a lack of quality of life UI improvements that came with later titles. 

For example, in modern PDX games, every army has a little number next to it, saying how many men are in it. Not so in EU:Rome, all you can see is an army marching towards you, and that's it. Now, you can pause the game, hover your mouse over the unit, and see the number, but it's quite grating to have to grind everything to a halt just to see some basic information. On top of that, if two armies are on the same province, and they both move to another province, one army's sprite will completely override the other, and there's no graphical indication the other army is there.

You are also inundated with events, on par with playing the U.S. in Victoria 2, every waking moment. Even a relatively experienced Paradox-game player like myself found it to be quite difficult to keep things straight when some loser named Gnaeus Barbilus spams you with Senatorial events over and over.

I tried to play nations besides Rome, but it felt second-class, quite a departure from later titles where even the smallest nation can be interesting. The Populist faction rivals Anarcho-Liberals in Vicky2, with how damned annoying they are to beat down. It's real fun to have to check the character screen for any Populist with better than 4 Charisma and imprison them, so they don't pull every Senator from Rome to Hispania to their faction.

The positives of the game are primarily related to the loyalty system. A general wins a few battles, a few legions think he's a pretty cool guy, then he decides to take his army, march on Rome, and install himself as leader. Quite the balancing act is required by the player to have effective leaders, while checking their power.

Little side notes:
Characters are all hideous potato-human hybrids.
x5 speed (a.k.a. the game runs as fast as your CPU can handle) on modern hardware is so fast, it's near suicidal to play on.
The map feels small with such massive provinces, can't really blame a game from 11 years ago for that, though.

As a player that tried +60 hours to understand and enjoy and Cursader Kings II, and failed, I can say that this game has been just the contrary experience: I enjoyed it from the very start and I'm still interested in it. I'm playing, of course, the Romans and in a few years I defeated Tarentum and Epirus, annexed their former territories and executed Phyrrus (by demand of the Roman People). Also I started colonizing the north and defeated a migrant horde of barbarians under the command of some Ariovistus. Just with a few hours and with my past experience with CKII I am able to do this review! Must buy if you love Roman Era.

Mix of Europa Universalis IV and Crusader Kings II with an Ancient Era theme?
As mentioned before this game somewhat finds the middle ground between Europa Universalis IV and Crusader Kings II set in the Classical Era, while keeping it a bit more simple. There are individuals with personal properties who are part of families which you can appoint to perform certain tasks in your realm, but you are not playing as a dynasty gaining and losing lands by inheritance. For some people this type of gameplay might make CKII a bit hard to comprehend (or even annoying when you lose your realm because of some patrilineal/matrilineal screw up, or lose your alliances at the death of your ruler), in which case Europa Universalis: Rome offers a nice alternative because you are playing as a state while still having a fun mechanic with indivuals with personal traits.

Trade
I really enjoy the fun mechanic for trade in which each province produces a type of goods that can be traded with neighbouring countries or countries linked by trade routes over land or sea. Each province can trade its good once, or more often when you construct buildings like markets or harbours.

Demographics
I like the way each province's population is divided into the three classes: slaves, free men and citizens. The three classes function as the base for tax, manpower and technology respectively.

Colonisation
It's fun to have a mechanic of colonisation in this Classical Era theme, and I like the requirement to have a somewhat developed population in an adjacent province. This mechanic could be improved however by giving it some more depth, for example with a colonisation policy, either nation wide or local. The way in which you colonise now is a bit too simple, and the requirement to reduce the barbarian population in the designated province sadly makes it necessary to position troops there and wait till you trigger an uprising.

Barbarian hordes
On the other hand, the barbarian hordes spawning in the non-state lands are an interesting mechanic, picking up strength when passing through different barbarian lands and reducing technological development in raided provinces, or even destroying colonies. There is quite some empty lands in central and northern Europe, so these armies can pick up quite some strength on the way.

Celtic and Germanic tribes/states
Partly as a result of the many barbarian hordes it is rather difficult to play as one of the celtic or germanic states. If you manage to survive the ravaging by these hordes, it is highly likely that the Romans or Carthagians come and sweep you up. The mechanics for playing with these states could definitely be improved. However, you can quite easliy create your own mods in text files in which you can create more, bigger, or wealthier "barbaric" states.

All in all, I love the game because of the Classical Era theme (including the music) and think it's a good change every now and then to the extensive micromanagement of Europa Universalis IV. Sometimes you just want to play a simpler game which still has a good variety of interesting mechanics to enjoy.

I can't wait to see what the follow up "Imperator: Rome" will be like!

Works fine on my 2011 win 7 laptop, except the game kept crashing if I loaded a saved game a few times and I get runtime crashes from the auto save. HOI 2 and 3 are the best of the genre. Have yet to really play CK or VIC. I did play some EU3 before, but I stopped for some reason. This game is really slow paced compared to EU. In Rome, you can only colonize, when an area is past a certain civilization level and you have enough people, which take a long time for it to happen. I couldn't get into Sengoku, because your subordinates do their own thing. With Rome, the main annoyance is that you are fighting your own people as much as the enemy. Having troops too loyal to a general, actually makes that general become disloyal to the empire. I either had to use 2 generals for each army or throw away the loyal troops to the barbarians. Eventually made enough money that I kept bribing them; however I don't like cycling through my guys, just to make sure everyone is on the same team. When you’re fighting an enemy that has a lot of territory, even if you take all their territories, you only can get a few pieces of territory from the peace treaty. Also taking over enemy territory only weakens them and usually only giving you money that you really can't use for anything important. I was idling for a good portion of the game, basically waiting for the peace treaties to expire or for my revolt levels to go down. Also there is the annoying Populists to deal with. 

There are 4 superpower nations at the start. I'm not sure I would want to try other lesser nations, because they don't get enough research points or men as compared to the superpowers. Mistakes I made during my first real game was not working on diplomacy and not building up my navy. Also it is important to put someone with high Finesse for your technology, but I was still lagging behind the AI for some reason.  

Might be a good stepping stone for the genre. I did get it for $2.50, but I think HOI2 or EU3 would be better. Maybe HOI4, but that looks a little too casual. - Placing a road can cause the game to freeze, and crash.
- Trying to save the game can result in a game crash
- Deleting old autosaves can cause the game to crash
- ALT + Tab can result in either the following 2 options. 
A: Your buildings will go invisible and FPS will drop to negative.
B: Your buildings come back to how it's supposed to be and you regain your FPS.
- Autosave takes too long for it to occur, and it's the safer method comparing to manually saving your game which can often lead to the game crashing.
- But even autosave can crash your game, but still less likely then the manual save.

Now those are what I have experienced in roughly 11 hours of playtime. 
Besides that, it's an old game. Mechanics are clunky and kinda bad, building roads for example is a pain.
No moving things around, no refunds on destruction.
Speaking of destruction, there seems to be no popularity gain when you construct certain things, but. When you remove them because you don't like the placement for example, then you will lose 5 popularity. Which I think is kinda lame, the game is pretty hardcore in a couple of ways.

I'm sure there's many things to like about the game, but these are things I've come across that make my playthrough a lot more frustrating, especially the saving part. I just had 2 campaign starts lost because the game crashed when I tried to save it, so after 2 attempts that was me done for tonight. 

The lack of updates also is a turn off for me, the game doesn't seem to have been updated to a more friendly user standard. Updates that would improve the game's mechanics or features. 
(small example: I build a Bakery and around it is plenty of space, but the automatically generated trees from the Insula get removed anyway, this is asthetically unpleasant. How can we built nice looking Roman cities when these things happen?)

If you're a fan of Roman games and city builders, you'll like this one for a number of reasons, it's an easy grab but honestly do so at a discount considering the above issues.
Nonetheless, will enjoy this game for plenty of hours, but also hate it at the same time xD

[h2]Perhaps the best Roman city-builder one can play today[/h2]

The "Roman" here is not a figure of speech, nor is it merely a decoration chosen for an otherwise generic builder. In addition to welcome yet ultimately expected things like temples and aqueducts we have 4 population classes with their own needs and quirks - patricians, equites, plebes and, notably, slaves - with the latter being more of a commodity. We have two campaigns that let us meet notable figures of Roman history and work for them - and sometimes against them (with some unique missions based on your choices). All of it, including the soundtrack, does the job to create the appropriate atmopshere and immerse you into what happens on screen.

Great customization and progression is something this game shares with Haemimont's Tropico 4 that came out a few years afterwards. You get to pick your character's name, portrait and one of the 5 families - each coming with its own set of perks to unlock and each representing a particular side of Roman fantasy. You may start at level 1 and slowly work your way up, getting a single skill point to spend per mission completed. Or, you may start as a level 25 character and get your perks right away - which I honestly recommend doing. There are 3 perk trees to invest into - City and Military which are the same for every character, and the Family branch, specific to your family. You get about 36 perks to choose from, meaning there is build crafting and some tough choices involved, since you won't be able to just grab all the best perks - they only become available after investing a certain number of points in the tree. 

There is also a secondary progression system called estates. You unlock new estates to buy and the money to buy them by completing side objectives during missions, and estates allow you to start a mission with a surplus of certain resources - ranging from money and research points to slaves or building materials. Another reason to start as a level 25 character is it makes every estate purchaseable from the get go, as opposed to forcing you to play in a certain way to complete side objectives, that can sometimes not align with your family's preferred playstyle. Speaking of families, the guide you might stumble upon here on Steam considers slavers Lucii and traders Valerii to be most powerful, however I personally swear by the scholarly Flavii - leading to the point that most families appear pretty balanced and fun to play, with different builds available even with a single family, contributing to the game's overall replayability.

As for the gameplay itself, this game's approach to it is pretty unorthodox for the time and can be considered a war crime by an old Caesar 3 veteran. You see, there is no simulation of individual citizens here, there are no "walkers". There is no need to watch haulers carrying your goods to warehouses... heck, there are no warehouses in this game to begin with. And the thing is... it works nonetheless. Instead of resource logistics the primary city-building challenge here comes from layout planning. You see, every building has a radius it affects and where it draws workforce from. Leading to a reality where any production building needs people living nearby. Those people need food, religion and entertainment. And, before you know it, you'll have small towns forming organically around farmable land or stone quarries. It's a satisfying gameplay loop that just makes sense. Or if you don't want to build an entire town for the sake of a single quarry, you can build a slave market instead, that's going to serve all hard labor jobs in its proximity, as opposed to a regular "1 house - 1 workplace" rule. 

A seemingly oversimplified city-builder, it's actually surprisingly deep and comes with challenges for you to solve, with bonuses and penalties being applied based on how you play. Went all-in on food quality? Your low-tier housing is now free to build. Your city mostly consists of equites and patricians, while your hard labor is carried out by slaves? You get the "city of nobles" modifier that doubles your taxation income. Ignored fountains and herbalist shacks? Congratulations, a plague. Once again, every family encourages its own approach to urban layout. For example, as Flavii you want to have a beautiful city with lots of gardens and plazas, meanwhile Julii thrives when you cram as many insulas next to each other as possible. 

And then there's combat. It ain't Total War, yet fairly impressive for a city-builder. You have morale, training, unit abilities, not to mention many, many unit types including Roman legions, gladiators, gaul berserkers, war elephants and everything in between. Combat is an important part of the game - while there are purely economic missions, there are many hybrid and even purely military ones. This serves as another aspect of your build as it makes you plan for how you're gonna handle the inevitable combat segments of the game. Lucii will flood the enemies with multiple squads of cheap light infantry, Flavii will call upon an elite squad of Praetorians, meanwhile Valerii are just gonna bribe enemies to make them go home - a neat trick if you'd like to skip most fights the game has to offer.

Back in the day it was regarded as visually stunning, so I gotta admit that for a 15 years old game it still holds up - to the point it's probably going to be prettier than most recent "labor of love" games half a decade in the making by a single indie dev. It still works like a charm on Win 10 and is surprisingly stable, to the point you can just buy, install and have fun - more than can be said for many old games!

Are there flaws? Of course. Some descriptions of how buildings work are inaccurate - for example, you'll read that artisan market makes goods out of clothes and olive oil, while in reality it only uses the latter. There are several mistakes like that, and they might be a result of balance changes by the Reign of Augustus expansion. Other than that, the gameplay can get repetitive, as after you've figured out your build you just repeat the same actions again and again every mission. This can be remedied by playing multiple characters in parallel, leaning into different playstyles. 

Overall, while Haemimont Games' titles tend to be hit or miss, Grand Ages: Rome was definitely a hit. I don't find myself recommending games very often, but the truth of the matter is this is perhaps the best Roman city-builder one can play today.

El juego en un principio parece atractivo, pero el tema de los incendios que se desatan cada dos por tres acaba siendo desesperante... No hay más que ver que Internet está lleno de foros preguntando por cómo evitar los incendios en este juego, por algo será. Llega a ser un problema, más cuando tampoco tienes gráficas ni indicadores claros sobre la gestión de la ciudad que te indiquen la causa, y especialmente si tenemos en cuenta que ya puedes haber construido la mismísima copia de Roma... Si tu Fundus sufre un incendio y se destruye, pierdes la partida y tienes que empezar de cero. Yo he jugado en paralelo a este y al Imperium Romanum Gold, y aunque este último gráficamente es inferior, a nivel de jugabilidad le da mil vueltas al Grand Ages: Rome, y yo diría que incluso es más realista. 

Y es que parece que los desarrolladores de Grand Ages: Rome (o Imperium Civitas 3) se centraron demasiado en el tema gráfico y menos en hacer un juego realista y adictivo; básicamente colocas tu insula, y ahí se queda, ni evoluciona ni nada... En el Imperium Romanum Gold por lo menos las casas y sus ocupantes pueden ir mejorando o empeorando, y es un juego super adictivo que te quita el sueño y en el que echas horas y horas y ni te enteras; aquí, no veo eso, lo siento. En fin, lo he acabado desinstalando después de dos partidas perdidas por los dichosos incendios, y me quedo con el Imperium Romanum.

Ceville is a point and click adventure set in the far-off fantasy land of Faeryanis. You play as one of three characters - Ceville, the tyrannical king; Lilly, a cute little girl; or Ambrosius, the bumbling and narcissistic paladin. The three characters work together to solve problems and stop the evil advisor Basilius from taking over the kingdom. The three of them travel Faeryanis, meeting its faerie tale denizens and learning more about the world and themselves along the way.

  Mechanically, Ceville is a point and click, and as such, follows the usual gameplay conventions of the genre. While it lacks many of the puzzle elements found in other point and clicks, it still includes the all-important apply-thing-to-other-thing-to-get-third-thing mechanic. The puzzles in Ceville are less explicit and more situational - which of the many objects should be applied to get to the end result? - but in some ways, this results in a stronger structure. The game isn’t slowed down by the artificial insertion of puzzles, but instead, flows more naturally from the characters’ own problem solving skills.

In thinking about what makes a point and click work, I tend to evaluate them on three criteria - puzzles/gameplay, their story, and their world. Each game may approach these differently, favouring one or another, but they all feed into that grand picture of what a game actually is while playing into what the genre strives to do.

Puzzles and gameplay-wise, Ceville is not explicit puzzle-heavy, but relies instead on situational puzzles, and figuring out what item does what. Its world does a good job providing hints for the next step through changing a mouseover icon based on how a player is meant to interact with a particular object. It is very much a game that sees its puzzle elements as fuel to move the player along rather than the element keeping the player hooked on the game in and of themselves. They are decent - nothing special, nothing particularly difficult, just a vehicle to keep the player engaged.

It’s in Ceville’s story that I find myself getting disconnected from the game. While it is a unique story, the characters within it are themselves not unique enough to make their struggles interesting, or, for those that are unique, they are unique in ways that make them unpleasant to engage with.

The main character, for instance, is Ceville. We first meet Ceville when he is deciding which of either the three little pigs or the big bad wolf to send to a labour camp. He is arbitrary, cruel, and the very picture of a tyrant who deserves to be overthrown. While the game shows his gradual transition into a redeemable character who recognises his flaws, it is a painfully gradual transition, and we as the players spend a great deal of time with this thoroughly unpleasant person. 

Evil can be fun, don’t get me wrong. Morrigan (Dragon Age), Sheogorath (Oblivion), and Handsome Jack (Borderlands) are all excellent examples of how to make an evil character compelling, fun, and one that the player wants to interact with further. Theirs is a charismatic evil, and one that recognises its own vileness while also justifying it as necessary, or at least worth doing for some other purpose rather than strictly for its own sake. Ceville is an evil character, but without this charisma, charm, or greater purpose - he is simply evil for the sake of it. As much as the game’s writing want me to laugh alongside him as he jokes about torture or executions, his presentation isn’t one that can carry that humour. Rather than being a comical villain-protagonist, Ceville just becomes a deeply unpleasant character with his transformation into someone less vile being too shallow and too slow to overcome that repulsion.

The same is true, albeit to a lesser extent, of Ceville’s two other protagonists, Ambrosius and Lilly. Ambrosius is narcissistic to the point of caricature. This is, again, an intentional choice on the part of the developers, but one that doesn’t lend itself to the humour the game’s writing is trying to cultivate. Much like with Ceville, the caricature is an unpleasant one to interact with, especially when the humour surrounding him is at his expense. It is a mean-spirited humour in a game that seems to delight in cruelty. Some of this is very much in-universe with the solutions the protagonists choose to take. Some of this, though, is in how the game asks the players to progress. It wants the players to choose the cruelest option that lays low the people of this world. In so doing, it creates an unpleasant play experience that clashes with the character development the game is trying to present. 

The world of Ceville is also a flawed one. While its explorations of faerie tales and subverting the tropes inherent to them are fun, the game chooses to engage with these in what often feels like the cruelest way. In some ways, it feels like Ceville became reactionary against the wholesomeness of Disney-fied faerie tales, choosing instead to rebel against them in a froth of teenage-gamer edginess. The world, much like the characters themselves, dives too far into caricature to feel meaningful or interesting to explore. 

This is, in some ways, compounded by its graphical style. Though this game is nearly a decade and a half old and can’t be too heavily criticised for its graphics, the choices it makes for how to portray its world evoke some of the worst elements of mobile games. The colours are garish, and the character designs flat and doughy. Much like with the other elements, however intentional or unintentional this may be, the graphical choices further cement the unpleasant experience that playing this game becomes. 

Ceville is a product of its time. It is the product of an old revival of point and clicks, but one that sought to ape better and more successful games. While some of its flaws are less flaws and more products of its time, its choices about what story to tell and how to tell it make for an experience that leaves the player struggling to find motivation to slog through. This game may be a more fun experience for those who are more interested in edgy subversions of faerie tales. For me, however, it was an unpleasant slog, and one I’m happy to be done with.

In Ceville, you play a former tyrant trying to get his throne back. This point-and-click adventure flips the usual hero story completely. Instead of playing some noble good guy, you control a snarky, scheming villain who's absolutely ruthless. The humor really carries this game. I found myself laughing at Ceville's conversations with characters like the stuck-up paladin Ambrosius and the clever orphan Lilly. The game constantly pokes fun at typical fantasy tropes. 

It follows the standard point-and-click format. You collect items, talk to other characters, and click on whatever looks interesting. The puzzles also felt just right to me. Challenging but not impossible. Switching between characters was a nice touch since they all have different skills. You might need Ceville for one thing but then switch to Lilly for something else.

pros

✅ gorgeous looking, cartoony and colorful background graphics and character models
✅ spacebar to highlight all hotspots so there are no pixel huntings
✅ there are three playable characters. you can easily switch and exchange items between them
✅ mostly nice variety and clever, satisfying puzzles. there are also inventory-based puzzles to solve, so you can also make multiple combinations in your inventory and create new items
✅ story is cartoony but sweet and funny. You take on the role of a greedy little tyrant named Ceville, who was overthrown from his throne and reign by the malevolent wizard Basilius. together with a young little girl and a gullible, conceited Paladin, you embark on a quest to defeat Basilius and regain your throne and realm.
✅ voice overs doing very good job
✅ nice background musics perfectly fits the game's style
✅ charming, likeable, quirky, humorous main character and cast of side characters
✅ there is auto save
✅ there is a quick travel map, which prevents some backtracking
✅ there are plenty of different, good-looking, and colorful places
✅ decent length

cons

❌ unfortunately, the game hasn't aged well and is plagued by technical problems. you need to check the Steam forums and make some adjustments to run this game properly.
❌ despite the solutions from the Steam forums, cutscenes still don't work.
❌ frustrating timed puzzles
❌ frequent and long loading screens
❌ there are some adventure game logic puzzles and quests.
❌ It crashed one time, but if you forget to save the game, autosave will rescue you.
❌ a hint system would be really helpful
❌ the story is quite cartoony, so older people could find this game childish
❌ there are some more than necessary conversations with side characters
❌ there are no steam achievements and cards

Questa è una avvenura difficile. Sgombriamo subito il campo da illusioni generate dalla bellissima ed accurata grafica del gioco e dall'ambientazione quasi fiabesca, ad onta del carattere di uno dei protagonisti, che è appunto tale Ceville. Costui è il crudele e perverso regnante di un fantasioso reame che ad un certo punto deve recuperarlo dalle grinfie del suo ancora più malefico mago suo consigliere: ma, appunto, il mondo che ci viene proposto è invece ironico e spensierato. Dico che è uno dei protagonisti in quanto questa avventura conta la bellezza di ben quattro (!) personaggi giocabili: due a tempo pieno ed altri due in brevi fasi del gioco.
Ora, perchè dico che è difficile? Perchè gli enigmi sono spesso molto subdoli e di non facile risoluzione. Il gioco usa spesso la tecnica di aprire degli scenari dopo che si sono risolti determinati enigmi, e questo senza evidenti notifiche o indizi rivelatori: per esempio come nel caso della segretaria che non ci voleva far passare. Oppure inganna con false ed apparenti risoluzioni che amaramente poi ci accorgiamo essere non valide spingendoci a riflettere meglio. Ed ancora c'è la modalità cooperativa per la quale un enigma deve essere risolto usando i vari personaggi giocanti, che possono essere anche tre contemporaneamente. Il gioco comunque mette a disposizione anche una modalità per cui si illuminano gli elementi dello scenario in base all'oggetto dell'inventario selezionato. Credo che una difficoltà aggiuntiva per noi del Bel Paese è che i testi in inglese ci rendono sfuggevoli molti particolri che invece ci aiuterebbero. E c'è da dire che di testi ce ne sono, ah se ce ne sono! Tutta l'avventura è un continuo scambio di battute tra Ceville e Lilly, l'altra protagonista principale; inoltre tutti sono più o meno logorroici e ci martirizzano con i loro commenti in inglese. L'intreccio narrativo è ben fatto e la colonna sonora ben impiantata.
Lati negativi? Perché l'ho abbandonata due volte ed anche la terza volta, questa ultima che ho giocato, quasi quasi mi stava portando ad abbandonarla? Il motivo non lo capisco bene: è come se questa avventura mi portasse stanchezza, ed alla fine noia. Eppure la grafica è molto bella, i protagonisti ben caratterizzati e gli enigmi molto validi e mai campati in aria, anche se non evitano la sindrome dell''ammucchiata', cioè del provare tutto con tutto. 
Giocatela, e mi sappiate dire.

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

This game is well worth playing, but I warn you before we even begin that it has serious, SERIOUS issues you should go in prepared for, or it’ll drive you halfway to madness. 

Ceville is a modernish 3D point and click adventure. Clearly inspired by the old days in terms of humour, it puts you in the boots of the titular deposed tyrant as you puzzle your way to revenge. In terms of the art, its style is similar to the telltale Sam N Max adventures or their ‘bone’ games. Ceville’s gameplay plays like any other 3D point and click – get things, rub them on other things, sometimes sensibly, sometimes ‘creatively’, talk to characters, unlock locations, rinse and repeat. 

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*]The game is very well humoured and quite funny, however the jokes are almost exclusively in-jokes… such as “I feel the need to read it [a horse] a story.” “Oh? What would you do with its teeth?” This is amusing if you know, if you don’t, it’s just going to be meaningless fluff that seems stupid and out of place. 
[*]The voice acting is on point and banter between the characters is nice and in character, it doesn’t feel forced or out of place (except for the above possible point) and has been written to include the player by way of shared experience. 
[*]The story itself is good fun, the characters are excellently done caricatures, and the puzzles are mostly well paced with only a few multistage ‘REALLY?’ moments.  
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Starting with the benign. The usual point and click irritations, such as; pixel hunting (until you discover the space bar), rubbing things on other things, illogical logic puzzles, repetitive dialogue, and everything else you’d expect from a pnc. 
[*] Moving into the less benign. The games load times are a joke. Several multi-minute load times on a game this old is just unacceptable and can be quite jarring.
[*] Finishing with the cancerous. The game crashes and freezes. This is so bad, that if the game wasn’t carried by just how well it is written, I’d have put it down really quickly. Multiple freezes that don’t even let your task manager shut it down, wont alt F4, and ultimately force you to reset? Even more crashes to desktop? EVEN MORE freezes, but ones that allow you to kill it via taskmanager?! This game spends almost as much time loading and stopping as it does playing, and its rage inducing. 
[*]The dev’s outright missed the opportunity to let you chose the end, deciding if Ceville had changed through his time with Lilly. A few slightly different puzzles to let the game end on a few different notes would have really given the game a strong finale.  
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] Fix. The. Bugs.
[*]A ‘watch cut scene’ library.
[*]A little optimisation.
[/list]

[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]

If you go in expecting the problems, Ceville is well worth a play through for any veteran point and click player. It’s not a bad length at ~8 hours (with an extra 2-3 hours of load times -_-). The story is so well written and the interactions so entertaining that it doesn’t hugely matter what the issues are. That said, they are extremely frustrating and as such, if you’ve made it this far, here are a list of the solutions I found to these bugs I encountered. 

1. Put on subtitles.
2. Change the resolution to max, or your monitor’s max, if lower. 
3. Patience is a virtue; if the game is going into a timed segment (which frequently crashes) don’t double click to enter it, don’t try and skip any of the dialogue, let it go in at its own pace.
4. Ain’t nobody got time fo dat; if patience is failing, try to skip everything before the game hangs again.
5. If it’s a cut segment crashing, turn the in-game Master Volume to 0%.
I have no idea why any of these fixes work, or how the people that discovered them did so, but they helped me out a lot throughout the game. If I haven’t put you off playing, I wish you luck, and an enjoyable experience.
