Das am 19.02.2009 veröffentlichte Point & Click-Adventure Ceville ist der Debuttitel des deutschen Entwicklerstudios Realmforge Studios (Dungeons-Serie, DARK). Trotz positiver Pressestimmen und -wertungen ist das humoristische Spiel doch recht bald in die Obskurität gefallen. Ein Grund dafür mag die Tatsache sein, dass gerade mal eineinhalb Monate später das sehr ähnlich geartete „The Book of Unwritten Tales“ erschien, mit dessen Polishing Ceville nicht ganz mithalten kann.
Dennoch ist auch Ceville ein schönes Spiel, welches Fans von parodistischen Humor, frechen Anspielungen und kunterbunten Fantasywelten jede Menge Freude bereiten dürfte.


[h1]Zwei Bösewichter im Kampf um den Thron[/h1]
Ceville ist ein kleinwüchsiger Tyrann, der über das märchenhafte Land Faeryanis regiert. Der Fiesling liebt seine Schurkenrolle und tut sein Möglichstes, um seinen Untertanen das Leben zu erschweren und seine Taschen mit Gold zu füllen. Dummerweise hat der Kurze ein verdammt schlechtes Händchen, wenn es um die Akquirierung von kompetenten und vertrauenswürdigen Personal geht. Sein Berater, der Lulatsch Basilius, spinnt eine Intrige, um Cevilles Tyrannenthron zu rauben und seinerseits als neuer Schreckensherrscher das Zepter zu schwingen. Es erklärt sich von selbst, das Basilius plant den Grad der Bosheit um ein vielfaches anzuheben, um den verhassten Ceville alt aussehen zu lassen. Seine Intrige äußert sich in Form einer Revolution, die vom ebenso inkompetenten wie selbstverliebten Paladin Ambrosius geleitet wird, und an der sogar Cevilles Leibwachen beteiligt sind.

Zwar gibt Ceville sein Bestes, um aus seinem eigenen Schloss zu fliehen, jedoch ist das Glück auf der Seite des doofen Ambrosius, weswegen Ceville geschnappt und eingekerkert wird. Doch unser Ex-Tyrann hat seinerseits Glück im Unglück, denn das kleine, herzensgute Waisenmädchen Lilly wird auf das Gegrummel des Protagonisten aufmerksam. Ceville erklärt ihr die Umstände seiner Gefangennahme, weswegen Lilly beschließt den kleinen Fiesling zu befreien und zusammen mit ihm die Pläne von Basilius zu vereiteln. Das ist freilich wesentlich leichter gesagt als getan.

Was die Handlung anbelangt, so ist diese sehr geradlinig und dient eher als Mittel zum Zweck, um das Abenteuer und vor allem auch die witzigen Dialoge und Situationen zu rechtfertigen. Ceville ist also kein Spiel, welches man sich wegen einer spannenden Story oder ausgefeilten Charakteren holt, sondern weil man einfach was zu Lachen haben will und auch mal in die Rolle eines kleinen Fieslings schlüpfen möchte, der für fast alles und jeden einen gehässigen Kommentar parat hält. Die niedliche Lilly dient da als ausgleichender Gegenpol zum Protagonisten und sogar Paladin Ambosius bekommt einige spielbare Abschnitte. Den Großteil des Spiels ist man jedoch mit dem Duo Ceville und Lilly unterwegs, welches auch hervorragend miteinander harmoniert.

Abgesehen von Cevilles fies-gehässigen Verhalten, baut der Humor sehr stark auf Anspielungen auf. Anspielungen auf andere Videospiele, Fantasy-Klischees und wirtschaftliche sowie politische Probleme sind in den meisten Fällen sehr gut gealtert und bringen immer noch zum lachen. Wenn es in den popkulturellen Bereich geht, wird es da schon schwieriger. So nimmt das Spiel etwa Jennifer Lopez aufs Korn, welche dieser Tage jedoch keine nennenswerte Relevanz mehr hat und daher vor allem bei jüngeren Spielern unbekannt sein dürfte. Somit werden jene Witze, die auf Lopez' Konto gehen, bei einigen Leuten nicht mehr zünden.
Ein wesentlich größeres Problem ist jedoch das schlechte Pacing der Story. Denn auch wenn die Handlung an sich, nicht wirklich die treibende Kraft hinter dem Spaß ist, so ist es doch enorm frustrierend, wie zäh die Handlung in den Kapiteln 1 und vor allem 2 voranschreitet.


[h1]Solides Standard-Gameplay mit einem schwachen Hauch von einem Gesinnungssystem und drei spielbaren Charakteren[/h1]
Was das Gameplay anbelangt macht Ceville keine Experimente. Das gesamte Spiel besteht aus Inventarrätseln und NPC-Dialogen. Man klickt sich also durch die Spielwelt, untersucht Hotspots, sammelt Gegenstände ein, welche in einer Inventarleiste am unteren Bildschirmrand gesammelt werden, kombiniert diese Gegenstände gegebenfalls untereinander und nutzt sie, um diverse Problemstellungen zu lösen. Einzige Ausnahme aus diesem Trott ist ein sehr simples Apparatur-Rätsel im Theater, wo man mit einem Scheinwerfer hantieren darf.

Das was das Spiel von vielen anderen Titeln unterscheidet, ist die Tatsache, dass man hier drei spielbare Charaktere hat, welche nach dem Einstiegskapitel auch zusammenarbeiten müssen, um voranzukommen. Zunächst agieren Ceville und Lilly als Team. Da muss Lilly auch mal einen NPC weglocken, damit Ceville einen Gegenstand stehlen kann, oder man hat variable Antwortmöglichkeiten in den NPC-Dialogen. Während Ceville seine Gesprächspartner gerne beleidigt und verspottet, reagiert Lilly freundlich, aufmunternd und charmant. Man hat sogar daran gedacht die Antwortoptionen mit unterschiedlichen Farben zu kodieren, damit man weiß, wer der Beiden die Antwort geben wird. In den meisten Dialogen und Situationen ist derlei zwar nur ein Gimmick, aber hier und da gibt es dann doch kleinere Passagen, wo man die Gesinnung seiner Spielfigur im Hinterkopf behalten sollte. Denn da wo sich Lilly weigert etwas fieses zu tun, hat Ceville freilich keinerlei Hemmungen. Es wäre schön gewesen, wenn das Spiel mehr aus diesem „Gut und Böse“-Gesinnungssystem herausgeholt hätte. Stattdessen wird man manchmal mit zeitkritischen Szenen konfrontiert, wo man nur wenige Sekunden Zeit hat, die Lösung zu finden bzw. eine entsprechende Handlung auszuführen. Diese Zeitpassagen sind etwas lästig aber kein Beinbruch.

Hat man Kapitel 3 erreicht, schließt sich dann auch noch der Paladin Ambrosius an. Hier agieren die drei Charaktere jedoch losgelöst voneinander, und müssen improvisieren, um sich Gegenstände zuzuschanzen, die der jeweils Andere benötigt. Folglich ist Kapitel 3 dann auch das spielerische Highlight im Spiel.

Absolut vorbildlich sind übrigens die Komfortoptionen, die zur Verfügung gestellt werden. So bietet Ceville Doppelklick-Funktionen, um die Charaktere rennen zu lassen und Ein-/Ausgänge abzukürzen, Autosaves die alle 5 Minuten durchgeführt werden, die Möglichkeit Zwischen- und Dialogsequenzen per Mausklick wegzudrücken, sowie eine Hotspotanzeige. Letztere ist aber leider weniger eine Option, sondern viel eher ein Muss. Das Spiel setzt nämlich auf 3D-Grafik mit Kameraschwenks, was es manchmal sehr schwer macht Hotspots und Gegenstände zu erkennen.


[h1]Grafik und Sound[/h1]
Anders als viele andere Point & Click-Adventures seiner Zeit setzt Ceville auf reine 3D-Grafik. Sowohl die Charaktermodelle, als auch die Umgebungen werden in 3D dargestellt. Für ein 2009-Adventure sieht die Grafik ganz ordentlich aus. Die Grafik profitiert deutlich von ihrer kunterbunten Farbgebung, weswegen sie auch ganz nett gealtert ist (aber trotzdem veraltet ist). Es werden auch höhere Auflösungsstufen unterstützt. Ich selbst konnte das Spiel immerhin in der Stufe 1920x1080 erleben. Auch das cartoonhafte Artdesign weiß zu gefallen und passt gut zum Humor. Es könnte für manch einen jedoch zu europäisch sein. Sogar die Animationen der Spielfiguren fallen für Adventure-Verhältnisse überraschend solide aus. 

Der Soundtrack des Spiels besteht leider nur aus debiler Märchen-Fahrstuhlmusik, welche – Gott sei dank – nur sehr unscheinbar im Hintergrund vor sich hin dudelt. An der deutschen Sprachausgabe gibt es hingegen nichts auszusetzen. Die ist super!

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
If cheesy point & click adventures are your schtick, this might be worth picking up; be sure to read the warnings though, as this game does suffer from some technical difficulties.

[h1]Technical issues[/h1]
Now, before I can actually start the review properly, let me begin by stating that I had to edit some game files to even get the game to run. Personally, I don't mind, since I'm used to doing tricks to get old games to run in DOSBox, but for the average Steam user, it might be a bit of a hassle. So be warned of this. Having said that, there's enough guides explaining how you can get the game to run, and it's relatively easy if you're a [i]somewhat[/i] experienced Windows and Steam user.

Once in  the game, I also had difficulties with the cutscenes between the acts. Even though the sound was playing normally, I didn't get the video to play at all with Windows 10. I never bothered to get them to work, since there's only a few and you don't miss much if you skip them. There's some guides with tips on how you can get them to run, which might or might not work; I simply watched them on YouTube.

Much more annoying was the fact that the further I got into the game, the more often the game would suddenly crash at seemingly random intervals. Luckily, the  game has a good autosave function, so I never lost much progress, but it was annoying nonetheless, especially since loading times at startup are quite long.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
In Ceville, you play as the evil ruler with the same name who, after being dethroned by his rebellious citizens and losing his throne to his former advisor, tries to take his throne back.

The game was released in 2009, but visually, it looks more like the 3d-games from the late 1990's or early 2000's. The graphics are ok, though, and reminded me somewhat of the Telltale "Sam & Max" and "Tales of Monkey Island" series (although those were both way better in the visual department IMHO). The character models are also "ok", although animations are pretty janky pretty often. Locations are interesting, varied and colorful; on some occasions, items blend into the background a bit too much to my liking, though. Nice touches are the camera swivels that are applied while walking through a location, as well as some "picture in picture" scenes during some of the puzzles.

The UI is overall very intuitive. Use left-click to move, talk or interact, right-click is the default to look  at things. Double-left-click makes the characters run instead of walk and exit points are obvious enough in each location. In the bottom, your inventory is shown; just a minor nuisance is that after you tried to use an item to no avail, the game automatically deselects said item. It would have been easier if the item would stay "selected", so you could easily try to use the same item with another person or item on the screen. Instead, you have to re-select the item over and over again.

Music-wise, the game is ok. Music is overall varied enough to not get boring or irritating while you're traveling through locations, but it might get repetitive if you're stuck in one location for a while. Sound effects are limited to footsteps, some birds in the background and some basic sounds in the in-game cutscenes. All dialogue in the game is fully voice-acted, though, and the voices are varied and fit the characters nicely.

As far as gameplay is concerned, the game is decent. Dialogue options (which can be skipped with a mouse-click) are fairly extensive, and at times rather amusing if you like cheesy humor. The puzzles aren't overly complicated, although you might miss an object or two because they either blend into the scenery a lot, or because interactable objects are sometimes very close to one another, so that you might miss the "hot spot", especially at certain camera angles (once you walk through the location, it sometimes becomes easier to spot objects or interact with them). A lot of the puzzles feature nice animations or mini-cutscenes, but sometimes, character animations are janky and rather slow, which can be a bit frustrating when you need to exchange inventory items between characters. And in several parts of the game, you [i]will[/i] be switching between characters and trying to get stuff from one character to another, in a somewhat similar fashion to using the time machines in Day of the Tentacle. Also, the game features a handful of "timed puzzles", where you have to do the right thing before a counter reaches 0. Even though you can easily retry them, I've personally never been a fan of these kinds of puzzles, but that's a matter of taste, presumably.

If you're an experienced adventure-player, you'll probably finish the game in around 10 hours or so. The ending neatly wraps things up, and even leaves room for a sequel (although I doubt that there ever will be one).

[h1]Pros and cons[/h1]
+ cheesy humor with many pop-culture references
+ colorful world with interesting locations and story
+ fully voice acted
+ sound and music are ok, albeit a bit repetitive after a while
+ decent autosave
+ play as multiple characters

+/- puzzles are ok, but never really, really hard
+/- timed puzzles

- you might need to tamper with some settings files to get the game to run in the first place
- cutscenes might not play on your PC
- random game crashes
- slow loading times at startup and  between acts
- some slight textual errors in the subtitles (although this is a very, very minor point)

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
If you overlook the technical difficulties, Ceville is a pretty decent point & click adventure for its time. It won't blow your mind away, but at the current price of 4 euro's, you get enough decent gameplay and story in return. It's worth the money at this price, even more so if it's on a sale. On a 10-point scale, I'd rate it at about a 6,5 or 7 out of 10.

👑 ОБЗОР НА TROPICO 3: ДИКТАТОР, КОТОРЫЙ МЕНЯ УСЫПИЛ 👑

★★★☆☆ «Ты — диктатор тропического рая. Твоя главная задача — не умереть со скуки, пока твои подданные неспешно строят очередную ферму»

---

🌴 ЧТО ЭТО?

Вы — Эль Президенте, правитель небольшой островной страны в эпоху Холодной войны. Вам предстоит строить здания, добывать ресурсы, удовлетворять потребности граждан, балансировать между фракциями (коммунисты, капиталисты, религиозные фанатики) и, самое главное, выигрывать выборы, чтобы вас не свергли. Смесь градостроительного симулятора и политической стратегии.

---

🔥 ЧТО ЗАЦЕПИЛО?

1. Атмосфера и юмор. Тематика «банановой республики» с карикатурными диктаторами, прослушкой, коррупцией и выборными обещаниями — это свежо и забавно. Радио и шутки в стиле «карибского кризиса» добавляют шарма.
2. Много способов играть. Можно стать добрым лидером, построить туристический рай, а можно — кровавым тираном с секретной полицией. Выбор за вами.
3. Переход в 3D. Третья часть стала первой в серии с полноценной трёхмерной графикой. По тем временам выглядело неплохо, да и сейчас смотрится симпатично.

---

😴 ПОЧЕМУ Я ЗЕВАЛ?

1. Медленно и непонятно. Экономика работает по своим законам, и не всегда очевидно, почему деньги уходят в минус. Строители могут годами возводить одно здание. Ты строишь фермы, ранчо, шахты, а толку — ноль. Всё идёт как-то само собой, без ощущения контроля.
2. Однообразие. Кампания из 15 миссий по большей части сводится к одной и той же схеме: построй то, настрой это, переизберись. Особых вызовов или неожиданных поворотов нет.
3. Скучно. Игра не торопит, не напрягает, не заставляет думать на опережение. Ты просто сидишь и ждёшь, пока накопится достаточно денег для следующего здания. В какой-то момент понимаешь, что заняться особо нечем, кроме как смотреть на бегающих человечков.
4. Управление — бесит. Строить дороги без привязки к сетке — тот ещё квест. Машины ездят криво, стройка встаёт, всё разваливается. Интерфейс на любителя — много статистики, но толку от неё мало.

---

💎 ВЕРДИКТ

Tropico 3 — это игра, которая пылится в библиотеке и ждёт своего часа. Вроде и задумка классная, и сеттинг живой, и юмор есть. Но исполнение оставляет желать лучшего: всё слишком медленно, однообразно и не всегда понятно. Вы либо втянетесь в эту вялотекущую рутину, либо (как я) закроете через пару часов и пойдёте искать что-то подинамичнее.

Берите, если:

· Обожаете SimCity и хотите попробовать что-то в тропическом антураже
· Готовы к спокойному, неторопливому темпу
· Любите политические интриги (пусть и упрощённые)

Проходите мимо, если:

· Хотите динамичного градостроя с понятной экономикой
· Не готовы ждать, пока строители соизволят закончить сарай
· Вам нужна игра, которая затягивает с первой минуты

P.S. Я так и не понял, зачем нужен швейцарский счёт. Вроде как для личного обогащения, но зачем он, если вся игра — это бесконечное «построй-подожди»? 🏝️😴

Итог: 5/10. Уютно, но скучно. Как отпуск на острове, где единственное развлечение — смотреть, как растут пальмы.

箱庭の街づくりゲームですが、街づくりやコロニーシミュというより政治シミュレーターに近い味付けの独裁政権シミュレーターです。
トロピコシリーズは複数ありますが、最初は安くて手に取りやすいんでこれでいいんじゃないかな？って思います。街を作って住民の経済・生活管理をするというより、個々に思想や行動指針をもったNPCの勝手ばらばらな不満を聞き、時には弾圧して、アメリカとソ連の外圧に耐えながらバランスを取り続けるというゲームなんで、カリブ海で楽しくハッピーにのんびりした街づくりをしようと思って手を出すと全く見当違いな料理が出てくるんで要注意です。

逆にコロニーシミュでよくある食料問題なんかはトウモロコシ農園を作ればすぐ解決しますし、ホームレス問題は住民たちが掘っ立て小屋を違法建築するためそもそも問題になりません。カリブ海の温暖な気候により通年で安定した環境なので冬は凍死の心配もありません。たまに地震とかありますが、例えば建物が壊れるだけで住人たちは揺れようがそれで職場が無くなろうが恐怖で大自然への畏怖を覚えるようなことはありません。そんなわけで、このゲームを遊んでいると無学の労働者は本当に独裁者にとって都合の良い家畜なんだなと強く感じます。

とは言えトウモロコシ畑を耕しているだけでは島が発展しないのである程度高度な技能を要する産業を興すことになるんですが、そういう工場などに従事するためには高卒程度の学歴は必要になり、そのための第一ステップとして学校を建築したりします。そうすると知恵をつけた労働者があれこれ権利を主張するようになったり、政治的な思想を持つようになったり、それはそれで苦労をさせられることになり、そういうあちらが立てばこちらが立たず、といったバランスを上手に取りながら島を発展させるゲームとなっています。

Steamストアの表示では実績はありませんがゲーム内実績はあります。

ゲームは英語ですが、有志の日本語化パッチがあるんでワンステップで簡単に日本語になります。

Tropico 3 stands as a noteworthy entry in the city-building and political simulation genre, developed by Haemimont Games and published by Kalypso Media Digital. Released in 2009, it puts players in the shoes of “El Presidente,” the ruler of a small Caribbean island navigating the complexities of governance during the Cold War. The game strikes a compelling balance between managing the island’s growth and handling the intricate political dynamics that define Tropico’s charm. It invites players to craft their own style of leadership, whether through benevolent policies or iron-fisted rule, creating a rich playground of strategic possibilities.

At its core, Tropico 3 tasks players with building and maintaining a thriving island economy. This involves constructing a variety of buildings—from residential housing and farms to factories and tourist attractions—each contributing to the island’s prosperity and stability. The economic systems are well-integrated, requiring players to carefully manage resources such as food, raw materials, and exports to sustain growth. What sets the game apart is how these economic considerations intertwine with political factors. Various factions within the island, such as capitalists, communists, religious groups, and environmentalists, all have their own agendas, and balancing their demands is crucial for maintaining power. Players must also manage relationships with global superpowers, making diplomatic decisions that impact aid, trade, and potential threats.

The political simulation aspect of Tropico 3 adds significant depth, allowing players to engage in election rigging, censorship, and the suppression of dissent, or alternatively, to foster goodwill through social programs and public services. This creates a dynamic environment where the player's decisions shape the island’s stability and its citizens’ happiness. The inclusion of advisors and customizable presidential traits further enriches this experience, enabling a tailored approach to governance that influences gameplay style and outcomes.

Visually, Tropico 3 employs a bright and colorful aesthetic that vividly captures the tropical atmosphere of the Caribbean. While the graphics reflect the era of its release and may not compare to modern standards, they still successfully evoke the lively and often humorous spirit of the game. The island environments are detailed and varied, ranging from beaches and jungles to bustling towns. The user interface is generally accessible, though it can become somewhat cluttered as the island grows larger and the number of management options increases, demanding more attention and strategic planning from the player.

The game’s audio design complements its visual charm, featuring a soundtrack filled with Caribbean-inspired music that enhances immersion and sets a relaxed yet engaging tone. Sound effects such as construction noises, chatter, and political broadcasts contribute to the atmosphere, while the voice acting imbues characters with personality and humor, reinforcing the game’s satirical take on island politics and Cold War tensions.

From a technical standpoint, Tropico 3 performs reliably on a broad range of systems, benefiting from the Source engine’s efficiency and flexibility. It offers modding support, which has helped maintain a dedicated community by enabling the creation of additional content and customizations. However, players on newer operating systems, especially macOS versions beyond 10.15, may encounter compatibility challenges due to the game’s 32-bit architecture, which limits native support without third-party solutions.

Overall, Tropico 3 remains a deeply engaging title for those who enjoy strategic city-building and political simulations. Its blend of economic management, factional politics, and diplomatic maneuvering creates a multifaceted gameplay experience. While some technical and graphical limitations show the game’s age, the depth, replayability, and distinct Caribbean flair ensure that Tropico 3 continues to stand out as a memorable and rewarding entry in the series.

Puzzle Quest: Galactrix offers an engaging blend of match-3 puzzles and RPG elements set in a sci-fi universe. The hexagonal grid and directional gravity add a fresh twist to the gameplay, enhancing strategic depth. While the variety of mini-games and ship customization options provide depth, some players might find certain mechanics, like the leapgate hacking, a bit repetitive. Probably the only puzzle game I keep coming back to. The story is fantastic and I love a good Sci-Fi game. This is one of those stories that could EASILY become a fantastic RPG like Dragon Age or Kingdoms of Amalur. 

Keep in mind, it's a puzzle game. So it's going to get repetitive. If you're not into puzzle games then this game is only gonna annoy the heck out of you.

There are different types of puzzles to do which elude to hacking certain gates, battling enemies and gathering resources. There are great personal themes you can do as side roleplay like choosing the factions you want to be pleasant with and those you want to be enemies to. And you get to grind for the guns and ship you want, being able to choose different ones.  There's also a ton of side quests to do so you can take breaks from the main plot if you want to. All in all, it's a classic puzzle adventure game.

One of the most irritatingly great match 3 games ever made. 

I finished the game 6 years ago and reinstalled it this year, It seems way harder now - but never TOO hard. 

Why great? Galactrix uses a mechanic I've never seen before in a match 3 game, where the direction in which you complete the match determines which way the new pieces fall in. It's meant to simulate anti-gravity, and really, it is brilliant. It makes every puzzle challenging. 
The space sim element and RPG elements also work for me. The dialogue isn't especially deep, but it's not bad, either, and you will get involved in personal stories of your crew (or ignore them if you choose.)  

Why irritating? Well, you will likely get into situations where you are trying to complete a mission in enemy space, and the further you get, the more you get attacked. If you quit the game before achieving your objective you will have to fight all those battles all over again, and these can be time-consuming. There is an option to use PSI points to avoid combat as you progress, but there is a certain amount of grindiness. 

And as other reviewers point out, yes, luck plays a big factor, and it can be frustrating when your enemy hits a chain of combos and suddenly you get wiped out in seconds. But the same luck can work in your favor, and as well, one does learn to anticipate how things can go wrong and thus play a bit more conservatively to avoid giving the enemy opportunities. It doesn't always work, but it adds an element of strategy missing from many match 3 games. 

But really, the positives so far outweigh the negatives here. This is an immersive, relaxing and fun game, and there are just enough variations in the enemy ships and the game boards to keep it fresh. The ending is a bit disappointing, but you'll likely have fun up till then. I would definitely buy a sequel.

Puzzle Quest Galactrix (PQG) definitely has its strengths and weaknesses, but for people who enjoy puzzle games it works out to the good.

On the positive side: the core puzzle game has easily-grasped rules that allow you to become more effective as you learn how to plan multiple moves ahead. The head-to-head puzzles have a few variations (the most annoying of which is the time-pressure variant, but more on that in a moment). There is a very lightweight story wrapped around it, nothing movie-worthy or anything like that, but it does give context. The soundtrack is also better than one might think; generic adventure-orchestra, but well done for that. I also find it to be stable for a game of its age, with a crash happening maybe once per 30 game hours. It frequently auto-saves, so even if it does go boom you don't lose more than a few minutes of progress. You also can retry any engagement that you lose without penalty, so even if you lose a given game, no big deal.

On the downside: there is a LOT of luck involved. Part of the game rules involve chaining of combinations, and given that the game board's refreshing really does seem to be random, you can end up with frustrating very long chains of bad luck that can cause a loss, possibly even so bad that you can lose without you getting even a single move in a battle. Of course, this can work in your favor too. The time-pressure variation of a PQG battle is also frustrating, but there are ways to deal with that. And for all the variations, in the end it's really just that: variations. If you like the core game, great, but if not, well, that's all there is.

Okay, summary then tips.

Summary: PQG is a one-trick pony. The core puzzle game has numerous minor variations that change things up. There is just enough story to incentivize playing further. For people who like board/puzzle games, it will be good fun.

Tips (and minor spoilers):

1. If you get frustrated by the timed "hacking" game, you can farm Psi (purple gems) with pirates with no consequences. Go to the northwest of the map and go back and forth between the two pirate systems there, engaging every enemy ship you find. Even if you get defeated it doesn't take away the Psi you've built up. Spend the Psi on hacking Difficult gates; don't even bother trying the Difficult ones. You won't succeed.
2. Remember to immediately sell contraband to the bases in the pirate systems before you leave them to avoid being hassled!
3. Do the quest chain for the Lost as fast as you can. That chain eventually allows you to go anywhere without being attacked (even in hostile systems like pirate-controlled); you get to choose where battles occur. HUGE luxury,
4. Pay attention to your ship's Red-Green-Yellow capacity; it dictates which modules you can fit. Ships also vary tremendously in cargo capacity. Remember to Haggle before selling or buying a ship, and remember that Haggle bonuses only apply to a single major purchase or sale (do it again after). Keep retrying til you get +30%, and in that variant, keep pulling from the edge to the center. 
5. Beta Centauri is money. Go to Terra and open that gate. You can then get all the in-game money you need through the asteroid mines. Asteroids seem to reset after you've mined three others, and with six asteroids in that system, you can fill your holds every single time before selling.
6. Use selling to build your faction standing. You can easily keep all factions positive, and a couple of cargo holds full of sold goods will earn forgiveness for almost any sin (or blown up ship). Take full shipments to shore up your reputation where it's needed.
7. Remember to have "utility" modules like shield rechargers, energy type-transformers, and board-clearing modules in addition to the missiles and lasers.
8. Your character maxes out at level 50, Just keep that in mind as you assign experience.
9. The planets with the little moons have "Rumors" (game backstory exposition dumps). Once you have the crew member that allows that, do every one you can. They help you gain experience very quickly. Don't try to chain in that variant; just tiny 3-gem combos pulling from edge to center, as close to the edges as possible. You can do each Rumor once.

Have fun!

I played the original. I saw the negative reviews on PQ:G and thought "It can't be THAT bad, can it?"

It can.

Galactrix's match-3 mechanics are a solid upgrade from the original Puzzle Quest; the hex grid is a new and interesting approach, and the ability to control where gems fall in from adds a huge amount of depth. Plus, 4-of-a-kind no longer gives a free turn, which makes the game so much less painful than in the original Puzzle Quest.

Unfortunately, the rest of the game is not so good. It's an unstable game and likes to crash, and while it does autosave aggressively, the crashes mostly happen right after completing a mission, before the autosave. Talk about irony.

You hit a wall early on requiring a money grind to get past as your opponents start showing up in bigger, beefier ships that vastly outclass your own, but to get a bigger ship you need TONS of money. Since you don't have a class any more, you are entirely left on your own to obtain and craft ship parts (ie, spells from the original PQ).

As far as I can tell, the random encounters scale to your level, making leveling up pointless - it just makes the battles take longer.

The main map is the most generic thing possible and makes me wonder if they built the game on a shoestring budget.

The main character is still a total doofus who will do anything that anyone asks of them, no matter how dangerous or morally questionable.

In short, don't make my mistake; if you liked the original Puzzle Quest, don't get this one just to see how it is, even if it's on sale.

--  The upgrades seem fairly expensive based on how soon you start running into the above OP ships

It's a very different game to the original Puzzle Quest, being played on a hexagonal board rather than a square board.  There's lots of RPG elements again, just as with the original Puzzle Quest.  You can upgrade your ship, buy new weapons, and there's an Elite like element of trading goods between planets.  There's lots of missions to be done, and the puzzle game element can be challenging, and is as fun as the original Puzzle Quest was.

Puzzle Quest: Galactrix has a lot going on in it...and that's kind of the problem.  3 hours of play in, and I don't feel like I've encountered a significant percentage of the different systems the game has inside of it.  There's just way too much going on, without much help to navigate and explore all these different systems.  This is also hurt by the fact that each system is propped up on more or less the exact same, multi-directional match-3 gameplay, which feels more luck-driven than the usual match-3 play, if only because the ability for gems to fall in any of 6 hex directions adds complexity in a way that makes it extremely difficult to foresee chain reactions or anything like that.

On top of that, the software itself is somewhat unstable - it's crashed on me a few times, and frequently has everything pause and the screen go black for a few seconds.

If you love match-3 games, this is a decent one that applies the gameplay to lots of different, deep systems, but otherwise, you can probably take a pass on this one.

In its category it is a solid game.

However, there are several drawbacks which did not let me finish (and enjoy) the game.
Namely two - poor design choices in several instances, and inability (because of the poor design choices) of the game to avoid succumbing to pointless, time wasting grind.
So, for the poor design choices: In short, all experience players will spot artificially injected cheap mechanisms which force the player to play.  In PQ: Galactrix this poor design choice is the forcing of players to go through pointless mining, instead of having fun by battling pirates and alien ships!  And unfortunately, as a player, i did not have any other choice but to mine in order to upgrade my ship, and in order to avoid infinite conflicts with unfriendly factions.
Also, this design choice also resulted in a bug - by completing a mission, i have shifted a Faction toward an aggressive stance toward me.  This made the ships of that faction attack me.  The ships were much higher level than me, and when i tried to cancel the combat and run, i ended up escaping into another planetary system of the same, hostile action, where - again! - i was being attacked by overpowering ships.  So, that was a specific example of one of the poor design choices.

Overall, i do still recommend until you get tired of the mindless mining grind fest.

Hours Played: Enough to feel like a one‑man (or one‑team) insecticide army
Verdict: ⚠️ Mixed‑Positive (Ridiculous Fun, Not Perfect)

Earth Defense Force: Insect Armageddon is unapologetic giant bug‑smashing chaos full of explosions, absurd weapons, and ridiculous enemy waves and that’s exactly why fans adore it.

The core gameplay is simple but gloriously so: hordes of giant insects, robots, and alien monstrosities swarm every mission, and your job is to blast them back into the tarantula‑sized history books. The sheer variety of weapons from machine guns to rocket launchers to “why does this exist” death machines keeps each firefight explosive and unpredictable.

This isn’t a tactical shooter; it’s arcade‑style, over‑the‑top action where strategy is often “shoot first, worry later.” Enemies explode, buildings crumble, and your squadmates call out cheesy lines that make you smile even as you’re swarmed by fifty ants the size of cars.

However, it is a bit rough around the edges. Visuals are dated, enemy pathing can be goofy, and missions sometimes feel repetitive once you’ve seen every bug type a few dozen times. The story is basically an excuse to blow stuff up, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything more.

What Insect Armageddon does right:

* Insane, explosive action against massive hordes
* Huge variety of fun, chaotic weapons
* Ridiculous, laugh‑out‑loud moments
* Great pick‑up‑and‑play arcade vibe

Where it struggles:

* Dated graphics and presentation
* Repetitive mission designs over time
* AI and enemy behavior can be goofy
* Story is minimal

Earth Defense Force: Insect Armageddon isn’t deep but it’s wildly entertaining when you just want to mow down giant bugs with a smile. If you love cheesy action, absurd weapons, and pure blast‑em‑up fun, this is a classic guilty pleasure. If you want polish or narrative depth, look elsewhere.

I went into this game as someone who was introduced into the series by EDF 5, and have since played all other EDF offerings on steam. I was looking at this as a kind of pilgrimage to see the earliest available EDF on steam, even if it is a spin-off.
The game had a very strong start as it actually gives you mechanics you would expect from "normal" games - primarily that every class can run. It was very wild to see fencer run, and outrun enemies. WD glides across the ground and can easily make the distance without consuming ANY energy. There is a god damn spectator mode if you go down. Enemies, while not very varied, are interesting enough. The big spider enemy is quite something to behold. There were very functional sentry nests, a tank and a mech (that spawn in-map), at least for Normal. Really, this game should have been a fever dream that I would be eagerly doing a 100% on and wanting more.
Sadly, this game has completely atrocious pacing. Instead of spawning all enemies at once it just keeps spawning them in small groups, and all around you. Personally, I found that this made the fights very annoying as instead of having this one big, clear horde going after you, it is instead a battle of attrition. Enemies are all around you, and there is a never-ending trickle of a few from every direction. There might be a bigger horde at the start, but when this spawning starts it just ends up feeling dragged out. This is because as the enemies get tankier/deal more damage and force you to rely on kiting them more and more, one graphical feedback you get is that the horde chasing you gets smaller and smaller. Here, instead, it feels like there is a dozen of enemies always around you and there is just no way to get rid of them. Add to that that the game chose a more "realistic" visual theme, and instead of giving you vibrant colors and sometimes absurd enemies to look at, you just have an endless mush of dark tones that you need to concentrate on to see where the enemies are. You can't even rely on the radar as for some reason it "pings" and only shows you the enemies for about a second every 5 seconds. Then there is also the fact that there are a lot of fights against minibosses, that, while look cool and create stress, are also very tanky. On harder difficulties this becomes even worse as it feels like the enemy health scales much faster than your weapons. I think just the switch from "Normal" to "Hard" gives enemy HP pool a 4x multiplier.
Your progress is locked behind your character "rank", basically levelling system from RPGs. There is a currency pool that you unlock most weapons with, but of course, some of them have to be locked behind weapon boxes. At the very least, those drop semi-consistently from bosses, and there are only a few of these weapons so it is not too bad. The bigger problem is that the weapons feel kinda underpowered and not that fun to use. Some are quite interesting, and at least the ones I tried were functional, but the reload to ammo count on them is just too much. It felt like at least half of the time I was waiting for the gun to reload. There is an unexplained, but somewhat intuitive mechanic to halve the reloading time by timing your reload correctly, but imo if I have the time to concentrate on that there are not enough bugs trying to kill me. Weapons feeling weak might be a product of me working up only through half the levels, but by the end of the normal campaign I was already struggling to motivate myself to finish this game. Ranks for every class have to be grinded out separately, so this slow start has to be repeated for every class before you see their peak.
Finally, voice acting. Characters deliver their voices in a very bland, almost bored manner, especially the HQ which drive the story. It was almost depressing to listen to. For some reason there are also random voicelines of your squadmates being played periodically that make zero sense. For one, these play even if you disable the AI squadmates and go in alone. For two, these are played completely randomly with zero regard for the situation you are in. These voicelines can go urge you to go close hive that spawns enemies when there are none, or complain that you are getting overrun when there is just one enemy left. Instead of being this endless source of possible slapstick comedy they are just annoying.

Overall, this is not a terrible game per se.
Campaign on normal took me about 5 hours to finish, and if you are an EDF fan it might just be worth it to witness what this game has to offer.
If you haven't seen EDF and think about getting into it, look into getting 5 and then 6, instead.

If you want EDF in the edgy West, this is it.

A lot of people don't like this one, but I think it's great.

The only other one I've played is 4.1, and a lot of it at that. This one has a very unique flavor that makes it very enjoyable. 

---THE GOOD---

- Multi-part missions with objectives give it an immersive feel
- Extremely cool bug/robot designs. The Hectors look less goofy than 4.1.
- I like the class design, from the Wing Diver's super speed, to the Fencer's blast radius, to the Tactician's turrets and mines. 
- Vehicle and turret options are frequent, mixing up the pacing
- A certain pulse-pounding urgency that comes from it being less of a sandbox and more of a directed experience
- Campaign remix
- Gritty style, including Steve Blum's voice acting
- A more "adult" story involving top secret projects, abandonment, and loyalty
- Weapons are often simple, but the goofy ones are still neat.
- The tone is a lot closer to the Starship Troopers vibe the series goes for.
- Miniboss portrayal is great. When they show up, there's a sudden beat where it makes you want to stop everything and take care of this problem. The whole thing has a certain gravity to it.


---The Bad---
- Fairly short, maybe 5-6 hours for the campaign. In some ways it's nice, like getting to play as other classes sooner. However, it leaves you wanting more.
- The ending is sudden, has no buildup, and reeks of the budget running out.
- 30FPS. However, this can be easily circumvented with a hex editor.

I bought this for like $10, and came away from every gameplay session feeling hype.

I think it's well worth it.

Depths of Peril is one of those rare action-RPGs that refuses to sit neatly in a single genre box. Developed and published by Soldak Entertainment, it blends fast-paced hack-and-slash combat with faction rivalry, political maneuvering, and emergent world simulation. What might look like a Diablo-style indie ARPG at first glance quickly reveals itself to be something more experimental: a dynamic world where your hero is only one part of a larger struggle for dominance among competing barbarian covenants. This blend of action and strategy gives the game a personality all its own, and even years after release, it still stands out as a bold and inventive take on established RPG conventions.

The central premise revolves around the city of Jorvik, where multiple covenants vie for leadership. You play as the chosen champion of your own covenant, responsible both for safeguarding its lifestone—your faction’s heart and anchor—and for driving the group toward victory. While you venture out into the wilderness to complete quests, defeat monsters, and collect loot, rival covenants are doing the same in real time. They level up, recruit followers, forge alliances, and even declare war. This dynamic creates a constant sense of pressure. You’re never truly alone in the world; every success or failure shifts the balance of power. Diplomacy, sabotage, alliances, and territorial skirmishes all feel meaningful because the world responds to your actions rather than waiting passively for you to act.

Moment-to-moment gameplay leans heavily into classic ARPG staples—slaying monsters, collecting gear, improving skills—but the strategic overlay transforms these actions into pieces of a larger puzzle. You not only develop your hero but also invest in your covenant: hiring guards, strengthening your base, trading with rivals, or forging non-aggression pacts that can quickly collapse if interests diverge. The AI-controlled factions behave independently, pursuing their own goals with surprising assertiveness. This gives each playthrough a distinct rhythm; sometimes diplomacy keeps the peace until late-game conflict erupts, while other times early wars erupt and reshape the political landscape long before you’re prepared.

Character building offers flexibility that supports this replay-friendly structure. You can respec easily, allowing experimentation with skill trees and playstyles without punishing missteps. Combat itself is quick and responsive for an indie title from its era. While the game’s visuals are dated—textures, animations, and UI elements reflect its 2007 release—they serve the gameplay well enough, and the clarity of enemy types and item icons keeps the interface readable. The world’s lore unfolds through discovered books and texts, offering backstory for those who want it without imposing lengthy narrative sequences on players who prefer action.

Depths of Peril’s biggest strength is the sense of a living world. The city doesn’t exist as a static hub but as a battleground of influence where events can unfold without the player’s involvement. Quests can fail because other covenants completed them first—or because monsters destroyed a town area while you were busy elsewhere. Your choice of when and where to intervene becomes a strategic decision rather than a simple checklist of tasks. This dynamism makes the game feel unpredictable, sometimes exhilarating, and occasionally overwhelming. For players used to traditional ARPGs where the world politely waits, the constant movement of AI factions is a refreshing shock.

There are limitations tied to its ambition. The learning curve can be steep, especially for players not accustomed to juggling diplomacy, base defense, and hero progression simultaneously. Although the strategic layer adds depth, some players may feel that the diplomatic options and covenant management systems could be fleshed out even further. The repetitiveness of environments and monster types eventually becomes noticeable, and while the faction system generates variety, not every procedural scenario is equally compelling. The game is also strictly single-player, and the absence of co-op or competitive multiplayer may disappoint players who imagine how well the game’s faction warfare could translate to shared experiences.

Despite its rough edges, Depths of Peril remains a remarkable and forward-thinking game. Its fusion of action RPG combat with emergent strategy and faction diplomacy creates a unique experience that rewards improvisation, adaptability, and long-term planning. It’s an indie title that aimed far higher than most of its contemporaries and succeeded in carving out its own identity. For players willing to overlook its dated visuals and embrace its hybrid nature, it offers dozens of hours of unpredictable, replayable, and deeply satisfying gameplay. Depths of Peril is a standout example of how a bold design vision can elevate familiar mechanics into something memorable and distinct.

An uncomplicated, arguably shallow action RPG that is fun and different, incorporating diplomacy and trading as mechanics.

Positive:
- Using your character's skills and managing their position during battles is challenging, engaging, and fast-paced. Sometimes this involves one or two enemies and other times the entire screen may be filled with monsters.
- There is plenty of loot to be found as drops from fights and as rewards from quests, but most will end up being sold to the town's vendor for cash or traded to other covenants for relationship points and profit.
- NPCs can be recruited to join your covenant and can also be selected to go adventuring with the player. They advance levels automatically with gained experience and can be customized in terms of weapons, some armor, and shields.
- Most quests are reminiscent of MMORPG quests, such as "kill a certain amount of these enemies", "collect a certain amount of this item", "kill this specific monster by name", "rescue this particular person", etc, but they remain solid and entertaining nonetheless.
- Replayability is relatively high. The game can be restarted and advanced (other covenants' levels, world difficulty, monster difficulty, etc) each time you become the leading covenant of the town and win.

Neutral:
- The story is optional. One may choose to read the flavor text from quests, items, and monsters or longform stories describing the world's lore from tomes that are found as you progress, but the writing is mediocre and the plot is so bland that I stopped bothering very early on.
- Although the game is all about action and obtaining the next-best loot, there is little or nothing to work toward in terms of any endgame goals. It's all about the level and loot grind and nothing else, really.
- While there is a decent amount of enemy and monster variety, none of the foes were created with much imagination. Most enemies fit into standard fantasy or horror-fantasy tropes and stereotypes.
- There are some issues with the user interface. For example, F11 brings up a screen for your recruits and can only be closed with the mouse, as pressing F11 again does not close it.
- Several quests often repeat between playthroughs. The worst part about this is that way too many low-level quests appear in the queue again between playthroughs. A player at level 30 should not be offered a quest that is level 2 or 4 for negligible experience points. That's a complete waste of time.
- Character attributes cannot be rearranged like skills points for cash. Once you commit to upgrading any of the character attributes (such as strength, dexterity, etc), this change is permanent and can never be reversed or altered.
- Sometimes town NPCs that are responsible for managing quests die because of a siege or disease and this halts your progress until the game decides to resurrect the NPC (this can take a very long, unreasonable amount of real time) or until you are able to complete a quest to heal the sick NPC. Sometimes dead NPCs simply do not resurrect after several hours of play time.

Negative:
- For a game from 2007, it performs poorly in 2020. I had to turn everything down to the lowest qualities while keeping a high resolution in order to keep the game running at a fluid 40 to 90 frames per second.
- Very basic builds and build variations available. It feels like there is only one true viable build per class, since there really aren't that many skills and even less good skills combinations to use and to experiment with.

Overall rating: 4.0/5.0

Depths of Peril combines basic hack-and-slash gameplay with an innovative NPC political system. While you're out questing, parties of NPCs from rival Covenants (clans) are also out slaying monsters. They will offer to sell you their loot, demand or offer tribute, and go to war with each other (and you). The actual win condition of the game is not killing the final boss, but control of the town through alliance or elimination of the rival covenants. 

In theory, this sounds pretty interesting. In practice, it means that NPCs bug you with the most annoying parts of the politics of a 4X game like Civilization, while you play a worse version of a hack-and-slash like Diablo. 

The core hack-and-slash gameplay is bad.  It is the most basic version of "click enemies until they die, find better loot so you can go click enemies with bigger numbers". Combat is not at all dynamic or exciting. Every area is literally a square about 4 screens wide, with a couple different terrain sets that repeat over and over, and filled with a few types of enemies that repeat over and over (just recolored and resized for different areas). The dungeons are randomly generated mini-mazes, with some enemies scattered around. The quests are all "kill x enemies" or "gather x items that are lying around in x area".

The political system is also bad. Trading with the NPC covenants is a chore, since they only send trade offers with their junk items, and constantly checking their inventories for interesting items every 10 minutes is tedious. Other than that, strong covenants try to bully you, weak ones suck up to you. The best way to gain favor is to wait for two of them to start fighting, and pick a side. But for everything I tried, the optimal strategy really is just to be the strongest, so you can bully weaker covenants into an alliance and kill the remainder.

Honestly, the game feels like a proof of concept. Like the studio had an idea for a Diablo-meets-Civilization game and threw a demo together in a couple weeks to sell the idea to a publisher. It's a really cool idea. The problem is that the game was released in that state. It's not often that I feel like my hours were wasted on a game, but this is one case where I do. In retrospect, I wouldn't recommend this game to myself.

There are a lot of ways to approach competition in ARPGs, but Depths of Peril came up with perhaps the most unique. The looting and questing you do here isn’t preparing you for a final battle against some great evil, but rather for crushing your allies and asserting your dominance. It changes the entire landscape of the game, taking emphasis off of simple leveling and gearing and puts it on making strategic decisions about when to set off, which quests to accept, and how best to use your resources. It can be a very compelling game, but it’s likely not many people will see that given how stiff and challenging the moment-to-moment action can be.

You run a guild of adventurers in Jorvik, a rough frontier village of barbarians. Beasts and monsters and all manner of evil are threatening to overrun the place, and your guild is there to take on quests meant to keep them at bay. The thing is, you’re not the only game in town. Other factions of adventurers are out there right alongside you, checking off quests and hoovering up loot that could have been for you. As I mentioned before your goal isn’t to crush the forces assaulting the city, but rather to grow in power and influence to crush your competitors, establishing you as the de facto ruler of Jorvik.

The tutorial does a decent job of introducing you to this unusual premise, sending you around to the different vendors and questgivers you’ll be making your bones with. There’s a ton of systems at your fingertips right from the start, and ones that you won’t find in any other ARPG either. You have relationships with other factions to manage, crystals and bookshelves to arrange in your guildhouse, and a surprisingly open skill system with five pages of talents you can freely invest in as you level up. You won’t have to worry about all of these from the start, of course, but in games of this nature it can be hard to recognize what is and isn’t important, especially if you start sliding down the power scale.

Regardless of how well you grok the systems you’re going to want to head out and kill monsters, and this unfortunately is perhaps the weakest part of the game. Depths of Peril is dated as hell and not exactly big-budget, and it shows in how stiff and canned all your animations are. Maps are also terribly cluttered with scenery which makes it hard to see where you’re going and impossible to see some item drops. But worst of all is the enemy spawns, which loves to produce a dozen or so monsters in tight formations that all descend on you at once. Battles are not going to feel very manageable for the first few hours, and you can expect to burn plenty of healing items on just surviving basic combat.

Once you start ticking off quests and gearing up some of these gripes start to fade away. It’s never going to be a smooth or polished experience, mind you, but the depths of the systems involved give you plenty to focus on instead of the goofy animations or weak combat. Learning how to influence other guilds and switch to war footings against them is quite interesting, and presents a very different challenge from conventional ARPGs. You can carry on questing and following treasure maps and such for a good long while, of course, but it’s the diplomatic aspect that’s an actual selling point here.

It’s hard to recommend Depths of Peril without some large caveats, but the concept is so unique I’d say it’s worth experiencing. Definitely don’t show up for the combat or the story or the graphics, as this is about as indie as you can get on all three fronts. The concept is also fleshed out more in Soldak’s subsequent games like Drox Operative, so I wouldn’t consider this an essential entry in the franchise either. But it’s strange and engrossing and works well enough to keep me hooked for a few hours, and if you give it a chance maybe you’ll get similarly sucked in to its weird little worlds.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]

- Diplomacy with other factions is nonsensical

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Spending 10 bucks or whatever money you are using in this game would be a waste. Wait for a 80% sale at least and then, buy only if you want a cheap hack'n'slash game in the dark corner of your computer to play with a little bit and have guaranteed fun for a little while.

[h1]Game description:[/h1]
This game is an old school hack'n'slash where you smash your skills buttons to kill hundreds of various monsters. It's mindless, repetitive, devoid of originality, but it's fun. You receive randomized quests from NPC in the "town" (which is called Jorvik, and that's all the lore you will get about it) such as: kill some unique monster, gather some zombie brains in the forest, or deliver a package (intriguing!) to some stupid guy who bizarrely lives in the middle of a desert surrounded by giant scorpios which throw lighting bolts. Some quests have a timer, which adds a bit of challenge. Each quest is associated with a location which is one of the big rectangles full of monsters and a monomochromatic texture that makes up the world (which by the way has weird borders which gives you a glimpse at the deep void on which this universe is floating; creepy!). As each location is associated with a teleporter (that needs to be activated in the first place, fair enough), you can rush and do as many of these random stupid quests as you want. As for the story, there is none: some big baddie is doing evil things so you must first thin out its forces by killing its main lieutenants (at least that's what people say to you but don't expect a dynamical world), and once you finally get to kill him, you just learn that there is an even bigger baddie which waits in line. Think of it as the endless loop it is and you have a good idea of the story you will be given in the game. 

[b]In short, there is always something to do in Depths of Peril and that's why it still manges to be fun. Plus, backtracking is minimal thanks to the excellent teleportation system.[/b]

So far, there is nothing original in Depths of Peril; the quests, character classes, monsters, setting, are all pretty generic (actually there are generically generic). The big novelty is the "covenant" system. You, random adventurer, belong to a covenant, or faction. The town hosts several of these covenants, and they all compete for influence by doing more quests than the others. They can also compete for hiring new recruits, which will ask to fulfill a quest (always: kill X monsters of that kind) or can be found wandering in the world, slaughtering monsters on their own. 

[b]You therefore has to compete with the other factions to fulfill the quests before them.[/b]

That seems fun! Unfortunately it's not. The problem is, you can also enter into open warfare with the other covenants. Then, you rush into their house (a hut exactly similar to yours) and strike some magic crystal until it breaks. Killing heroes from other covenants also damage the crystal. When you go into war, there is no way to stop it. You constantly suffer raids into your house so you cannot go adventuring anymore. Since you do not gain XP by killing other heroes, you no longer improve your character. 

Worse, in your covenant, you can have recruits. Some of these recruits (the screenshots show several but at level 15 it is still only one) can join your party (i.e. help you in all the questing stuff), while the others will have to stay home, quitely hanging around the magic crystal for days. However, as you can get XP from adventuring only, those who stay cannot gain new levels. On the other hand, the AI can send as many recruits as it wants in quests, so they will all gain XP. Which means: unless you contantly hire better recruits, you will end up with a covenant full of guys utterly useless against the rival factions. But of course, if you are at war, you cannot recruit anyone anymore (anytime you are questing the enemy will raid your crystal and you will have to go back defend it), so you better have to end the matter quickly, or you will get overwhelmed. 

Which means, it's not fun. The competition only surfaces in these wars (the AI seems pretty ineffective in fulfilling quests, but they gain XP nonetheless) which are the most boring thing in the world (guys show up by teleporting next yo your crystal and you have to chop off their heads one after the other until you get killed, resurrected, and restart). 

[b]As a result, the most original mechanism of the game, which is the competition between covenants of heroes, is broken and does not bring on any fun.[/b]

Puzzle kingdoms is a solid concept that ends up becoming a little too bloated for it's own good. Ostensibly an interesting combination of a strategy game and a puzzle game, Puzzle Kingdoms offers an interesting and engaging blend of match-3 and tactics - but this isn't without problems.

Without a solid strategy, fights can often feel overwhelming or far too overtuned - but with a solid grasp of the fundaments, battles are almost always laughably easy. There's a lot of grinding that the game expects you to do, for an assortment of troops, relics, spells and heroes - but you're extremely limited by the points system in terms of what you can bring at any one time - making most of that grinding ultimately pointless, unless you know exactly what you're looking for. While the randomness of match-3 doesn't always clash against the concept of tactical planning and strategising, it's clear that the turn-based approach offered by Puzzle Kingdoms clashes with it. Setup is essentially impossible, as the AI will happily foil any attempt to do so, often leading to quick 3-cost matches being the only real consistent path forward.

The minigames (or rather, alternate ways of playing the match-3 game) are also entirely devoid of the combat and strategy aspect, just being "do this in X amount of time, or X amount of moves", which can often feel more like filler than engaging gameplay. In addition to this, the only real opposition that the player will run into is bad luck - as the AI will not move, or attack you, leading to "battles" often feeling like a one-sided slog. This isn't to say that Puzzle Kingdoms is a bad game per se, just that for the amount of time I felt was required to finish it, i ended up being very bored by the end.

While it looks a bit like a modern Match3 RPG, it's actually quite different from the modern form, but sadly not in a good way. The match3 part is played on a shared board with your opponent, and you take turns  pushing a row or column one block at a time, and then do damage/acquire manna  for any set of 3 adjacent matches. There's no chance to set up combos since you take turns on the same board, which takes all the fun/skill out of it. As for the RPG the leveling up of your single hero is essentially linear, so there's no strategy there as well; it's just a way to balance the gameplay by offering some grinding if you are losing the match3 battles. It was nice to play a game that didn't have ads or constant pushes to buy a resource pack, however, so in that one way this game is superior to modern match3 RPGs.

After playing the legendary Puzzle Quest: Challenge of the Warlords on PSP back in the day and absolutely loving it, I had to give this a try. Seemed like the next best game from this developer based on reviews, and caught it on sale for cheap so why not? 

Game starts out a bit rough around the edges, with a UI that is somewhat difficult to figure out, but the in-game tips help, and I started to figure stuff out as I went along. It's nice not having everything so simple. After all, this is a puzzle game!

Gameplay is fun, and you move the rows in up/down/left/right directions to match colors instead of swapping two pieces. Somewhat different than Challenge of the Warlords, which was a nice change. 

Here's where I fell in love: UNLOCKABLES! So many great items, skills and troops to earn through the side-quest puzzles, and it feels so rewarding when I solve some of the higher level ones. These items can be used to customize your Kingdoms and Heroes, with all sorts of RPG-type stats and effects to play with. 

My only complaint is being unable to exit a Kingdom once you enter it. There have been times when I wanted to tweak my build, but had to complete the entire Kingdom first (about 30-60 minutes) before I could go back to customize. Maybe there's a way to do it (without dying), but I haven't figured it out yet. 

All in all, I'd give this an 8/10 and estimate about 25-50 hours of gameplay.

Puzzle Kingdoms is an old match-3 style game from 2009.  The developers added a lot of window dressing for the game, including a Heroes of Might and Magic style campaign and a few other things.  Matching-3 in this game gives your troops little boosts.  The AI gets a turn on the same board you're playing on, which is a fun twist as you need to think on your feet and account for AI moves.

The game hasn't aged so great.  The graphics look old and pixely, the hand drawn art is a little mediocre.  There's no true widescreen support, they display the game artificially pillarboxed.   Despite being such an old game, and barely better than a mobile match-3 game, they want $21.50 for this.  It's totally not worth it.   If they modernized it, added 4K support and fixed a few of the gameplay issues it would be more viable.

I hate this game.  The campaign option uses some variations on 'match 3' games to advance a basic plot (good you versus evil demons), but everything is very unpolished and unclear.  For example, your 'heroes' get bonuses for 2 colors and penalties for 2 others when assigning points for relics and spells, BUT while the base points and color-bonus/penalty points show on the assignment screen, when you actually make the assignment, a different value is used! 

Other gripes: 
 - heroes have two colors, but you only get to see one unless you go through a convoluted series of screens.  
 - while you are given a choice to play as male or female, the story always refers to you as a male.
 - just one save per campaign, and lots of places where the game auto-saves -- which means if you aren't sure whether you want to do one thing or another, you won't be able to save, try one way, then go back and try the other.  Nope. You can save at most any time, but if you want to try that other option, you pretty much have to start a new campaign.
 - why, oh why does this game basically require you to pick a small set out of a large list of heroes to advance, and then make its point system tie varying priced gear to the hero rather than the kingdom?  That would have fixed so many problems!
 - the mechanics just suck.
    - for the timed game, the clock keeps running while automatic matches are being made, but you can't keep playing the game, so you are just watching the animation while clicking on a control that will not respond.
    - you get a limited number of points per conquered kingdom (which also have two colors) but any assigned hero will advance such that they become too strong for various assignments ... which would be fine if the game didn't stop you from doing anything else at all when you scroll through the kingdom list and happen upon the over-assigned situation.  At that point, you have to HAVE to either remove your hero or change their equipment (which has different costs for each kingdom with any given set of gear because of the color-based point system).
    - even if you have NOT changed gear, doing all the little tasks at the end of each round auto-equips new equipment on your current 'hero' so they become too expensive to use for its 'current' kingdom.
 - the help system is not helpful.  It is very brief and does not cover much of anything.
 - the game re-uses character profiles, so at one point, I had a character as my Hero for one battle, switched for the next round, and found myself battling my *previous* Hero because...? the game makers were too lazy to make another character?  The system is that buggy? I don't know.
 - When I got to the end, and the game actually have the words, "The End", AFTER THAT, there were a couple little anti-climactic things to do (final Tavern/Dungeon games). 
 - the quick-battles (not in campaign mode) give you and your enemy random equipment instead of letting you choose, which -- combined with the one-save, no backsies in campaign mode -- makes the quick battles useless for training purposes.
 
I shouldn't complain that the AI is too 'smart' because I might just be a bad player, but ... I played on Average and found the 'Tavern' game to be mostly unplayable at the highest levels (the ones costing 100-800 gold were fine, but the 1500 gold one felt mean spirited for anyone wanting an average challenge).

非常早期的结合三消玩法的RPG游戏
三消部分的玩法并不是常见的那种点击交换，而是将整行或者整列向着某一个方向移动一格，使得大等于3个的相同颜色的方块堆叠即可消除

战斗部分主要是依靠英雄+单位
其中单个英雄部队可以最多携带4个不同的兵种单位，每种兵种单位都有自己的攻击、防御以及最重要的属性能量
属性能量和可消除的方块颜色种类基本一致，消除对应颜色的方块可以进行充能，三个堆叠的方块增加一点能量，四个堆叠的方块增加两点能量，依次类推
当能量全部充满后即可主动选择攻击（界面上方靠近己方一侧的剑形状的按钮），如果同时拥有多个单位填充满能量，攻击按钮上会显示+1~+3的字样
此时单位之间的攻击力会有额外加成（+1~+3），这个也是后期比较实用的buff，让一些单位直接秒杀掉原本攻击后还差1、2点血的敌人
除此之外，消除的方块颜色如果没有对应的单位可以填充能量（或者对应单位的能力已经全部填充完毕），可以使得英雄单位恢复魔法值
从而发动一些特殊符文技能（效果可以是直接对地方造成伤害的、回血的、或者消除一定或者随机颜色的方块）

每张大地图的胜利目标是击杀场景里的敌方英雄单位，你可以长驱直入进行斩首行动，也可以一路上把各个据点打下来慢慢积攒经验增加总分
每场战斗的胜负条件分别是消灭全部敌方单位或者失去己方所有单位，如果中途撤退，则己方损失的单位不会恢复、但生命值回满，敌方全部单位复活，也就是如果打不过可以选择逃跑、然后重新招募部队再次挑战

除了主线的挑战任务外（世界地图上显示问号的城池），还有一些支线任务（世界地图上显示问号的城池），主要是两种小游戏，有自己的时间限制或者步数限制，以及挑战金币限制
失败不会扣除金币，但成功后会扣除对应的金币，并获取一件装备、符文，或者解锁一个新的英雄、兵种单位
不过奖励设置应该是有固定的，并不能在一个城池上无限挑战支线任务，所以有钱了就可以把能做的支线任务都给解了

游戏价格不算便宜，但如果喜欢类似三消游戏的还是听推荐的，大概全流程可以有20~30个小时的游戏时间，还不包括特意去练级，算是挺耗时间的小游戏

I was about to give Puzzle Kingdoms a negative vote: the battle screen is an interesting match-3 variant and the side puzzles are not bad, but there is no possible comparison with Puzzle Quest:

- The interface is atrocius. Its usability reminds me of cascading menus of early 1980's accounting software; it is utterly incomprehensible and some choices are, appropriately, puzzling: buttons that visually click but don't do anything because they are disabled, oversized "time left" texts covering the game board, higher-level timed puzzles made almost impossible by disabling moves while block animations are slowly playing... while the clock goes down!

- The influence of luck in battles is very high and the block entering from above are different from those depicted. Moreover, I believe the AI player cheats (as in Puzzle Quest), in the sense that it knows which blocks will enter from above.

- There is no strategy or tactic on the main board, none in war boards and only very little tactic in battle. The game is basically a corridor.

- Character progression is ludicrous: I think I was offered a grand total of two, maybe three, binary choices (e.g. add 1 point to attack or to defense?) in the whole game.

So why the positive vote? 

- First, I played the game to the end: despite its many shortcomings, it has a sort of hypnotic "one more battle" effect.

- Second, try to consider the interface as a puzzle game in itself: when I finally discovered how to configure the hero and, over all, how to get more points [I don't want to spoil your fun] the game became almost playable, maybe even too easy.

- Third, I found the non-timed puzzles interesting and challenging.

So, definitely not a good design but a decent pastime.

I'm not the most avid match 3 gamer out there, but I appreciate that the concept can be made to be entertaining. Puzzle Quest 1 has a lot of interesting features and good music and art, but honestly I feel the battles last far too long and end up being boring to me or entirely based on luck, so I'm hoping some improvements have been made. Kingdoms has some big shoes to fill as a sequel to that game, but as I am a researcher of the Warlords franchise and Etherian universe in general, I took the plunge.

Lets start with the pros, what this game does right:
- The setting, as always with Warlords games, is interesting. There's definitely a feeling that the preestablished universe is helping to set the scene.
- The gameplay has gone back to more of an original Warlords style, where the player searches ruins for artifacts, builds armies, recruits heroes and uses combinations of these to defeat opponents. There's a massive amount of variety in the way each unit attacks, each hero casts whatever spells you've selected them to cast and even the initial setup has type-based advantages or disadvantages depending on which kingdom's army is used. There is a lot of strategic depth to be found here, which is very surprising.
- Heroes can be customised as the player wishes, selecting items and spells for them to use, each with additional costs or discounts based on the chosen kingdom.
- I am very pleased that the combat is much faster than it is in PQ1. Most battles only last around 3-5 minutes, with the harder ones going on towards 10. I absolutely love this, as it makes the combat more virulent and helps to keep it fresh. By comparison, Puzzle Quest 1 just sits there dawdling every time you encounter what is essentially a Zubat because everything has SO MUCH HP.

Things which are neither good nor bad:
- The music is kind of mediocre to me. There are a few delightful tunes, but most isn't memorable and is there to get a job done.

Cons
- As should be noticed immediately before even buying the game, the art. For a game made in 2009 in particular, very little of it passes the check, with most failing and looking like ugly cardboard cutouts. Everything just looks so bright and flat, why is everything lit from all angles? Any sense of depth is completely lost because there's basically no shading in most areas.
- You yourself have to be a human warrior from some village in the borderlands. I much prefer PQ1 here, where you got to personalise your own character and play with them in a much more RPG-orientated format. Instead, Kingdoms has you use heroes that you find across Etheria for battles.
- Border-blocks are a nice new feature which can help stale boards function better. Unfortunately, this feature is mired down by some serious issues. Firstly, when matching anything, new block randomly generate from the top instead of being of the type seen around the border. Secondly, as others have said before, there are simply too many colours, too many block types. Because of this, boards have a much higher chance of being completely stagnant even with the border blocks. You will definitely encounter a lot of boards like this, where no-one gets to do anything for multiple turns and the combat becomes unnaturally long.
- Dubious balance. Some units are just outright better than others. Why would anyone choose a crossbowman when an elven archer is directly superior? Yes it costs 25 gold more to produce, but by the time you've conquered around 2 or three kingdoms, you always have the gold and your hero's build starts to combo off more smoothly meaning you're unlikely to lose them anyway.
- There's no point in being able to field more than one hero. By the time you get to the end-game kingdoms, it's highly likely that you'll have one max level hero and a bunch of level 1-3's, which are completely useless at this stage of the game. The thing is though, you need to min-max your hero XP otherwise the game will likely be considerably harder.
- The game is so long. You'll be playing hundreds of matches and that's more than enough to burn out the gameplay. It gets incredibly monotonous and by the time you reach the Doomwood you'll want to just complete the game as quickly as possible or drop it.
- Throughout the game, you will be collecting and destroying boxes which are linked to some sort of curse. This wouldn't be a problem if you didn't have to complete one of the most tedious matches in any Puzzle Quest game. It's so completely unnecessary and unrewarding, and it often takes well over a hundred turns to clear the board (it's a special game type where you have to clear the entire board with no random blocks coming down. Instead, you have to use the side blocks which are randomly generated every time they're used). These types of matches never give you what you need to proceed, so it ends up being an endurance match which I admit, I have actually lost one or two times (when I went to 200+ turns and gave up).
- If you're aware of the Warlords universe, well suffice to say that Kingdoms is most definitely not something to be considered canon. If you're not, ignore this con. There are mistakes - some blatant, some minor, riddled throughout this game's lore. The story is completely implausible, the map is broken, locations are scattered more than they've ever been and there are few new things to discover. I feel like this is definitely a waste of a well-setup universe, which has immeasurable detail and a good timeline that's existed since Warlords 3. It makes me sad that the immense detail this game franchise has may never even see the light of day (except in The Protectors that is).

Overall, Puzzle Kingdoms tries to make some improvements on the original formula of Puzzle Quest. In some areas, I think it has actually succeeded, but in most others it failed. Gameplay is faster and the strategy is there, but the RPG aspect has suffered and the characters and story are no where near as good as PQ1 (and they weren't particularly good in that imo). It feels like Kingdoms was rushed, and there is evidence of that even in the text where some incorrect syntax has been input in a couple places. If you're a PQ or match 3 veteran and can't get enough, there is definitely something to be had in Puzzle Kingdoms, if you can bare the empty void that was the RPG aspect (or the art for that matter). Otherwise, I would recommend skipping this game.

Ancak oyunda özellikle dikkatimi çeken ve ayrı bir yere koyduğum bir DLC var: Taurus Mountains – Toros Dağları (Ulukışla – Yenice).

Türkiye'nin eşsiz coğrafyasını demiryolu üzerinden deneyimlemek gerçekten güzel bir his. Adana Yenice'den başlayıp Toros Dağları'nı aşarak Ulukışla'ya uzanan bu 125 kilometrelik güzergâh, yalnızca manzarasıyla değil, sunduğu sürüş deneyimiyle de öne çıkıyor.

37 tünel, 60'tan fazla köprü, zorlu eğimler ve değişen rakımlar arasında ilerlemek, makinistlik deneyimini çok daha keyifli hâle getiriyor. Özellikle meşhur Varda Köprüsü'nden geçmek, rotanın en etkileyici anlarından biri.

DLC'nin en güzel taraflarından biri de yerli demiryolu kültürümüzü oyuna taşıması. DE 24000 lokomotifiyle yolcu ve yük taşımacılığı yapmak, Türkiye'deki demiryolu atmosferini hissetmek açısından oldukça başarılı.
